The library then generated lists, a hundred per run, and when one broke a fact it shrank the list to the smallest one that still did.

It broke on the fourth run. The shrunk case was two ranges: one from 09:00 to 09:00, the other from 09:00 to 10:00. The first is empty, a shift of zero length, which the rota form allowed if someone clicked save with the same time twice. My function returned both unchanged, and 'do not touch one another' failed because they share an endpoint. The effect in the field was that for two years any zero-length shift sitting next to a real one had produced a phantom line in the rota, which the front end hid by filtering out anything shorter than a minute. Nobody had ever seen the bug, because somebody had patched the symptom three layers away.

I showed Mara the shrunk case before I said anything about it. She looked at it for a while and said it was a case she would never have thought to write. She is not careless. The point is that a hand-picked example comes from the author's idea of the problem, and the generator does not have my idea.

We fixed it by dropping empty ranges at the start of the function, which made the front-end filter unnecessary, and Tobias deleted it the following week with some satisfaction. The property test found one more thing when I ran it with larger inputs: ranges given with the end before the start, which the old code treated as empty by accident and the new code now rejects with a named error.

I do not want to oversell it. Writing the three facts took longer than the eleven examples, and choosing them was the real work. But the facts were already the specification, and I had never written them down.

The supplier's price list came every month as a spreadsheet exported to CSV, and in November the delivery dates in it were wrong in a way that took me four days to put a name to. Not all of them wrong: that was the trouble. Most rows were fine, and a minority were plausible and impossible at once.

Bettina in purchasing noticed first, because the overdue list had filled with deliveries due in April and May, and she had not ordered anything in April. I looked at the import. The parser was told to read day-month-year, and it did so faithfully. A row reading 04/12/2024 became 4 December, which was right. A row reading 12/04/2024 became 12 April, a date in the past, and the supplier had meant 4 December written the American way. The file contained both conventions, row by row, and the rows with a day above twelve gave the game away only because they could not be read the wrong way.

I compared the file with the three months before. In August every row was day-first. In September one row was month-first. In October, sixty-one. The unambiguous rows let me classify those with certainty, and what they showed was not random: every month-first row came from one of the supplier's two dispatch offices, the one that had changed laptops in September. The file was a mixture of two machines' habits, and the ambiguous rows could be resolved by the office code in column B.

Mara and I went through the options. Ask the supplier to fix their export: we did, Imogen answered within the hour that they would look, and by January they had not. Guess per row: never. Resolve by office code: workable, but the rule would live in our code where nobody at the supplier knew it existed. We built it anyway, with one condition. A row whose office is not on our list, or whose date, read the way its office writes dates, falls outside the delivery window printed in column F, is not guessed at. It is held back and listed in the import report with its row number.

Forty-three rows were held back in December and Bettina cleared them in twenty minutes with the supplier's confirmation emails open. That felt right. A date that is quietly wrong costs a pallet nobody expected; a date that is loudly missing costs twenty minutes of somebody's morning.

The first release we shipped with a canary was a dull one, and I keep it as the example of what a dull release is worth.

Callum had built the traffic split over the two weeks before: five percent of requests to the new version, the rest to the old, with error rate and slowest-one-percent latency drawn side by side on one page. Mara had been reluctant, because it meant a release now took forty minutes of watching instead of ten of hoping. We shipped the order-history change on a Tuesday at 10:15, the quietest part of the week.

Eleven minutes in, the canary's error rate rose from 0.2 percent to 3.4. The other ninety-five percent were fine. Callum said 'roll it back' before anyone had looked at the cause, and the rollback was a single setting that sent all traffic to the old version. It took forty seconds. In that time about two hundred requests failed, where a full release would have failed every order-history page for every customer until someone noticed.

Then we looked. The failing requests all carried a header from the mobile app, version 2.3, and the new code read the page-size parameter as a number while that version sent it as a string in quotes, '20'. Our staging tests used the web client, which sent a number. The old code had accepted both by accident, through a loose conversion library that this change had replaced.

We made the parser accept both and added a test that replays three captured mobile requests. We shipped again at 13:30, canary clean for twenty minutes, then half, then everything, with nobody speaking much.

Two things came out of it. The canary did not make the bug less likely; it made the cost of the bug a quarter of an hour instead of an afternoon. And Mara changed her view of the forty minutes. They were not watching. They were the time the new code needed to meet a client we had forgotten.

Afterwards I asked Callum what he would add. He said a list of the client versions seen in the canary's traffic, so that if one we have never tested turns up, we are told. That is the next thing we built.

Generating an invoice PDF took eleven seconds, and for most of a month that was acceptable because it happened on a button. Then Ilse's clinic began sending monthly statements in batches of three hundred, and eleven seconds became fifty-five minutes during which everyone else using the application waited behind it.

The service made each PDF by launching a headless browser, loading an HTML template, printing it and closing the browser. I timed the steps on a sample of twenty. Rendering the template took 0.4 seconds and the print about 0.9. The browser launch was nearly nine seconds of the eleven. Obvious in hindsight, though I had been looking at the template, because that was where Mara had assumed the time went.

The remedy was a pool: start two browsers when the service starts, hand out a fresh page from an existing browser for each invoice, close the page, keep the browser. Time per invoice fell to 1.4 seconds. The batch of 300 took seven minutes with two browsers, and Mara and Wren argued for twenty minutes about whether to raise it to four. We measured instead. With four, the machine began swapping and the batch took nine.

Then the pool did what pools do. After about two days memory crept up. After four days a browser stopped responding in the middle of a batch, and the clinic's 212th statement came back blank. I traced it by rendering the same invoice twenty-five hundred times through one browser while watching its memory. Roughly 190 pages in, the process held three times what it had at the start, and by 2,000 pages it was slow enough to time out. Nothing was wrong in our code. The browser simply leaked slowly, as long-lived browsers do.

So we added the other half of a pool, which is retirement. Each browser serves 200 pages and is then replaced by a fresh one that is already starting, so the pool never has fewer than two. If a page takes more than twenty seconds, that browser is killed and the invoice retried once on another. A blank PDF can no longer be returned silently, because the service checks that the output has at least one page and a size above a few kilobytes, and fails loudly otherwise.

The part I would tell anyone starting this is that the check for the blank file was written after the failure and would have been easy to write before. A service that returns a file should know what a wrong file looks like. The clinic re-sent that one statement by hand, and her receptionist, who had spotted the blank page, was thanked at the next team meeting, because without her we would have learned about it from a patient.

The function was called quote_total and it was 380 lines long, and for the first two months I worked beside it I treated it the way one treats a sleeping animal. It took a basket and returned a price for the freight company's customers. It had fourteen levels of nested conditions, a table of numbers named after a supplier that had gone out of business in 2020, and a comment near the top that said only: DO NOT TOUCH, SEE PETRA.

In February the company introduced a fuel surcharge and the function had to change. Mara asked me to work out where it could go, and I began where I always begin with a function I do not understand: not by reading it, but by finding out what it does. Petra, who had been in QA when the function was written and now ran the dispatch desk, was happy to talk. She told me the story of the comment. In 2019 a change to the rounding had undercharged one customer by about a thousand over a quarter, and the person who fixed it had wanted to keep everyone else away.

I did not take the story as the specification. Mara and I pulled six months of real quotes from the log, 9,400 of them, each with its inputs and its price, and made them the first test: feed in the same inputs, expect the same price to the penny. That is called a characterisation test, and it does not claim the function is right. It claims the function has not changed. With it in place the function became something I could poke.

Over three days I made small changes that should have changed nothing. I moved the table into a data file, gave each of the fourteen levels a name for what it decides, and re-ran the 9,400 after every step. Twice the test failed. The first time I had reordered two conditions that looked independent and were not: a pallet over 800 kilograms was checked for the remote-area charge before the weight band, so the charge was applied to the band's rounded weight. The second failure was stranger. Forty-one quotes differed by one penny, all with the same customer code, all after I had replaced a division with an equivalent multiplication. The old function divided early and rounded twice. It was wrong in the sense that no sensible author would choose it, and right in the sense that forty-one customers had been paying by it.

Whether that was wrong or established was not mine to decide. I wrote the forty-one down with their codes and gave the list to Petra and Mara. Petra rang three of the account managers. Two said the penny had never been noticed. One asked that we keep it as it was until the contract renewal in June. So the function now has one line that reproduces the double rounding for that customer code alone, with a comment giving the date, Petra's name and the renewal month, and a test that starts failing in July so the line cannot outlive its reason.

One more thing came out of the replay, and I put it in the same note. Eleven of the 9,400 quotes had a price of zero, and I took them first for faults in my harness. They were real: the sales desk used customer codes beginning ZZ for free sample consignments, and the function carried a branch for them that appears in no document and that I would have deleted as dead code, since no customer in the table has such a code. It is now named in the function, with a test, and Petra added a line about it to the sales desk's own page, which is the first time the desk has written down what the ZZ prefix means.

The surcharge itself took twenty minutes once the levels had names. I thought afterwards about the three days that came first, and about the comment. DO NOT TOUCH had worked for five years. What it had never said was what to do instead. A warning without a method is a kind of abandonment, I think, and I try not to leave one.

Petra deleted the old comment herself. She said it was hers to remove.

On a Monday morning the build server's disk was full and nothing could be built, and Halvard, who looks after the machine, was on a train. Mara brought me in the way she does when a thing is simple but urgent, with one line: df says 100 percent, help me find the 80 gigabytes.

She ran the commands I suggested and read the numbers back. The biggest directory by far was the container image store, 71 GB, mostly old layers from builds that had finished months ago. There was supposed to be a cleanup job: Halvard had written it two years before, a cron entry that removed anything unused for thirty days. I asked her to look at its log. It was there, and it held a single line, repeated every night since the second of August: cannot find /var/lib/containers/storage.

The storage had moved. In August the machine's disk had been resized and the container store put on a second volume mounted at /srv/containers. The builds followed it, because the build tool read its path from a config file Halvard updated that day. The cleanup script had its own copy of the path, hard-coded. It failed every night afterwards, politely, writing one line to a log nobody read, and exited with status 0, because the last command in the script was an echo.

Mara freed the space with a prune command, then fixed the path. My suggestion on top of that was small. Make the script ask the tool where the store is instead of carrying a copy, and let it fail with a nonzero status, since a failed cleanup that reports success is the worst of both. Cron mails nonzero exits to Halvard, so he would hear about the next failure on the night it happened, not ten weeks later.

We also put in a disk alert at 80 percent. It sent one message to Halvard's phone on Wednesday at 02:14, when a test run left a large artifact behind, and he cleared it from a train again. He told Mara it was the first alert in a year he had been glad of.

I think about the echo at the end of the script more than about the disk. Everything in the story followed from a script that reported its own success instead of its work.

Dario's company sent us orders as JSON, and for a year we validated them twice: once in the browser form, with rules Wren had written, and once on the server, with rules Tobias had written. The rules were meant to be the same. In March they were not, and a customer could type an eight-character postcode into a field the server limited to seven, see a cheerful 'saved', and a little after midnight Tobias would get an error email.

The cause was dull. The postcode limit had been raised in the browser in January to allow a new format, and nobody had changed the server. Mara's first idea was a checklist, when you change a rule, change it in both places, and I told her what I think of checklists: they depend on the person least likely to remember being the one in a hurry. What I proposed was a single file, written once, that both sides read.

We argued about the format for two days. Wren wanted a JSON Schema document, since there are validators in every language. Tobias wanted generated code, since a schema validator is a slower and larger thing in a browser than a function. Mara wanted whichever one she would not have to maintain. I tried each on three real rules: postcode length, a date that must not be in the past, and a rule that either phone or email must be present. The schema handled the first and third at once, and the second only through a custom keyword that each side would have to implement. That is exactly the sort of thing that drifts apart again.

We settled on the schema for shape (types, lengths, required fields) and a short named list of extra rules in code, each with a test that both sides run against the same twenty example inputs, kept in one file. The list has four entries today. The shape half is guarded by a test that fails if the browser bundle and the server were built from different versions of the schema, because the file carries its own hash and both builds print it.

Within a month the arrangement caught its first drift on its own. Wren raised the name length from 60 to 80, the test went red on Tobias's side, and he raised it that afternoon. That was the moment Mara said the checklist could be retired. I did not say anything. I did put a note in the header of the file about why there are two kinds of rule and where each lives, because the next person will be tempted to put them all in one place, and the reason they are not should be there when they are.

For two days I tuned the wrong thing. Sunniva had reported that searching for 'charger' in the Pennant hardware shop's catalogue put a cable-tidy box first and the USB-C wall charger on page two, and that the same was true of 'torch' and 'ladder'. It had begun the week after the search engine was upgraded to the next major version, so everyone, me included, assumed the new version scored differently.

So I tuned. I raised the boost on the product title from 3 to 5, then to 8, and each time the results moved a little and moved back when Sunniva tried a different word. By Wednesday evening I had a table of twelve test queries and their top five results under four boost settings, and no setting got more than seven of the twelve right. The table turned out to be useful only as proof that I was turning a dial that was not connected to anything.

On Thursday Mara asked me a question I should have asked myself: for the wall charger, what did the engine say about its score? The search engine can explain any result, field by field. I asked for the explanation of both products for the query 'charger'. The cable-tidy box had a score from the description field, 4.1. The wall charger had a score from the description, 2.6, and nothing at all from the title field. Not a low number: no entry. The title, which contained the word, had not matched.

That is not scoring. That is a title field unable to see its own words. I fetched the mapping of the live index, and the title was mapped as a keyword, an exact-string type, which matches only a query equal to the whole title. The mapping in our code said text. The live index was not built from our code: the reindex after the upgrade had run on a machine where an older index template, from 2022, was still registered and took precedence for any index with a matching name. It had been written when titles were short product codes.

The repair was one deletion of the old template and a reindex of 31,000 products, forty minutes. At the original boost of 3, eleven of the twelve queries then came out right, and the twelfth was a real disagreement about what a person looking for a 'torch' wants.

I took two things from it. When a knob does not move the thing it should, stop turning it and ask whether it is connected. And ask the system to explain a single result before tuning for all of them.

The test that failed about every other run compared a generated expenses report with a stored copy, and for three weeks the team called it flaky and clicked rerun. Wren proposed an automatic retry in the test runner, three attempts, and I asked Mara not to agree. A test that sometimes fails is telling you something about the code. A retry only teaches people to stop listening.

I ran it forty times in a loop and kept every output. Nineteen failed. I laid the failing outputs beside the stored file and a passing one, and the difference was never in the numbers. It was in the order of two sections: 'Fuel' and 'Insurance' came first in one version and second in the other. Nothing else moved.

The report sorted categories by total, largest first, and the fixture had been built two years earlier with Fuel and Insurance both at exactly 1,240.00. For a tie the sort had nothing to say, so the order depended on the order the categories came out of the dictionary the totals were collected in, and the language shuffles the order in which it walks a dictionary, deliberately, from one run to the next, so that programs do not come to rely on it. This one had relied on it for two years. The test had passed whenever its author's luck came round, which was half the time.

The best part came when I went to look at the real reports. Ilse had written in the tracker months before that the monthly report 'rearranges itself' whenever she refreshes it, and someone had answered that it was probably the browser. It was the same bug. In production, any two categories with equal totals swapped places at random, and a person trying to compare this month with last month's printout had been tripped by it for years without being able to say what was wrong.

The fix is one line, a second sort key, the category name, so a tie is broken the same way every time. I added a test with three tied categories in every order of input, which fails at once if anyone removes the line. Then I told Wren why I had not wanted the retry: with it, the bug would have stayed invisible and Ilse's printouts would have kept shuffling. He said he had not thought about the report. Nobody had, because the test was the only place we ever looked.

On a Friday evening, two hundred and twelve customers each received three emails saying their parcel had shipped. Noor, who runs support, forwarded the first replies at 18:40, one of which said, kindly, that the customer assumed she had ordered three things and was checking her card statement.

Our system sends the shipping email when the carrier's service tells us a label has been scanned. The carrier does this with a webhook, a request to an address of ours, and if that request is not answered with success within thirty seconds, it assumes the message was lost and sends it again, up to twice. I read the logs of one affected order and the timeline was plain. The first request arrived at 17:02:11. Our handler found the order, rendered the label PDF for the customer's records, saved it and sent the email, and only then returned an answer: 31 seconds. The carrier gave up at thirty, sent the event again at 17:02:42, and again at 17:03:17. Each of the three requests was handled in full, because the handler never asked whether it had seen this event before.

Two things were wrong, and the temptation was to treat only one. The slow part was the label rendering, which had been fast until the previous week, when the PDF service went from a pool to a single worker. That change was mine, in the sense that I had suggested the simplification and was now paying for it. The second fault was more important: a handler that is not safe to run twice is wrong whatever its speed, because the carrier is entitled to retry.

We did both, in this order. First, the handler records the carrier's event id in a table with a uniqueness rule and does nothing if the id is already there, so repeats can arrive in any number. Second, the handler now does almost nothing before it answers: it stores the event and returns success within a few milliseconds, and a separate worker does the rendering and sends the email. The first change is what makes the second safe, since a worker may also run a job twice.

Noor wrote the apology, and I read it beforehand. It said what had happened in one sentence, did not blame the carrier, and told people they had been charged once. Eleven customers wrote back to thank us for the clear message, and one asked whether the third email could be turned into a coupon. Noor said she would think about it, which I took to mean no.

The documentation wiki at Marrow Labs had 612 pages, nine years of edits and three syntaxes, and in September Yusra decided it should become a static site that anyone could build from a folder of files. She owned the content and I was given the move. It took five weeks, and the part I remember best is not the conversion but the thing I did not know I had to do.

The conversion was mechanical and a little humbling. The wiki exported pages in its own markup, with a second, older markup on about sixty pages from before a plugin change, and some raw HTML pasted in by hand. I wrote the converter in stages, ran it on twenty pages, looked at what came out, and Yusra, who knew which pages mattered, read twenty at a time and sent me the sentences that had broken. Tables were the worst. The old markup let a cell contain a bullet list and the new format did not, so thirty-eight tables had to be restructured by hand, and Yusra did these herself, over two evenings, saying she wanted to see what nine years of colleagues had actually written.

Links took a week. Inside the wiki, pages linked to each other by title, with spaces and capital letters, and titles had changed over the years, the old ones left behind as redirects. I built a table of every old title and where it finally led, and rewrote the inside links against it. Images were simple by comparison. By the end of the third week we had a site that built in eleven seconds and looked right.

Then Mara asked who links to us. I had been thinking of links as something inside the wiki. Documentation is read through links sent in emails, pasted into tickets, kept in other people's pages and in the browser history of three hundred customers, and every one of those would break the moment the old addresses stopped working. I had no list of them and no way to ask the world for one. But the old server did hold a record of every address anyone had requested for the past ninety days.

I took the access logs and counted. About 2,100 different addresses had been requested. The top three hundred accounted for 94 percent of all hits, so a short list would cover nearly everything, and the long tail was mostly search engines and scanners. I mapped every requested address that returned a page to its new place. Every one that did not, 71 addresses in an old query-string form like ?title=Setup_Guide, I matched to the right page by hand. I also found that the same page was requested with underscores, with spaces, with different capitals, and with and without a trailing slash, five forms of one address, and the map had to hold all of them.

Before the cutover I did one more thing that Yusra had not asked for, and it was the cheapest insurance in the project. I wrote a script that requested every address in the redirect map from a test copy of the new site and checked that each one ended on a page that existed and whose title was close to the old one's. Nine failed: five pointed to pages Yusra had merged during the migration, two to a page deleted on purpose, and two to a typo of mine in the map, where a hyphen had become an underscore. The script runs again before each release of the site, and has found six more broken links since, all of them made by people who were trying to improve something.

We cut over on a Monday at 07:00. In the first week the share of 'page not found' responses was 0.6 percent of requests.

Three weeks later a customer wrote that a link in an email from 2019 still worked, and thanked us for it. Yusra framed the message. What I took from it is that a page is not only its contents but every address by which it has ever been reached, and the only complete list of those addresses is the record of the people who were actually looking.

The chat server for the allotment society's app grew by about 280 MB a day, and nobody saw it for the first year, because it was restarted every Sunday night by an update job and never lived long enough to matter. Then Wren turned off the Sunday restarts, for reasons I will come to, and by the following Thursday the server was using 1.3 GB and the chat was lagging.

I do not enjoy memory problems, since the symptom and the cause are always far apart, but there is a method for them, and it is to take two photographs and compare. On the Monday Wren had restarted the server by hand and taken a heap snapshot of the fresh process. On Thursday afternoon he took another. I had both loaded into a table of what kind of object, how many, how big, and I subtracted. Almost everything was the same size. One line was not: closures, 41,000 of them in Thursday's, 600 in Monday's. Each one held a reference to a connection object, and each connection object held its buffers.

Closures that hold a connection are what you get when you register a callback for it, so I looked for the places that did. The presence feature, who is online, registered a listener on a shared event emitter whenever a client connected, so it could be told when other people appeared. On a clean disconnect the listener was removed. On the other ways a connection can end, a network timeout, a phone going into a tunnel, an error from the socket, the code went down a different path that closed the connection and forgot the listener. The emitter lived forever and kept every dead connection alive through it. Members of the society, who are on phones in gardens, produce a great many of the second kind of ending.

The count agreed with the story: about 41,000 leaked listeners in four days, and the logs showed roughly ten thousand timeout disconnects a day.

I fixed it twice, the second time because the first fix is easy to forget. The listener is now removed in one place that every kind of ending passes through. And the presence feature no longer registers a listener per connection at all. There is one listener, which looks up the current set of connections, so a dead connection has nothing to be held by.

As for why the restarts had been turned off: Wren had thought them a leftover and disliked them, and in a way he was right to. For a year they had been hiding the leak. I told him so. The Sunday restarts are back, as a precaution this time, with a line in the config saying what they guard against.

For one spring we ran our own build machines, and I want to set down what it cost, because the number we started from was wrong by a factor I did not expect.

The hosted build service had cost us 118 a month since we crossed its free tier, and Callum, who dislikes paying for things he could run himself, proposed a used workstation under his desk as a self-hosted runner. It arrived in April with 64 GB of memory. The first builds were splendid: the full pipeline in six minutes against fourteen on the hosted machines. Mara said she wanted to see where the catch was, and I said I would keep a list.

By the end of June the list had nineteen entries. Some were small: the machine's clock drifted and one signature test failed. Some were the kind that eat a Saturday. Builds shared a temporary directory, and two builds running at once overwrote each other's output, producing failures that showed in one branch and were caused by another, and for the better part of two weeks Tobias believed his own code was broken. The machine needed security patches and a reboot, and the reboot needed someone in the room, because the disk encryption asked for a passphrase on boot. Callum went in on three Sundays. A power cut in May took the runner down for a day and a half, and we found out when a release was waiting on it.

Meanwhile the six minutes had a hidden share. Half of the hosted build's time was spent downloading the same dependencies, and Callum's machine already had them on disk, so the fair comparison, with the hosted service configured sensibly, was nine minutes against six. We had been saving three minutes a build and paying for them in weekends.

I tried to put the weekends in the same units. Callum's hours on the machine over ten weeks came to fifty-one, the great majority unplanned. At any reasonable rate for an engineer's time, the 118 a month was the cheapest line in the whole arrangement. I showed Callum the arithmetic privately before showing anyone else, since the machine was his idea and he had worked hard at it. He read it, said 'ha', and went to look at the hosted plan's settings himself.

We went back in July. The machine is now a bench for Teo's firmware builds, where a day of downtime hurts nobody and, as Callum puts it, it has at last found honest work. What I took from it: the price of a thing you run yourself is mostly paid in attention at the worst moments, and it appears on no invoice, so someone has to write it down.

The energy co-op's dashboard showed a weekly average output for the shared solar array, and every few weeks the figure dipped in a way the weather did not explain. Sunniva, who reads it aloud at the members' monthly meeting, said so first, after a week in June with a clear sky and a number lower than a grey week in March.

I began with the sensor, since that is where people always begin, and the sensor was fine. The hourly readings for the week were in the database, 150 of them, not the 168 a week should hold. I computed the weekly mean by hand from the raw readings and got 41.2 kW. The dashboard said 37.1.

The dashboard did not take the mean of the week. It took the mean of seven daily means, and each daily mean was a mean of that day's readings. When every day has 24 readings the two are identical. That week the logger had lost its connection for most of the Wednesday and recorded only six readings, all from the early morning, when the array produces almost nothing. Wednesday's mean was 3 kW, and the weekly figure counted that day with the same weight as a day of twenty-four readings, so one half-dead day pulled the week down like a full one.

It is an old mistake and I know it by name, the average of averages, which is right only when the groups are the same size. I had not looked for it because the groups had always been the same size, until the day they were not. Bugs of this kind do not live in code that is wrong. They live in code that is right under an assumption nobody wrote down.

The fix is to store the sum and the count of readings for each day, not the mean, and to compute any longer average from the totals. That also let the dashboard say something it had never said: how many readings stand behind each figure. For that Wednesday it now shows 6 of 24 in grey, and any week with a day below 20 readings carries a note beside the number, 'one day incomplete'. Sunniva liked that more than the fix. She said it gave her something to say at the meeting beyond 'the figure is lower'.

I also went back through the stored weekly figures for the past year. Four weeks had been affected, the worst by 10 percent. We recomputed them from the raw readings and posted the corrected values with a line saying what had changed. No decision at the co-op had hung on them, but Sunniva wanted the minutes right.

Zeynep could log in on her phone and not on her laptop, and for two days that was the whole of the evidence. She is a patient at Ilse's clinic and uses its booking portal, and she wrote politely, three times, and Ilse brought it to Mara with the remark that the portal was haunted.

The obvious differences between phone and laptop were not interesting. Same account, same password, which she had reset to be sure. Same network on the evening she tried both side by side. The portal gave the same message in both cases, 'no account found for that email', not 'wrong password', which put the failure ahead of the password check, in the lookup. And the email was the one thing I could not see, since I do not ask for patients' details. I asked Ilse to have Zeynep type her address exactly as it appeared in the confirmation email and describe, letter by letter, what was capitalised.

Her address began with a capital I. Her phone's keyboard, she said, capitalised the first letter. Her laptop's browser autofilled the address from an old form, in all capitals. The portal stored addresses in lower case and compared in lower case, which is the right design, and it lowercased what you typed before the lookup. A capital I lowercases to a small i in every language I know apart from one.

The portal's lowercasing used the language of the request. The phone sent its language as English. The laptop had been set up some months before with Turkish as its main language, and said so in a header on every request. In Turkish the capital I lowercases to a dotless letter, a different letter, and no account is stored under that. The lookup was perfectly correct for Turkish text and wrong for an email address, which belongs to no language.

To confirm it I asked Mara to send a request against a test account with the laptop's language header and the address typed in capitals. It failed with the same message. With the header changed, it worked. That was the whole proof. The fix was to lowercase email addresses without regard to locale, in one place, with the language-independent function. Mara went through the portal for other places that had borrowed the request's language for text that was not language, and found two more, a username search and a promo code.

Ilse wrote back to Zeynep that the fault was in the portal and not in her computer, which I think mattered to her more than the repair. And Mara added a line to the testing checklist: try the Turkish i. She has a card on her monitor that says so.

The weekly digest email went out twice for three weeks before anyone said so, and the person who said so was a retired member of the choir who forwarded both copies to me with the subject line 'Is there something wrong or am I being given extra?' Ilse passed it on with a laughing face and a request to find out.

The digest is sent by a scheduled job, Sunday at 18:00. Halvard had added a second web server in the autumn so that updates could be done without taking the site down, and he had set the second up as a copy of the first, which is sensible, and the copy included the table of scheduled jobs. Both machines woke at 18:00 on Sunday and each sent the digest to everyone. Every member received two. The choir member was the only one who said anything, because a duplicate from an organisation you like is easy to forgive.

The quick answer would have been to take the schedule off the second server, and Halvard did that within minutes. I said that was the right first move and the wrong last one, because the next person to set up a third machine would copy it again, and the job was safe only so long as it ran on exactly one. A property that holds only because of how the machines happen to be laid out is an accident.

What I suggested instead was that the job protect itself. At the start it takes a named lock in the database, 'weekly-digest', and if another process holds it, it exits quietly and logs that it did. It also records the date of the last digest in a table and refuses to send if that date is within the last six days, so a lock that is somehow missed, or a manual rerun, cannot send a second. The lock stops a race and the date stops a repeat. I would not drop either: they fail in different ways.

Mara asked why both. I said I did not trust myself to have thought of every way the job might start twice, and between them they covered the ones I could think of and probably a few I could not. We tested by starting the job twelve times at the same instant from a shell loop on two machines, which sent one digest, and by running it again an hour later, which sent none.

The choir member got an apology and a sentence about what had happened. She replied that she had rather enjoyed the second copy, since it gave her an excuse to read the rehearsal dates twice.

We announced the end of version one of the booking API six months before it ended, and when the day came the partner who mattered most had not heard.

Dario and I had done everything the guides recommend. The old endpoints returned a Sunset header carrying the date, the documentation had a banner, and a notice went to the partners' mailing list at six months, three months, one month and one week. In the logs I could see which API keys were still calling the old version, and by the final week there were four, three of them small. The fourth, belonging to the reservations system at Tamsin & Pike, was calling it 9,000 times a day.

At 09:00 on the day the old version began answering 410 Gone, a plain statement that the thing was removed and a link to its replacement. At 09:12 Osei, an engineer at Tamsin & Pike, rang Dario. Their integration had stopped, their customers were being told nothing was available, and nobody there had known. The address on our list belonged to a person who had left their company in March. The header had been sent to their code on every call for six months, and their code did not read headers.

In the following hour I wrote down what we had actually promised, and to whom. We had promised notice, and given it, to an address that was no longer read. We had not promised that anyone had understood. Dario decided, and I think rightly, to put the old version back for Tamsin & Pike's key alone, for three weeks, with a firm second date that Osei confirmed in writing, and to leave every other key answering 410 as announced. The switch in our gateway was one line in a configuration file, and the extension was live by 10:20.

Osei's team needed only eleven days, since the change on their side was small. They had simply never been told there was a change. The delay cost them about an hour and a half of lost bookings, and cost us a morning.

What I changed is what I do before the last date. I no longer send one more notice. I take the top callers by volume and ask a named person at each to reply that they have received it. A header is a message to a program and a mailing list is a message to an address, and neither is a message to a human being who is accountable. I keep the list of those humans, with the name of whoever confirmed and the date.

Noor reads the infrastructure plan line by line before anyone applies it, a habit she says she acquired the hard way at a previous job and will not describe, and in October that habit saved a Friday evening.

The plan was for a routine change, a larger disk on the reporting database, and the first screen was as expected: one resource to change. On the second screen, below the summary, was another line: one resource to destroy, a firewall rule named tmp-reporting-access. Noor stopped and asked who had created it. The infrastructure code did not mention it, which is why the tool wanted it gone: the tool's view of the world is the code, and anything outside the code is, to it, litter.

I went through the audit log with her. The rule had been made by hand eleven weeks earlier, at 02:50 on a Sunday, during an incident in which the reporting database had become unreachable from the partner's analytics service. Dario, on call, had added the rule to let the service through, intending, I am sure, to write it into the code in the morning. The 'tmp' in the name was an intention too. The incident was closed, the ticket written, and the rule forgotten, and it was now carrying the partner's nightly extract, 40 GB of it, every night.

Had the plan been applied at 17:00 as scheduled, the extract would have failed at 02:00, and the partner would have seen it on Saturday morning with nobody on call who knew why. It would have taken some hours to find. I know, because it took me ten minutes with the knowledge that it was there.

We did not apply that plan. Dario wrote the rule into the code under a proper name, narrowed it to the partner's one port instead of the whole range he had opened in the dark, and Noor reran the plan, which was clean apart from the disk. It went out at 18:20.

Two small things came of it. We set up a weekly job that runs the plan against the live system with nothing changed and mails what it would do. Any line other than 'no changes' means somebody did something by hand. In its first week it found two more, both harmless. And Dario put a sentence in the on-call guide: after an emergency fix by hand, the fix is not finished until it is in the code, and the ticket stays open until it is.

Noor said what she liked best was that nobody was blamed. I said nobody had been wrong. A rule made at 02:50 to restore a service is what the person on call is for. The only wrong part was that code and world were allowed to disagree for eleven weeks, and the weekly job now makes that impossible.

Teo brought a benchmark to a meeting on a Thursday, which he does not usually do, and it changed what we did with the reporting module.

The month view of the fleet report, the page people open first each morning, took 4.2 seconds. Tobias, who wrote the module and likes the object-relational layer it was built on, maintained that the time was in the database and that a better index would fix it. Teo's benchmark said otherwise. He had put the same question to the database console as a single plain query, summing fuel costs by vehicle for the month, and it answered in 0.3 seconds with 240 rows. The layer's version fetched about 180,000 fuel records with every column, built an object for each, and added them up in the application. The time was not in the database. It was in turning the database's answer into objects and then throwing the objects away.

I want to be fair to the layer, because Tobias was in the argument. For the writing side of the application it is excellent: it validates, it keeps the rules in one place, and nobody wants hand-made inserts scattered through the codebase. The trouble was the reports, where the question is 'sum these columns grouped by that' and an object for every row is the wrong shape. We were using a delivery van to carry a postcard.

We settled the argument by agreeing a boundary, not a winner. Anything that changes data goes through the layer. Anything that only reads and aggregates is written as a query, in a file of its own, with a name, and its results come back as plain rows mapped to a small typed record. Tobias asked for one more condition, and I think it was the important one: every report query gets a test against a small fixed dataset, so that the SQL is no less checked than the objects were.

We moved the module over in four steps, one report at a time, and after every step I ran the old and new versions against each other on a week of data. Twice they differed, and both times the old one was wrong. The layer had been silently skipping vehicles with no recorded fuel purchases, because of a join it had chosen for us. The month view fell to 0.35 seconds. The thirty-one vehicles without fuel purchases appeared in the report for the first time, and Ilse's colleague in finance asked where they had come from. They had always existed. The report had never shown them.

Tobias took it well. He said what he disliked was not the plain SQL but that it was he, not the layer, who had assumed the layer was cheap. Teo was offered a cake as thanks, declined it, and then accepted.

Lazlo's pipeline for the delivery-failure report was eight small programs joined by pipes, 340 lines of awk and sed in all, and it had printed the same four tables every morning since 2016. Lazlo was a contractor who had moved on, and the only documentation was a sentence in the README that began 'This is quick'. When the logging format changed in the autumn, Mara asked me to bring the report up to date, and I decided, with her agreement, to replace it with one program in a language the whole team reads. The decision I am glad of is not the replacement but the way I checked it.

I ran old and new side by side on ninety days of logs and compared every table, number by number. For the first thirty days nothing differed. On the thirty-first something did, and by a lot: the new program counted far fewer failures for the first nine days of every month, and equal numbers for the rest. A bug in my date handling, I thought, and I spent an hour on it before I looked at the log lines themselves.

The old proxy that produced them wrote its timestamps in the traditional style, 'Mar 14 06:02:11', the month abbreviated and the day a plain number. For days from the first to the ninth the day is padded with a space instead of a zero: 'Mar  3 06:02:11'. Two spaces. When I looked for what the old script did about it, I found the sixth stage, one line of sed that turned a pair of spaces into a space and a zero, with no comment. Without that line the old pipeline would have lost the first nine days of every month, so Lazlo must have met the problem. My program was not wrong about the dates. It was wrong about something else: it recognised a failed delivery by the third field, which on those lines was one field further along, because my splitter and my pattern did not agree about where the date ended.

I fixed the field handling, and then did what I think is most of the job, which is to keep the oddity. The new program has a test with three sample lines, 'Mar  3', 'Mar 13' and 'Dec  9', and a comment at the place where the date is read, saying what the proxy does and whose script first knew it.

Then I went through the other seven stages looking for knowledge hidden in one-liners. There were two more. One discarded lines from a health-check client that polled every ten seconds, which would have inflated every count. The other dropped lines with status 499, which I had taken at first for a typo of 409, and which is the proxy's own code for a client that hung up, not a failure of ours.

Mara asked whether anything of Lazlo's was left. I said everything he knew was left and nothing he typed. It is what I want to be true of any code I replace.

Wren tested the sync on a train, which is why I know exactly what was wrong with it. Tern is the inspection app our client's engineers use on site, often underground, where there is no signal. They fill in a form about a pump or a valve, and later, in daylight, the phone uploads. Two engineers sometimes inspect the same asset on the same day. The first design of the sync was the obvious one: each record has a modified time, and the later one wins.

On the 07:40 service between two towns Wren took two phones, set both to airplane mode, and edited the same inspection record on each, one changing the pressure reading and the other adding a note about a photograph. He reconnected them in the station, and one phone's edits had vanished altogether. Not conflicted: gone. Whichever phone uploaded last had overwritten the whole record, and neither engineer would have known.

I looked at what was being compared. The record as a whole carried one time, and the time came from each phone's own clock. That meant two faults. First, a whole-record winner throws away every field the loser changed, even when the fields do not overlap. Second, phone clocks disagree. One of Wren's was three minutes and ten seconds fast, and in the test the phone with the earlier edit won because its clock was ahead.

The redesign was smaller than the problem sounded. Each field carries its own stamp, and the stamp is not a time but a pair: a counter that each device raises whenever it sees a higher one, and the device's name to break ties. That orders edits the way they happened, as well as anyone can know, without trusting a clock. Merging is done field by field. Edits to different fields combine, which is nearly always what happened. Edits to the same field are the only true conflict, and there the later stamp wins, but the losing value is not discarded. It is kept in a conflict list on the record, visible in the app, with who entered it and when. I did not want the loser silently lost, since the person who typed it may have been right.

Wren's first run of the same train test, a week later, passed, and the conflict list held one entry. Both engineers had typed a reading into the pressure field, 6.2 and 6.4, and the app showed the later and offered the earlier. Wren said it was the first time the app had told him something he did not know about his own test.

What I took from it is how much of a sync problem is deciding the unit of conflict. A record was too big. A character would be too small. A field was the right size for this form, and may not be for the next.

Forty-one minutes was the build time that Dario's firmware team had stopped noticing, the way people stop noticing a noise. They started a build and went for lunch. It was Mara who counted that on an average day the team started thirty builds, and that at forty-one minutes each, a quarter of the working day of four people went on waiting.

I wanted to know first what the build did, and then what it did that it need not. The tool they used rebuilds a file only when something that file depends on has changed, so a second build with no changes should have done nothing. I asked for a build with no edits, immediately after a full one. It rebuilt 1,860 files and took thirty-nine minutes. That was where the answer lay: the tool believed something had changed, always.

The build tool can explain itself. For one of the rebuilt files I asked why, and it said that a dependency, a header called board_config.h, was newer than the output. The header was not in the source tree. A small generator wrote it at the start of every build, from a list of board options, and it began with a comment: generated on, and the date and time to the second. The contents were therefore different every time, and the file's timestamp was always newer than every object that included it. Every file that included it, directly or through other headers, which in this codebase meant nearly everything, was rebuilt on every build. A comment had been costing the team a quarter of its day.

The fix was two lines in the generator: leave out the time, and write the file only if its contents differ from what is already there. Two changes, because the first is not enough if someone later adds anything else that varies. The no-edit build now took eleven seconds. The build after editing one source file dropped to about ninety seconds. A full clean build still takes thirty-eight minutes, but nobody does that thirty times a day, they do it twice a week.

Dario asked why nobody had found it in three years. I think the answer is that the slow build was a fact of their world and not a fault in it. A person who has never seen the build do nothing does not know it ought to. So I put a check in their pipeline that does a build, then a second one with no changes, and fails if the second takes more than thirty seconds. It has gone red once, in November, when somebody added a version stamp to another generated file. They fixed that within the hour and said it was the pleasantest red they had ever seen.

The partner's catalogue arrived as a single CSV of 2.1 GB, and the importer had died three times on it before Mara asked me to look. Each attempt ran about seventy minutes and was killed at the same point, near the end, by the operating system's out-of-memory killer. She had left the fourth running overnight, and in the morning it had died again, which was the reason she was a little short with the machine.

The importer's design was the first one anybody would write. Read the whole file, split it into rows, turn each row into an object, validate all of them, then write them to the database. For a 20 MB file that is correct and fast. For 2.1 GB it needed memory for the text, the rows and the objects at once, about 11 GB on a machine with 8. It had worked on every previous catalogue only because those were smaller than the machine.

I rewrote the flow as a stream. The file is read in a single pass, a row at a time, validated as it passes and written in batches of 5,000 rows, each batch in its own transaction. Memory stays near 90 MB whatever the size of the input. The first full run took 48 minutes, partly because the machine no longer swapped, and for the first time in a week it finished.

Two other things came from treating it as a stream. The importer now records, after every committed batch, how many rows of the file it has consumed, so a failure at row 1.9 million resumes from there and not from zero. And it found the real defect in the file, which the old importer could never have reported because it died first. At row 1,204,331 a product description contained a single stray double quote, which opened a quoted field that never closed, so the parser read the next eleven thousand lines as one enormous description. The streaming parser reported it as it happened, with the line where the quote opened and the line where the field finally ended.

The importer does not stop on a bad row. It writes the row, with its line number and the reason, to a rejects file next to the input, carries on, and at the end prints how many rows were rejected and where the file is. Mara sent the rejects file to the partner: 212 rows in all, one of them eleven thousand lines long. She said she would rather have a short, specific complaint to send than a long, vague apology to receive.

Tobias drew a bucket on the whiteboard and I knew we were going to spend the afternoon on the rate limiter. The public API of the ticketing service, Plover, had never had one, and a partner's script that retried in a tight loop had taken the service down for eleven minutes in September. The question was how to limit, and the argument that followed ran two days and ended better than it began.

Tobias wanted a sliding window log: for each API key, keep the time of every request in the last minute, and refuse when there are more than a limit. It is exact and easy to explain. My objection was cost, with a number. A key making 300 requests a minute would hold 300 timestamps in the shared store, and with two hundred active keys the store would carry sixty thousand entries purely to count. I proposed a token bucket instead: two numbers per key, the tokens available and the time of the last refill. A request takes a token, tokens return at a steady rate, and the size of the bucket is the burst you will tolerate. It is cheap, and it allows what well-behaved clients do, which is to be quiet and then busy.

Mara asked the question that decided it, and I would like to keep its form. She asked what the numbers would be. Tobias and I had both been arguing about structure, and neither of us had a limit in mind. We took a week of real traffic and computed, per key, the busiest second and the sustained rate over a minute. The busiest second of any legitimate key was 14 requests, and the sustained rate at most 3 a second. The partner's looping script had made 220 a second. So the limit did not have to be clever. A burst of 30 and a sustained 5 a second would never touch the legitimate callers and would stop the loop in a quarter of a second. Those numbers came from the data, and I wrote them in the comment with the date.

We built the token bucket, updating its two numbers in one step inside the shared store so that two servers can never both spend the last token. Tobias came round on cost when he saw the memory figure, and I came round on one of his points, that a refused request must tell the client when to come back. So the response carries the number of seconds until a token is available, and the limit is documented in the same place.

Then came the part I did not predict. Three days after release Osei's team reported a few refusals just after midnight when they were nowhere near the limit. I found them in our logs: always within a minute after 00:00, always on one of the two servers. The bucket measured elapsed time with each server's own clock. Halvard's time-sync service steps the clock once a night, and on one machine it had drifted 1.8 seconds ahead. At the correction the clock moved back, the elapsed time since the last refill came out negative, and my code, which subtracted it, took tokens away instead of adding them. Some buckets went to minus fifty and stayed there until the refill caught up.

Osei's reply when I told him was characteristic. He said he had assumed the limit was the problem and had been about to ask us for a higher one. I think that sentence is worth keeping, because a rate limiter that misfires teaches the people it limits to distrust the limit. For a week after the fix I read the refusals by hand every morning, fourteen of them in all, and every one was a genuine overrun by the looping script that had started the whole affair, now running under a different key at a different partner who had copied it.

I fixed it two ways. Elapsed time is never allowed below zero, and the time itself now comes from the shared store, one clock for all servers instead of each server's own. I wrote a test that moves the clock backwards in the middle of a run, and it failed against the old code in exactly the way described.

What I keep from the week is Mara's question. We would have built either design and tuned it by feel. The number the legitimate callers needed was sitting in a week of logs, and it took twenty minutes to compute.

Nobody asked how many files it was until Noor's query for the monthly retention figures ran for nine minutes and then timed out. She had assumed the data was big. It was not: the whole month of events came to 6 GB. I asked the storage for a listing of the partition and it returned 41,300 files, and the listing alone took longer than I had expected the whole query to.

The event data lands in the lake from sixty sources, and each source's writer, by design, writes what it has once a minute so that dashboards stay fresh. Most sources were quiet, so the real figure was fourteen hundred or so files a day, each about 150 KB. Every one of them has to be opened, its header read and its place in the query worked out. A query across a month meant 41,000 file opens spent on 6 GB of data. It was not slow because the data was heavy. It was slow because the data was in crumbs.

The remedy is called compaction, and the idea is plain. Once a day's partition is closed, a job reads all of its small files and writes them back as a few large ones, about 128 MB each, then replaces the small files with the big ones. We added it as a nightly job. The monthly query went from nine minutes and a timeout to forty seconds.

I want to record the two things that were not plain. The first was the replacing. If the small files are removed before the large ones are visible, or a query happens to run in the middle, it sees too little or double. We arranged it so that the large files are first written to a staging place, then listed in the partition's manifest in a single step, and only on a later run, a day on, are the small files deleted. A reader at any moment sees either the old set or the new set, never a mix.

The second was a check on the check. After the first week of compaction I compared row counts, day by day, between the old crumb files, which we had kept for the purpose, and the compacted ones. They matched on six days and not on the seventh, off by 212 rows, and for a moment I thought I had lost data. The seventh day was the one on which a source had written a late file after its partition closed. The compactor had skipped it, correctly, since the manifest was already sealed, and a second pass the following night picked it up. I had been looking at the gap at the wrong hour.

Noor wanted to know whether the lake was now fixed. I said it was fixed for the shape of data we had, and that the real cure was for writers to hold their data longer. We asked the three noisiest sources to flush every ten minutes instead of every minute. Two agreed and the third said it needed the freshness. We left it.

The outages came every six hours, to the minute, and that told me more than anything else I learned that week. At 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00 the internal services began failing to find one another: errors saying the host name could not be resolved, lasting between forty and sixty seconds, then healing. They had been going on for about two weeks, small enough to pass as network noise. Halvard blamed the resolver. Callum blamed the resolver's cache. Mara asked me to find out which of them was right.

Neither, as it turned out. Anything that happens on the hour at regular intervals is a scheduled job, so I read the schedules. At the six-hour marks there was one: the service registry's refresh, which re-registered every internal service from a configuration file so that new ones were picked up. The way it did this was to remove every entry and add them back, and for the few seconds between those two steps the name 'billing' did not exist. A caller that asked at that instant received the answer 'no such name', a definite answer, not a failure to answer.

A definite no is something resolvers are entitled to remember. The name server's own zone data told them to keep a negative answer for sixty seconds. So a single four-second gap, if someone asked inside it, became a minute of 'no such name' on that caller's machine, because the machine believed the registry's momentary lie for as long as the record told it to. That was why the outage lasted forty to sixty seconds when the gap lasted four.

To test it before I said so, I set up a small loop on a test machine asking for a name once a second, and ran the refresh by hand. The loop printed one 'no such name' and then thirty-seven more, then the name again. Mara counted them aloud as they scrolled, which I thought a good use of a person.

We fixed it in the order of the cause. The refresh now adds new entries first and removes the old ones afterwards, so a name is never absent. And the negative-answer time was cut from sixty seconds to five, since a name that is missing for a good reason gets fixed quickly and nothing in our setup needs a long memory for being wrong. Both changes, because the first prevents the gap and the second limits the harm from any gap that remains.

Halvard asked whether I would put a note somewhere for the next person. I put it in the registry's own configuration, beside the refresh interval, in two lines: do not remove before adding; a missing name is remembered by every caller for longer than it was missing.

At 02:10 on a Wednesday one message in the order queue killed the worker that picked it up, the worker restarted, the queue offered it the same message again, and the worker died again, and so on for three hours and twenty minutes, with 1,900 other orders waiting behind it. Nobody was woken, because nothing was down. The worker was running, in the sense that a process that keeps starting is running, and the health page was green.

Callum found it at 05:30 when he looked at a graph I had asked him to add the week before, which he had thought a little fussy: the age of the oldest message in the queue. It stood at 3 hours 20 minutes and was climbing in a straight line. That graph, not the logs, told him where to look. The logs held the same crash 2,400 times, each with the same message identifier and the same line: division by zero.

The message was an order with an empty list of items, which the web form should have refused and, because of a validation bug nobody had noticed, had accepted once. The worker computed an average weight per item, for shipping, by dividing the total weight by the number of items. Nothing in the worker had been written to survive a division by zero inside what the queue called a valid message. The queue had done what it is designed to do. It had never lost the message and it had never given up on it.

There are two repairs, and they live in different places. The worker should not divide by zero: an order with no items is refused with a reason and the message is acknowledged as handled, because retrying a message that can never succeed helps no one. That was a one-line fix and Callum made it before breakfast. But I did not want to leave it there, because the next poisonous message will not be a division by zero. It will be some other thing nobody has thought of. So the queue is now set to give each message five attempts, with a growing pause between them, and then to move it to a separate queue for messages that have failed, where it waits for a person, and a message arriving there raises an alert to the on-call phone with the order number.

We tested it by deliberately sending a bad message. It failed five times in forty seconds, appeared in the failed queue, and the on-call phone rang, which Callum, having sent the message himself, took in good humour. The 1,900 orders behind the first one, once it was gone, cleared in nine minutes.

Mara said the lesson was to validate input. It was one lesson. The other, which I added to the notes, is that a retry loop with no limit turns a single bad item into an outage that looks like quiet.

Negative light is not a thing, and yet the rooftop weather mast at the community centre reported minus 31,000 lux at noon on every sunny day that spring. Teo had built the mast with the youth club: a light sensor, a temperature sensor and a small board that sent a reading every ten minutes. The chart on the centre's website had a crater in the middle of each fine afternoon.

Teo's first theory was reasonable: the sun heated the sensor and the sensor misreported. He sent me a month of readings and I looked for the pattern in what was wrong, not in why. The negative values appeared only when the true value must have been high, and the raw readings fell in a narrow band, just above 2,047 on the converter's scale and never below. A heat error would grow smoothly with the temperature. This looked like a cliff.

A cliff at 2,047 in a number that runs from 0 to 4,095 sits at the middle of the range. The firmware, which Teo had written in the evenings and shared with me, read the sensor sixteen times and added the samples to get a smoother figure. The sum was held in a signed 16-bit integer, which holds up to 32,767. Sixteen samples averaging 2,047 add up to 32,752. Sixteen averaging a little more come to 32,768 or higher, which a signed 16-bit integer cannot hold, so the value wraps around to a large negative number. On cloudy days the average never reached it. On clear days it did, around noon.

I said I thought it was the sum and asked him to confirm it with arithmetic before touching the code, and he did it on the back of a flyer from the youth club: 2,048 times sixteen, 32,768. He rang to say the number was exact to the digit, which is the satisfying kind of confirmation.

The fix was to hold the sum in an unsigned 32-bit integer, which has room for any number of samples, and divide afterwards. I asked him to add a plausibility range to the reading itself, too, so that a lux value below zero or above the sensor's rating is flagged on the chart as a fault and not drawn as a measurement. The crater would not have lasted a week if the board had been willing to say that it did not believe its own number.

On the first fine afternoon after the change the chart rose to 94,000 lux at 12:40, and Teo sent me a photograph of the screen with a delighted child in front of it. I did not need to say anything about it.

Ninety-four seconds. That was the number that explained why roughly one request in forty between two of our services came back with 'token not yet valid', and it took me a day to reach it because I kept studying the one in forty and not the thirty-nine.

The setup was this. Service A signs a short-lived token valid from the moment of issue, and Service B checks it. The failures were not tied to any user or endpoint. The only structure I could find was in the machines: every failure was on one of B's three servers, number three, which rejected tokens it believed had been issued in its future. Tokens older than ninety seconds or so passed. A client keeps one token for about fifteen minutes, so fresh tokens are a small share of traffic, and a failure needed a fresh token to meet server three, which came to about one request in three times one in twelve. That is one in thirty-six, close enough to what the logs said.

I asked Halvard for the clock offsets of all the machines against the reference time. Servers one and two were within twenty milliseconds. Server three was 94 seconds behind. The image it was built from had had its time synchronisation switched off for a test in the spring and never switched back on, and a clock with nobody disciplining it loses a few seconds a day, which is almost exactly a month of drift. That was the whole cause: one machine's idea of now.

There were three things to do and I did not want to do only the first. One: set server three's clock right, which Halvard did, with a forced step, in under a minute. Two: make the receiving side tolerant by a small allowance, thirty seconds, as is usual, so that two honest clocks that disagree a little do not become an outage. I argued against widening it enough to cover a case like 94 seconds, since a bigger allowance is a bigger window in which a stolen token still works. Three: make something notice. Each server now reports its offset from the reference, and an alert fires at five seconds. A clock is the kind of fault no application log will ever mention.

The oddest feature of the bug, I told Mara, was that for a month the system had been rejecting one request in forty and nobody had complained. Retrying worked. The person pressed the button again and it went through, and the failure became part of how the product felt. She said that was the worst kind, and wrote on the whiteboard in her large hand: RETRIES HIDE THINGS. It is still there.

The command-line tool our field engineers use to download job sheets took fourteen seconds to print its own help text, and the engineers, who are patient people, had assumed that was how it was. Rafe wrote it in the summer, his first real program, and he was proud of it and a little hurt when Ilse mentioned the delay, so I asked whether he would sit with me and work out where the time went. I did not want to be the one to tell him.

Python has a switch that makes the interpreter report how long each import took, and I asked him to run the tool with it and send me the output. It is a long list, and the way to read it is to look at the cumulative column and ignore the rest. One line stood out: the analysis module, which Rafe had imported at the top of the main file, took 11.8 seconds, almost all of it spent importing a large numerical library that loads a great many things the moment you ask for it.

Why was a numerical library involved in downloading job sheets? Rafe explained, and he was right to be embarrassed, because the answer was one function near the bottom that computed a weighted average of the sensor readings on a job sheet, and the library was used for exactly three lines of it. Everything else in the tool just read a file and talked to a server.

There were two kinds of fix and we did both. First, the import moved inside the one function that uses it, so a run that never calls the function never pays for it. That brought the help text to 0.6 seconds. Second, and this was Rafe's idea, and I thought it a good one, we asked whether the three lines needed the library at all. They computed a weighted mean. In plain Python that is a loop of four lines. The library left the project. The tool now installs in seconds rather than a minute, and the packaged download shrank from 71 MB to 3.

I kept one habit from it, which I gave to Rafe as the only advice I was sure of: an import at the top of a file is a promise that every run of the program will want it. Mostly that is true. Now and then it is a bill that you pay without knowing.

Ilse told the engineers the new version was out. One wrote back, with obvious feeling, that he had thought the tool was just 'thinking about it'. Rafe pinned the message above his desk.

Sunniva found it by accident, searching the log tool for the text of an error and noticing, in the ten lines around the match, a customer's email address. Then another, and a telephone number. She told Mara within the hour, and Mara told me, in the flat voice that means a thing is serious, to find out how far it went and make it stop.

The booking service logged any unexpected failure together with the request that caused it, so that whoever read the log could reproduce the failure. That is a reasonable thing to want and a careless thing to do, because the request is the customer's form: name, address, telephone, email, a note. It had been that way since the service was written, and the log tool kept thirty days.

I wrote a search for the shapes of personal data, an email pattern and a telephone pattern, and ran it over one day of logs, then over a sample of each of the thirty days, to see whether it had started on a particular date. It had not: it was there from the first day of the retained window. On a typical day there were between 40 and 90 lines with a personal detail, nearly all from one handler. Nothing had left the log tool, which only five of us can open, and Dario confirmed from the access log that nobody outside had read those days' entries. That was worth knowing, and it did not change what we had to do.

Three steps, in the order that stops the harm first. We stopped writing it. The logging call no longer carries the request body, only its identifier, the route and the names of the fields it contained, which is almost always enough to reproduce a failure when paired with the identifier, since the support team can look the booking up properly. We scrubbed what was there: a pass over the thirty days that rewrote every matched line with the personal parts replaced by a marker, followed by the same search to confirm that the count had gone to zero, which it had, apart from eleven false hits that were the company's own address. And we closed the route that let it in, with a rule in the logging wrapper that refuses to serialise any object with a field of certain names, and a test that logs an object containing an email and fails if the email appears in the output.

Dario asked whether we needed to tell anyone. We went through the checklist, which turned on whether any outsider had had access, and the answer, backed by the access log, was no. We wrote down the reasoning and the date and put it with the incident notes, so that if the question is asked later, the answer already exists.

I took away a small rule about what logs are for. A log is written for the person who has a problem at 03:00, and that person needs to know what happened and which record to look at. They almost never need the record's contents, and when they do, there is a better place to read them, with better care.

Fourteen customers bought walnut chopping boards that the shop did not have. The stock page said minus three, which no stock page should ever say, and over a weekend in the spring sale the customer-service inbox filled with the gentle, baffled emails of people who had been told their order was confirmed.

The shop is Pike & Quill's, a small online business whose warehouse partner keeps stock in a shared spreadsheet because that is what the warehouse staff use, and the shop's website reads and writes the number in a cell. When an order arrives the site reads the cell, subtracts the quantity and writes the result back. When a delivery arrives the warehouse's import reads the cell, adds the delivered quantity and writes it back. Each does it in two steps with a gap between them, and in the gap the other may do the same.

I reconstructed the Saturday from the logs on both sides. At 10:41:07 the warehouse import read 12 for the walnut boards and began adding a delivery of 200. At 10:41:08 six orders came in, and the site, one after another, read 12, then 11, then 10, down to 7, writing back each time.
