At 10:41:09 the import finished its sum and wrote 212 over the cell, so six boards had been sold from a number that no longer existed, and the site's six writes were lost. The stock was overstated by six. That is a lost update, the oldest bug in any system that two things write to. The minus three came later, from the mirror image: a clash during a stock count that erased an addition. Together the clashes made up the fourteen oversold.

I wrote the real cause on one line for Mara: the number had two writers and no arbiter. A spreadsheet cell cannot arbitrate, because it has no way to say 'add three to whatever is there now'.

The repair moved the number of record out of the spreadsheet and into the shop's database, where an update can say exactly that: set stock to stock minus the quantity, as one statement that the database performs with nobody in between. The warehouse keeps its spreadsheet, which they like, and it has become a view. A small job copies the numbers into it every minute, and deliveries are entered on a sheet that the shop reads and applies as additions, never as replacements. I asked the warehouse manager, Odile, whether she could live with entering 'received 200' in place of 'now 212', and she said she had always thought of it that way and only typed the total because the cell was there.

Pike & Quill's honoured all fourteen orders late, with a voucher, and the boards were reordered. The shop's owner wrote that the spreadsheet had never lied to her before. I did not say that it had not lied this time either. Two honest writers had simply never been told about each other.

The storefront's worker processes began dying one Tuesday afternoon, not all at once but one every few minutes, each with a stack overflow, a crash I had seen perhaps twice in the codebase's life. Sunniva, whose shop it was, noticed because the pages for cookware and for gifts returned an error while the rest of the site was fine. That was the clue I held on to: two sections and nothing else.

Each page of the shop builds a breadcrumb, the line at the top that reads Home, Kitchen, Cookware, by walking up from the current category to its parent, and its parent's parent, and so to the top. The walk was a function that called itself, and it ended when it reached a category with no parent. I asked Mara for the parent of Cookware and the parent of Gifts, and they were each other. Cookware's parent was Gifts. Gifts' parent was Cookware. A walk up from either never reached the top. It went round, getting deeper, until the process ran out of room and fell over.

The history of the category table showed how. At 13:52 someone in the shop's back office had dragged Cookware under Gifts by mistake, then dragged Gifts under Cookware to put it right, and the second move had been accepted with the first still in force. Nothing in the back office or the database had ever asked whether a move would make a category its own ancestor. People had moved categories for years, and none of them had been the one to make a circle.

The repair had to stand on both sides of the wall. On the way in: before any move is saved, the code walks up from the proposed new parent, and if it meets the category being moved, it refuses with a message that says which category is in the way and why. On the way out: the breadcrumb walk now carries a depth counter and stops at twenty levels with a typed error that names the category where it gave up, so a bad circle in the data becomes a line in the log and a plain page for the visitor, not a dead process. The shop's deepest real category is four levels down. Twenty is not a number anyone will come near by honest means.

Sunniva put Cookware back under Kitchen by hand, once I had checked that she was going to, and the pages returned at 15:10. If you now try to put Gifts under Cookware, the back office says that Cookware is already inside Gifts. She thought that a very civil way for software to say no.

After the database outage, the thing that hurt was the recovery. The outage itself lasted four minutes, a storage hiccup that Halvard cured with a restart. What came after lasted twenty-six, and what I did that evening was draw the graph that showed why.

When the database came back at 14:07, every one of our twenty-odd services had been failing, and every service had been written by someone sensible to retry with a growing pause: wait one second, then two, then four, then eight. It is the standard thing. The trouble with the standard thing is that all twenty services had been failing since the same moment, and so all of them tried again at the same moments. At 14:07:01, a wall of requests. Then silence. At 14:07:03, a wall. At 14:07:07, a wall, and at 14:07:15 and 14:07:31. The graph of connections to the database during those minutes was a row of fence posts, each taller than the database could take, because a freshly started database handles each wall slowly, which keeps more clients waiting, which keeps the next wall tall. It fell over twice under its own recovery, and the second time it took a restart to clear.

I could see the synchrony in the logs by lining up the timestamps of the retries from four different services. They matched to within a few hundred milliseconds. Four independent services had become one.

The remedy is well known and I think I explained it badly at first, because Mara asked why adding randomness would help. The pause should be a random number between zero and the current limit, not exactly the limit, so that two clients that began failing in the same second do not wake in the same second. With the pause chosen at random from the interval, the wall melts into rain, and the database sees a load it can absorb, one that rises as it recovers. We made the change in the one shared client library, since twenty private copies of a retry loop were precisely the problem.

We added two more things there, both small. A cap on how many requests one process will have in flight to the database at any moment, so a service cannot send a hundred at once even if it wants to. And a circuit breaker which, after five failures in a row, stops trying for thirty seconds and answers callers at once with an error, so the service neither queues work it cannot do nor adds to the pile.

I tested it on the staging database by pulling its network for four minutes and letting the services recover on their own. They recovered in just under three minutes, against twenty-six, and the graph was a smooth ramp. Halvard asked for it to be printed and pinned beside the fence posts from the day.

The clinic's reception software used a single SQLite file on a shared network drive, and on a Monday morning it said that the database disk image was malformed. Ilse rang Mara at 08:05 with three receptionists standing behind her and a waiting room that had begun to fill.

I want to be careful about the order in which we did things, because the urgent thing and the important thing were different. The urgent thing was to get reception working. The important thing was not to make the damaged file worse. So the first instruction I gave, through Mara, was to copy the broken file as it stood, with its companion files, to a safe place, and to stop all three reception machines from opening the program. The second was to open the copy, not the original, with the database's own recovery command, which reads whatever is readable and writes a new file.

It recovered everything except the last forty minutes of Friday afternoon, about thirty bookings. By 08:50 reception was running on the recovered file, and the receptionists re-entered Friday's missing bookings from the paper diary that Ilse, to her credit, had never let anyone throw away. The paper diary was the best backup that clinic had.

The cause took me longer. SQLite is a very reliable database in the circumstances it was built for, and one of them is that a file is opened by processes on one machine, which can coordinate through the operating system's locks. A network drive passes those locks across a wire. Some of the time, on some drives, under some load, the lock is granted to two machines at once, and then two receptionists writing in the same second write over each other's pages. The clinic had run like that for two years without a fault. On Friday at 16:20 the drive's own firmware had been updated and restarted, in the middle of the afternoon, and for a minute the machines wrote into a file none of them could properly lock.

We did not move the file to a better drive. That would have been treating the symptom. What I proposed to Ilse and Mara was to make the database one owner's property. One program, running on the one machine that is always on, opens the file and nobody else does, and the three reception programs talk to it over the local network as clients, asking it to make bookings and to say what is booked. It is a small program, four hundred lines. Wren built it in a week.

Two weeks later the drive was restarted again by a power cut, and the reception programs said, for ninety seconds, that they could not reach the booking server, and then reconnected. Nothing was lost and nothing was malformed. Ilse asked whether the paper diary could finally go. Nobody has thrown it away yet.

For one week in September we deleted feature flags, and the most useful thing I did all week was refuse to read a file.

The shop platform had accumulated sixty-three flags over four years, the way a drawer accumulates keys. Each had been added to ship something gradually, and each was meant to be removed once the thing was everywhere, and almost none had been. Mara called it flag debt and set aside a week. The plan was simple, and it was mine: for each flag, decide which branch of the code production actually runs, delete the flag and the other branch, and keep the live one. Sixty-three small deletions, each reviewed by Tobias.

The first step was to find out what production ran, and the obvious place to look is the configuration file, where each flag has a value, on or off. I began there, and by Monday lunchtime I had half drawn a table of sixty-three flags and their values. Then I stopped, because I realised I was about to make claims about the live system out of a document that describes how the live system is supposed to be set, and I had not looked at the live system.

A flag's value on this platform can come from three places: a default written into the code, the configuration file, and an environment variable set on the server, in that order of increasing power. The file shows only the middle layer. The running server can tell you what it is actually doing, and ours has an internal endpoint, meant for debugging, that prints the resolved value of every flag along with the layer that decided it. I asked Callum to call it on each production server and send me the output. It took him four minutes. I then compared its sixty-three values one by one with the table I had drawn from the file.

Sixty-two agreed. One did not. The flag was called pay_retry_v2, and it controls how the checkout retries a payment that the provider has answered with a temporary error. In the file it was off. In the code its default was off. On both production servers the resolved value was on, decided by the environment layer, and that environment variable had been set on a night in April. The audit log named Dario, and the note beside it said 'while provider flaky'.

If I had worked from the file I would have deleted the flag and kept the off branch. At the next deploy, production would have gone back to the old retry behaviour, which treated a temporary error as final, on the very path where a customer has just typed a card number. No test would have failed, since tests run on defaults. Nothing would have said anything until some Saturday when the provider next flickered, and orders began to fail that would have succeeded for five months.

I took it to Dario with the evidence. He remembered, and was quiet for a moment, and said the provider had been flaky for a week in April and he had turned it on during the worst of it and then had not put it back in the file because it had worked. For five months, the setting that kept payments alive had lived in a place no one reads. We kept the on branch, deleted the flag, deleted the variable, and wrote in the commit message why. That payment path has since been the most thoroughly tested of the sixty-three.

The rest of the week was routine. By Friday we had deleted fifty-one flags and kept twelve on purpose, each with a line in the file saying who owns it and when it should go. A flag now carries a date. The change I care most about is smaller: the endpoint that prints resolved flags is now part of the deploy checklist, and the cleanup rule says that the truth about a setting is whatever the running system says, and the file is only a claim.

The CSV library we vendored into the toolchain was 2,300 lines of C written by a stranger in 2011, and it had never given us trouble, so when a customer's file lost a value I began by assuming the fault was ours.

The customer, a laboratory, sent measurement files exported from a spreadsheet, and in one file the last row came through with its last column empty. Tobias checked the export: the value was in the file. Callum checked our mapping: correct. I truncated the file by halves until I had the smallest input that still showed the fault, and it was two lines, a header and a single row, with no newline after the final value. Add a newline and the value appeared. That was a strong hint and a narrow one. It pointed at the end of the buffer, not at the spreadsheet or our code.

Then I read the C, and I will own that it took me an hour longer than it should have, because I looked in the main loop for something clever and the mistake was dull. The tokenizer scans characters until it meets a comma or a newline, and then it emits the field. At the end of the input there is neither, so the last field is emitted by a separate piece of code that runs when the scanner reaches the end. That code tested whether any characters were left with a comparison that read: position less than end minus one. For a final field in a file without a closing newline, the last character sat exactly at the position the test excluded. One character short. The last field of every such file had been silently dropped, and in any file with a final newline the code was never reached.

I ran the library under a memory checker, mostly to be thorough, and it was clean. The mistake read nothing it should not. It read one character too few, and that is why nothing had ever complained.

We fixed our vendored copy with a one-character change and added the two-line file as a test. We did not stop there, because the library is somebody's work and others use it. I wrote an upstream report with the two-line input, the expected and actual output, the line number, and the change as a patch. Its maintainer answered in three days, a little sheepishly, thanking us and saying it was the first report of its kind in years, and released a fix the following week.

Our patch file now carries a header saying which upstream version it applies to, with a link to the report and a note to delete it on the next update. Mara says it is the first time she has seen a one-character fix arrive with a bibliography.

We rehearsed the database failover on a Thursday evening in staging, and the rehearsal found the defect that would have cost us on the real night, which is the argument for rehearsals in one sentence.

The planned maintenance was a move of the primary database to new hardware. The plan, written by Halvard and reviewed by me, was a sensible one: the new machine is already a replica, so we wait until it has caught up, promote it, point the application at it, and retire the old one. Seven steps, with a window of ten minutes of tolerated write errors.

At 21:00 Mara and Halvard ran the seven steps against staging while I watched row counts on both sides and wrote down times. The promotion went through at 21:06. The application, however, kept writing. For ninety seconds after the replica had been promoted, test orders from the staging load script were accepted and acknowledged, and I could see them landing, and when I looked at the new primary they were not there. They were on the old one. The application's connection pool held open connections to the old primary, which was still running and still willing to accept writes. For ninety seconds there had been two primaries, each with a different history, and I could not have said which was right. In production that would have been ninety seconds of customers' real orders on a database we were about to throw away.

The missing step was not at the end but before the promotion, where the plan said 'wait for the replica to catch up' and did not say what stops the old primary moving on in the meantime. It needed fencing. The first action is to make the old primary refuse writes, set read-only. Only then do we wait for the replica's position to equal the old primary's final position, promote, move the pointer, and restart the application's pools so that no old connection survives.

I rewrote the plan with eight steps and a verification after each. The check after the read-only step is that a test write is refused. The check after the promotion is that the replica's last position equals the old primary's final one, as printed, not as assumed. The check after the pool restart is that every application connection reports the new primary's address. We rehearsed again the following Tuesday. No orders in the wrong place. Eleven seconds of refused writes.

The real maintenance was on a Sunday at 06:00 and took nine minutes, with the same eleven-second blip. Halvard took the old machine out of the rack that afternoon and wrote the date on its lid in marker.

Dario's customer wanted proof that the firmware they were running had been built from the source they had been shown, and the only honest proof is to build it again and get the same file, bit for bit. We tried on two machines, one of them Callum's. The files had the same size and different hashes.

There is a tool that compares two builds and says where they differ, and I ran it on the two outputs. The differences were not random. They fell into three groups, and I took them in order of how much each annoyed me.

The first: both binaries contained the path of the directory they were built in. Callum's machine had built in /home/callum/work/fw, the other in /srv/build/fw, and the compiler had stamped the path into the debugging information and into the text of an assertion message. Nothing wrong with that, except that no one could ever reproduce another person's build without standing in the same directory. We solved it by building inside a container with a fixed path, and telling the compiler to map the path to a constant.

The second: the output was packed into a firmware archive, and the archive recorded each file's modification time. The files had been written at different moments on the two machines, so the header bytes of the archive differed. The accepted remedy is to tell the packer that every file's time is a fixed date, taken from the date of the last commit and not from the clock. A rebuild of the same commit therefore produces the same dates in any year.

The third was the one that taught me something. With two groups fixed, the hashes still differed, and the tool showed that the archive contained exactly the same files in a different order. The packer took the files in the order the filesystem listed them, and filesystems promise no order. Callum's listed them by creation. The build server listed them by name, usually. A machine under load once listed them differently again. We sorted the list before packing.

There was also a smaller fourth, which I found when the three were gone and one machine of three still disagreed: the version string embedded the name of the host that built it. We removed the host name. Someone had put it there because they wanted to know where a build came from, which is a fair wish, and it is now served by a line in the build log that sits outside the binary.

After that the hashes matched on three machines, a laptop, the build server and a spare desktop, on five commits in a row. Dario sent the customer's auditor the recipe, a six-line script and the container's identifier, and the auditor ran it on her own machine and wrote back one line to say the hash had matched.

What I liked about the work was how little of it was clever. Each difference was a place where the build had let its surroundings into the product: somebody's directory, somebody's clock, somebody's filesystem, somebody's hostname. The product had been carrying small pieces of its builders about, and the test of reproducibility is whether it can be made to stop.

The Spanish checkout page had been showing strings like checkout.promo.label for nine days when a customer sent a screenshot with the message 'is this meant to look like this?' That was how I learned that forty-one of our Spanish strings had vanished, and the order in which I learned the rest is worth recording, because the cause was not where either of us looked first.

Wren looked at the loader, since it was the thing that read the file. I looked at the translations, since they were the thing it read. The file was valid JSON; it opened in every tool. The keys were there for the other sections of the Spanish file, the basket, the account page, the footer. The missing section was checkout, and when I opened the raw file I found the word checkout as the name of a section twice, forty lines apart, at the same level. The first held forty-one strings and the second held nine.

JSON does not forbid repeating a name in an object. The standard says only that names should be unique, and parsers deal with a repeat as they please, and ours kept the last one. So nine strings were visible, and the forty-one above them had been quietly overwritten at the moment of reading.

How it got there is a small story about merging. Two translators, Noor and an outside freelancer, had each added strings to the checkout section of the Spanish file in separate branches during the same week, Noor near the top and the freelancer near the bottom. Git joined the branches without complaint, since they had touched different lines, and the freelancer's tool had, for reasons of its own, written its whole section out as a new block with the name repeated. The text was syntactically perfect and said two things at once.

The repair was easy: join the two blocks by hand, fifty strings, and Noor checked each against the English. The prevention took more thought. I wrote two tests. The first loads every language file with a parser told to refuse a repeated name, and on the day I wrote it, it caught a second duplicate in the Portuguese file that had been harmless because the two copies were identical. The second checks that every key in the English file exists in every other language, and every key in every other language exists in English, so a missing string is a failing test and not a screenshot from a customer.

Noor said that for nine days the company had been telling its Spanish customers to enter checkout.promo.label, and that she wanted it on a t-shirt. I told her I would not make the shirt, but that I would make sure the sentence could never appear again.

The churn model scored 0.99 and I did not believe it. Noor was delighted. She had spent six weeks on the features, and the area under the curve on the held-out customers was higher than any I have seen for any question about human behaviour. I said the number was too good to be a finding and would turn out to be a finding about the data, and I asked for a day to learn which.

When a prediction is that good, it is usually because the answer is already inside the question. I asked for the model's most important features and looked at each. The first was ordinary, the number of support tickets in the last quarter. The second was a column Noor had built called days_since_last_activity. The third was named plan_status.

I asked how days_since_last_activity was calculated. Noor said: today minus the date of the last activity. Today meant the day the feature table was built, which was in July. The customers in the training set who had churned, though, had churned months earlier, in the spring, and for them 'days since last activity' was measured up to July, a quantity that grows from the moment they leave and is large for exactly the people who left. The model had learned that customers not seen for 120 days are customers who have gone. True, and of no use whatever. Plan_status was the same, read in July: cancelled or active. The model had been shown the outcome in the form of its own shadow.

The honest version of the question is: knowing only what was known at a certain date, can you predict who leaves in the next ninety days? That requires every feature to be calculated as of a date, the same date as the start of the label's window, and nothing after it. We rebuilt the feature table with a cut-off date for each training example, which took Noor and me three days, and a good deal of care with the plan table, whose history was overwritten and not kept, so we reconstructed it from the billing events.

The new model scored 0.74. Noor was disappointed for about an hour and I did not try to talk her out of it. Then I showed her what 0.74 meant in practice. The top tenth of customers by predicted risk contained 31 percent of the customers who actually left in the following ninety days, three times what picking at random would give. For the retention team, who can ring perhaps eighty people a month, that is a useful list. What 0.99 would have given them was a list of people who had already gone.

She took the 0.74 to the retention team, and the team rang the top eighty. A few weeks later she told me they had kept eleven. We do not know how many of the eleven would have stayed anyway, and she was careful to say so. I put the cut-off rule on the first line of the project's notes, because the next person to build a feature will be tempted by 'today'.

Deleting a demo customer took forty minutes, and while it ran nothing else could touch the table. Yusra started the deletion on a Tuesday at 11:00 before a sales call, because the demo account's data was cluttering her presentation, and by 11:20 two colleagues had messaged to say their pages hung.

I looked at what the database was doing. The delete had been issued for one row in the customers table, and the schema, sensibly, had foreign keys that cascade: deleting a customer deletes its orders, its users, its files, its events and so on, nine tables in all. That is the right design for removing someone completely. The cost is that for each child table the database must find the rows that belong to the deleted customer, and to find them quickly it needs an index on the customer column of that table.

Eight of the nine tables had one. The ninth was the audit-events table, which had 38 million rows and no index on customer. For the cascade the database read the whole table from top to bottom, and while it read, it held a lock that made the customers table wait. Forty minutes was how long it took to read 38 million rows. The demo account had 212 of them.

Yusra asked the right question, which was whether she could stop it. She could, and I told her what would happen: the whole delete would be undone, a rollback taking about as long again, and the account would remain. She chose to wait. At 11:41 it finished.

The repair was an index on the customer column of the audit-events table, created in the background mode that does not block writers. It took twenty-six minutes on 38 million rows, and Mara watched it with the vexed look of someone watching a progress bar. Afterwards I ran the same deletion on a copy for a second demo account. Four-tenths of a second.

I looked for others like it. A short query lists every foreign key in the schema whose referencing column has no index at its front, and it returned three tables, all small. I indexed them anyway, since a foreign key without an index is a habit worth not having, and I put the query in a test, so that a new table with a foreign key and no index fails on the day it is written.

Yusra's call began at 12:00, ten minutes late, with the demo account gone and an apology for the delay that did not mention what had caused it.

For seven weeks the team's data flows were drawn, not written, and I want to say fairly what was good about it before I say why it ended.

Marguerite's group had adopted a visual tool for moving data between systems, where you drag boxes onto a canvas, draw lines between them, and each box is a step: read this table, filter these rows, join with that, write to there. The pitch was that analysts who did not write code could change a flow. In the first fortnight that was true, and rather lovely: Bettina, who does the purchasing, added a step to a flow herself on a Thursday afternoon and the data was right on Friday. Fourteen flows were built that way.

What went wrong was ordinary, and it was all about change. The tool saved a flow as one large XML file, 9 MB for the biggest, with the positions of boxes on the canvas mixed in among the logic. When Bettina's change and another by a colleague were made to the same flow in the same week, the second save replaced the first. Nobody had done anything wrong, and a week of Bettina's logic vanished. There was no way to see what had changed between yesterday's flow and today's. The tool kept a history, but it showed that a file had changed, and the file was a block of generated text. A review, which Mara considers the minimum for anything that touches money figures, was impossible: Tobias opened a diff of 4,000 lines in which the logic of the change was perhaps fourteen.

What finished it was a Wednesday in week seven, when a flow that joined orders to payments began to produce duplicates and I could not tell why. I could not read the join. I could see a box with the word Join and a dialog with settings, and the setting that would have said whether duplicates were possible was three dialogs deep. Marguerite and I spent two hours opening boxes. The fault was a join on a column that was not unique. In code it would have been one line, and one I would have seen in the first minute.

We moved to plain scripts: six hundred lines in all for the fourteen flows, each a short program with a name, in version control, reviewed like anything else. Bettina still changes things, but she now does it by asking for the change in plain words in a ticket, and the change arrives as a diff of five lines that she can read herself.

I do not think the tool was bad. It was good at making the first version and poor at the thousandth change, and our flows were going to see a thousand changes. We kept one thing from it: the diagram. A small script now draws a picture of each flow from the code, so the people who liked boxes still have them.

Marguerite said afterwards that the tool had taught the group what their data flows actually were, and that was worth the seven weeks. I think she is right, and I would still not run the experiment again.

One file would not upload, and it was always the same file. A swimming coach had recorded forty-eight megabytes of a relay start on her phone, tried four times over an evening to attach it to the club's training notes, and each time the progress bar reached the end and the app said the upload was incomplete. Other clips went through. Wren, who built the uploader, assumed her connection and asked her to try on the pool wifi, and it failed there too.

A failure that repeats exactly for one input is a gift, because it means the input is the cause. I asked her for the file's exact size in bytes. It was 50,331,648. That is exactly twelve times four mebibytes, and four mebibytes is the size of the pieces the app sends. Twelve full chunks and nothing left over.

The protocol was simple. The phone cuts the file into 4 MiB pieces, sends each, and finishes with a call that says complete. The loop that cut the pieces was written to continue while there was data and then send the remainder, and the remainder, for a file that divides exactly, was zero bytes. The phone sent a thirteenth chunk with nothing in it. The server refuses empty requests as a general rule, because empty requests are almost always mistakes, so it answered 400, and the app, after retrying, gave up.

To prove it I made files of 4 MiB, 8 MiB and 40 MiB, with the same sizes less one byte and plus one byte, and ran all nine through the uploader against a test server. The three exact ones failed. The other six passed. Nobody had thought about the sizes of a coach's phone video, but it is a classic place for a fault: a loop that handles 'the rest' and has never met a file with no rest.

Wren fixed the client to send only chunks that have contents. I did not trust a fix on one side alone, so the server's completion step now checks that the number of bytes received equals the size declared at the start of the upload, and no longer depends on seeing a last piece of any particular shape. The nine-file test is now in the suite, with its sizes written as multiples of the chunk size and a comment saying why.

The coach's clip went up the next morning. She wrote that she had begun to believe the relay start was cursed. It was the arithmetic.

At 07:40 on a Tuesday every build in the company failed within seconds with the same message, and the message said that one package could not be found. The package was called trimline. It was 23 lines long, it removed spaces from the ends of strings, and its author had withdrawn it from the public registry overnight after an argument with the registry's operators that none of us followed.

We had lockfiles, and I had thought of them as a protection. They are one, against a surprise upgrade. They are none against a disappearance, because each build ran in a clean container that fetched everything fresh, and a pinned version that no longer exists is a pin in nothing. Fourteen of our projects failed. None of us had ever chosen trimline. I traced it through the lockfile: it was a dependency of a dependency of a dependency of our test tooling, four levels down, and none of the four had been written by anyone we knew.

Mara had the builds working again by 08:30. Callum's laptop still held the package in its local cache from a week before, and she copied it to a shared folder and told the build containers to look there first. It was an hour of improvisation and I was not comfortable with it. She was not either, but there was a release that day.

The afterwards is what I want to record. I counted: our 41 direct dependencies brought in 1,214 packages in all. We had chosen forty-one, and we trusted 1,214 strangers' decisions to remain true every day, and the most trivial of them had stopped a company. Mara sat back from her screen when I said the number.

We did not try to reduce the 1,214. We set up our own mirror, a caching proxy that sits between our builds and the public registry and keeps a copy of every version of every package that any of our builds has ever fetched. Builds read only from the mirror. If the registry loses a package, or a maintainer removes one, or the registry itself cannot be reached, nothing of ours notices. The setup was a day's work for Halvard and a little disk.

The public registry restored trimline two days later, under a policy it had apparently not wanted to need. The mirror has not been used for what it was built for since. It has been used for something else: in June the registry was unreachable for forty minutes, and our builds went through without noticing, which Callum found out only when he read about it the next morning.

On the twenty-ninth of February the warranty page of the appliance shop returned an error to everyone who tried to register a product bought that day. There were twenty-three of them, and it was Odile, who runs the shop, who noticed, because three of the twenty-three rang her.

Once I had the error message the cause took a minute: 'day is out of range for month'. The code worked out the end of a one-year warranty by taking the purchase date and building a new date with the same month and day in the following year. For a purchase on the twenty-ninth of February, the following year has no twenty-ninth of February. Everyone else's warranty had always worked, because every other day exists every year, and the code had run for three years without meeting its own corner.

The repair is easy, and the question it raises is not one for an engineer. What is the end of a one-year warranty that begins on 29 February? The twenty-eighth of February of the next year, or the first of March? Either is defensible, they differ by a day, and a day is what a warranty dispute is made of. I did not choose. I wrote both down with the customer-facing wording each would imply and asked Odile, since the shop's terms are hers. She asked her own adviser and came back an hour later with 'the first of March, and write it in the terms'. We made the code produce that, with a test for purchases on every day of a leap year and the day after.

Looking at the same function, I found its quieter cousin. The report of warranties expiring this month added 365 days to the purchase date, which is one year only when the year has no leap day in it. For anything bought between March and December of the year before a leap year, the report put the expiry a day early. Nobody had complained, because nobody rings a shop to say their warranty lasts a day longer than they thought. It was still wrong, and it was the same fault: the belief that a year is a number of days. Both places now ask the calendar for a year and not for a count.

The twenty-three customers were registered by hand that afternoon, with an apology. Three of them were delighted to hear from the owner herself, and one of them had bought a kettle.

After the power cut on Saturday morning, three of the eleven touchscreens in the museum's galleries showed a black screen with white text asking the visitor to press Y to repair the filesystem. There are no keyboards on them. Teo, who looks after the kiosks, heard from a volunteer at 10:20 and drove over, and I got the story at lunch with a photograph of one of the screens attached.

The kiosks are small computers with a flash card for a disk, running a program that tells the story of a local object. They are powered by whatever is on the gallery's circuit, and the building loses power about four times a year. Each time, a machine in the middle of writing to its card can wake up with the card in an inconsistent state, and the system's honest response is to ask a person, and nobody is there to answer. Eight of the eleven had been lucky. The three that were not had been caught writing.

I asked what they were writing. The answer should have been nothing, since a display that shows a story has no need to save anything, and it turned out to be three small things: the system log, a visitor counter that the program updated whenever somebody pressed Start, and a cache of images the program kept in a temporary directory. None of it mattered, and all of it gave a power cut something to interrupt.

The principle for this sort of machine is to make the disk read-only, because nothing can be damaged if nothing is ever written. We set the root filesystem to read-only and gave the system a small memory-based layer for anything that wants to write, which disappears at reboot and is no loss. The visitor counter, which the museum does want, goes to a separate small partition, written once a minute, with a check at mount that formats it if it fails. That is the one place a power cut can now hurt, and what it can hurt is a count of how many people pressed Start.

Teo tested it by walking down the row of kiosks pulling plugs, forty times in all, at no pattern, including during the minute in which the counter writes. Every machine came back to its story in 38 seconds. He said it made him feel brutal and then pleased.

The counter lost a minute's worth of presses twice. We wrote the museum's volunteer coordinator a sentence about it for her report, and she said that with eight thousand presses a month she could live with two minutes.

The split should have been even. The new signup page, version B, was shown to half the visitors and version A to the rest, and after nine days the counts were 52,104 for A and 47,896 for B. A difference of four thousand is far more than coin tosses produce at that size, and the conversion rate said B had won by six percent, which was the answer Sunniva had hoped for, and which was why I put off sending her the numbers.

An uneven split is not a result. It is a symptom: something in the system treats the two groups differently before the visitors have decided anything. I looked for what was different about B. Its page lived at another address, and visitors assigned to B were sent there by a redirect from the original page. They were counted when they reached the B page, not when they were assigned. Anyone assigned to B who left before the second page loaded was never counted. A visitor on a slow mobile connection, or one who closed the tab at the sight of a blank screen, was lost from B and kept in A. The lost people were the impatient and the poorly connected, who are exactly the people least likely to sign up. B was not better. B was a page whose worst visitors had been taken away.

I tested the story against the data. I split the traffic by connection type, and the gap in counts came almost entirely from visitors on mobile networks, nine percent short in B, whereas on wired connections the split was even to within a few visitors. That was enough for me to say with confidence what had happened, though it could not tell me what the true effect of B was.

I explained it to Sunniva by telling her she had been shown a race in which the slowest runners of one team had been taken off the track before the start. She was quiet for a while, and then said that she would sooner know. We reran the test with the assignment made on the server, before any redirect, and the visitor counted at that moment whatever happened afterwards, and with a standing check that the split is even, which stops the test and says so if it is not.

The second run, eleven days, ended with 50,010 and 49,990. B's conversion was 0.4 percent above A's, well within what chance produces. We kept A, and Sunniva kept the first set of numbers on her desk, at her request, as a souvenir of how good a win can look.

From the middle of March, patients of Ilse's clinic began telling her that the password reset email never came. It came, as it turned out, but into the junk folder of one particular webmail provider that about forty percent of her patients use, not into the inbox, and the people who wrote to say so were only those who had thought to look.

The change that preceded it was ours. In the first week of March we had moved the sending of the portal's emails to a new mail provider, cheaper and with better reports, and Wren had updated the domain's records as the provider's instructions said. Everything worked in testing, because we tested with our own addresses, which are all at the company's domain, and which trust it.

I could not see what the webmail provider thought, but I could ask. There are services that give you test inboxes at several providers and report where a message landed and what the provider's checks said, and I sent one email to twenty such inboxes. Seventeen delivered it to the inbox. Three put it in junk, all at the provider in question, and the report from that one carried two lines of its own that I read with interest. The first said that the sender policy check had a permanent error. The second said that the signature was valid but belonged to a different domain than the one in the From line.

The sender policy first. A record in the domain's settings lists the servers allowed to send for it, and a check is limited to ten lookups of other records. Ours, after years of adding services, was made of includes, and the new provider's include pulled in four more of its own. Counted down the tree it came to thirteen. A receiver that counts past ten stops and gives an error, which it treats as a fail. Some providers are lenient about that, and one was not.

The second line. The new provider's default was to sign our mail with its own domain, so the signature said 'I am the provider' while the From line said 'the clinic'. Valid but not aligned, which the receiver reads as a stranger speaking for the clinic.

We made two changes. We gave the provider a dedicated sub-domain for our mail, with its signing key published under our name, so that the signature and the From line agree. And we removed from the main domain's policy the three services we no longer used, which brought the count down to seven. I sent the test again to the twenty inboxes: twenty in twenty.

Ilse wrote to the patients who had complained. Nine found the earlier emails in junk. Two were relieved to be told it was not their fault. One wrote that she had thought she was being quietly removed from the clinic's lists, and I think that sentence was the true cost of the bug.

Nothing was wrong with our servers, and that was what made the afternoon hard. Processor load was low, memory was fine, the database was idle, and the whole shop had stopped answering. At 15:12 on a Wednesday pages simply hung until the browser gave up, including pages that touched nothing but the product catalogue.

The first thing I looked at was threads. The shop's web servers handle each request on one of two hundred worker threads, and when I asked for a snapshot of what every thread was doing, a hundred and ninety-eight of them were doing the same thing: waiting for a reply from the address-lookup service, the third-party one that fills in a street when a customer types a postcode at checkout. I looked at the two that were not. One was serving my request for the snapshot.

The lookup service was slow, and I confirmed it from outside: replies in thirty or forty seconds instead of two hundred milliseconds. That was their trouble. Ours was that the code which called them had no timeout at all. A customer typing a postcode would hold a worker thread until the answer came, however long, and the threads, which are finite, filled with waiting customers within four minutes. The catalogue pages hung because there were no threads left to serve them. A fault in one small feature had taken down the rest of the shop, which had nothing to do with it.

There was a fix on three levels, and I tried to keep them in the order of how much each would have mattered. First, the obvious: a timeout, one second to connect and three for the whole reply, after which the lookup fails and the form falls back to asking the customer to type the address. Second, a limit on the damage: calls to the lookup service now run on their own small group of twenty threads, so that in the worst case twenty customers are waiting and a hundred and eighty threads are free. Third, tell somebody: the number of lookups that time out is a metric with an alert, so that the next time the service goes slow we hear it from our own graph before anyone's page hangs.

Then I went through the codebase for other outbound calls without a timeout, which I should have done the moment I saw the first. There were eleven. Tobias fixed all eleven on the Thursday, and found that one of them, the tax lookup, did have a timeout already, of ten minutes, set by someone who had meant ten seconds.

The lookup service recovered at 16:05. The shop was working again at 15:31, from the moment Tobias switched the lookup off by hand. For nineteen minutes the whole shop had been waiting for one input field.

Callum's branch was six weeks old and touched 212 files, and he had the look of a man carrying a full cup across a room. It was the multi-currency change. Until then the shop priced everything in one currency, and the branch taught every price, total and report to carry a currency with it. Three people had told him it would be impossible to merge, and he had begun to believe them.

Mara's view, which I share, is that a change nobody can review is not a change, it is a rumour. She asked whether it could be cut up. Callum said that it was one idea and could not be cut. I did not think so, and I asked for a day with his diff.

I read all 212 files and sorted the changes into piles by what they did, not by where they were. There were four piles. Some changes only introduced something new that nothing yet used: a Money type that holds an amount and a currency, with rounding rules for each currency, and its tests. Some moved existing code onto the new type without altering what it did, because the shop had one currency and the answer was the same. Some added currency columns to the database, with a default that made every existing row what it already was. And a few actually did the new thing: let a price be in a second currency, display it, convert it.

The point of sorting was that only the last pile changes behaviour. The first three can be merged into the live system while the shop is still single-currency, and do nothing, which means they can be merged on any Tuesday. I proposed fourteen slices in the order of their dependencies, and Callum and I cut the branch along the lines. Each slice was small enough to read in half an hour and had one rule: it must not change what a customer sees. Mara added a second: nothing lives on a branch longer than three days.

The first slice, the Money type, merged on a Thursday with 31 lines of change outside its own file. The second moved the basket total onto it. Every slice went through the existing tests, and for several I ran a before-and-after comparison on a week of real orders and expected no difference. Slice nine produced one. Sorting products by price in the admin list sorted by the number of minor units, so that once there were two currencies the list would have placed a price of 900 yen beside 900 cents. It was no trouble for a single-currency shop, it passed everything, and I saw it only because I had asked what in the code compares two amounts. We fixed it with a comparison that refuses to compare different currencies without a conversion, a typed error and not a quiet answer.

Tobias reviewed all fourteen, and said afterwards that it was the first change in the codebase of which he had read every line. The reviews took between ten and forty minutes. I kept a plain list of the slices in the branch's description, with what each does, what it must not change and what was checked, and ticked them off as they merged. It was the only paperwork I allowed, because that list was what stopped the unmerged remainder of the work from being forgotten.

By the sixth slice Callum's anxiety had gone quiet, and I noticed that he was eating lunch. By the eleventh he was the one proposing the cuts. The last of the slices that change behaviour, the one people had said could never be merged, was forty-two lines.

Six weeks of branch became fourteen merges in nine working days. In the shop's first week with two currencies there was one bug, a rounding in the price display for a currency without minor units. A customer found it on the sixth day and it was fixed in twenty minutes, because it lived in a slice small enough to find. Callum asked whether he could write up the method. I said it was his, and that I would be glad to be named in a footnote.

When we changed the logs to structured form, each line a JSON object with fields instead of a sentence, Halvard said he would never forgive us, and for a month he did not.

The reasons for the change were good ones. A sentence like 'order 4417 failed for customer 90 after 2.3 s' is easy to read and almost impossible to ask questions of. To learn how many orders failed per plan over a week I had to write a pattern that took the sentence apart, and every time someone reworded a message the pattern broke without saying so. With fields the same question was a line in the log tool: group failed orders by plan. In the first two weeks we answered three questions nobody had been able to ask, one of which showed that failures were four times commoner on the smallest plan, because of a limit that no one had known applied there.

The cost was Halvard. He works in a terminal at 03:00 with the tools of thirty years, and a line of 400 characters of braces and quotes is as hostile to him as a closed door. He said it was like being asked to read a telephone directory aloud in a thunderstorm. He was not wrong, and I did not argue with him about the form of the logs. I argued about whether a person should have to read them raw.

The remedy was a small program, thirty lines, which Wren and I wrote in an afternoon and Halvard rewrote in the evening because he disliked how it coloured things. It reads the JSON lines and prints each as one short line: the time, the level in colour, the message, and the other fields in dim grey after it. You pipe the log through it and see what you used to see, in the same order, and when you need a field you can still search for it. A flag turns it off, for when he wants the raw lines for another program.

A few weeks later he was called out on a Saturday, and I found him on the sofa in the office kitchen grepping the raw logs, which I had not expected. He said it was faster for what he wanted. We did not discuss it. The structured form was the same file both ways, which was the point, and he was free to use the data in whichever shape suited the hour.

The one thing I insisted on was that the message itself stays readable: a real sentence with the important values in it, in addition to the fields. A log that is only fields is a database, and the person at 03:00 needs a line that says what happened.

The workbook was called month_end_FINAL_v7.xlsm, and Bettina inherited it with her job. Gunnar, who had built it over eleven years and then retired to a smallholding, had left two pages of instructions and a note that said, in full, 'it just works'. It did work. Every month Bettina pressed one button and eleven minutes later the month-end figures appeared in the right places, and in nine months nobody had had a reason to open the box.

She opened it because the auditor asked how it worked, and Bettina, who is honest, said she did not know and would find out. She asked Mara, Mara asked me, and the arrangement was that I would read and explain it, and that nothing in it would change without Bettina's say.

It had thirty-one sheets, one of them hidden and named z, and 2,100 lines of macro. I read the macros first, then the sheets, and the hidden sheet last, since it seemed to be the heart of it. It held 4,000 rows mapping account codes to the categories on the report. The macro did the mapping with a lookup that takes a code and finds it in the list. There are two ways to do such a lookup: exact, which finds the code or says it is not there, and approximate, which assumes the list is sorted and finds the nearest code below. The macro used the approximate kind. On a sorted list it behaves exactly like the exact one, which is why Gunnar would never have noticed.

The list was not quite sorted. Somewhere around row 2,300 a code, 6190, had been added at the bottom in a hurry. With an approximate lookup, a search for 6190 could land anywhere near it, and I wrote a small check that did the same lookup both ways for every code that had appeared in the last year. Four codes disagreed. For one of them, 6190, the macro had been putting the amounts into the catering category, where they did not belong, for fourteen months. The total was 2,310, in a company whose month-end is read to the unit: not trivial, and not alarming.

I told Bettina, with the evidence beside it, before I told anyone else. She was not upset. She said it was exactly why she had asked. We did not replace her workbook, because it was her tool, and she knows every corner of how it behaves and would have been lost in a different one. We made three changes. The lookup became exact, so a code not in the list says so in a message instead of being filed nearby. The hidden sheet became a visible one called Mapping, sorted, with a note at the top. And Bettina wrote one page, in her own words, on how the month-end works, to live next to the file.

The auditor was given the page and the four codes. She said she had rarely been so well answered on a Tuesday, and asked for the same for the supplier ledger.

The customer's machine had thirty-two cores, our laptops had four, and the bug lived in the difference. The dairy cooperative's quality system counted the samples processed in each batch, and now and then the final count came out a few short: 4,998 of 5,000, once 4,991. Dario's team could never make it happen at a desk. On the customer's server it happened about one batch in six.

An intermittent count that is a little short, and more often short when there are more processors, is almost always two threads updating the same number at once. I did not need to see the code to say so; I needed to find where. We have a tool that watches a running program and reports any memory touched by two threads without proper protection. It slows the program badly, so I asked Dario to run it on a rented thirty-two-core machine for an hour, with a generated batch of samples, instead of on the customer's server. It named the line in two seconds.

A statistics object kept a running total, and each worker thread added to it with a plain increment, which is three steps: read the number, add one, write it back. If two threads read the same number before either wrote, one of the additions was lost. With four cores that needed bad luck. With thirty-two it happened in one batch of six.

The tool found a second thing, which would have bitten later. The same statistics object kept a table of counts by sample type, and the table could be read by the reporting thread while workers were adding new types. Reading a table while it is being rearranged is not a lost count, it is a crash, and it had not crashed yet only for want of enough luck.

The fix for the first was an atomic increment, one indivisible step. For the second, the table is guarded by a lock held only for the instant of the update. Neither is clever. What I had to decide was whether to keep the watching tool, and the answer was yes, as a nightly job: it now runs the whole test suite under the watcher on a machine with sixteen cores, along with a stress test that starts sixty-four workers and counts. It has caught two more since, both in code from before I knew the system.

The customer's next batch of 5,000 came to 5,000. Dario sent me the line from their report with no comment except the number.

For three days we made the service faster, and it did not get faster, and the reason was that we were measuring the wrong end of the wire.

Teo had run a load test that showed the booking service topping out at 1,900 requests a second. That was well under what the clinic group's growth needed, and Tobias spent two days profiling the service. He found two real wastes, a JSON conversion done twice and a database call inside a loop, and fixed them. The next test showed 1,950. He fixed another thing, and the number was 1,940. Whatever had been the bottleneck had stopped being one, and the number would not move.

On the third morning I asked a question I should have asked on the first, and I am not proud of the delay: how busy is the machine that sends the load? Teo looked. The load generator was a single script on a single core, and it was at 100 percent. It could create and measure about 1,900 requests a second, and the service had simply been answering as fast as it was asked. We had been tuning the service to meet a ceiling that belonged to the instrument.

Teo ran four copies of the generator on four machines. The service handled 7,800 a second, and now the number moved when we changed things: Tobias's two fixes had been worth about eleven percent. And at 8,200 the service stopped scaling for a different reason, its database connections, which was a real finding and one that the first three days had hidden.

I kept two things. The first is a rule for load tests: before believing a ceiling, look at the processor of whatever produces the load, and the network between, as carefully as at the thing being loaded. If the tool is saturated, the number is a fact about the tool. The second is a line Teo added to the test's report after the throughput: generator CPU, as a percentage. When it is over 70 the report says the result is invalid, which is better than a number that looks like a fact.

Tobias took the three days well, and then said, rather quietly, that his two fixes were still worth having. He is right. The eleven percent is real. It was just not the thing we had been looking at.

The shop's passwords were stored with a hashing method that had been fine in 2014 and was now fast in exactly the wrong way: a modern graphics card can try billions of guesses a second against it. Dario's security review put the finding at the top of the page, and Mara asked me how to move 38,000 accounts to a better method without making 38,000 people reset their passwords.

The trick is that you cannot convert a hash. You can only learn the password at the moment someone types it. So the migration is a patient one. Every stored hash now carries a label for the method that made it. At login the system checks the password against whatever method the label names, and if it is correct and the label is the old one, it quietly makes a new hash with the better method from the password it has just been given, and stores that instead. The person notices nothing. The accounts of people who log in migrate on their own, and in the first month 61 percent of them did.

The part that needed thought was the remaining 39 percent, the people who had not come back. Their hashes stay weak for as long as they stay away, and they are the ones most exposed to an attack from an old copy of the database. I proposed a second step that Mara did not like at first. We wrap the old hash in the new method: take the old stored value, run it through the better hash too, and store that, labelled 'old inside new'. This needs no password. It makes every account as slow to attack as the new method makes it, at once, with the old check tucked inside. At the next login the password is checked by running the old method and then the new on top, and the stored value is replaced by a clean new hash.

The test that mattered was one I wrote after Callum asked a nasty question: what happens if the migration is interrupted halfway through writing an account? We tested it by killing the process at every step and logging in afterwards. In one case, between writing the new hash and removing the old, a user could have two valid hashes. We made the write a single step.

By the end of the quarter 94 percent of accounts had been migrated by login and the rest by the wrapping. Dario's finding went from the top of his page to a line at the bottom that says closed, with the date.

Four thousand and ninety-one files in the shared drive had the words 'conflicted copy' in their names, and Noor was the one who finally said something, with the air of a person admitting to a secret.

The drive synchronised folders between everyone's laptops, and when two people changed the same file while one of them was offline, the service kept both and renamed one, politely. Over three years of that, for a team of eleven, the folders had filled with offspring: 'Q3 forecast (Teo's conflicted copy 2023-09-14).xlsx', and so on. Most were harmless debris. Some held the only copy of somebody's afternoon of work, and nobody could tell which.

Mara's first idea was to delete everything with the phrase in its name and see who complained. I asked for a day first, and told her what I wanted to know: for each conflicted copy, is it different from the original in any way that matters?

I wrote a script to find out. For every conflicted copy it found the file it came from and compared the two: contents for text and spreadsheets, size and checksum for anything else. It sorted the 4,091 into four piles. Identical to the original: 2,466. An older version of the original, all of whose content had been carried forward: 1,031. Different, with content the original lacked: 347. And files with no original left, the originals having been deleted: 247.

The first two piles, 3,497 files, I could prove redundant, and with Mara's agreement I moved them into a folder rather than deleting them, to be removed after sixty days. For the last two I made lists, a sheet per person with the file, what differed and the date, and sent each of the eleven theirs. People went through them over a fortnight. Of the 347, about forty held work that had never made it back, and one, in Teo's folder, was a firmware table he had spent a weekend on and believed lost.

We changed the way the drive is used as well, since cleaning is not curing. Most of the conflicts came from a handful of big shared spreadsheets that several people kept open all day. Those moved to a tool built for editing the same document at the same time, and the drive's folder for them now holds a link and nothing else. In the two months since, the count of new conflicted copies is nine.

The sixty days ended in June, and the folder of the provably redundant went into the bin. Teo's table, I am told, is backed up in four places.

The balances in the loyalty app were wrong for about one customer in two hundred, and always wrong in the same direction: too high. Sunniva noticed because a regular reported that she had 1,400 points when she should have had 900, and the shop, being fair, wanted to understand before it did anything about it.

Points are awarded and spent by events. A purchase sends 'earned 100', a redemption sends 'spent 500', and a service reads them off a queue and applies them to the balance. A customer's balance is the result of applying them in order. I looked at her events and they were all there: earned 500, earned 400, spent 500, earned 100, and so on, summing to 900. The balance said 1,400, as if the 'spent 500' had never been applied.

The service was written to validate a spend: a redemption is refused if the balance is too low. In her case the 'spent 500' event had reached a worker before the 'earned 400' that came ahead of it. The queue was split into several lanes for speed, and events from one customer could go down different lanes and be handled by different workers at different speeds. The spend arrived while the balance was 100, so it was refused as insufficient and dropped, and the earning arrived a moment later. The customer had spent the points in the shop. The service had said no after the fact. The till showed the discount given, the balance ignored it, and the difference of 500 stayed in the account.

There were two cures, and I wrote both down. One: make all events of a single customer go down the same lane, so that they are applied in the order they were produced. It is cheap and standard, and I would do it whatever else we decided. Two: stop the consumer from refusing a spend. The decision to allow a redemption was made at the till, with the customer standing there. The event is a record of something that has already happened, and the right answer to it is to apply it, and if the balance goes negative for a moment, let it be negative until the earning arrives.

Mara and Tobias argued for the first alone, on the grounds that ordering is the ordinary solution. I argued for both, because ordering within a lane holds only while the lanes are set up the way we expect. The day somebody changes the number of lanes, or replays old events into a new queue, the first fix will quietly stop holding and the second will not. We did both.

For the customers who were already wrong, I recomputed every balance from the full history of events under the new rule and listed the differences: 187 accounts, all too high by an amount the till had already given away. We took no points back. That was Sunniva's decision, and I think a kind one. The shop wrote off 71,000 points and sent no apologies, since no customer had noticed anything but a pleasant surprise.

For a month the uptime monitor woke somebody roughly twice a week to say the booking site was down, and each time, by the time the person had found a laptop, it was up again. Callum was on call in the second week of March and said he had begun to resent the sound of his own phone.

The monitor was a service outside our network that requested the site's front page once a minute from a single location and raised an alert after two failures in a row. I pulled the history of its alerts and our own server logs for the same minutes. In ten of eleven alerts the server had no record of the failed requests at all. They had never arrived. Our systems were fine, and the only thing that had been down was the road between the monitor and us.

So the monitor was measuring one road and calling it the site. The cure is a fact people tend to know and not to apply: never treat a single observer as the truth. We changed the monitor to check from four locations, on different networks and in different countries, and to alert only when at least three of the four fail at once, twice in a row. A single bad route can no longer wake anyone.

Mara asked whether we were making the system less sensitive. We were, to one kind of event, and I wanted to say so. Before, a failure of the monitor's own route looked like our outage. Now, if the site is reachable from only two of the four places, no alert fires. I thought that gap worth closing with a second, quieter kind of alert, so that two of four failing sends a message to a channel and not a phone call, to be looked at in the morning.

The last piece I had not expected. In the twelfth alert, the one that matched real failures, the monitor had seen the failure, so had the load balancer's logs, and the first customer complaint arrived four minutes later. For all the other alerts the customers had said nothing. I added the number of complaints per hour to the page that the on-call person sees first, since it is the best check on whether an alert is true.

In the two months afterwards the phone rang twice. Both were real, a ten-minute disk problem and a provider outage. Callum said the sound had become informative again.

The geocoding quota for the whole month was gone by 14:00 on the third, and the address lookup in the delivery planner began returning 'limit exceeded' to the dispatcher, who rang Mara in the voice of a person with eleven vans waiting.

A monthly quota used up in two and a half days means a loop. The provider's usage page showed 41,000 requests an hour from our key between 02:00 and 13:00, against a normal fifty. I looked at what ran at 02:00. A nightly job refreshed the coordinates of each delivery address that had been edited that day, calling the geocoder once for each. On the second a data fix had touched every address in the table, 1,900 of them, and the job treated them all as edited. That would have cost 1,900 requests, not forty-one thousand an hour.

So I looked again. The job retried failures. On the second a clerk had saved a batch of 140 addresses with the street line missing, and the geocoder had answered each with 'not found'. The job's rule was: retry anything that fails, up to ten times, with no pause. And, being an old script, it put each failed address back at the front of the queue. Each of the 140 bad addresses came round again and again, as fast as the provider would answer. One hundred and forty addresses at three hundred requests an hour apiece is 41,000.

The sentence I put in the note was: a retry rule that cannot tell 'try again' from 'it will never work'. The geocoder's answer 'not found' is a final answer for that address, and a network timeout is not. The script now retries only the errors that can change, with a pause that grows, and records a not-found address as unresolved, with the reason, in a table that the planner shows to a human.

For the immediate trouble Mara paid for more quota for the month, which cost 90, and we added a ceiling in our own client: no more than 2,000 requests a day from this key, with an alert at 1,500. A bug that spends money at that rate should meet our limit before the provider's.

The clerk, I should say, had done nothing wrong. The form allowed a missing street. It now does not. The unresolved table has had 31 entries since, and the dispatcher clears them herself before the first van leaves.

For a day and a half a deployment succeeded on one server and failed on the other, and I believed, for much of the first morning, that the problem was the deployment.

The deploy tool copies a new build to each of two application servers, stops the old process, starts the new one and checks that it answers. On Monday at 16:10 it did this for a routine release. Server one came up in four seconds. Server two did not come up at all: the process started, died and started again, and the tool, after a minute, rolled back. The error in the logs was 'address already in use'. Something on server two was already listening on the port the application wanted.

My first thought, which is the usual one, was that the old process had not stopped. I checked and it had; there was no process by that name from our deploy. I asked Halvard to list who owned the port. The answer was a process with our application's name, started at 03:10 that morning, running a build from March. It was a stranger on our port, wearing our name, and Halvard said with unusual care that he had not started it.

What had started it was a job that Callum had added the previous Thursday to make the application reopen its log files: stop everything whose service name begins with 'app', rotate the logs, start everything whose name begins with 'app'. On both servers the application ran as a unit called app-live. On server two, from before the deploy tool existed, there was also an old unit called simply app, disabled and forgotten. A disabled unit does not start at boot, but a command that names it starts it, and the pattern matched both. After the stop, the old unit came first alphabetically, took the port, and started the March build. App-live then found the port taken and gave up. Since Friday at 03:10, server two had been serving a build from March to half of our visitors.

It took me longer than it should have to see that, because I was reading deployment logs. The question that turned it was a different one: what version is each server serving? The application reports it at a path nobody visits. Server one gave Monday's release. Server two gave the March build, seventy-one commits old. Customers had not noticed, because the visible difference was a footer.

Half our traffic for three days on an old build is the thing I most wish I had known earlier. Nothing flagged it, because every health check asked 'does it answer' and none asked 'what is it'.

I went through the commits between the March build and Monday for anything a customer could have felt. There were two. The order list's date filter, added in April, was missing on the old build, and a customer had written on Saturday to ask where it had gone, and been told by support to refresh the page. And a corrected shipping estimate for one region was missing too, so some people on server two had been quoted four days instead of three. Noor wrote to the nine customers who had been quoted wrongly. None had acted on it, but I wanted them told.

The repairs were these. Halvard removed the old unit, one command. Callum changed the job to name the unit instead of matching a pattern. The deploy tool now refuses, before it starts anything, if the port is held by anything other than the process it just stopped, and says which process and since when. The health check compares the version each server reports with the one that was deployed and alerts on a mismatch. And a script now compares the services, scheduled jobs and listening ports of the two machines every Monday and prints the differences. On its first run it found three more: a leftover cron entry, a different version of a command-line tool, and a firewall rule that one machine had and the other lacked.

What I took from it is that two machines supposed to be identical are a claim, and the only way I know to keep a claim honest is to check it on a schedule. The script has printed nothing since.

At 00:00:01 every night a handful of customers got a server error, and it had been so for months. Ten to fifteen requests, never more. In a day of 90,000 they were invisible, and I noticed only because I had been asked to count errors by minute of the day for something else, and the minute 00:00 stood alone on the chart like a post in a field.

A fixed minute means a scheduled job, and the job in question was the log rotation, which runs at midnight. Its configuration told the application server to reload after the logs were moved, so that it would open new files. Reload, on this server, sends the process a hangup signal, which tells the workers to finish what they are doing and be replaced by fresh ones. A worker is supposed to complete its requests first. Ours did not always, because the worker timeout was set to one second, and any request in progress that took longer was cut off. At midnight, with the shop's nightly price-feed import also running, a few requests took two or three seconds.

I confirmed it with the simplest experiment: a forced rotation at noon, with a slow request open in another window. The request died at one second with a 500.

The fix is the plain one. The application server can reopen its log files on a different signal, without replacing its workers at all, and the rotation now sends that one. Nobody's request is touched. I also raised the graceful-shutdown timeout from one second to thirty, since it had been set once, to make restarts quick on a developer's laptop, and never revisited.

A small thing I like about this one: nobody was hurt much, and nobody would have found it. The shop's error rate was fine by any threshold. What gave it away was a chart drawn for a different reason. I now draw that chart, errors by minute of the day, once a quarter. It is cheap, and it shows what is scheduled.

At about 11:00 on busy mornings the payment service began to fail with 'too many open files', recovered when it was restarted, and failed again the next day a little earlier. Yusra reported it first, with the sort of specificity I like: it dies sooner each day.

The error means the process has used up its allowance of file handles, and sockets count as files. The default allowance on that machine was 1,024. I asked for the list of open handles of the live process at three points in a morning, and the count climbed: 212 at 08:00, 640 at 09:30, 1,011 at 10:55. Nearly all of them were network connections, in a state that said the other end had finished and ours had not closed.

The service called the card processor over HTTP, and the code that did it fetched a response, read the status and the body, and moved on. In one branch, when the processor returned an error status, the code returned early, and the early return skipped the line that closes the response body.
