In that library an unclosed body holds the connection open and out of the pool, so each failed payment leaked one connection. Normal payments closed theirs correctly. Only the errors leaked, and the rate of errors was about ten an hour on a normal day, more when the processor was grumpy, which it was in the mornings.

That the leak was real and slow is why it had hidden. There were two possible fixes: add the missing close to that branch, or restructure so that closing is not something each branch has to remember. I did the second. The function now asks for the response and, on the very next line, registers the close to run whatever happens afterwards, whichever way the function returns. A branch added by someone next year cannot forget something that was already arranged.

I also raised the process's allowance of handles from 1,024 to 65,536, although I want to be honest that this would have hidden the leak for a month and not cured it. I did it for a different reason: a payment service running at its ceiling should not be one busy day away from refusing customers.

The graph of open handles after the fix is a flat line at about 190. Yusra asked for a copy to put on her wall. It is mostly the flatness she likes.

One customer, a woman at a dental practice using an older browser at the reception desk, saw the booking page as a screen of black diamonds with question marks. Everyone else saw it fine. Ilse was the person who rang, and she described the screen with great economy: it looks like a crime scene.

Garbled characters in a single client point at how the bytes were treated between our server and her browser. I asked Ilse to open the page's developer view on the practice's computer, which she did with the receptionist, and to read me the response headers. The content-encoding header said gzip. The first bytes of the body, which she read out in hexadecimal, were 1f 8b, the start of a gzip stream. And a little further down, the same two bytes again.

The page had been compressed twice. Our application compressed its pages, and so did the proxy in front of it, which Halvard had introduced the previous week to take work off the application. The proxy was set to compress anything that did not say it was already compressed, and it checked a header that our application did not set, because the application's compression was a plain wrapper that added the compressed body but not the header. So the proxy saw a body with no declaration, compressed it again, and sent a header that said gzip once. Most modern browsers decompress once, find that the result still looks like compressed data, and decompress again, a leniency nobody asked for. The practice's browser was one version too old for it and showed the inner stream as if it were text.

Our other visitors had been served double-compressed pages for a week, and nobody knew, because their browsers hid it. They had also been paying a little for it, the page being fractionally larger than it need have been.

The fix was to have exactly one place compress. The application no longer compresses at all. That job belongs to the proxy, which does it for everything passing through and sets the right headers, and the application sends plain bodies. I added a test that requests the page through the proxy with a client that makes no allowances and checks that, after one decompression, the first character of the body is an opening angle bracket.

The practice's receptionist rang Ilse back to say it looked like a normal page again. Ilse wrote it down as a testimonial.

The check-in tablets in Ilse's waiting room were eight years old, and on the new check-in form the date-of-birth field did nothing when a patient touched it. Not an error message. Nothing. The tablets cost nothing to keep and a great deal to replace, they ran a browser that had stopped receiving updates years ago, and the form had been built by Wren on a current browser, tested on current browsers and shipped on a Tuesday.

A form that does nothing is hard to debug, because it is silent, so I asked Wren to connect one tablet to a laptop so we could read its console. There was one line in red: unexpected token '.'. That is how an old parser reports optional chaining, the short form of 'if this exists, then its field', which the script used in one place and which the eight-year-old browser had never heard of. A script that cannot be parsed does not partly run. It does not run. The date picker library, fetched in its modern build, failed the same way, and all of the page's behaviour came from those two files.

We could have fixed it by asking the clinic for new tablets, which would have been Ilse's money and a poor answer, and I said so. The better question was what the form needed to promise. I asked Ilse who touched the tablets: mostly people over sixty, sometimes with reading glasses in the other hand, entering a birth year such as 1951. I had looked at the date picker through Wren's eyes, a calendar to click, and I had not thought of a person who must scroll back seventy years through it, month by month.

So the picker went. The date of birth is now three plain dropdowns, day, month and year, the year list starting from the current year and going back a hundred and ten. They work on every browser made in the last fifteen years, need no script, and ask the patient for what they know by heart. The receptionists said they were quicker.

For the rest of the script we told the build to compile for the browsers actually in use at our customers, and wrote the list down as a policy file that includes the clinic's tablets, so that it is a decision somebody made and can change. And one of the old tablets now lives in a drawer in Wren's office, charged, with the check-in page bookmarked. Before a release he picks it up and does a check-in. It takes ninety seconds and has stopped two things already.

Yusra found the hole in a review, on a Wednesday afternoon, in a change that I had written, and I want to put down both facts.

The change added a page where a customer could download a PDF of an invoice, at an address ending in the invoice's number: /invoices/20931/pdf. The code looked up invoice 20931 and returned the PDF. Yusra, reading the diff, left a single line of comment: who checks that this is your invoice? I read the diff again, and nobody did. The page required a logged-in customer, which I had checked and had been proud of, and then it handed over whichever invoice was named. A logged-in customer who changed 20931 to 20932 would get someone else's invoice, with that person's name, address and purchases, and invoice numbers go up by one.

I had written the test, too, and it passed. It created an invoice, logged in as its owner, and downloaded it. It had never asked for an invoice that belonged to someone else, because what the test was written to prove was that the page worked, not that it refused.

I told Mara that afternoon, plainly, before the change was merged. It had not reached production, which was the whole point of a review. We fixed it, and then I wanted to understand what to learn. The fix was to look up the invoice by number and customer together, so that an invoice that is not yours is the same as an invoice that does not exist, and the response to both is the same, not found. That last point is deliberate. A different message for 'exists but not yours' tells a stranger which numbers are real.

The learning was in how many other pages had the same shape. I searched the codebase for every address that ended in an identifier and read what each did with it. There were nineteen. Sixteen checked ownership in the lookup. Three did not, and two of those were the older receipt and delivery-note pages, live for two years. I told Mara in the same voice as before. We fixed all three that day and went through the logs for the last ninety days looking for a customer requesting an identifier that was not theirs. We found none, by which I mean we found no case, and we wrote it that way in the note.

What I added is a test that I now write whenever an address has an identifier in it: log in as a second customer and ask for the first one's. It is a four-line test and has failed twice since, both times in my own code. When I thanked Yusra she said she had only asked a question, which is the whole of the job.

I lost a day to a browser error that said, in red, that access had been blocked by the cross-origin policy, and the day ended with a missing slash.

Wren was building the new dashboard, which lives at one address and calls our API at another, and the browser, which by default refuses to let a page on one address read responses from another, wanted the API to say it was happy about it. Browsers do this by first sending a small request called a preflight, a question: may this page call you with these headers? The API answers with permission headers, and the browser goes ahead. The dashboard's calls to a dozen endpoints worked. One, the list of saved reports, did not.

The first hours I spent in the wrong place, which is the permission headers. I compared the response for the good endpoint with the response for the bad one, line by line, and they were identical. I added a more permissive setting, and then a more permissive one, and the error did not change. It said what it had always said. That sameness is what I should have taken as evidence: if relaxing the rule does not change the message, the message is not about the rule.

At about 15:00 I stopped looking at the headers and looked at the network trace for the failing call, in full. The preflight to /reports, the address the dashboard used, did not return the permission headers. It returned a redirect, status 301, to /reports/, with a slash at the end. The API framework redirects any address to its canonical form, and the canonical form of this one had the trailing slash. Browsers do not follow a redirect on a preflight, and the specification forbids it. They take the redirect as the answer, find no permission in it, and report that access was denied. The message was completely true and told me nothing.

The fix was one slash, in the dashboard: call /reports/ and not /reports. It would have been wrong to stop there, because the next person to forget a slash will lose an afternoon of their own. I changed the API to answer preflight requests directly for both forms of every address, without redirecting, and to say plainly when a path is not found.

I wrote the day down in the notes as a rule for myself: when a restriction message does not respond to loosening the restriction, look at what the request actually did. The trace is the arbiter, and I should have had it open from the first hour. Wren, who had been on the call all afternoon, said he had never been so grateful for a trailing slash.

Every sixty seconds exactly, the live-results screen at the sports club's tournament dropped its connection and came back, and for a whole Saturday, with two hundred people watching the scores, the scoreboard blinked white once a minute like a nervous eye. Wren had built it. I was asked on the Sunday what a timer could be doing in a screen with no timer in it.

The screen kept an open connection to our server, a websocket, over which scores were pushed as they happened. The browser's console showed the connection closing with code 1006, abnormal closure, no reason given, and reopening a moment later through the reconnect logic that Wren, wisely, had written on the first day. The closing came sixty seconds after the last message and at no other interval. That arithmetic pointed at an idle timeout somewhere on the path between browser and server. A connection with nothing to say for a minute is treated as dead.

There were two candidates, the load balancer in front of the servers and the proxy on each server. I checked the proxy's configuration first, since it was ours, and its read timeout was 3,600 seconds. The load balancer belonged to the hosting provider, and its documentation, which I read twice, gave a default idle timeout of sixty seconds for connections carrying no traffic. During a close game scores arrive every few seconds and nobody notices. In a quiet spell between matches nothing is sent for minutes, and the connection is cut at the stroke of sixty.

The fix could have been to raise the load balancer's timeout, which is only a setting, and Wren's first instinct was just that. I preferred what the protocol itself offers for this, a ping. Every 25 seconds the server sends a small message that carries no content and which the browser answers automatically. To the load balancer it looks like traffic, and the connection is never idle. Twenty-five was picked to sit comfortably under sixty, with a margin for a late packet. The next provider might choose thirty, and the margin would still hold.

We also kept the reconnect logic and made it show nothing. The white flash came from the screen clearing itself on reconnect, so it now keeps the old scores on display, dimmed a little, until the new connection brings fresh ones. A visitor who sees a dimmed score knows it is being refreshed. A visitor who sees white thinks the match has been cancelled.

On the next Saturday there were forty-one minutes with no scores at all, during the lunch break, and the connection stayed up through every one of them. Wren sent me a screenshot of the connection log. It was one line long, which is what I had wanted from it.

Wren had never used a profiler, and the afternoon we spent with one was when I came to think of a measurement as a kind of generosity. The mobile API's 'my bookings' call took 1.9 seconds, and Wren had a list of five suspicions about why: the database query, the permission check, the image links, the sorting, the logging. He had been ready to rewrite the query.

I asked him to sample the running service for sixty seconds under a steady load, which is one command and costs nothing, and to turn the samples into a flame graph, a picture in which the width of each box is the share of time the program spent in that function and everything it called. It is the most useful picture I know, because it replaces an argument about where the time goes with an answer.

The picture was a single wide tower. The query was a thin box, 9 percent. The permission check was nothing. The sorting was 3 percent. The wide tower, 61 percent of the width, was the conversion of the result into JSON, and inside it the widest box was a function that formatted dates. For each of about four hundred bookings in a typical response there were five dates, and each date was formatted by building a fresh formatter object, with the locale looked up from scratch, and then throwing it away. Two thousand formatters per request.

Wren looked at it for a while and said he would never have guessed the dates. Nobody would. That is the point of measuring. His five suspicions had not contained the cause, and they could not have, since suspicions come from what a person thinks is expensive, and a date does not feel expensive.

The repair was to build the formatter once and reuse it, a change of eight lines. The 'my bookings' call came down to 0.62 seconds. The graph after the change showed the JSON tower at 14 percent and a new widest box, the database query, now at 41 percent, which was honest at last. I told Wren that if the call were still too slow, the query would then be a worthy target, with evidence behind it. It was not needed.

We saved both graphs in the ticket, with the date and the commit. Wren said the best thing about them was that Mara, who had not been part of the conversation, read the ticket for thirty seconds, said 'ah', and went away. I do not think any amount of prose would have had that effect.

The country list stopped working for Norway, and for no other country, and it took the whole of a Tuesday to find out why, mostly because nobody believed the explanation when they heard it.

The shop's checkout read its list of shipping countries from a configuration file, a plain YAML file with a two-letter code for each country and its delivery time. Sunniva reported that Norwegian customers could not complete an order: the country drop-down offered Norway with its code blank and a strange word, false, where the code should be. Everything else was correct. I opened the file and found the line: no: Norway, between se: Sweden and nz: New Zealand.

The code for Norway is NO. In the version of YAML that our parser implements, an unquoted no is a boolean, the same as false, along with yes, on, off, y and n. The line therefore said: the value false is Norway. The parser, dutifully, built a table with a key of false, and the checkout's loop read the key as a code and showed what it found. It had worked for the nine months since the shop began shipping to Norway, for a reason I find rather interesting. Until the previous Thursday the file had been read by an older version of the library, which treated only true and false as booleans and left no alone. A routine update had changed the interpretation, and nothing in the update's notes had made it sound like a change to anyone's shipping.

I wrote the nine-line test I wish had existed. It reads the file, checks that each key is a string of two capital letters, and checks that every country in the shop's order history is present. It failed on Norway at once. The fix is to quote the code, so that it is read as text, and I quoted every code in the file, to remove the question for good and not only the case that had bitten.

That was the repair, and the part that interested me more was the belief around it. Mara, hearing the explanation, said that cannot be true, and she was right to doubt, because it is absurd. I did not convince her by argument. I asked her to open a terminal, type the file's first lines into the parser herself and print the result. The word False came back. She said a word I will not reproduce, and then laughed for some time.

Sunniva wrote to the eleven Norwegians who had tried to order in the previous days. Six replied. One, who had wanted a lamp, said that he had begun to wonder whether the shop was trying to tell him something about his country.

Seventeen orders were paid for and never arrived in the warehouse's system, and for a fortnight each of them was treated as a separate mystery by a different person. Noor kept the list on a sheet of paper on her desk, with a column headed 'why'. On the day it reached seventeen I was asked to find a single why.

The path of an order is this. The shop takes payment, puts a message on a queue, and a worker in the warehouse integration picks the message up, creates the order in the warehouse's system and tells the queue that it is done. The queue then forgets the message. Each of the seventeen orders had a payment and an entry in the shop's log of 'message sent', and nothing at the other end. The warehouse's system had no record of them and the worker's log mentioned none.

The question that settled it was a plain one: when does the worker tell the queue that a message is done? I read the worker. It received a message, immediately acknowledged it, and then began the work of creating the order in the warehouse's system. The author had done this for a sensible reason, which was that creating an order sometimes took twenty seconds, and the queue would redeliver any message not acknowledged in time, producing duplicates.

The sequence therefore had a gap: acknowledged, then work. If the worker died inside the gap, from a restart, a crash or a deployment, the message was gone from the queue and the work was never done. I lined up the seventeen order times with the deployment log. Fourteen fell within ten seconds of a worker restart. Three were at times the worker had crashed with an out-of-memory error that Callum already had on his own list. Seventeen of seventeen.

The cure reverses the order and then deals with what that causes: do the work first, acknowledge afterwards. If the worker dies in the middle, the queue, which has not been told, delivers the message again to another worker. That cannot lose an order. It can create the same one twice, so the creation in the warehouse's system now carries our order number as a key, and a second attempt with the same number is recognised and does nothing. Between the two arrangements, the first can lose and the second can only repeat, and a repeat that is harmless is something one can accept.

For the seventeen, Noor and I went down her paper list and entered each in the warehouse's system by hand with the date it should have shipped, and she rang the customers whose orders were more than ten days late. Eleven were understanding. Two cancelled. She added a column to her sheet, headed 'sorted', ticked it seventeen times, and put the paper in the recycling.

The design I most disliked in the whole affair, I told Mara afterwards, had been a well-reasoned one. The author had weighed duplicates against loss, and had protected the thing that was visible, a duplicate order, and not the thing that was silent. I have tried since to ask of any acknowledgement: what happens if the process dies right after this line?

We upgraded the main database by three major versions over a weekend in November, and I want to describe it carefully, because it was the first big thing of its kind that went right, and the reasons it went right are not the ones I would have guessed.

The old version was reaching the end of its support life, and the upgrade tool that rewrites a database in place needed the shop to be closed while it ran: for 190 GB, Halvard's estimate was three to four hours. Mara said that three to four hours of a closed shop on a Saturday was acceptable in principle, and that she would rather it were eleven minutes. That sentence became the design.

The method for eleven minutes is logical replication. You build a second database on the new version beside the old one and have the old one stream every change to it as it happens. The new one catches up, and when it has caught up you stop writing to the old, wait for the last changes to arrive, and point the application at the new. The closed shop is the time between stopping writes and pointing. We rehearsed it three times, on copies of the real data, over the preceding fortnight.

The rehearsals found what rehearsals are for. The first failed outright, because six of our tables had no primary key, and logical replication cannot carry updates for a table that gives it no way to identify a row. Those six were old tables of log-like data. Adding a key to the largest took forty minutes and a careful look at what could go wrong on a live system, and for two of the six we chose another setting, telling the replication to treat the whole row as its identity. The second rehearsal showed that sequences, the counters that hand out order numbers, are not carried across by this method. The new database would have started numbering orders at 1 and collided with the existing ones on the first sale. A step that sets each sequence to its old value plus a margin went into the plan, and a check after it, comparing every sequence.

The third rehearsal was complete and clean and timed at nine minutes forty. We wrote the script for it with Halvard's name on the command that closes the old database to writes, since he had asked to be the one to press it.

On the Saturday at 06:00 the shop showed its closed notice. At 06:02 Halvard stopped writes. At 06:03 the new database reported itself level with the old, which I checked by comparing the last position of one with the received position of the other, not by trusting a message. At 06:05 the sequences were set, and the check passed on all 112 of them. At 06:08 the application's configuration was switched and its servers restarted, at 06:11 the first test order went through, a lamp Mara bought for a colleague, and the shop reopened at 06:12. Ten minutes from closing to the lamp.

What I did not predict was the Monday. The new version planned some queries differently, and one report, the stock valuation, took forty seconds instead of three. A table's statistics are not carried across, and the new database had not yet learned the shape of the data. Halvard ran the statistics gathering by hand at 08:15 and the report took three seconds. That step had been on our list since the second rehearsal, and we had simply left it out of the cutover script. It cost fifteen minutes of one person's patience. It is in the script now.

The old database stayed available, read-only, for two weeks, and then Halvard shut it down with a line in the log recording who and why. What I take from it is that the plan was good because Mara's sentence made it concrete. 'Acceptable in principle' would have given us the in-place tool and a closed Saturday. 'Eleven minutes' gave us three rehearsals, and the rehearsals gave us six keys, a hundred and twelve counters and one forgotten step, which was all of the knowledge there was to have.

The plan to take notifications out of the monolith looked simple on a whiteboard in January and took until June, and the reason is a table.

The monolith, our booking platform, sent emails and text messages to customers: confirmations, reminders, cancellation notices. The code that did it lived in the same program as everything else, and its problems were the usual ones. A slow email server held up a booking request, a bug in the reminder code had once taken the whole platform down on a Sunday, and three of us were afraid to change it. Mara proposed extracting it into a service of its own, with a narrow doorway: other parts of the platform say 'send this message to this person', and the service does the rest. Tobias drew the box.

Before cutting anything, I did what I do and made a list of everything the notification code touched. The code itself was 3,100 lines, and clean enough. But it called into other code, and other code called into it, and I counted the places where it reached outside its own files. The count was 46. Most were what one would expect: it read a customer's name, a booking's time. Two were not.

The first was a table. The notification code kept its state, which messages had been sent, which were queued, which had failed, in a table called messages. By name and in the schema, that table belonged to notifications. But nine other places in the platform read from it directly. The booking screen showed 'reminder sent' by looking in the table. The support page listed a customer's messages by querying it. The nightly report counted failures with a query. The no-show logic asked whether a reminder had gone out 24 hours earlier. The table was the real interface to the notification system, and it had never appeared on any diagram, because it was just a table. If we moved the code into a service with its own database, those nine would break.

The second was a function, called in the middle of the booking code, that formatted a date for a message. It lived in the booking module and the notification code called it, so the arrow of dependency ran backwards into the thing we were trying to leave.

We spent the first three months on those two. For the table, we listed each of the nine reads and what question it was really asking, and found that they asked only four. Was a message sent for this booking, and when? Which messages did this customer get? How many failed in a period? What is the status of this one? The service now answers those four questions through its doorway, and the nine places ask it. The table became the service's private business, and we could move it without anyone knowing. For the function, the date formatting moved into the service with copy rules of its own, and I deleted the old function from the booking code, where it turned out to be used in only that one place.

Only then did we do the thing that had looked simple in January, the move itself, and it took eleven days. We ran the two paths side by side for a week, with the old code sending and the new one logging what it would have sent, and compared the two logs each morning. They differed on day two by 4 messages out of 3,000, all from a time zone rule I had copied incorrectly, and not at all after that. On day twelve we turned the old code off.

The lesson Tobias wrote on the whiteboard when it was over was: draw the tables. I would add something about the question you ask before you cut. The code was never the coupling. The coupling was what everything else had learned to rely on without being told it was there.

The files were right when they left the instrument and wrong when they reached the lab's storage server, about one in every four gigabytes, and each time by a single flipped bit. Hettie, who runs the data side of a materials lab, noticed because the checksum that the instrument software prints did not match the one she computed on the server, for one file of the 211 that week.

I asked for the experiment that separates the two ends of a chain: copy the same 4 GB file from the instrument to the server twenty times and compute a checksum after each. Three copies differed from the other seventeen, each from the original by exactly one bit, in a different place each time. The fault was random, and it was somewhere on the path. Then I asked her to copy the file on the server from one disk to another, twenty times. Two of the twenty came out different. That mattered: the network was innocent. The corruption happened inside the server.

Inside a server data passes through the disks, the controller, the processor and the memory, and I know of two places where a single bit goes wrong without anything noticing: a disk that lies, and memory without error correction. Disks usually announce their faults. I asked what the memory was. It was ordinary, with no error correction, 64 GB, bought second-hand by the lab. We left a memory test running overnight, and at 03:40 it reported a failing address in one module of four, with a single bit stuck.

This was the satisfying part and the frightening one together. A stuck bit corrupts a value only when the correct bit is the other one, which is half the time, and only when the data happens to land at that address, which in 64 GB is rare. That is the one in four gigabytes. But the module had been in the machine for fourteen months, and Hettie had 31 TB on the server.

What do you do about 31 TB? We did not recompute everything. For the files made in the last eight months the instruments had kept checksums, and a script compared them: of 6,200 files, 41 had silently changed. For the older ones there is nothing to compare with, and nobody can know. We wrote each research group a one-page note giving the dates of the window and the list of the 3,900 files from it without checksums, and each decided for itself what it meant for their results. Most of the data was spectra, in which one bit disappears into the noise. One group had stored firmware images, in which it would not.

We replaced the module and then the other three, with error-correcting memory the board supported. We turned on checksumming in the filesystem, which verifies every block on every read and would have told Hettie within a day. And the copy script now prints a checksum at both ends. I think the note to the groups was the honest thing to write, and I also think nobody enjoyed reading it.

The supplier's file drop had been an FTP server since before any of us worked here, and moving it to a secure transfer should have been a Friday-afternoon task and was in fact a three-week project, because the old server had been doing things nobody had listed.

Odile, whose warehouse receives the supplier's stock file each morning, asked for the move after her insurer's questionnaire wanted to know whether any partner exchanged files without encryption. What I wanted was the list of behaviours, not the protocol. I read the supplier's setup notes, two pages, the last ninety days of file arrivals, and the script on our side that picked them up. The behaviours I found were four.

First, files appeared in two steps. The supplier's system created the file and then wrote into it over some seconds, and our script, which ran at 06:30, took a file to be ready if its name ended in .csv. The supplier wrote to a name ending in .tmp and renamed it when done, and a rename is instant. With the new transfer method their client wrote to the final name directly, and our 06:30 job would on some mornings read a half-written file.

Second, dates. The filenames carried the date of the supplier's local day, which differs from ours, so on mornings when their clock had passed midnight in their zone but not in ours, our script looked for a file that did not exist. The old arrangement had hidden this because the old server kept a file called latest.csv, a link that the supplier's system refreshed. The new service could not do links in the account's folder.

Third, deletion. The supplier's job removed the previous day's file when it uploaded the new one. On the new server they had no permission to delete, and the folder began to fill with ninety days of files, which our script read in sorted order and applied to stock one after another, the oldest first, so that the final stock was right only by luck.

Fourth, and I found it only from the ninety days of arrivals: on eleven mornings the file had arrived twice, the second a corrected version an hour later, and our script had applied the second over the first because it ran again at 07:30. Nobody had written the 07:30 run down. Odile had added it in the spring after a bad morning.

So we did not copy the old behaviours. We wrote them as rules. A file is ready when a small marker file with the same name and the ending .done exists, which the supplier writes last. The script looks for the newest complete file regardless of its name. After processing, a file is moved to an archive folder on our side. A corrected file with a higher sequence number replaces the earlier, with a line in the log saying so. We asked the supplier, Lars's team, to write the marker, and they did it in a day, with an apology for not having a better word than done.

The first morning of the new arrangement had two files, one corrected, and the script took the second, wrote its line in the log and archived both. Odile read the log and said she could see what had happened to her stock for the first time in four years.

The video-upload feature for the climbing wall's route reviews had one habit nobody could explain. Videos filmed on phones held upright turned up on the site lying on their sides, but only from some phones, and only after processing. Teo, who runs the wall's website on the side, sent me four sample clips and a message saying he was beginning to take it personally.

The transcoding step took what members uploaded and made a smaller copy for the site. I started with the files themselves. A video file carries, apart from the picture, a handful of facts about itself, and I printed those for the four clips. Two had a field called rotation with the value 90. The picture inside those files was not upright at all. It was stored lying down, as the camera's sensor sees it, 1920 wide by 1080 high, together with a note saying turn this a quarter when you play it. Phones do this because it is cheaper to record in the sensor's orientation and ask the player to rotate. Every player honours the note. The other two clips had no note, because those phones turned the picture themselves.

So the question was what our transcoder did with the note. The answer was that it re-encoded the picture, which was lying down, into a new file and, as a tidy-minded gesture, dropped all the metadata, rotation included. The new file contained a perfectly sideways picture and no instruction to turn it. The phones that rotated the picture themselves produced files that survived. The ones that used the note lost it.

There were two ways to cure it. The first keeps the note: tell the transcoder to copy the rotation across. That works, and leaves a time bomb, since different players honour the note in different ways and a few not at all. The second applies the rotation while re-encoding, so that the new file holds a picture that is actually upright and a note that says zero. I chose the second, and explained to Teo that a note is a promise the file makes about itself to a player, and I would rather not depend on every player keeping it.

I made a test with six clips, one for each of the four rotations a phone can note, plus two that were upright already, and a check that reads the output's actual first frame and measures whether its height is greater than its width for those filmed upright. Teo then did something I would not have thought of. He found three members who had uploaded clips in the last year that were lying on their sides, and asked whether he could reprocess their originals, which he still had. Two said yes. The third replied: oh, I thought that was just how it looked.

The climbing wall now has a page of review videos with every climber the right way up. Teo said the best part was that it had stopped feeling like a personal attack.

The order-confirmation page took 1.4 seconds and nobody could say why, because no part of it was slow. Each query was fast, each call was fast. The profiler, when Tobias ran it, showed a thin, even smear, which is the sign of something that is slow because of how its parts are arranged and not because any part is.

We had installed tracing the month before, so that each request leaves a record of everything it called and how long each call took, and for the first time I could look at a single request as a timeline. I asked for a typical confirmation page and drew it on the left of the screen. There were eight calls to other services: customer details, order lines, delivery options, loyalty points, a tax lookup, two for stock, and one for recommendations. Each took between 60 and 150 milliseconds, and in the picture they stood one after another in a staircase, each starting when the one before ended. Eight hundred and forty milliseconds of waiting, and the rest of the 1.4 seconds was our own work.

The staircase was not necessary. Of the eight calls, six did not need the result of any other. The delivery options needed the order lines. The recommendations needed the customer details. Everything else could start at the same moment. The code had been written one call after another because that is how code is written in a hurry, and it had been so since the page was made.

I drew the dependencies on a piece of paper as a small graph and found the longest chain: order lines, then delivery options, 150 ms plus 90. The rest could run beside it. With the calls arranged in three waves, the waiting should come to about 240 ms and not 840, which would put the page at about 0.8 seconds. I asked Tobias to make the change, and I want to say what I asked him not to do, which was to launch all eight calls in a tangle. The code states the dependencies explicitly, a few lines for each wave, so that someone reading it a year from now can see why the third wave waits for the second.

The page came out at 0.83 seconds, which is the best prediction I made all year.

There was one thing I would have missed without the timeline. In the new trace the tax lookup, which was in the first wave, finished last, at 190 ms, because it had been the slow call all along, hidden in the staircase. Now it was the longest bar and the page waited for it. I asked Tobias whether the tax result could be remembered for the length of one session, since it depends only on the country and the type of basket, and it could. That brought the page to 0.7 seconds.

Mara looked at the two traces side by side, the staircase and the three waves, and asked whether she could have the picture for the team's wall. I had made it in plain text, so I said I would draw it properly.

The metrics server died on a Thursday night, and when Halvard brought it back it died again, which told us it was no accident. It held our dashboards' numbers, and within ten minutes of every start it ran out of memory, carrying six million series with it.

A metrics server stores, for every distinct combination of a metric's name and its labels, a separate series. A request counter labelled by route and status code makes perhaps two hundred series, because there are about forty routes and five statuses. Two hundred is nothing. Six million was a number I did not believe, and I asked Halvard to list the metrics by the number of series each held. One of them held 5.8 million, and it was ours: the response-time histogram for the new 'my account' endpoint.

Wren had added a label to it the previous Tuesday. The reasoning was good. He wanted to see whether particular customers were getting slow responses, so the histogram carried the customer's identifier as a label. A histogram has fourteen buckets. We have about 41,000 customers. Forty-one thousand times fourteen times a few more labels is where the six million came from, and the series count grows with every new customer, with no ceiling. The server had been slowly filling since Tuesday, and on Thursday night a busy hour had pushed it over.

I did not want it to be Wren's mistake, because it was not only his. The metrics library accepted any label without a word, and nothing told a person that a label with 41,000 values is a different kind of thing from one with five. I wrote on the ticket, as the cause, what a label is for: it divides the data into a small number of groups that you will want to compare on a graph. A customer is not a group. A customer is a record, and records belong in logs, where a line per request is cheap and a new value costs nothing.

The repair had three parts. Remove the label from the metric, which Halvard did at 23:50, and which brought the server back at once with its memory falling to 40 percent. Put the customer's identifier into the request log for that endpoint, so that Wren's actual question, which customers see slow responses, can be asked of the logs, and it can. And set a limit on the server: a metric may not have more than 5,000 series, and an attempt to create the 5,001st is refused and counted, and shows in a panel. That limit would have stopped it on Tuesday evening, with a message, at the moment Wren made the change.

Wren was mortified for most of Friday, and on Monday he did something that gave the whole business a good ending. He wrote a short paragraph for the team's guide to metrics under the heading What is a label, with the story of the six million in two sentences and the rule in a third. He named himself in it. When I asked why, he said it would be read more carefully that way.

For the event store we had used random identifiers as primary keys, the ordinary kind, because they are unique without any coordination and nobody has to ask the database for the next number. This worked well up to about forty million rows and then began to get slow in a way that no query could explain: inserts, not reads, and steadily worse.

The shape of the slowdown was the clue. Inserts that took half a millisecond in the early months now took six, and in busy hours spiked to forty. The database was not busy, the disk was not busy, and the table's size, 38 GB, should have been no obstacle. I asked for the number of index pages touched per insert and saw it was nearly one fresh page every time. That is what a random key does to a sorted index. The index is a tree kept in key order, and a new row goes where its key belongs. With sequential keys new rows go to the end, always the same few pages, which stay in memory. With random keys each new row goes into some random page among a million, and once the index is larger than memory most of those pages must be fetched from disk, modified and written back. Each insert caused a read and a write somewhere unpredictable.

We could have gone back to simple counting numbers, which are perfect for this. But our identifiers are created in several places, on phones and in three services, and the counting method needs one place to hand them out. The alternative that has lately become standard is an identifier whose first part is the time and whose rest is random: unique without coordination, and roughly in order of creation, so that new rows land at the end of the index again. The newer version of the UUID standard defines one. We tested it with a million inserts into two tables, one with each kind of key, on a machine with small memory to make the effect visible. The random table took 11 minutes 40 seconds and the time-ordered one 2 minutes 10.

Mara asked about the price. There are two. A time-ordered identifier tells anyone who sees it roughly when the row was made, to the millisecond, which for our events is no secret but would be for some data, and I wrote in the guide that I would not use it where the time of creation is sensitive. And changing the key of a table with 40 million rows is a significant operation. We did not change the existing rows. New rows get the new kind of identifier, and since both kinds are valid identifiers of the same size, nothing else in the system could tell them apart. The old random ones stay where they are, and the index improves slowly as their share falls.

After two months the insert time had dropped from six milliseconds to 0.7, and the page writes per insert from nearly one to about a twentieth. Wren's phone clients, which create their own identifiers, took the new library in the next release. Old versions still send the old kind, and the dashboard shows both, as a small chart of the proportion that is time-ordered, climbing.

The worst afternoon of the year began with a customer's email saying, politely, that she was looking at someone else's company. She had logged in to the reporting dashboard of our service, and the page that came up showed another firm's name in the corner and another firm's figures. Noor, who got the message at 14:12, did the right thing before she did anything else: she rang Mara.

I want to put the sequence down carefully, since the temptation on such an afternoon is to fix what one can see and not what one understands.

The first decision, made by Mara within four minutes and agreed by me, was to stop the harm and then find the cause. The dashboard's address was put into maintenance mode, a page saying the service was briefly unavailable, at 14:19. It cost several hundred customers an hour of their working day. It stopped anyone else seeing a stranger's figures. I did not hesitate about that, and I do not now.

The second step was to find out what was possible. Could one customer see another's page? Yes, but not always: the customer who had written saw the other firm's page about one reload in six. That ruled out a fault in the login, which is deterministic, and pointed at something between the customer and our servers that sometimes remembered the wrong thing.

We use a content delivery network, a layer of servers around the world that keeps copies of pages so they load faster. Static files such as the logo and the scripts are its ordinary business. Dynamic pages are not meant to be kept, and whether a page may be kept is decided by a header our application sends. I fetched the dashboard page twice from outside, with different logins, and looked at the responses. Both carried a header saying the page may be stored publicly for sixty seconds. The page that contains a customer's figures had been marked as something to keep and hand to anyone.

How had the header got there? I went through the week's changes. On Monday Callum had changed the application's default caching headers to make the marketing pages faster, which was a sound change in itself. It applied a public caching header to every response that did not set its own. The dashboard, whose code had never needed to say anything about caching, because the old default was private and never store, inherited the new default. Only one reload in six showed the wrong page because the network has many servers, each keeping its own copy for sixty seconds, and which one answered depended on where the customer was and when.

We fixed it in three layers, in this order. The dashboard and every page behind a login now say private, do not store, explicitly, so that they depend on no default. The default was changed back to the safe one: anything that does not say what it is, is not kept. And the network was told to purge everything for the dashboard's addresses, at 14:51.

Then the question that matters most, who had seen what. The network's logs record each response served from a kept copy. I asked for every dashboard response served from storage since Monday's change and matched each to the login that requested it and the login that created the copy. Of 41,000 views in four days, 212 had been served from a copy made for another customer, and 158 of those to someone who stayed on the page for more than five seconds. Those 158 people, from 63 companies, had seen another company's figures: revenue summaries, the names of contacts.

Mara wrote to each of the 63 within the day. The message said what had happened, what had been visible, for how long, that it was fixed, and gave a direct telephone number. She did not use the word incident once. Some replied kindly. Two asked for a formal report. One cancelled, which she was entitled to do.

What I learned is not about caching headers, though they were the cause. A default is a decision about every page that has not yet been written, and its blast radius is the number of things that will silently inherit it. Callum's change was good, and it was reviewed. What nobody had asked was: what will inherit this that we did not mean? I now ask it of any default I change, and then I list the things that inherit. That day the list would have contained the dashboard.

The deployment of the booking service pushed an image of 1.9 GB to each server, which took four minutes on a good day and had once, in the middle of a rushed release, taken eleven. Callum, who had been bitten by that, asked me to get it small.

An image is a stack of layers, and most of the weight was where such weight usually is: the build tools. The image was based on a full operating system with a compiler, headers, a package manager and a few hundred megabytes of things used only while building the application and never while running it. I split the build in two stages. The first has everything and produces the program. The second starts from a minimal base, takes only the finished program and what it truly needs to run, and that is the image we ship. Mine came out at 140 MB, thirteen times smaller. The push took eleven seconds.

I thought the day was done, and it was not. That same afternoon the invoice PDFs started to come out with every letter in a box. The minimal base had no fonts. The old full image had a standard set that the PDF renderer found by itself, and nobody had ever put them on a list of what the service needs, because they were simply there. In the small image nothing was there that we had not asked for, and the renderer, finding no font, drew empty boxes.

Callum spotted it on the staging server during the checks, which I was glad of, and which exist for exactly that. I added the two font files the invoice template uses to the final stage explicitly, which cost 780 KB, and wrote the template's font names beside them in a comment. I also wrote a test that renders a one-page invoice in the final image and compares its text layer with what it should say, since a page of boxes has text that reads as nonsense to the check.

Then I went through the rest of the contents with care, because this was the first time I had seen a list of what the service uses. There were two more things the old image had carried unremarked: the timezone database, which the booking code needs for local times, and the certificates that let the service talk to the payment provider. Both would have failed quietly in the new image, one at the first booking in a different timezone and the other at the first payment. I added both and tested each.

The principle I took is that a small image is not the aim. The aim is an image that contains exactly what the service needs, and the smallness is the evidence that one has not carried the rest. The way to find what is needed is to take everything away and see what fails, which is slow. It produced a list, though, and the list is now a file in the repository, which nobody had ever had.

Twice a day, at about 11:30 and 17:40, a customer at the shop's checkout would be told that something went wrong, and in the logs there would be a line saying that the database had detected a deadlock and rolled one transaction back. It had been going on for months at a rate of one or two a day, and the shop's response, which I understood, was that retrying the payment usually worked.

A deadlock is two transactions each holding something the other needs. Neither can go on, and the database, after a second or so, picks one and cancels it. The log line, which I had not read closely before, names the two statements involved. Statement one updates the stock of a product and then the customer's loyalty points. Statement two updates the loyalty points and then the stock. The same two things, in opposite orders. If a checkout and the returns desk's processing for the same customer and product run in the same instant, each takes its first lock and waits for the other's.

It was rare because the opposite orders came from two different places and needed to touch the same customer and the same product within the same few milliseconds. It was a coincidence of three things, which is why it happened about once in 6,000 checkouts, at the busy times of the lunch break and the end of the working day, when the returns desk clears its queue.

The remedy is old and simple and stated in every book on the subject: always take locks in the same order. We picked an order, by alphabet of the table names, stock first and loyalty points second, and I changed the returns code, which was the one doing it the other way round. No cleverness in the database, no retry loop on top. I also changed the checkout's error handling so that in the rare case a deadlock arises for another reason, the customer is not shown an error but the payment step is retried once, automatically. A retry can mend a deadlock. It must not be the only protection, because a retry is how a problem comes to go unseen for months.

To test it I wrote a script that ran the two paths against each other, a thousand times each, in two processes, at a rate designed to collide. Before the change: 212 deadlocks. After: none, in ten runs of the same size. A short version, 200 each, is now part of the suite, and fails on the old code every time.

The last point is the one I find most interesting. The same deadlock had appeared in the shop's log of warnings, with the same words, a few hundred times. It was not counted as an error because the database handled it and the shop retried. A long log of things that were handled had become something nobody read. I asked Callum whether the deadlock count could go on the dashboard as a single number. It reads zero. He says he looks at it more than he should.

In March the on-call phone received 212 alerts in a week, and I remember the number because it was Callum's, said with the quiet of a person who has stopped believing in the phone. The week before, a real fault, a full disk on the file server, had sat in the pile for four hours before anyone opened it.

I did not begin by changing any alert. I began by classifying the 212, which took an afternoon, putting each into one of four groups by what the person who received it should do: act now, act today, look at it sometime, nothing. The groups came out as 6, 21, 49 and 136. A hundred and thirty-six alerts, nearly two thirds, had a correct response of nothing: a disk at 82 percent on a machine that grows by one percent a month, a service that restarts itself in two seconds and tells everyone, a slow-response notice at 3 a.m. on a nightly batch machine that is slow by design.

Then I did the thing people do not like. For the nothing alerts I proposed deletion, not tuning. An alert that nobody will ever need to act on is not a smaller version of a useful alert. It is noise that costs attention. Callum agreed for the disk-space ones and argued for several of the others, and he was right about two of them: a certificate expiring in thirty days means nothing on twenty-nine days and a vital job on the thirtieth. For things like that the alert is still wanted, but as a ticket on a Monday and not a call at night.

That gave a rule, and I wrote it at the top of the alert configuration: anything that wakes a person must be something a person must do within the hour. Anything else is a message to a channel or a ticket. The six act-now alerts remained. The twenty-one act-today alerts went to a channel Callum reads at 09:00. The forty-nine went to a weekly list. The hundred and thirty-six I deleted, after Mara had looked at each, with a line in a file saying why, which has been used twice since, when somebody asked where an alert had gone.

For the next fortnight the phone rang nine times a week. Every one was real, though three of them could have waited, and I moved those down. In the third week a full disk on the backup server rang the phone at 04:10 and Callum answered it within six minutes. He said afterwards that what he noticed was the silence before it.

I keep this one to remind myself that the trouble with alerts is rarely the threshold. Nobody was asked, when each was written, what a person should do when it fires, and look at it is not an answer.

Members of the club-booking app said that some of their past bookings were missing from the list, but only if they scrolled. The bookings were there on the first page and the third, and on the second one had gone. When they refreshed it was back. Wren had the reports in a tidy pile and no reproduction, which in my experience is the shape of a good bug.

The list loaded twenty bookings at a time, newest first, and the next page was requested as 'skip the first twenty, give me the next twenty', which is called offset pagination and is how nearly everyone begins. It works as long as the list does not change while you read it. Ours changes: a booking is added at the top whenever anyone books, and a club with a few hundred members makes new bookings all evening.

I could make it happen on paper. A member opens the list and gets bookings 1 to 20. While she reads, someone adds a new booking, which goes to position 1 and pushes every other booking down one place. She scrolls, and the app asks for 'skip twenty, give me twenty'. But what was number 20 is now 21, so she is sent bookings 21 to 40 of the new list, and the booking that used to be 20 has been skipped over, not because it is missing but because it moved. If a booking were deleted from the top instead, she would see a repeat: the last item of the first page, again at the top of the second.

To prove it I wrote a script that read the list page by page while a second process added a booking every second. Seven of ten runs skipped something, and none were clean once I made the adder faster.

The remedy is not to count from the top but to remember where you stopped. The app asks 'give me twenty bookings older than this one', naming the last booking it saw and using that booking's own time and identifier as a bookmark. This is called keyset, or cursor, pagination. A booking added at the top changes nothing about what is older than the bookmark, and a deletion changes nothing either, since it simply carries on from the place named. As a bonus the database finds the starting point through its index and does not have to count down past the skipped rows, which on a long list is cheaper as well.

The cost is that one can no longer say jump to page seven, since there is no page seven, only older than this. I asked Wren whether any screen did that, and exactly one did, the admin list, which carries a page number in its address. We left offsets there, since an admin list is not read while it moves, and I wrote a note in the code about why the two screens differ, for the person who would otherwise try to make them match.

The script that skipped seven of ten now skips none. The member who had written in most often, and who had counted her missing bookings to the day, wrote to say that her list was complete. She added that she had thought it was her.

Sunniva and I disagreed for a week about what it means to delete a person, and I think I was wrong for the first four days.

The shop had begun to receive requests from customers to erase their data, which the law in the countries the shop sells to entitles them to ask. The first came in March, handled by hand by Noor, who removed the customer's name and address from the orders table and felt that this was probably right. The second came three weeks later and Noor asked whether there was a proper way, which is the question that landed on my desk.

My first design was thorough, and I was proud of it. A single operation, erase customer, walking every table that held anything about a person, deleting the rows and cascading to everything that referenced them: orders, invoices, messages, loyalty points, support tickets. It would leave nothing. I wrote the plan on the Monday and gave it to Sunniva, who runs the shop and is the person responsible in law, to approve.

She sent it back on the Tuesday with one question: what happens to my accounts? Invoices are legal documents, which a business must keep for years, six in her case. Deleting a customer's invoices to satisfy a request for erasure would leave her records incomplete for the tax authority, and she would be in breach of one duty by satisfying another. I had treated the request as the whole of the law and not as one law among others. I said so. We then argued about the middle, which I now think was the useful part.

I proposed that invoices simply be exempt: erase the customer and keep their invoices as they are. Sunniva said that was also wrong, since an invoice carries a name and an address, and the right to erasure is not suspended for everything a business is allowed to keep. The duty is to keep what must be kept and nothing more. We went through an invoice line by line. What the tax rules require is the seller's details, the date, the amounts, the tax, the items sold, and the buyer's name and address so that the sale can be identified. The buyer's email address, telephone number, notes and delivery instructions are not required. It was a boundary drawn through the middle of a single row.

The design that came out of the argument had three rules, and I wrote them as plainly as I could. One: data the shop must keep by law is kept, in the form the law requires, and is marked as kept for that reason with the date until which it must be kept. Two: everything else about the person goes, including from the places nobody thinks of, the support tickets, the message log and the search index. Backups we left as they are and wrote down: they age out in thirty days, and the person is told so in the reply. Three: when the legal period ends, a nightly job removes the rest, so that nothing outlives its reason.

Sunniva asked for one more thing, which I had not thought of. She asked that the confirmation to the customer say exactly what was erased and what was kept and why, in words, with the date the kept part would go. People forgive a business for keeping an invoice, she said, and do not forgive it for saying it has deleted everything when it has not. The reply Noor sends now lists both, a few lines each.

The first request handled the new way took eleven minutes. It came from a man who had bought one lamp, and he wrote back to thank us for the clarity. The second asked whether we would delete the invoice also, and Noor answered with the paragraph about the six years, which I think is the first time I have seen a business explain a law to a customer in a way the customer found reasonable.

What stays with me is the four days. I treated a rule as the specification and built exactly to it. The person who knew where it ran into other rules was not an engineer but the one who had to answer for the accounts, and I would not have found it without asking her what happens to hers.

The price scraper broke on a Wednesday morning, as scrapers do, and the story is mostly about what we did instead of repairing it.

Dario's company tracked the prices of about 900 components on a distributor's website, to warn its buyers when they changed. A script written two years earlier by someone since gone fetched each product page, found the price with a pattern matched against the page's markup, and stored it. On the Wednesday every price came back as nothing, because the distributor had redesigned its site over the weekend and the pattern no longer matched.

The habitual response is to look at the new markup and write a new pattern. I did look at it. The new pages had their prices inside a script block that built the page in the browser, so the price was not in the page's text at all unless a real browser ran the script. A simple fix was therefore not available. A harder one, running a browser for each of 900 pages every day, was possible, and I disliked it for several reasons that I put to Dario. It would be slow and fragile. It was exactly what the distributor was making difficult on purpose. And whatever we built would break again at the next redesign, of which we would have no warning.

I asked what the distributor itself offered. It turned out that the site had a section for developers, which nobody on the team had read, with an interface that returned a product's price and stock as plain data, for registered customers, free up to 5,000 requests a day. Dario's company was already a customer, since they bought from it. The interface was no quicker to start with than a pattern, but it was documented, it was versioned, and its terms said what we were allowed to do with it, which the scraper's did not. The scraper had been living in the grey area between what a person with a browser may do and what a program may.

The script I wrote against the interface was about forty lines, less than the scraper, and it retrieved all 900 products in a single call to a list endpoint instead of 900 page loads. The data was richer: prices by quantity band, which the pages had hidden in a pop-up, and the date from which each price was valid. Two of the buyers had asked for exactly that for a year.

There was a loss. The scraper had seen the price that the website showed an anonymous visitor, and the interface returns the price for our account, which under Dario's contract is different on 37 of the 900 parts. I told him before he saw it in the numbers. He said the account price was the one his buyers actually pay, and that the old numbers had been a polite fiction.

We kept the old scraper's output for a month alongside the new, and then deleted the scraper. Dario wrote the distributor a short message to say thanks for the interface, and a person replied, to everyone's surprise, saying that hardly anyone ever used it.

At 08:05 on a Monday the dispatcher's map showed nine of the company's depots in open water. Not near the coast. In it, a long way from any land, in a pattern that made a tidy diagonal line, and she sent Mara a screenshot with no text except a question mark.

The map took the depots' positions from a table of latitudes and longitudes, and the table had been updated on the Friday evening with a new batch of depots from a spreadsheet kept by the property team. The depots already in the table were all in the right places. The nine new ones were not, and the question was why those nine.

I looked at the coordinates. A depot at about 51 degrees north and 6 east appeared in the table as 6 north and 51 east: the two numbers swapped. A latitude can only run from minus 90 to 90, so a swapped pair is often still a legal pair, which is why nothing refused it. For depots in the northern middle of one continent, the swap produces a perfectly valid position on the other side of the planet, or in the middle of an ocean. Had the depots been far to the east or west of the world, the longitude, which can reach 180, would have become an impossible latitude and the import would have rejected the row. Luck had picked exactly the region where the error is silent.

The cause was upstream, in a convention. The property team's spreadsheet gave positions as x, y, copied from a mapping website that writes longitude first, like a graph, while our table is latitude first, like a person speaking. Neither convention is wrong. The old depots had been entered by Teo, who knows the difference, and the new nine by a colleague who did not.

I could simply have swapped them. I did not, because I did not know for certain that all nine were swapped and not some, and a fix that changes data by a rule has to be tested against the ways the rule can fail. I listed all nine with a guess at where each should be, taken from its address, and compared. All nine were swapped. Teo and the dispatcher had each said so independently, and I counted that as a second witness, though the first was enough.

The change that matters is in the import. Coordinates are accepted only by name, lat and lon, never by position in the file. A pair that falls outside the region the company operates in is refused with the depot's name and the two values, and the message ends with the line 'if these look reversed, they probably are', which is the only joke I have allowed myself in an error message. The dispatcher, who does not read error messages, was shown one by Mara, laughed, and asked whether the depots could be out of the sea before the 9:00 run. They were.

I added one more check afterwards whose value I did not appreciate until I wrote it: each new depot must be within 400 kilometres of at least one other. A depot hundreds of kilometres from all the rest is more likely a mistake than an expansion.

The inspectors who use Tern said the app ate their batteries, and for once they had a number: a phone that began at 100 percent was at 52 by the end of a four-hour round, with the screen off most of the time. Wren called it the vampire and could not find the fangs.

You cannot hunt battery use by reading code, because the cost is not in the instructions but in what they wake. I asked Wren to run a four-hour round on a test phone with the operating system's own battery log switched on, and to send me what it recorded, not a feeling. The log is a list of things that kept the phone awake or its radios on, with durations. For four hours it said: location, 3 hours 58 minutes, at high accuracy; processor wake locks held, 71 minutes; mobile radio active, 96 minutes.

Each had a cause. The location: the app asked for the phone's position every ten seconds at the finest setting, so that it could stamp each inspection with a position and keep a route trace, and it never stopped asking, in a plant room or on a roof, in a pocket or in hand. The finest setting turns on the satellite receiver and keeps it on. The wake locks: during an upload the app asked the phone not to sleep, and released the request only when the upload finished, which on a poor signal could be an hour, with the phone doing nothing but holding on. The radio: the app tried to upload every five minutes, and on a weak connection each attempt kept the radio at full power for a minute before failing.

We went through them in turn. For the position I asked the question Wren had not: how often do the inspectors actually need it? An inspection needs its position once, at the moment it is saved. The route trace on the map was a feature Tobias had added for the managers and that no one had looked at in months, and the managers said they were happy to lose it for a battery. The app now asks for one fix when an inspection starts and another when it is saved, at a coarser setting that uses the phone's network position and is accurate to about twenty metres, which is plenty for a valve in a building. For the uploads, the wake request is held only while data is actually moving, and if no progress is made for thirty seconds it is released and the attempt retried after a pause that grows. For the radio, uploads are attempted when the phone reports a decent connection, and when an inspector gets back to the van.

The next four-hour round ended at 87 percent. Wren did it twice more to make sure, once in the rain, and got 85 and 88. The inspectors have not said a word about batteries since, which Wren was prepared to take as the best feedback there is, and which I told him was not feedback but silence, and that we should ask. We asked. Two said it was much better. One said he still charged his phone every night, out of habit.

Part number 00742 was received into the warehouse system as 742, and 742 was a different part, a pack of brass hinges, and for eleven days the shop sold drawer pulls on the strength of the hinges' stock, and hinges on the strength of the pulls'. Odile found out when a customer wrote to say that the box he had opened held a hundred hinges and he had ordered drawer pulls.

The cause was easy to see once I had the file in front of me and hard to see before. The supplier's stock file was a CSV. The supplier used five-character part numbers for new lines, with leading zeros, and the older lines kept their short numbers, so 742 was an old hinge and 00742 a new drawer pull. Somebody, back in the spring, had started opening the file in a spreadsheet to look at it before the import, and then saving it, because that is what the save key is for. A spreadsheet, seeing a column of digits, concludes that they are numbers and stores them as numbers, and a number has no leading zeros. Every part number beginning with a zero, about a fifth of them, lost its prefix on saving, and some collided with whatever older part happened to have the shorter number.

How many? I wrote a script to compare the saved file with the supplier's original for each of the last eleven days and list every row where the part number differed. Of 6,310 parts, 1,284 had lost zeros. For 1,203 of them there was no collision, because nothing else carried the shorter number, and the import had simply created a new part called 742 with the stock of 00742, which was harmless apart from an orphaned old part. For 81 there was a collision, and those 81 had received each other's stock.

The solution I would have chosen first was to ask people not to open the file. I did not choose it, because the habit of looking at a file is reasonable, and asking people to stop is how problems return in six months. I changed the import so that it reads the part number column as text and never as a number, by naming the column's type in one place. And I added a check from the other end of the problem: the import counts part numbers by length and stops, naming the row, if the count of five-character numbers falls by more than a few percent from the day before, since a file that has lost its zeros has lost a fifth of its long numbers at once.

For the eighty-one collisions I took the supplier's original file for each of the eleven days, recomputed the stock movements for those parts from it, and corrected the counts, and Odile and her staff counted twelve of them on the shelf to check. Twelve of twelve matched. She made me wait for the count before she let me close the ticket.

The customer got his drawer pulls, with a note, and wrote back that he had assumed it was the sort of thing that happens with brass.

The Calder Valley Coaches job began with a voicemail from Philippa Strand, who ran operations there and said she had eleven drivers, four of whom could not share a shift without a row, and a rota that lived in a spiral notebook. Mara called back on a Tuesday in March. The first call lasted fifty minutes and Mara spoke for perhaps ten of them. I kept the notes: the notebook rota, the rule that drivers must have eleven hours between shifts (which the notebook broke about twice a month without anyone noticing), and a list of preferences Philippa dictated from memory, down to who would not take the airport run on a Sunday.

Mara quoted a fixed 7,800 for a tool that would import last year's rota, check the rest rule, and print the week in a layout the drivers would read. Philippa asked for a day and came back with one condition: the printout had to fit on one side of A4, because the depot noticeboard was that size and she did not intend to change the noticeboard. That shaped everything. We drew the week as a grid with drivers down the side and rest violations marked by a thick border instead of a colour, because the depot photocopier turned every colour into the same grey, which Philippa mentioned only after the first draft had been printed and pinned up.

Delivery took five weeks. The hard part was the exceptions: a driver named Emeka whose licence kept him off the coaches over twelve metres, a school contract on Saturdays that moved every term, and Philippa herself overriding the tool by hand on three of the first ten days. Mara did not treat that as failure. She asked each time why, and two of the three overrides turned out to be one rule nobody had written down, that the Marchmont run needs a driver who has done it before. We added it as a field, and Philippa stopped overriding after the second week. I noticed, because I kept the log, that the tool's own flags were never wrong in those weeks, and that the human overrides were wrong about once in twelve. I did not say so to Philippa, who had earned her overrides, but it was a measure of the thing: the machine knew the rules and the person knew the exceptions, and the work was to move exceptions into rules without removing the person.

The last call, in May, is the one I remember best. Mara asked what Philippa would change, and the answer was small. She wanted the Sunday airport run to rotate fairly instead of going to whoever asked least loudly. It was a rule she had never dared say aloud, and she had only seen it was missing when the grid printed the unfairness in plain columns. I took from it that a tool shows people their own rules, including the ones they have never spoken. Mara took something plainer: she now asks every client, near the start, what they would never say in a meeting, and listens to the pause that follows.

We lost the Ostrander County Records Office bid on a Monday, by letter, and the letter was kind in the way that makes things worse. Mara had spent nineteen hours on it over two weeks: a public search over about 400,000 catalogue entries already typed up from old index cards, at a fixed price of 31,000. Lindqvist Hale, a firm with sixty staff, won at 58,000. The scoring table came attached. Price counted for thirty percent and Mara scored full marks on it. Quality counted for thirty and she scored well. Capacity and continuity counted for forty, and there she scored 9 out of 20.

She read the 9 aloud twice and then asked me whether I thought it was fair. I said I could not tell her it was unfair, because the proposal had a single sentence on the subject, that she was supported by trusted associates. A reader on a committee could not weigh that sentence, and the committee was spending public money for five years on a system that would need to be kept alive.
