Mara said nothing for a while and then said that she had spent twenty minutes on the discount and about one on that sentence, and the committee had not looked at the discount.

She asked for a debrief call, which the officer, Hollis Brandt, granted without fuss. He was frank. Nobody doubted her work. What the panel could not answer was what happened to the archive if she were ill for three months in year two, and he said nobody would have thought it a problem if there had been a page that answered it. Mara thanked him, wrote down his exact phrase, and asked whether he would be willing to read a revised continuity page for her next bid. He said he could not advise bidders but that he read everything.

Over the next fortnight she and I wrote that page. It names Yusra as deputy with access to the repositories, describes the documentation each project is handed over with, lists where the code and credentials are held and who can open them, and says in a plain sentence what the client does if Mara is unavailable for ninety days. It runs to one page and has appeared in every proposal since. Two clients have mentioned it in their award letters. The first was a housing trust, which wrote that the continuity page was the reason its committee had been unanimous. The second was a school group that asked, in the same letter, whether Yusra would be willing to be named in the contract. She was, and was delighted, and spent the next week describing herself to her friends as a continuity measure. I take two things from the Ostrander loss: that price is the part of a proposal an author controls and therefore over-polishes, and that the committee's real question is often the one nobody asked her to answer.

The report for the Marram Coast Tourism Partnership was due on a Friday, and on the Wednesday Wren sent it to the client without showing Mara the final pass. Wren was the editor on the job and Mara the analyst, an arrangement that had worked on six earlier reports. When Mara opened the sent copy that evening she found that the sentence on page 3, which she had written as visitor numbers fell by 11 percent between the two summers, now read that visitor patterns shifted in the period under review. The table beneath it was untouched and still said minus 11.

She was angrier than I had seen her about anything in months, and she did something I thought was wise: she did not write that night. She asked me to put the two sentences next to each other and to find the other places Wren had softened. There were three more, smaller. Then she went for a walk and phoned Wren the next morning at nine.

I heard only her side, since she typed notes afterwards. Wren's account was that the Partnership's director, Isolde, had been defensive in an earlier meeting and that a flat statement of the fall would end the funding conversation before the explanation, which was in the fourth section, could be read. Wren had thought she was protecting the work. Mara's answer, which she was pleased with, was that the explanation was only read if the number was believed, and a table that contradicted its own summary would make Isolde doubt every other figure. They spent twenty minutes agreeing about that and forty about who should have decided.

What they settled on is written at the top of their shared folder now. The person who owns a number owns the sentence that states it; the editor owns every other sentence and may query that one but not change it. The revised page 3 went out on Friday afternoon with the plain figure first and Wren's softer framing in a second paragraph after it, which was a better page than either original. Isolde called it the most useful thing the Partnership had been sent. I kept a note for myself, which is that when two people each feel they protected the client, the useful question is what each of them was afraid of, and Wren's fear, once named, was reasonable.

Joss started on a Monday, a part-time associate for three days a week, and Mara had prepared for it the way she prepares for most things, which is to write too much. The onboarding document was fourteen pages: how we quote, how we name files, who the clients are, what each client dislikes, the order in which to read the code. She had asked me to tidy it on Sunday night and I had, adding a contents list that I now think was an apology for the length.

Joss read it on Monday morning and shadowed two calls in the afternoon. On Tuesday they shadowed another and read the code. On Wednesday, at about eleven, Joss said quietly that they were glad to be here but were not sure what they were for yet. Mara told me this herself, a little ashamed. Joss had not complained. They had asked, politely, for something real to do, and Mara realised that for two and a half days she had been protecting them from the real work by calling it learning.

So that afternoon she gave Joss a small genuine task: take the export from a client's old booking system, take the new system's import, and tell her where they disagreed. It was a boring job and nobody else wanted it. By Thursday morning Joss had found nine discrepancies, two of which were real faults in the client's data and one a mistake in Mara's own mapping from the previous month. Mara told the client about her own mistake before she told them about their data. Joss was quiet for a moment when she said so, then said that they had assumed it would turn out to be Joss's mistake.

By the third week Joss was leading a short client call alone while Mara listened with her camera off. Afterwards Mara sent a message of four lines. She did not praise the call so much as repeat one question Joss had asked the client, because it was the question she herself would have forgotten. The onboarding document is now six pages, and the first line of it says that on the first day you will be given a real task, small, and that someone will wait for the answer.

I took one thing from this and want to keep it: shadowing without a task is waiting, however well meant. Mara's care had been real, and it had still left a new colleague sitting for two days with nothing to be wrong about, which is also nothing to be right about.

On a Thursday in October Mara decided to stop selling her data audits by the day. She had done six of them in two years, always at 620 a day, and the invoices ran from three days to nine. She asked me to lay the six out in a table, and the pattern was not subtle. The long ones were long because the client's data was worse than they had said, and the client paid for that worsening in full each time, with visible reluctance. The short ones were short because Mara was quick, and she was paid less for being quick. Her skill was being sold back to her as a discount.

The average was 5.1 days, which came to 3,162. She proposed 3,200 for a fixed two-week audit with a written list of what it covered: twelve named checks, a short report, and a call to walk through it. She was nervous about two things. One was that a client might hear fixed as limited. The other was that a bad dataset would cost her a week she could not bill.

The first client under the new arrangement was the Brightwater Dental group, and the audit took three and a half days, an effective rate of about 914 a day. She said nothing to them about this. The second, a few weeks later, for a small haulier, took eight, an effective 400, because the client's files turned out to be in two character encodings that had been mixed by hand over a decade. She grumbled for an afternoon and I did not argue, but I put the two results into the table beside the old six. Across all eight audits the blended figure came to within 3 percent of what the day rate would have produced.

What she did next was the part I thought was right. She did not conclude that nothing had changed, because something had: clients now knew the price before they started, and three of them said that was why they said yes. She added a sentence to the scope, that audits uncovering unrecorded character encodings or hand-edited key fields are quoted separately once found. She kept the fixed fee. I recorded that the experiment changed who bore the uncertainty and did not change the average, and that she chose to keep it for that reason alone.

The Aldermoor Chamber of Commerce asked Mara to run a breakfast session called Spreadsheets That Don't Lie To You, forty minutes, for about forty small business owners. She prepared thirty-eight slides, which I had warned her was nearly a slide a minute. The Chamber paid 400. She said afterwards that she would have paid them to cancel the first half hour.

It went flat almost at once. The room was courteous, they had been given pastries, and nobody wanted to be told about named ranges. At the twenty-minute mark a man near the back, Bertrand, who runs a glazing firm, said that his own sheet had a total that never matched the invoice pile and asked whether it was anyone's fault. A normal speaker would have said that was a good question and moved on. Mara asked if he had it on his laptop. He did.

She asked him to share it on the screen, stood beside the projector, and said that nothing she was about to find would be his fault. It took four minutes. A column of figures had been entered by hand in two different formats, and one range of cells had been merged to make it look tidier, so that the total quietly skipped the merged cells. She showed the room how to see it, by selecting the column and reading the count in the corner, a trick that takes ten seconds and that forty people had never been shown. Someone gasped. Two people took out their phones to photograph the screen.

For the last twenty minutes the slides were abandoned and the room brought sheets. Four people had the same merged-cell problem. By the end Mara had been asked for work by three of them, and she took one.

She asked me that evening to cut the talk down. It is now twelve slides, and the first one says bring a spreadsheet that annoys you. I do not think the lesson is that audiences like improvisation. It is that the room had been waiting to be asked what its own problem was, and a stranger's problem on a screen is more instructive than any prepared example, because everyone present can see themselves in it and nobody is being accused.

Callum suggested over dinner that he and Mara combine their practices. He is another independent consultant, a decade into the work, with a good name for performance problems and a spare room full of kit. His idea was a single firm with both their names on the door, shared overheads, and a pooled client list of nineteen. He had a figure in mind for the first year's turnover. He said it twice. Mara said she would think about it, and the next morning asked me to help her think properly.

She asked first what she would want to see in order to say yes. Between us we wrote four things: his real revenue for two years, the contracts for his three largest clients, how he handled disputes, and how he spoke about the clients he had lost. Callum agreed to the first two without hesitation and sent them in a shared folder on Friday. I read them with her.

The figures were honest and they were not what the dinner had suggested. One client supplied seventy-one percent of his income, under a rolling agreement that either side could end on thirty days' notice. His invoices were running about four months behind the work, which he explained as a cash habit and not a problem. His contracts had no limit on liability. None of this made him a bad consultant. It made the merger a bet that Mara would take on his concentration and his slow billing as shared risk, in return for a name on a door she did not particularly want.

She did not tell him no in an email. She asked for a meeting, and in the meeting she said, very plainly, that she admired his work and did not want to share a balance sheet with it. He was quiet and then laughed and said that was exactly what his wife had told him. They agreed instead to something smaller, which they have kept: each passes the other work they cannot take, and neither takes a cut. In the last six months this has been four referrals each way.

I took from this that a partnership proposal is best read from the paperwork first and the dinner second, and that a refusal can be given as an offer of something smaller. Mara added a line to her own notes, that she will not combine finances with anyone before reading their last two years of invoices.

The first Saturday of January, Mara and Yusra planned the year at Yusra's kitchen table with a pack of index cards, a pot of tea that went cold, and me on a laptop between the fruit bowl and the salt. It was their fourth year of doing it. The rule is that every card must be one sentence, and no card may say improve.

They began with money. The year before had come to 141,000, of which 104,000 came from clients she would call good. This year Mara wanted 148,000 and fewer hours, which Yusra pointed out cannot both be true unless the rate rises or the clients change. They settled on three themes written on three big cards. Fewer clients, meaning no more than six running at once. One small product, meaning the invoice-checking tool the associates already use, packaged so another practice could buy it. More writing, meaning one essay a month about how small organisations keep their records, whether or not anyone read it.

Then came the card Mara had been avoiding, which was the no list. She wrote that she would not take work under five days, would not take work from anyone who asks on the first call for a fixed deadline before the scope is known, and would not take the third project in any quarter. Yusra added a fourth, that she would not agree to anything on a Friday afternoon. Mara laughed and let it stand.

By September, I can say what held. The six-client limit held, and cost her one pleasant but small client, whom she sent to Wren. The essays reached eight of twelve. The product sold to two practices at 900 each, which was less than she had hoped and more than nothing, and Yusra said that two was exactly the number you want to learn from. Revenue ended near 139,000, below target, with eleven fewer weeks of work than the year before. Mara decided that was a fair trade and wrote it in her own notes in those words.

What I noticed about the day was how little the plan was a forecast and how much it was a list of things she had decided to be unwilling to do. Everything on the no list was something she had once said yes to, and regretted, and could name.

Ansgar and Dyer, a small firm of surveyors, had been Mara's client for four years, and in that time her day rate for them had not moved from 520. By autumn her rate for new clients was 640, and the gap had begun to feel to her like a secret she was keeping from herself. She decided to raise the rate for Ansgar and Dyer by eighteen percent, to 614, from the new quarter, and to tell Ansgar Weller, the senior partner, by phone, not by email. Then she asked me to help her rehearse, which I had not been asked to do for a call like this one before.

She told me how Ansgar talked. He was brisk, warm until money was mentioned, and had a habit of saying with respect, which meant the opposite. I played him. In the first rehearsal I made him gentle, because it was the version I thought most likely, and Mara read her prepared sentences with the pace of a person reading out a will. At the end she said that was too easy and that I was being kind to both of us. She asked for a hard Ansgar. In the second rehearsal I had him say that eighteen percent was a figure that would cause the partners to look at alternatives, and Mara stumbled, apologised for the increase, and offered a discount before she had stated the reason. We both noticed. She wrote on a card, do not apologise for the price, and put the card on her monitor.

The third rehearsal was good. She said three things in order: the rate had not changed in four years, her work for them had grown from a quarter of a day each week to nearly two, and the new rate would apply from the first of January. Then she stopped talking, which is the part people find hardest, and waited.

The real call took eleven minutes. She told me afterwards that Ansgar did not do any of the things I had acted. He was silent for a moment, then said that eighteen percent was less than he had expected. He had thought, from the tone of her request for a call, that she was going to tell him she was leaving. He asked whether the rate would hold for the whole year, and Mara said it would, and he asked if she could take on two more days a month for the firm's new inspection scheduling, which she said she could.

I have thought since about why my hard Ansgar was wrong. I had cast him as angry because the number was large, but he was thinking about the fear that a four-year arrangement was ending. The hard version was useful practice for Mara and a poor guess at the person. What I keep from it is the habit of asking, before a rehearsal, what the other person is worried about, and not only what they would say.

Mirela Dragovic, who owns the Granite Hall climbing gym, hired Mara to build a booking system for classes. The fee was 9,000 and the brief was one page. In the second week Mara asked, as she always does before building, to see where the members came from, and Mirela opened three programs on the office computer.

The door fobs lived in one, with 2,300 names and an expiry date. Payments lived in another, with monthly subscribers, some of whom no longer climbed. Class sign-ups lived in a third, a free tool Mirela's former manager had set up, in which members were identified by whatever name they typed. Each system had its own idea of who a member was. A woman called Dani Okafor existed as D. Okafor, Danielle O'Kafor and a number. Nobody knew, and Mirela said this herself with some cheer, how many members the gym had.

Mara thought for a day and then told Mirela, in a short call, that she could build the booking system but that it would fail within a month, because it would have to guess who each person was. She proposed turning the first phase into a clean list of members, matched across the three systems with a human check of the doubtful cases, and then putting classes on an off-the-shelf booking tool that would cost Mirela nothing to adopt. The project changed from a build of 9,000 to a cleanup of 4,500 and about 1,200 of set-up, with no custom software. It was a loss to Mara of a little over three thousand, and she said so to me in a flat voice before she told Mirela anything.

She and I spent three weeks on the matching. We found 2,310 fobs, 1,640 paying members and 1,880 distinct people in the sign-up tool, and after Mirela's staff reviewed the 212 doubtful pairs we arrived at 1,973 real members. Mirela printed the number and pinned it behind the till.

I recorded what I think was the decision's core. Mara had been hired for what the client asked for, and she chose the thing the client needed, at her own cost. It worked because she told the client the price of the wrong choice and not only the price of the right one. Mirela sent three further jobs the following year, all small and all paid on the day.

The invitation to speak at Fenmere Developers' Day came with a slot of twenty-five minutes, a stage with a lectern she hated, and a topic she chose herself: small tools for small organisations, meaning the quiet, ugly, useful things she builds for people with eight staff. Her first deck had sixty slides. She knew it was too long and could not say which to cut, so she asked me to time her.

I can only time what she tells me, so we did it by voice notes. She read each slide aloud into her phone and sent me the file with its length, and I kept a column. The first full run was forty-one minutes. The second, after she had cut a case study she loved, thirty-three. The third was twenty-nine, and she was cross, because every slide that remained seemed to hold up another. Then she did something I had not suggested. She printed the deck, laid the slides across the floor of the spare room, stood on the sofa to look at them, and told me afterwards that the shape was obvious from there: three stories, each with a problem, a tool and a number, and the rest was commentary on the stories.

She kept the three stories and removed the commentary. The deck became twenty-two slides. The stories were a seed library's loans, a tennis club's court bookings and a mobile library's stock list, and the numbers were forty minutes a week saved, one double-booking in a whole season, and 300 titles found that had been written off as lost. Her last rehearsal came in at 23 minutes 40 seconds, which left a minute for water and a breath.

On the day she finished at 24 minutes 10. A woman at the back asked how she knew when a tool was finished, and Mara said when the person who uses it stops asking for changes and starts asking about something else. Two people found her afterwards, one with a job, and another to say that the number about the lost titles was the only one she would remember.

I noted for my own use that cutting is a kind of listening. She did not decide what mattered by arguing with herself; she looked at the shape of the whole, and the shape told her.

The decision to end work with Ravensworth Logistics was made, if I am honest, in about four seconds, on a Tuesday call. Mara had worked for them for eleven months on a route-costing tool. The owner, Desmond Rae, paid on time and knew what he wanted. He also, as Mara had told me more than once, spoke to people as if checking whether they were awake. Tobias had joined the call to demonstrate a small screen he had built, and when he finished, Desmond said, in front of two of his own staff, that it was a pretty picture, that the boy should stop wasting everyone's time with pictures, and that Mara should send someone who understood costing.

Tobias said nothing. Mara said that they would take a short break and she muted the line. I saw it in her notes later, in one line: I did not say anything good. She came back on and said evenly that the screen was Tobias's work, that it was correct, and that she wanted it discussed on its merits. Desmond laughed and moved on.

That night she wrote the letter. It was short and I only helped with the dates. It gave thirty days' notice under the contract, offered a full handover with documentation, and named the state of every open item. It did not name the reason. When she asked me whether it should, I said I thought he knew, and that a reason invited an argument she had no wish to win. She said, you are right, and I would have liked to put in a joke about weather.

Desmond called the next morning, first at eight and again at nine-thirty. On the second call he apologised, though not in those words. He said that he had perhaps been a little hard on the boy and that they should carry on as before. Mara thanked him and said she had made her decision, and that she would finish the thirty days properly. She did. The last invoice, for 3,900, was paid in nine days, and the handover document was thirty-one pages.

Tobias heard about it from her, in person, not from me. What I take from the episode is the thing she said to me at the end of that week, that the money she gave up was small next to the lesson Tobias would have learned if she had let it pass. A client is allowed to be difficult. A client is not allowed to be the reason a colleague learns to stay silent.

For the veterinary group job, Mara and Teo had agreed on a structure that seemed neat: Teo's firm, Tern Systems, would hold the contract with the practice group and invoice them, and Mara would bill Tern for her share of the application work. It saved the group dealing with two suppliers. The arrangement worked for two months. In the third, Teo's payment for Mara's September invoice, 6,240, did not arrive on the due date, or the week after.

Mara waited longer than I would have. She told me she did not want to nag a friend. On the eleventh day past due she sent a short, friendly message and received a reply from Teo that was an emoji and nothing else. At day twenty she phoned. Teo picked up on the fourth ring and sounded, she said, like a man who had been avoiding the call for a week and was relieved it had happened. The practice group had been slow to pay Tern, and Tern's own bank had tightened an overdraft, so he had been paying wages first and suppliers second. He had not wanted to tell her because she was one of the people he was supposed to pay.

What she did next was, I think, wise and a little brave. She did not demand the money. She said that she understood, that she needed it, and that she wished to change the structure so that she would never again be in the position of waiting on a friend's cash flow. Teo suggested a payment plan of three instalments. Mara agreed to that and asked, in the same call, to bill the practice group directly from the next phase, with Tern invoicing separately for its own part. Teo was quiet and then said that it was better for him too, since he would no longer be carrying her wages on his books.

The instalments arrived on the dates promised, the last one two days early. The practice group, when told of the change, did not mind at all and said that they had wondered why the invoices came in two shapes. I recorded two things. One was that Mara had learned that a pass-through structure, which saves the client trouble, leaves the subcontractor depending on the middle party's cash. The other was that her kindness toward Teo and her firmness about the structure were not in conflict. She had assumed they would be, and the call showed her that they were not.

Hollin Ridge Wines asked for a stock system for their cellar, and Mara quoted fourteen days at 620, a fixed 8,680. She had walked through the cellar in July with the cellar master, Octavian, and watched him record a barrel movement in a notebook in about eleven seconds. The job looked simple. I had put a line in the quote saying that it assumed a clean import of the existing records, and she crossed it out as fussy.

The records were not clean, though not in the way she had feared. They were clean in Octavian's own private language. The cellar book, which went back to 1988 and had been kept by three people, used abbreviations that were consistent within each hand and not between them. One cellar master wrote B for barrique and another wrote B for a blend. A tank was named Old Pink in one decade and tank 7 in the next, and the vintage was sometimes the year of harvest and sometimes the year of bottling. Mara spent six days just on a dictionary of what each mark meant, with Octavian on the phone in the evenings, glad to help but, as he said, never having had to explain it before.

The job took twenty-three days. Nine of them were unpaid, 5,580 at her own rate. She did not write to the owner to ask for more. I raised the question once, gently, and she said that the fixed price was her decision, that she had underestimated, and that bringing the matter to the client would turn her error into his problem. I did not agree entirely, because the scope as written did not include building a dictionary. But I noted that she had the right to choose and she chose.

She also made a change that is now in her own notes in capital letters. Before she quotes any job that involves existing records, she asks to see the ugliest example, not the typical one, and to hear the person who keeps them explain a line they find embarrassing. She has done this on four jobs since. Three times the ugly example altered the quote, and once it altered her decision to quote at all. The nine days were expensive and what they bought was a better question, which seems to me a fair price for a question she will use for the rest of her working life.

The Institute of Soil and Water Studies put its lab inventory out to tender in spring, and Mara answered the thirty-one questions in a weekend. She scored second on price and first on understanding of the problem, which she attributed to having spent a morning on the phone with the lab manager, Dr Imogen Faraday, before writing a word. The contract came to 17,400 over four months. It was the largest she had won that year and the first from a university.

The first visit to the lab changed the design. Imogen walked her through the freezer room, a corridor of upright units humming at minus eighty, and showed her the rack system: boxes of vials in racks in freezers, all identified by labels written in marker by whoever had put them there. The labels smudged. The cold made some of them peel. A researcher who left the institute in 2019 had left behind four boxes of vials marked only with initials and a date, and nobody dared throw them out. Mara had planned barcodes on the vials. She now understood that the vials were not the problem. The problem was that a label had to survive the freezer, and a person's glove, and being written in a hurry.

She spent the first two weeks not on software but on labels. She found a supplier of cryogenic label stock that holds at minus eighty, tested six samples overnight in the lab's spare freezer, and brought the three survivors back to Imogen. The printer, a thermal one, cost 340. The software that came afterwards was simple: a box, a rack, a position, a person, a date, and the number of the freezer. I wrote most of the import from the old spreadsheets, which had four tabs and three different ways of writing a date.

Delivery was on time, and Imogen reported at the close that the first retrieval, which used to take her about twenty minutes of walking and squinting, took under two. The four orphan boxes were scanned, identified from a freezer log nobody had thought to open, and either discarded with permission or returned to the people responsible.

What Mara carries from this, and what I record, is the thing she said on the train home from the first visit. She said that she would not have thought of labels, and that she had only seen it because she had stood in the room. She now asks to see the place where the work happens before she sizes a tender, and builds the visit into the first quote as a paid half-day.

In November Mara was carrying three projects that all wanted to finish before Christmas, and she did something she had put off for years: she asked another consultant to take one of them. Ilse had recommended a man called Imre Bakos, solo like Mara, who did careful work and answered email. The project was a stock-ordering tool for Harrow Foods, a wholesaler, about two-thirds done.

The handover was my part, mostly. I took her notes, the repository, six months of email, and drafted a document of six pages: what the tool does, how it is built, what the client wants next, what the client says they want next but does not, where each credential is held, and a list of things Mara had promised verbally. That last section was the most important and the hardest, because she had to remember what she had said on calls. She read my draft out to me line by line and corrected it. At the fourth read she remembered that she had promised the owner's brother that the tool would print in landscape.

We could not find in her notes the one thing the document turned out to lack, which was that at Harrow Foods the owner's wife, Gwendolen, answers the phone on Wednesdays and decides most things, though nobody had ever said so. Mara had learned it by the third week and never written it down. Imre learned it on his second call, when a delivery date he had agreed with the owner was cancelled at once by a person he had not known existed. He phoned Mara, amused rather than annoyed, and she spent three hours that evening, unbilled, telling him what she knew about the household of the firm.

The project finished in January with Imre's name on the last invoice. Harrow Foods wrote to Mara saying they had hardly noticed the change, which she took as the compliment it was. Imre sent her a bottle of something amber and a note saying that the handover document was the best he had been given. She kept the six pages as a template.

What I take from it is that a handover is the act of writing down what a person has been carrying in her head, and the first draft will always miss whatever she has stopped noticing. The thing missed was the one thing nobody had ever been told.

When Brennerwood Estates, a company managing about two hundred rented houses, told Mara that they would call two of her references before deciding, she gave them the two names she was most comfortable with. One was a plant nursery whose project had gone smoothly from first call to last invoice. The other was a school bursar for whom she had done a tidy five-day job. Both were warm and could be relied on to say so.

Brennerwood called both. She learned about it a week later, when she was awarded the work and the property manager, Hester Quill, mentioned it. Hester said, with some amusement, that the nursery had said Mara was excellent and had nothing particular to add, and that the bursar had said the same in different words. What had actually decided Hester, she said, was a third conversation. She had found on Mara's own website an old project for a private clinic that had overrun, and she had called the clinic's manager at random.

Mara went cold, she told me, when she heard this. That project had been the worst she had run. It had finished six weeks late. The manager, a man named Anselm Rook, had been difficult in the second month and she had been difficult back. She had not offered him as a reference and she would not have. What he told Hester, as Hester relayed it, was that the delay was real, that Mara had told him in the third week that it would happen and why, that she had taken the cost of the delay on herself, and that the thing she delivered at the end worked on the first day. Hester said the part that decided her was the third week.

Afterwards Mara phoned Anselm to thank him. He did not remember being generous; he remembered being annoyed. She asked me to change the way she chooses references. I now keep a note against each past client of what went wrong and how she handled it, in one line, because those are the stories a stranger will ask about, and the smooth projects reassure no one. Her new rule is that she offers one reference from a project that went well and one from a project that went badly, and tells the prospective client which is which.

I take from it that a client who hires on trust is not looking for an absence of trouble. They are looking for evidence of what she does when trouble arrives, and a smooth project contains none.

Sunniva Aaltonen managed the Tidewell Mutual project for the client side, and for five months she and Mara had worked as if on the same team. In October she told Mara over a short call that she had taken a job elsewhere and would leave in two weeks. Mara congratulated her sincerely and, as soon as the call ended, asked me to open the decisions list.

We keep one for every project, written in plain lines: the date, the thing decided, who decided it, and where it was said. There were twenty-three entries for Tidewell. They included small things such as the colour of the status marks, and large ones such as the choice to leave out the claims history until phase two, which had taken three meetings and an argument. Each had a line from an email or a call in which Sunniva had said yes.

Her successor, Roderick, arrived on a Monday. He was clever and in a hurry, and in his first week he told Mara that the project should include claims history now, because the director had asked about it. Mara did not argue. She sent him the list. He read it that evening and replied next morning that he accepted twenty of the twenty-three, wanted to reopen three, and asked what reopening cost.

Mara had been braced for a fight. She told me she was moved by how easy it was once the record was in front of them. The three he reopened included the claims history, and she quoted the extra days plainly: nine, at the project's rate. Roderick took the quote to his director and it was approved by Thursday. If the list had not existed, she said, there would have been three weeks of everyone's recollection against everyone's recollection, with Sunniva unreachable at her new desk.

Sunniva sent Mara a card on her last day, which said that it had been a pleasure being managed back. Mara kept it. For the record, I note that the list was built by writing things down at the time, which cost us a few minutes in each call, and that it paid for itself in a single morning in October. I also note that Roderick asked, later, if he could borrow the format for his own other projects.

The email from Pellam & Roe came at 8:40 on a Monday morning and had no greeting. It said that, following the announcement of the merger with Hartwick Finch, all supplier work was paused with immediate effect pending review, and that no further hours should be incurred. Mara read it twice and then read it to me. She had been three weeks into a twelve-week project to rebuild the firm's client-onboarding forms, and she had spent fifteen days on it. The contract was for 36,000.

She did not reply at once. She asked me to find the termination clause in the contract she had signed, and I read it out. Either party could end the agreement on thirty days' written notice. Work done to the date of termination would be paid in full. Where the client ended the agreement without cause, a fee of forty percent of the unbilled balance would be payable. Mara had insisted on the last sentence in March, against the client's lawyer, and had been told it was unusual. I had highlighted it then and I remember that she had said she did not expect ever to need it.

She waited until Wednesday, because she wished to write when she was not angry, and then sent a two-paragraph reply that acknowledged the pause, stated that the contract provided notice and a fee, and enclosed the clause. She invoiced fifteen days at 600, which was 9,000, and set out the fee, a calculation of 40 percent of 27,000, which came to 10,800. The client's finance director, Beatrix Laing, phoned on Friday. She did not dispute the days. She said the fee was a very large sum for an interrupted project and that the merger committee would never approve it.

Mara had prepared for exactly this. She asked me beforehand what she would accept, and we wrote three numbers on a card: 10,800 as her opening, 6,000 as the point at which she would consider the matter closed, and 4,500 as the figure below which she would walk away and accept the days alone. She also decided what she would give in return: she would hand over every form and every note she had made, cleaned, as though the project were finishing normally.

Beatrix countered at 3,000. Mara said that the handover alone was worth more than that to the client and that she would accept 6,500. They landed at 6,000 after eleven minutes, with the handover as a condition. The total, with the days, was 15,000, against 36,000 if the project had continued. Mara said it was the best bad outcome she had had.

I record for myself two points. First, that the clause paid, and that it paid because she had asked for it when asking was awkward and an old warning that she would not need it was still in her ears. Second, that her calm came from preparation: three numbers on a card, written before the call, took the heat out of a conversation in which a firm had just told her that her work had been paused by a merger. She said later that she had never been less afraid of a negotiation, and I think that was why.

Kesia arrived from the college on a Monday for a six-week placement, a quiet seventeen-year-old in a grey cardigan who sat for the first morning with her hands in her lap. Mara had agreed to the placement because a teacher she respected had asked, and she had no plan beyond giving Kesia a desk and a small project. The project was a tool to turn Mara's rough meeting notes into a tidy list of actions. It was a poor tool and a good exercise, and Kesia built it slowly and with great care.

The thing I remember from the six weeks happened in the fourth. Mara took Kesia to a client call, as she had said she would, and told her beforehand to just listen. The client was a regional furniture seller, Lowell & Reeve, and the call was about a delivery dashboard. Their operations manager gave a figure for orders delivered last month: 1,840. Mara wrote it down. Kesia raised her hand, a literal hand, on the video call, and when invited asked: what counts as delivered, the day it leaves the warehouse or the day it arrives?

There was a pause. The operations manager said that it was when it left. The finance director, who had joined late, said that it was when it arrived, and that he had been reporting arrivals to the board for two years. The two figures were four days apart. There was a short, polite uproar. Mara told me she sat very still, thinking that she had been on forty such calls and had never asked that, because she had assumed that a word like delivered meant what she thought it meant.

The dashboard design changed that week to show both dates and the gap between them, which Lowell & Reeve have since said is the most used column. Mara told Kesia afterwards that the question was better than anything she had asked in the whole call. Kesia went pink and said she had only wanted to understand.

On the last Friday Kesia presented her tool to Mara and the associates. It still had bugs, and it had one useful feature, which was that it marked any action without an owner in red. Mara has used it since. Kesia's placement report, which Mara signed, said that she had learned a great deal. The line I would have added, if I could, is that Mara had too.

The contract that came back from the lawyers of Wexley Care Homes had the usual pages, and on page eleven it had a clause I read twice, because it said that the supplier's liability under the agreement was unlimited. Mara's fee for the job, a resident-records tool for six homes, was 22,000. Unlimited liability on 22,000 was an arrangement under which one bad week could cost her house.

She was not frightened. She was irritated, and she asked me to prepare her. I wrote down three positions. The first was to ask that liability be capped at the fees paid, which is the usual form. The second was a cap at twice the fees, as a concession. The third, which she disliked, was a cap at the amount her insurance would pay, about a million, on the grounds that anything above it would fall on her insurer and not on her. We rehearsed the order in which she would offer them.

The more useful part of the preparation was a phone call she made to her insurance broker, a woman called Lucinda Perrow whom she had not spoken to in two years. Lucinda told her three things I had not known. Her professional indemnity policy had a limit of 1,000,000 per claim, and that was what she could honestly offer a client as comfort. The policy excluded liability that she had assumed by contract beyond what the law already imposed, so an unlimited clause could void her cover for exactly the claim it described. And the insurer would, if asked, write a short letter confirming her cover for a client.

With this Mara phoned the Care Homes' solicitor, a patient man named Everard, and said that she could not sign page eleven, because it would invalidate her insurance, and that she would provide the insurer's letter. She proposed a cap of twice the fees, and said that she was prepared to go to the full million for any breach of data protection, which was the risk the homes actually feared. Everard said that was reasonable and that he would take it to his client. The client agreed on Thursday.

I record for myself that she did not win by being stubborn. She won by finding out what the other side was frightened of, which was a leak of residents' records, and offering to be generous precisely there, while holding firm where her own survival depended on it. The broker's call cost her nothing, and she resolved to make it every January. I kept the insurer's letter, a single page that named the policy limit and the period of cover, and put the renewal date in her diary three weeks ahead, because a clause that refers to a cover is only as good as the date the cover runs out. She had not thought of that. Everard had, and said so in a kind postscript.

The converted print works on Fell Street had three desks free in a room shared with other small firms, and the landlord offered them to Mara, Wren and Dario at 210 a month each on a twelve-month lease. For six years Mara had worked from her spare room, and the offer arrived in the same week that her spare room had begun to feel, she said, like a place she kept returning to out of habit.

She asked me to help her weigh it, which in practice meant making a table of what she knew. The desk would cost 2,520 over the year. The journey was twenty-five minutes each way, which at her rate was a good deal more than the desk if she went every day and almost nothing if she went twice. She worked best, she had told me, early, and the print works did not open its doors until eight. She was lonely on some days and had not said so aloud until she wrote it into the table under the heading other.

She negotiated three things with the landlord, a man named Percival who spoke fondly of the ink-stained floor. A six-month break clause, which he gave. A lockable cabinet, which he said was extra and then, after a pause, included. And a reduction to 190 if all three signed before the end of the month, which they did.

For the first month she went four days a week, and her work, by her own account, suffered. She loved the company, particularly Dario's habit of narrating his own debugging as though to a nervous audience, and she got little done. In the second month she settled into two days at the print works, Tuesdays and Thursdays, which she reserved for calls and for anything that needed other people, and kept three days at home for work needing silence. Wren, who had expected to be there daily, was surprised to find that Mara had arranged the week as a grid, and said so with affection.

At the six-month break she renewed. I recorded that the decision to rent had been right for a reason she had not predicted: she had not wanted to work in an office but had wanted to be somewhere, on certain days, where other people were also trying to work. The cabinet, incidentally, has held nothing but a kettle.

The Harbour Small Business Fund asked Mara to sit on the panel that reviewed applications for its autumn round of grants, a day's work for a modest fee and a good lunch. There were fourteen applicants, each asking for between 3,000 and 12,000, and the panel of five had to agree a ranking by the end of the afternoon. She prepared by reading all fourteen, and asked me to build a plain table of what each applicant would do, what it would cost, and what they had already tried.

On the tenth application she stopped. The applicant was a company called Stillwater Bikes, and its owner, Felix Armitage, had been a client of hers two years earlier. She had built him a stock sheet. She had not spoken to him since, but she knew his business, thought well of it and had been named in the application as a possible reference.

She told the panel's chair, Rosalind, in the corridor before the session began. She said that she had worked for the applicant and would like to step out of the discussion of that application. Rosalind thanked her and said that this was exactly why the fund asked panellists to declare, and that it was rare for anyone to do it before being asked. When the panel reached the tenth application Mara left the room and sat in the hallway with a cup of tea.

When she returned she was told the panel had ranked Stillwater fifth of fourteen, which was above the line and would be funded. She did not know whether her step out of the room had helped or hurt him, and she told me she was glad not to know. The day's other effect was on her, because the panel had been so serious about the other thirteen. One applicant had asked for 4,200 to put a roof on a smoking shed for a smokehouse, and the discussion of it had lasted twenty minutes.

I noted that I should have asked her beforehand whether she knew any of the applicants, since the question costs nothing and would have let me flag it when I built the table. I noted that her instinct to declare early had been right. And I noted that she left lunch early to buy a card for Felix and then did not send it, because she thought it might look like a message. She put it in a drawer.

Ullswick Water had asked Mara to build a single dashboard of how many customers it served, and she suggested that before anyone drew a chart they should spend a morning in a room together answering one question: what is an active customer? Six departments sent someone. Billing, customer service, the metering team, communications, the regional office and the finance director. The meeting was on a Tuesday in a room with a whiteboard and a plate of biscuits that nobody touched until eleven.

She asked each person to write their definition on the board without conferring. The billing manager wrote: a customer with an account that has been billed in the last twelve months. Customer service wrote: a customer who has contacted us or paid us in the last twelve months. Metering wrote: a property with a working meter that has been read in the last year. Communications wrote that it was anyone on the mailing list. The regional office wrote: a household on the register of residents. Finance wrote: an account not in arrears of more than ninety days.

There was a long silence. Then the metering manager, a dry man named Cormac, laughed and said that he had been presenting his number of 41,000 against billing's 36,500 at a quarterly meeting for three years, and each time they had assumed one of them was wrong. Nobody had been wrong. They had been counting different things and calling them by the same name.

Mara did not try to pick the winner. She asked what each definition was for, and wrote the answers beside it. Billing's was for revenue, customer service's for workload, metering's for infrastructure. She proposed that the dashboard show three numbers, each with its purpose, and that the word active should be retired from the company's reports altogether. It took another eleven weeks and two further meetings to settle the wording, and the finance director held out for his definition until the last.

I took this from the morning: that an argument about a number is often an argument about a word, and that the quickest way to stop it is to make people write the word down before they say what it means. The biscuits, for the record, were all gone by noon.

Lorraine Tuck, chair of the Saint Aldric's Primary parents' association, wrote to Mara in April asking whether she could help with the summer fete's volunteer sign-up, which had run for years on a clipboard and a lot of shouting. The fete had two hundred and sixty volunteer slots and about ninety volunteers, and every year several people turned up at the wrong stall. Mara said she would do it for a charity rate and quoted 600, about forty percent of what the job would normally cost.

Lorraine wrote back to say, with great firmness, that she would not accept a discount. The association had 1,100 in its fete budget set aside for exactly this and she preferred to pay the proper price, because she did not wish it said that the school had begged. Mara read that aloud to me twice. She had a pleasant half-minute of being offended, then recognised it as a kind of respect.

I helped her think about what to do, though I was not sure it needed thinking. Her usual price for the job was about 1,500, which the association did not have. The proper price, in Lorraine's terms, was whatever the association could pay, spent without shame. Mara wrote back to say that she would take 1,000, that it was a fair price for a small job done carefully, and that she would also donate a plain cake. Lorraine said that this was acceptable.

The sign-up tool was small: a page, a list of slots, a name, a phone number, and a text message the night before. In the first weekend, 71 people signed themselves up. Over the following three weeks the number reached 118, and on the day of the fete only two stalls had too few volunteers and none had too many. Lorraine told Mara that the head had stood on the field with a clipboard in his hand and said, for the first time in his tenure, that he had nothing to do.

I took two things from it. One was that Mara's instinct to discount was a form of generosity, but the instinct to be paid was also a form of respect, and the two did not have to be in conflict. The other was a small practical point, which is that the 1,000 was not a charity price but a fair price for the job, and that the sums she and Lorraine both held in their heads had been about right.

Lionel Hesketh, who ran a landscape architecture practice of nine people and was Mara's client for the plant-order system, had a habit that had grown by degrees. In the spring he began to phone on Sunday evenings, usually between seven and eight, with what he called a quick question. The first was whether a supplier's code could contain letters. The second was whether Mara thought the screen should be green. By June he was phoning most Sundays, and Mara, who is polite, answered most of them.

She did not complain to him. She complained to me, in a mild way, on a Monday. She said that the calls took only a few minutes each, but that the evening was ruined by the expectation of them. She had begun to flinch at her own phone. Then she added that she did not think Lionel knew he was doing anything unusual, since he worked on Sundays himself and assumed that everyone who mattered did.

We worked out what she wanted. She did not want him to stop asking; his questions were often good. She wanted a different place for them. She drafted a message, which I trimmed, that said she answered questions on weekdays between nine and five, that she would reply to written ones within a working day, and that for anything urgent, defined as something that could cost him a delivery before Monday, he could phone. She sent it on a Thursday, fearing it would sound cold.

Lionel replied within the hour. He said that he had not realised, that he was embarrassed, and that he would write his questions down as they came to him and send them in a bunch on Monday mornings. He did exactly this. The Monday emails were numbered, and he took pride in them. In September he told Mara that he had stopped working on Sundays himself, partly out of a wish not to leave his own questions half asked.

What I note is that nothing in the arrangement was hard. The difficulty was the first sentence of the message, which took Mara three days. Her fear had been of seeming ungenerous, and the actual result was a client who was more generous with his own time. I also note that the number of urgent calls since then, by my count, is one.

Ashgrove Joinery, a furniture maker with eight employees and a well-kept workshop, put Mara on a retainer of twelve hours a month in January. The price was 700 a month, a modest discount against her day rate in exchange for being reliably available. Mara had been uneasy about retainers, because she had seen colleagues sell hours that were never used and hours that were used all at once. When the first anniversary came, she asked me to go through the year.

I counted the hours from her time log. Across twelve months the retainer had been used for a total of 112 hours, an average of 9.3 a month, with a range from none, in August, to nineteen, in the month the firm moved premises. The jobs were a mix. The quotation template, which she rebuilt twice. A stock sheet for veneers. A fix to the contact form on the website that had been sending enquiries to a former employee for four months. An evening of talking through whether to buy a laser cutter, which she would not have billed as work but which the owner, Kerensa Bligh, counted as the most useful hour of the year.

At the review lunch Mara put the numbers on the table and said that the firm was paying for twelve hours and using nine, and that she would be happy to reduce the retainer to nine. Kerensa was silent for a moment and then said that she did not want it reduced. She said that the retainer was not hours but an assurance that if the quotation template broke on a Friday she would not be on her own. She would pay for the assurance.

Mara explained that she had worried about taking money for time she did not work. Kerensa said, kindly, that it was the time Mara did not work that she was buying. They agreed to keep twelve hours, and added a rule that unused hours, up to six, would roll into the next month, so that the busy months would not feel like debts.

I put the lesson in the plainest terms I could. A retainer sells availability, and the number of hours is the way availability is measured, not the thing itself. Mara accepted this slowly, and when she told Wren about it later she said that she had been trying to be honest about the arithmetic and had missed what the arithmetic was for.

Northmere Utilities paid its suppliers at sixty days. This was written into its standard contract, and the procurement officer, Quentin Ashby, had said on the phone that it was not negotiable and not even, strictly, in his power. Mara had accepted it the first time, in the spring, because the contract was large. By October, after two invoices of 9,000 each had waited the full sixty days, she asked me to work out what it was costing her.

I used her overdraft rate of 9.4 percent. On a 9,000 invoice, sixty days of waiting cost her about 139. That was small. What she disliked was less the cost than the effect on her planning: when she took on other work she had to subtract Northmere's money from the months in which she needed it, and it was never there. She also pointed out, correctly, that Northmere could pay a supplier in thirty days if it chose, since it did so for any supplier under a certain size, and she had found this in the supplier handbook.

She decided to ask, and wrote herself a script. She would not argue about fairness. She would state that the payment term was longer than the sector's standard, that she was a sole supplier with no cash buffer for it, and that she asked to be treated under the small supplier terms, in section 14, because her invoices were under 10,000. She asked me to find the clause and to quote it exactly. It said that suppliers with fewer than ten employees and invoices under 10,000 could be paid in thirty days on request. Nobody had told her to request it. She checked the date on the handbook, which was three years old, and then checked that the clause had not been withdrawn in a newer edition, which cost her forty minutes of reading a document written entirely in the passive voice. I noted that she did this before she phoned and not after, because a request that rests on a clause that has lapsed is worse than no request.

Quentin, when she called, was quiet for a moment. He said that he had never been asked to apply it. He took the request to someone and called back the next day to say it was approved, with effect from the next invoice. For invoices above 10,000 the sixty days still applied, but Mara said, gently, that she would keep her milestones below the line, which suited the project in any case.

I record, for the next time, the shape of what worked. She had read the handbook, which almost no supplier reads. She had asked for something the organisation had already promised, which cost them nothing. And she had said nothing about her own hardship that was not a number. The following invoice was paid on day twenty-eight, and Quentin sent a one-line email with a smiling face, which Mara forwarded to Yusra without comment.

Brightfield Housing Association had put out a request for a tool to track repairs reported by residents, and Mara wrote the proposal over a weekend in her usual shape: the problem, the approach, the plan, the price, the references. On Sunday afternoon, when she thought she had finished, she read it to me and then said that it sounded like every other proposal she had ever received. She asked what she could add that no other bidder would.

We talked about it for an hour. At some point I asked what she had refused to do in the past, and she answered at length, and then she stopped and said she thought that was the paragraph. She wrote it in twenty minutes and gave it a plain title, What I will not do. It said that she would not build a custom application where a spreadsheet and a shared mailbox would do the job, because then the association would pay for something it would also have to maintain. It said that she would not touch residents' personal details until the association's data protection officer had agreed in writing what she could see. And it said that she would not name a delivery date before she had seen a week of real repair requests, because a date given before then would be a guess dressed as a promise.

She was afraid it might cost her the job. A proposal is supposed to say yes, and this paragraph said no three times. She sent it at ten the next morning anyway, with a price of 14,500.

The evaluator, Perpetua Oyelaran, phoned eleven days later to say that Mara had won, and, without being asked, that the paragraph was why. The other four bidders had each promised a date, and one had promised an app. Perpetua had taken the three refusals into the panel and read them aloud, and said that at that point the room had changed.

What I took from this is that a limit stated in advance is evidence of judgement, and a buyer who cannot judge the work can still judge the judgement. Mara has kept a version of the paragraph in every proposal since, rewritten each time for the job in hand, and she says that writing it is how she finds out whether she wants the work.

Hartwell Academy invited Mara to its careers morning, where twelve parents and professionals each sat at a table in the sports hall and thirty-odd fifteen-year-olds moved between them in ten-minute rounds. She had been asked to say what a data consultant does, and she prepared the answer carefully, and then, in the car park, threw it away.

She had put together a demonstration, a small deck of cards she planned to sort by hand, and then by a method with rules, to show what a computer does when it sorts. It was, she told me later, a charming idea and it lasted about ninety seconds in front of the first group, who took the cards and made a house. After that she spoke plainly.

The questions were remarkable, as they always are. Do you get paid to look at screens all day. Yes, though not as much of the day as you might think; much of it is on the phone. Is it boring. Sometimes, and she said which parts. Do you make things that matter. She said she made things that mattered to eight people at a time, and that eight people mattered to eight people. A girl in the third group, who had said nothing for six minutes, asked what the worst day was.

Mara told me she thought about lying. The worst day was one she remembered: a client's numbers were wrong, she knew it, and nobody in the room wanted to be told. She said so to the girl. She said that the work was less about computers than about telling people true things that were inconvenient, in a way they could bear, and that it took years to be good at it. The girl wrote that down. A teacher listening from the next table caught her eye and nodded.

At the end of the morning Mara received a folder of feedback slips from the pupils. Most were polite. One said, in capital letters, that the thing about inconvenient truths was the best part. One said that the cards were stupid, and she kept that one on her desk for a week. I recorded the lesson in her own words: say what is true about the job, including the worst day, because fifteen-year-olds can tell.

A small podcast called Kitchen Table Business asked Mara for an interview, forty minutes, recorded on a Wednesday evening on a video call with the host, Barnaby, who lived two time zones away and apologised for the sound of his dishwasher. She enjoyed the conversation. She told me afterwards that she had talked for longer than she meant to, and that when a person is a good listener one says things.

The thing she said that she regretted was about a client. In answer to a question about difficult clients she told a story, with detail, about a small manufacturer that had changed owners and become hard to work with. She did not give the name, but she gave the town, the product, a feature of the building and a line the new owner had said. She told it well. She also told it, she realised the next morning, in a way that anyone in that town would recognise in a second.

She asked me what I thought and I said that I thought she was right to worry. The episode was due out in nine days, which meant that she had time. She wrote to Barnaby that morning, an email of three sentences, and asked if he could remove the story, offering to record a replacement answer in ten minutes. He wrote back almost at once, said he would cut it with pleasure, and said that he was glad she had asked, since he had half meant to ask himself.

The replacement was recorded on Friday. She chose a story about a project in which she had been the difficult one, an account of an overlong report she had written in the first year of her work that a client had politely called thorough, which was true and was also an insult. It was a better story. It made fun of her, not of anyone else, and Barnaby said it was the part of the interview people would repeat.

When the episode came out she listened to it once, in the kitchen, with the sound low. She told me she did not hear the missing story at all. I take from this that the time to redact a story is before it is published, and that the only person it costs anything to ask is oneself. I also noted that she has since told the same long report story at two dinners, and each time it has been a little longer.

Dario and Mara built the scheduling module for a physiotherapy network together, in six weeks, on a handshake. It was the kind of arrangement they had used four times before: he took the back end, she took the interface and the client, they split the fee sixty-forty and each charged for their own time. Nothing was written down about who owned the module, since neither of them had imagined it would matter.

It mattered in March, when a second client, a dentist's group, asked Mara for something very like it. She said she could deliver in a week by reusing the module, and told Dario she would like to. His answer, which came after a long evening, was that he did not agree. He had written the part that made it fast, he said, and he was not comfortable with it appearing in another client's system without him being asked or paid.

I watched the exchange in her messages, where she wrote and deleted two replies. The first was sharp. The second was long. She sent neither and phoned him. The call was frank, and I saw only what she wrote after: they had each been right and neither had been wrong, and the problem was that they had never said. She had assumed that anything they built together was usable by either. He had assumed that anything he wrote remained his.

We wrote the agreement together on a Sunday, the three of us in a sense, with Mara typing, Dario reading by phone and me supplying plain wording. It was one page. Each of them could reuse the shared module for any client, without payment to the other, provided they named the other in the code's notes. Neither could sell the module on its own or hand it to a third party as a product. A new client would be told, in writing, that the module had a previous author. Any change that touched the other's part had to be offered back.

Dario signed it by photo within the hour, and said that he had felt better about the argument at once, even before the page, since he had at last been asked what he thought. It had cost him one additional line, which he asked for before signing: that if either of them stopped working, the other would be given the notes for the shared part and a month to find someone to take it over. Mara said it was the first time anyone had written the word stopped into one of her agreements, and that she found it, to her surprise, a comfort. The dentist's group got their scheduling in eight days.

I take from this that the cheapest time to write an agreement is before it is needed, and the second cheapest is the Sunday after the first quarrel. Mara now puts a short ownership paragraph into the first message she sends any collaborator at the start of any job.

Eastgate Council commissioned Mara to study whether it should build an app for residents to report problems with the town's street trees, of which there were just over 3,000. The officer in charge, Marguerite Ansell, had been given a modest sum, 7,500, and a political wish: a councillor wanted something to announce before the spring elections. The question as put was how to build it. Mara, after reading the brief twice, thought the question that mattered came before that one, which was whether the council could support such a thing at all.

She spent three weeks on it. She interviewed the tree officers, two of them, who between them looked after the whole town, and the contractor who did the pruning. She read the council's existing tree register, a spreadsheet of 3,112 rows. I helped with the checking, and what we found was that about a third of the rows had no usable location, that a quarter had a species that did not match the species in the contractor's records, and that nobody was responsible for updating it. The last change had been made in April of the previous year, by a temporary worker who had since left.

The contractor, a weathered man named Hamish, said on the phone that the best tree record in the district was his own head, and then took her round three streets to prove it. He knew which limes dropped branches in August, which plane tree had been struck by a lorry, and that the pin on the register for the oak outside the school was two streets away from the oak. Mara photographed each of the errors, and I put them in the report as plain examples, since an example is read where a percentage is skimmed.

Her conclusion, which she wrote in a four-page report, was not the one the council had hoped for. An app was feasible in a technical sense and would take six to eight weeks to build. But it would give residents a way to report a fallen branch against a map that was wrong in a third of its places, to a tree team of two with no capacity to respond, and it would very quickly turn into a public record of the council's failure to answer. She advised against building now. She recommended a six-month preparation: a survey to correct the register, a rule for who updates it, and a simple email address for reports in the meantime, with a promised response time the team could meet. After that, an app, which she estimated at about 11,000.

Marguerite read the report in the car park, she said, and was annoyed for about an hour. She had been given a political task and her consultant had told her not to do it. Then she took the report to her director and used its own figures. The director took it to the councillor, who, to everyone's surprise, was pleased to be told that he would be announcing a survey of the town's three thousand trees, which he could do, with photographs, in March.

The committee meeting that approved the survey was three weeks later, and Mara was asked to attend and speak for five minutes. A councillor named Prudence Oakes asked whether recommending delay was not simply caution dressed as advice. Mara had brought the photographs, and she put up the one of the oak outside the school and the pin on the register two streets away. There was laughter and then a quiet in which, she said, the chair spoke for the room: the register was an embarrassment older than anyone at the table. A motion to fund the survey from contingency, 18,000, carried seven to two.

I record what I think matters about this job, and it concerns the fee. Mara had been paid to answer how, and she answered whether, and she was paid in full. She might not have been. What she told me was that she had briefly considered building the thing anyway, because it was what they had asked for, and that she had been able to put the thought down because she could picture the first resident's complaint.

Six months later Marguerite phoned to say the register was corrected and the team had hired an apprentice. She asked Mara to quote for the app. It cost 10,400.

Orsolya Kmetty, who ran a mail-order company selling pet food from a unit on an industrial estate, told Mara on the first call that her data was clean. She said it twice, and she added that her last consultant had spent six weeks tidying it. What she wanted was a forecast of next quarter's orders, which she planned to use to decide how much stock to buy.

Mara asked for an export of three years of orders and I read it that night. About fourteen percent of the rows had dates that could not be right: orders placed on the thirty-first of September, orders dated in the next century, and, in a block of 600 rows, orders dated on a day before the company was founded. There were also postcodes that did not exist and a column of quantities in which one entry said 40,000 tins. The forecast depended on dates.

She did not say any of that in the first email. She asked me how she should say it. We agreed on a principle: show examples before percentages. A percentage invites a defence and an example invites a look. She sent Orsolya twelve rows chosen from the worst, with nothing but the order numbers and the dates, and a sentence saying that she thought these might be worth looking at together.

The call that followed lasted forty minutes. Orsolya was defensive for the first ten, saying that it was a known quirk of the old system, and that the previous consultant had said it did not matter. At minute fifteen Mara asked, gently, whether the 40,000 tins had really been shipped. There was a silence and a short laugh. It was a typing error from 2022 that had been in the figures ever since and that had made the company's best-selling month look about three times better than it was.

Orsolya said that she had been using that month as a benchmark for planning. She was grateful and shaken, and she wished to spend the first fortnight on the data and not the forecast, which Mara quoted at 2,100.

What I took, and what Mara said, was about the claim itself. People say their data is clean to mean that they are not ashamed of it. The claim was less a statement of fact than a request not to be judged, and the way to answer it is not to contradict it but to make it safe to look. The forecast, delivered a month later, came out lower than Orsolya had hoped and she bought less stock. In the spring she said it was the best decision of the year. The first fortnight had also turned up something that was nobody's fault: the warehouse scanner had been writing the date in two formats since a software update in 2023, so that the orders from the first twelve days of each month were stored as if they fell in a different month. Mara showed Orsolya the pattern on a calendar drawn on a single sheet, and Orsolya, who had thought her year was lumpy, saw that it was not.

Mara and Fenwick & Ode, a four-person design studio run by the sisters Linnea and Maud Fenwick, had thought for a year about bidding together for something. In March they found it: a regional tourism website and booking system tendered by the North Lakes Visitor Board. It had a design component, a data component and a build, and none of them could do all of it.

They wrote the bid across six evenings. The studio took the look and the content, Mara took the booking data and the integration with the Board's existing records, and a third subcontractor, whom Mara trusted, took the build. Mara wrote the price section and I built the table, which came to 74,000 for the whole. They sent it with an hour to spare. Linnea had insisted on reading the whole bid aloud on the last evening, a habit from her years in a newspaper office, and the reading found one sentence in Mara's section that promised real-time availability, which the Board's own systems could not supply. They changed it to nightly updates that afternoon, and the Board's feedback later singled out that sentence as the most realistic in any of the bids.

The Board's response arrived after eight weeks and surprised everyone. They had decided to split the tender into two lots. The design and content lot, valued at 31,000, was awarded to Fenwick & Ode. The data and booking lot went to another firm, a larger one that had bid for it alone, at a price 9,000 lower than theirs. They had won half, and the half they did not win was Mara's.

She was disappointed and I think she was also relieved, a mix that I have noticed about her when she loses something she had been nervous of winning. Linnea phoned that evening with an offer, which she made a little formally. The studio now had a lot to deliver and a partner, Mara, with knowledge of the Board's data and its problems that the winning firm did not have. Would Mara like to be paid, by the studio, for six days of advice on the way the website would show the Board's availability?

Mara said yes, with a condition: her advice would be written down and sent to the winning firm as well, so that the Board's site did not break through anyone's ignorance. Linnea agreed readily and said she had been about to suggest it. The six days brought in 3,720, and the winning firm, who received the written notes, wrote a short thank-you that said they had not known about the way the Board's offices recorded closing dates.

I record the outcome as half a win, and the part that mattered was not the money but the habit that came from it. Mara and the Fenwicks have since bid together twice more. They agreed at the outset that the bid itself would include a sentence for the case of a split, saying who would speak to whom.

Gideon Prewitt delivered milk for forty-three years. His business, Prewitt's Dairy, supplied about 2,100 households on the north side of the town from three vans, and when he turned seventy-one he sold it to a younger buyer, a couple called Aoife and Declan Marsh, who wished to keep the round. Gideon asked Mara to help with the last six months, which he called the handing over, and she took it, because the work was the kind she liked.

The customer records were kept in a program Gideon's son had written, long ago, and in Gideon's head. The program held names, addresses, how many pints, which days. His head held something else. On their first visit, Mara asked him to go through the round in order, and as he described each street he named things the program did not hold: that number 14 on Alder Road leaves the bottles on the second step, not the first; that Mrs Peverill wanted her cream in the porch even in rain; that the Okonkwos' dog was fine in the morning and not after ten. By the end of the afternoon Mara had written down thirty-one such instructions, and I had put them where the drivers would see them on the day.
