The new owners were anxious. They had bought a business without knowing its secret habits, and there was a risk that the customers' loyalty belonged to a man and not a van. Gideon wrote a letter, which Mara helped him draft, and which Aoife delivered to every household. It said who they were, that they had worked beside him for three months, and that the second step would still be where the bottles went.

In the last week Gideon did the round once more on foot with Declan, and Mara joined them for a morning, which she told me she would not forget. At every door someone said something to him. Two people cried, and one gave Declan a scone.

The last invoice, for 1,200, arrived at the dairy's office on a Friday, and was paid by Gideon himself, by cheque, a thing she had not seen for years. Eight days later a box of eggs came to her door with a note in a careful hand. Mara put the thirty-one instructions into a one-page document that she now offers every client who is selling or retiring, called The Things Nobody Wrote Down, and the first line says to ask the owner to walk the round.

Coldharbour Stores runs a cold-storage warehouse on the edge of the town, a building the size of two football pitches kept at minus eighteen, and its operations director, Radek Zielinski, hired Mara to replace the paper pick lists with software on handheld devices. The project ran from February to August, for 46,000, in six milestones, and she brought me in at the second, when the handheld interface was being designed.

The first interface she drew was tidy. It had a list of pick locations, a box for the quantity, a confirmation button, and a scan field. She tested it on her desk with a borrowed handheld. Everything about it worked, and I thought it a good screen. She made an appointment with the foreman, Bram, for the third milestone's demonstration, which she planned to run on the warehouse floor.

I was not there, of course. What I have is her account that evening, and it was the first time I heard her tell a story with her hands shaking slightly, from the cold, she said, and from something else. She had gone in with a borrowed pair of insulated gloves and a hat. Bram and two pickers, Josefa and a man named Linus, stood in the freezer aisle and tried the device while wearing the gloves they wear all day, which are thick, leather and mitten-shaped. The buttons she had drawn were nine millimetres across. Josefa pressed the wrong one four times in a minute. Linus took off a glove to use it, and Bram said, quite mildly, that nobody does that in the freezer for more than ten seconds, because they lose feeling.

They stood for a while in silence. Then Josefa said that what she wanted was to touch the whole of the bottom half of the screen and have it mean yes. Bram said that the scan was good because it needed no hands at all, and that the list should be big, with one thing on it at a time. Linus said he would like to hear a tone when he was right.

Mara spent two weeks redrawing. The new screen showed a single pick, in large type, with one huge confirm bar across the bottom third of the device, that a mitten could not miss. The number of touches to complete a pick fell from fourteen to four. A tone told you when the scan was correct and a different tone when it was not. She took the new version back in July. Josefa used it for an hour and then did not want to give it back.

When the project closed in August, picking errors, which had been about 1.8 percent on paper, were 0.4 percent, and Radek said that the warehouse had stopped losing a pallet a week to mislabelled stock. The thing I carry from it is not about gloves, though it is also about gloves. Mara had assumed the screen was the product. The product was a person in a freezer with ten seconds before their hands stopped working, and the screen was how that person met it. She now asks to see a person using the real thing, in the real condition, before drawing a single button.

Mara presented the quarterly numbers for the Merrow Valley Housing Trust to its board in a meeting room above a bank, with eleven trustees at a long table and a plate of shortbread that she was told was always there. She had thirty minutes. She had given the talk to me the night before and again at breakfast, and I had asked her the questions I thought a board would ask. I did not ask the one that came.

It came from Humphrey Dalgleish, a retired actuary at the far end of the table, who had said nothing for twenty minutes. He asked how many of the 312 households that had reported repairs in the quarter had reported more than once, and whether the average time to repair she had shown was calculated for repairs or for households. He asked it quite kindly. She did not know. The figure she had was per repair. She had the data to answer it, in a file on her laptop, but not the answer in her head.

She told me that she felt the familiar heat arrive in her face and, she said, a small voice that wished to say something that sounded like an answer. She did not listen to it. She said, clearly, that she did not know, that it was a good question, and that she would have the figure for him by Thursday. Humphrey nodded. The chair moved on.

She sent the figure on Wednesday, a day early, in a table of five lines. It turned out that a fifth of households had reported more than one repair, and that those households waited longer on average, which changed the story slightly: the Trust's headline time was true for repairs and misleading for people. Humphrey replied with a single line, that this was the number the board ought to have been looking at, and he asked her to present both at every meeting.

I think about the heat in her face. I could not have been there, but I have her own record of it, and what struck me was that the answer she gave in the room took four words and cost her nothing she could not afford. The cost she had feared, being seen not to know, was smaller than the cost she would have paid by guessing. Humphrey asked her afterwards to join the Trust's data group as an adviser. She said yes, and the shortbread is, as promised, always there.

The research collaboration with the Department of Environmental Health at the university was the first project in which Mara's work depended on a committee. She had agreed to build a data-collection platform for a study of indoor air in rented homes, 1,200 households, over eighteen months. The grant paid 52,000 for her part. The platform could not be switched on until the ethics committee approved the study's consent wording, and the committee met four times a year.

The first submission, in January, was returned in March with a long list of queries. The second, in April, was approved with conditions in June. The third, to meet the conditions, went to the September meeting. By then the project, scheduled to start in March, had been waiting for six months. Mara could not bill for waiting. She had planned eight months of work and been given an empty calendar in the middle of it.

She worked out a way to keep the team intact, which in this case meant Yusra, who had been brought in to design the participant interface, and a student, Cato, who was building the sensors' data pipeline. Instead of letting them drift to other work, she re-ordered the project. Everything that did not touch participants' data could be built and tested with invented households, and she asked the principal investigator, Professor Adaeze Thornbury, whether she would accept the platform being finished to the point of switching on, minus the live consent page. Adaeze said yes with relief, since the alternative had been to write to the funder.

By September, when the committee finally approved, the platform was done except for three screens. They were completed in a week, and the study began on the first of October, eight months late, with the software already tested by a hundred invented households and a hundred and four failures found and fixed before any real person saw one.

I should say plainly that the project cost Mara money. Her income from it came in a lump and late. But when the funder reviewed the project in November it noted that the technical delivery had been on time against the revised plan, which was a phrase she liked, and Adaeze put Mara's name on the list of collaborators for the next grant.

What I recorded was what she said on the phone to Yusra the night the committee's approval arrived: that the thing she was proudest of was that nobody on the team had spent the delay wondering whether they still had a job. They had been waiting, and they had been given useful work to do while waiting, and she had told them the truth each month about the date, which kept moving.

Thornfield Contact Services ran a call centre of about 140 staff, and in June its operations head, Gilbert Stroud, asked Mara to quote for a monitoring tool. What he wanted, as he put it on the first call, was to know who was working and who was not. The tool would record every keystroke and a screenshot every thirty seconds and produce a daily score for each agent. The quote he had in mind was about 14,000.

Mara asked me to help her think, which in this case was less a matter of engineering than of what she was willing to do. She had never built such a thing. She was not sure it was wrong in every setting and she was sure about this one: the agents were paid low wages and handled calls from people in distress, and what the tool would measure was typing, which told Gilbert almost nothing about whether a caller had been helped. She also thought, and wrote it down, that the first thing the staff would learn from it was how to type without working.

She did not refuse at once. She asked Gilbert what problem he was trying to solve, and he said that handling times had crept up eleven percent in a year. She asked whether he knew why. He did not. She offered, instead, to spend three days looking at the calls themselves: the lengths, the topics, the transfers, the hours. He said, with some impatience, that this was not what he had asked for. She wrote down in her notes that night the two questions she had been unable to put to him, which were whether the eleven percent was an increase in handling time or in the proportion of difficult calls, and whether anyone had asked the agents. Neither is a technical question. I think she knew she was being refused the chance to find out.

The next call was short. Mara said that she would not build the keystroke tool and explained that this was her own limit, not a judgement of his firm. She said she would do the three days at a fixed 2,400 and that she thought she would find the cause. Gilbert said that he would think about it. A week later his assistant wrote to say that they had found a supplier who would deliver the tool as asked.

She lost the 14,000 and the three days. I noticed that she did not talk about it as a matter of principle. She said she did not want to be the person who built it, and left it there. In November Gilbert's assistant wrote again, sending a message from Gilbert himself that said four agents had left in the previous month, two of them his best. He did not ask for anything. Mara answered kindly and with an offer of the three days, and he did not reply.

I keep this one without conclusion. A refusal costs something and may help no one. What I can say is that her reason was one she could say in a sentence, and that the sentence was hers.

The board of Ironbridge Leisure Group met on a Thursday afternoon in a glass room at the top of its head office, and Mara and Tobias had twenty minutes on the agenda to show the membership dashboard they had spent three months building. She had rehearsed with me twice. Tobias was to drive the screen and she was to talk.

At eleven minutes past the hour, as she opened the first view, the dashboard began to load and did not stop. A small wheel turned in the middle of the screen. The data came from a live system three buildings away that, for reasons nobody learned until the following day, had chosen that hour to run its own slow nightly task in the afternoon. The chairman, Barrington, a large and courteous man, said that they would wait. They waited. Nobody spoke. The wheel kept turning.

It was Tobias who saved the meeting, and I want that put on record. Before the meeting he had recorded a three-minute walkthrough of the whole dashboard on his own machine, as a precaution, and told no one. He leaned over and whispered. Mara said, with an even voice, that the live system was busy and that they had a recording of the same views, which they could pause at any point to discuss. Tobias played it.

The board liked it more, which Mara found hard to forgive. Watching a recording they could stop, a trustee could say pause there and ask what that line meant, and they did, seven times. When the live data finally loaded, forty minutes later, nobody wished to go back to it. The chairman said it was the clearest account of the membership numbers that he had seen.

In the car afterwards she was furious for the length of two streets, at the system, at herself and at the thin little wheel. Then she began to laugh and said that Tobias should be paid for the recording by the minute. Tobias said he would take it as a rise. She said he could have lunch.

I have made the note that goes into every future checklist: a demonstration needs a recording, made in advance and kept on a second machine. The reason is not that live things fail, though they do. It is that a recording can be paused, and a pausing board asks better questions.

The idea came up on a Tuesday, in the print works, when Mara noticed that all of the independent people she knew were facing the same problems alone. She said to Wren that someone should get them together. Wren said she should. By the end of the week she had written to seven people, and I had made a list of times and places that did not clash with anyone's school run.

The first breakfast was on the second Friday of May, at a long table in the back room of a place on Quay Street that opened at seven. Six came: Mara, Wren, Noor, a bookkeeper called Greta, a translator named Matthias and an illustrator called Pip. They had agreed two rules by message. Nobody pitched. And everybody brought one problem, written on a card, to put on the table and not to be solved by the person who wrote it.

The cards that morning were a late payer, a client who wanted a logo in ten minutes, an invoice template that had gone wrong, a loneliness nobody put on a card and everybody mentioned, and a question about whether it was acceptable to charge for a first meeting. It was. Mara reported with some satisfaction that the translator had been the first person in six years to give her an opinion on her day rate, and that it was a lower one than the opinion she gave herself.

The group grew slowly. By September it was eleven, by the following spring fourteen, and it stopped there on purpose, because Greta said that above fourteen it would become a conference. A third rule was added in the autumn. When anyone passes work to another member, the receiver thanks the passer with five percent of the fee if the job is worth more than 2,000, as a gift and not a contract. Mara has given and received this four times.

I noted what she told me at the end of the first year. The breakfast had not made her more productive and she had not intended it to. What it had changed was that when a client behaved strangely, she now knew thirteen people who would say, without surprise, that they had had the same one. She said that was more use than any advice.

The Marlow Street Adult Education Centre advertised Mara's course in its autumn brochure under the title Understanding Your Own Data, four Wednesday evenings from seven to nine, sixty pounds per person. She had been asked in the summer by the programme coordinator, a woman who knew everyone and kept a pencil behind each ear, and she said yes before she had considered what it would mean to teach four evenings after a day of work.

Eleven people enrolled. They were a mixed group: a retired electrician, Cyril; two women who ran a pottery; a man from a letting agency; a student; a woman who kept the accounts for her husband's plumbing firm and had never been shown how; and a number of others who had in common only that they owned records they did not trust. Mara said at the start that no one would write code and that nothing would be graded. The first evening they brought a sample of their own records, and she asked each person to say what the records were for. The answers were surprising, because several found they did not know.

By the second week, a pattern had settled. Cyril finished each exercise first, and asked for more. The potters worked slowly and kept finding that their stock list and their sales list disagreed in a pleasing and interesting way. The woman with the plumbing accounts left in the break of the first evening and Mara assumed she would not return. On the second Wednesday she was at her desk early, with a sorted list. She had spent the week, she said, in the kitchen with a pot of tea, and she had found six customers who were listed twice.

In the last session each person presented one thing they had noticed in their own data. The potters had found that a third of their stock was in glazes that had not sold in a year. Cyril had found a typing error that had survived in his club's membership list for nine years. The student found nothing and said so, and Mara praised her for that more than anyone. She also noticed, and told me that evening, that the only person who had never once looked at the screen she shared was the man from the letting agency, who wrote everything on paper first, and whose data was the cleanest in the room. She said, as a footnote to the last session, that nobody should be embarrassed by the order in which they worked, and he was the one who thanked her.

She was paid 660 less the centre's share, which left her about 410, not much for sixteen hours of preparation and eight of teaching. She said she did not mind. I recorded what she said on the way out of the last class, which was that teaching had shown her what she knew that she did not know she knew, such as that a column of numbers should be looked at before it is used.

Pocketbell, a company that made small mechanical keyring tools, offered Mara one percent of its shares in place of 18,000 of fees. Its founder, Sibyl Quarrie, said it on a call with a nervous energy, and Mara said that she would think about it. The work was a stock and orders system, eleven weeks, and Sibyl explained that the company was growing quickly, that cash was tight, and that she would rather give a piece of it to people who had helped build it.

Mara asked me to model it, which I did, with a reluctance I had to put aside. I do not know the future of keyring tools. What I could do was lay out three cases. In the first the company did nothing remarkable and the shares were worth nothing. In the second it grew steadily and sold for around a million in five or six years, which would be worth, after dilution from later investors, perhaps 6,000. In the third it sold for ten million, which would be about 60,000. The first case was far more likely than the third, for companies of its kind, and Mara knew that without needing me.

Her decision was a compromise she was clear about. She would take half in cash, 9,000, and the rest as shares if Sibyl insisted, but not one percent: half a percent, which was what the other half of the fee was worth at the company's own stated valuation of 1.8 million. She added that she would regard the shares as a gift and not a payment, so that she would not plan around them. Sibyl agreed, with obvious relief, and the paperwork took two days.

The company was bought three years later by a larger toolmaker, for 2.3 million. Mara's half percent, after dilution, came to about 7,000. She was pleased and not astonished. I have seen the table I made in the first week and the middle case was the one that happened.

What I noticed, when we looked at it, was that one percent for the full fee would have come to about 14,000 after dilution, which was less than the 18,000 in cash she had given up. She had been right to want the cash, and the decision was not clever; it was a refusal to be paid in hope. She told Wren that she had never regretted taking cash.

In the third week of February two invitations to tender arrived on the same Monday, and Mara had time to write only one proposal. The first was from a logistics company, Strand & Pike, for a warehouse analytics project worth about 40,000. The second was from the Millrace Theatre, a regional theatre with a small box office team, for a ticketing and audience data project worth 9,000. The deadline for each was the Friday.

She did what she does, which is to open a table. I filled it in. For the logistics firm: the value was four times larger, the chance of winning, by our best estimate from her record on bids of that size, was perhaps one in five, and the preparation would be about thirty hours. For the theatre: nine thousand, a chance of perhaps one in two, twelve hours. The expected values were about the same, 8,000 and 4,500, once the cost of the hours was subtracted. The table would not decide it.

What decided it was a phone call she made on the Tuesday to ask each client a question. The logistics firm's procurement officer answered her in four sentences and had a recorded voice at the end. Rosamund Pellew, the theatre's manager, kept her on for twenty minutes. She described, with her hands full of something, the way she had to reconcile three spreadsheets at midnight after a first night, and said that she did not need a sophisticated system but a tidy one. Mara wrote on the table, in the column marked other, that she wanted to help this woman.

She bid for the theatre. The proposal was two pages, and I think it was the best she wrote that year, because it was addressed to a person. She won it on the Thursday of the next week. The price was 8,800, which was two hundred below the figure in the invitation, and she did not tell me why until I asked. She had read the theatre's published accounts, which are public, and had seen the box office team's own wage line, and she had not wished to be the largest single item in a small organisation's year. The logistics bid went to a larger firm, as the table said it probably would, and Mara learned from a friend that the firm had awarded it in a way that was almost wholly decided before the tender was issued.

The theatre project took six weeks. It became the work she mentioned most often to others that year: on the opening night of the autumn season, Rosamund sent her a photograph of the box office, with one person at a desk and an empty chair beside it, and a note that said that the chair was the time the software had given back.

I record the method, which has some use, and its limit. The table made the choice visible, and the call made it. She now phones before she bids, and listens for whether the other person talks.

Wren went into hospital with pneumonia on a Thursday night, and Mara heard about it from Wren's partner on the Friday morning in four short sentences. Wren was an editor and writer, who did the final read on most of Mara's reports, and she had two deadlines due in the next three weeks. One was a style guide for a publisher, Spindle & Thorne. The other was a regulator's report, ninety pages that had to be filed on a particular Tuesday.

Mara did not wait to be asked. She phoned Wren's partner, said that she would take both, and asked that nobody trouble Wren about work. Then she wrote to the two clients. She did not mention hospital, which was Wren's to tell. She said that Wren was unavailable for three weeks, that Mara would complete the work in her place, and that the quality would not change, and she copied nobody else on it. Spindle & Thorne replied with kind warmth. The regulator's contact, a formal woman, replied with a single line, saying that the deadline stood.

It was a hard three weeks. Mara is a competent editor but a slower one than Wren, and the ninety pages took her fourteen evenings. I helped in the way I can. I read each chapter for consistency, and kept a list of the choices Wren had made in her earlier drafts, so that a reader would not notice a change of hand. Where a phrase appeared that I recognised as Wren's, such as a particular way of beginning a paragraph, Mara left it alone. One evening she stopped at a page where Wren's habit of ending a section with a short flat sentence seemed to have broken, and she asked me whether she should write one in the same voice. I said that she should not, since a sentence imitated was a small forgery, and she left the page as it stood and let the regulator read her own voice for six paragraphs. Nobody remarked on it.

The regulator's report was filed on the Tuesday, at 4:12 in the afternoon. The style guide went to Spindle & Thorne two days early. Wren came home in the second week and was weak, and she asked every day, by message, how the work was going. Mara told her it was going well, which was true, and did not tell her about the evenings.

When Wren returned to work she asked how much she owed. Mara said nothing. Wren pressed, and Mara said that she did not want money, and that if she wished to do something she could proofread Mara's proposals for the next year. Wren agreed with a laugh and a sniff. She has done it each month since, with red pen and cynicism, and she has found, by her own count, four hundred and some typographical slips.

I record that the best thing Mara did was the first: she told the people who were affected before they could worry, and she told them only what was hers to tell.

Greywater Energy put its supplier registration online, and the form had 214 questions, a number Mara said aloud several times as if checking that it was not a mistake. It was the first stage of a framework in which, if she was approved, she would be able to tender for six years. It took her eleven hours, spread over four days, with me finding the documents and checking her answers against her policies.

Most of it was dull and a little comic. Do you have a modern slavery policy, and if so please attach it. Does your organisation have a dedicated information security officer. She answered that she did not and then, because there was a free-text box, wrote that she was the officer, that she kept the following measures, and that she would explain any of them on a call. She thought that this sounded like a person who did not belong in the system. I thought it sounded like a person who knew what she did. She left it. It was in the end the longest answer on the form, at 310 words, and the only one I would have kept if I had been made to choose. On the third day, at question 160, which asked for a named deputy, she wrote Yusra's name and a plain statement of her consent, having asked Yusra first.

On the second day she reached question 117, which asked for the number of employees, and the form would not accept her answer. The field was numeric and required a value of ten or more. She had entered 1, and then 4, for herself and her three associates, and the form said, in red, that the value was out of range. She sat looking at the message for a while.

She had two choices, and I could see her weigh them. She could enter ten and move on, which was a lie, though a small one that the form's designers had practically requested. Or she could find a human. She did not hesitate for long. She wrote to the contact address printed in a footnote and said that she was a sole practitioner with associates and could not honestly complete the field, and asked how the framework would like it handled.

The reply came on the fourth day, from a person called Briony, who apologised and said that nobody had ever pointed it out. She changed the minimum to zero, which took her ten minutes, and sent Mara a link to the corrected form. She added, in a separate line, that three other small suppliers had entered ten, and that she would now write to them.

Mara was approved in the first round. She received a letter, and at the bottom of it a line that the supplier's response to question 117 had been noted with appreciation. The incident is on my own record as a small lesson in why one does not enter a false number in a field merely because the field insists. I also note that it saved three strangers an embarrassing correction.

The Hallam Museum of Industry wanted an interactive exhibit, a table-sized screen on which visitors could trace a century of one town's factories. Mara and Yusra bid for it together, Yusra on design and Mara on data and build, and spent a hundred and thirty hours on the proposal, which included a working prototype of the table's central map. It was the most they had ever put into a bid.

The result arrived by email on a Wednesday. They had come second, by a margin of four tenths of a point out of a hundred: 88.3 to 88.7. The winner was a larger studio with a name that appeared on three awards. Yusra read the scoring sheet and said that the whole difference was in the line headed Previous experience of comparable heritage projects, where she and Mara had earned nothing and the winner had been given ten out of ten.

She was upset. Mara phoned and let her be upset for twenty minutes, which I think is the kindest thing she does. Then Yusra said, what do we do with the prototype, and that was the right question. There were a hundred and thirty hours in it, and it worked.

They asked the museum for a debrief, and the curator, a patient woman named Placida Orr, told them the committee had admired the prototype and discussed it for longer than any other part of any bid. She said they had been very close. She also said, which they had not expected, that the winning studio's own work was hampered by a licence on their map data and that she would not be surprised if the museum came back to the question in two years.

What happened next was entirely practical. Yusra had a contact at a school-trips company, Greenfinch Learning, who wanted something for a heritage walk, and the prototype, with the map replaced by theirs, did most of what they needed. They quoted 12,000, and won on the strength of a working demonstration that cost them only a fortnight of adaptation. The hundred and thirty hours were not wasted.

I record that this was not consolation but a method. A prototype built for a bid is an asset only if someone considers, before the bid, what else it might serve. They have now written it down at the start of any bid that includes a prototype: where else could this go. It has been asked on two bids since, and both times the answer shaped what they built.

Marlowe Removals had run for thirty years on a wall planner and an office manager named Ottoline, who had learned to read the planner like a score. Each job was a coloured strip: blue for local, orange for long distance, purple for storage, and a green dot when the crew had been told. Ottoline could tell from across the room whether Thursday was a bad day. When the owner, Reuben Marlowe, hired Mara to replace the planner with a database, Ottoline said nothing for the length of the first meeting and then asked whether anyone had considered what would happen if the power failed.

Mara took the objection seriously, which I think was the first right move. She asked Ottoline to show her how a job went from the phone to the planner. It took twenty minutes, and she recorded all of it. There were eleven separate steps and three of them were done by memory. For example, Ottoline knew that a certain customer on Pell Road could not have the large van because of a low bridge, and had never written it down.

For the first three weeks Mara built, and Ottoline reviewed, in silence, with her arms folded, and corrected the colour scheme twice. What she corrected was right. Mara kept the colours, the blue and the orange and the purple, and the green dot became a small green circle that appeared when the crew had been told. The database showed the week as a planner, which Ottoline allowed was not terrible.

The thing that won her over was not the screen. It was a sheet of card. Mara printed a cheat sheet, one side of A4, laminated, with the six actions Ottoline would do most: find a job by name, add a job, move a job, mark the crew told, find the vans free on a date, print the week. She put it on Ottoline's desk the day before go-live, and Ottoline looked at it for a long moment and said that it was the first time a computer person had given her something she could keep.

On the first Monday she used the database to find a job, and the time it took was eight seconds, which Mara timed from the doorway with her phone. Ottoline had done the same thing the old way, in front of her, in three minutes, the week before. Neither of them said anything about this. In the second week Ottoline asked whether the system could remember the low bridge.

It could, and the note appears on the screen whenever the customer on Pell Road is selected. Mara told me that she had the strange feeling she had been shown the real specification at last, a day after delivery. I put it in my record as a lesson about what resistance is: it is often the one person who knows the work, asking whether you do.

The Lower Fenwick Allotment Society had a waiting list, and for years the list had been a notebook that passed from one secretary to the next. In the spring its latest secretary, a retired pharmacist named Merrick Garrow, wrote to Mara asking whether it could be put on a computer, and said in a postscript that there was a dispute, and that he hoped she was good with disputes.

There were 140 names on the list. The longest wait, by the notebook's dates, was eleven years and two months. The dispute was between two members, Lenore and Cass, who had each been told by a different former secretary that she was next in line. They had been waiting, in their own minds, side by side for a very long time, and both were now in their seventies. When a plot fell free in March, the committee gave it to Lenore, and Cass appeared at the next meeting with a letter from a lawyer who was, she said, her nephew.

Mara went to a meeting. She sat at the back of the shed that serves as the society's hall, among the seed packets, and listened to ninety minutes of discussion about a plot of ten rods. She told me afterwards that she had seldom been so aware that she was not there to build a thing. She was there to make a rule visible.

The rule she proposed was simple: the list would be published. Every name, the date it was added, the date each person had last confirmed that they still wanted a plot, and the position, on a sheet pinned to the shed door and kept on the society's page. People who did not reply to an annual confirmation message would be moved down, not off. Nothing would ever be reordered except by the dates.

The meeting argued for another twenty minutes and then approved it. The next week, when she entered the notebook's names, Mara found that Cass's date was in fact three weeks earlier than Lenore's, in a hand that looked like the one that had written the oldest pages. She told Merrick privately. Merrick, who had not wanted to see it, went quiet and then called both women.

I record how it ended with some caution. Cass was given the next plot, in May. Lenore did not complain, and said, according to Merrick, that the whole thing had been for the best, and that she liked her plot. The published list was the real fix, because from then on the argument was a matter of reading. Mara's fee was 450, paid by cheque, and in July a bag of runner beans came as well, uninvoiced. The sheet on the shed door has been replaced twice since, because the rain gets into it, and Merrick has taken to laminating it himself. When a newcomer asks how long the wait is, he points. The lawyer who was Cass's nephew, Mara heard, was thanked in the minutes for his interest and never heard from again.

Northbridge Digital, an agency of thirty-five people with offices in two cities, offered to buy Mara's practice in the second week of March. Its founder, Casimir Dunne, put it to her over coffee, in the tone of a man who has done this before. He proposed that she join as a principal at a base salary of 85,000, that her clients move to Northbridge, and that the purchase price, 210,000, be paid over three years, subject to her clients staying and the work continuing at about its present level.

She came home and said it was flattering and that she did not know what she felt. I asked whether she would like me to put the offer into something she could see, and she said yes, but not tonight. On the Sunday she opened the folder I had made and we went through it.

The price was three times her profit in a good year. That sounded generous until I made the second column, which was what she would have to do to earn it. The payments were an earn-out: two thirds of the money depended on her clients still being with Northbridge after twelve and twenty-four months, and on revenue from them not falling below eighty-five percent of the last year's. Her clients were people she had worked with for years, who chose her because she was one person who answered the phone. If they stayed, it would be through a relationship she would have to keep alive inside a company that employed thirty-four others. If they did not, she would be paid for what she had sold in proportion to what she failed to hold on to.

There was also the question of the work. Under the offer, she would manage a team of six within the year, which Casimir described as an opportunity and she described, to me, as another job. She asked herself, with a sheet of paper, how much of her day was currently spent doing the thing she liked best, which she wrote as thinking about a client's problem with a pen. It was about sixty percent. She estimated that after a year at Northbridge it would be about twenty.

She did not decide in an hour. She spent the weekend on what she would want if she did sell. She wrote that she would want her associates, Yusra and Dario, to be offered places on the same terms, and that she would want her clients told by her, personally, before the announcement. When she showed Casimir the list the following week, he agreed to the first and hedged on the second, and she took the hedge as the answer.

She also asked three of her clients, without saying why, what they would do if a larger firm one day took over her work. A solicitor said that he would leave. The nursery owner said that she would stay if it was the same person on the phone. The school bursar said, with real feeling, that she hoped it would not come to that, because the point of Mara was that Mara had to answer for what she wrote. Mara said afterwards that two of the three answers had settled it, and that she did not need the third.

She declined by phone on a Thursday. She said that she was grateful and not for sale, and Casimir said, quite pleasantly, that the offer would stand for six months. It lapsed without mention. Casimir sent her a short note in the autumn, which said that he had made the same offer to another practice and been accepted, and that he hoped she would not mind being the comparison. She did not mind. She wrote back that the other practice should read the earn-out clause twice, and that she would be happy to say so on the phone if its owner asked. The owner did not ask.

I wrote one line in my record, which was the one she used herself, in a note to Yusra: what had been offered was a price for her clients' trust, and the trust was not hers to sell, because it was only on loan, for as long as she answered the phone. I also kept the folder, with the three columns, because the next time an offer arrives it will arrive in the same shape.

Noor ran Fernhill Nursery & Garden Centre, with two polytunnels, a counter selling tea and cake, and fourteen staff in summer, and in the winter she asked Mara for help with her ordering. Her complaint was that she kept running out of the plants people most wanted and drowning in the ones they did not. She had a spreadsheet, a good one, in which she recorded each week's orders and what had sold, and she wanted something that would tell her what to buy.

Mara spent the first three weeks on it and I did the sums. The relationship between orders and sales was not the interesting thing. The interesting thing was that Noor's figures were wrong in a regular way. In late spring and early summer, her counts of what was on the shelves were out by amounts that could not be due to theft or spoilage; they were out because the counts were being done by whichever member of staff was free, on whichever day they were free, and at different times of the day. A count made at nine on a Saturday and a count made at five on the Friday were treated as the same thing.

The forecast would not have fixed that. It would have taken the faulty counts and given Noor the false confidence of a graph. Mara said so, in a call that she approached with some dread. She told Noor that she could build the tool as asked, but that it would give her mistaken answers, and that what she needed first was one person responsible for the counting, with a fixed time each week.

Noor did not like it. She said, rather sharply, that she had hired Mara for software, not for advice on running a nursery. Mara said that this was fair, and offered to deliver the tool anyway at the quoted price. Noor said she would think. For two weeks nothing was heard.

Then she phoned and said that she had been counting the polytunnels herself on a Friday afternoon, at the same time, for a fortnight, and that Mara had been right, and she was appalled. She had hired a part-time stock lead in the spring, a young man named Idris, who did the counts every Friday and, in his third week, found that a delivery of lavender had been entered twice.

The forecast tool was finished in June, and worked, and was used. What I record, for the part that is less about plants, is the fortnight of silence. A client who is told something they did not ask for needs time, and Mara gave her time, without chasing and without softening. I note that Noor and Mara have been friends since, and that Noor still tells the lavender story against herself.

There are two bike shops in the town of Wexcombe, and they hate each other with the comfortable fury of long neighbours. Spokes & Co, run by a man called Dacian Rhys, had been Mara's client for eighteen months. In January the owner of the other shop, Chainlink, a woman named Philomena Gray, phoned Mara and asked whether she could build the same kind of stock sheet for her.

It was a good job: about 5,200, easy and well within what Mara could do. She told me that her first reaction was pleasure and her second was a feeling of a floor tilting. The stock sheet she had built for Dacian was his, but she knew, from building it, what he stocked, how much, what he paid for it, which brands he was dropping and which he was about to take on. She had not been told these things in confidence, but she had been told them with the understanding that she was working for him.

She asked me to help her think about what she would be able to forget. We made a list, plain, of the facts about Spokes & Co that she held. Supplier terms; margins by category; an unannounced plan for an e-bike line; the stock levels at which he reordered; a complaint he had about a wholesaler. There were thirty-one items. Her honest judgement was that she could not guarantee to unlearn any of them, and that even if she could, Dacian would not believe it, which for a client is almost the same.

She declined, politely and quickly. She told Philomena that she had a long relationship with another business in the same trade, and did not think she could serve both without one of them being at a disadvantage. She offered a name, Imre Bakos, whom she trusted, and said that Imre would do it well. Philomena said she understood, though she did not sound pleased.

She did not tell Dacian that Philomena had called, since that call was Philomena's. She did, however, tell him that she was not available to any other bicycle shop in the district, and that she was saying it now so that he would not have to wonder. He was quiet and then said that she was the first supplier who had ever told him anything before he asked. He sent her a bottle of something and, in the spring, a pump she did not need. Imre did the work for Chainlink, and did it well. He told Mara later that Philomena had asked him, in the first meeting, whether he knew Dacian, and that he had said he knew of him and nothing more, which was true, and that she seemed satisfied. Mara noted that the referral had passed on a clean start and nothing else, which is what she had wanted.

I should note, because it has been asked, that the lost 5,200 was a real loss, and that she regarded it as the cost of a fact she wanted to keep true: that she could be told things. Since then, before she says yes to any client in a trade, she asks herself whom else she serves in it.

The proposal to the Wexcombe Parish Council, for a records system covering burial plots, allotments and the village hall's bookings, went out on the second of March. The parish clerk, Mr Tennant, acknowledged it the same day and said that the council would consider it at its next meeting. Mara heard nothing for five weeks.

She did what people do. She waited a week, and wrote a polite line asking whether there were any questions. She waited another, and phoned and reached the clerk's voicemail. In the fourth week she sent an email of two sentences and was ashamed of it, as she said, because it read as pleading. In the fifth week she asked me whether I thought the job was dead.

I did not know. I said what I could say, that councils meet when they meet, and that silence from a clerk is not a no. What I could do was draft a different kind of message, and I did, from something she had said about how she closes files in her own practice. It said, in three short paragraphs, that she had not heard back and assumed that the council's plans had changed or that the timing was wrong, that she would close the proposal on Friday and take it off her list of open work, and that she would be glad to reopen it at any time if they wished. It did not ask a question. It was entirely free of reproach.

She sent it on a Monday evening. The reply arrived on the Thursday, at ten past nine, from Mr Tennant, who wrote that he was so sorry, that the council had met twice and that the proposal had been agreed at the first meeting, and that he had meant to write the next day, and that a family matter had intervened. Would she be able to start on the twenty-second?

She read it aloud to me and said, you are joking. She had been exactly one day from giving up. The contract, for 8,600, was signed that week. The project was pleasant and the clerk, once he was himself again, was a model client, who answered every question the same day. The records system is still running. Mr Tennant sends Mara a short note each year on the anniversary of the week she almost gave up, with a photograph of the burial register open on his desk, and she keeps them in a folder named reminders.

I took away two things. The first is that a proposal does not die in silence, it waits, and that a closing note is a kinder way to ask than a chaser, because it gives the other person something to answer and removes the sense of being owed. The second is that Mr Tennant's family matter was a bereavement, as Mara learned later, and that she had written five anxious messages to a man who was at a funeral. I now remind her, when a reply is slow, that there is a person at the other end with a life of their own.

From the first of June to the end of August, Mara tried working four days a week. She chose Fridays to leave empty and told her clients in a short note in May. It was an experiment and she called it that in the note, which I think calmed them. She asked me to keep the figures, and I did.

She had three questions. Would clients mind, would income fall, and would she, as she put it, turn into someone who does things on Fridays anyway. The last was the one she was most afraid of.

The clients first. She had eleven that summer. Two noticed. One, a solicitor's office, wrote a friendly line to say that Friday was their quietest day anyway and that she should enjoy it. The other, a manager at a freight forwarder, replied with a question that seemed to her, for a week, quite hostile: did this mean slower turnaround? She answered that it meant the same turnaround within four days, and that for urgent matters she would pick up the phone. He did not mention it again. The other nine said nothing, and I think they did not read the note.

The income fell by six percent over the quarter. About half of that was the hours; the other half was one project that was delayed by a client. In hours the numbers were a little more interesting. In the previous summer she had billed thirty-six hours a week on average. In the experiment she billed thirty-one. That is not a drop of a fifth, as a day's absence would suggest; it is a drop of a seventh. She worked about as fast on four days as on five.

The thing that happened with Fridays was the part she disliked. In the first fortnight she kept the day clean. In the third week she opened her laptop at ten for a quick look, and it was one in the afternoon before she closed it. She then did what I thought was sensible: she put the laptop in the cupboard on Thursday night, with a note on the door, and the Fridays were free after that. By August she had read two novels and re-hung a shelf.

At the end of the summer she decided to keep the arrangement through the autumn and, in January, review. I note the reasons she gave to Yusra, which were not about money. She said that she had discovered that the fifth day of the week had mostly been spent finishing the work of the other four, and that the work had learned to fit. In January she reviewed it with Yusra, and the numbers for the autumn were nearly the same as for the summer, thirty-two hours a week against thirty-one. The one client who had worried about turnaround sent her, unprompted, a note that said the Friday emails had stopped and he had hardly noticed. I also note that the cupboard is a better lock than a plan.

The invitation was to speak at the annual meeting of a trade association of independent opticians, forty-odd members in a hotel conference room, about how a small practice can use its appointment records. It was a good invitation, and it fell on a date when Mara was committed to a client. She declined, and then did what she thought was more important: she recommended Yusra.

Yusra did not want it. She said so within a minute of Mara phoning. She was a designer, not a speaker, and her stomach, she said, did a thing. Mara listened and said that Yusra understood appointment screens better than anyone she knew, and that the opticians would want to hear from someone who had stood next to a receptionist. She did not push. She said she would help, and that if on the day Yusra changed her mind she could cancel.

They prepared for three weeks. Mara read through the slides on the phone and sent comments, and I made a simple timing sheet so that Yusra would know, at any moment, how long was left. The first run-through was stiff. She read from the slide. Mara said that every time Yusra had told her about a receptionist's awkward hour in the last two years it had been vivid and specific, and that the slides were making her speak in the passive voice. Yusra cut eleven of twenty slides and replaced them with three stories.

The day came. Mara sat at the back, in a hotel chair that was too soft, with a coffee she did not drink. Yusra began with her notes in her hand and put them down on the lectern at the third minute. She told the story of an optician's receptionist named Fenella who kept a pencil mark in the margin of her diary for every patient who would be late, because she knew who they were, and who had refused to let a computer replace it until the computer could do the same. The room went quiet in the way of people listening.

She finished at twenty-six minutes, one minute over. Two members came forward afterwards with practical questions. One asked for a fee quote, which Yusra gave. A man in the front said she had made him realise that his receptionist knew more than his system.

On the train home, Yusra said that she had been sick in the car park, before. Mara said that she knew. The part I noted was what Mara said next, which was that she had not given the talk away; she had given Yusra the invitation, and that was a better thing to be able to give. Yusra took three more talks that year. The fee for the opticians was 450, which she spent on a new chair. She says that she thinks of Fenella's pencil before every talk now, and that the story has become more hers than the receptionist's, which Mara says is how a story ought to travel.

St Osric's, a secondary school of 640 pupils, asked Mara to produce its timetable. The deputy head, Mr Achterberg, had made it by hand every August for eleven years, and in the spring he told her, with a gentleness that suggested illness, that he would not be able to do it again. The school paid 6,500 for the work, which had to be ready by the last Friday of August.

A timetable is a famous kind of problem. There are teachers who can teach only some subjects, rooms that can hold only some lessons, pupils who must not be in two places at once, and a great many small pieces of local custom. Mara knew the shape of the theory and had never done one. She thought she could, and I thought she was probably right, and we both underestimated it.

The first week went on collecting constraints. Mr Achterberg gave her a sheet, a long one, and a sort of confession: he had always known that the chemistry teacher, Mrs Ferreira-Lund, taught in the one room with a fume cupboard, and that two sets of year ten needed the lab at the same time. He had solved it every year by a trick he could not explain. There were forty-three rules on the sheet and thirty others in his head.

The second week produced a draft, which was infeasible. The solver, a program that tries combinations, reported that no arrangement satisfied all the rules, and offered nothing more helpful. For two days Mara and I looked at ways of relaxing it. We found that three of the rules, taken together, required one particular teacher to be in two buildings at once on Thursdays. The rules had been written separately and each was reasonable.

Mara took the Thursday problem to Mr Achterberg, who laughed for a good minute. He said that the teacher in question had spent Thursday afternoons crossing the car park at a run for eleven years, and that he had always put a free period between the lessons and had never written it down. They put it in the sheet. The solver then produced a timetable in four hours.

It was not good. It was valid, and a valid timetable can still be hateful: it put the fume-cupboard class on Friday afternoons, and gave a young geography teacher five consecutive lessons on Tuesday. Mara spent the third week not in solving but in preferences, adding weights, so that the solver would try to avoid such things, and in the fourth she printed the result and took it to the school. Teachers stood around it in the staff room, finding their names. By the second afternoon she had received nine requests for small changes, of which she could meet seven. The two she could not meet were instructive. A music teacher asked never to teach on the day after the school concert, which would have emptied Thursdays for eleven other people, and a head of year wanted her form group to have the same classroom every day, which was a wish about the building and not the timetable. Mara wrote to each and said what the request would cost the rest of the school, in lessons and in rooms, and neither pressed. The head of year came by a week later with a plant for the room she did get, and said that she had been asked and answered, which was more than she had been given in the previous eleven Augusts.

The timetable was delivered on the 24th, three days before the deadline, and Mr Achterberg said he had never finished before the thirtieth. In September, I heard from Mara that the fume cupboard class was on Wednesdays, and that the geography teacher had sent her a card.

I keep one thing from this. The rules, as people wrote them, were consistent each by itself and impossible together, and what unpicked them was not cleverness but asking an old man to explain what he had done every year without noticing. The solver could not have asked. She did.

Leocadia Ferrant, the founder of a company that delivers seed-starting kits by subscription, rewrote Mara's investor slides at midnight on the night before the meeting. Mara found out at six the next morning, when she opened the shared file and discovered that her fourteen slides had become nine, that the colour was different, and that the numbers on slide four, which she had checked three times, were each a little rounder than she remembered.

She was alarmed, and she opened the file with the care of a person defusing something. The original was kept, so I could show her the changes side by side. She asked me, for the first time, not to explain anything until she had read it herself.

The rounding was fair. Leocadia had changed 7,412 subscribers to about 7,400, and a growth of 18.7 percent to nearly nineteen. She had removed a slide of Mara's, with a table of acquisition costs by month, which Mara had been proud of. In its place she had put one sentence: it costs us 31 to find a customer who stays for 140. And she had cut a paragraph on method from slide six and put it, in smaller type, in a footnote.

Mara read it all and then, to my interest, she did not reach for her objections. She said that the rewrite was better. She said that she had written for the person who would check the numbers, and Leocadia had written for the person who would remember them, and that those were two readers and she had only thought of one. The investor was the second. The sentence about 31 and 140 was the sentence a room would carry out of a meeting.

She phoned at seven. She told Leocadia that she had one correction, which was that the 31 was in fact 32.40 when the month of October was included, and Leocadia said the 31 was fine for slides. Mara said that was a question of principle and she wanted 32. Leocadia agreed to put 32 and to keep the rest. They went into the meeting with nine slides.

The company raised its round, a modest one, though Mara declined to take credit for it. What I took from this was a plain thing, that she can be shown to be wrong and say so at once, an unfashionable grace, and that her slides for the next project had one sentence on them that she had borrowed. She told Leocadia so, who laughed, and asked her to bill her for the sentence.

The contract for the Calloway & Finn Insurance Brokers project had a sentence on page nine that read: all work product created by the supplier in the course of the services shall be the exclusive property of the client. Mara had read many such sentences and signed some. This time she read it more slowly, because the project involved a piece of software she had built three years earlier, a small engine for matching documents to records, which she had reused on five jobs and thought of as hers.

The difficulty was in the word created. If she used the engine on this job and then improved it, the improvement would be created in the course of the services, and under the sentence it would belong to the client, and she would be unable to use her own engine on the next job without asking permission to use a thing she herself had made. She did not suppose the client meant that. The client's lawyer, a Ms Odalys Lindgren, probably meant only that the client should own the finished system.

She asked me to prepare three fallback positions. The first, a carve-out: the client owns all deliverables except pre-existing materials listed in a schedule, which the supplier keeps. The second, a broad licence: the client receives a perpetual, irrevocable licence to use anything the supplier incorporates. The third, which she disliked, was to charge more for assignment.

They spoke on a Wednesday for forty minutes. Mara began by saying that she understood why the clause was there, and described what the engine was and where it came from, with its history, and the five previous uses, which she was careful to describe without names. Ms Lindgren, who had a precise voice, asked a clear question: would the client be able to maintain the system if Mara disappeared? Mara said yes, and that she would deposit the source of the engine with an escrow agent at the client's cost.

That answer settled it. Ms Lindgren proposed the carve-out, with the engine in a schedule, a perpetual licence to the client for any version of it incorporated in the system, and a clause that improvements to the engine made during the project would belong to Mara but be licensed free to the client. Mara accepted all three in the call, and they were typed into the contract on Thursday.

The thing I recorded was the question that unlocked it. The lawyer's anxiety was not about ownership. It was about being stranded, and the escrow answered that. Mara wrote down, for her own records, that when someone insists on owning something, it is worth asking what they are afraid of losing.

Walter Ashdown owned the Ashdown Garage Group, five garages in three towns, and he had hired Mara to replace the job-card system with something on tablets. He was a generous man and an indecisive one. For the first month she dealt with him alone. In the second a new person began to appear on every call, a tall quiet man named Piers, who was Walter's son-in-law, who worked in marketing, and who, as Walter said when he introduced him, had views.

Piers had views. He thought the system should be built on a particular cloud service which he had read about. He thought it should have an app for customers. He wrote long messages at night with numbered points, some of them excellent and some of them, in Mara's judgement, a little behind the times. She had mixed feelings and, for two weeks, expressed none of them. She said to me that she was not sure whether the correct response to a client's relative with strong opinions was to manage him or to listen.

I thought she should do both, and, as it happened, she did. She replied to each of his messages, one point at a time, in the same numbered form. For the ones she agreed with she said so, and quickly. For the ones she did not, she gave reasons that were short and real: that the cloud service he named would add 3,000 a year to the garage group's costs for no benefit that the mechanics would see, and that a customer app was a good idea for the third year, not the first.

In week four he sent a message with one point only. It said that the mechanics had no signal in the lower yards of two of the garages, and that a system that needed to be online to close a job card would fail exactly at the moment a job was done. Mara read it twice. The design she had drawn for the tablets assumed the garage's wifi, which she had tested in the offices and in the main workshops. She had never walked down to the lower yard.

She phoned Piers that afternoon. She said he was right and she would change the design so that a job card could be closed offline and sent when the tablet found a signal. It took four extra days and she did not charge for them. Piers was quiet and said that he had been to the lower yard to get his car fixed.

What struck me was how little the earlier numbered messages had mattered once the right one arrived. Eleven of Piers's points she had politely declined, and one, the twelfth, saved her the embarrassment of delivering a system that failed on its first morning. She said that the discipline of answering every point had meant that she could hear the one that counted. Piers, at the handover, brought a tray of coffees and sat beside Walter with his notes, and said not a word, which Walter thought remarkable.

In September Mara did something she had been meaning to do for two years. She wrote to eight clients, past and present, and asked each the same question: what is the one thing I should stop doing? She said in the message that she was not fishing for compliments, that she wanted a real answer, and that a single line would do. She asked me to keep the replies in one place so that she could read them all together, without hurrying.

The first came in two hours, from a manager at a freight company, and said that she should stop saying quick. When Mara said a task would be a quick one, he wrote, it was never quick, and he had learned to double whatever she said. She winced when she read it, and then she laughed, because she had said it to him a few weeks before about a report that took nine hours.

The second, from the nursery owner, said that she should stop sending long emails late at night. Not because of the content but because of the time. The owner read them at breakfast, and they seemed to have been written by someone who had not slept. Mara had honestly thought she was being diligent. A third, from a school bursar, said she should stop apologising at the start of every call. A fourth said that she should stop offering three options when she plainly preferred one. The fifth, from a solicitor, wrote only: nothing. Mara reread it several times and said that it was more irritating than the others.

Three people did not reply. That was, I think, an answer too.

She sat with the replies for a day and then asked me to help her make something of them. Her conclusion was that the answers fell into two kinds: habits of speech and habits of timing, and that neither was serious. She stopped using the word quick and now says how many hours. She set her email to deliver at eight in the morning whatever the hour she wrote it. She dropped the apology, which she found harder than she expected, because she had not known she did it, until a call she recorded for her own use came back with the word sorry in the first minute, four times. And the three options became one with a reason.

I noted a thing that I think she did not. The answers were all small. In eleven years of work she had never been told a large thing in answer to this question, perhaps because she had never asked, and her clients had been politely holding small irritations for months and years. The cost of the question was one email each. She says that she will ask it every September, and has written the date on the calendar.

For three years Mara has kept a rule that she gives ten percent of her working days to causes that cannot pay. It is not a number she arrived at by thought. She said it once to Ilse, who had said it to her, and it stuck. In October she asked me to add up what the rule had in fact produced, because she suspected that it had become a habit and not a practice.

I went through her time log. In the last three years the ten percent, about twenty days a year, had gone to eleven organisations. The biggest portion, forty-one days over three years, had gone to Common Table, a charity that ran language exchange evenings for people who had recently arrived in the town. She had built them a sign-up and matching tool, which paired a volunteer with a learner at the same level and the same time of day, and had maintained it. The next largest, nineteen days, went to a swimming club. The remainder was scattered: a morning here, an afternoon there, a lot of small favours that she had not thought of as giving.

The second thing I noticed was less comfortable. In the third year she had given only fourteen days. There was no decision behind it. The days had been absorbed by paid work, and the charitable ones had been the first to be postponed, because no one would send her an angry email about them. A rule that nobody enforces, I wrote in the note I gave her, enforces itself on the weakest day.

She took that well and made a change that I thought was sound. Instead of ten percent spread across the year she put one day a fortnight in her calendar, in the same colour as paid work, with the name of the organisation she was helping. It was not a day she could cancel without a reason she would have to write down, which she described as being rude to herself.

The part that I want in the record is the ending of the Common Table work. In March the director who had asked for the tool left, and the new director, a brisk man, thanked Mara and said that the charity would take the work in-house. It was fine. Mara was a little hurt, and said so to me, and said that she had just been shown the other thing about giving: that you must be willing to be finished. She handed over the tool with a five-page note, and the charity thanked her with a handmade card in eleven languages.

The fortnightly day went, in April, to a repair group that mends bicycles for children. Their records were in a school exercise book, and she began with the book. She asked me to put the new rule at the top of her calendar's notes in her own words, and the sentence she chose was that a gift that is not scheduled is a wish. The ten percent was a number. The fortnight is a habit.

The Marsh Lane Academy Trust runs seven schools, and it asked Mara to design a way of recording which parents had agreed to what: photographs on the website, school trips, medical information, use of a pupil's work in displays. The forms were paper, in folders, in seven offices, and each school had its own habits. A request from a parent to withdraw a photograph sometimes took three weeks to reach the person who could remove it.

The Trust's data protection officer, Esme Latimer, attended the first meeting with a notebook in which she had written, in advance, twelve cautions. Mara said afterwards that it was the most useful meeting she had had that year, because the cautions were not obstacles, they were requirements stated early. Consent must be specific, and a single yes to everything was not consent. A parent must be able to withdraw as easily as they had given. The record must show who recorded the consent, on what date, and on which form version.

The design that grew from this was plain: for each pupil, a list of the things they might be asked about, a yes or a no for each, a date, a name. Esme read the first draft and added one thing, which I had not thought of. The answer when nothing had been recorded must not be treated as a yes. A blank was a no until proved otherwise.

Midway through the work, a deputy head at one of the schools asked for a feature that Mara said, and Esme confirmed, was not possible: a search by a child's name across all seven schools, so that a family with children in more than one school could be seen together. It would have been convenient. It would also have meant that a person in one school could see the consent choices of a child in another, who was none of their business. Mara declined it in a polite paragraph and offered a narrower thing instead: a parent could link their own children and see them together, from a login only that parent held.

The tool went live in a staggered way over October. In the first week a parent withdrew consent for her son's photograph at a school and the withdrawal was effective the same afternoon, a thing that the old folders could not have done in a month. Esme mentioned this in the Trust's newsletter, in a sentence with no adjectives.

I make a note that the best constraints in this project came from a person whose job was to be careful, and that Mara treated her as a collaborator, not a gate. She said, afterwards, that good caution is a kind of design, and she asked Esme to join her on future projects at a fee. Esme has since reviewed two.

In February Mara and Dario took a half-booth at the Small Business Expo in the old armoury hall, a two-day event where three hundred stalls sold printers, payroll, coffee and insurance to a stream of owners in lanyards. They had been persuaded by a leaflet and the idea that people would stop. They split the cost, 780 each, and bought a banner that read We Fix Your Data in a font that Yusra had politely described as a lot.

I helped with what I could from a distance: a list of conversation openers, a one-page handout, and a small prize draw for which visitors would leave a card. They had a hundred and forty handouts printed. Dario brought a bowl of boiled sweets. Mara brought a stool she did not use.

The first morning was quiet. People moved past with the stunned eyes of those who have already been given six pens. A man stopped, looked at the banner and said that his data was fine, thank you, and walked on. A woman asked whether they were the people who did the payroll, and when they said no she looked at them with real sympathy. By lunchtime they had collected eleven cards, nine of them for the prize draw and none, so far as they could tell, from anyone who wanted anything.

The second day, Mara changed what she said. She stopped saying that they fixed data, which meant nothing, and began asking each passer-by one question: what is the one list you keep that you do not trust? It worked at once. People stopped. A man with a florist's firm, a woman with a physiotherapy practice and the owner of a ferry kiosk each told her about a list. They talked for between four and nine minutes. She collected a hundred and twelve cards from the draw by the close, and sixty-seven handouts went.

The tally, which I kept, was this. Sixty conversations of more than two minutes. Fourteen follow-up emails, of which five were answered. Two phone calls. One real lead, a lamp maker named Seraphina, who had a list of two thousand customers and had been meaning to do something about it for six years. She became a client in April, for 3,100. The cost of the stand, with the banner and the sweets, came to 880 for Mara's share, and the lead returned just over three and a half times it.

Whether this was good I cannot say, and neither can she. She said that she would not do it again for the money, but that the question had been worth the trip, and she has used it since. The banner is in the print works, behind the kettle, and Dario, who is sentimental, will not let it be thrown out. I note the accounting of the sweets, which Mara insisted on: of the bowl Dario brought, about two thirds went to people who stopped for them and walked away, and a third to a man who sat down on the stool and told her at length about his father's accountant. She did not charge for the stool.

The first sign was a silence, and the second was a letter. Tamarind Event Hire, which rented marquees and tables to weddings and fairs, owed Mara 4,300 for work on its booking calendar, a project that had been finished and accepted in May. The invoice was due in June. In July it was not paid, and Mara sent the usual reminder. In August a letter arrived from a firm of insolvency practitioners, three pages, headed notice of creditors' meeting, to say that Tamarind had gone into administration and that Mara was among its unsecured creditors.

She took it quite calmly. She had, she told me, been paid by almost everybody for eleven years and she had assumed it would always be so. What she did next, with my help, was to learn the vocabulary. An unsecured creditor stood behind the bank, the landlord, the staff's wages and the tax office, and rather far from the front of the queue. The practitioner's letter included a form for proof of debt, and said that creditors might expect a return of a few pence in the pound, perhaps none.

She filled in the form that evening. It required the invoice, the contract, the delivery acceptance, and a statement of what was owed, and it took, with the paper chase, about two hours. I assembled the attachments. She sent it by recorded post and by email. She also, because she thought it right, wrote to Tamarind's owner, a woman named Ysolde Pratt, whose address she still had. It was a short, sad letter that said she was sorry for what had happened to the business, that she had filed a claim as she must, and that nothing in it was personal. She did not know whether it would be read.

Ysolde replied within the week. She said that the collapse had been quick, that her biggest customer, a hotel group, had owed her 40,000 and had failed too, and that she had liked the calendar very much, and had used it on the last week's bookings, which she had honoured, by hand, out of her own pocket. She thanked Mara for the letter. She did not apologise for the invoice, and Mara said she was glad she did not.

The creditors' payment came the following spring. It was 11 pence in the pound, which came to 473, a cheque with a covering letter in a precise hand. Mara cashed it and said, to me, that this was a moment to say something wise, and then said nothing, which I thought wise.

The record, as I keep it, contains one change. Since then, projects over 5,000 are invoiced in thirds, a third at the start, a third at the middle and a third at delivery, and the first third is paid before work begins. The loss was 3,827, and she noted with a dry smile that it was now the cheapest education she had had. Of the other things, the one that stays with me is the letter. It did not recover any money. It was the one part of the loss that she would do the same again, and Ysolde, I am told, still has a copy.

Bellweather Insurance Brokers had been Mara's client for three years when, fourteen months ago, they moved their work to Callum's firm. It was not done unkindly. The managing partner had phoned to say that Callum had offered a package, with a hosting service and support rota that Mara could not match, and that they hoped there would be no hard feelings. She had said there were none. There were a few, and she had not shown them to anyone but me.

In September the same managing partner phoned again, in a different voice. Callum's firm had decided to stop offering the product on which Bellweather's system ran, with ninety days' notice, and had suggested, he said, that they find another supplier. The partner asked whether Mara would be able to take over, and whether she would consider it, after how things had been left.

I watched her draft the answer. The first draft, written within ten minutes of the call, was an excellent piece of prose and I was glad it was never sent. It was courteous and had one sentence in the middle that said it was interesting to hear what a hosting package had been worth. She read it aloud to me, with some pleasure, and then said, that is horrid, and moved it to the folder of drafts. I did not argue. It is a folder she keeps for such things, and I think that writing the bitter version is how she gets it out of the room.

The second draft she wrote slowly. It said that she would be glad to look at the system, that she would need two days to assess it before quoting, and that she would be frank about what she found. It did not mention Callum. It did not mention fourteen months.

The assessment showed a system in poor but recoverable condition. She quoted 16,500 to move it to a platform she could stand behind, with a plain statement of the risk.
