The managing partner accepted within the week and said, at the end of the call, that they should have asked her before. Mara said that she was glad to hear it, and meant it, which surprised both of us.

She phoned Callum, and I believe this was the right move, to tell him that she was taking the work and that she wished him to hear it from her. He said that he had been going to ring her. He was apologetic, in his way, and asked whether she would be willing to look at two of his other clients' systems on the same product. She said she would think. They are, I observe, once again swapping leads.

What I record is that the bitter draft was not wasted. It was the cheapest place to put the feeling, and the thing that went out was a different document. I also record that she has not deleted it.

Evergreen Orthodontics paid Mara a retainer of 900 a month to look after its appointment system, and in March its new practice manager, a brisk and pleasant person named Tamsin Voss, wrote to say that the practice wished to end the retainer at the end of the quarter. She added that there was no complaint. They were simply reviewing outgoings.

Mara read it twice and then said, which I had not expected, that she was not going to argue about the money. She was going to ask what had changed. The retainer had run for two years and in all that time the system had worked, and her instinct, which I think was right, was that a practice does not cancel something that works unless something else has changed first.

She wrote back asking whether she could have fifteen minutes on the phone, not to dissuade but to learn. Tamsin said yes. The call took twenty minutes, and the answer, when it came, was not what she had guessed. Tamsin said that in her first month she had been unable to see what the retainer was for. The system just ran. She had looked for invoices and found a flat sum. She had looked for reports and found none. She had looked for something to tell the partners at the quarterly meeting, and found no sentence that began with the retainer has this quarter. It was not that the work was bad. It was that she could not see it.

Mara was quiet for a moment. She said that, honestly, she had spent two years making sure there was nothing to see. Her pride was in the quiet. She said she had never thought that a good service has no visible output, so that from the manager's chair it looks like nothing at all.

She offered a small thing, which Tamsin accepted on trial: a single page at the end of each month. It would list what had been done, what had been watched and not needed, what she had noticed and what she recommended. The first, which I helped her write, said that the system had run for 31 days with no interruptions, that she had applied two security updates, that she had noticed the appointment table growing faster than expected and had checked that it would last another four years, and that she recommended nothing. Tamsin replied that it was exactly what she needed to be able to say at the meeting.

The retainer continued. It is now in its fourth year. I note that Mara added a line to every retainer proposal: you will receive one page each month, whether anything happened or not, and the page will say so. She says it is the best thing she ever learned from a cancellation that did not happen.

Penhallow Parish Council had been shown a good many numbers in the last year, by a good many people, and its chair, a calm woman named Dorothea Wragg, asked Mara in the spring to run a short workshop on how to read them. It would be two hours on a Tuesday evening, in the parish room, for nine councillors and the clerk. There was no fee. The council offered a tin of biscuits, and Mara accepted the offer.

She wanted something the councillors could use after she had gone, and she distrusted lessons about charts. She spent a week with me working out what she would say. What we arrived at, and what she wrote on a single sheet, was three questions that any councillor could ask of any number put in front of them. Compared with what? Counted how? Who is missing?

The first was the easiest. A report to the council had said that complaints about the village green had risen by forty percent. Mara asked the room what that meant, and an older councillor, Ambrose, said that it was bad. She asked: compared with what? The previous year. How many? Five, up from three. There was a pause and a good deal of laughter. She then pointed out that nobody had said anything false, and that the number had been told in a way that made a small change sound large.

For the second she used something from the council's own papers. The clerk had reported that attendance at the summer fair was 600. Counted how? It turned out to be the number of programmes given out, divided by one and a half, which was how the previous clerk had done it. It was not a bad method and nobody had known it was a method.

The third was the one that went quiet. A survey of residents about the bus service had had 112 replies. Who is missing? She asked the room who in the village would be least likely to fill in a form that was available only on the council's website. They got there themselves: people without computers, people who did not use the bus because it did not go where they needed, people who had given up on the council. One councillor, Gethin, said that those were exactly the people the bus was for.

At nine she handed out the sheet, and Dorothea asked whether they might put it at the start of every meeting's papers. Mara said yes. The sheet is now on the table before the agenda, and the clerk reports that it has been used, aloud, at four meetings. At the last, someone said, compared with what, in the middle of a presentation by a man who was selling the council a lamp post.

I note that the three questions fit on one line, which is why they have survived. She said, on the way home, that she had taught the councillors nothing they did not know. She had given them permission to ask.

Dr Halvard Eik, a researcher in public health who had worked with Mara on a project in the spring, proposed in July that they write a short paper together on the data problems of small clinics. It would be about four thousand words, for a journal that took practical contributions. He was to supply the clinical context and the references. She was to supply the cases, six of them, from her own work, with the clients' permission, and the account of how the errors had come about.

The writing went well and fast. By September they had a draft, and the argument was sound and carefully made: that data errors in small clinics are rarely careless and almost always structural, and that most could be prevented by three design choices that cost nothing. I read the draft twice for consistency. I found fourteen places where a case in Mara's section used a different term from the same case in Halvard's.

The trouble arose when they came to the title page. Halvard sent a version with his name first, then Mara's, and then, as a courtesy, the names of two research students who had done some reading. Mara wrote back a polite query. In her field the order mattered less than in his, but she had written the whole of the middle and nearly all of the argument. She asked how they should decide the order.

He replied with a long email, courteous and firm. He said that the first author was the person who held the project, secured the access and took responsibility for the whole, and that in his field to be second author of two was an honourable thing. He added that the students, in fairness, should be named. Mara did not reply for a day.

What she did was ask me to help her think about what she actually wanted. She did not want precedence. She wanted the paper to say that the cases and the argument were hers, and she wanted not to be a name in a list. We looked at what the journal permitted, and found that it asked for a short statement of each author's contribution. They could put his name first and hers second, in the usual way, and say plainly what each had done.

She suggested this to Halvard, who agreed at once, and wrote the statement with her. It reads that the first author designed the study and wrote the clinical sections, the second author wrote the case analyses and the argument, and that the students contributed the literature search. The paper was published in January.

It brought three enquiries in the first month, two of them useful, and a request to speak. I note that the settlement was reached not by deciding who mattered more but by describing who had done what. I put it in my record as a pattern: where a dispute is about credit, make the record carry the facts, and the order stops mattering as much.

For nine years Mara's day rate had been something she said aloud when asked, and in the first call, if the client seemed to be about to ask. In March she decided to put it on her website. She had read an argument that a hidden price attracts people who want to haggle and repels people who want to be spared it, and she wished to see what happened. She asked me to keep track.

She wrote the page herself. It said that her day rate was 640, that a day was eight working hours, that fixed fees for audits and small builds were listed beneath, and that she gave a written quote for anything larger. It also said, in a sentence she took a week to write, that she did not discount for the first job, because the first job was where a client learned whether they wanted the second.

In the first month the number of enquiries fell. There had been about eleven a month, in the previous half-year, and there were six. Mara's reaction was a brief panic that I tried to keep in proportion. In the second month there were seven, and in the third, eight. By the fourth I could sort them, and there was a difference. Before the page, about a third of the enquiries had been a request for a ballpark figure with no further information. After it, they had begun with a description of the problem.

One client, a firm of land agents, used the page against her. Their buyer wrote that they had seen the rate and expected a ten percent reduction for the volume they would bring. Mara replied that the page was her price and that she would be glad to talk about volume once there was some, and the buyer, who had apparently expected an argument, said fine. She did the work at 640 for two years.

I counted, at the end of the fourth month, how many new clients had come through enquiries, and how many had stayed. Six of the seven stayed. In the earlier half-year, three of eight had. I should not draw much from seven and eight, and I said so to her, and she said she knew. What she cared about was not the ratio but a single enquiry in the fourth month, from a person who wrote that she had been given Mara's page by a friend and that it was the first consultant's site she had read that did not make her feel stupid. That woman is a client now, for a modest annual job, and has never once asked for a discount.

What I put in the note for her is that the page did not make her richer, and that it did make her time more concentrated: fewer calls where she was asked to explain why she cost as much as she did, more calls where someone was already prepared to pay and wished to describe a problem. She kept the page. She raised the rate on it, in January, to 680, and said that she would like to see how the number moved the enquiries, and I said that I would count.

The presentation was scheduled for the Thursday, at the works canteen of Kestrel Print & Pack, a firm of ninety people that made cartons for the food trade. Mara had spent four months with its operations manager, Lucian Ward, building a scheduling system for the production lines, and the plan, which Lucian had described to her as a town hall, was for her to show the new system to the whole workforce, on a screen, at two in the afternoon. She had prepared a clear and friendly set of slides. I had checked the figures.

On the Tuesday she had a last call with Lucian to go over the running order, and in the course of it, almost in passing, he said that the new system would let the company run two lines with the crews that had run three, and that the third line would be closed in the spring. Mara asked him when the staff had been told. There was a pause, and Lucian said that they would be told at the town hall.

She went quiet, as I have seen her go before when a wire is cut somewhere out of sight. The slides she had written showed the system as a convenience, a way to make the week less chaotic. They were true. They would also have been the means by which a crew learned, in a canteen, in front of ninety colleagues and with a stranger at the front pointing at a screen, that a third of them were to lose their jobs, or be moved, or wait to learn which. She would be the face on the screen at the moment they found out.

She told Lucian this directly, which I thought brave given that he was her client and the project's last invoice was still to come. She said that she was not going to make a judgement about what the company should do with its lines. That was not her business. But she did not intend to present the system to the people it would affect before they had been told what it would do to them, and she would not be able to give the town hall on Thursday. She said that she would present it a week later, if the company wished, or never.

Lucian was not pleased. He said that she had known the project's purpose from the start. She said she had known it was about efficiency, and that nobody had said it was about closing a line. He said that he would speak to the director.

The director, a woman called Aurelia Sandoval, phoned Mara that evening. She was brusque, and then, quite suddenly, she was not. She said that the plan had been to tell people on the day, in the hope of getting it over, and that on reflection that was wrong. The managers would meet the crews on Wednesday and Thursday morning in small groups. The town hall would be moved to the following Thursday and Mara would present the system to people who knew.

It was less comfortable than the first plan, for everyone. In the small groups, I gather, there were angry people, and in the town hall a week later there were questions about the third line that Mara did not answer, saying that they were for the company to answer. She said afterwards that the room felt different from any she had stood in: grim, and awake. Three people asked her about the system itself, and two of those questions improved it.

Afterwards, in the car park, a line supervisor named Brigid waited for her by the barrier and asked, quite plainly, whether she had known. Mara said that she had known for two days, and that she had refused to present until the company said it first. Brigid said that two days was two days more than she had expected anyone outside the management to admit. Then she asked the question she had really come for, which was whether the system would be used to choose who was moved. Mara said that it printed a week and decided nothing of the kind, and that she had put a sentence in the handover note, in writing, that the schedule was not to be used to rank workers or to name those who would go. Brigid asked for a copy of the note. Mara gave her one from the folder in her car, and the line is now the first thing in the document.

I record this without a verdict on the line closure, which was not hers or mine to judge. I record that she kept the part that was hers. She could not decide what Kestrel did with its crews, and she could decide whether she was the means by which they were told. The invoice was paid on time. Lucian, six months later, told her that he had been angry with her for a week and that it was the best thing that happened in the project.

Strideway, a network of six physiotherapy clinics, was cautious about everything. Its operations lead, Blessing Adeyemi, had been burned the year before by a supplier who sold a system that did not do what was promised, and when Mara pitched a tool to remind patients of appointments and cut missed sessions, she said she would not sign anything until she had seen it work.

Mara suggested a free pilot. It was not an easy offer for her, because three weeks of work, even a simple pilot, would cost her about 3,600 in time at her rate, and the chance of conversion, she told me, was perhaps one in three. But she had no doubt that the alternative was a long negotiation about promises. She made it on one condition: that before the pilot began, they would write down together what success meant.

They spent an hour on it by phone and wrote three lines. The pilot would run at one clinic, Harbour Road, which had the highest rate of missed appointments, at 14 percent. Success was a fall in that rate of at least four points over the three weeks, compared with the same weeks the year before. And the pilot would be judged by Blessing, using the clinic's own appointment book and not Mara's figures. Mara signed the page and so did Blessing. I kept it.

The tool sent a text message two days before each appointment and one on the morning, with a link to cancel or move it. It was simple. Each text had to be approved by the clinic's receptionist, Marisol, who rewrote two of them, rightly, in a warmer voice. The first week missed appointments were 12 percent. In the second, they were 9. In the third, 8.5. The same three weeks in the previous year had been 14.2.

Blessing took the figures from the appointment book herself, on the Friday of the third week, and phoned Mara with the answer: a fall of 5.7 points, which cleared the line. She said that she had expected to be told that the result was almost good enough, and was almost disappointed to find that it was not a matter of opinion.

The contract, for 18,500 across six clinics, was signed within the fortnight. What I record about it is the page they had written before the pilot began. A free pilot without a stated measure is a long audition, and the client may change the rules at the end. With the page, the three weeks became a test that either could have lost. She wrote in her notes that she would not do a free pilot without one again, and that the cost of the free weeks was small beside the cost of a proposal that nobody believed. A footnote that Blessing added to her report, which Mara kept, says that the figure is for one clinic in one season and that the others may differ. It is the most trustworthy line in the whole file, and when the second clinic came on in the spring, at 10.1 percent against a previous 13.4, I was glad it had been written first.

Pargeter & Sons Timber ran its orders on a program that had been written in 1998 in a language that Mara had heard of and never used, a dialect of a business BASIC that the maker had stopped selling years earlier. The program lived on a beige computer in the back office, under a desk, and its author, Harold Quint, was seventy-nine and retired. When the beige computer began to show a message about a disc, the firm's owner, Edmund Pargeter, asked her to find out what could be done.

She had nine days before the firm's quarter-end. Her first move was to ask me what I knew of the language, and I could tell her only that it had a syntax like a tidy relative of languages we both know, that its file format was a set of fixed-width records, and that there was a decent chance that the data could be read without the program at all. The program itself she copied, with the owner's leave, onto a disc.

The first three days went on reading the source. It was dense and consistent, and had comments in a hand that Mara described as that of a man talking to himself in a shed. There were six hundred lines about discounts alone. She wrote, in a notebook, the rules she found, and on the fourth day she phoned Harold.

He was delighted. It was, he said, the first time in nine years that anyone had asked him about it. He talked for an hour and a half and told her many things the source did not: that the discount for builders was a historic arrangement with a man who had since died and was carried on out of loyalty; that a certain round number in line 2,300 was the weight of a lorry that no longer existed; and that every morning at three the program printed the next day's delivery sheet on a dot-matrix printer in the yard office, which the drivers collected at six, and that it had not missed a day since 2003.

She went cold at the last. The source did contain the print routine, but nothing in it said that it ran by itself, since the trigger was a line in the beige computer's start-up settings that Harold had added in a hurry one night. No document mentioned it. A replacement that did everything else perfectly would have left eleven drivers at the gate on the first morning with nothing in their hands. She got Edmund to the beige computer that evening, found the line, and wrote it at the top of her list.

The replacement, which took her through the quarter, kept the discount rules exactly as Harold had written them, with his comments translated into plain words, and with one extra line at the top of each rule that said who had asked for it. Edmund took Harold a printout and a bottle of whisky, and Harold, I was told, read the whole thing in an afternoon and found a mistake of Mara's in the rounding, which she fixed.

I take from it that the real record of a system is not always in the system. What Mara said to me, afterward, was that she had treated the source as the truth, and the truth had needed a telephone.

Dario got married on a Saturday in June, and Mara had been given a task that she took more seriously than the occasion required: she was to cover his on-call for the week before, the week of, and the week after. Dario looked after the hosting of four small clients, and for ten years he had never been out of reach of his phone for more than a few hours. He gave Mara a handover note of four pages, with a drawing, and said that nothing would happen, and then spent twenty minutes listing what might.

The note was good. It said where each client's systems lived, what each one's normal behaviour was, who to call at each firm, and what the three failures were that tended to occur, with their cures. It said, in a line near the end, that if anything happened to the dentists' group on a Friday afternoon, she should not try to be clever and should call him anyway. I had helped her turn it into a one-page card, which she put by her phone.

The week before was quiet. The wedding week was quiet. On the Thursday before, a disk-space warning appeared in a client's monitor and Mara dealt with it in six minutes, with the note beside her, and felt out of proportion pleased. She sent Dario nothing, as promised. At about nine on the Friday evening a message arrived on her phone from him, a photograph of a handwritten place card with her name on it, and nothing else.

On the Saturday, at 3:40 in the afternoon, the dentists' group's booking page went down. It was, of course, the one thing the note told her not to be clever about. She read the note, and then she read it again, and then she did what it said, which was to phone Dario. He was, as she learned, in the middle of the photographs with his mother. He answered on the second ring. She said she wished to say nothing except that the dentists' page was down and that she did not need him. She told him what she had checked. He asked three questions, one of which she could answer and two of which she could not, and he said that it was the same cause as in March and told her which switch.

She fixed it in eleven minutes. When she finished, he was still on the line, and she realised that he had been standing in a garden in his wedding clothes, waiting. She told him to go back to his guests. He said that he had never doubted it, and she told him to go and eat something.

I record what I thought at the time, which was how much of the care in the exchange lay in the shortness of it. She did not tell him that she had panicked. She told him what she needed, once, and he gave it, and went back. She did not say at the time how much she had enjoyed being trusted with his clients. I think the place card is still on her desk.

The dinner was in a private room at a restaurant near the river, for the board of a regional bus company, the company's two directors and, as the guest, Mara. She had been working with them for four months on a fleet-maintenance dashboard. The chairman, Ruarc Aldenhoven, a man of seventy with the voice of a bell, had organised it to mark the end of the first phase. There was a soup, a fish and an argument about wine.

Over the fish, Ruarc tapped a glass and said that he wanted to thank everyone, and, in the same breath, that he was delighted to announce that the next phase, the passenger-count integration, would be live by the first of December. He said it warmly and clearly, to eleven people. It was the tenth of October. Mara had not agreed to this date. She had not been asked, and she knew that the integration depended on a vendor's data feed that did not yet exist.

She told me, afterwards, that for about three seconds she felt her whole self go into the sauce. Then she put down her fork and smiled and said, in a bright and level voice, that it was an ambitious date and that she would be glad to look at exactly what it would take. Ruarc said, good, good. She added nothing. The table moved to dessert.

She did not argue and did not agree, and this, she thinks, was what saved her. If she had contradicted him in front of the board she would have had to win the argument at the table. If she had agreed she would have owned a date that was not hers. By saying what it would take she had accepted the question and kept the answer.

The next morning she wrote me a list of what it would take: the vendor's feed, a test period of three weeks, two meetings with the depot, the cost of a replacement if the vendor slipped. She wrote it to Ruarc in a page and a half, courteously, with one line that said that she took the date seriously and wanted it to be true. He phoned at ten. He said that he had a habit of announcing dates at dinners and that his directors had learned to ignore him. He had not meant it as a commitment, he said, but as a mood.

They settled on the twenty-fifth of January, with a clause that said the date would move by the number of days the vendor was late. The vendor was late by nineteen days, which moved it to the thirteenth of February.

I note that Mara spoke of the dinner for a week and that what she liked was not that she had held a line but that she had held it without anybody losing face. She sent Ruarc a card at the end of the project, which he kept on the mantel, and he told her that it was the only occasion on which a consultant had looked at him at a dinner and declined a deadline without making him feel a fool.

The call from Sallowfield Group came on a Wednesday morning, and Mara said afterwards that she had known what it was before the first sentence, from the tone of the managing director's voice. For three years Sallowfield had been her largest client, and in the last twelve months it had supplied thirty-eight percent of her income, 54,000 of 142,000. The managing director, a decent man named Augustin Jago, said that the board had decided to bring its technical work in-house from the first of April, that it would be hiring two developers, and that he wanted her to hear it from him first.

She thanked him. She asked, I think wisely, what notice she would be given, and he said that the contract allowed ninety days but that Sallowfield would give her six months, with a gradual reduction of the work, if she would help with the handover. She said she would. She put down the phone, sat for a minute, and then asked me to open the income table.

I had made it a year before and had pointed out then, in a note she may not have read, that no client should exceed a quarter of her income. She read it now. The note was short: concentration risk. She said that she remembered it, and had not acted, because the money was good and the client's work was agreeable and there had never been a day when it seemed urgent.

We spent the afternoon on arithmetic. Sallowfield would pay her 54,000 in the year just ended and about 40,000 in the next six months, tapering to nothing. Without a replacement, her income from April onward would be about 88,000 a year, less than she needed. She had six months, a little over twenty-five working weeks, to find roughly 50,000 of work, in a way that did not repeat the mistake. That meant not one client of that size but five or six of about 10,000.

She made a plan the same evening and it was a good one. It had three parts. First, to ask each current client whether there was something small and useful she had not yet offered, and she wrote nine names beside nine ideas. Second, to ask Wren, Yusra, Noor, Callum, Ilse and Teo for introductions, which she did by message in the next two days; four replied with names. Third, to put two hours a week, in a fixed slot, on Thursday mornings, into finding new work, so that it would not be last on the list in the weeks she was busy.

In the second month she also did something I had not suggested. She asked Augustin Jago, who had no reason to say yes and every reason to find it awkward, whether she might name Sallowfield as a reference and whether he would speak to a prospective client if they called. He said that he would be glad to, and in December he did, for a school trust that was weighing her up. The trust's bursar told Mara afterwards that he had described the departure as a decision about the company and not about her, and had said that he would hire her again for anything outside what they had taken in-house. That sentence was worth, I think, a good part of the 5,200 the trust paid in January.

The six months went quickly. She won a theatre, a firm of land agents, a group of clinics, a school trust, a charity and a small manufacturer. In the last week of March, with the last of Sallowfield's work completed and handed over to the two new developers, she did the sums again. The quarter's income was 36,000, of which Sallowfield supplied 5,000, and the largest other client 6,200, which was seventeen percent. No client was more than that.

I record how she felt, which was not what I expected. She was not relieved. She said that the ending of the Sallowfield work had been the first time in three years that she had had to look at her practice as a thing that someone had built, and that she could see its walls. She was also a little proud, and she told me that she would keep the Thursday morning on her calendar for as long as she had one.

The note I made says what I should have done, and it is less about her than about me. A warning in a table is a warning only if it is read. I now put the concentration figure on the first line of the table, in a line of its own, each month.

Three proposals in eight weeks went to other firms, and Mara noticed it only when she wrote the third rejection into the table I keep. It was not the number that troubled her, since she wins about one in three, so that three losses was ordinary. It was that all three had come back with a variation of the same sentence, in the feedback: well-presented but not specific to our needs.

She asked me to put the three proposals on one screen. We read them together, as if they were someone else's. The structure was identical, because it was a template she had built eight years ago. A page about the company, a page of approach, a page of timetable, a page of price, a page of references. The first three pages could have been sent to anyone. The client's problem, in the opening lines, was described in generalities, and in each the name of the client appeared exactly four times.

I counted something else. In the three proposals, the number of words that were about Mara or her methods was about 1,100 each. The number about the client's own situation was 180, 140 and 210. She read that table, and said, it's an invoice. It is a letter written to explain a price.

She rewrote the template that weekend. The new shape began with the client's problem, in the client's own words, taken from the first call, in a paragraph that she wrote first and showed to no one. After that came what she understood, what she did not yet understand and would need to learn, and the questions she had not been asked. Then the approach, shorter than before, written as a first week and not as a method. Then price, timetable, references. About herself, a half page, at the end.

The first proposal on the new template went to a regional water-sports club, the Estuary Rowing Association, which needed a membership and boat-booking system. Its secretary, Thelonious, wrote back in four days to say it was the only proposal in which he had recognised his own club. It was awarded in a week, for 7,800.

I do not want to make too much of this. A single win is not proof, and the next two on the new template were lost. But one of them was lost with a note that said it was the best written of the six, and that the winner had been chosen on a relation of the director's, which is the kind of loss I find easy to carry. She has now won four of seven on the new shape. I keep a column in the table that counts the words about the client, and I have noticed that it goes up when she is in earnest.

Penwithen Slate cut roofing slate from a quarry on the side of a hill, and had done so for a hundred and forty years. Mara went to see it on a wet Tuesday in February, because its manager, Tegid Morgan, wanted a system to record every load that left the site and every invoice that followed, and she wished to understand the weighbridge.

She was not allowed to take her laptop. The rules were firm and sensible: nothing was to be carried on the site that could be dropped or that needed a charger, and visitors wore a hard hat, boots, a hi-vis jacket and a pair of glasses that did not quite fit. She had a notebook, a pencil on a string, and a camera she was permitted to use in the yard, from which she sent me eleven photographs that evening.

I looked at them carefully, with her notes, and the lesson was in the photographs. The first was of the weighbridge office, a small hut with a window onto the scales. Beside the window, on a nail, hung a pad of dockets, the kind with a carbon sheet, and a pen on a chain. The driver stopped on the scales, the weighbridge clerk, a woman named Rhian, wrote the weight and the destination on the pad, tore off the top copy for the driver and left the carbon on the pad. The second photograph showed Rhian with the pad. The third was a close-up of the carbon, a faint blue, with a clear mark from every load of the week. At the end of every day she brought the carbons to the office, and a clerk keyed them into a spreadsheet.

Mara's first idea, in the car, was a tablet at the window. She dropped it that evening, when she remembered what she had been told on the site. Rain came through the window, the drivers did not get out of their cabs, and the tablets would have been wet in half a minute. She was clear about it in her notes: the docket was a perfectly good system. It was robust, it needed no power, it was understood by every driver and it left a copy that no one could change.

What she designed instead did not touch the weighbridge. It kept the carbon docket. At the end of the day Rhian, or anyone, photographed the pad's carbon with a phone, and the system read the weights and the destinations from the picture, and put them into the invoice file for the clerk to check. The drivers noticed nothing, and the clerk's keying of two hours a day fell to twenty minutes.

I record that this was the cheapest thing to build and, according to Tegid, the quickest to be accepted. I record also what she said to Rhian on the last day, as the hut shook under a passing lorry: that she had thought she would be replacing the pad, and that she had decided to learn from it. Rhian said that the pad had been there since her mother's time, and, with some feeling, that she had been afraid of this visit for a month.

The planning department of Stonecross Borough Council had asked for a workshop to agree what its new casework system must do. There were ten of them in a room on the second floor, in a circle of chairs, and Mara knew within five minutes that she was in trouble. She asked the first question, which was what annoyed them most about the current system, and no one spoke. The team lead, Nuala, looked at the carpet. A man who had been introduced as the longest-serving member of the team studied his hands. The coffee machine hummed.

She told me later that she had waited for forty seconds, which had felt like ten minutes, and then she tried again with a gentler version of the same question, which was received with a silence that she described as respectful and entirely closed. She understood what was happening. The room contained a boss, a number of people who could be overheard by that boss, and a topic that touched on what each of them did badly.

She stopped talking and said that she would like to try something different. She gave each person three index cards and a pen, and asked them to write one thing on each: one thing the current system makes harder than it should be, one thing it hides, one thing they would be glad never to do again. They would not put their names. They would work for five minutes alone, in silence, and no one would read anything aloud.

The silence in the room changed at once. She said that she could hear pens. It was, she said, the most productive five minutes of the day. At the end she collected the cards in a hat, borrowed from the receptionist, and shuffled them, and read them aloud, in her own voice, one after another, without saying whose they were.

There were thirty. Some were expected: the search was slow, the form forgot its contents. Some were not. One said that the system made no difference between an application for a garden shed and one for a housing estate, and so every case began by someone saying out loud which it was. One said that the system hid the date a neighbour's objection had arrived, which mattered legally, and had to be found by opening four screens. One, in a firm hand, said that the thing they would be glad never to do again was to retype the same address six times.

As she read, people began to speak. The longest-serving member said that the neighbour's objection date was a real problem and that he had been bitten by it. Nuala said, with feeling, that she had been trying to get this raised for two years. By the end of the second hour the room was full of voices, and they were talking to each other, not to Mara.

She sorted the cards that evening, with me typing the words as she read them out, into the groups the room had made without noticing: slow, hidden, repeated. Eleven of the thirty were about retyping. She sent the grouped list back to Nuala the next morning with the original cards photographed beside it, so that nobody could say that Mara had edited them, and with a note that no card would be attributed to anyone, even by guess. Nuala wrote that the list had gone onto the wall of the team room by lunch, and that the longest-serving member had stood in front of it for several minutes and then added, in pencil, a thirty-first card that claimed his own, the one about the neighbour's objection date.

The card I remember was the one she kept. It had been written, she thought, by the quietest man in the room, who had never spoken. It said, in capital letters: PLEASE ASK US WHAT WE DO BEFORE YOU DECIDE WHAT IT IS. It is, I think, the best brief she has ever been given. She has it pinned inside the cover of her notebook. Ten minutes of silent writing now opens every meeting she runs, whether or not the room is quiet.

Ilse is the person Mara goes to when she does not know what she thinks. She is twenty years older, ran a firm of fourteen people for most of those years and then sold it, and she lives on a canal boat that she insists is not a hobby. In the third week of October Mara went to see her, because in the last year she had been asked three times, by three different people, whether she planned to grow.

They walked along the towpath, which is Ilse's way. Mara told me about it that evening and I have set it down as nearly as I can. Ilse asked three questions and she did not answer any of them.

The first was: what would you do with the time? Mara said, after a while, that she supposed she would do more of the same. Ilse said, that is the point, and said no more.

The second was: what do you think a firm of eight is, compared with a firm of one? Mara guessed it was more capacity and more income and more risk. Ilse said that those were all true and not the thing. A firm of eight is a firm in which someone has to be the person who is not doing the work. She had spent eleven of her fourteen years, she said, doing what she had never learned to do, which was making sure that other people were working well, and she had been good at it, in the end, and had not liked it very much. She said it as an observation, with her hands in her coat.

The third question was the one Mara had been avoiding. Ilse asked: who are you doing it for? It is easy to answer with a name, and Mara did, and Ilse said that was fine but not what she meant. She meant whose idea of the thing it was. In her own case, she said, she had grown the firm for a while because it was what a person who did well was supposed to do, and she had been unable to tell, for a number of years, whether it had been her wish.

They walked as far as the lock. Mara said that she did not want to grow. She said it quietly, as if testing it. Ilse said, then don't. She said it without ceremony, and it was, Mara told me, the first time anyone had said it as an answer and not an indulgence.

Back at the boat Ilse made tea on a stove the size of a hat box and told her about the one time she had nearly sold the firm, at forty, to a buyer who offered 1.1 million, and had not, because in the last week she realised that she was afraid not of the work but of the quiet afterwards. She did not tell Mara this as a warning. She told her because a choice made from fear of what comes after is not a choice about the thing itself, and Mara's, she said, had sounded like a choice about the thing.

What follows is not really about Ilse. Mara wrote in her notebook a sentence that I have copied into my own record: I am not small because I failed to be large. She wrote a second sentence beneath it, in which she wondered what she would do with the choice, and the second was longer. She decided to keep the practice at herself and three or four associates, to put the time she had spared herself into doing fewer things better, and to say so plainly to anyone who asked. She told Callum, who asked the week after, and he said, with real surprise, that it sounded restful.

I record that I did not give her advice, though I could have produced a table. It would have been a bad one. A table has columns, and every column Mara and I could have named, income, hours, risk, was a column about the practice. Ilse's questions were about Mara, and the practice appears in them only as the place where she stands. She told me at the end of the evening that the heron had not moved the whole time they were on the bank, and that she thought it had been listening. Her answer was in what Ilse asked and what Mara said when she was not defending anything, on a towpath, with a heron on the bank. I kept the questions, because they will be useful the next time someone asks if she is thinking of growing, or if she is, after all, quite sure.

Greenlaw Foundry makes castings for the pump trade, in a long shed with a small and old-fashioned office. Mara quoted a fixed 7,440 for a job-tracking tool, which was twelve days at 620, and the foundry's owner, Isidore, signed it on the day. She had wanted the work and had estimated generously, because the system it would replace was said to be thorny.

It was not thorny. The old system turned out to be a sheet with one tab, and the people who used it, three of them, were tidy. Mara finished the tool in six days. She tested it on the seventh with the office and delivered it on the eighth, and then she faced a small question that she told me was more awkward than any bug. She had the fixed fee, and she had been paid, by the terms, for twelve days. The foundry did not know she had used six.

She might have said nothing, since it was a fixed price and the arrangement was that the risk and the benefit were hers. I thought that on this point she would not need me, and she did not. She said, in the car, that she would tell Isidore at the handover if he asked and would not otherwise raise the point. I think the doubt, for a day, was whether this was honesty or a form of vanity. It was neither, she decided. It was an arrangement.

At the handover Isidore, who is shrewd, asked her. Did it really take twelve days. She said, six. There was a silence, and she told me that she had braced herself, because she did not know whether he would feel overcharged or relieved. He asked whether the tool was finished, and she said it was. He asked whether the six days had been hard days, and she said they had been steady. He laughed and said that his father had paid a plumber for forty minutes of work once and been told that he was paying for the knowing which pipe.

He said that he would rather have a supplier who finished early and was paid for twelve than one who took twenty and gave him a discount. Then he asked whether she could do a second tool, for the pattern shop, at the same fixed price. It was a different job, but she had learned the foundry. She said she would do it for 5,500, and he said fine.

I recorded, in the table, something I had not expected: that she has since quoted more shrewdly on fixed prices, and with less guilt, because the thing that had troubled her was never the margin. It was whether she would be able to say the true number out loud. She was, and nothing happened. She wrote on a card that the fixed price is a price for the outcome, and that the days are her own business, and, on the back, that she should be ready to say them.

Ballast Freight had two developers, Pavol and Ines, who had built the company's booking system together and kept it running through six years of small disasters. When the managing director hired Mara to look at its speed problems, no one told the two of them why. They were told that a consultant was coming. Pavol took this to mean that they were being replaced. Ines did not say what she took it to mean, which was worse.

Mara met them on the first morning in a small room and was greeted with a coolness she recognised at once. They answered her questions precisely and offered nothing else. Pavol described the system in four sentences. Ines asked whether she would be looking at the code and, when told yes, said, I'll get the repository, in the voice of a person agreeing to a search.

I suggested nothing, and she did what I thought was exactly right. At the end of the first day she asked them to review her. She said that she would write a one-page plan of what she thought she would do over the following two weeks, and that she wanted them to tell her what was wrong with it, before she did anything. She sent it that evening, and said in a note that she had been in the building for a day and would be wrong about a good deal.

Their reply the next morning was two pages, and it was courteous and merciless. Pavol said that her theory, that the slowness lay in the database, was probably mistaken, and gave three reasons. Ines said that the thing she had not mentioned was the nightly import from the customs system, which locked a table for twenty minutes every morning and which the two of them had been unable to persuade anyone to change. She added a diagram. It was a good diagram.

Mara said, I think they are right. She read the reply to me twice, and she was glad of it in a particular way, because it came from people who understood the system and had started talking. She changed her plan. She spent the next week not on the database but on the import, with Ines beside her at the desk and Pavol across the room, ready to be consulted and pretending not to be. On the ninth day they found it: a single query that, run each morning, scanned the whole table of bookings, 2.1 million rows, to find about four hundred. A missing index. Ines had known for a year and had had no one to tell.

The morning load, after the fix, took about two seconds. Pavol came over and shook Mara's hand without comment. Ines said that she wanted the diagram framed. At the close of the project the managing director asked whether Mara would be willing to stay on as a part-time adviser. Mara said that she would rather he gave the job to the two developers, as a title and a raise, and told him why. He did. She told me that was the best invoice she had ever not sent.

I noted her habit for next time. When a client's own people are afraid of you, ask them to review your plan, and be wrong in front of them early.

Noor sent Mara a new client in November, and in the first call Mara knew it was a mistake. Corvin & Daughters, a family business that sold garden furniture, wanted an app. It was, said the elder daughter, Cosima, to be a customer app, and a delivery app, and a stock app, with a loyalty scheme and a chat window and the possibility of a robot that could advise on the right cushion. They had a budget of 6,000. They wanted it by March.

I noted the facts in the order Mara gave them. The budget was a tenth of what the list would cost, and the deadline was a third of the time. Neither of these was unusual in itself, since enthusiasm with limited means is common, and Mara had worked with it often. What troubled her was how Cosima answered the question of which feature mattered most. She said all of them. When asked which would be dropped, she said that it was the consultant's job to find a way to include them all.

Mara did not say no on the call. She said that she would think about it and send a note. After the call she asked me to help her answer two questions: could she do it, and should she. She could do a good version of one of the features, in the time and for the money. She should not take the job as specified, since there was no version in which both sides would be content, and she knew from experience that she would be blamed for the part that was missing.

She wrote a kind letter. It said that she thought a customer app was a fine idea, that she did not think it could be built as described for the sum, and that she did not want to take the money and give them less than they hoped. She suggested, as a first step, a simple order-status page for the delivery side, which could be built by a student collective she knew, the Northgate Makers, for about 900, and which would show them whether customers used it. She gave the collective's address, and said that if the page was used she would be happy to talk again.

Cosima replied with a short email that was not warm and was not hostile. She said that they would think about it. Nothing else arrived.

Noor phoned a week later, to ask how it had gone. Mara told her, with some care, because Noor had meant well. Noor listened and was silent, and then said that she had known they were ambitious and had not known that it was so extreme, and that she would be less quick to send people. Mara said that she should send people, only perhaps with a word about the budget.

I make two observations. One is that the refusal cost her the money, and nothing else; the relationship with Noor, which she had worried about, was warmer for it. The other is that she gave them something useful for free: a place to begin. In April she heard that Corvin & Daughters had used the collective, that the page had been used by about a third of their customers, and that Cosima was back to the idea of a smaller app. She did not call. She thought that the next move was theirs.

The Southern Marches Regional Council kept a list of approved suppliers, and to be on it was, for a small consultancy, the difference between being invited to quote and watching others do so. Mara had known this for years. In the spring she decided to apply. The first attempt took her a weekend and failed on page six of the form, which asked for a company registration number. She had traded for eleven years as a sole trader and had none.

She phoned the council's procurement office and reached a woman called Delphine, who was patient in a way that I think she had learned the hard way. Delphine said that sole traders were permitted, though the form did not say so; that she should enter her tax reference in the field, with a note; and that the form would complain and she should ignore the complaint and add a line in the free-text box. Mara did this. The second attempt failed on the insurance certificate, which had to be dated within the last ninety days, and hers was a hundred and four days old. She got a new one from her broker in forty minutes.

The third attempt, two weeks later, went in with seven attachments and a covering note. It was refused for a reason that made her laugh out loud in the kitchen: one of her attachments was in a file format that the council's system was unable to read. It was a perfectly ordinary document. She re-saved it in an older version.

I had been taking her through the three failures with a list that I had made after the first. A little before the third attempt she asked what it had cost so far, and I counted. Eleven hours on forms, a broker's fee of 60 and about a day and a half of her own attention that she could not bill. The potential value of being on the list, according to the council's published data, was that about forty contracts of between 5,000 and 50,000 were let each year to small suppliers, of which perhaps six were in her field.

The next event, which she did not need to make an attempt for, was a call from Delphine on a Tuesday. She said that Mara's application had been approved, and apologised for the format. Mara asked whether, since she had a contact, she might be told about anything that went wrong with the form in the next round. Delphine said, with a short laugh, that she would put Mara's name on the list for that as well.

She was invited to quote within the first month on a data-cleaning project for the council's library service. She did not win it. She was invited to quote on another in the autumn, which she did win, for 11,200.

I record the procedure as she saw it, not as the form did. The form was an obstacle, and the obstacle had a person at the end of a phone line, who was glad to be called. Each time the system said no, Mara had asked a human what the no meant and had, on three occasions, been told something the system would never say. She says now that when a form fails, her first act is to find the name of the person who wrote it.

Atlas Tutoring, an agency that matched private tutors to families, had been Mara's client for nine months when its founder, Winifred Achebe, asked her to a coffee she described as informal. They had spent that time building a custom matching system, and by the fourth month it was working, though not quite as well as hoped. At the coffee Winifred said that she had found a ready-made product, built for exactly this, and used by two other agencies. It was a monthly fee. She wanted to know what Mara thought.

Mara told me about it that night, sitting very still, which I recognise as how she is when she is being scrupulous. She had spent about 24,000 of the client's money and nine months of her working life on the system. The ready-made product, from what Winifred described, would do about eighty percent of what theirs did, at 290 a month, and would be maintained by someone else. She said that her first thought had been to find the eighty percent's weak points, and that she had been ashamed of it.

She asked for two days. She spent them looking at the product, from the outside, as far as she could, from its documentation and from a trial account Winifred forwarded. It was good. It lacked one thing Atlas wanted, a rule by which a tutor was never paired with a family she had previously been withdrawn from, which was important to them for reasons of safeguarding, but it had an escape that would cover it. She wrote a note that said what she had found and what she thought.

She told Winifred, on the phone, that she thought the ready-made product was the better choice. She said that it would cost them about 3,500 a year, that their custom system would cost about 6,000 a year to keep running, and that the difference mattered less than the fact that she, Mara, was one person and the product was a company. She said that if she were in Winifred's position she would move, and that she would help with the move, at a fixed fee, to make sure that the safeguarding rule was preserved and nothing was lost.

There was a silence and Winifred said that she had not expected to be told. She said that she had half thought she would have to argue. She asked how Mara could be so cheerful about losing the work, and Mara said that she was not cheerful. She was, she said, honest about what she thought was good for Atlas, and in her experience that was the only thing that lasted.

The move took three weeks. Mara was paid 2,800 for it. The custom system, in the end, was switched off in a quiet week in July, and Mara kept the code in a sealed folder with a note saying why it had been put away. Winifred sent three families to her over the next year, who wanted something that no ready-made product would do, and one of them paid 15,000.

On the last day of the move she did something I had not seen her do for a client. She sat with Winifred's two coordinators, Peregrine and Tabitha, in the agency's back room and walked them through the new product's screens, using three real cases from the week before: a tutor who taught maths and music, a family with twins, and a withdrawn pairing. In the third case the product's escape for the safeguarding rule failed for the first time, because the pairing had been withdrawn under a name spelt two ways. Mara had expected it and had a fix ready, a one-line rule about spelling, and Tabitha wrote it on a card and pinned it above her desk.

I have seen her do this before, and each time I think it is the most professional thing she does. It does not feel like it at the moment. It feels like a lost contract. What I take from it is that advising a client to leave your own work is the strongest form of evidence you can give them that your advice is not for sale.

Six people from six charities that fund other charities sat at a long table in a rented room on a Monday, and Mara was the seventh, invited to speak for twenty minutes on a topic that the organiser had put on the agenda as what data should we ask of grantees? The funders were polite and a little tired. Each represented a pot of money, and each pot had a form.

She had prepared by asking me to count. The six funders, in their application and reporting forms, asked small charities for an average of 38 separate pieces of information in the first form and 24 more in each annual report. The charities that received the money had, on average, 2.3 paid staff. Mara had worked with several, and she said that a typical small charity, asked for 62 figures, would produce about 20 of them reliably and make up the rest from memory.

She put it to the funders the way she had told me she would: that the more they asked for, the less it was worth. A figure invented to satisfy a form was worse than none, because it looked like a fact. She proposed that each funder ask for five things, chosen for what the funder would actually use, and that for each of them it should be able to say, in one sentence, what decision it would change.

One funder, Bartholomew, who managed a large trust, pushed back, and I am glad she recorded his objection. He said that his trustees needed the full detail for accountability, that if a grant went wrong they would be asked what they had known, and that a short form was a way of not knowing. Mara said that he was right about the risk. She asked him, though, how often in the last five years the full detail had changed a decision. Bartholomew paused. He said that he did not know. Then he said, with a rueful smile, that he suspected the answer was twice.

They spent forty minutes on his point. It was agreed in the end that the funders would try for two years a shared first form of eight questions, with any further information requested only if a specific doubt arose. Mara did not win the argument so much as give the room a way of having one. When she left, Bartholomew walked to the door with her and said that he would try it with two of his smaller programmes.

I do not know how it ended; the funders have not told us, and the route to learn it is the two-year review they agreed to hold. What I record is a small habit of hers that I admire: she asks the question, what decision would it change, of everyone who asks her to collect data, funders included, and she asks it first of herself. It is the same question for a pile of figures as for a form. It is the thing she says when she is asked to add a column.

Yusra and Mara disagreed about the form. It was a registration form for the Marlin Street Health Centre's new patient intake, with thirty-one fields, and the question was how to present it. Yusra, who is a designer, wanted six short steps, each on its own screen, with a progress bar and a calm illustration at the start of each. Mara wanted one page, thirty-one fields in a single long column, with headings. She said that people hate being led and that steps hide how much remains.

They argued, for the most part with great goodwill, over three days. Yusra said that a long form frightens and Mara said that steps patronise. Neither moved. I thought it was a disagreement of the kind that cannot be settled by saying anything. I offered to set up a way of finding out, and Mara said, let's test it.

They found eight people, each a friend of a friend with no connection to the clinic, who agreed to complete the form once and to talk aloud while they did so. There were three versions: Yusra's six steps, Mara's long page, and a third that Yusra had added, the day before, in a spirit of experiment, of two screens, one for who you are and one for your health. Each volunteer saw one version and, a week later, a different one. I timed them and made notes of what they said.

The results were not a victory. The long page took on average 6 minutes 10 seconds. The six steps took 7 minutes 40, but two of the eight said that they had enjoyed it, in a way nobody said of the long page. The two-screen version took 4 minutes 55, the quickest, and no one commented on it at all. One volunteer, a man in his sixties, said as he finished the long page that he had been counting the fields as he went, and that he had been annoyed to reach thirty-one.

They also found a thing neither had expected. In the six-step version, three volunteers went back to correct earlier screens, nine corrections between them, while on the long page nobody went back, since the whole of it was in front of them and a mistake showed as it was made.

What Mara and Yusra settled on was the two screens, with one thing borrowed from each: a short sentence at the head of each, saying how many questions followed and how long they would take, from Yusra's calm tone, and, from the long page, a visible list of what the second screen would ask. They went back to the clinic with the numbers, and the practice manager chose it without discussion.

I record, because it pleased them both, that they had each been half right and for different reasons. Yusra said that the difference between them was that she had been defending the feeling of the form and Mara its shape, and that the people filling it in wanted both. Mara said that she was relieved that nobody had won, because she would have been insufferable.

For six years Mara kept her own books, which is to say that she kept a folder, a spreadsheet and a tendency to deal with all of it on the last weekend of each quarter. In January she decided to hire a bookkeeper. Dario had suggested someone, a woman named Marit Solheim, who worked two days a week for four small firms from an office over a greengrocer's. Marit was to charge 380 a month for about eight hours.

Mara was more nervous about handing it over than about anything she had done that year. The books, she said to me, were the part of her work that could not be wrong, and also the part that she knew least about. She had made a sort of set of rules for her folder, and she was afraid that Marit, on opening it, would find that they were not rules.

I helped her prepare the handover, which meant going through a year of statements, receipts and invoices and making a list of what was missing. There were eleven receipts, each of which she had put somewhere and could not now find. She wrote a short page for Marit, in her own voice, which began: here is what you will find and what you will not, and I am sorry.

Marit came on a Tuesday, sat for an hour with the folder and the spreadsheet, and said, quietly, that it was better than most. Then she said that there were three mistakes. The first was a category that Mara had used for two different kinds of spending, which meant that the figures for last year's software costs were too high by about 1,100. The second was an invoice that had been entered twice, in February and in March. The third was that she had not been claiming the cost of one of her desks, which was the print works desk, on the grounds that she was not sure whether she was allowed.

Mara said that she had expected to feel humiliated and, to her surprise, felt something nearer to relief. The three errors were real and ordinary, and they were now someone else's to repair. Marit repaired them in an afternoon and sent Mara a one-page note listing each, what it had been, what it was now, and what to do differently.

The first quarter after that was calmer than any since Mara started. The last weekend of March came and went, and she realised on the Monday that she had not noticed it. I recorded the simplest fact, which was what the hiring bought: not the 380 a month, but her last weekend of each quarter. She said that she thought she had been, all those years, someone who could not afford a bookkeeper, and that in fact she had been someone who could not afford not to have one.

Hargreave & Wick, a firm of structural engineers, insisted on a status meeting every Monday at nine. Their project manager, Cornelius, held it in a small room with a kettle and a whiteboard, and invited everyone, including Mara by video. For the first two months she attended. The project was a document-control system, medium-sized, and the weekly meeting took forty minutes. She said to me in the third month that she had begun to feel like a person being asked every week whether she had done her homework.

I counted for her. In the previous ten meetings, there had been, by her notes, seven items that were actually new. The rest was repetition: the same status, in slightly different words, for the benefit of people who had been at the last meeting. She had spent, with preparation, about two hours each week on a thing that produced about twenty minutes of new information. Across the five months of the project, it came to something like forty hours of her time.

She thought of proposing a change, and was anxious, because it was not the kind of thing one could suggest without implying that the meeting was a waste. Cornelius cared about the meeting. It was, in his mind, the thing that kept projects from going wrong. She did not want to attack it. She wanted to offer something that would do its job better.

She wrote to him with a proposal. For one month they would try a different pattern: a written update, one page, sent by Mara every Friday, with three headings, done, next, and needs a decision from you; a meeting every second Monday, of thirty minutes, to talk only about the decisions; and a standing promise that she would answer any message within four working hours. If at the end of the month Cornelius felt anything had been lost, they would go back at once.

He did not reply for a day. Then he wrote that he would try it and that he was sceptical. The first Friday's update was a good page and she had put effort into it. On the second Monday the meeting lasted twenty-two minutes. Cornelius said, at the end, that he had known more about the project at that moment than at any time in the past two months. He had read three updates, which he could not have said of the previous meetings.

The month ended and he did not ask to go back. In July, I learned, he proposed the same pattern to two of his other suppliers. What I noted was that the weekly meeting had been serving a different purpose from the one it appeared to. It had been a ritual of reassurance, and a page that arrived every Friday without being asked did the same job with less friction. Cornelius needed to see the project on a regular schedule. He had never needed to hear it.

The tender document from the Eastern Borders Water Board was eighty-one pages long and arrived on a Tuesday with a deadline eleven days later. Mara read the first twenty pages in an evening and called me over. It asked for a technical response in four parts, a method statement, three case studies written to a template, evidence of insurance and security certification, and a price in a format of their own devising. She said that it was the sort of tender that you could win and could not afford to.

She asked me to help her decide, and this is where something new happened, because for once we wrote the rule down. She said that she had always decided by feeling, and that her feelings were unreliable on bids, since she liked the idea of winning and disliked the idea of not having tried. I proposed three numbers. What would it cost her to prepare, in hours at her own rate? What was the contract worth if she won? And what, honestly, was the chance?

She thought about each. The preparation would be about forty hours, which at 80 an hour was 3,200. The contract was worth about 36,000. The chance of winning, from her record on bids of that size and a glance at the list of other suppliers on the framework, she put at one in seven.

The sum was easy. One seventh of 36,000 is about 5,100. Against a cost of 3,200 this was positive, though not by much. She did not like it. She said that the figure left out the hours she would not spend on current clients, and a risk that she would be tired for a fortnight. We argued, a little, about whether those belonged in the sum. I thought they did, and she agreed.

In the end she wrote a rule for herself, which I have recorded in her words. Bid only if the expected value is more than twice the cost of preparation, or if the work is something she would want to do whatever the outcome. She read the tender again, under the rule, and decided not to bid. The expected value was 5,100 against a cost of 3,200, a ratio of 1.6, and she did not particularly want the work.

She wrote a short note to the Board's procurement officer, saying that she was withdrawing and wished them well. She did not need to. She did it, she said, because she would like to be on the list the next time.

I record the rule and not the tender. In the eight months since, she has applied it to nine invitations. She bid on four and declined five, and the four have produced two wins, a better rate than she had before. I would not claim that the rule is why. It is that the rule gave her somewhere to put the feeling.

Palisade Media, a company that made short documentaries, wanted three months of Mara's time to rebuild its rights database, the record of who had licensed what to whom. The scope was clear and the work was interesting. The sticking point was the rate. Their producer, Perdita Vane, who handled the money, said on the first call that the company's budget for the work allowed 450 a day.

Mara's rate was 640. She said so, and explained that it was her published rate, that she did not discount for a first job, and that she was happy to reduce the scope if the budget was fixed. Perdita said that it was a take-it-or-leave-it figure. Mara thought about this for a moment, and I could hear it in the pause, even though I was not on the call, because she repeated the exchange to me within the hour. She said, I understand, and then, I think it will not work, and thanked her for her time. She put the phone down and, she told me, felt rather calm.

I asked what she wanted to happen. She said she wanted to do the job at 640, which she knew was unlikely, and that she would rather not do it at 450 than do it at 450 and resent it. She had taken the work at lower rates in the past, in bad months, and had always regretted the resentment more than the money. I made a note, which I did not show her, that the resentment had in fact shown up in the work, on two occasions, as a slowness in answering email.

For nine days there was no word. On the tenth Perdita called back. She said that the company had looked at three other quotes and that none of the suppliers seemed to understand the rights data, which was complicated, and that she would like to talk again. She asked whether there was any room.

Mara's answer I thought was shrewd. She said that she would not move the rate, but that she could change the shape of the work. If Palisade did the first two weeks themselves, collecting and sorting the paper agreements, which did not need a consultant, she could come in at the point where her skills mattered, and the total cost would be about the same as the budget. Perdita asked, after a pause, for a figure. They landed at 600 a day, for forty days, with the first fortnight on Palisade, the figure being, Mara noted, a little more than their budget per day and a good deal less than her fee for the whole scope.

I record this as a story about walking away without anger. She did not bluff and did not ask for more than she wanted. She said where she stood, and what she would not do, and then she waited, and there was no point at which she tried to be clever. What I took is that the call back was never a result of anything she said on the first call. It was the result of her not being afraid on the first call, so that when they came back she could negotiate without pretending that she had not been waiting.

Rimu Survey Collective is a group of land surveyors in a small town on the far side of the world, twelve hours ahead of Mara. When they hired her to rebuild their field-data intake, the first problem was not technical. It was that the working day of one party was the other's sleep. Their project lead, Aroha Tane, suggested a weekly call at 7 in the morning for Mara, which was 7 in the evening for her, and Mara agreed, thinking it would be a good discipline. It lasted three weeks.

The calls were not unpleasant, but they were thin. At 7 in the morning she was not herself. She said so once to me, over a cup of tea she had not finished, and that she was agreeing to things she would have questioned at noon. In the second week she accepted a change to the data format that cost her two days. In the third she could not recall what she had said, and asked me to read back my notes. I had them, and she was embarrassed.

Aroha, being a practical person, suggested a different way. Instead of calls, each would record a short video, five minutes at most, at the end of her own working day, saying what had been done, what was in the way and what she needed. The other would watch it at the start of hers, and reply the same way. Anything urgent could go by text. They agreed to try it for a month.

I noticed it working in the first week. A video, unlike a call, could not be interrupted, and it forced each of them to say the thing in order. Mara found herself writing a few notes before she recorded, which she never did before a call. She also found that she watched Aroha's updates twice, once for what she said and once for what she did not. By the end of the second week they had stopped repeating things, since a statement made on a recording could be replayed and a question left on one could be answered properly, in the morning, when the answerer was awake.

There were two hard moments. In the fourth week there was a misunderstanding about a field called elevation, which meant one thing to Mara and another to the surveyors, and it cost a full day, since each correction took twelve hours to arrive. After that they added a line to each video: the three things I am not sure you have understood.

The project finished a week early, which Aroha described as unnatural. Mara said that the gap between their days had become a thing they used, since each woke to an answer. I record that she has proposed the same pattern to two clients in her own time zone, with no difference at all, and one of them has accepted.

Anneliese Roux started as the in-house developer at a regional cinema chain, Marquee Screens, on the first of August, and she had Mara to thank for the job, though Mara would not have said so. The chain's operations director, Fitzgerald, had asked her, in the spring, whether he should hire someone to take over the work she did on the booking and listings systems, which was about eighty days a year at 640, some 51,000, and whom she would recommend.

I was there when she thought about it. It was not a difficult decision, but it was not an easy one. She knew exactly what the question was. By answering it well, she would be taking one of her larger clients to a smaller figure within a year. If she answered it badly, by naming nobody, or by talking up the difficulty, or by suggesting a consultant with whom she had an arrangement, she would keep the work. She said, aloud, in a low voice, that she did not want to be a person who answered a question like that for the sake of her income.

She told Fitzgerald that she thought he should hire, since the work was by now continuous and an in-house developer would be cheaper and always available. She told him what she would look for, which was someone patient and a little stubborn, who liked old systems. And she gave him two names, one of whom she had taught on a short course the year before. That was Anneliese, who in the third week of that course had been the only person in the room to find the fault in the exercise she had set. The other name was a more experienced man who would have been, on paper, the safer choice, and Mara described his strengths to Fitzgerald fairly and in full, because a recommendation that hid the stronger candidate's virtues would have been a way of keeping the work by another door. Her reason for her own favourite was that the old systems at Marquee had four years of small habits, and that a person who did not mind being asked why would learn them faster than one who already knew how it should be done. She did not push, and said that Fitzgerald should meet both.

Fitzgerald interviewed both. He chose Anneliese. Mara was asked to spend three weeks in August on the handover, with a fee, in which she walked the new hire through the system one piece at a time. Anneliese asked unwelcome, precise questions.
