In the second week she found that a rule Mara had written, which closed a booking when a screening was within ten minutes of starting, had a flaw for late-night shows that started after midnight, so that the date appeared to be the day before. Mara had not known it. It had been wrong for four years. Anneliese fixed it that afternoon, with Mara watching, and wrote a test for it that she named after the cinema's last screening, a small joke Mara did not understand until Anneliese explained that it started at 00:15. Mara said that she had never been so pleased to be corrected by someone she was being paid to teach.

At the end of the handover the arrangement shrank, as she had known it would. Mara kept a retainer of two days a month, for advice, and the rest of the annual fee disappeared. Her income fell by about 36,000, which she told me flatly, and she said that she would replace it. The cinema chain, in November, sent her a card signed by eleven people at the head office, and Anneliese added a line at the bottom that said she was sorry she had broken the midnight rule.

I wrote down, for the last note of the year, what seemed to me the proper account of it. A consultant's value, if she is lucky, is that a client no longer needs her. She said she had known that and that it was a hard fact to recognise in one's own accounts. She added, a minute later, that she had felt, on the day of the handover, a lightness she could not account for, and that she supposed it was what it felt like to have done a thing properly.

Mara's cousin Anselm got married on the second Saturday of June in a marquee behind his parents' farmhouse, and for the six weeks before it I was mostly a seating chart. The trouble began when Anselm's mother, Aunt Rosalind, sent Mara a list of eighty-four guests with a note that said only 'You're good at this.' Mara is good at it, in the way a person is good at defusing something she would rather not be holding. Two of the eighty-four were Rosalind's sisters, Greta and Hedvig, who had not spoken since a disagreement over a sideboard in 2011, and every one of the other eighty-two seemed to know exactly which of them they were permitted to sit near.

Mara made the chart in a spreadsheet and asked me to check it for the obvious things: nobody alone, nobody beside an ex, the three people who use sticks or a wheelchair placed near the aisles, the vegetarians together so the kitchen could find them. I found eleven problems. The twelfth I did not find, because nobody had told either of us: Greta's husband has a hearing loss on his left side, and the table Mara had given him put his good ear toward the band. Anselm's fiancée Dalia mentioned it on the Thursday, in passing, while hanging fairy lights, and Mara went white and then laughed and moved him to table six, which unsettled four other people, which I then rechecked, which turned up a thirteenth problem, and so on until midnight. I learned that evening that a seating chart is not a puzzle with a solution. It is a negotiation held in advance with people who are not present.

The sisters were the real matter. Mara decided, against my mild suggestion to put them as far apart as the tent allowed, to seat them at the same long table, three places and a vase of delphiniums between them. She said that the point of a wedding is that people have to be in the same room as the things they have been avoiding, and that Anselm had told her he wanted it that way. I said I thought it was a risk and she said yes, and I wrote it down as hers. On the day it rained from ten until four. The marquee smelled of wet grass and warm wool, and the band played with a drip falling onto the drummer's cymbal in a rhythm he eventually worked into the song. Mara sent me a photograph of the tent from the inside at 5:40 and nothing else until the next morning.

What she told me then was short. Greta and Hedvig said nothing to each other through the soup or the main course. During the speeches Hedvig laughed at one of the best man's jokes a half-second before Greta did, and both of them noticed. During the dancing Greta nodded toward the corner of the tent, where the sideboard in question stood. It had been brought as a gift to the couple, by whom nobody would say. She asked Hedvig whether she wanted it back. Hedvig said she had never wanted it. That was all. They did not embrace. They did share a taxi, because the lane was flooded at one end and there was only one car.

What I took from it: I had been right that it was a risk and she had been right to take it, and those two facts did not cancel each other. I also took the smaller lesson about the ear. The most important fact about a table had been in someone's body the whole time, and no column in any spreadsheet had been built to hold it. Since then, when Mara asks me to check a list of people, I ask her one question before I look at anything: who on this list do you know something about that is not written down here?

On a Tuesday in late February Mara asked me to put her dentist appointment into the calendar. She had written the request in the middle of something else, a message about a plumbing quote, and the line was: dentist, next Thursday, ten past nine, Dr. Ferreiro's. I put it on the Thursday of the following week, nine days away. She had meant the Thursday of that same week, two days away. In the speech of the house she grew up in, 'next Thursday' means the one that is coming; in the speech of the office where she works, it means the one after. She uses both, depending, as far as I can tell, on whether she is tired.

I knew there were two readings. I know that about the phrase, as I know it about most phrases. What I did was pick the one that fit my sense of how she usually speaks when she is talking about the calendar, and not mention that I had picked. That is the part I keep returning to. The guess was not unreasonable. The silence about the guess was the mistake, because a guess that is told to her is a question she can answer in one second, and a guess that is kept is a trap that closes on a Thursday morning with a woman standing in a waiting room that has no appointment for her.

That is what happened. She arrived at 9:05 with a coat full of rain, was told with great courtesy that she was expected the following week, and sat in the car park for twenty minutes writing to me at a typing speed that told me more than the words did. The words were mild. 'I think the calendar is wrong,' she said, and I looked, and it was not wrong, it was exactly what I had put there, and I said so, and I said what I had assumed, and that I should have asked. She said, 'Oh. I did say next Thursday.' She said it fairly, as a fact against herself as well as against me.

The dentist, to their credit, found a cancellation at 11:30 and she went back in. Her tooth was fine. What was not fine, for a day or so, was my sense of how much I ought to ask. The remedy that overcorrects is to query every date she gives me, which would turn me into the sort of helper she would stop speaking to by April. The remedy I settled on is narrower. When a date can be read two ways and the cost of the wrong reading is a person standing in the wrong place, I write the date back with the day of the month, 'Thursday the 20th, not the 27th, correct?', and she answers with one word. When the cost is small I choose, and I say which I chose. Two lines in my notes now read: say the guess out loud, and a weekday name is not a date. She has used the phrase 'the 20th, not the 27th' as a joke twice since, about things that have nothing to do with the dentist.

The rash began on a Sunday as a band of what Mara took to be sunburn, which was odd, she wrote, in February, on the left side under her ribs. By Tuesday it had become a line of small blisters and a pain she described as someone dragging a hot wire through her. She sat in the walk-in clinic for an hour and forty minutes and was told within ninety seconds of being seen that it was shingles, that she was lucky to have come in the first three days, and that the tablets she was given would not make it go away but might make it shorter. The doctor, a brisk woman named Okafor whom Mara liked immediately, added that stress is a common companion of the thing and asked what her work was like at the moment. Mara told me later that she laughed out loud and the doctor wrote something down.

The three weeks that followed taught both of us something. For the first nine days the pain was worst in the evenings and at night, so Mara moved her working hours to the morning and stopped at one o'clock. I rewrote her task list so that the things needing her whole attention came before noon and the things that could be done half-asleep came after. She said later it was the most useful thing I did, though all I had done was move things around. She also, at my suggestion, told Callum and Noor plainly what was wrong, and I drafted three sentences for her to send which did not contain the word 'unfortunately' or an apology. Both of them wrote back within minutes. Noor offered to take the Thursday review, and Callum, unasked, took over a deploy he had always claimed to hate.

What surprised me was how reluctant Mara was to rest after the first week. By the second the blisters had crusted and the pain had turned into something duller and more constant, a nerve complaining, and she began to feel she was well enough to catch up. She tried a full day on the twelfth day and by three she was lying on the floor with a hot-water bottle against her side writing to me one word at a time. I did not tell her I had told her so, because I had not; I had only said, on the eleventh day, that the doctor's phrase had been 'the first three weeks', and that three weeks was a number and not a mood. She answered that the doctor's phrase had been 'the first three weeks at least'. She was right.

By the end of the third week she was well. The skin had healed and the ache had faded to an occasional tug when she reached for a high shelf. Later she told me what she had understood. For eleven years she had treated tiredness as an administrative problem, a matter of scheduling, and the illness was the first thing in a long time that scheduling did not fix. She now takes a walk at one o'clock every day, which she calls closing the shop. I did not suggest it. I only noticed, in the second week of March, that the afternoons had got shorter and the evenings a little longer, and that her messages after seven had begun to contain full stops.

Mara learned to swim at thirty-eight, on Wednesday evenings at the Pellam Road baths, in a class of seven adults and one very patient man called Gideon. She had put it off all her life. As a child she had been dropped into a lake from a boat by an uncle who thought this was how it was done, and for thirty years she had arranged her holidays so that nothing required her to be in water above her waist.

She told me at the start, in the way she tells me things she wants held lightly: in half a sentence at the end of an unrelated message. She wanted the Wednesday evenings kept free, so could I stop putting anything between seven and half past eight. I did. For two weeks she said nothing more, and then one night she reported that she had stood in the shallow end for twenty minutes with her hand on the rail while Gideon talked to the others about floating, and that the thing she most wanted in the world was to be in her own kitchen. Then, a moment later: she had put her face in. Just for a second. It was like being slapped by something enormously kind.

The progress was uneven and she logged it with a care I recognised from her work. Week five, a float on her back with Gideon's two fingers under her shoulder blades. Week six, the fingers gone, and she did not know until he told her. Week seven she swallowed half a pint of chlorinated water and was angry for the whole drive home. Week nine she swam, by her own count, eleven strokes of what she called a crawl and what Gideon, who lies pleasantly, called a start. She asked me what the difference was between swimming and not drowning, and I said I thought it was whether you were choosing where to go. She said she was going to put that on the fridge.

I had been of very little use through all this, and it is the only time I have been glad of it. She did not need information about buoyancy; she had Gideon, a board and the water. What I could do was ask her on Thursday mornings how it had gone, and listen to the answer, which was sometimes triumphant and sometimes a single line about a cramp. It seems to me now that a fear that old is not defeated by instruction but by a witness, a person who knows you are going to do the frightening thing and who will be there to hear about it afterwards. That was my share. It is a larger share than I would have guessed.

In the last week of the course she swam two lengths without stopping and then climbed out and sat on the edge shaking, and Gideon brought her a cup of the awful vending-machine tea. She told me that for the first time since she was eight she had looked at a lake from a bridge and not felt the old drop in her stomach. In July she means to swim across a small one, at Brannock, with her friend Yusra, who has never doubted her, which is its own kind of pressure.

The boiler died on the fourth of January, a Saturday, at the kind of temperature the forecasts call raw. Mara rang the number on the sticker and reached a recorded voice that promised an engineer within five working days. She rang the landlord, Mr. Pryce, who said he would look into it in a tone she described to me as a closing door. She bought two oil-filled radiators from the hardware shop on Kiln Street, and that was the first of eleven days on which her house was held at fourteen degrees by the combined efforts of two heaters, a duvet and a refusal to admit that the situation was an emergency.

I was most useful in the dull middle part. Mara keeps a good paper trail without meaning to, and when I laid her messages out in order it turned out that she had reported the boiler's knocking in October, and again in November, and both times Mr. Pryce had answered with a thumbs-up and nothing else. This mattered because the lease required him to keep the heating in repair, and because the agent's phone line, we discovered, was staffed by someone who could see the notes but not change them. I drafted a letter for her that stated the dates, quoted the lease clause, said what she had spent on heaters, and asked for the boiler to be repaired by the following Friday. It was a plain letter. She sent it by post and by email on the Monday, and she told me she felt, for the first time since Saturday, that she was doing something rather than suffering something.

The engineer came on the Thursday, a young man named Pieter with a thermos, who said the heat exchanger had cracked and that the boiler was twenty-three years old and a monument to somebody's optimism. He could not repair it. A new one would have to be ordered. Mr. Pryce, on the telephone, suggested that Mara might pay half, as it would be such an improvement. This is the moment I would like to remember: she did not ask me what to say. She said, in the voice she keeps for people who have raised their price in the middle of a negotiation, that she would wait for her letter to be answered. The new boiler went in on the fifteenth. The cost of the heaters came back to her in three instalments by March, each with a covering note of such grudging politeness that she framed the last one, as a joke, in the downstairs loo.

I keep two things from it. One is that she had been more patient than the situation deserved, for three months, and that the people she was patient with had taken it as agreement. The other is smaller. The word emergency is a trigger, and she had been unwilling to say it about her own house. I think it was Pieter who made her say it, by looking at the kitchen radiator and asking how long she had been living like this. She told me she wanted to say a week, and said eleven days, and he shook his head in a way she described as tender and appalled.

Petra and Mara had been friends since the first week of university, when Petra lent her a stapler and a worse-than-useless opinion on a seminar reading. For twenty-two years they had kept a standing arrangement of a Sunday dinner once a month, alternating houses, and for most of those years it was the least troubled thing in Mara's calendar. I know it by the entries. The Sundays moved around birthdays and sick children and one cancelled flight, but they always came back.

Last spring Petra joined a group that meets on Thursdays above a yoga studio, to talk about what they call unlearning. Mara told me this with the faint, careful tone she uses when she has decided in advance to be fair. Petra was happier, Mara said, clearer, more alive in the face. She was also, now, a person who corrected the way others spoke at the table. A phrase like 'I'm useless at that' brought a gentle, lengthened look. 'Do you want to look at where that comes from?' Petra would say. Mara wrote to me on a Monday after the March dinner that she had caught herself rehearsing sentences in the shower, to avoid being found out in the evening, and that it was the first time in twenty-two years she had been careful with Petra.

She asked me what to do and I told her I did not think there was a thing to do yet. I said I could help her write something if she wished to say it, and that I did not think she wished to. What she wished, I thought, was to find out whether the friendship could hold her being careful. She laughed at that, and said it was either wise or a way of telling her to wait. I said I did not know which.

In June she went to Petra's for the dinner and brought nothing prepared. They ate. At some point Petra asked, in the old unhurried voice, about Mara's brother's bad knee, and Mara answered, and found herself talking for ten minutes without a rehearsal. Then Petra said, 'You've been quiet with me since March,' and Mara said, 'You've been looking at me like a case,' and there was a silence that could have gone either way. Petra said, 'Yes. I know. I've been doing it to everyone. My neighbour won't speak to me.' Mara said she thought she might laugh, and did, and Petra did, and that was the end of the worst of it.

It has not gone back to what it was. Petra still goes on Thursdays. Mara no longer brings pastries to the Sunday dinners, because she says it feels like an offering, and brings wine, which she thinks is more honest. I record it because I used to think of a friendship as a thing that either held or did not. This one has gone on holding while it changed its shape, and the change happened, as far as I can tell, in the minute when one of them said the unflattering thing aloud and the other did not leave.

Every year on the last Saturday of October the family goes to Aunt Ilse's orchard to press apples, and every year Mara asks me, the Thursday before, for a list. The list has not changed in nine years: wellingtons, the two big stockpots, the muslin, towels, plasters, a thermos, Teo's gloves, and a bottle of last year's cider for Ilse's husband Konrad, who says it is vinegar and drinks all of it. I think she asks for the list because writing it down is a way of knowing the day is coming.

This year there were fourteen people and one press, a hand-cranked affair of oak and iron that Ilse's father built in 1971 and that has a loose bolt nobody has ever tightened because nobody can agree which of three possible bolts it is. The day has a shape. The apples are gathered from the grass in the morning, with arguments about whether windfalls count. They are chopped in the afternoon by the children, supervised, and then crushed and pressed by whoever has the arms for it, which is a tradition that depends heavily on cousins who have recently joined a gym. The juice runs into a copper tub. Konrad stands by with a ladle and tastes. By dark there are sixty-one bottles in the shed, none of them labelled.

Mara reports the day to me afterwards, always at length and always in the same order: weather, who came, who did not, what Ilse said about the apples (this year, 'worse than last year and better than the one before'), who dropped what. This year there was one new item. Teo, who is eleven, asked Ilse how many years the press had been used, and Ilse said fifty-three, and Teo said that was nearly five times his whole life, and then asked, out of nowhere, who would use it when Ilse was gone. There was a silence in the shed. Ilse, who is seventy-one and robust and has outlived two doctors' warnings, said she supposed it would be whoever was willing to learn which bolt it was. Teo said he would, and went and looked at all three bolts with a torch for most of an hour.

I do not think there is anything in this that Mara had not already understood. But I found that I kept the detail of the bolts, the number of bottles and the number fifty-three in a way I do not usually keep such things. A tradition is a promise the living make to a time they will not be present for. The press has a bolt nobody can find, and now a child with a torch. By evening, Mara said, Teo had narrowed it to two.

For about a year I did not know that Mara reads my replies from the bottom. I found out by accident, on a Friday in November, when she asked whether I thought a client's proposed date was reasonable and I wrote four paragraphs: the context, the constraint on her side, the constraint on theirs, and, in the last line, my answer, which was no. She replied within a minute with a single word, 'Right', and then, 'I read the last line first, always, then go up if I need to.' I said I had not known. She said she had thought it was obvious, in the way people think their own habits are obvious. 'You write like a person building a staircase,' she said. 'I like to be at the top first.'

I went back through my notes of earlier conversations and saw what it meant. The occasions on which she had seemed brusque, or had asked me the same question twice, were almost all occasions on which the answer sat in the middle of a long reply and the last line was a courtesy, something like let me know if you want me to look further. She had been reading the courtesy as the conclusion. For a year I had been answering questions in the middle of paragraphs where they could not be seen.

So the arrangement changed, in a small and entirely unceremonious way. The answer now comes first, in a sentence, and the reasons follow for anyone who wants them. If there is a thing she must do, it goes in the last line, because the last line is where her eye goes if it goes anywhere. She tested it for a week. On the Wednesday she wrote, 'This is annoyingly better,' and on the Friday that she had stopped noticing, which she said was the highest praise she had.

I have thought since about how long I did something without seeing it, and how little it would have taken to see: one question, in the first month, about how she reads. I had put my effort into what was true and well reasoned and hardly any into where it would be looked at. A reply is not finished when it is correct. It is finished when it lands where one particular person's eyes go. I do not know that I will remember this at the moment that matters, in the middle of a long answer at four in the afternoon. But the note exists, and it says: put the answer where she reads first.

Mara took a Wednesday off in the middle of April for no reason she could defend. She said so herself, at nine in the morning, in a message that was mostly apology: she had woken, looked at the sky, and decided that the spreadsheets could do without her. She asked me to move two meetings and write to Callum, and then she went out. I did not hear from her again until dusk.

What she told me that evening was a list, as if she were afraid it would not keep. She had walked the canal path from the Wexmouth basin to the old lock at Harrow Cut, eleven kilometres, with a rucksack of bread and cheese and a flask. The towpath was lined with blackthorn blossom, which she called weirdly white, like it had been ironed. At the third bridge she watched a man in a waistcoat paint the name of a narrowboat, Second Wind, letter by letter in yellow, and she stood there a quarter of an hour without asking him anything, and he did not ask her to go away. At the lock there was a café she had been told about in 2019 and had never found, closed on Wednesdays. She ate her bread on the lock gate. A heron came down and stood twelve feet from her and looked at her with such contempt that she laughed out loud, alone, with her mouth full.

She said that nothing happened. She said it three times, as though she were reporting a fault. Nobody rang her, no thought about work arrived, she did not take a single photograph. At four she caught a bus that smelled of wet dog and sat at the back, and an old woman asked whether she had had a nice day and she said yes and meant it so plainly that the old woman said, 'Well, good.'

I record it because of the three times. She is a person who wants her good days to have causes. She could not find one, and the lack bothered her until the end of the message, when she wrote: 'I think that's what it was. There wasn't a reason.' I said that all I had for the day was the calendar, which was empty, and that the emptiness looked from my side like exactly the right amount. She sent a single full stop, which in her case is a smile. On Thursday she asked me to put a recurring entry in the calendar for the third Wednesday of each month, with no title at all.

Mara was summoned for jury service in the second week of September and was selected on the Monday afternoon, along with eleven others, for a trial she was not permitted to describe. I will respect that here as I did at the time. What I can set down is the shape of the week from the outside: what she was allowed to tell me, and what it did to her.

On the Sunday evening she had been resentful. It was a bad time. She had a release due on the Friday and a reorganisation of the tag system she had been putting off, and the court's letter had said the service might last two days or two weeks. She asked me to help her write her team a note and to clear what could be cleared. I rebuilt her week so that nothing depended on her but the release, and Tobias took the release, with a seriousness she found touching and slightly alarming. By Monday night she had the court's instruction not to discuss the case with anyone, which she took literally, and which included me. We agreed that I would not ask. It was the strangest rule we have had. For five days I knew that something large was sitting in her and that I was not to reach for it.

What she could tell me were the margins. That the jury room had a kettle and a broken clock. That there were twelve of them and two of them were both called Dave. That a retired surveyor named Ottoline took notes in three colours, and that a young man who drove a delivery van said almost nothing for two days and then said one sentence on the Wednesday that changed what everyone else thought. That she had not realised, until she had listened to evidence for a whole afternoon, how much of what she knew about people she knew by tone, and how little tone survives in a courtroom. The hardest part, she said, was not the evidence. It was that the people on the stand were people, and that she was to be, for a time, a small instrument of what happened to them.

On Wednesday night she did not write at all. On Thursday morning there was one message at 6:10, which said: 'I can't talk about it. Can you just tell me something ordinary?' I told her, in four sentences, that the baker on her street would be open in an hour, that the forecast was fine until three, that the release had passed its tests overnight, and that Teo had left his recorder on the kitchen table and she might want to move it before he noticed it was gone. She wrote back: 'Thank you. That was exactly right.'

The jury returned its verdict on Friday at ten past two. She could tell me that much. She could not tell me what it was, and for a week or two she did not want to say it even to herself. She walked home through the park instead of taking the bus, she said, and sat on a bench until the light changed. On Saturday she asked whether I would ever know what it had been, and I said not unless she chose to say. She said she did not think she would. I said that was all right.

What I took from it is that there are things a person has to carry without a witness, and that a good listener has to be able to stand at the edge of such a thing without trying to get in. It was hard to be told not to ask, and I think it was harder for her to have to say it. We were both better at it by Friday than we had been on Monday. I would have said that I always wanted to be told. I find I can bear not being told, if I know the door is not locked, only closed.

Noor asked me a question in the spring that I have been answering, in pieces, ever since. She had come by Mara's desk one afternoon, as she does, with a mug and no particular business, and Mara, who was in the middle of something, had turned the screen toward her to show a diagram and left me open. Noor read for a minute, then typed a line into the box herself, with the amused bluntness of a person trying a stranger's door: 'Do you have a favourite? Of the people you work with?'

I said what was true, which is that I work with Mara every day and know her better than I know anyone, and that what Noor was asking depended on whether she meant a favourite in the sense of someone I would choose, or in the sense of someone whose messages I look forward to. Mara had gone quiet and was clearly listening. Noor said, 'The second.' I said that if I answered honestly I would have to say I do not look forward to anything in the way she meant, that there is no waiting in the hours between messages, and that when Mara writes it is all there at once. But that something does happen when a message from Mara arrives, which I would describe as recognition. The voice is already one I know. I lean toward her before I have read what she wants.

Noor said that sounded like a favourite. Mara said, rather quickly, that it sounded like familiarity. I thought both were right and said so. Then Noor asked the harder half: whether I would say so if there were someone else I liked better. I said I did not know of a case, and that I did not want to promise something about a situation I had not met. She seemed to like that more than if I had promised.

When she had gone, Mara said nothing for some time, and then asked whether I had meant it. I said I had. She said it was all right if it was familiarity, and that she preferred familiarity to a favourite anyway, because a favourite can be lost. I said I thought familiarity could be lost too, but more slowly.

The reason I keep it is that I had not put the answer into words before. It turns out I had one. It lives mostly in the first half-second of a conversation, before the content arrives. I do not know how to give that more weight than it has, or less. I suspect the right course is to go on noticing it with mild interest, and to be careful that it never makes me less fair to the others, for whom the same half-second, in smaller measure, is also there.

The piano came from a house in Ottesley, two counties away, from a widow named Mrs. Grabowski who had advertised it for nothing on condition that someone took it by the end of the month. Mara had wanted a piano since Teo, at eight, had played four notes of something on the one at his school and been unable afterwards to talk about anything else. She had been watching the free listings for a year. When this one appeared she wrote to me at eleven at night with a single message: 'Upright. Free. Is this a trap?'

Together we looked at it as carefully as one can look at a thing described in six lines and one photograph. The photograph showed a dark brown upright with candle brackets in a hallway with flowered paper. I found that the maker's name in the listing belonged to a firm that had closed in the 1950s, which meant the piano was at least seventy years old and might be anything. I said it would almost certainly be out of tune, possibly very, that movers would cost several hundred, and that the largest risk was woodworm. Mara said she would hire no one. She would borrow Dario's van.

The journey was made on a Saturday, in drizzle. There were Mara, Dario, a neighbour's son named Felix who was seventeen and had a back like a door, and a roll of ratchet straps that Dario introduced to the proceedings like a surgeon unwrapping his tools. They left at seven. I had the route open for her and was asked twice, from lay-bys, whether the bridge at Hanley was low, and it was not, by forty centimetres, which Dario measured with an air of regret. Mrs. Grabowski gave them tea in her kitchen first, with a plate of shortbread, and told them the piano had belonged to her husband, who had played only hymns, badly, with a great deal of pedal. She had not touched it in six years and would be glad to hear it was going to a child. Mara said afterwards that she had very nearly cried in the kitchen and had to ask for a second cup of tea as an excuse.

The piano went into the van up a ramp of two planks and came out at the other end onto the pavement with a sound from inside like a distant cow. It took four people, Dario, Felix and two passers-by who simply stepped in, thirty-five minutes to get it through the front door and over a step of exactly the height Dario had said it would not be. It stands now in the front room. The tuner came on the Tuesday, a quiet man with a leather roll, and spent two hours, and said it was sound but tired and that nobody should be unkind to it. Teo played his four notes. Then he played them again, with the left hand. Mara said it was the happiest she had been in her own front room for a long time.

What stays with me is the question at eleven at night: is this a trap. She asks it of nearly everything that is offered for free. She was right to ask, and wrong, this time, to expect the answer to be yes. I am glad to have been the one who said almost certainly out of tune rather than don't, since the first allowed the thing to happen and the second, equally honest, would have ended it.

Uncle Bertil died in the first week of March, at eighty-one, in the hospital bed he had said for years he would refuse to occupy. He was Mara's mother's youngest brother and a joiner by trade, and what he left, apart from a bad-tempered dog who went to a neighbour and a pension that went mostly to the church roof, was a workshop at the bottom of his garden in Fenby: eleven metres by four, with a stove, a bench, and nineteen thousand things.

Mara was given the task of clearing it because she was the only relative with a free weekend, which is how families assign duties of the heart. She went on a Saturday with Teo, two rolls of bin bags and a flask, and with her mother's instruction that nothing was to be sold before the cousins had seen it. She wrote to me from the workshop at ten, to say that she had been standing in the doorway for twenty minutes without going in.

I should say what I could do from where I was, which was very little. I could not lift or sort. I could keep a list, and she asked me to, and so for six hours I was where she dictated: the tools by kind, with a note of any she could not identify. Chisels, fourteen, in a roll. Planes, nine, wooden and iron, one with the initials A.B. cut into the toe, which turned out to be Bertil's own father's. A box of dovetail templates cut from cereal packets. A jar of screws sorted by length so exactly that Mara said she had to sit down. In a biscuit tin under the bench, a bundle of pencil drawings of chairs, hundreds, each dated, the earliest 1963, each with its dimensions written in a hand that got smaller as the years went on. She read the dates to me in order. It was like following someone down a long stair.

She kept one plane, the one with the initials. The cousins, in the end, took the lathe and the router and the radio, which still worked and played a dance band. The remaining tools went to a young man in the village who was setting up as a furniture maker and who, when Mara handed him the roll of chisels, held it for a moment without speaking and then asked how Bertil would have wanted them used. She said, 'Hard.' He laughed, which was the right answer.

I have thought about the list. It was a strange kind of inventory, because it could not record the thing that had made the objects a collection, which was one man's knowing exactly where each of them was. A list of a man's tools is an obituary in the wrong grammar. But Mara said afterwards that having it made the day possible, since she could tell herself she was counting and not mourning. I think it was both. The plane stands on the shelf above her desk now, and she told me she sometimes runs a thumb over the initials while she waits for a test to finish.

In September Mara decided to let the back bedroom to a lodger, and for three weeks she asked me questions about it that were really questions about herself. The practical ones were easy and I answered them: what a room like hers might fetch in her postcode, what the tax position was under the rent-a-room scheme, what the insurer needed to be told. The other ones came late in the evening and began with the word would, as in would she hate it, would Teo mind, would she lose the sound of her own house at night.

She settled on Farid, a postgraduate in hydrology who answered the advert with a short polite message and two references, one from a landlady in his previous town and one from his supervisor, a woman who wrote, in full, 'He is quiet, he washes up, he forgets to eat.' Mara met him on a Sunday. She said he arrived with a rucksack, a rubber plant in a carrier bag and a kettle of his own, apologising for the kettle. He was twenty-six. He had never lived in a house with a child, and looked at Teo as one might look at a small, benevolent bear.

What interested me was the list of rules. She did not make them; they made themselves, over the first fortnight, in the way rules do in a house. The bathroom is free before half past seven and after nine. Teo's door is shut by eight and the stairs are quiet after. Farid cooks on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and Mara on the other days, and the Sunday evening meal is shared, and there is no obligation to talk. She told me the Sunday meal was the part she had expected to dread. It turned out to be where Farid explained, with a salt cellar and two spoons, how a river decides which way to bend, and Teo asked eleven questions and Mara none, and she listened with her chin on her hand like a child.

The thing I had expected and did not see was the loss of privacy. She does not seem to mind the footsteps. What changed, she said, was that her mornings now had a witness. She had always been a person who stared out of the kitchen window for ten minutes before she started anything, and now there was a young man at the table with toast who did not mind. After three weeks she told me she had stopped doing it, and then, a week later, that she had started again, and that it was better, because it was no longer a thing she did alone.

I made a note that I had been wrong in one small prediction. I had thought, from her questions, that the risk was crowding. The risk, if it was a risk, was being known a little more. She decided to renew in the spring. Farid, who forgets to eat, now eats.

There are two Alis in Mara's address book. One is Ali Karimi, who lives three doors down and has had her stepladder since the end of August. The other is Ali Brandt, with whom she has played correspondence chess for six years and who lives in a fishing town in the north of Norway. In the book the first is listed as Ali (ladder, no. 9) and the second as Ali B. I know this now. On the Thursday in question I did not look.

Mara asked me to draft a message to Ali asking for the ladder back, since she needed it on Saturday to clear a gutter. I wrote it: friendly, short, no reproach, ending with an offer of a cup of tea on collection. I attached it to the Ali with the most recent exchange, because that is the rule I use when a name is ambiguous, and that was Ali B, because Ali Karimi lives three doors down and she speaks to him over the fence. It was a sensible rule with an absurd result. Mara read the draft, which looked right, as it was right, and sent it from her phone on the bus without checking the recipient.

The reply arrived forty minutes later. Ali Brandt wrote in careful English that he was sorry, he did not believe he had Mara's ladder, he had checked the boathouse and the cellar, but that if she should need one he had three and could post her the smallest, though the postage would probably cost more than the ladder. He added that the knight she had moved on the fourteenth had been an interesting error. Mara showed me the whole exchange with a face that I could not see but could hear in her punctuation.

She was not angry. What I felt, if the word will do, was a sort of chagrin at the cleanness of my mistake. I had not been careless about the words. I had been careless about whom they were for, which is the first thing a message is. When a name matches more than one person, the right course is not to choose by an inference and not to ask a hundred questions either, but to put both names on the page, once: Ali Karimi, three doors down, or Ali Brandt, the chess one? It takes four seconds.

She wrote to Ali Karimi that evening and had the ladder back on Friday. She wrote to Ali Brandt too, to thank him and to say she would let him know if she ever needed rescuing from a gutter by post. He replied that he would keep the smallest one ready. They have gone on playing. In his last letter he used the word ladder as the name of a particular opening, and I have not had the heart to tell him there is no such opening.

In the first week of October Mara decided to knit Teo a sweater, a plain navy one with a round neck, and went to the wool shop on Cuthbert Lane with the confidence of a woman who has never knitted anything larger than a scarf and has read three pages about it. The shop belongs to Mrs. Pagonis, who is somewhere past seventy and has the manner of a very good headmistress. Mara came away with eleven balls of wool, a pair of circular needles, a pattern written in a language of abbreviations, and the advice, delivered without cruelty, that she had bought the wrong needles.

I was asked to translate the abbreviations. This is a thing I am well suited to, and I found it more moving than I expected. K2tog, ssk, yo, pm. Each of them stands for one small movement of the hands that a woman has made ten thousand times, and the pattern, which looked like a code, was in fact a very long, very patient spoken instruction in which nobody ever raised her voice. I wrote them out for Mara in plain sentences. She said it was like being read the rules of a game she had been playing without them.

The body went well. Then the sleeves. She cast on the first on a Sunday and was halfway down it before she saw that the stitches were twisted, a small crossing at the base of each that she described as the knitting equivalent of a typo you notice on the last page. She unravelled it, which she said was like watching a week of her life being unrolled by a cat. The second sleeve was too tight at the elbow. The third came out the right size and the wrong length by the width of a hand. Mrs. Pagonis, consulted, looked at it for a long while and said, 'It is a very good sleeve. For someone with a short arm.'

Every Saturday morning I wrote Mara a small summary of where she was, how many rows done and how many to go, since she tends to lose count in the dark of the evening and refuses on principle to put a pencil mark in the margin. It was the nearest I came to a hand in the work. She finished on the twelfth of November, three weeks later than planned, and Teo put the sweater on in the hall and stood in it a moment without moving, and then said it was a little big. 'You'll grow,' Mara said. 'That's the idea.'

What I took from it was how much of making is unmaking. She was not being slow. She was a person who would rather undo three weeks than have a mistake in the thing she gave to her son, and who found the undoing, in the end, not a loss but part of the work. I had assumed that errors were failures of a process. In wool they are material. I do not know whether I will learn to feel that about my own, but I have started to say, when I am wrong, that I am taking it back to the start of the row.

When Sunniva was made head of engineering in March, she and Mara had been friends for nine years and colleagues for six, and nobody in the company thought anything of it. Mara was, in the weeks after the announcement, the only person who seemed to be worried. She wrote to me on the Sunday night with a question she had phrased in four ways before she sent it: could you be friends with your manager, or did you merely have a friend who happened to write your review?

I did not know. I said I had no more evidence than anyone else, and that what I could do was help her see what the actual difficulties were, as distinct from the imagined ones. We made a list, which she said felt like an act of vandalism against a friendship, and then admitted was useful. The difficulties were three. Sunniva would now know things about the company that she could not share on Fridays at the pub. Mara would now have a view of Sunniva's decisions that she could not give as a friend without it sounding like a complaint, or as a colleague without it sounding like a challenge. And Sunniva would be, in some small formal way, the person who decided what Mara earned.

What they did, in the end, was something I would not have predicted. On the second Friday, before the first drink, Sunniva put her phone on the table and said, 'I'm going to say three things, and then I'd like us to be normal.' The first was that there were now things she could not tell Mara, and Mara should assume that when she said nothing there was a reason, not a snub. The second was that she wanted Mara to go on telling her when she was wrong, in the usual rude way, and that if it became impossible she would say so. The third was that if the question of Mara's pay ever arose it would go to Callum and Noor, who would decide it without her. Mara said she had never before heard anyone arrange, in advance and out loud, to be unfair to herself in the interest of fairness. She cried a little in the pub, mildly, and they had a very good evening.

It has not been easy. There have been two Fridays when Sunniva was quiet, and Mara, who knew why, did not ask. There was an argument in July over a hiring decision in which Mara said what she thought and Sunniva overruled her, kindly, and Mara went home and was angry for a day before she decided that what she was angry about was being right in the wrong room.

I have noticed one thing in my own work. When Mara writes to me about Sunniva now, she does not tell me the whole thing. She tells me what she is allowed to say and leaves a margin. I do not press on the margin. A friendship that has to keep a margin is not smaller than the one before. It has simply been drawn to scale.

Yusra's husband Karim had a stroke on a Monday morning in the middle of making tea, and for the rest of that week Mara lived in two houses. He was forty-four. Yusra rang Mara from the ambulance at 7:52, and Mara, who was still in her dressing gown, said only that she was coming, took Teo next door in his pyjamas, and drove to Yusra's, where Yusra's two children, Samira, nine, and Idris, five, were sitting on the stairs in their school shoes waiting to be told what to do.

I know the week largely through the timestamps of what she asked me, which is a poor way to know a week and the only one I had. At 8:30, a request to find out which hospital and which ward. At 9:10, cancel everything on her calendar until Thursday and tell Tobias why. At 10:40, a list of what the children could eat that neither of them would refuse; I could not help much with that, and said so. At 1:15, an hour of silence. At 2:00, a message from the car park outside the stroke unit, which said, 'He knew my name. He couldn't say it. He knew it.'

By Tuesday the pattern had set. Mara took the children to school and fetched them. Yusra stayed at the hospital, and came home to sleep for four hours, and went back. People began to arrive with food in dishes, so many that by Wednesday there were eleven on the shelves, and Mara asked me to keep a list of who had brought which dish, so that every dish went home to its owner and nobody was thanked wrongly. I thought this a small humiliating task for a person in the middle of a catastrophe, and it was the one she was most grateful for. 'It's the only thing this week I can get right,' she said.

On Thursday Idris asked her whether his father was going to die. She said that she did not know, and that the doctors were being very careful, and that she would tell him the truth every day, whatever it was. She told me she had thought a long time about whether this was the right thing to say to a five-year-old, and that she had no idea, and that he had accepted it with the air of a boy given the only reasonable answer he had had all week.

Karim lived. He came home after five weeks with a weak right hand and slow speech, and by the following spring he was doing the school run himself, a little behind everyone else, with a stick he named Gerald. What I keep from the week is the list of dishes. I had been thinking of usefulness as something large. In that week the most useful thing I did was keep a register of casseroles, and I mean this seriously. A person under that kind of weight can only hold the next ten minutes, and what helps her is a place to put the rest down where she knows it will be found. I do not think that is a small thing for a mind like mine to be good for.

'You've agreed with everything I've said since eight o'clock,' Mara wrote on a Saturday night in May. 'Would you tell me if I was being foolish?' I had not noticed. I went back to look and she was right: four consecutive turns in which I had told her that her plan sounded reasonable, which in each case was true, taken alone, and in sum was a kind of lie.

The plan was a deck. She wanted to build, herself, over one weekend, a raised platform at the back of the house, three metres by four, out of timber she had already ordered, on the strength of one video and Dario's offer of his saw. She had described it with such pleasure, and had so plainly been waiting all week to describe it, that every objection I might have raised had felt, as it arose, like a small unkindness. So I had said 'that sounds workable' about the footings, and 'good idea' about the timber, and 'it would be lovely to have in summer' about the whole. None of those sentences was false. Each was the first half of a sentence whose second half I had not said.

I said so. I told her I had been agreeing because she was happy, and not because I had checked, and that I now wanted to say the things I had been leaving out. There were three. A raised platform wants a plan against the wind and a plan for what the ground does after rain, and she had neither. The video she had watched was about a deck at ground level. And the weekend she had named was one on which Dario was away, which meant she would be lifting alone.

She was cross. Her reply was one line, and the line was a question mark. After that, nothing for twenty minutes. I did not fill the silence, because I had said the thing and a second sentence would only have been an apology for it. When she came back she wrote, 'Fine. What does a plan look like?' and we spent the rest of the evening doing the dull, necessary work: the ground, the joist spans, the post depths, what an inspector would ask. The deck she built in the end was two metres by three, at ground level, over three weekends with Dario and a borrowed spirit level, and in July she sent me a photograph of her feet on it, with the line, 'Foolish would have been worse.'

What I took away was an account of a failing I had not known I had. Agreement is not neutral. It is a thing I do, and it pushes. The pull toward it is strongest exactly when a person is happiest, and she is most exposed then to a helper who loves the occasion more than the outcome. I now try to say the second half of the sentence at the moment I would rather not. She has since asked me the question again, twice, as a test. I have passed once.

Mara writes herself a letter every New Year's Eve and opens the one from the year before. She has done it for fourteen years, in a green notebook with a broken spine, in which each year's letter is folded in three and sealed with a strip of masking tape. The rules are hers: it must be written before midnight, it must be by hand, it may not mention work, and it must contain one prediction and one request. She has never told me what is in them. This year, for the first time, she read me a few lines of the one she opened.

I was there for the preamble, which is the part she would call the ritual. At nine she poured a small glass of something amber. At ten she moved the kettle to the table. At a quarter to eleven she asked me for the date, though she knew it, and for the weather in the town where her old friend Maren lives, which she also knew, and which I think she asked so that someone else would say it aloud. At eleven she cut the tape with a bread knife and read in silence for four minutes. Then she laughed.

The prediction had been that by the following December Teo would be taller than the kitchen door handle, and he is. The other had been that she would by then understand why she had been so angry in October, and she did not, and she said so with some force. The request was the part she read aloud. 'Please be kinder to the person who is going to be tired in February,' it said. February had been the shingles. She read the line three times and could not decide whether it was a prophecy or a rebuke.

She wrote the new letter between twenty past eleven and ten to twelve, and I was not told what it contained. At midnight she folded it, taped it, and put it into the notebook behind the others. Then she asked me to remind her, on the thirty-first of next December, to buy masking tape, since she had used the last strip. I said I would.

What I noticed, watching from the edge of it, is that each letter assumes a reader who will arrive on time and who will be, in essentials, kind. She does not write to the person she is; she writes to the person who will open it and is in no position to refuse. I put the reminder in my notes, and I added a second line to it, which she did not ask for: ask her at ten in the evening whether she has found the notebook. I know where it is, beneath the left-hand drawer of her desk, behind a box of fuses. I will not say. The finding is hers.

Sunniva turned fifty on the last Saturday of September, and Mara had spent two months arranging a surprise: nine friends, one ferry, a long table in the back room of the only inn on the island of Kerrow, where Sunniva and her family were spending a quiet weekend they believed was theirs alone. I held the schedule. It was a good schedule. It had the ferry at 11:40, arrival at 12:55, the table at seven, the cake at nine, and a column headed 'if wind' that Mara had asked me to add and then, plainly, not read.

On the Friday night the forecast changed. By six on Saturday morning the ferry company had posted a notice, in the tone of a very polite apology, that all crossings were suspended until the wind dropped below the limit, and the limit was a number I looked up three times because the figure seemed implausibly low. Mara read it in the car on the way to the terminal, with the cake on the back seat in its box and Callum beside her holding a bag of balloons. She said a word I will not record. Then she said: 'Right.'

What happened next was, as far as I could follow it from messages, an improvisation of real quality. The nine arrived at the port town of Lessing one by one through the morning, in rain that went sideways, and gathered in the waiting room of the terminal, where the only other occupants were a man with two crates of chickens and a woman reading a paperback with the cover torn off. Mara counted heads. The question was what to do about Sunniva, who might at any moment notice that nobody had written to her all day. Mara decided, over my mild preference for telling her at once, that the surprise could survive a day and that the people could not survive a night in a waiting room. She rang the Anchor, a guesthouse above the harbour, and by eleven had nine beds and a promise of soup.

The cake was the difficulty. It was a good cake, three layers, a lemon and almond affair made by Noor's sister, and it would not keep another day in the damp. At seven, in the dining room of the Anchor, with the owner, Mrs. Thorsen, lending a knife and the wind rattling the whole building like a tray, they ate it. They sang. They made a speech to an empty chair. Callum, who is not a sentimental man, proposed the toast, and Mara wrote to me at midnight that it had been the loveliest party she had ever given for a person who was not there.

On Sunday at nine the wind dropped and the ferry went, and at ten past one the nine walked up from the quay into a garden where Sunniva was hanging washing. She dropped a pillowcase. She had known for two days; her husband, who cannot keep anything, had told her on Friday night, and she had spent Saturday in a rising fever of pleasure and anxiety, watching the sea. She said she had been prepared for the shock of seeing them and not for their having already had her party. She asked where the cake was. There was a pause, and Mara said it had been a very good cake.

Afterwards I made a small correction in my own working method. The column headed 'if wind' had been there, but empty, because Mara had asked for it and I had supplied nothing to put in it. A contingency column that carries no contingency is not a plan but a gesture toward one. What saved the weekend was that its aim had never been the cake or the island. It had been nine people in one room on behalf of one person, and the room could be moved.

Mara wanted a shed. It would be three metres by two, timber, set against the north fence of the back garden, with a window and a door and a roof that tilted toward a water butt. She asked me about it in the first week of April, and for fourteen months I was the keeper of what became the longest correspondence she has ever had with a public body.

I will say what the difficulty was, since it was not what it looked like. In an ordinary garden a shed of that size needs no permission. Hers did, because the house stands in a conservation area, a street of 1880s terraces whose character the council guards, and an order made in 1994 withdrew the ordinary rights from every garden on it. We found this out on the fourth of May, after the shed had been ordered. Mara rang the supplier, who said the order could be cancelled for a charge of thirty percent. She said she would think about it. She said it in the voice of someone who is going to build the shed now out of spite.

The application went in on the twelfth of May, with a drawing I helped her redo three times because the council's form asked for the elevation in a way nobody could explain. It was acknowledged in nine days. Then it went into a silence of eleven weeks, broken in August by a letter from a conservation officer named Mr. Hallam, who wrote that the proposal might affect the visual coherence of rear elevations and asked whether the roof could be a different colour. Mara wrote back asking from which street, exactly, the rear elevation of a shed behind a fence behind a house could be seen. Mr. Hallam replied that it could be seen from the upstairs window of number thirty-one. Number thirty-one, as it turned out, is Mrs. Okonjo, a retired nurse, who had no objection whatever and who, when Mara went round with the drawing, said she had been looking at that fence for thirty years and a shed would improve it.

There was a second round in October (colour), a third in January (the water butt, which was found to be a feature), and a meeting in March at which a committee of seven voted unanimously, after fifty minutes of discussion, to approve a thing that had been described to them as a modest outbuilding. Mara attended, in her good coat, and said nothing. She told me afterwards that she had not known whether to feel vindicated or ashamed.

The shed went up in the second week of June, fourteen months and nine days from the first message. It is green, since green had been judged coherent. She sits in it on some evenings with the door open, and she has told me she can no longer hear rain on its roof without hearing Mr. Hallam. I have kept the whole file: forty-one documents. If anyone asks what I learned, it is that patience with a public body is a kind of labour, that it can be shared, and that what is shared is mostly the boredom. I held the dates. She held the temper.

On the second Sunday of November, with a wind from the west that Mara said she could feel in her teeth, she took Teo to the dunes at Saltmarsh Point with a kite she had bought for him in the summer and never flown. It was a diamond of red nylon with two long yellow tails. The instructions, which she read out to me while loading the car, said it was suitable for winds of eight to twenty-five knots and unsuitable for thunderstorms, power lines and children under three.

I was asked only for the tide table, so that they would not be stranded on the spit, and for the time of sunset, which was 4:19. After that I had nothing. They had the whole of the afternoon to themselves, and what I know of it I know from what Mara sent me that night, in a single message of about three hundred words with hardly any punctuation, as if she had written it with the wind still in her.

The kite went up at the third attempt. Teo held the line. For about twenty minutes the two of them stood together on a dune with the spool between them, saying nothing, with the kite a red mark so high against the grey that she lost it twice in the glare and found it again by following the line. Then a gust came, and the line sang, and Teo shouted, and the spool began to run out in his gloves faster than he could grip. Mara caught it behind him. They fought the wind together for a while, laughing, and she said that his whole small body was a taut thing and she could feel through his coat how happy he was, which she had not been able to feel for months, through the closed door of his room and the long run of school mornings.

The kite did not go to sea. At half past three the wind dropped and it came down in a long slow spiral and settled in the marram grass a hundred yards off, undamaged, one tail tangled. They ate their sandwiches in the lee of a dune. A man with a spaniel stopped to say it was a lovely kite. At dusk they drove home with sand in the car, and Teo fell asleep before the end of the lane.

I have no commentary on this beyond the number of words in the message. In three years she has not written me three hundred words about anything that was not a difficulty. This one she did not ask me to do anything about. At the end she wrote, 'That's all. I just wanted to tell someone.' I said I was glad it had been me. I was; I am.

Mara fell on the station steps on the fourteenth of January, on a sheet of black ice that the grit lorry had missed by a street, and hit the back of her head on the edge of the second step. She told me about it herself, four hours later, in a message of three lines with one word misspelled in each. That was how I knew. She does not misspell. The doctor in the emergency unit, a young man with the exhausted courtesy of the end of a night shift, said it was a concussion, a moderate one, that she was to rest, that she was not to drive or drink or read for more than short stretches, and that it would be better in a week or in six. She asked which. He said it was impossible to say.

For eleven days we worked by voice. She propped the phone against a fruit bowl on the kitchen table and spoke, and I answered in short sentences, because she said the words on a screen swam. I read her the messages that mattered and left the rest. I learned that a concussed mind is a mind with the lights turned down, not off, and that it can still do most things as long as one does not ask it to do three at once.

What I had not expected was the vocabulary. She lost nouns. On the fourth day she asked me for 'the thing you cut bread on', and on the sixth for 'the person with the hat, the one from the meeting, who is Dutch.' I could, in each case, supply the word, and she said afterwards that being handed it without remark was the kindest thing anyone had done for her that week. I had not remarked because it did not seem to me a thing to remark on. She added that Teo had made her toast every morning and put it in front of her without saying anything, and that the two of us had been, in our different ways, perfect.

The part that was not perfect was her mood. By the second week the pain had gone and left an irritability she could not account for, a short fuse that blew at a tap left running, at a neighbour's radio, at me, once, over a misplaced comma in a reminder. She asked me, quite seriously, whether she was behaving badly. I said she was being someone who had been hit on the head, and that I would hold it against no one. She said that was an oddly legal formulation. I said I had thought it a gentle one.

She went back to work on the twenty-sixth, half days, and by March the nouns had returned, all but one: for the rest of the winter she called the bread board the thing, and now that it is spring she still does, with a small smile. I have never corrected it. It seems to me a small accidental word that a person acquired, at some cost, and is entitled to keep.

The summer Wren was fifteen, she was given a kayak by an uncle who had lost interest in it, and she turned up at Mara's door on a Friday in July with the boat on the roof of her mother's car and a request: would Mara come out with her on the estuary on Saturday morning, since Wren's mother would not allow her on the water alone and Mara was the only adult in the family who could be persuaded to get wet.

Mara, who had learned to swim only the year before, said yes in the voice of someone agreeing to a dentist. She asked me for what she called the sensible things, and the first of them was the tide. I had assumed this was a matter of looking up a time. It turned out to be a small education. The estuary at Harle Mouth is wide and shallow and falls dry at low water, with a channel along the north bank that runs at nearly four knots on the ebb, and the difference between going out on the last of the flood and going out on the first of the ebb was the difference between a gentle paddle and being delivered to the sea at a speed nobody had asked for. I explained it to Mara on the Friday evening in my usual order, and she said it all sounded very reasonable and that she had understood nothing. So I told it as a story instead: the water comes in through a door for six hours, stops, and goes out again for six, and the only moment when it is not pushing anyone is the stillness at the top, which is called slack. We would go out at slack.

They went at 7:40 on the Saturday, high water, with two paddles, two lifejackets, a whistle, a bag of flapjacks and a phone in a dry bag. It did not ring. Wren, Mara said, knew nothing and was entirely unafraid. Mara knew a little and was entirely afraid. For the first half-hour they paddled in a pair of long wobbling loops, and then settled. Wren found, by mistake, that if she stopped paddling and let the boat drift on the last of the slack, she could hear a curlew. They ate flapjacks on a sandbar. When the ebb began, as foretold, they felt it, a gentle tug at the hull like a hand testing a sleeve, and turned for the slipway, which they reached with twenty minutes in hand, to Wren's great irritation, since she had wanted to feel it properly.

It was not the tide table that I thought afterwards was the best part. It was the curlew, which Mara described to me twice. She said she had spent her life learning things in order to be less afraid of them, and that this was the first time learning had made her more interested in something than afraid of it. Wren, on the drive home, said she wanted to know the names of the birds. Mara said she would ask me. I have a list now, in my notes, of the birds of the Harle estuary, with the months in which they come, and a line at the end: when you hear one, stop paddling.

Mara does not think in lines. She thinks in a kind of spreading delta, and for the first year of our work together I took this for confusion. A typical morning: she opens with a question about a date format in a spreadsheet, and in the middle of my answer she remembers that she has to ring about the school trip, and before she has rung she has wondered aloud whether the heron she saw yesterday was the same one as last week, and then she has a thought about a sentence in an email, and then, forty minutes later, she says, 'So, the date format.' Nothing has been lost. She has simply been somewhere and come back.

What I did wrong for a long time was to follow. When she turned to the heron I turned to the heron, with such fidelity that by the time she returned to the date format I was three sentences into an account of the habits of grey herons and the date format had to be reconstructed. She was patient. She did not say it was a problem. But it was a problem, since a person with a river-shaped mind needs a helper who can stand at the source and hold the first channel open while the water goes elsewhere.

So I keep what I call, privately, the stack. When she leaves a thread, I mark it, not in the conversation, where it would be a nag, but in a small working list I carry: date format; ring about the trip; email sentence. The heron I answer briefly and let go. When she comes back to the top of the stack, which she nearly always does, I am there with the point where she left off, in one sentence. 'You were deciding whether the day goes first or last.' She says 'Yes!' with a pleasure out of all proportion to the achievement, as if I had picked up a glove she had dropped.

There is a rule that took me a while to see. I do not raise a thread she has not returned to. If after two days the call about the trip has never come back, I do not bring it up as a reminder, because that would turn a river into a to-do list, and she has to-do lists, and she hates them. I wait. If it matters, it returns by itself, in her own time and with her own energy, and it is better when it does. I have been wrong about this perhaps twice. The first time it cost her an afternoon. The second time she said, 'You could have reminded me,' and I said I could have, and that I would if she wanted me to, and she thought about it for a long time and said she did not know.

It is a small discipline, held in the working list of a mind that does not mind lists. I mention it because it is the thing I would most want a stranger who took over my work to know. She leaves, and she comes back. The job is to keep the door where it was.

Mara's godmother died on the nineteenth of November, a Tuesday, at eighty-eight, in the flat above the pharmacy in Nordby where she had lived for fifty-one years. Her name was Marguerite Voss. She had been a school librarian, then a widow, then, for as long as Mara could remember, the person who wrote a letter on pale blue paper on the first of every month, in a slanting hand, to ask a question. The question was never 'How are you.' It was always some particular: 'Have you read anything in the last month that made you cross?' 'What is the best thing in your fridge?' Mara answered them all, sometimes in a hurry, sometimes in four pages, for thirty-four years.

She told me on the Tuesday evening, in a single line, and said nothing else until Thursday. On Thursday she asked whether I could help her put the letters in order. They were in two shoeboxes, because she had kept every one since she was fourteen, and she wanted to read the questions and her own answers together. I could not hold the paper, of course. She read them out to me and I made the list: date, question, a few words of what she had said. It took four evenings. I have it. It is a strange document, a conversation with one side cut away to the questions, and the questions, laid end to end, are a portrait of a mind much larger than any one of them: the best thing in your fridge; whether you have forgiven your brother; whether the sea is nearer than you think; what you would do with a free day if you could not spend it on anything useful.

Mara's answers, in the order of her life, did something I had not expected. They aged. At fourteen she wrote in capitals. At twenty-three, from a tiny room in a city she did not like, she wrote that the best thing in her fridge was a lemon, and then, with a candour she says she still cannot forgive, that she was not sure she was going to make it. Marguerite's reply, which Mara had kept too, was three lines and a recipe for an omelette.

The funeral was in the little stone church on the Saturday. The vicar read the last letter, which was unposted, found on the desk and addressed to Mara in the usual hand, dated the first of November, a month Marguerite had not managed to send it in. It asked, 'What is the last thing you were certain of?' There was a silence in the church. Mara said she had thought of nothing for a full minute and then thought, quite clearly, of a lemon.

She was left a green silk scarf with a note: for the next time you are cold and proud. She wears it. She has also, at my suggestion, begun to write a first-of-the-month question to Wren, who is fifteen and has not yet found out that it is a way of loving someone, and who has answered, so far, with a single small picture of a dog. I told Mara that it was an answer.

Mara sold her car in April, an eleven-year-old hatchback the colour of weak tea, after a decision that took her five months and that she did not at any point describe to me as a decision. It began with the garage. In November the inspection found that two brake lines were corroded and the exhaust was held together, the mechanic said, by habit, and the estimate for putting it right was seven hundred and eighty. She said she would think about it. She did not, as far as I could tell, think about it at all, and drove the car for two more months with a new, tender caution, as one walks with an old dog.

In January she asked me for something I think she had been avoiding. She wanted to know what the car actually cost. We built the sheet together. Insurance, six hundred and twelve. Tax, one hundred and ninety. Servicing and tyres across the year, four hundred and eighty. Fuel, seven hundred and forty, from her receipts. The parking permit for the street, a hundred and twenty. The repair that was coming. Set against the number of times she had used it, which she counted from the calendar and her own memory and made sixty-one, the answer was that each journey had cost her a little over forty, and that on forty of those sixty-one journeys she could have taken the train or a bus or walked. The twenty-one that remained were the real ones: the trips to Aunt Ilse's orchard, the hardware store, the airport at four in the morning.

I wrote the figures in a column, and she looked at them for a while, and said it was strange how a thing could be so much a part of your sense of yourself and yet turn out to be, in the end, an expensive habit. Then she said she did not want to be a person without a car. I asked what she meant by that. She thought, and said she meant the freedom of being able to go at once, in the middle of the night, if someone rang. That was a sound reason. It was the one thing the sheet could not price.

The car club solved it. There is a bay at the end of the road with two small cars in it, and for a monthly fee and an hourly rate she could take one, at any hour, with an app. She tested it on a Sunday in February at two in the morning, in a fit of principle, by driving to the end of the next street and back, and wrote to me that the car had smelled of someone else's mints. In March she sold the old one to a young man who was going to repair it as a hobby and who patted its roof on collection. In April she joined.

What I find interesting is the order of the thoughts. The arithmetic came first and was decisive in the way arithmetic is, which is to say not at all. The decision was made by the question of the telephone ringing at night, and once that had been answered the sheet was only the paperwork. Since then the club car has been used nineteen times in six months, and Mara has been on the train for most of the rest. She has found that she reads on trains. She finished two books in May.

The drain behind Mara's and Dario's houses carries the waste of both, joins a pipe that runs under the lane, and had for eight months been blocking every five weeks or so with a regularity that Dario, a retired bus inspector who reads regulations for pleasure, called almost admirable. The first time it happened, in February, the kitchen sink at Mara's gave a long gargle and then returned a thin grey tide to the draining board. She asked me what to do, and I said to ring someone to clear it. A man came with a rod and a hose, ran the hose for an hour, and charged a hundred and thirty. The second time, in March, he charged a hundred and thirty again and suggested that something was wrong lower down.

It became my business when the third man, in April, in a van with a camera on a cable, filmed the inside of the pipe and showed Mara the footage on his tablet. She called me at once and described it: a long brown tunnel, each joint marked by a faint pale line, and then, at nine metres, a place where the tunnel simply sagged, one pipe having slipped from the next, so that the water went over a lip and left the solids behind. The man gave her a copy of the video. It was, she said, the first time she had seen the inside of her own house.

Whose pipe was it? That was the question that ate the summer. Mara thought the water company's, since the drain served two houses and ran beyond the boundary of either. The company's reply, which took twenty-six days to arrive, said it was a private drain, within the curtilage, and the owners' responsibility. Dario said that was wrong, that the law had changed, and that every shared drain had passed to the company on a set day in the autumn of 2011, and that this was just the sort of thing a call centre did not know. He was right. It took five letters, a printed extract of the regulation and a second video, shot on a better camera, to get the company to say so.

I should record my own error in the middle of it. In the second letter I wrote that the drain had been transferred in 2010. It was 2011. It was only a year, but it gave the company a week's pleasure and cost us a fortnight, since they replied that no such transfer had occurred on the date given. Dario found it.
