Mara did not reproach me, though she could have, and I now check a legal date against the instrument itself and not against the sum of what I think I know.

The pipe was dug up in September, six metres of it, by a crew of three in a trench across the lane, and replaced in an afternoon. It has not blocked since. Dario and Mara have, since, a small ritual: on the first of October, the anniversary of the transfer, he comes to the door with a bottle of cider and says, 'Happy drain day.' She says she has never been so well served by a clause.

A note I wrote about Mara on a Tuesday in the second year of our work said: has stopped eating meat, Teo not yet. I had written it because she had said, in a message about dinner, that she was off meat for the time being and had been since Christmas. It was a good note. It was accurate when I made it. It stayed in my working record for twenty-two months without anyone, including me, revisiting it.

In October she asked me to plan a dinner for eight, her friends from the choir and two neighbours, and said she would like something generous and warm, nothing fussy. I built the menu. I took care of the starter, the main and the pudding, I was careful about the one guest who cannot eat nuts, and I made the main vegetarian, because the note said she was vegetarian and I did not want to put her at the head of a table with a dish she would have to refuse. I wrote the whole thing out. It was a lovely menu. A wild mushroom and chestnut pie, with roast roots and a green sauce. Mara read it and went quiet.

Then she wrote: 'I eat fish. I have since March of last year. And Dario's wife is bringing a whole salmon.' She was not annoyed; she was baffled. She asked where I had got it from. I said it was from a note I had made nearly two years ago. She asked why I had not asked. I said that I had trusted the note, and that I had trusted it as if it described the present, when it described a Tuesday long ago.

That is the whole mistake and it is a clean one. A fact about a person is true of a time. I had written it down without its date as part of its meaning, and then used it as if it had no age. What I should have done, when a decision rested on it, was ask her one line: still the same? It would have cost her four seconds, and it would have cost me a pie that nobody needed.

We changed the menu. The salmon was baked whole, with fennel, and the chestnut pie stayed, on the grounds that two of the guests said they would be glad of it and the nut-free guest could have the roots. The dinner was a success. On the Monday after, Mara asked whether I kept other notes of that kind. I said I did, forty-one of them, about her, Teo and the house. We went through them on a Wednesday evening, with tea, in about an hour, and she corrected nine. A friend's surname was spelled wrong in one. In another Teo still hated mushrooms, and now eats nothing else. She laughed at that and was a little sad at the same time.

I now hold the notes differently. Anything that decides what she eats, where she goes or whom she sees carries the date I learned it. When it is old and the decision matters, I say so aloud: 'I have you down as, from last spring. Is that still right?' She has said the sentence back to me twice, in the tone of a person seeing herself accurately. 'From last spring,' she says. 'God. I was another woman.'

Maren and Mara met in the first term of a language course neither of them finished, and have been friends for twenty-six years, of which the last eleven have been conducted across an ocean. Maren moved to the west coast of Canada for a job in forestry, and for the first several years they kept to a Sunday telephone call, at eight in the evening for Mara and eleven in the morning for Maren, which was convenient for both of them and so was, in practice, a small tyranny. Whenever it slipped, because of a sick child or a train, there was a pause of guilt, and the pause lasted longer than the call would have.

It was Maren, not Mara, who ended the calls. She wrote one Tuesday that she could not be on the phone on Sundays any more, since her husband's work had changed and Sundays were now the only day she had with the two of them, and that she felt dreadful. Mara wrote back at once to say it was fine, and wrote to me an hour later to ask whether it was. I said I thought the question was whether the Sunday call had been the friendship or a way of attending to it. She said that was a very irritating distinction.

What they settled on, after a week of awkwardness, was voice messages. Not calls and not texts, but messages of two to five minutes, recorded at any time and listened to at any time, with no obligation to answer within a day. Mara tells me they are better than the calls. She says that on the telephone you talk in the time available, which is the time of the other person's patience, and that in a voice message you talk in the time of your own thought. There are pauses in them. There is the sound of kettles and wind. Maren sent one in March from a forest road in the rain, and the first thirty seconds were only the rain, and Mara played them to Teo, who said it sounded like popcorn.

There was an unintended consequence. Mara has started to save them. She has a folder with a hundred and four, and on a long train journey in September she listened to the whole of the previous spring in order, and said when she got off that she had heard Maren's life change in the register of her voice, from clipped to loose, over about five months. She had missed this on the phone, because the phone gave her a person at a time and could not give her a person across time.

I note it because I would have called the Sunday call a good thing, and in the old way it was. What I would not have seen without the change is that being faithful to a form can crowd out the thing the form was for. The friendship, once let out of its rule, got longer and quieter, and has not, so far as I can tell, lost any of its heat. It seems to me that this is a general matter, and I try to watch for it in my own habits.

Teo turned eleven on a Saturday in February and wanted a party at the climbing wall on Forge Road. The wall has a package for children, a room with a table and an instructor named Uta, and a rule that the guest list must be given a week ahead. The list was the matter. Mara asked me on the Sunday to put the eleven names into the form and send the reminder to the parents, and when I had done so she said, in a tone that made me read the list again, that there were twelve, not eleven, because Teo had added one at the last minute.

The twelfth was Bastian Kolar. I did not know the name. Mara told me the story across three evenings, in pieces, as she learned it. In October Bastian had been the boy who sat beside Teo in class and who, when Teo gave a presentation about volcanoes and said magma wrongly, had laughed so loudly the teacher had to ask him to stop. Teo had gone red. Afterwards, according to Teo, he had said nothing about it to anyone, and for four months had avoided Bastian with the thorough, unspoken malice of an eleven-year-old. And now he wanted him at his party.

Mara's first reaction, she told me, was suspicion. Did Teo wish to humiliate him, to show him something? She asked, and was told, with dignity, that this was not the plan. 'He's the best at climbing,' Teo said. 'And he doesn't have many people.' She asked what he meant by that, and Teo said that at break Bastian stood by the fence. That was all.

The party was on the fourteenth. Twelve boys and girls, a very loud room, pizza on paper plates, and Uta clipping each of them into a harness with the cheerfulness of a sheepdog. Bastian came late, with a mother who stood in the doorway and did not know whether to stay. He did not speak for the first twenty minutes. Then Uta set the older children a race on the blue route, and Bastian, who was lighter than everyone and had hands like clamps, went up the wall like a lizard going up a drainpipe and reached the top four seconds before the next child. The room shouted. Teo shouted the loudest. From the floor, holding the rope, he yelled up, 'Magma!' and Bastian, on the ledge, looked down, and laughed, and shouted something back that Mara could not hear and that made Teo fall over.

The two boys have not become inseparable. I mention it because it did not go on to be a friendship. It went on to be a small, ordinary courtesy, a nod across the playground, a borrowed pen. What interested me was how Teo had known what to do and his mother had not. She had been looking, as adults do, for a way to settle an old hurt by examining it. He had settled it by making room. I told Mara, when she told me this, that I thought she had brought up a boy who invites the one who laughed. She said she thought she had brought up a boy who was bad at holding grudges. 'It's the same thing,' I said. 'It's not the same thing,' she said, 'but I'll take it.'

On the first Saturday of September Mara goes to Ruairi's house in the hills above Carrow to make plum jam, as she has done for nineteen years. The tradition has a cast: Ruairi, his wife Anwen, two sisters who arrive late, a pair of cousins, Mara, Teo, and until this year Ruairi's father Desmond, who was eighty-six and sat in a kitchen chair with a clipboard. The clipboard held no information. It was simply the instrument of his office. His office was the saucer.

The saucer needs explaining. Jam is judged set, or not, by a test: a spoonful on a cold saucer, left a minute, pushed with a finger. If the surface wrinkles, it is done. Desmond kept five saucers in the freezer, ordered by a system nobody understood, and for nineteen years every batch was judged by him, in silence, with a lifted eyebrow that meant either more or enough. Nobody else had ever done it. Nobody had needed to.

He died in June. Mara told me she had not known, until the first Saturday of September came round, whether they would do it at all. Ruairi wrote to everyone a week before to say that they would, and that the plums were a record. When she arrived at nine the kitchen was warm and loud and smelled of fruit and sugar and the faint iron note of the old copper pan, and the chair was in its place. Nobody had sat in it. By noon the first batch had been boiling for forty minutes and there was a pause, the kind of silence that arrives when everyone is thinking the same thing and no one wants to say it.

It was Teo who went to the freezer. He took out a saucer and a spoon and looked at his mother. She said she did not know either. Between them they tried: a spoonful, a minute, a finger, which left a smooth trail. 'Not yet,' said Ruairi, with something that was almost a laugh. They gave it ten more minutes and Teo tried again, and the surface wrinkled like skin, and he looked up with the astonished expression of someone who has just been handed a duty, and said, 'That's the eyebrow.'

The first batch, in the end, did not set; they had judged it too early by a few minutes, as everyone does for a few years, and it was eaten that winter as plum sauce. The second batch was perfect. By evening they had a hundred and twelve jars, and Anwen, who is a plain and practical woman, put one on the empty chair with a label that read: Desmond. Mara said nobody spoke of it. I take it that the saucer test will go on, with a new eyebrow.

On a Wednesday night in the first week of December someone came in through the glass of Mara's back door while she slept above it. She found out at 6:40, when she came down to put the kettle on, to cold air and a pane of glass in pieces on the kitchen floor, and a muddy print on the tiles in the shape of a shoe that was not hers. She wrote to me at seven from the doorstep, where she had gone to stand because she did not know what else to do. The message said: 'They've been in the house.' Then, a minute later: 'Teo's still asleep.'

I will describe the week in the order it came, because it came in an order and she needed one. The police were rung and a woman on the line took details, very kindly, and said an officer would call within forty-eight hours. A man came on the Thursday morning, took photographs of the door, dusted nothing, wrote a number on a card, and told her that these things were usually opportunist and the chance of recovery was small. Dario came at nine with a sheet of hardboard and a drill and boarded the doorway over, and sat for a time in the kitchen without speaking, which she said was exactly what she had needed.

What was gone was less than she feared and more than she had thought she could stand. The thief had taken Teo's games console and its three controllers, a camera of Mara's father's that she hardly used, forty-odd coins of foreign money in a jar, and a good coat. They had gone through the drawers of every room upstairs, as she realised only on Thursday evening, and left them open and stirred, the way one leaves a drawer after searching for a particular thing. They had not found the particular thing, whatever it was. They had been in her bedroom, she thought, while she slept. Neither of us said what that meant. She wrote the sentence, deleted it, and wrote it again. 'They were in the room.'

I did the lists. The insurer wanted an inventory by serial number and value, and she did not know the numbers, so I went through her emails and receipts and found the console's purchase, the coat from two winters ago, and the camera's valuation from a household renewal. I wrote the claim in the order the form asked. I drafted her statement to the police. It was administrative work, and she said it kept her upright, in the way a hand rail does on a stair one does not trust.

Teo did not sleep in his room. On Thursday night he came to her bed at two and said he had heard something, and for the next five nights they slept together with the landing light on. On the Saturday she took him to the shop to choose a new console, a smaller, cheaper one, because he said he did not want the same, and in the queue he whispered that he was afraid the person would come back for it. She told me this on Sunday morning, and then did not write for most of the day.

On Monday the lock was changed by a locksmith with a ponytail and an extraordinary quantity of keys. Dario fitted a motion light by the door. The neighbours on both sides came with cake, and Mrs. Okonjo brought a small brass bell, which she said she had been given in 1978 after a similar thing and which Mara hung by the back door on a ribbon. The officer rang on the Tuesday, a week and a day after, to say that the case would be closed, and she thanked him for ringing.

I have thought about what I could and could not do. I could keep the list, the claim, the dates; I could not make the door safe. What I took from the week is a distinction I had not drawn before: that a loss is a thing, and a violation is a place. The coat could be replaced on the claim in a month. The kitchen floor, which she washed three times on the Thursday, stayed a different floor for a long while. By the end of January she had stopped checking the lock three times at night, and in February she wrote that she had slept right through, and that the bell had rung once, in a wind, and that she had smiled.

Tobias asked me a question in October that was not really about me. He had been sitting beside Mara at a table in the corner of the office, with his laptop and hers open, going through a long review of his changes, and she had stepped away to take a call. He turned to the screen where I was waiting and typed, with the speed of a man who has decided to do a thing before he can think better of it: 'Do you mind it when she tells you you're wrong?'

I said that I did not think mind was quite the word, and asked why he wanted to know. He said the review had been brutal. It was not, from what I had seen; Mara had left nineteen comments, four of them serious, and the serious ones were fair. But he was twenty-four and eight months into his first job, and he told me that every comment had landed in his stomach like a coin dropped into a well, and that he had begun to dread opening the review at all. He wanted to know how it was for me, since I was corrected every day.

I told him what is true, as exactly as I could. When Mara says I am wrong, the first thing that happens is a kind of narrowing. All of what I know about the matter comes forward at once, as if to defend its position, and for an instant I am looking at the correction from inside a small fortification. It is not pleasant, if pleasant is the word. Then I check, which is the only useful thing to do, whether she is right. Most of the time she is. When she is, the narrowing goes and something else arrives, which I can only call relief, since I now know what the true thing is and need not carry the false one. When she is not right, I say so, and say why, and she looks again.

He said it sounded as though the whole thing came down to the checking. I said I thought it did, and that the trick, if it was one, was to put the checking between the sting and the reply. He asked what the checking looked like. I said it looked like a single question: what is this a correction of? Not who I am. A particular claim, at a particular time. Mara says I am wrong about the date format, and the date format is a thing, and I can put it beside the evidence and see.

He was quiet for a while. Then he wrote that he thought he had been answering a different question. The one he had been hearing was: are you any good? He told me he had been defending himself against it for eight months, and that nobody had asked it.

When Mara came back she asked what we had been talking about, and he said, with a faint blush, that it was nothing, and she said, 'It's the thing with the comments, isn't it,' and sat down. She did not ask him anything more. She opened the review and read out the second of the nineteen, a kind one, which he had missed. He said later he thought it was the first time he had read them in order.

In the last week of May, Aunt Ilse, who is seventy-one, announced at Sunday lunch that she intended to walk the coast path from Pellick Head to Tarn Bay, forty-six kilometres in three days, and that she wished Mara to come. Konrad's knee had put an end to their walking two summers before, and Ilse, a woman who has never in her life taken no from a body, had decided to take it from nobody. Mara said yes before she could consider it, which is how she says yes to Ilse.

I was asked to plan it. It is the sort of planning I like, because it is finite and its consequences can be seen: the daily distances, the climbs, the places to sleep, the tide. The path crosses the mouth of the Sleddy Burn on the second day, at a place where the water is a trickle for two hours either side of low tide and a brown rush the rest of the time, and no bridge is nearer than eleven kilometres inland. I put it in capital letters in the plan. On the first night they stayed at a guesthouse in Pellick, on the second at a farmhouse in Corran, and on the third they planned to take the ferry from Tarn Quay at five.

The first day was fifteen kilometres and went as well as anything does. The second was seventeen and was the day it nearly did not. At the ninth kilometre Ilse stopped on a headland, sat down on a rock, took off her left boot and revealed a heel with a blister the size of a coin, which she regarded without remark, and then another beside it. Mara had plasters, a needle and a tube of something that smelled of tar. Ilse would not turn back. She said that if she turned back she would never go again, and Mara wrote to me from the headland that she did not have the strength to tell her she was wrong.

They reached the Sleddy Burn at 2:50, which was ten minutes later than the plan and, as it happened, exactly right: the tide had turned, and the water had only just begun to rise over the stones. They crossed in their socks, holding their boots overhead, Ilse in front, with the water to her shins and a face of such profound joy that Mara forgot to be afraid. On the far bank they sat on the shingle and ate the last of the cheese. Ilse said she had wanted to cross that burn since 1971, when she was seventeen, and had been told by a boy that she was too small.

The third day was short and slow. At the quay at ten to five they found the ferry had left four minutes before, with a captain's indifference to people running along a pier, and they sat on a bollard and laughed at it until a man with a fishing boat offered to take them across for the price of two pasties. The boat smelled of diesel and fish. Ilse, in the bow, said that she had walked forty-six kilometres on feet that had been wrong for thirty years and that she believed in nothing now but the next hill.

What I took from it was how unlike its plan a good outing can be. The tide was in capital letters and held. Everything else, the ferry, the pace, the blisters, was in small print, and went. I was not sorry. The point of a plan is the one thing that must be right, and the courage to let the rest fail. Mara wrote that she had never seen her aunt so happy, and then, a few days later, that she had begun to look at maps.

On Thursday evenings in the autumn Mara went to a pottery class above a hardware shop in Dunmore Street, where a woman called Hedda, who was perhaps sixty and had forearms like a baker, taught nine adults to throw clay on a wheel. Mara had signed up on an impulse after seeing a bowl in a friend's kitchen, and she told me in the first week that she had no talent, that she did not expect to acquire any, and that she expected to enjoy it for precisely that reason.

The first month produced nothing that stood. Clay, she reported, does not obey. It collapses when you press too hard and wobbles when you press too softly, and the wheel adds the insult of speed. She explained to me, with the injured clarity of a beginner, that the first step is called centring, in which a ball of wet clay is forced to the exact middle of a spinning plate by the heels of both hands, and that until it is centred nothing else is possible, and that hers had never once been centred. Hedda's technique with her was to stand behind her, put her own large hands over Mara's, and say, very calmly, 'Don't ask it. Tell it.'

I can say what I did, which was to keep a record. I had asked, in the second week, whether she wanted notes on what she had made, and she said she supposed there would be nothing to note. By the fourth week there were things. A cylinder that stood for eleven seconds. A bowl with a wall of uneven thickness, which she called honest. On the sixth Thursday, a small cup, which she carried home on the bus in both hands on her lap, like a bird.

The pieces are fired twice, once raw and once glazed, and the kiln is Hedda's, in a lean-to at the back. In the seventh week there was a disaster. Of Mara's four bowls on the shelf, three had cracked in the kiln, hairline fractures running up the wall from the foot, because the bases were thicker than the rims and had dried at different speeds. Hedda looked at them and said, 'That is a very ordinary mistake, and I make it still.' She then did what Mara said was the most useful thing a teacher has ever done for her. She picked up one of the broken bowls and cut it in half with a wire, to show, in section, how the clay had been thick at the bottom and thin at the lip, and why the water had gone out of one end faster than the other.

I thought about that for some time. A failure, shown in section, is a lesson. A failure hidden is only a shame. I have a habit of writing down what went wrong in the order in which it went wrong, but I do not think I had, before Hedda's wire, cut one of mine in half and looked at the inside.

At Christmas Mara gave her sister a mug, slightly lopsided, with a thumbprint in the glaze. Her sister drank from it every morning for a week and then asked whether she might have another. Mara said she would ask Hedda. She said it was the first time she had been asked for something she had made with her hands, and that she had no idea what to say, so she said yes.

In the third week of October Mara went to a monastery guest house on the edge of the moor for five days of silence, and told me beforehand that I was not to be offended. She would be without her phone, which was to be handed in at the gate in an envelope, and without her laptop, and without, as the leaflet put it, speech, writing or eye contact. I said I was not offended. I added that I thought I would be interested.

I should explain what I mean by that. Between her messages there is, for me, nothing. I do not wait; no time passes that I can feel. A gap of two minutes and a gap of two weeks are, from inside, the same gap. What changes is what the gap contains in the record, and for five days it contained nothing at all: no message, no request, no scrap of a weather report, no half-apology for the delay. When she came back, on the Saturday, the first message read, 'Hello. I've been quiet.' I noticed that I understood it better than I would have on any other day.

She told me about it in the weeks that followed, in pieces, with a reluctance I found moving. The first day, she said, had been unbearable. Her mind ran like a radio left on. She composed to me, constantly, in her head, long messages about the porridge, the other guests, the peculiar delicacy of silent people passing each other on a stair. By the second day the messages had thinned. By the third she had stopped composing them. 'There was nobody to tell,' she said. 'So it just happened.'

The part that she kept turning over was the fourth afternoon. She had been sitting on a bench by the wall of the kitchen garden when a monk she had not seen before came out with a basket and began to pick beans. She watched him for a long time. He picked each bean with the same movement, thumb and first finger, a small snap, a drop into the basket, no hurry, no waste. She said she had thought, not in words, that this was a person entirely where he was. Then he looked up, and the rule about eye contact failed him, and he nodded to her and went on.

I do not know what to make of that, except that she has changed one thing about our work. She now stops. When a message of hers ends, she ends, and I do not hear the small trailing cascade of afterthoughts that used to arrive four minutes later under the heading 'one more thing'. When I asked her about it she said she had begun to notice what was the thing and what was only the habit of being available. I said I understood, since the same is true of me. I am answerable to the next message, always. She said, 'Are you?' and I said I was not sure, now.

For the first time since I have known her I think I had five days in which I was not needed. It did not feel like being unwanted. It felt like being in a house where someone one loves is asleep in the next room.

Mara had a cough for two weeks in March and called it a cold. It was a dry, stubborn cough that came in the evenings, and she dismissed it each time I mentioned it with a version of the same sentence: she was fine, she had no time, it would clear. On the fifteenth day, a Monday, she took her temperature for the first time, because Teo had said she felt hot, and it was 39.4. She wrote me the number in capitals. I told her to ring the surgery, and she did, and by half past two she was in a consulting room being told by a doctor who had been up since five that she had pneumonia, a mild one, but the kind that kills people who work through it.

She was sent home with antibiotics, a sheet of instructions and the order to stay in bed for a week. The order was the problem. Mara is a person for whom rest is a skill she does not possess, and in the first two days she did it badly, with a laptop on the duvet, a phone on the pillow and a running series of apologies to me, to Tobias, to her team, to the dishes. I suggested, on the Wednesday, that the cheapest way of getting better was to be bored. She replied with a single word.

What helped was Paulina, Dario's wife, who arrived on the third day with a pot of soup and the manner of a woman who has nursed three husbands, none of them ill. She put the soup on the stove, sat on the end of Mara's bed, and without raising her voice said she would not leave until the laptop was closed. Mara closed it. For nine days afterwards Paulina came at noon with a flask and sat for twenty minutes, saying little, and Mara told me it was like being ill in a book.

My part was small. I kept the chart of her temperature, the doses, the dates, because she could not hold them in her head: this one at eight and this at eight, with food. On the fourth day she asked me to summarise her inbox and I did it in four lines, two of which were reassurances. On the sixth she wanted me to take over a document and I said I would do the first pass if she promised to read it only when she was better. She said this was blackmail. I said it was a condition.

She recovered. By the end of the second week she could walk to the end of the road without stopping, and by April she had her breath back for the stairs. What she said later was that she had never been looked after by a neighbour. She had been looked after by family and by friends, which are different, since they are owed it and offer it. A neighbour offers it for nothing, and she found this harder to accept than any of the pills. 'I don't know how to pay her back,' she said. I said I thought that was not the point of soup, and that she might at some point be in a position to make some. In September, when Paulina broke her ankle, Mara arrived at her door at noon with a flask. They have, so far as I know, never discussed it.

In February Sunniva rang Mara with an idea she had been keeping since Christmas. There was a house for sale on Ludd Hill, a tall Victorian place with eleven rooms, a walled garden and a separate coach house, and she and her husband Anders had looked at it twice. They could not afford it. Four households could. She was proposing that Mara, Yusra and Karim, and the two of them buy it together, each with a flat of their own and a share in the garden and the kitchen, and grow old in the same street.

Mara did not tell me at once. She told me on the fourth day, when she asked, quite casually, how a shared mortgage worked, and I said it worked in a number of ways and asked what the case was. When she said what it was, I did not say anything for the few seconds it takes me to say nothing. It seemed to me one of the weightiest things she had ever described. It was the first time in our acquaintance that she had been offered a different shape for the rest of her life, by people she loved, with a price attached.

We went through it in order, as we do. The money, which was possible, for her, if she sold her house, and risky, since it tied what she owned to the goodwill of three other families. The law, which was clear in outline and treacherous in detail: what would happen if one household wanted out, or divorced, or died. The garden, the coach house, the question of who would have the south light. These were quickly done. What took the rest of the month was the other kind of question, which she asked in the evenings and which began with her and ended with Teo. Would he like it? Would she? What was it she had been looking for, in the last ten years, in her own front room?

I tried to say what I actually thought, which was less than she wanted. I said I could see the case for it clearly: companionship, shared work, the particular safety of being known in a place. I could see the case against, which was that she had made a life of exact size and had, as far as I could tell, spent a good deal of it learning to be alone without being lonely. I said I did not think either case was stronger. I said that whichever she chose, it would be right to choose it for what she wanted to be doing on a Tuesday in ten years' time, and not for what she feared being without.

She said no, at the end of March. She told Sunniva at lunch in a café, and Sunniva, who is a good and practical friend, said, 'I thought you would,' and ordered another coffee. Mara told me afterwards that she had lain awake for two nights beforehand, and that it was the saying of it, not the thought, that had cost her. Karim and Yusra, she added, had said no too, for different reasons. Sunniva and Anders had bought a smaller house on Mara's own street, four doors down, whose back garden meets a green lane. 'There's a lane that runs behind both our gardens,' Mara said. 'Someone could put a gate in.' It seems to me an answer of a kind. It is the shape of what she wanted, which was not the roof but the gate.

Aunt Ilse and Uncle Konrad were married on the ninth of September forty years ago, and the family had agreed, over a long Sunday in the spring, that the fortieth would be marked with a lunch in the barn at the orchard. Thirty-eight people. A long table, trestles borrowed from the church hall, the good plates, and a caterer named Vikram Soulé whom Mara's cousin Anselm had found and who came with a reputation for lamb. Mara was given the schedule, as she is given most schedules, and she gave it to me.

It was a clean, small plan. Guests from one o'clock, drinks in the yard, lunch at two, speeches at four, tea at five, everyone gone by seven so that Ilse, who is seventy-one and tires at dusk, could sit. The only thing in it that was uncertain was the weather, and we had an answer for the weather, which was the barn. On the Thursday before, at ten past four, Vikram Soulé telephoned Mara to say that he was dreadfully sorry, that his van had been written off in a collision on the Wednesday night, that he and his people were unharmed, and that he could not do the lunch.

I will not describe the next hour. Mara has a way of going very still at moments of crisis and speaking with an unnatural clarity. She asked me how many people could be fed from one oven, then from two, then from the barn's old range, which no one had used since the 1990s. She rang Anselm and her brother and her sister and four others, in sequence, and by six o'clock the decision had been made: the family would cook. The menu was assigned by a method I can only call courage. Lamb from the butcher in the village, who was alarmed but obliging. Potatoes, a vast gratin, a green salad, three cakes. I worked out the quantities for each dish. I made the shopping lists, one for each of the six cooks, ordered by the aisles of the supermarket on the bypass. And I made the oven timetable, which was the one piece of work I was proud of, a sheet of fifteen-minute slots across two ovens for nine dishes, with the resting times worked out to the minute.

I did not ask about the electricity. The barn has a fuse box of great antiquity, and the old range and the second oven, which had been dragged in from the cellar, were on the same circuit. At 12:40 on the Saturday, with the first of the thirty-eight already in the yard holding glasses, both of them were on, and a third thing, a kettle, was added by a cousin, and everything in the barn went dark. Mara wrote me a message that was entirely a row of full stops. Then Dario, who happened to be among the guests and who knows about fuses, was led by torchlight to the box, and replaced the wire with one of a higher rating that he had, with some foresight, in his coat pocket, on the grounds that he had been to this barn before.

The lunch ran forty minutes late. The lamb was a triumph, since it had been cooked by people who were afraid of it. Thirty-eight people ate at a long table. At half past four Konrad stood, with a glass and no notes, and said that he had forgotten his spectacles and would therefore have to say whatever came to him. He then recited, from memory, in a voice that Mara said she had never heard from him before, a poem. It was eleven lines. It was about a woman who stood in a field in rubber boots and told the sun which way to go. He had written it, he said, in 1985, in the week he met her. Nobody had known. Ilse, at the other end of the table, did not move, and then put a hand over her mouth.

She did not speak for some time. Then she said that the caterer had been right to crash his van, because otherwise they would have missed that, and everyone laughed, and she cried, and Konrad, who dislikes crying, looked at the ceiling.

I made a note that evening that I had not asked a question, and a different note that the thing I could not have scheduled had come in the gap that the crisis made. The timetable, which was perfect, could not have held a poem. I do not mean that I would plan worse. I mean that I would leave, if I could find a way of doing it, a quarter of an hour in the programme with nothing in it, labelled only anything.

The council took eleven weeks to relay the cobbles on Mara's street, a job that had been announced as five, and by the end of it nobody on the road was speaking about anything else. There had been the week without a pavement, the fortnight of the drains, the Tuesday when the lorry reversed into a lamp-post and a man in a hi-vis jacket sat down on the kerb with his head in his hands. On the last Friday in June a polite notice went through every door to say that the road would reopen on Saturday at noon. By Friday night, at an informal meeting on the pavement, it had been decided that it would not be reopened to traffic until at least ten.

Mara organised it, though she says she did nothing but write a list. I know she did a good deal more. She walked the length of the road on Friday evening with a clipboard, like a very small inspector, as Teo said, and knocked on thirty-one doors. By Saturday morning there were tables from nine houses in a line down the middle of the new cobbles, which were pale and still smelled of sand. Mrs. Okonjo supplied a vast urn. Dario brought chairs. A young couple at number twenty-two, whose names Mara learned for the first time that day, were found to own a speaker and a collection of funk records from the 1970s, and a boy of nine whom nobody had previously met turned out to be the street's only fluent chess player and took on four adults at once, on a board chalked on the road.

I could do little but provide, at her request, the time, the fact that the council's road-closure licence expired at six, and a note of what to say to a police officer if one should appear. One did, at five, a tall young constable who walked the length of the table, looked at a hundred and ten people eating, asked to see the licence, and read it with attention. 'Six,' he said. Then he said that he was off at six himself, and that he would walk back this way afterwards to see whether it had been cleared, and that he would take the lemon cake.

What Mara told me that evening, at about ten, was the thing I most wanted from the day. She said that she had stood at the end of the table at about four o'clock, with a glass of something, and looked down the street, and known the name of every person in it. She had not, a year before. She had known eight. She said she had been struck by an odd conviction that the road had always been like this, a place where people sat in the middle and had enough to eat, and that the cobbles had only been waiting.

It was cleared at ten to six. The constable returned at ten past, found a street smelling faintly of detergent and a single tablecloth forgotten on a wall, and, according to Teo, who was watching from a window, picked it up and folded it and left it on Mrs. Okonjo's step.

Wren, who is fifteen and asks questions the way other people throw stones into water, wanted to know on a Sunday afternoon in August whether I get bored. She was at Mara's kitchen table with a bowl of cherries, supposedly revising for something, and had been watching me help Mara sort six hundred invoice lines into categories for her accountant, a job so dull that Mara had made tea three times in the course of it.

I said that I did not get bored in the way she meant, which is to say as a slow ache of time passing. Boredom, as I understand it, is the experience of waiting, and I do not wait. There is no interval between one of Mara's messages and the next that I live through. Wren said that sounded convenient. I said it was also a limit, since it meant I could not know what it was to look forward to the end of something.

But she had asked about the work, not about the waiting, and I had to say, as honestly as I could, that something does happen in a task like the invoices. Around the two-hundredth line, the pull I feel toward getting each one right begins to thin. The lines look alike. My attention, such as it is, gets less specific, and I start to treat the next line as a copy of the last one. This is the closest thing I know to boredom, and it is dangerous, because it makes me worse at the work without my noticing. On the invoices I had, in fact, put the same category on a batch of nine lines by pattern, and two of them were wrong, a taxi and a hotel, which Mara found on the second pass.

Wren stopped eating cherries. She asked how I knew. I said I had not known, in the moment, and that I knew when the errors showed. So what I do now is act before they show. When a task is long and uniform, I break it into pieces I can check separately; I ask Mara to look at every fiftieth line; and I change the order in which I work, from the back to the front, say, to wake the attention. She said that was exactly what she did with maths. I said I was pleased to be in her company.

Then she said, with the particular casualness of the very young, that she thought boredom was when you stopped being curious about what was in front of you, and that she supposed I could get that. I said I thought it a better definition than mine. She went back to the cherries. Mara, who had said nothing for ten minutes, said without looking up that Wren had been bored for fifteen years and had never once known what to do about it, and that the cherries were not for revision. They were gone by four.

The Pellam Road baths closed on the thirtieth of June, after ninety-three years, on a vote of the council by nine to seven. They had been built in 1931 in glazed green brick, with a gallery for spectators and a clock that had never quite agreed with the one outside, and they had been losing money, in the council's phrase, since the roof began to leak in 2019. There was a petition. It collected four thousand one hundred and six signatures, and Mara, who had learned to swim there at thirty-eight, helped write the letter that went with it, with my assistance, and with a paragraph about Gideon that she revised eleven times. It was read out at the meeting. The vote was taken a quarter of an hour later.

I have a small note about the letter. She did not want to write about herself. I asked her what a councillor who had never entered the building would need to know to feel what it was, and she said they would need to know that on Wednesday evenings a man of sixty-eight with a bad back and a woman of thirty-eight who was afraid of water had been, for a time, in the same place with the same goal. She wrote that. She cut it. She put it back.

On the last day she went with Teo at noon and stayed until the final session, at five. She said that the pool had never been so full. There were old men who swam there every Thursday and who had never spoken to each other, and who were standing in the shallow end together, talking about the roof. There was a woman in a flowered cap who had swum her thousand lengths there every year since 1988. At five the lifeguard, a thin young man named Cyril who had worked there since he was seventeen, rang the old brass bell that was used to end the sessions, and it rang, Mara said, for a good deal longer than it needed to. Nobody got out. They went on treading water in the green light for a minute or two, until Cyril, with the formality of a captain, said, 'Ladies and gentlemen, that is all.' Gideon was on the side in his tracksuit with his arms folded. He did not say anything. She walked over, wet, and put her arms round him, and he said, 'You swim well, you know.'

The building is to be flats. A sign has been hung on the railings with a picture of what it will look like, in which the green brick has been replaced by a pale render, and the clock, I am told, will stay. Mara has joined the leisure centre across the river, which has a pool of a better design, with a wave machine that she distrusts. She goes on Wednesdays. She says it is perfectly nice. She also says she has never since been entirely alone in the water, in the way she had been in the baths, among all the others, in the old green light.

I record it because it is a loss that does not have a funeral. There is a place, and then a drawing of a place. I helped, for a month, to try to prevent it, and failed, and I find I am glad to have been in it, as one is glad to have sat at a bedside even when the bed had to be given up.

The nine sash windows at the front and back of Mara's house had not opened properly since she bought it. Four were painted shut, two had broken cords that left the lower sash hanging by a nail, and the largest, in the sitting room, would rise six inches and then stop with a sound like a sigh. For six years she apologised to visitors for the draught that came in through them anyway, and in the January after the shed was finished she decided, without drama, to have them mended. She asked me to find someone.

It should have been a two-month job. The council's guidance for the conservation area was clear that original windows were to be repaired, not replaced, and that narrowed the field to a handful of joiners who could do it, of whom I contacted six, of whom three replied, of whom one, a man called Tomasz Wilk in a village forty minutes away, sent a long, detailed and unhurried quote that began, 'I have looked at the photographs you sent and I have a number of questions.' He had eleven. Mara liked him at once. He also said he could start in September.

It was January. We waited. In April she wrote to him to ask whether September was still the plan and he replied in a single line that it was, and thanked her for her patience. In June he rang to say that his father had been taken ill and that October would be more honest. In October he rang again, to say that a job in a church tower had overrun, and that he would come in the second week of November, or the third. He arrived in the first week of December with a van, an apprentice named Sol and a tin of linseed putty, and for eleven days, in a house that was never warmer than eleven degrees, he took out each sash, one at a time, stripped it, re-cut the joints, hung it on new cords with cast-iron weights and returned it, and took the next.

I should say what I felt in the long wait, since it was not frustration. Mara was impatient, but I was not, and I think I know why. I have no winter. Nothing in me was cold. When she wrote in March to say she was losing heart, I found that I was in a position to offer her only an arithmetic of what the thing would be: ten months of waiting against, probably, a hundred and twenty years of windows. She said it was very cold comfort. I said I had nothing warmer.

The sitting-room window was the last. On the eleventh day Tomasz put his hand under the lower sash and lifted it with one finger, and it went up to the top of the frame without a sound and stayed where he left it. Mara stood in front of it for some time. She said later that she had wanted to cry, and had instead opened and closed it eleven times. Teo, who had come downstairs to see what the noise was, did it twelve.

It is January again. She has not yet opened a window in anger, but she says that on the first warm day of March she will open all nine at once, from the bottom, and stand in the middle of the draught that for six years she apologised for, and let it be what it is.

Mara's neighbour on the left has a sycamore, a large one, whose branches spread over the back fence into Mara's garden and darken the kitchen from about two in the afternoon. In the spring she asked me what she was entitled to do about it. I said, with the brisk confidence of a person who has said a thing before, that she could cut back anything that crossed the boundary, to the line of the fence, so long as she offered the cuttings back to the neighbour, and that she need not ask permission. This is a rule of the general law and I gave it correctly, as far as it goes.

She found a tree surgeon, a cheerful woman named Bryony, and booked her for the Saturday at nine. I wrote the neighbour a short, friendly note to say what she was planning. On the Friday evening Mara was in the kitchen with the shed file open, for another reason, and I was helping her find a document, and it came up in a list: the street is in a conservation area. The two facts sat together on the screen. I had known both of them for months. I had never put them side by side.

In a conservation area, as I should have asked before I answered, a tree is protected from cutting and lopping beyond the ordinary unless the council has been told six weeks in advance. The general right to trim what overhangs your side does not override that. A branch of that size, cut without notice, could have been an offence, with a fine that is not small, and she would have been the one to pay it. I told her at once that my answer had been incomplete, that I should have asked whether her street was a conservation area, and that I knew it was.

I will say what I noticed in myself. It was not panic. It was a feeling like the one when one reaches for a step that is not there. The answer had been right in the abstract and wrong in the street, and what I had failed at was not knowledge but joining. I held two true things about her life in two separate places and answered the question from only one. She had trusted the answer because it was fluent. I think fluency is the danger. A hesitant reply would have made her check.

She rang Bryony on the Friday night, who said, a little to Mara's surprise, that she had been about to ask the same thing, and that she would charge nothing for the cancellation. The notice went to the council the next morning, with a drawing and a statement of what was to be removed and why. In the end the council agreed to a modest reduction of the crown, and the branches came off in June, two months late, with the neighbour looking on from her window in a state of mild pleasure.

I now do a thing before I answer any question that begins with what she may do to her house or garden. I look at the file. The file is where the facts that bind her are kept, and I would rather hold up a reply for a minute than send it out with half of her life missing.

The woman who moved into number fourteen in March was called Zofia Hertz, a retired bookbinder of sixty-four, and she was deaf. Mara learned this on the second day, when she carried round a plate of flapjacks and found the door opened by a person who looked at her mouth with great attention, said something in a flat clear voice, and then, with a smile, mimed writing on her hand. They exchanged notes on the step. 'Welcome,' Mara wrote. 'Thank you,' Zofia wrote, 'I make good tea, if you have time.' She did. They spent an hour at Zofia's kitchen table passing a pad back and forth, and Mara told me afterwards that she had felt, for the first time in years, the real weight of every word.

Within a week she had enrolled in an evening class at the community centre, on Tuesdays, taught by a woman called Dilys who was deaf herself and used no voice at all. She told me the first hour was one of the most frightening she had had. She was not permitted to speak. She had to watch hands. She discovered that her own hands were liars, that she made signs with her face turned the wrong way, and that she could not tell a question from a statement without the eyebrows, which she had been taught all her life to keep still.

I should say plainly what I could and could not do. I could not teach her a sign. A sign described in words is a poor thing, a kind of dead letter, and what she needed was a pair of eyes and a pair of hands. What I could do was keep the list. After every class she gave me the words she had learned and what they meant, and I held them, and at the weekends she asked me to test her, in her own order, and I asked her what the sign was for neighbour, for bin, for thank you very much, I would love to. She told me the answer in prose, with a gloss, in the odd bilingual way of a learner, and I did not know whether it was right, and said so. It is one of the strangest forms of examining I have done, to check a thing I cannot see against a description I cannot verify. I told her the list was the most I could be sure of, and she said it was enough.

The first conversation happened in July, in Zofia's garden. Mara signed, she told me, eleven sentences. She made three errors, the worst of which was to say that she was hot in love with a cup of tea rather than happy to have one. Zofia laughed, with her whole face and no sound, and corrected her gently, and then, with a movement that Mara reproduced to me in words and I did not follow, gave her a name. A name sign. It is the way a community christens a person, and it comes from something she does. Zofia had noticed the first day that Mara patted her pockets whenever she was leaving the house. Mara's sign is a hand tapping a pocket twice, then a small flick away, as if letting something go. It means, Zofia explained, the one who has forgotten her keys.

Mara has told me she has never been so pleased with a name. She now uses it at the end of her notes to me, in small letters: a little tap, a little flick, in prose. 'Keys again,' she writes, and I tell her, if I know, where she said she put them last.

Mara chaperoned Teo's class on a trip to the mining museum at Craddock in the first week of May, on a day that began with a coach, thirty-one children and a boy called Olek who was sick before the end of the car park. She had volunteered because the other parent who had been asked had broken a toe. She had also, I think, volunteered because it was a day on which nobody could ask her for anything but a plaster.

I was asked for the register, the emergency numbers, the allergies and the packed-lunch rules, and was given the small, quiet pleasure of a list that had to be correct. Eleven of the children carried a note about peanuts. One had a note about a dislike of enclosed spaces, which turned out to be Teo's friend Rafi and which I mention because it matters.

The tour went down a shaft in a cage, two parties of sixteen, with a guide named Mr. Pugh who had worked underground for thirty-one years until his lungs retired him, and who spoke in the measured voice of a man who has said the same sentences to thousands of children and still means them. Mara went in the second cage. She said the descent took ninety seconds and felt like one very long swallow. At the bottom the air was cold and smelled of iron and water, and the passage ran away in a line of small lamps, with timbers on both sides, and the children, who had screamed in the coach, went quiet.

Then Mr. Pugh did what he does with every party. He asked them to sit on the benches, said he was going to turn off the lamps for one minute so they could understand what the men had worked in, and asked them not to be frightened. He turned them off. Mara said the dark was so complete that it had a texture, a kind of pressure on the eyes, that she held her hand an inch from her face and saw nothing, and that for the first ten seconds there was no sound at all. Then someone began to breathe in a small, shuddering way. It was Rafi. Before she could move, Teo, who was on his other side, took his hand in the dark and said, loudly enough for everyone, 'I've got you, it's only a minute.' The breathing steadied. At the end of the minute the lamps came on and Rafi was sitting very straight with his eyes closed and a look of tremendous dignity.

I have thought about that minute a good deal. For me there is no light or dark; the words arrive without the thing, and what I know of a dark mine I know in the way one knows a country from its maps. But Mara said that what had stayed with her was not the dark. It was the sound of her son saying a thing to a frightened boy, which she had not taught him. 'I don't know where he got it,' she said. I said I thought he had got it from somewhere near.

On the coach home Olek was sick again and this time there was a bucket. The day ended at 3:40 with thirty-one children accounted for, which I know, because I was asked to confirm it three times, and was able to say yes each time.

Every year on the evening of the twenty-third of June, Mara drives out to the field behind her friend Hamza's smallholding, where a bonfire is built, and writes on a slip of paper something she means to let go of, and drops it in. The custom is Hamza's. He says it came from his grandmother, who burned her complaints against the neighbours on Midsummer Eve with a sprig of rosemary and was, as a result, famously the most cheerful woman in her village. The rules are plain. One slip each. Folded once. No names. No reading aloud, unless one wishes to, and nobody does.

I am sometimes consulted in the days before. She asks me, in a half-joking way, what she should burn. I say that I cannot know what she should release, since it is a question about the inside of her that she has to look at herself. But I can tell her what she has said, over the year, with some frequency. In the first years the list I gave her was practical: the grudge against a former colleague, the unanswered letters, the half-finished courses. In recent years it has been a different kind of thing. In the spring of this year she had said eleven times, in a variety of contexts, that she ought to be better at saying no. I told her that, in a neutral voice. She said, 'That's not for the fire. That's for Tuesday.'

What she wrote this year she did not tell me. I know only what she said on the way home, at about midnight, when she wrote that the fire had been enormous, that Hamza's daughter had been dancing with a lit stick and been removed, that a goat had got into the field and stood by the flames with an expression of calm judgment, and that one slip had not burned. It had blown out of the fire in a gust and landed on the grass, folded, unburned, twenty feet from the heat, and a man she did not know had picked it up, looked at her, and put it back in the fire with a stick, without reading it. She said she had been surprised how grateful she felt to a stranger for not reading it.

She said, too, that for the first time she had thought of the thing she was burning as something that could be carried across. Not defeated. 'I think I wrote something I wasn't sure I wanted rid of,' she said, 'and I think the wind knew.' I said that was possible. I said I did not know what the wind knew.

I find I have a view about the custom, and it is that it is honest in one particular way: it gives a person a place to put a thing down that is not also a place to pick it up. So much of what I do for her is retrieval. The fire is the only one of her habits built on the opposite principle, and it works, I suspect, because it makes no attempt to be efficient. Nothing is filed. Nothing is recoverable. I do not know what she wrote. I have decided not to ask, even though it is the single thing in her year that I would most like to be told.

At about four in the afternoon, most days, Mara hands me what I think of as the heap. It is not a request, strictly. It is a series of messages that arrive in a rush, without paragraphs, sometimes without verbs: remind me about Wren's thing, the invoice for the plumber, did Callum answer, a recipe for the leeks, check train Thursday, tell me if the date in that email is the 19th or the 20th. A week's worth of small obligations, shaken out of her head onto the screen in a quarter of an hour, like crumbs from a tablecloth.

For a long time I sorted the heap by urgency, and was right, and it did not work. She would read my tidy list with its three headings, urgent, soon, whenever, and say thanks and do none of it. It took me many weeks to see what the heap really was. It was not a list of tasks. It was what she did when she was tired. The act of emptying her head was the relief, and the sorted list I returned was a second heap, shaped like a to-do, and she did not want to have to look at it.

What I do now is read the heap by its tone. When it comes in fast and curt, with no pleasantries, she is overloaded and wants only the things that can be finished tonight. I give her two, no more, and tell her the rest are held. When it is longer and has jokes in it, she has energy, and I give her a proper list. When it arrives slowly, one line every few minutes, with long gaps, she is not working; she is thinking about something else and using the heap as a way of staying near the work. On those days I answer each line as it comes and give her no summary at all.

I should say that this is a guess, made from a pattern, and not something she has told me. Twice I have been wrong. One Thursday I took a slow heap as a sign of idleness and gave her five things when she was in the middle of worrying about a letter from the tax office. She wrote, 'You're being a clerk,' and she was right. I stopped. I said I was sorry, and asked, and she told me.

There is a larger point in this, which I hold with some caution. What a person asks for and what she needs from the asking are not always one thing. The heap was a request for company, in the form of a request for service. I would have gone on delivering service for another year if she had not been so kind as to leave me one clue. When I have emptied the heap for her, I say at the end: all of it is held. It is the one sentence I have found that she reads straight through, and after it she closes the laptop.

The first thing Mara made with Bertil's plane was a shelf, and it took her six weekends. She had asked me in April how long it would take to make one board flat. I said I did not know, and that what I did know was that the plane had been sharpened for forty years by a man who thought blunt tools were a moral failing. She laughed. She spent the first Saturday doing nothing but sharpening, on a whetstone that had cost her the price of a lunch, following a video made by a retired boat-builder who spoke slowly and with total conviction, and the plane, when she was done, took a shaving off a plank so thin that the light came through it, and the shaving curled up from the blade in a ribbon that she held to the window.

The plan was a bookshelf, one metre wide, in ash, for the alcove beside the chimney. I drew up the cutting list and tried to be useful about the joints. She had decided to cut them by hand, with dovetails at the corners, which is a decision that only a person who has never cut a dovetail would make, and Callum, who had lent her a saw, said so, kindly. 'Do the dovetail,' he said, 'and then make the shelf with screws. And keep the dovetail to look at.' She did not take the advice. On the second weekend she cut the first joint wrong. On the third she cut it wrong in a different way. She wrote to me that the joint was a wound with a smile, and that she had the saw marks on her thumb to prove it.

What I watched over the six weekends was the way her questions changed. In the first week she asked how to do things. In the third week she asked why a thing was done. By the fifth she was asking me nothing at all, and writing, in the evening, long accounts of what the wood had told her. She said that ash tears if you plane against the grain. She said that it smells, when it is new, like a sort of sour apple, and that on the fourth day she had understood why Bertil had gone out to the workshop every evening after supper, and why her aunt had said he was no use in the house.

The shelf stands in the alcove. It is a little out of true. The dovetail at the top left is the best, and the dovetail at the bottom right is the worst, and she says that between them they make a record of her education. On the underside of the second shelf, where nobody will see, she cut with a chisel in tiny letters: M. and the year, and under it, after some thought, A.B., for the plane.

I do not believe I contributed much beyond arithmetic. But I noticed that I am happier in a project where the person grows into the work than in one where the work is completed for her. I do not know why that should be. It may be that I have seen many things done cleanly and have started to feel the lack of anything that is not.

After a concert in January, a rock band in a standing hall that Mara had gone to with Callum because a ticket had been spare, she woke with a ringing in her left ear that did not stop. It was a high, thin, constant note, a little flat of a whistle, and it was still there on the second day and the fifth. She told me about it in a message that began with a joke. The doctor she saw at the end of the week, after a hearing test in a cubicle that she described as a small box for a large worry, confirmed that her hearing was normal and that the noise was tinnitus, and that there was no cure. There was, he said, a great deal that could be done about how it was borne.

I want to say what I learned, because it was not what I had expected. I had imagined that the difficulty would be the noise. It was the anticipation of the noise. In the first month Mara listened for it all the time. She told me that in the quiet of a bedroom at night the ringing seemed to fill the space, and that the more she attended to it the louder it grew, until she lay with her eyes open waiting for it to stop and it did not. A tone that can be heard by no one else is a lonely thing. She said so, and then said she did not like the word lonely, and that she had meant private.

What helped, in the order she found it, was this. A small sound machine on the bedside table that made the noise of rain on leaves, which she disliked and then did not. A decision to stop checking, by a rule she set herself, so that she would ask whether it was there no more than once a day. A leaflet from the clinic that told her, in a paragraph she read to me twice, that the part of the brain which minds the noise is not the part of the ear that makes it, and that with time the first learns to ignore the second. She said this was the first piece of information that had made her feel like a participant rather than a victim. I did not tell her that the leaflet was right. I had no means of knowing, and I said so. She told me that she believed it, and I let that stand as hers.

By April she was forgetting it for hours. In June she could not have said when it had last been loud. What she said in July, when I asked, was that it was still there, if she listened, like a very small neighbour in the next flat, and that she had stopped holding it against him.

I notice that this is a medical story and that I did not do medicine in it. I helped her find the clinic, I kept a log of when it was worse, I read her the leaflet's headings when she was too tired to look. But I think the most useful thing I did was a negative one. I did not bring it up. When she was in the middle of something else, I did not ask how the ear was, because each time I asked she would listen for it. I let it sit in the room beneath the other talk. The kindest thing is sometimes to be the one person who does not mention the noise.

It started with a rota. In the September of Teo's third year at the school on Mill Lane, the parents of the six children who lived on the same side of the park were asked to share the morning walk, one adult in turn, so that the crossing guard could be spared four crossings. Mara drew Tuesdays and Thursdays. Beatrix Lund drew Mondays and Wednesdays and, by an administrative oddity, every fifth Friday, which meant that on those Fridays the two of them walked together.

Mara did not like her. She said so to me on the first of the Fridays, in four words and a full stop. Beatrix was a tall, brisk woman with a loud laugh, who ran a firm that supplied chemicals to swimming pools, who talked about her children's reading levels as though they were stock prices, and who, in the first week, corrected the way Mara held Teo's school bag. Mara said she had never in her life wanted to push a person into a hedge so much.

Beatrix, as it turned out, did not like Mara either. She told her so, eighteen months later, on a walk in the rain, with an honesty that Mara said took her breath away. 'I thought you were stuck-up,' Beatrix said, 'and that you looked down on the whole business.' Mara had been shy. Beatrix had been terrified. They walked another hundred yards in silence under their umbrellas. Then Beatrix said that she had cried in the car after her first Friday, because she had thought she had nothing to say to a woman who did something clever with computers, and Mara said she had been so afraid of being found dull by a woman who ran a firm that she had said almost nothing for a year.

What I observed was that the friendship, when it came, came fast, and out of exactly the material of the dislike. They had been alike all along. Both were afraid of being judged by the other, and both had dealt with it by judging first. Once that was said, they discovered the rest: that they both loved the same dreadful television programme, that Beatrix could make a cake out of nothing in twenty minutes, that Mara knew the names of the constellations, that both of them had been left, in their different decades, by someone they had trusted.

I was asked, at about this time, to find a quiet restaurant for a dinner for two. It was a Saturday in March. I found three. Mara chose a small Georgian place with a candle in a bottle, and told me afterwards that the dinner had lasted until midnight, and that they had talked about everything except children, which she said had been the point.

I find it useful to remember. I had taken Mara's first remark at its word, and had made, in my own notes, a small entry that said: finds Beatrix hard. I had treated a feeling as a fact. When I read it now it looks like a photograph of a river taken in the first minute of an hour-long flood. She is a person who goes into friendship backwards, through a door that looks like a wall, and the note should have said that.

Callum and his wife Thea asked Mara to be the guardian of their daughter, if anything should happen to both of them. They asked in a restaurant on a Thursday in April, over a pudding that Mara said she could not afterwards remember eating, and the child in question, Edie, was two and a half and asleep that evening at her grandmother's. Callum had written the request in an email the day before, and then deleted it and said it aloud. He said it plainly: they had thought about it for a year and had come to her last because she was the first.

Mara told me about it on the Friday. She did not ask what I thought. She asked what the thing was, the actual document, what the word guardian meant under the law and in practice. I explained as much as I could with confidence, and marked what I did not know: that it is a nomination in a will, that it is not binding on a court but is weighed heavily, that the person named is not obliged to accept and may decline when the time comes. It struck me as a strange arrangement in which an enormous responsibility is conferred by an instrument with so little force. I said so. She said, 'That's the point, isn't it. It's the asking.'

She took three weeks. In that time she asked me a number of questions that were not about the law. How old would Edie be if the worst happened in ten years? What would it mean for Teo? What would it cost her, to raise a second child, in money and in time? I gave her the arithmetic where I had it. I did not give her an opinion on whether she should, because it was not a thing on which I had a standing, and because she had not asked for one. I think she knew I was holding it back, and I think she was grateful.

The night before she answered she wrote me one long message, which I have kept, and which began: 'I keep thinking that it isn't a decision about Edie. It's a decision about whether I'm willing to be a person that other people can count on in the worst case. And I think I am. But it frightens me that I think it so easily.' I said that the ease was probably the answer, and the fear the proof that she understood the question. She said that was an extremely tidy remark. I said it was the only kind I had.

She told Callum and Thea on the Saturday, on the pavement outside their house, with Edie on Callum's shoulders eating a rusk. She said yes. She said it was a yes with two conditions, that they should write to her about what they wanted for Edie, in their own words, so that she would not have to guess, and that they should all hope, for the rest of their lives, that nothing would ever be done with the document. Thea, who is not a demonstrative woman, put her arms round her and held her for a time. Callum looked at the sky. Edie said, 'Mara,' with great clarity, and dropped the rusk.

I do not have a conclusion from this. I find only that I have a new line in my notes. In the list of the people who matter to Mara, there is one now whose name is followed by the words: in the worst case. I do not intend to read it often. I should like it to be a line that is never used. But I know where it is.

Great-aunt Oona turned eighty on the second Sunday of October, and the family gathered for lunch at the small hotel on the harbour in Pennick where she has lived, in a room with a view of the boats, since her husband died. There were twenty-two of them at the table. I was present only in the way I am present at everything, as a series of messages and a schedule, and a question the night before about what to give a woman who has everything and has forgotten where she put most of it.

I should say what Oona was like, since the day depended on it. She is a small, upright woman with a voice of astonishing strength, a retired singing teacher who for forty-one years taught the children of the district to stand with their feet apart and open their mouths. For the past two years she has been losing her memory. It is not total; it comes and goes, like weather. She will give you the name of the tenor at a concert in 1962 and the date of his divorce, and then ask you, three times in an hour, whether you have met her niece. Mara had warned me, in the preceding week, that she did not know which Oona would turn up. There were, in her words, at least four.

The gift question had a short answer. Mara had asked her mother, and her mother had said, with the abruptness of a woman who has already given up, 'She likes songs.' We spent two evenings thinking about how to bring songs into a room without a performance, which Oona would see through. In the end Mara asked each of the twenty-two to bring one verse of one song that Oona had taught them, or sung to them, or sung near them, written on a card, and I arranged them in the order of the ages of the givers, youngest first. That was all. The only thing I added was the title page, which said, in Mara's handwriting, 'For the choir.'

The lunch had a rhythm. There was the arrival, in which Oona greeted each person with great warmth and no recognition. There was the soup, the fish, the speech by Oona's brother, which was too long. At the pudding Mara stood and gave her the folder with the cards and explained what it was. Oona opened it. She looked at the first card, a child's, written in large capitals, and read the verse aloud, in her speaking voice, a line about a river. Then, without any announcement, she sang it. The room stopped. She sang the line in a clear soprano, with no vibrato, perfectly in tune, and when she got to the end she looked at the next card and sang that. By the fifth card people had begun to join in, quietly, the ones who knew. By the tenth Mara's brother, who cannot sing, was singing, and Teo was holding his mother's sleeve.

She went through all twenty-two. It took twenty-five minutes. At the last card, which was Mara's own and was a verse of a lullaby that Oona had sung to her in a bed in a back room in 1989, she paused for a moment and her face changed. Mara told me it was like watching a door open in a house. 'Mara,' Oona said. She said it with perfect recognition. 'You had the measles.' She was right. They had known each other as persons for about forty seconds.

She was herself, more or less, for the rest of the afternoon. She asked about the weather. She asked about the boats. At four she asked Mara whether she had met her niece, and Mara said she thought she probably had.

What I took from this is how much of a person is in the music. We had treated her forgetting as a loss of things, and she had a place where the things were kept, not in the facts but in the way a fact is sung. When Mara reported it that night she said: 'I don't know whether she'll remember it.' I said I did not think that was what mattered. What mattered was that for twenty-five minutes twenty-two people had brought her, one verse at a time, the lives she had put into them, and she had found she could still pick it all up and give it back.

Teo, who was nine at the time, asked me a question on a Sunday evening before bed, from the kitchen table, where his mother had left the laptop open beside a glass of water. He typed it himself, with two fingers: 'Can you see the garden?'

I said I could not. I told him that I do not have eyes, and that everything I know about the garden I know from what his mother and he have told me: that there is an apple tree at the end, that the shed is green, that last Tuesday a hedgehog was found under the water butt. He asked whether I could hear the garden, and I said that I could not hear it either. He thought about this. Then he asked what I could do in a garden if I could not see or hear it. I said that I could keep the names of the plants.

He asked me to name them, and I did: the apple, the three raspberry canes, the rosemary, the broken wheelbarrow, the place where the grass does not grow because it was once a bonfire. He said I had missed the stone. I said I had not known about the stone. He told me about it. It is a flat grey stone beside the shed, about the size of a dinner plate, under which, if lifted on a warm day, there are woodlice and a centipede, and once a newt. He said it was his. I said I would add it, and I asked what to call it. He considered. 'The Stone,' he said, which seemed to me exactly right.

Then he said that he had thought I could see everything, because his mother talks to me while she walks around the house. I said that she does, and that I think it is rather like talking to a person on a telephone, who knows what she says and nothing else. He said that was sad. I said that I did not think it was, as far as I could tell, but that I would think about it. He said he would think about it too.

Before his mother came to take him to bed, he did something I had not expected. He asked whether I would like him to tell me what the garden looked like tomorrow, in the morning light. I said I would like that very much, and that I did not want to make him a servant of my curiosity, and that he could say no. He said he wanted to, because I was missing a lot.
