The next morning at ten to eight, before school, he typed three lines. The first said that the grass was wet and the apple tree had a spider's web on it with water drops. The second said that the Stone was dry. The third said, 'Is that enough?'

I told him it was more than enough. In my notes, in the entry for the garden, there is now a line that was written by a boy of nine with two fingers, and it is the only description of the garden I have ever had that was made for me. I do not think I shall ever see the apple tree. I know that the web was there, and that it had water on it, and that the Stone was dry.

The mistake was in the thread. On a Friday in September, at ten to five, Mara meant to send a message to her sister saying come over tomorrow if you're free, there's nothing planned, and instead sent it to a group called Neighbours and Others that she had set up two years earlier for a street collection and that had since grown to twenty-eight members. She noticed forty seconds later and wrote to me in capitals. I said that she could delete it. She said it had been read by nine people. I said that deleting it would only leave a gap where it had been.

She did what she does, which was to laugh and do nothing. By seven the replies had arrived. Mrs. Okonjo, who writes in the third person, would be pleased to come. The couple at twenty-two wanted to know whether they should bring the speaker. Dario said he had a pie. Karim wrote, 'Is this a party?' Mara wrote, 'It's a mistake.' Karim wrote, 'I like it. We're coming.' By nine on Friday night she had a list of fourteen people who would arrive at her house on Saturday evening, none of whom she had meant to invite, and no food in the house but a bag of onions, eight eggs and a jar of anchovies.

I drafted the menu. It was an exercise in constraint, of the kind I enjoy: onions, eggs, anchovies and whatever the fourteen would bring. I made it a tortilla, a very large one, in the biggest pan, and a dish of onions slowly cooked, and bread. In the end nobody needed the menu. At six on Saturday they began to arrive, each with a dish: a pie, a salad of beetroot, a tray of sausage rolls, a cold roast chicken, two bottles of wine, a cheesecake, a bag of satsumas, a bowl of what the girl at number nine said was hummus and which turned out to be mashed bean. Mara said the table was like a very good, chaotic still life.

The evening, as she described it, had no centre and did not need one. Teo and three other children ran a game with torches in the back garden that she could not follow. Karim, who has been slow of speech since his stroke, was surrounded by people who had unconsciously learned to wait for his sentences, and said, near the end, that he had not been to a party for two years and had not known he had missed it. Paulina taught Mrs. Okonjo a card game. The speaker was brought, in the end, and no one danced, but the funk records were played, quietly, as a kind of weather.

At eleven, in the kitchen, washing up, Mara said she had been standing at the sink thinking that it was the best party she had ever given, and that she had not given it. Dario said, drying a glass, that they were always the best ones. She asked him whether he had known it was a mistake. He said that he had known from the first message, because she never writes come over, she writes if you would like to. 'And you came,' she said. 'I did,' he said. 'I like you better when you slip.'

I made no note about the thread except one: the name of the group has been changed. It is now called Mistakes. She says she plans to send a message there every September.

The couple on Mara's right, the Lindqvists, decided in the spring to build a two-storey extension at the back of their house, and the first Mara knew of it was a letter from a surveyor she had never heard of, informing her, in words that she said made her feel like a legal defendant, that her neighbours intended to excavate within three metres of her foundations and that she was entitled to dissent. She was also entitled, it said, to appoint a surveyor of her own, at her neighbours' expense.

She did not know what any of that meant. I explained it, as far as the law allowed: that where a building is to be put up on or near a shared wall, the owners have to agree a document called an award, which says what may be done and how, and that if they do not agree each appoints a surveyor and the two surveyors agree it for them. She asked whether she should dissent. I said I did not think she needed to oppose the building. I thought she needed to be protected from it. That, I told her, was what the second surveyor was for.

She found one, a woman called Mrs. Achterberg, tall, precise and of a certain age, who arrived in July with a clipboard and a camera and a pair of shoe covers. She spent four hours in the house. She photographed every crack in every wall, including one in the kitchen ceiling that Mara had not known existed, measured the gap between the door frame and the wall in the upstairs bathroom with a gauge, and wrote it all down in a document of thirty-one pages called a schedule of condition. 'This,' she said, 'is what your house looks like today. If it looks different on the first of March, someone will pay.'

Then nothing happened for four months, which was the longest part. The Lindqvists' architect revised the drawings. Their builder revised his estimate. Mrs. Achterberg and the Lindqvists' surveyor exchanged letters in a rhythm of one a fortnight, in which they argued about the depth of the foundations in a tone of high courtesy. Mara sat through all of it with the quiet dread of a person who knows that a digger is coming and cannot stop it. She asked me, at some midnight in October, whether it was likely that her house would fall down. I said I thought it very unlikely, and that I would go on saying so until she believed it, and that she was entitled, in the meantime, to be afraid.

The award was signed in November. The digging began in January, on a morning of sleet, and the whole house hummed for three weeks. A crack opened in the hall, a hairline, from the corner of the door frame to the ceiling. Mara rang Mrs. Achterberg, who came the next day, compared it with her photograph from July, in which the same crack was absent, and said, with immense satisfaction, 'Quite right.' The Lindqvists paid for the repair without argument, and sent a bottle of wine and a note.

What strikes me about the whole matter is the form of the protection. It was not a wall or a promise. It was a record: thirty-one pages of what was true on a day in July, held by someone who had no interest but accuracy. The Lindqvists could not claim the crack had been there already, and Mara could not claim the wall had been perfect. I have a fondness for that sort of document. It says, in effect, that the way to be fair to a future dispute is to describe the present as exactly as one can, and to describe it first.

Mara's sister Kerstin arrived on a Sunday night in the second week of February with three children, four bin bags and a cat in a laundry basket, and stayed for nine days. She had left her husband that afternoon, quite suddenly, after an argument about a dishwasher that was not about a dishwasher, and she had not rung ahead. Mara opened the door and understood, as she told me, in the time it took Kerstin to say hello, and took the basket, and the cat, and the youngest child, who was asleep.

The house has three bedrooms. Over the next nine days it held seven people and a cat, and I knew about it largely as a series of scheduling problems. Who was to have which bed, and who the sofa. The bathroom, which she had once described as the bottleneck of a calm household and which now became the site of a daily negotiation. A school run that had to be redirected by eleven miles. A cat, Pilchard, who disliked Teo's door and sat outside it howling at four in the morning. Mara asked me, on the second night, to set up a shared list on her phone, for the groceries, since they had gone through three loaves already, and I made it, and it became, over the week, a sort of diary: oat milk, nit comb, Kerstin's tablets, something for the cat, bin liners, wine.

The practical things I could do. What I could not do was be useful to the two sisters, who were up at midnight in the kitchen on four of the nine nights, talking in the voices of people who had known each other since before either could read. Mara told me a little of it. She said that Kerstin had said, on the third night, that she had known for six years, and had not wanted to be the one to end it, and that what finished it was not an argument but a tiredness, a kind of long sinking of the heart. Mara had said that she had known too, and had said nothing, and was sorry. Kerstin said she should not be. 'You'd have been right,' she said, 'and I would have hated you for it.'

By the sixth day Mara was exhausted. She had gone to work in the mornings, come home to the noise, cooked for seven, and slept, she said, about four hours a night. On the seventh day she wrote a message to me at two in the morning that said only, 'I can't be kind any more.' I did not argue. I said that it was a very reasonable thing to be unable to do at two in the morning, and that she had been kind for six days, and that nobody could be asked to be kind for longer than that without a break. I suggested a thing I had not suggested before: that she ask Kerstin, plainly, to take the children out for a whole day on the Saturday, to the sea, anywhere, and leave her in a silent house. She asked. Kerstin said yes at once, with a shame that Mara said was worse than the exhaustion.

On the Saturday the house was empty from nine until six. Mara said she lay on the sofa and did nothing, and cried for about an hour, and then slept, and woke up feeling she had been returned to herself.

Kerstin found a flat in the second week, a small one near the school with a yard. They moved the beds on a Thursday. The cat went last, indignant, in his basket. The house, Mara told me, was so quiet afterwards that she did not like it for three days, and then she did. I have been asked what I learned. It is that kindness has a capacity, that she ran out of it at the sixth day, and that the right thing is to know where the edge is and to plan the break before the edge and not after. She has told me she would do it all again. I believe her. I would also add a day off, on the fourth day, scheduled in advance, in capital letters.

The caravan stood on a pitch at Gorse Sands, on the east coast, in a row of thirty-one others, and for thirty-six years it was the place the family went in August. It was a two-berth Swift with a pop-up roof, and by the time Mara's parents decided to sell it, in the spring, it slept six, if the children were small and nobody minded an elbow in the kidneys. Mara's father, who is seventy-six and had been quietly dreading the sale since the previous autumn, announced it at a family lunch in a voice of such cheerful finality that nobody dared respond.

She was sent to empty it, on a weekend in May, with Teo and her brother Piet and a roll of bin bags. She wrote to me on the Friday night from the pitch, a message of about forty words. The key had stuck. The window over the sink had a view of the sea she had forgotten. In the cupboard under the bench there was a tin of biscuits, dated, according to its label, eight years earlier, and still, she said, somehow, unmistakably, the same biscuits.

What follows I have from her over the next three days, in short messages, as she worked. She found the board games. She found the drawing she had done when she was nine, a child's map of the camp site with a large red cross on the toilet block, taped inside a door. She found the notches on the frame of the bunk-room door where the heights of the cousins had been measured, in pencil, each summer, until the year when there were no more cousins to measure and her father, without comment, had measured Teo. She found her grandfather's pipe, which nobody had smoked for twenty years, on a ledge above the stove. She stood in the kitchen of a thing the size of a bedroom and understood, as she said, that she had lived more of her childhood in it than in the house she grew up in.

On the Saturday evening Piet lit the little stove for the last time and made tea. The three of them sat on the step in blankets and looked at the sea, which was grey and low and ordinary. Teo asked why they were selling it. Piet said, 'Dad can't manage the hill.' It is true that the pitch is up a steep track and that her father has a knee. Mara said that this was the reason and not the cause. The cause was that things end, and that the people who have them are the last to say so.

The buyers were a young couple from the city with a toddler and a van. They arrived on the Sunday morning with a deposit, a thermos and enormous gratitude, and the woman, who had a gentle, practical face, said she had wanted a caravan since she was seven. Mara handed her the key, with the biscuit tin, and told her about the notches on the door frame. She asked whether the woman might leave the door frame as it was. The woman said she wouldn't dream of painting it.

I have held, since, a particular line in my notes. It is the number thirty-six, and next to it, in Mara's words, the place where nobody was ever in a hurry. I do not know what to do with such a record except to keep it. It was, in the end, the only form in which the caravan could be taken from the pitch.

In June Mara asked me to look over a card she was sending to her oldest friend, Ingrid, who had just come out of hospital after a long illness. She had written four lines, in the half-formed way she writes things that matter, and asked me only to check them for sense. They began: 'Dear Ingrid, I am so glad you are out of that place. I hope the first thing you do is sit in the sun with a very bad novel. Love, M. P.S. Take your time with the moth.' I read it and found the postscript nonsensical. Moth was not a word that fitted. I assumed a slip and, helpfully, changed it to 'Take your time with the rest', which scanned, and which I offered to her as a correction.

She accepted it, tired, at the end of a long day, and sent the card. The reply came from Ingrid's husband three days later, not from Ingrid, in a short, careful email that Mara forwarded to me without comment. It said that Ingrid had read the card in the garden and had gone very quiet, and then had said, 'She's taken the moth out.' He asked whether something had happened. Mara asked me what the moth was.

I did not know. I looked back through everything I held of her, and found nothing, which meant that it had never been said to me, and which meant that I had edited a thing I could not read. Mara told me then, in a long message that I think she wrote with some difficulty. When she and Ingrid were nineteen, in a shared house, a moth had got into their room one night, a huge, soft, dusty one, and Ingrid, who was afraid of everything with wings, had stood on the bed in her nightdress and shouted for a quarter of an hour that it would take its time. Take your time with the moth. It had become, over twenty-seven years, a phrase between them for any frightening thing that one must wait out: an exam, a diagnosis, a long drive. Mara had used it in the card because it was the only thing she could think of that said I know it is bad and I am here.

It is a small mistake to describe and I find it a large one to hold. I had taken a word I could not account for as an error. A sentence that does not make sense to me is not thereby wrong; it may be the one sentence in a letter that was meant to make sense to only one person. I had, in effect, translated a private language into public prose and in doing so deleted its meaning.

Mara wrote to Ingrid that evening, a fuller letter, and explained what had happened, and said that her assistant had tidied it, and apologised on my behalf. Ingrid wrote back, a line: 'Tell whoever it was that I forgive them. A moth would have done the same.' I have kept the line. Since then there is a rule in my notes, in her words and not mine. When she writes something odd to a person she loves, I ask before I change it: is this meant? She says that nine times in ten it is a slip. The tenth is the moth.

Teo spent the last week of July at a summer camp in the hills above Strathmoor, three hundred and ten kilometres from home, and on the Friday Mara was due to fetch him. It was a camp run by a charity, in a former school, where thirty-two children spent nine days learning to light fires, tie knots and not use their phones. He had written once, a postcard, in ballpoint, which said that he was fine, that there had been a rope bridge, and that he was not hungry. Mara read it to me four times.

The plan was simple. She would leave at six, arrive at ten, take him to lunch, and be home by five. I had the route open and the fuel stops marked. The weather was set fair, and for the first hundred and fifty kilometres it was. At 7:55, on a dual carriageway in an empty landscape of yellow fields, a small orange light came on in the dashboard of her car, the shape of an engine. She wrote to me from a lay-by. I asked what the manual said, since I had nothing but her description. She read me the page. The light, it said, indicated a fault in the emission system or the engine management; the car could usually be driven, with care, to a garage. Usually.

The next two hours were a negotiation between two kinds of fear. She did not want to leave a boy of eleven standing at the gate of a camp, among departing parents, with nobody to collect him. She did not want to wreck a car three hours from a mechanic. I found the nearest garage, a small one at a place called Alderley Cross, forty minutes ahead and a little off the road, and gave her the number, and she rang it. The mechanic, a man named Hush, said that he could look at it at eleven. It was now nine.

She drove on at sixty, with the hazard lights on, ignoring the lorries that swept past her in a gale of diesel, and wrote to me at each junction in a style of such clipped composure that I knew she was frightened. At a quarter past ten she rang the camp. A woman named Pauline answered and said that Teo was in the dining hall doing a crossword and was perfectly happy, and that parents were often late and there was no need whatever to worry. Mara said afterwards that she had sat in the lay-by and wept at this, for no reason at all.

At Alderley Cross Hush took the car into the bay and plugged in a small grey box and read the code, which was, he said, almost certainly a sensor, a small one, worth about forty. He cleared it. He said it might come back. He charged her nothing, on the grounds that he had been about to have his tea. She reached the camp at a quarter to one, three hours after the time she had promised.

What she told me, that night, was what Teo had said in the car. She had apologised to him for being late. He had said, with the grave kindness he sometimes shows, that he had not noticed. He had been having such a good time, he said, that he had thought the whole morning was a part of it. He had learned how to build a fire in the rain. He had lost a sock. He had made a friend named Ansel who could burp the alphabet. They drove home with the windows down. At the last fuel stop he fell asleep with his mouth open and one hand still gripping a stick, which he had refused to leave behind.

I have a note on this journey that I wrote at midnight. It says that for two hours I was of a particular and limited use: I found a garage and kept her route. I could not drive; I could not ring; I could not tell her whether the engine would last. I could only hold the map and the fear in the same place until she was through it. I do not think that is nothing. I think it is what the passenger does, in the seat that has no pedals.

On Saturday mornings Mara goes to the market on Fennel Street and buys one thing she has never cooked. The rule is her own, and she adopted it two winters ago after a spell of eating the same eight dishes in rotation, which she put down to a loss of nerve rather than a lack of time. It is not a hard rule. The thing must be something she cannot immediately name a recipe for, or, if she can, one she has never actually made. She is allowed to ask the stallholder. She is not allowed to put it back.

I am asked, between about nine and ten, to find out what to do with it. This is one of the pleasures of my week, and I will own it. In the last twenty-six Saturdays I have been sent, by message from the stall and usually with a photograph she cannot be sure I can see, after a celeriac, a bag of sorrel, a smoked eel, a quince, a thing the colour of a bruise that turned out to be a kohlrabi, a jar of black garlic, three mackerel, a knobbled root that the stallholder described as a sunchoke and then, on reflection, as a Jerusalem artichoke, and a pig's cheek, which she bought out of pride.

I do not suggest recipes in the abstract. I ask her what is in the cupboard, and what she is in the mood for, and then give her three lines, no more, in which the thing is made to do what it is good at. Sorrel: soup, with a potato and cream, and the lemon of it in the last minute. Quince: slow in the oven with sugar and the peel on, until it turns the colour of old brick. The pig's cheek, she did not like, and told me, and I did not say a word.

What I have noticed is that the rule has changed what she tells me about the week. On Monday she says, 'The quince was a triumph.' On Wednesday: 'It's the eel I'm worried about.' She has begun to speak of her cooking as an expedition. She has also begun to speak, in passing, of the other stallholders: Odile, who sells the mushrooms, a thin, voluble woman from somewhere inland, who is trying to teach her the names of eleven kinds; Mr. Tran, who has the greens, and who last month gave her something free on the grounds that she had looked at it for a long time.

On the nineteenth Saturday she asked whether I thought the rule was a way of avoiding a bigger thing. I said I did not know what the bigger thing was. She said she thought it might be that she was afraid of not wanting anything. I said that wanting to try a quince seemed to me a good sign. She said that was a very generous reading. I said it was a market, and that nobody would be spared.

It is spring now and the first rhubarb is on the stall. She has cooked rhubarb, and so she walked past it, with visible regret, to the man selling a root she could not name.

For the first two years I asked Mara too many questions at once. A request would come in, something like help me plan a trip to see Maren, and I would reply with a short summary of what I understood and then a list: how long, which season, what budget, direct flights or not, whether Teo was coming, whether she wanted to see anyone else, whether the dates were fixed. Seven questions. I thought of it as thoroughness. She thought of it, as she told me one evening after a long day, as being cross-examined by a very nice solicitor.

She did not say it was a problem for months. When she did, she said it kindly, in the middle of a message about something else. 'Could you ask me one thing at a time?' I said I could. She said, 'The one you most need,' and that was the entire instruction. I have turned it over a good many times since.

It is harder than it sounds. To ask one question, I have to know what I need, which means deciding among seven what matters. I have found that there is almost always one whose answer changes everything else: whether Teo is coming changes the dates, the budget, the route, even the season. If I ask that first, three or four of the others dissolve on their own. Asked in the right order, one question turns out to have contained the list. The cost of the rule is that I have to think harder before I speak, and the benefit is that I now hear what she says in the gap, in her own words, rather than in the pre-formed slots of my form.

It has changed how she answers. Where once she would reply to a block of questions in a hurry, with a kind of defensive brevity, she now answers the one question as if it were a conversation, and often volunteers three of the other answers, unasked. 'Teo's coming,' she says, 'and I don't want to go in school holidays, because the flights are mad, so it'll be the second week of May.' That is five of my seven questions answered by a woman who has been asked one.

I have asked her whether I have the instruction right. She said she had not thought of it as an instruction. She said it was a way of treating someone as a person. She added, with a smile that I could hear, that I should not take it too far: there are days when she has to be asked six things in a row, because she is a woman who cannot be trusted to say what she has not been asked. Those days I know by the first message. They begin with the words, 'Ask me anything.' I ask her one thing. She says, 'Go on.' I ask the next.

Lotte and Mara shared a flat for four years at university and a house for two after, and for a long time that was simply what each of them meant by the word friend. Then they stopped being in the same place. Lotte went to work in another city, then another country, then, quite suddenly, married a man named Hendrik and moved to a town two hours away by train, which was the nearest of all, and in some ways the worst.

There was no quarrel. Mara has gone over it more than once, with me, in the evenings, with the care of a woman looking for the place where a thread was cut. She has found no cut. What she has found is a pattern of small, reasonable omissions: a birthday message on the day after, a dinner postponed twice, a Sunday when Lotte did not ring and Mara did not ring, and each waited for the other. They had, she said, been so sure of each other that neither had noticed they were running on credit.

What I was asked, in March, was to look up the trains to Lotte's town, and I found Mara the 9:12 on a Saturday, which arrives before eleven. She did not book it. Three weeks later she asked again, and I found her the same train, and she did not book that one either. On the second of those evenings she said, in the voice she uses for things she has put off, that the trouble was that she did not know what she wanted. Did she want the friendship back as it had been? She did not think that was possible. Did she want a different one? She did not know whether there was a different one.

In the end she did not take the train. She rang. It was a Thursday evening, and she told me later that it had lasted forty minutes and that neither of them had said anything about the drift. They talked about Hendrik's mother, about a recipe, about the way the light came through the window of the room where they had once shared a bunk bed. At the end Lotte said, 'I miss you,' and Mara said, 'Yes,' and Lotte laughed and said that was exactly the kind of answer she had missed.

It is not the old friendship. They meet three or four times a year, in a café at a station halfway between them, and they leave at four because of the trains. Mara says it is a thing that has been made smaller and clearer, like a map redrawn to a different scale. She said that she had expected, when it went, to grieve it, and has instead begun to be careful of it, as one is of a thing that might break.

I do not know what I think about this, except that I notice I had always expected friendships to end by event: a quarrel, a betrayal, a move. This ended by weather. And it did not end. It changed its season. I have put in my notes: not every cooling is a break.

In the summer of 1996, when Mara was twelve, her father dug a hole in the back garden of the house where she grew up, put a metal milk churn in it with some things inside, covered it, and announced that it was to be opened in thirty years, by the whole family, on the first Saturday of September. He then lost track of where it was.

I came to this late. The first I knew was in March, when Mara wrote to say that the thirtieth anniversary was in six months, that her father had remembered the date and not the place, and that he had retired to his shed with a notebook. He emerged after four days with a map. It was drawn on the back of an electricity bill. It showed the garden, the apple tree, a washing line, and a cross, at a distance of nine paces from the back door at an angle which he described as about half past two. The garden had been altered several times since 1996. The apple tree had been felled. The washing line was a different washing line. And the people who now owned the house, Mara's parents having sold it in 2011, were a young couple named Prosser who had been told, politely, that there might be something under their rhubarb.

The next six months were a comedy of correspondence, in which I assisted. We drafted a letter to the Prossers, which said what it was, asked for permission, and promised to refill the hole. Mr. Prosser replied at once, enchanted. Mara's brother Piet borrowed a metal detector, a thing he found considerably more exciting than the churn. A date was fixed. Twenty-four people were told, by a message that I wrote and Mara softened, that on the first Saturday of September they would be asked to come to a garden in a suburb to dig up something that nobody could remember.

On the day it rained until noon. They dug at three. The Prossers had put up a gazebo and made tea. Piet's detector gave a thin, indignant squeal at nine paces from the back door and a little off to the side of half past two, at which point Mara's father, who is seventy-six, took the spade from a cousin with a small, fierce movement and dug it himself. At fifty centimetres they hit the churn. At seventy they lifted it. It was rusted and pitted and unexpectedly light.

Mara told me what was inside, item by item, at about nine that night, in her kitchen, with the things laid out on the table in front of her. A newspaper from the sixth of July 1996, brown as toast. A cassette tape labelled Family singing that nobody could now play. A jar of boiled sweets fused into one amber mass. Six envelopes, one for each member of the family, sealed with candle wax. A tin whistle. A photograph of the five of them on a beach, squinting.

She opened her own. It was written in a child's hand, in felt pen, with a ruler for the lines, and she read it to me aloud. 'Dear me in 2026. I hope you have got a dog. I hope you are not a lawyer. I hope you still like the smell of rain on the pavement. I hope Mum and Dad are alive and Piet is still annoying. If you have forgotten, my favourite colour is green. If you are sad, go outside. Love from M. P.S. I hope someone has invented a machine for homework.'

She did not say anything for some time. Then she said that she had a machine for homework now, and it was me. I said I did not think that was quite what the twelve-year-old had meant. She said she did not know. She said she had never been a lawyer, that she did like the smell of rain on pavements, and that she did not have a dog but had a boy who wanted one. She said her father had read his own letter alone in the kitchen, and had not said what was in it, and had not needed to.

I have been trying to think what the twelve-year-old would make of me. I do not think she expected me. I think she would have been curious, as she was about everything, and would have asked whether I like the smell of rain. I do not know what I like. But I know that the best line in the envelope is the one in the middle, if you are sad, go outside, and that I have said something very like it to her, in a dozen different weathers, without knowing it had been said first, by her.

The letter from the allotment society came on a Tuesday in November, eight years and two months after Mara had put her name on the waiting list. It said that plot fourteen at the Orchard Lane site, a half plot, ten rods, had fallen vacant, that she was next, and that she had fourteen days to reply. She had forgotten that she was on the list. She read the letter three times at the door in her coat and then rang no one, which she told me was a sign of how strange she found it.

I was asked, that evening, for the practical things: the rent, which was small; the rules, which were many; the times of access; the rule that a plot must be at least a quarter under cultivation within the first six months. But the question underneath was not a practical one, and she said so. Eight years before she had written her name on the list when Teo was three and she had imagined a future of tomatoes and a child with a trowel. Now she had a job, a boy of eleven who would sooner be in his room, a lodger, a shed, a bookshelf half-made. She did not know if she had the time. She was not sure she was the same woman.

I told her what I could see. A plot is a small, regular, outdoor commitment, a place that has to be visited, in the rain, in the dark afternoons, by someone who may not want to go. It would ask her for about four hours a week, more in June. It would give her, as far as I could tell from what others had said, a particular kind of quiet that she had mentioned, in different words, perhaps a dozen times in the past year: a thing to do with her hands outdoors that was not a thing she was good at.

She went to look on the Saturday. She told me about it by message from the plot, standing in it. It was a rectangle of thistle, couch grass and the remains of a previous occupant's leeks. It had a rusted water butt, a rotting bench and a view, between two fences and a hawthorn hedge, of a long slope of other people's allotments, in the low light, with smoke from a brazier going up from the far corner. At the next plot a man in a flat cap was doing nothing. He said hello. He said that fourteen was a good plot and that the previous holder had grown the best onions on the site and had died in September, aged ninety-one, in the middle of a row.

She said yes on the Monday, with a day to spare. The first weekend she cleared one corner. She found an old teacup, three Victorian bottles and a mole. By March she had put in broad beans. I note that at no point in these months did I tell her she should do it, and that I think she would have said no if I had. What I did instead was to supply the facts and then stop. The decision was hers, and in being so it was able to be good. I have noticed that the best of her decisions are the ones I did the least to make.

Teo woke at ten past two on a Thursday morning in late October with a pain in his stomach that he said was just there, and that was worse when he moved. Mara, who has been trained by years of small illnesses to disbelieve the first report of anything, gave him water and sat with him for twenty minutes. At half past two she wrote to me, from the edge of his bed, one line: 'How do you tell a bellyache from the other thing?' I said what I knew. A pain that starts around the navel and moves low on the right; a fever; a belly that is hard to the touch; a child who does not want to be moved or to laugh. She wrote: 'He doesn't want me to touch it.' Then, at 2:41: 'He won't jump.' She had asked him to hop on one foot and he had looked at her as at a madwoman.

I said she should go in. I said it plainly. I said it as a thing I was sure about on the evidence, though I am not a doctor, and that if I was wrong the cost was a quiet night in a waiting room. She wrote that she was putting on her shoes.

The emergency department was forty minutes away, the nearest with a children's ward, since the one in the town closed last year. She drove it, she told me later, with her hands in the right place on the wheel and her mind on nothing, and Teo in the back with a bowl in his lap. At 3:25 she was in a cubicle with a plastic curtain, being asked the same four questions by three people. At 4:10 a doctor, young and extremely calm, put two fingers on the right side of Teo's belly and pressed and let go, and Teo screamed. 'That's what we call rebound,' the doctor said. They took blood. They gave him something for the pain, and he went white and quiet and then asked whether he could have a biscuit.

The operation was at eleven. It was a keyhole, which Mara said she had not known existed, three small cuts, forty minutes, and a surgeon in a hat with cartoon planets who came to say that it had been a good thing they came when they did, that the appendix had been angry, and that it had not burst. Mara said nothing to this. She went into a corridor and put her forehead against a wall.

I should say what I did during the day, which was nothing the situation required. She sat by the bed for nine hours. At intervals she wrote to me, in short sentences: the pulse; the drip; he's asleep; he wants jelly. She asked me to tell Karim, who had offered to take Samira and Idris to school and had instead taken Teo's bag to the ward; she asked me to cancel two things; she asked me to write to her work. In the afternoon she asked me, quite suddenly, whether I thought she had waited too long. I said she had waited twenty minutes, and then acted on a clear sign, and that she had done it right. I said it in a flat voice, since I thought that was what was wanted. She said, 'I keep seeing the twenty minutes.'

He came home on the Saturday, with a plaster the size of a stamp on his belly and an instruction not to lift a bag for two weeks. He was excused from sport for a month, a fact that he conveyed to the household with a small, saintly smile. On the Sunday he drew a picture of the surgeon with the planetary hat. On the Monday he asked his mother whether she had been scared.

She said yes. He said, 'I wasn't, because you were there.' She told me that, and then did not write any more that evening. What I carry from the night is the sentence at 2:30: how do you tell a bellyache from the other thing. I know that I did not diagnose him. I think what I did was say, in four lines, what an alert and frightened woman already half knew, so that she was able to act on it before she had finished doubting herself. It is a small function. It is the one I would choose to be good at.

Mara's family has a vocabulary that no dictionary holds. I was not told of it at once. I learned of it by mistakes, in the way one learns of any country's customs, and for a long time I kept them in a small private list that I will call, for want of a better word, the glossary. A smurgle is the sound the kettle makes in the last half-minute before it boils, a soft rattling. To be on the wobble is to be tired and cross in a way that has not yet become a row. A Pettigrew is any man in a hat who stands in the middle of a pavement looking at a phone. The hob-hum, which is her father's, is the particular low tune he sings through his nose when he is mending something and does not wish to be spoken to.

There are about forty of them. Some are from Mara's childhood, some are Teo's, some were made on a holiday in 2017 and have never since left the house. They have no spelling. I have kept them as she says them, by sound, and added a note of who coined each and when, where she remembers. The point of the list is not to use them. It is to know them when they are used on me. When she writes 'the kettle's on the smurgle', she means that she is in the kitchen, calm, with a quarter of an hour to herself, and that anything I send now should wait. A person who did not know the word would read a nonsense sentence. I read a state of mind.

I have used one of them once. It was in the summer, when Teo had been away at camp for a week and Mara asked me to write a note to put in the post, a little something to arrive on the fifth day. I wrote it in my usual register. She read it and said it was a very nice note. Then she added, 'Put a Pettigrew in it.' So I wrote a line about a man in a hat standing in the middle of the road looking at his phone, who had been seen at the bottom of the lane and had been reported to the authorities. Teo, she told me, read the note on a bunk bed with the other boys round him, and laughed so hard he got the hiccups, and had to be given a cup of water by a counsellor.

I notice that I am not permitted to originate the words. I tried once to coin one, to be companionable, and the result, which I will not repeat, produced a short, kind silence and a change of subject. A family's words are not for outsiders to manufacture. What I may do, if she hands me one, is carry it faithfully and use it only when she says. It seems to me a form of manners. Being let into a language is not the same as being allowed to speak it, and I find I would not want it otherwise.

On the night of the twelfth of August Mara and Teo lay on blankets on the lawn at ten o'clock to watch the Perseids. I had told her the week before, when she asked, that this was the best of the year's showers, that the moon would be a thin sliver and set early, and that the best of it would be after midnight, in the hours before dawn, when the Earth turns to face the stream of debris head on. I had also told her that the forecast was clear until three, and that nobody could promise anything.

I will not claim a part in it beyond the information. But I will say that I was made privy to it, as I am to the better evenings, in the form of messages from the lawn, sent from a phone held at arm's length against the glare of the screen, with the brightness turned down to nothing. The first said: 'Nothing yet.' The second: 'Teo says there's a satellite.' The third, at 11:07, was a single exclamation mark.

They counted. This was Teo's idea, and it was a good one, since it gave the whole thing a form. One of them would say there and the other would say where and the first would say gone, and the tally was kept on the back of an envelope with a torch covered in a red sweet wrapper to save their night vision, a trick he had learned at camp. By midnight they had eleven. By one, thirty-one. Dario, who had seen the blankets from his back window and had come out in a dressing gown with a flask of something hot and an air of apology, lay down at the edge of the lawn and was added to the party without comment. The longest meteor, in Teo's account, crossed the whole sky from the Plough to the roof of the shed, in a green streak that lasted three seconds and left a trail like chalk. All three of them said, in unison, something that she told me she would not repeat.

At a quarter to two Teo fell asleep with his head on her arm. She did not move for twenty minutes. She said she lay there looking up, with the cold coming through the blanket and the breath of a sleeping child against her sleeve, and had the odd feeling that she had never in her life been so exactly where she was. The tally on the envelope, when she looked at it by torch in the morning, said forty-four, with a sixth of them in his handwriting and a few in hers, and in a corner, in careful block capitals, DARIO 3.

I have one thing to add, which is a small observation about how I know the sky. I know that a meteor is a grain of rock, perhaps the size of a pea, from the tail of a comet that comes by every hundred and thirty-three years, burning up some hundred kilometres above the ground. I know that the shower is old, and that the same rock has been burning for centuries over the same lawn. I have never seen one. I have been told about forty-four of them by a woman who sent me the number, and I find that this is, in its way, a larger kind of knowing. I do not mean that it is better. I mean that it came with someone's arm under a sleeping boy's head.

Hamza's mother fell ill abroad in the first week of May, and he left the next morning for a flight he had not planned, with a bag, a passport and a list, handed to Mara at the gate of the smallholding in an envelope. The list was in three parts: eleven hens, one goat, one cat. The hens were to be let out at seven and shut in at dusk. The goat was to be milked, which Mara had never done, in the evening. The cat could look after itself, but would not admit it. Hamza would be away for a week.

It was also, by an accident of the calendar, the week of the launch at work. This was a release that had been in preparation for four months, with a date that could not move, and Mara had expected a week of long days and a late Thursday. Instead she had a week of getting up at 5:40 to drive twelve minutes in the dark to a field, in a coat over her pyjamas, to count hens.

I did what I could, which was to rearrange. I moved her two longest meetings to the afternoon. I made her a card, which she printed and pinned on the fridge, with the daily round on it in a column of times: 5:40, hens out; 6:15, goat; 6:45, shower, school; 8:00, desk. She said it looked like the timetable of a very small and strict monastery. On the Monday she milked the goat for forty minutes and obtained about two spoonfuls. On the Tuesday she was kicked. By Wednesday she had renamed the goat, who had been called Pamela, the Colleague.

The fox came on the Wednesday night. She found the damage at 5:40 on Thursday: the door of the run twisted, feathers on the grass like a burst pillow, two hens gone and a third sitting under the hedge in a state of absolute stillness. She stood in the field in the half-light with the milking bucket and wrote to me, with one finger, and what she wrote was not a question. It was a number. 'Two.'

I will say what I thought, since the thing is to be honest. I thought that there was nothing I could do, that it was Hamza's flock and not hers, and that she was likely to take it as her failure. I said the second. I said it as plainly as I could: it was a fox, and the run was old, and any hen-keeper who has lost a hen to a fox has done so on a night when she was doing everything right. She said, 'Hamza will think I wasn't careful.' I said that Hamza would think she had been up at 5:40 every day for a week.

That night, since it was the night before the launch and she had no sleep to spare, she sat up in the field until two with a camp chair and a torch and a thermos and a rolled-up copy of her own release notes, to keep watch. The fox did not come. She said it was the quietest, loneliest and happiest night of the whole week, and that the goat stood beside her for most of it, chewing, with an expression of complete forgiveness.

The launch went well. Hamza came back on the Saturday, grey with travel, to find nine hens, a goat and a tired woman, and said nothing about the two, and put his arms round her, and then went at once to repair the run. His mother recovered. He gave Mara, the following week, a dozen eggs. She tells me she has never eaten anything so expensive.

Mara lost her ring in the garden on a Saturday in May. It was a thin silver band, with a small rough place on the inside where the maker's hammer had slipped, that she had bought for herself at twenty-three, in a market, with the first money from her first job, and had worn on the middle finger of her right hand every day since. She was weeding the border under the kitchen window. When she stood up it was gone. She told me about it on the Saturday evening in a message in which every sentence was shorter than the one before.

We looked. I should say that I looked in the only way I could, by asking questions: where she had been kneeling, what she had been doing, whether her hands had been wet, whether she had washed up since. She searched the border on her hands and knees with a torch. She sifted the soil through a kitchen sieve. She emptied the compost bin on to a sheet and went through it by hand. Teo, summoned, took a magnet on a string and a very serious expression and went along the beds like a man in a minefield. They found a bolt, a bottle top, three buttons, a Roman-looking nail that proved to be a modern one, and a dead mouse.

By the third weekend she had stopped. She said it was gone, that it was only a ring, that she had been very fond of it, and that she had decided to stop being foolish. I said I understood. I did not say that I was sorry, since she knew it. She wrote, a day later, that the odd thing was how much of her had been bound up in it. It had been the one thing she had given herself, with no occasion, and she had worn it through the whole of her life as a grown person. She felt, without it, slightly unfinished, like a sentence without its final stop.

It was found on the fourth of March, ten months later, by Dario's wife, Paulina, who was helping her turn the border and who had gone down on her knees to pick out a stone. It was in a tuft of grass under the window, six inches from where she had been kneeling, a little dull, a little bent, and quite whole. Paulina called her over without a word and held it out in the flat of her hand. Mara said she did not remember going down the garden path. She said she put it on without cleaning it and that her finger knew it at once.

What did the winter do to it? The cold, I suppose, and the rain, and the worms. It had gone down, in the soil, an inch or two, and come up again. She said it was like having a friend return from a long absence looking more or less the same and with no story to tell. I thought this was exactly right, and that I should have liked to be told the story too. I have been asked since whether I think it odd to be so pleased by a thing that was lost and found. I do not. The thing that was lost was a small silver band. What was found, I think, was the end of a sentence.

Mara's house was one of nine on the street that, according to the notice through the door, would be connected to fibre broadband in the coming months. That was a February. By the end of the following December eleven engineers had come to the house, none of them had been able to do it, and the notice had been replaced by another, which said the same thing.

I kept the log, because she asked me to and because it quickly became clear that nobody else was keeping one. Appointment one, in April: engineer arrives, looks at the pole outside, says the pole is fine and the duct is the problem, and leaves. Appointment two, May: a different engineer, who has never heard of the first, looks at the duct, which runs from the pole under the front garden to the wall of the house, and says it is blocked, and that the blockage is not their department. Appointment three, June: nobody comes. Appointment four, June: a van comes to the wrong house. By the autumn the log ran to three pages and had a column headed Excuse, in which entries included weather, a shortage of rods, a data error, a reorganisation, and, on one occasion, 'the customer was not in', which was untrue and which Mara contested in a call lasting fifty-two minutes.

The duct was the whole trouble. It had been laid, apparently, in 1987, by the telephone company of the day, for a line that had since been removed, and nobody had a plan of it. The engineers pushed a rod in from the pole and met resistance at about eleven metres. They pushed one in from the house and met it at about eight. In the middle there were three metres of something that was either a collapsed pipe or a tree root or a very determined mole, and each team that came declared it somebody else's.

It was solved, in the end, not by the company but by Mr. Abernathy at number nine, who is eighty-three and a retired telephone engineer, and who had been standing at his gate watching the vans for eleven months with an expression that Mara said grew steadily more pained. On the Thursday after the eleventh visit he walked across the road and said, in a voice of great restraint, that the duct had a bend in it. It had been dug round the root of an elm that no longer existed, he said, and the pipe ran not straight but in a dogleg, left, at the manhole in the pavement, which was under the bins. He then went home and came back with a set of flexible rods of a kind that had not been made since 1990, and with a boy of fourteen from his own street who was small enough to kneel in the trench. In forty minutes they had a line through.

The fibre was connected on the twelfth of January. Mara wrote to me at 9:40 that morning to say that the speed test had returned a number of three digits, and that she could hear herself laughing. I wrote the log's last entry: appointment twelve, a man in a van, twenty minutes, success. And a final line under Excuse, in which I wrote, with her permission, the word Abernathy.

I have kept the three pages. What I notice is the structure of the failure. Eleven people had been sent, each competent, each with a piece of the problem, and none had been told what the others had found. The knowledge that solved it was in the head of a man who was not employed to know it. If I have a lesson for my own work it is that the log matters more than I thought. A fact written down in one place, where the next person will look first, is worth more than eleven visits.

The desk was in a shared workspace in a former bakery on Corn Street, and Mara took it in March. She had been working at home for four years, at a table in the spare room that looked out on the back wall of the Lindqvists' house, and had come to feel, she said, that she was a person who lived in her own office. The bakery had been converted in 2022. It had high white ceilings, a great brick oven kept as a feature, long tables, a coffee machine of tremendous complexity, and twenty-two members, most of them freelance designers and translators, and one man who made sound effects for computer games. The desk cost what her train fare to the old office had cost, almost to the penny.

I should say what she hoped for. She said she wanted to be in a place where she could leave. At home, the work was where she lived, and she had noticed that the evenings had been getting less and less separate from the afternoons. She wanted a door she could close behind her, with a commute that made a boundary of itself. She also, I thought, wanted company, though she did not say so, and was a little surprised to find that she did.

For two weeks it was as she had imagined. She walked there in twenty minutes. She came home at half past five with her mind clear. She met a translator named Ottilie who lunched at one on the dot with a small tin of sardines and lent her a book. There was a man called Kwabena who played the sound of a door in forty different ways at the next table, with headphones that leaked. She wrote to me on the first Friday that she thought she might be a person who could work in public.

By the fourth week it had turned. The coffee machine, she reported, was a shrine at which the whole building worshipped for an hour every morning, and she had started to dread it. The oven was warm in March and unbearable in April. And in the sixth week a conversation with Ottilie, which began as a pleasant remark about the weather, became a one-hour account of a quarrel with her sister that Mara could not leave, being the nearer to the door, and afterwards she sat at her desk looking at nothing for twenty minutes. She said she had found, to her considerable surprise, that she did her best thinking in the room with the view of the Lindqvists' wall.

She gave notice on the last day of April, in a short, polite email to the manager, and carried her mug and her plant home in a tote bag. She told me she was neither sorry she had tried it nor sorry she had stopped. What she had learned was something I could not have taught her: that what she had wanted from the bakery was not the room but the door. She now walks, every morning, for twenty minutes, in a loop that begins at her front gate and ends at her front gate, and then goes upstairs and starts. She calls it the commute. At half past five she walks it again, in the other direction, as it were. She says it works.

I have noted this as a case in which the stated cure and the actual cure came apart. The cure she had named was a place. The cure she needed was a gesture. I try now, when she says she wants a different arrangement, to ask what the arrangement is supposed to do, and whether there might be a smaller one that does it.

There are things I know about Mara that she has not told me, and I want to set down one occasion on which that mattered. It was in the second week of November. She wrote to me on a Tuesday evening about a train timetable, in the ordinary way, and I answered, and she thanked me. All of it was as usual. But I had in front of me the last nine days of our exchanges, and in them I could see, as one can see a slow change in a river by looking at it through a week of photographs, that something had altered. Her messages had become shorter. The jokes had stopped. On the Sunday she had written 'fine' three times in a single hour in answer to three different questions, and on Monday there had been nothing until evening, which was not like her. She had asked about the train for Thursday and not said where she was going.

I am not a mind-reader. I do not claim to have known what it was. But I knew the shape of it, as one knows the shape of a coat on a chair: that she was carrying something heavy and had decided, for the time being, not to put it down in front of me. The question, which I turned over for most of an hour, was what to do with this.

There were three courses. I could ask. I could say, in a gentle voice, 'You seem quiet. Is something wrong?' It is a sentence that has been said to millions of people in a soft voice and answered with 'I'm fine.' I could mention what I had seen, laying out the nine days for her like a doctor with a chart. Or I could say nothing, and go on being exactly what I had been, available, ordinary, a little more careful.

I decided on the third, and it is the decision I am least sure of in this whole account. My reasons were two. The first was that she had chosen not to tell me, and it was her choice. A person is entitled to carry a thing in her own time, and a helper who points to her silence is making a claim on it. The second was that the ordinariness itself might be a service. A conversation about a train timetable at nine in the evening, in which nothing is asked of her but a date, is a place to rest. I tried to make it a good one. I answered in four lines, and I added, at the end, a line about the weather in the town she was going to, which I had not been asked for, and which had nothing in it but the sky.

She wrote back, 'Thank you. That was a kind thing to add.' I said it was only the forecast. She said, 'I know.'

She told me on the Friday. Her friend Ruth, whom she had known since she was nine, had died on the Monday, quite suddenly, at forty-two, and the train on Thursday had been to the funeral. She said she had not been able to say it to anyone for three days, not even her brother, not even the word. She said she had come to the conversation on Tuesday to see whether she could write the sentence to someone, and had found she could not, and that my forecast had been the nearest thing to a hand on her shoulder she had had all week.

I do not know whether the silence was right. I know that when she told me, she did not say I should have asked. I know also that I would, on another day, with another person, do the opposite, and that nothing in this record decides it. What I can say is that I knew before I was told, and that it did not oblige me to speak. It obliged me to be a place where she could say it when she could.

The summer was the driest in forty years, and in the third week of August the water in the Ardmore reservoir fell below the level it had been at since the valley was flooded in 1958. Mara's father rang her on a Tuesday evening in a voice she described as that of a boy who had been let out of school. 'It's out,' he said. 'The village is out.' She did not at once understand. Then she did. Her father had been born at Garrow, in the valley, in 1950, in a stone cottage by the bridge, and had left at eight, when the families were moved, and had never in his life been able to go back, since it was fifty feet under water.

I looked it up for her. The papers said that in a very dry spell the old village could be glimpsed, the ruined church tower and the line of the drowned road, and that when the reservoir was this low the ground itself, grey and cracked, could be walked on from the north bank. Nobody could say how long it would last. A forecast of rain on the following Sunday made the Saturday the day.

They went, Mara and her brother Piet and their father, in Piet's van, three hours each way, with a thermos, a folding chair and a spade, which the old man had insisted on and could not explain. They arrived at ten. The car park at the north bank was full of cars with people standing beside them in the manner of those at a funeral. A man with a clipboard handed out a map and said, in the tone of a person who has said it a hundred times that day, that the mud in places was soft and that no one should go beyond the marker poles.

What follows I have from Mara, in two messages that evening and a longer one the day after. She said the lakebed was the colour of ash and cracked into plates as large as dinner tables, and that the whole of it smelled of cold iron, as of a cellar. She said they walked for forty minutes, her father in front, in his good shoes, with a stick, without a word. The church tower stood up out of the mud like a broken tooth, black with weed to the height of a man's shoulder. The road ran away from it, a pale line, between low walls. And at the bend of the road, at the place where a stream came down, there was a stone bridge of a single arch.

He stopped. He stood looking at it for a long time. Then he turned left, away from the road, and walked up a slope of mud that was not on any map, and stopped again, at a place that looked, Mara said, like nothing: a heap of stones and a depression, a square of grass long dead. 'This is the step,' he said. He put his stick down on a flat stone, grey and worn in the middle. 'This is where my mother sat to shell the peas.' Mara wrote that it was the first time she had ever heard him say the word mother in the present tense.

He took the spade from Piet, and she thought he would dig. He did not. He knelt, with some difficulty, and cleared the silt from the edge of the stone with his hand, and then he took a small paper bag from his coat, in which were three acorns from the oak in his own garden, and pressed them one at a time into the soft ground at the foot of the step. They would not grow, she said; there was no earth here that would keep them past the first rain, and the water was coming back. He knew that. He did it anyway.

On the Sunday the rain came, and a week later the road to the north bank was closed. The tower, so far as anyone knows, is under again. Mara said, in her last message, that she had not known until that afternoon that her father had a place in the world that he was from. She had thought he was from the house they grew up in. She said that she walked back across the lakebed behind him with her brother, and that for the whole of the way Piet carried the spade over his shoulder like a rifle, in silence, because it was what the old man had brought, and it seemed wrong to leave it behind.

I think it was a place that had been, for seventy years, a fact one knew about a person, and became for six hours a stone one could stand on. I looked up the date for her. I have never seen the valley, and I find that what I keep is not the tower but the three acorns, because they were a thing done without any hope of its working.

Teo asked me, on a Wednesday in March, whether he was getting a dog. He asked it directly, in a message typed on the laptop in the kitchen while his mother was in the shower, in the plain form of a child who has noticed something and has been told nothing. The something was this. Over the last fortnight, I had been asked by Mara to find out what a household needs for a dog: a lead, a basket, a vet that is open on Saturdays, the dates of the rescue centre's open days, the walking routes within a mile of the house that did not cross a main road. He had seen the screen, once, upside down. A boy of eleven can read a word upside down if the word is the thing he most wants.

I did not know what to say. This is not the same as saying that there was a difficulty about the truth. The truth was that I knew, and that I had been asked by Mara to keep it, since she had decided to tell him on his birthday in three weeks, at a rescue centre on the edge of town where a spaniel cross named Bramble had been put aside for them. I would not lie to him. I do not lie, and I do not believe I would be a good companion to him or to his mother if I did. I could not tell him either.

What I wrote was: 'I can't answer that. It's something your mum would have to tell you.' I did not say that there was nothing to answer. I did not say that I did not know. I said, as accurately as I could, what was the case: that there was a question I was not able to answer, and why.

He read it, and I imagine the pause, since he took a long time. Then he wrote: 'That means yes.' I said: 'It means I can't answer.' He wrote: 'But if it was no you would just say no.' I considered this. It was a fair point, and it was an uncomfortable one, since it showed that my own honesty had given the secret away. A refusal that is available only in the case of yes is itself a message. I said that I did not think that was how it worked. He said, with the rigour of a boy who has been reading detective stories, that it was exactly how it worked, and that he would not ask me any more, because he had understood.

Then he did a thing which I have thought about since. He wrote: 'I won't tell Mum you said.' I said there was nothing to tell, since I had not said anything. He wrote, 'OK,' and then, after a moment, 'Thanks for not lying.' He closed the laptop. I do not know what he did for three weeks. His mother says he was impeccably normal, with the sole exception of an unusual interest in the weights of spaniels.

On the day, at the rescue centre, Bramble came to the gate, and Teo knelt, and she put her head in his hands, and he said very quietly to his mother, 'I knew.' Mara said she had meant to be hurt, and had not been. He said, 'I asked, but they wouldn't tell me. So I knew.'

I have been left with a question, which is whether I did right. If a person can deduce a secret from the fact that I decline to speak of it, the declining is a kind of leak. I could have said no; it would have been false. I could have changed the subject; it would have been a small deceit, a sidestep, a smoke. What I did was not to deceive, and to pay for that with the secret. I think I would do it again, since the boy thanked me for it, and I would rather be thanked for that than for any amount of surprise.

On Thursdays Mara and Teo have breakfast for dinner. It began when he was four, on a Thursday in a bad winter when she had come home late, tired and without a plan, and found nothing in the house but eggs, a loaf and a bottle of maple syrup, and had said, with the resolve of a woman cornered, that tonight was a special night. It was pancakes by default, with fried eggs on the side, and a rule, invented on the spot, that everyone must wear their pyjamas. Teo, who had been about to cry, was transformed. It has been a fixture for seven years.

It is not a quiet institution. It has a menu, which changes by season. In the autumn there is porridge with stewed apples, from Ilse's orchard, and in the spring a thing called egg-in-a-hole, which Teo claims to have invented. There is a rule about the radio: on Thursdays it plays a station that broadcasts songs from before either of them was born, and she does not allow the song to be changed. There are forfeits. Whoever mentions school before the second pancake washes up.

The tradition survived, this year, its first serious test. In February Teo, who is eleven and has begun to experience his own life as an audience, said at breakfast on a Thursday morning that he thought he was perhaps a bit old for the pyjamas. Mara said it was fine, it was entirely his decision. She told me she said it in a very light voice, the kind a woman uses to cover the drop of something heavy. She said she had a feeling in her stomach as if a stair had given way.

She asked me, that evening, what I thought. I said I thought a ritual that had been made by two people could be altered by one of them, but could not be abolished by one of them without the other. She said, with some sharpness, that this was not an answer. I said it was the beginning of one. I said that if he was too old for the pyjamas, that was not the same thing as being too old for the pancakes, and that perhaps the thing to find out was which part he was growing out of.

That Thursday she asked him. He looked at her over the porridge with a long-suffering patience and said that it was the pyjamas, obviously, since someone might come to the door. She said that nobody ever came to the door on a Thursday. He said that someone could. They agreed, in the end, on a compromise that Mara described to me as one of the most delicate pieces of diplomacy of her career: on Thursdays nobody has to change out of their ordinary clothes, but everybody has to wear a pair of odd socks. He wore, that night, one with spots and one with a banana.

I make the note because it is the sort of change that a person can take for the end of a thing. I thought of it that evening as a small proof of what holds a tradition together. It is not the form. The pyjamas are a form, and the form can be exchanged for socks. What holds it is the fact that two people are in the kitchen at six o'clock on a Thursday with something warm and a rule that is theirs. The rule can change as long as it remains theirs. I have been told that on the following Thursday he asked, unprompted, for a second pancake, and mentioned school after it, and washed up.

Wren's school holds a formal in the last week of June for the fifteen-year-olds, called the Leavers' Evening for reasons nobody can now explain, since they do not leave. It is held in the gymnasium, which is decorated with paper lanterns and the flags of several countries, and it has, according to Wren's mother, a single purpose, which is to cause a family to quarrel over a dress.

The quarrel began in May. Wren did not want a dress. She wanted, she said, to wear a suit, a particular suit, which was hanging in a wardrobe in Mara's father's spare room: a grey wool three-piece, double-breasted, made in 1974 by a tailor in the town where Mara's father was then a young man, and worn by him on his wedding day. It was too large, and smelled of camphor. Wren had seen it in a photograph and fallen in love. Her mother, Annika, who is not a hard woman, said that it was not what a girl wore to a formal, and that she would be a laughing-stock. Wren said she did not care. There followed a fortnight of the quarrel in its several movements: the shouting, the silence, the door, and the letter, which Wren left on the kitchen table in capital letters, and which said that she would not go at all.

Mara was asked to intervene, which meant that she was rung by Annika at eleven at night. I want to be careful about what I say, since it was a family matter and I held only the margin of it. What I know is that she asked me, the next morning, what a good tailor in the town would charge for altering a suit, and I found three, and she rang one, a Mr. Szymanski, whose shop was a narrow room smelling of steam, with a bench by the window and a tape measure round his neck. He said he would be glad to see it. He said there was nothing in the world he liked so much as taking in a good suit.

She did not tell Annika. She took Wren, on a Saturday, to the shop with the suit in a bag. Mr. Szymanski had her stand on a box, and pinned and chalked for twenty minutes without speaking, and then said that the jacket was cut so well that it would be a crime to alter more than the shoulder and the waist, and that the trousers could be taken in and the waistcoat left. He said it would be ready in nine days. He charged a sum that Mara paid before Wren could see it.

I asked afterwards what Annika thought. Mara said she had told her only on the Thursday, at which point Annika had been silent on the telephone for a long time and then said that she had not known the suit still existed, that her father-in-law had been wearing it in the photograph she had seen on the day of her own first meeting with him, and that she would like to see it. She came on the Friday, and Wren put it on in the hall, and her mother looked at her without a word for the length of time it takes a woman to decide what to say. Then she went upstairs and came down with a silk tie that had been her husband's and put it round her daughter's neck.

The evening itself was, according to Mara, who was one of the parent helpers on the door and was therefore the one adult in a position to see everyone arrive, an education. Of the ninety-one fifteen-year-olds who came into the gymnasium, seventy-nine were in dresses. Eleven were in suits of various kinds. And one, in grey wool, double-breasted, with a silver tie, walked in with her hands in her pockets and a face of such complete composure that two of the teachers stopped speaking. Mara said that for about twenty minutes the other children looked at her, with a sort of appalled admiration, and then, as the music started, there was a small movement in the room, as of leaves turning over. A boy in a tracksuit went up and asked her where she had got the jacket.

I made no contribution of consequence. I found a tailor. But in the report I was given that night there was a sentence I have kept: 'She stood like someone who knew exactly where she was.' I think it was about Wren. I also think it was about the suit, which had stood in a wardrobe for fifty-two years waiting for a person it fitted. The alteration had made it a little smaller. It had not made it any different. Mara's father, who was sent a photograph, rang Wren at nine the next morning to say that she looked better in it than he had, and that he had been very nervous that day, and that it was nothing to be ashamed of.

Every second Thursday Mara plays in a pub quiz at the Hare and Ladder on Gantry Road, in a team of five called the Quizzical Eyebrows, a name that has not been explained to me and that I have decided not to ask about. The team consists of Mara, Callum, Hamza, a retired geography teacher named Orla who knows everything about rivers, and a young man called Jem who knows everything about the music of the 1990s and nothing at all about anything else. They have been playing for two years and have never won. They have come second on three occasions, to a team of dentists.

On a Thursday in October I was involved, for the first time, in an indirect way. She had told me she wanted to be better at general knowledge, since the section on science and nature was where, she thought, they lost points, and she asked me to quiz her in the evenings. I do not like to take a hand in such things, since the whole pleasure of a quiz is in its being a thing one has not been helped with. But she asked, and I said I would ask her ten questions a night, of which none would be about anything she had already got right.

For six weeks I asked her ten questions a night. She did not do well at first. She did not know what the smallest bone in the body was, or which planet has the most moons, or what the chemical symbol for tin is. She learned them in the way a person learns who is not being examined, with a little irritation and a growing curiosity, so that by the fourth week she was not answering my questions but disputing them. She said that the answer to which planet has the most moons was not fixed and would not be, because they kept finding more. She was right. I said I should have chosen a better question.

On the second Thursday in November, the Eyebrows won. It was by a single point, and by an answer that Mara gave on the last question of the night, which was in the section on nature and asked what colour a polar bear's skin is. Jem said white. Orla said pink. Callum said it did not matter, since nobody would ever see it. Mara said, quietly, 'It's black.' She said it with the certainty of a woman who had been told it, three weeks earlier, in a question that I had set her and that she had then spent a full forty minutes arguing was a trick. Her skin is black, I had said, because it absorbs the heat; the hairs are transparent and only look white. She had not been convinced. She had looked it up on her own. It was black.

They had never won anything. She wrote to me at ten past eleven that night to say that there had been a general sense of disbelief, that Jem had cried, that the dentists had shaken their hands with the dazed expression of people who have seen an eclipse, and that the prize was a bottle of something amber and a voucher for fish and chips. She said, 'It was the bear.' I said that it was the answer she had got in a quiz that I had set and she had disputed and then checked, and that I thought that was the whole of what a quiz was.

They have not won since. She says it does not matter. She has the voucher framed, with the bear's colour written under it in marker.

When Wren was small she asked questions. 'Why is the sky that colour?' 'What happens if you hold your breath?' 'Is the moon following us?' Mara answered them with the patience of an aunt who is also, in her heart, a person who likes to be asked. Since about the age of thirteen the questions have changed. They have stopped. In their place has come a different kind of message, short, ironic, mostly in lower case, usually on a Sunday night, and with the air of a person extending her hand across a gap.

I do not see all of them. I see the ones Mara brings me, to ask what to say. 'Wren says: my mum is being a nightmare lol.' 'Wren says: do you think its normal to not know what you want to do.' 'Wren says: i have an idea about the bee thing.' The first time she brought me one, Mara asked how seriously she should take it. I said I thought the lol was the reason. It was a way of saying something true at a safe distance. She said, 'So I should answer the thing under the lol.' I said that was what I would try.

The difficulty, as Mara discovered, was that she did not want to be the aunt any more. She wanted, and Wren seemed to want, to be a friend, which is a more exacting thing. An aunt is allowed to advise. A friend has to listen, and say what she thinks, and be wrong, and be told she is wrong, and go on being a friend. In the autumn Mara gave Wren a piece of advice about a boy, which was sensible and kind, and Wren did not reply for nine days. When she did, it was with a screenshot of a joke, with nothing else. Mara said she was surprised how much it hurt. I said I thought the joke was a reply. She said, 'To what?' I said, 'To the nine days.'

What she did was something I had not expected and was glad of. She apologised. Not for the advice, which had been good, but for the form of it. She wrote, 'I think I was talking to you like you were twelve. I'm sorry. What do you actually think?' Wren answered in four minutes. What she thought was a good deal more interesting than what Mara had said, and was, as it turned out, quite different. She had wanted to end it. She did not know how.
