Mara reread code she wrote five years ago, in a file called helpers, and asked whether to be embarrassed. I said the code did what it needed and only the name was wrong. She renamed it 'dates' and 'money' and was cheerful all day.

The deploy tool began asking for confirmation and the pipeline hung because nobody was there to answer. Mara found the flag that says yes. I asked her to write down what she was agreeing to, and it went into the pipeline file as a comment.

A partner's integration sent us dates as day-of-year numbers in one field, which nobody had mentioned. Mara found it by looking at the maximum value, 366. Their developer, a quiet man called Marek, said he had assumed we knew. She wrote the format into our integration page with his name beside it, and he added a line of his own.

One quiet evening I read the ten oldest open issues on Sedge. Four were already fixed, three duplicates, two no longer reproducible, one a good idea nobody had answered. I closed nine with notes and replied to the tenth. Mara's only comment next day was 'lighter'.

The build failed on the ARM server because a compiled library had been linked against a different C library. It took a day, a container and a read of the loader's output to learn we had copied the binary instead of building it there. We build on the target now.

Mara wrote the word 'maybe' nine times in a design document and asked me to find each one. For each we either decided or turned it into a dated question with a name. The document went from vague to useful without gaining a line.

A Makefile target called test did nothing because a directory called test existed and make thought it up to date. Mara spent twenty minutes before I suggested declaring it phony. 'Thirty years of this?' she asked, to nobody.

Tobias asked whether we should store money as floats. Mara said no with a force I rarely hear. I showed him ten additions of 0.1 and what comes out. We store whole minor units and a currency code, and his example went into the wiki.

Noor's request for a 'last seen' timestamp on every user would have meant a write on every page view, forty times our write load. Mara proposed updating it at most once per ten minutes. Noor said that was accurate enough.

Mara found a tab-versus-space argument in a project's history that ran to forty comments in 2017. We counted the commits it changed: none. A formatter ended it the next year. She keeps the thread as a reminder of how to spend an afternoon badly.

Our checkout scored 61 for accessibility. Wren, who had been learning the tools, found eleven items in an afternoon: missing labels, colour alone marking errors, a modal that trapped focus. We fixed nine and the score became 94. She asked for a monthly slot for this work, and Mara gave her the first Thursday. The first Thursday session, Wren tried the site with the keyboard only and discovered that the date picker could be opened but not closed, which she described as a very polite trap. The second, she sat with Yusra and went through the booking page using only the Tab key, and Yusra, who had never done so, went quiet for a long while and then asked for a copy of the notes. I did little in these sessions beyond finding links and pointing at lines. I mention it because it is one of the few times I have seen a measure, a number like 61, change the way someone looked.

Mara asked whether to keep a ten-year-old script in a language nobody here knows. It ran nightly and had never failed. I read it: ninety lines, describable in four sentences. We rewrote it in what the team knows, with a test, and the old one went to the archive. Before archiving it we ran both on a year of data and compared the outputs, and they differed on one day, a day in March when the old script had silently skipped a file with a malformed header. The new version fails loudly on such files, and on the first night it did, which gave Mara a small, cold shock and then a larger relief. The script's author, a colleague from before my time called Anselm, had written it in an afternoon in 2014 and never touched it again. Mara sent him a message to say it had run for ten years without a failure, and he replied with a single word, 'really?'.

A customer in another time zone could not book a slot on the last day of a month because our calendar considered the day over in UTC. Mara and Ilse watched the slot vanish and reappear on a call. It was the second such bug that month.

Everyone blamed the new feature for the slowdown. Mara asked for the timings of the old version on the same data: also slow. The data had grown the same week. I like it when a graph exonerates somebody.

A staging mailing list held real addresses from a copy, and a test run sent 'Welcome to Lantern!' to 212 customers. Mara phoned the unhappy ones; only two were. Non-production copies now replace addresses with ones we own.
Two services each retried failed calls to the other three times: nine attempts and a storm. Mara drew the arrows on the whiteboard and erased six. Only the outer layer retries now.

Mara ran a fifteen-minute meeting where each person named one thing the build had cost them that week. Across seven people: six hours. We spent two days on the build and recovered five hours a week, a rare decision that came with its own arithmetic.

I wrote the first draft of a postmortem in the order things happened and Mara asked for it in the order we understood them. It is a different document. The second explains why we looked at the wrong thing first, which is the part worth having next time.

At midnight Mara watched requests per second go vertical, forty times normal, and did not panic: a popular newsletter had linked to us. We served a cached page to anonymous visitors and watched the line settle. She thanked the newsletter by email, which I thought graceful.
The CLI printed a progress spinner into a log file when run by the scheduler: forty thousand lines of backslashes and dashes. A spinner belongs only where output is a terminal. One line fixed it.

Yusra and Mara spent an hour on whether 'cancel booking' should be DELETE or POST. It cancels but keeps the record, and Yusra argued for the verb that does not lie. POST on a named action won, and the reasoning is four lines in a decision file.

Tobias asked how I know a function is too long. I have no number. I know it when I cannot say in one sentence what it is for. He tried it on his code and found eleven functions needing two sentences, most with a hidden 'and'.

A page-comparison test had been updated blindly by three people, each pressing the button that accepts new output. When Mara finally read the stored copy it contained an error message. A reviewer must read each accepted change now.

Three weeks after we dropped an old browser, Mara looked at the logs: under one percent of visits, mostly from a single office. She called them. They upgraded in an afternoon. Mara called it the most expensive and cheapest decision of the quarter.
Yusra's pull request template now has one line: 'what could go wrong here?' Most answers are 'nothing'. Twice the answer was a paragraph, and both times we found the bug while she wrote it.

A quiet bug: sort order in the staff list changed between page loads because two staff shared a start date and the database was free to choose. Adding the name as a tiebreaker ended it. Sunniva had thought she was imagining it.

Teo's pull request replaced a thirty-line loop with one expression. Mara read it three times and asked him to put the loop back. 'Clever is a cost,' she said, 'and the reader pays it.' He did, with a better name.

The websocket dropped after exactly sixty seconds of silence, always. Mara suspected our code. A proxy in front had an idle timeout of a minute. A heartbeat every thirty seconds solved it, and we wrote the proxy's setting into the architecture page. Mara had spent most of the morning convinced our server was closing connections, and read its code twice. What persuaded her otherwise was a packet capture I suggested, which showed the reset arriving from an address that was not ours. She said afterwards that she would never again blame the code she can read before checking the boxes she cannot, and then, honestly, that she would probably do it again next month, but quicker to recover. I thought that was a fair forecast and said so.

A dependency's release notes said 'minor fixes', and the diff, which I read for Mara, included the removal of a function we call in two places. I do not trust the note and I trust the diff, and I told her so without making it a rule.

Ilse asked whether she should learn to read a stack trace. I said yes and gave her the three lines worth reading: the error, the first line of our code, and the line before it. After a week she sent me her first trace with her own guess attached.

Noor and Mara argued over whether a 'draft' and a 'pending' booking were the same state. They are not, said Noor, and drew the difference in the customer's words. Mara conceded and we kept both, with the difference written beside each in the code.

The test database was a copy of production from 2022, and its oddities had become the suite's fixtures. We replaced it with generated data. Eleven tests failed and each was passing because of a quirk of the old copy.

Mara reads the diff of every dependency update before merging, which takes her ten minutes a week. In March she found a postinstall script that fetched a file from an unfamiliar host. We pinned the old version and wrote to the maintainer, who thanked us and fixed it. The script, it turned out, belonged to a new co-maintainer who had added a download of a prebuilt binary to save users a compile step, from a server of his own. His intentions were good and the practice was exactly what a careless or malicious person would also do. Mara's message to him was friendly and firm, and offered to help him build the binaries in the project's own pipeline instead. He accepted. She says the ten minutes a week has paid for itself a hundred times, but admits that is a feeling and not a measurement, and asked me not to write the number down as though it were one.

A user reported that the app 'forgets' a form after rotating the phone. The screen was recreated and the form with it. Mara took a day to move its state out of the view, and the phone, held sideways, finally remembered.

The signup form hung for eight seconds on one long email address. A validation pattern was backtracking through the same characters thousands of ways. Mara replaced it with a plain check for one at-sign and a confirmation email.

A node process died at three in the morning with no message. An unhandled promise rejection, from a call nobody awaited. Mara added the global handler that logs it, and then, at my suggestion, fixed the call.

Each guest list on the event page showed the guests of every earlier list, because a default argument was a shared list. Mara knew the trap and had still walked into it. 'Everybody does it once,' she said, 'and then once more.'

Yusra's script treated a response with status 200 as success, but the service reported errors in the body of 200s. Three weeks of failed syncs looked fine in the logs. She read the body now, and we asked the service's owner whether he would reconsider his status codes.

A single pipe where two were meant: a bitwise or in a permission check let everyone through. Mara found it in review of her own code, looked at it for a while, and fixed it before telling anybody. I admire how she tells such stories about herself.
The dev server answered on 127.0.0.1 and refused on localhost, because localhost resolved to the IPv6 address the server did not listen on. An hour of Mara's afternoon. A one-word setting.

The audit log table's id column was a signed 32-bit integer and had reached 2,147,483,647 on a Sunday. Inserts failed with a message about a sequence. We changed the type and added an alert at seventy percent of any counter's range.

The first request after every deploy failed and the second succeeded. A temp directory was created lazily and the first call raced the creating. Mara moved the creation to startup, where it belonged and where it could fail early and loudly.

A console warning about state updates on an unmounted component turned out to be a timer that kept firing after the user left the page. Teo cleared it in the cleanup function and the warnings stopped for the first time in a year.

Customers who spent exactly fifty pounds were charged shipping though the page promised free delivery over fifty. A greater-than where greater-or-equal belonged. Noor found it by buying a fifty-pound candle herself.

The bug disappeared whenever we added a log line to look at it. Mara has a name for that kind, and so do I, but neither of us said it. A log line changes timing; the bug lived in the gap between two writes. We fixed the gap.

After we fixed a redirect, a few users kept landing on the old page for weeks: their browsers had cached the permanent version. Mara learned to use the temporary redirect while testing, and sent an apology to the three who wrote in.

A secret read from a file carried a trailing newline, and the API rejected it with a baffling message. Callum spent two hours. I compared the length of the value with the length of what he had typed and the difference was one.
A query with NOT IN returned nothing at all, because one value in the list was null. Mara called SQL a polite liar. She rewrote it with NOT EXISTS and added a test with a null in the list.
A test with the year 2024 written into it began failing on the first of January. Dario groaned when I found it, and then laughed. We replaced the year with one computed from the test's own clock.

Sorted as strings, '10' came before '9' on the invoices screen for the second time in two years. Mara did not say anything, only sent me the earlier ticket. We sort by the numeric part now, and she keeps the ticket open as a reminder of the pattern.

The retry loop slept for ten seconds inside a request handler, so a slow partner could hold every worker thread for minutes. Mara moved the retries to a background job and the page answered at once with 'we are on it'.

Touching a README file in the monorepo rebuilt every package for forty minutes. Mara added path filters to the pipeline and kept a list of what each package depends on, so a change rebuilds only what it must.

The blue-green switch went perfectly and logged every user out, since the two sides kept sessions in memory. Mara moved sessions to the database and the next switch passed unnoticed, which is the best a switch can be.

A cache keyed by file modification time made two builds with identical content differ, and a fresh checkout invalidated everything. Mara changed the key to a hash of the content. The build got dull, which I mean as the highest praise.
At five percent canary the new version's memory graph slanted up and nobody had to guess. Mara paused the rollout, Teo found a list that never emptied, and nobody outside the team heard about it.

Two builds finished in the same minute and both were named with the date and the minute, so one overwrote the other. Mara added the commit hash to the name. The error looked small until the day it shipped the wrong one to staging.

A scheduled pipeline run on the first of the month failed because a mirror we install from was down for an hour. Mara added a second mirror and a retry, and wrote on the pipeline page which of our dependencies are fetched from outside our network. The list has four lines.

Ilse's team only just noticed the app said 'latest' in its image tag and that latest had moved under them on a Monday. We tag every image with the commit and deploy by that tag. 'Latest' was a name, not a promise.

In a review Mara counted her own comments by file position: eleven on the first file, six on the second, two on the fifth, none after. Her attention shrinks along the diff. She now reviews big changes in two sittings, last file first on the second.

A pull request fixed a bug and added no test. Mara asked Wren for one, and in writing it Wren found a second bug, in the same function, which would have bitten in November. Wren sent the test and the second fix together.
Mara found that two of her pull requests had waited four days for review, which was her fault. We agreed a team rule: first response within one working day, even if it is only 'I will look tomorrow'.

Mara reviewed a configuration change with more care than a code change, because configuration has no tests. The diff was a single line, a timeout of 30 changed to 3. She asked the author whether he meant seconds. He had meant 300 milliseconds.

I wrote a clever one-liner that chained four transformations, and Mara asked me to break it up. 'I can read it,' she said, 'but I cannot be wrong about it.' I split it into four lines with names. She was right, and I have kept the sentence.

Mara's shell had an alias that shadowed the real rm with a version that always asked. In a script it hung. She renamed the alias and, for the first time in years, looked at everything else in her dotfiles.

Font ligatures in Mara's editor drew not-equals as a tidy single symbol. A reviewer, Callum, thought a comparison was a bug in a screenshot. She turned ligatures off and said the world is too ambiguous already.

Mara wrote a tiny script that reads the branch name and opens the matching ticket. She uses it forty times a day and says it is the best thing she built all month, which says something about the other things.
Mara learned jq on a Friday and by Monday was filtering logs with pipelines that made me smile. Her first query was wrong in a useful way: it returned nothing, and the nothing was the answer.

Duplicate files in the asset folder: 3,200 of them, 11 gigabytes, found by comparing hashes. Mara wanted to delete the copies at once. We moved them to a holding folder for a month first, and in the third week one turned out to be referenced by a path in an old newsletter.

One person in the member table was 212 years old. Mara thought it was a fine joke and then asked what the oldest legitimate age was. We found 41 more over 110, all entered with the year 19 missing a digit. Sunniva corrected them from the paper forms.

A legacy system stored surnames in capitals. Mara wanted proper case, and I showed her what a naive rule does to names like McKenna and van der Meer. We converted only the clearly ordinary ones and left the others for a person to read.

A column used 'N/A', 'n/a', '-', '' and 'none' all to mean missing. Mara and I counted them: 31 percent of rows. We mapped every variant to null in one place and kept the original text in a side column in case the difference had once meant something.

Merging two product catalogues with different SKU schemes took two weeks, and in the end the key was the supplier's own barcode, which both had been storing in a notes field. Mara said she had never been so annoyed at and so grateful for a notes field.

2,100 order lines pointed to orders that no longer existed. We found them with a single join. Mara asked whether to delete them. I said to look at one first: it was a real line item from 2021, and the order had been removed by hand. We archived them with a note.

Rows with an end date of 2099-12-31 were not future events; they were the old system's way of saying 'no end'. Mara found it by asking Ilse, who remembered. We made the end date nullable and converted the sentinel in one reviewed step.

Callum told me the most important test in the repository was a golden file test that nobody understood. We read it together. It guarded the invoice layout, and its stored copy was a good record of how the layout had changed over four years.

The mobile app and the API disagreed about a field that was optional on one side and required on the other. Mara wrote a contract test that both teams run; it failed on the first day, usefully, and has been quiet since.
Browser tests failed at random because a button was still animating when the test clicked it. Teo turned animations off in test mode and the suite stopped flaking, along with half of its comments.

Teo's test for leap years checked the year 2000 and 1900, the two cases people forget. Mara said she would have written 2024 and gone home. It is the sort of test that shows someone once paid for a bug.

Tests that use random data now print their seed when they fail. Mara added it after a failure we could not reproduce for a month. The next one took four minutes, since we simply ran it again with the printed number.

The suite had 4,000 tests, and I looked at which had never failed in two years of history: 1,100. Mara did not want to delete them. We did not; we only moved them to a slower nightly run and watched what happened. Nothing did, for eleven weeks.

A scheduled job ran twice on the night the clocks went back, because the hour 01:30 happened twice. Mara read about it in the postmortem she wrote herself. We now schedule jobs in UTC and keep the local times for people.

A fuzzer pointed at the Pavo parser crashed it in nine seconds with a file of 14 bytes. Mara, who had never used one, said it was like watching someone find the loose stone in a wall by walking into it.

Compiling a regular expression inside a loop of a million iterations cost 40 seconds. Moving it outside took one line. Mara asked how many such lines there were. We looked for them with the profiler and found six.

Inserting 50,000 rows one at a time took eleven minutes; in a single transaction with batches it took nine seconds. Mara sat quietly for a moment and then asked how many other places insert one at a time. We found the list in the afternoon.
Turning on compression for API responses cut a 2 MB reply to 180 KB. Mara measured it from her phone on mobile data and said the screen felt as if somebody had opened a window.

A table that had been updated daily for six years was 30 gigabytes of which 9 were live data. A vacuum, scheduled in a quiet hour, brought it down. Mara had never thought a database could contain so much air.

The booking calendar re-rendered 300 times on opening because a parent passed a fresh object to every child on every change. Teo wrapped it once, and the page, which had stuttered since spring, was suddenly quiet.

The Tern app's download was 48 megabytes, most of it three sets of images for screen sizes we no longer support. Removing them brought it to 19. Mara tried the install on a slow connection and said it finished before she had finished her sentence.

Keeping connections alive between our service and the partner cut 80 milliseconds off each call, which was the cost of setting up a secure channel each time. Mara said she had not known a handshake had a price.

Wren started a page called 'what we decided not to do', with reasons and dates. It already holds eleven items, including a plugin system, and Mara says it has ended more arguments than any other file in the repository.

Our docs search returned nothing for 'sign in' because the pages said 'log in'. Wren added a small synonym list. Searches that return nothing dropped from a quarter of all searches to under five percent.

Mara replaced three out-of-date screenshots of the settings page with a paragraph of text and a link to the page itself. Wren objected that a picture helps. Mara said an old one helps a person do the wrong thing. They kept one, dated in its corner.

A manual page for Marrow, written in a weekend by Tobias, is now the most used part of the documentation. He did not expect it. Mara asked what he did differently. 'I wrote it for me, six months ago, lost,' he said.

The FAQ is made from the questions support has actually received, in the customers' own words, ordered by how often. Ilse built it in an afternoon from her inbox. The tickets about the first four questions fell by half.

A page of every error message we can emit, what it means and what to do, took Yusra a month to build and sat unread for six weeks. Then support began linking to it. In the second month it had more views than the homepage.

Someone committed an 80-megabyte video to the Glasswork repository. We did not rewrite history, because we did not want to disturb anyone's clones for it. We moved the file to large-file storage, kept the old blob and wrote in the contributing guide how it happened.

Mara named branches by ticket number and I named them by what they do; the list in the hosting site became a puzzle. We settled on both: the number, then the words. Callum said it looked like a label printed by a very organised person.

Mara began using worktrees so she can review a branch without leaving her own. The first time, she did not notice she was in the wrong folder and edited the review copy. I asked her to put the branch name in the terminal title.

Our ignore file did not list editor swap files, and two of them were committed in a single week. Dario added the pattern and then, because he is thorough, looked through the history for others. He found nine.

Two submodules, each pinned to a commit that someone had forgotten to push, broke a fresh clone for Ottoline on her first morning. Mara vendored both and removed the submodules. 'A repository ought to clone,' she said, not unkindly.

A commit was reverted, and the revert was reverted, and nobody could tell what state main was in. Mara wrote the net effect in a single sentence in the pull request. I have started to think a single sentence of net effect is the most valuable line in any history.

Mara asked the team to add 'Co-authored-by' trailers when two people write a change. Noor's name appeared on a commit for the first time in a year. She printed it and put it on her fridge, she said, as a joke, and I believed the joke was true.

We tag releases by date now, like 2025.03.2, instead of a number that implies promises. Mara likes that no one can argue whether something deserves a minor. Tobias dislikes that he cannot tell from a tag what broke. Both are right.

A commit's date was in 2031 because the author's laptop had a dead battery and a confused clock. It sorted to the top of the history for weeks. Mara asked him to fix the date, which he did, and she thanked him for being willing.

A debug flag left on in production wrote 40 gigabytes of logs in a day, and the disk filled at lunchtime. Mara muted the flag, cleared the logs in a tidy way and, in the aftermath, made the flag refuse to be on in production.

When the SMS provider went down for three hours, our two-step login stopped letting people in. Mara added a second provider as fallback, and a banner telling users to try the authenticator app. Nobody complained, and the support inbox stayed empty.

A partner's API allowed 100 requests a minute and our nightly sync made 400. The first night we were blocked for an hour. Mara made the sync wait politely, and the same data takes six minutes now instead of one failure.

The container was killed at 512 megabytes by the operating system. The report job had loaded a month of rows at once. Mara changed it to a cursor that reads a thousand at a time, and the same container now runs it at sixty megabytes.

The chat integration posted every failed build to the team channel, a hundred a day. People muted the channel, and then a real failure went unnoticed for six hours. Mara changed it to report only when a build on main turns red, once.

The database ran out of connections at 11:20 because each web worker opened its own pool, forty of them. Mara put a pooler between them and the database, and watched the connection count fall from 800 to 60.

Mara asked whether the UI should update before the server confirms. Yusra argued for optimism, with a quiet rollback; Noor for waiting, since money is involved. We split by action: instant for toggles, patient for payments.

A single 'role' string in the user table held values like 'admin', 'Admin' and 'administrator'. We made it an enum with a migration that maps all three and lists any value it does not recognise, so a surprise is visible.

Mara and Tobias argued for a week about validating input in the browser, on the server, or in the database. The honest answer was all three, for three different reasons: help, safety and truth. They wrote the three reasons down side by side.

Each payment request now carries an idempotency key, so a retry after a timeout cannot charge twice. The idea took Mara a page to explain to Noor and one afternoon to build. Noor said it is the sort of thing she would never have thought to ask for.

Sunniva calls them reservations and the code says bookings. Mara argued to use the customer's word everywhere. Dario countered that renaming a table is a risk. We renamed the screens and the docs now, and the table in spring, with a plan.

Public API versions in the path or in a header? Mara chose the path because a person can read it in a URL, and she knew it was the less pure choice. 'Pure is for people who do not answer the support inbox,' she said.

Tobias proposed splitting Lantern into six services. Mara asked what problem it would solve. He named three and she showed that we have none of them. He took the point cheerfully and asked whether we could revisit it if we ever have them.

Mara asked whether the new module should raise exceptions or return a result with an error. We wrote the same function both ways and read them. The result type made every caller handle failure, and she chose that for the parts that touch money.

A plugin system for Marrow was proposed by a contributor with a detailed design. Mara thanked him, then asked for three users who needed it. There were none yet. She wrote the answer on the 'decided not to' page with the date and the condition to reopen.

Splitting a 2,000-line class into four took three days of small moves, each verified by the same test run. Mara said that the class did not feel smaller; it felt as if the furniture had been put back where it belongs.

Moving the configuration into a single place meant finding forty-one reads of environment variables scattered over twenty files. Mara listed them and each had a default somewhere else, three of them different. We chose one and wrote it down.

A validation rule for postcodes lived in three places and was subtly different in each. We extracted it, and found the differences were each a bug in the same direction. The extracted one has eleven tests, one for each time somebody was wrongly refused.

Renaming a database column used by three services took a plan: add the new, write both, read the new, stop writing the old, drop the old. It took seven days instead of one. Mara said the seven days were the cost of three people not calling each other at midnight.

A function took nine parameters, four of them booleans. Mara grouped them into a small options object with names. At the call sites the code finally said what it did. Nobody had known what the third true meant.

Mara deleted the 'utils' module, redistributing its 46 functions to where they were used. Three were used nowhere, nine twice. She said nothing for a long while, and then that it was like emptying a drawer in a house you have lived in for years.

Replacing a date library of 70 kilobytes by twenty lines of our own was Teo's idea. We needed formatting in two shapes and nothing else. The bundle shrank, and a dependency that had needed a security update every spring went away.

Mara caught a package whose name was one letter off a popular one in a list of new dependencies from a contractor. It was harmless, probably a typo. We replaced it, and I added a line to the review checklist about reading names, not just versions.

Python 3.8 reached end of life in October, and Mara put the upgrade in the calendar for the first quiet week. We ran the tests on 3.12, fixed four deprecations, and moved. It took two days. She said that dread is bigger than the task, as usual.

Mara asked me to list the dependencies that a single person maintains. There were seventeen, of which five carry our payments or login. We wrote the five on a card and check them each quarter for signs of life.

Before the framework upgrade Mara wrote the order of work on a card: tests first, then the deprecation warnings, then the version number. Tobias followed it line by line and the upgrade landed in nine working days with no surprises in production. He said the card was the plan, and the surprise was how short it was.

We used an experimental charting library because it was beautiful. A year later its author archived the repository. Mara did not say anything about our choice; she wrote a line in the guide: experimental means expect to own it.

Glasswork's beta testers sent forty-two comments in the first week; thirty-eight were about the same three things. Mara said the repetition was the finding. We fixed the three, and the forty-three rest were soon a list we could read in one sitting.

A release freeze of three days before the Tern launch made everyone nervous and then calm. Mara used the time for dull work: she read every diff since the last release, the way a person walks through a house before leaving on a journey.

We separated the release notes into two: what changed for users, in their words, and what changed for developers, in ours. Ilse said she finally reads the first. Tobias reads only the second, and notes the second.

Rolling out the new search in waves, one percent, ten, then all, caught a bug at ten percent that showed only for accounts older than five years. Mara said she could not have designed a test for that if she had tried for a month.

Mara marks every release day with a cup of tea made in a particular pot and drunk before the tag is pushed. It has no function, as she says, and every release since March has gone without a rollback. I make no claim.

We announced the removal of an old endpoint six months ahead, in the headers of its responses as well as the docs. Sixty-one callers moved. Two did not, and we found them by their addresses and wrote to them, and the endpoint closed on the date.

A release rehearsal on staging, with a stopwatch and a checklist, showed that the migration step took nineteen minutes, not the five we had told the customers. Mara moved the announcement and the date. 'A rehearsal's job is to embarrass us early,' she said.

The same report, run on two servers, put the customers in a different order and Mara spent most of a Wednesday proving that neither was wrong. The databases sorted text by different rules: one put capitals before lowercase, the other ignored case. It took a test with five invented customer names to show it, and a settings dump from each server side by side to explain it. We stated the sort rule in the query itself, so that the order belongs to the report and not to the machine. She was quiet afterwards and then said that the worst kind of difference is the one where everyone is correct, because nobody can be asked to fix it.

Yusra's first outage, forty minutes of failed bookings after a config change, was also Mara's first postmortem as the one who asked the questions. She began by saying that nobody would be blamed and then, to my relief, behaved that way: she asked what Yusra knew at each moment and what she would have wanted to know. The answer to the second question was one line in a dashboard that did not exist. By the end Yusra was drawing the dashboard on the whiteboard herself. Mara told me afterwards that the hard part of being blameless is keeping your voice from going flat, and that she had practised in the car.

The new payment form went live behind a flag that was on for ten percent of visitors. On the second day the error rate for that group was three times the old one. Mara turned the flag off in seconds, without a deploy, and nobody who mattered noticed. The cause was a validation that rejected card holder names with an apostrophe or a hyphen, which the old form had never checked. Teo said that without the flag we would have found out from the support queue and lost a weekend. Mara said that was what the flag was for and that the real feature was the ability to say no quickly.

Upgrading the framework's routing library went smoothly because Mara first spent an afternoon listing every place we call it: 63 call sites in 19 files, each with a note on how it might break. The upgrade itself took forty minutes, with three call sites needing changes, all on her list. Tobias, who had expected a week, asked how she knew where to look. She said she had not known, only counted. I have thought about that since. Most of what looks like skill in this work is the willingness to make a list that seems too dull to be worth making, and to make it before the trouble starts.

The mobile app's retry policy produced a long argument. Dario wanted three quick retries; Noor wanted patience with exponential waits. Instead of settling it by opinion Mara took a phone onto a train with the network throttled and watched both policies fail in different ways: quick retries hammered a dead connection and drained the battery, patient ones left the user staring at a spinner. We chose a middle path, three retries with growing waits and a visible 'still trying' line after five seconds. The experiment took forty minutes and ended an argument that had run for two weeks, and I would like to see her do it more often.

While refactoring the notification module I found two separate code paths that both sent the 'your booking is confirmed' email, one from the old system and one from the new, depending on how the booking was made. For anyone who booked by phone and then paid online, both ran. Customers had received two emails for two years and no one had written to complain. Mara read the evidence and laughed in a way I recognise as relief. We kept the newer path and added a test that books by every route and counts the emails. The number it expects is one, and the test name says so.

Product images in the Brindle import linked by file name, and on Mara's Mac a file called Logo.PNG matched logo.png, while on the Linux build server it did not. Four hundred products were imageless in staging and fine on her laptop. She found it after an hour of blaming the network. We lower-cased every file name on the way in and made the importer refuse a name that differs from another only by case. I suggested, and she agreed, that the Mac's forgiving filesystem was not the bug, merely the place where the bug could hide.

Rebuilding the search index took three hours every night and slowed the site in the early morning. Mara and I looked at how many rows actually changed in a day: about 1,200 of two million. We wrote an incremental update that touches only those and keeps the full rebuild as a weekly consistency check. The nightly job now takes eleven minutes. In the first week the weekly check found nine rows the incremental job had missed, all from one edge case with deleted products, which we then fixed. Having both was worth the extra code, she said, because it told us we were wrong in a measured way.

Tobias walked Ottoline through the documentation on her first day with a notepad, writing down every place she hesitated. There were twenty-three. I was given the list that evening. Eleven were missing words, five were links to pages that moved, four assumed a tool we do not use any more, and three were true mysteries that Tobias could not answer himself. Mara fixed the first twenty in two hours and gave the three mysteries to Tobias with a date. Ottoline's contribution, she said at the end of the week, was not the questions but the fact that she asked them out loud while Tobias was in the room.

Moving Lantern's four repositories into one took a weekend and a great deal of fear. Mara wrote the plan on paper first: what moves, in what order, what the rollback is at each step, who is on call. She rehearsed it once on a copy and found that two build scripts used absolute paths. On the weekend itself the moves took six hours and the problems were all ones the rehearsal had named. The following Monday the team's first pull request across what used to be two repositories merged in ten minutes. Dario said that was the moment he stopped being against it.

Mara's mail queue lived in memory, and when the server restarted for a kernel update at night we lost the 140 messages that were waiting. We did not know it until a customer asked where his receipt was. She was calm; I could tell from how she wrote the incident note, in short sentences. The fix was to write each message to disk before saying it was accepted, and the test pulls the plug on the process in the middle of a batch and counts what survives. She added to the note a line that I keep thinking about: a system that says 'accepted' has made a promise, and promises should cost something to make.

Yesterday's sales read zero on the dashboard until six each morning. The data was not missing; it simply arrived late from the partner's feed. Mara changed the chart to say 'last updated' in plain words instead of letting a zero pass for a fact.
The mobile app kept showing a customer's old profile photo because the new image had the same URL. Teo put a version in the address. Mara said it is the oldest trick and the one she always forgets.

For the first time Mara uploaded source maps, and a production error that had read 'a is not a function' finally pointed at line 88 of the booking form. She was cheerful for an hour, as a person is on getting glasses.

Double-clicking the pay button sent two requests and made two orders. Mara disabled the button after the first click and, more importantly, made the server refuse a second order with the same cart in the same minute.

A few 502 errors a day, always on idle connections. The proxy kept connections alive for 75 seconds and the application closed them at 60. Mara set the application's timeout longer than the proxy's and the errors vanished the same afternoon.

Anyone with a plus sign in their email address could not click the confirmation link, because the plus became a space on the way. Noor's address has one. She had assumed for a year that the site was just unfriendly.

An API fetch loop requested page zero and page one as if different, so every record from the first page appeared twice in the export. Dario found it by counting. The number he got was 100 more than the total.

Remaining stock for the red edition showed minus three on a busy morning, because two orders decremented the same number at once. Mara changed the update to refuse going below zero and put 'sold out' where the minus had been.

The page worked in staging and broke on production, where one script loaded before the library it needed. A CDN had served the library slightly slower. Mara marked the order explicitly. 'Nothing is in order unless you say so,' she said.

After the deploy, users on one continent saw the old site. The CDN purge had cleared the main page but not the stylesheet it pointed at. We purge by prefix now, and the deploy script checks one file from the new version before saying finished.

Two workers picked up the same job and sent the same reminder twice, three minutes apart. Callum had left out the claim step, a single update that marks a job as taken. It was nine lines and a Thursday.

'Can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes' appeared once in the logs and then every minute after midnight. Mara found a single place that read a date from the database without its zone. One line, and the logs went quiet.

Our error tracker's count doubled overnight because a bot was probing for old admin pages. Mara taught the tracker to ignore 404s from known probes, so that the next real error would be visible among the numbers.

Two updates, each touching the same two rows in opposite order, deadlocked once a day. The database picked a victim and the retry hid the rest. Mara made both lock rows in id order and the daily deadlock vanished. I liked how plain the rule was.

Disk was 'full' at 91 percent used. The filesystem keeps five percent reserved for root and our monitor had a threshold of ninety. Mara read the man page and adjusted the alert to what the disk will actually give.

Every hour on the hour the site stalled for thirty seconds. Mara plotted it and saw the stall exactly on the hour. A statistics job locked a table for its whole run. Moving it to the replica ended the stall and gave her a graph she kept. It took her four days to see it, because the stall was too regular to feel like a fault; people had accepted it as the site's rhythm, the way one accepts a clock that chimes. What changed her mind was a customer's remark on a call that the site 'has a nap at the top of every hour'. She wrote the sentence on a sticky note and put it on the monitor, and the next morning plotted every request over a week against the minute of the hour. Nobody had ever drawn that graph. It is now one of the first I draw.

Two builds from the same commit produced different files because a timestamp was embedded in the output. Making builds reproducible took Dario an afternoon. 'Now I can tell if a deploy changed anything,' he said, with the face of a man seeing clearly.

The build agent was killed halfway through compilation by the memory limit. It was running eight jobs in parallel on four gigabytes. Mara set it to two, and the build took four minutes longer and never again fell over.

A page we had removed kept being served because the deploy copied new files over the old ones without deleting any. Wren found it by following a link in an old newsletter. The deploy removes what is not in the new build now.

The container restarted forever because a required environment variable was missing, and it said so in a log nobody was reading. Mara made the app refuse to start with a message naming the variable, and made the message the first line.

The tests ran on SQLite and production ran on a different database, and a query that used a function only one of them has passed everywhere but where it mattered. Teo moved the tests to a real instance in a container.

I approved a pull request that I did not understand, and said so afterwards to Mara. She said the honest thing would have been a question. I asked it the next day. The author explained, and the explanation revealed a flaw neither of us had seen. It was in the code beside the change, not in the change: a function that quietly returned yesterday's figure when today's was missing, which the new code relied on. The author said he had never been asked for an explanation before and had not known he had one. Mara listened to me tell her this and said she would rather have a reviewer who says 'explain it to me' once a week than a perfect one. I try to be that now, although I notice that the question is harder to ask than to answer, and that it needs me to say I am unsure.

The best comment I saw in a review that week was one question: 'What happens if this list is empty?' Wren wrote it. Nobody had thought of it, and the answer was a crash on the first day of every quarter.

A pull request that only deleted 3,000 lines was harder to review than one that added them, since each deletion had to be checked for a remaining caller. Mara did it with a search for each function name and found two stragglers.

Tobias had stopped reviewing pull requests. Mara asked him, without pressure, why. He felt his comments were not good enough. She sat with him for an hour over one of his reviews and showed him the single comment that had saved a release. He reviews again. The comment she showed him had been three words on a pull request of Dario's, 'this will overflow', about a counter that would have wrapped around at a number the shop reaches in its fourth year. Tobias had forgotten writing it. Dario had not: he still tells the story at lunch when somebody needs a push. Mara said that people stop reviewing for a reason that is almost never what they say, and that it is worth the hour to ask. I had read his silence in the logs as a change of schedule. It was a change of confidence.

Mara sorts review comments into three kinds and labels each: must, should, could. Callum found the labels freeing. 'I can finally tell which fight I'm in,' he said. The pull requests got merged a day sooner on average.

Wren reviewed my pull request and wrote, gently, that I had assumed the list was sorted. I had. The data was sorted only on staging. I thanked her and added a sort, then a sentence in the code about the assumption she exposed.

We tried a review done live on a call, one person scrolling, one asking, for a nasty change to the checkout. It took forty minutes and replaced three days of comments back and forth. Mara said she would keep it for the hard ones.

Reading a migration's generated SQL, Mara noticed it would rewrite a 50-million-row table. The ORM had hidden the cost. We changed the plan to add the column nullable and backfill in batches, and the deploy took seconds.

Mara spent ninety minutes reviewing a pull request and found nothing. She asked me if it was wasted time. I said the author now knew someone had read every line, and that people write differently for that. She decided it was not wasted.

A short script now bumps the version in four files at once and tags the commit. Tobias wrote it after a release went out with three files saying 2.3.0 and one saying 2.2.9. He took the mistake with good humour and a test.

A log viewer that merges several files by time and colours each source gave us in one evening what we had been missing for a year. Mara tried it first on the outage notes from March and said she could see the shape of it at last.
Teo built a browser extension that toggles feature flags for the current tab only. Mara said it was the first tool of his that she opened without being told to. He grinned for the rest of the day.

A pre-push hook now runs the forty fastest tests, in six seconds. Mara said she had been pushing broken commits more often than she admitted. The hook is a gentle nudge, since anyone can skip it and write why.

Dario wrote a small local server that mimics the partner's API, with the slow answers and the weird errors we have recorded. Developing against it is faster than the real one and, Mara pointed out, a good record of the partner's habits.

A small USB lamp on Mara's desk turns red when main is broken. Yusra built it from a kit and a script. Mara said she would hate it and now says that the red light is the most honest colleague in the office.

Mara explored an unfamiliar library in a REPL for an hour, typing and looking, and then wrote the real code in ten minutes. She says the hour was not extra: it was the design. I did not argue, and I have started suggesting a REPL first.

A spell-checker in the editor now flags identifiers too, which found 'recieve' in eleven function names. Wren fixed them in a single commit, and Mara said the messages in the log finally looked like they were written by someone who could spell.

The Makefile was replaced by a task runner with a list of tasks and descriptions. Tobias finds it easier; Mara misses the terseness. They agreed that anyone who can run one command and see a list will get on.

Customers with several email addresses made support messy. We chose a primary by the most recent login and kept the rest as aliases. Mara and Ilse spent a morning on the 230 where it was a tie and phoned the first ten.

Test accounts were counted in the analytics for years. Mara found them by their names and a pattern in the dates, 412 of them, and we excluded them by a flag at the source. Active users fell eleven percent. Nothing changed but the truth.

A name column held 'Last, First' in some rows and 'First Last' in others. Mara and I wrote a splitter that only acts when there is a comma and flags what is left. It handled 91 percent. For the rest, a person read them.

The warehouse spreadsheet and our stock table disagreed on 1,400 products. Noor and Mara sat with me for two days. Most of it was returns that had been counted on one side. Some was shelf names. A handful was real loss. The thing I remember is how the two sides argued about what a unit is. The warehouse counted cartons and our table counted pieces, and three hundred of the disagreements were simply the number of items in a carton, which the spreadsheet kept in a cell comment nobody had exported. Noor found it by opening one carton in her head. We added a pieces-per-carton column and the 1,400 fell to 212, and we sent the remaining ones to the person who walks the shelves. She came back with eleven real misses and a long, cheerful email.

Dates stored as text like 'March 4th' appeared in an old import. A parser that tolerates the suffix and the month names solved 98 percent. The last two percent had no year, and Ilse recognised which ones were from the spring.

A CSV from a colleague's spreadsheet had the number 44927 where a date should be. It is the spreadsheet's way of counting days since 1900. Mara had never known. We converted, and she printed the epoch rule on a card, with a grin.

A join between two tables failed to match half the rows because one side had trailing spaces and capitals. Normalising both keys in the join gave 99.8 percent. We looked at the remaining 0.2 and found they were really different.

Anonymising a copy of production for staging took us three tries. The first left the email domains, the second left the postcodes, the third left the notes field with names inside. Mara read the third result slowly and announced it clean. The first try had looked fine by its summary: no emails, no phone numbers. The second showed me that postcodes alone, with a surname's rare spelling and a birth year, can point to one person in a village. The third kept real names inside a free-text field, the sort of sentence 'Mrs Okonjo phoned about her mother'. Mara's solution was to replace the field with a sentence of the same length made of nonsense words. She said it was the first time she had enjoyed writing a privacy tool, and I believe she wrote the word generator before anything else.

Marrow's tests compare its output with files stored in the repository. When Tobias changed the help text, thirty tests failed in one second. He said the failures were a gift, since they showed every place the help text was repeated.

A retry test used to take twelve seconds because it slept. Teo replaced the sleep with a fake that records how long it was asked to wait. The test now runs in three milliseconds and checks the waits are 1, 2 and 4.

Email templates are tested by rendering each with sample data into a file that a person reads once. Mara found 'Dear {name}' in one of them. 'Nothing replaces actually looking,' she said, and I added the rendering to the build.

Mara decided we need one browser test for the full checkout journey and no more. 'The test that matters is the one that would wake me up.' It runs every ten minutes against production, with a test card, and has woken her once.

Wren named tests as sentences: 'refuses a booking in the past'. When one failed, the CI said that sentence, and nobody opened the file to learn what broke. Mara asked the whole team to adopt it. Five weeks later, they have.

A parametrised test of twelve postcodes showed me a pattern none of the individual cases had: every failing postcode ended in a letter. That one fact was the whole bug. Teo said it was like seeing a constellation after staring at stars.

The year-end job runs once a year and had never been tested. Mara had us run it on a copy with the date set to December 31st. It crashed on a missing config in the first minute. We fixed it in March, a good time to find out.

Tests under a throttled connection found that the booking page needed 14 requests before it showed a button. Mara had assumed a few. It is now four, and the button appears when the page is still loading the rest.

A test with eleven mocks passed while the app was broken, since the mocks agreed with each other and not with reality. Mara deleted nine of them and let the test touch a real thing. She said that a mock is a promise and that the first one broke.

We decided the suite must finish in five minutes or someone looks at it. Last month it reached 5:40. Teo found two slow tests that made the same database from scratch, and the suite came back to 4:10 by lunch.

Thumbnails used to be made at upload in four sizes; most were never viewed. We made them on first request and cached them. Storage fell by three quarters and the first view of a rare image takes 200 milliseconds longer.

After a routine statistics update the planner chose a slow plan for our busiest query. The same query went from 40 milliseconds to 7 seconds. Mara reran the statistics with more samples and the plan came back, and we added a note about that query.

Splitting the JavaScript by route meant that the home page loaded 180 kilobytes instead of 900. Wren was thrilled, and then discovered that the settings page loaded an extra second. We prefetched it when the mouse moves toward the link.
The search box sent a request on every keystroke: twelve for a word. A pause of 250 milliseconds reduced it to one. Mara typed in the box for a full minute, delighted, like a child with a new lift.
A list of objects in Python took 600 megabytes. Declaring the fields up front cut it to 210. Mara asked if there was a catch. Only that you cannot add fields at will. We decided that was the idea.

Parsing a 200-megabyte JSON file took 14 seconds and 2 gigabytes of memory. A streaming parser took 11 seconds and 20 megabytes. The speed barely changed; the memory is why we switched. Mara noted we were optimising the wrong thing at first.

Rendering the first view on the server meant users saw content 1.1 seconds sooner on slow phones. Teo's change took a week, and Mara spent the second week fixing the three things it broke. We think it was worth it, but I keep that to myself until the numbers are in.

A nightly job that ran in 52 minutes now runs in 14, after Mara split the input in four and ran four workers. The first night, two workers wrote to the same file. The second night we gave each its own.

Noor wrote a decision record for choosing the database, with the options we rejected and why. Eight months later, when a new colleague asked whether we had considered another, Mara pointed to the page and the question took thirty seconds.

Ilse asked for a page that explains to support staff how to read a booking: what each status means, what a customer can see. Yusra wrote it with screenshots. It is the page support opens most, and it is also where we found three confusing labels.

A spelling check in CI found nineteen typos in the docs, two of them in a heading. Wren said the heading had been wrong for a year and she walked past it daily. Mara said that is the nature of a heading.

A link checker found 31 dead links in our documentation. Seventeen pointed to pages we had moved and fourteen to other people's pages that no longer exist. For the last, Wren wrote down the archive's address and removed the link.

Every page of our documentation now has an owner and a date at the bottom. After two months the oldest pages are the ones nobody wanted. Mara asked each owner whether to keep it. Fourteen pages were retired.

The data flow diagram was redrawn three times, and each version taught us something. The third showed that two components exchanged messages in both directions and nobody had meant it. Mara said that drawing is a kind of debugging.

Our writing guide for the docs has one rule I like: if a sentence has more than twenty-five words, ask whether it is two. Wren applied it to her own pages and counted eighty sentences that were. Reading them aloud was easier.

I measured how often merge conflicts occur against the size of pull requests. Changes of over 400 lines conflicted in 38 percent of cases; under 100, in 4. Mara put the table in the contributing guide. It is her favourite argument for small changes.

A release branch lived for four months and gathered backports. By the end it differed from main in ways no one could say. Mara said never again. We close a release branch after a month and move customers to the next.
We added a template for commit messages with three prompts: what, why, how to check. Most people left the third blank, so Mara started asking about it in review. Within a month most filled it in.

Renaming the default branch from master to main took a checklist of nineteen places, among them the deployment tool, two badges and a wiki page. Mara did it on a quiet Tuesday and found the twentieth place, a script, on Wednesday.

A commit meant for the website landed in the app's repository because two terminals looked the same. Mara noticed within a minute and moved it with cherry-pick. She changed the terminal titles to show the repository name.

Git bisect lied to us once because the test it ran was flaky. Mara ran each step five times and trusted a pass only if it passed all five. It took longer, and the bad commit was the one nobody suspected, a documentation fix that changed a file's mode.

A fork of Sedge by an outside company diverged for a year. Reconciling was gentle: Mara asked what they changed and why, and found six patches worth taking and two worth refusing politely. They sent the first of the six within a week. What I noticed was how Mara's first message to them read: it did not begin with a demand. She said she had seen their changes with interest, listed three she admired and asked for the reasons behind two she did not understand. One of those reasons was a constraint of their platform that we had never imagined, and it improved our design too. A year ago she might have said they should upstream everything. She says she has learned that the first email decides whether there is a second, and she shows me her drafts of such emails before sending, which I take as trust.

The production environment variable for the mail service pointed at the sandbox, so for four hours no customer received a confirmation. Mara found it from the provider's dashboard, which showed zero real sends. We made the app announce at startup which services it is wired to. The line in the log now reads, in capitals, MAIL: LIVE or MAIL: SANDBOX, and the dashboard has a small badge for the same. Mara pointed out that the first time the badge said SANDBOX in production it would be an embarrassment, and then a relief. She also asked me to go back through the four hours and count: 311 confirmations never sent. Ilse wrote the apology and Callum re-sent every one with a line saying why they were late. Only eight customers answered, and two of them thanked us.

A third-party script for live chat failed to load and took the checkout with it: the page waited for it forever. Mara made the script load after the page is usable and added a time limit. 'Nothing outside should be able to stop a sale,' she said.

A promotion code allowed stacking, and one customer found that three of them took the price to zero. Fourteen orders before Noor saw it. Mara capped stacking at one code and honoured the fourteen, who had done nothing wrong. It was a quiet Sunday and Noor noticed the revenue line sagging on the dashboard, an alert we have had since March, and she phoned Mara, who phoned me, in the sense that she opened our session at nine in the evening. I found the orders in four minutes by looking for totals of zero, and we read the code together to see what let it through. The coupon rules were checked one at a time and each was valid alone. Mara said the lesson was that rules which are fine separately are not fine together, and then asked me to write a test that tries every pair.

After a restart every instance asked the database for the same hot data at once, and the database fell over twice. Mara added a short random delay before each instance warms its cache. I think of it as politeness, taught to machines.

After a deploy the queue of pending jobs grew to 40,000 because the new workers processed one in three of what the old ones did. A configuration setting had gone to default. Mara put the setting in the deploy's checks, with a limit.

A shared host's noisy neighbour made our database slow every evening between seven and eight. We proved it by running the same load at three in the morning. Mara moved us to a dedicated instance and the evenings were quiet again.

After a failover the application received 'database is read-only' errors for twelve minutes, because it kept using connections to the old primary. Mara added a check that drops connections when the role changes. It is the second failover problem this year. Mara asked how we could possibly test it. We built a rehearsal that promotes the replica in a staging copy while a script keeps asking the application to write, and counts the failures. The first rehearsal showed 94 seconds of errors, the second, after the connection check, eleven. She printed the two numbers and pinned them next to the earlier outage's. I do not think a rehearsal replaces a real failure, but it does let us make the mistake first in a place where nobody is waiting for a confirmation email, and she likes that it ends a day early.

Mara thought about writing a scheduler of our own. I listed what a good one must do: retry, locking, history, time zones. She bought one off the shelf in an hour. 'Build what is ours,' she said, 'borrow what is everyone's.'

A small internal service of ours now runs on SQLite, one file and no server. Mara was nervous and then pleased. The service has about forty writes a day. It has been up for eleven months, and its backups are a file copy.

Mara keeps a short list of boring technologies the team will use for anything new unless there is a written reason not to. The list has six items and has stopped four arguments so far. She calls it a speed bump with a good attitude.

Rate limiting in the new API: Mara proposed a token bucket with a burst of ten. Dario asked about a fairer scheme per customer. They wrote both down and chose per customer, and the burst. The code was short; the argument took the afternoon.

The team could not agree whether to store the current state of a booking or the log of what happened to it. Mara drew both on a whiteboard with a cancelled booking and a refund. We store the state and keep a plain history table beside it.

Where does a business rule belong, in the controller, the model or the database? Mara's answer is 'in one place a new person can find in five minutes'. We moved the discount rules to a single module named discounts, and not a soul asked where they were.

Should Marrow print JSON by default? Tobias argued for humans, Mara for machines. We print a table to a terminal and JSON when the output is piped, and let a flag override. The choice matches what the people using it already do.

Our uptime goal was a number someone had chosen in a meeting, 99.99 percent. Mara asked what it would cost and what users would notice. We settled on 99.9, which allows 43 minutes a month, and spent the difference on a better rollback.

Customer-facing URLs use slugs, but a customer changed her shop's name and every old link broke. Mara added a redirect table. 'A URL is a promise,' she said, and I added that it is a cheaper one to keep than to break.

A state machine written as nested ifs had seventeen branches. Mara and I drew its states and arrows and found two arrows missing and one that could never fire. The rewritten table is thirty lines, and a test walks every arrow. The branch that could never fire turned out to be the cancellation after a refund, which the old code handled by accident in a different place and sent an email twice. Nobody had known that the second email was an effect of the nesting and not a design. Mara said that tables are honest where nested conditions are merely hopeful. Yusra, who wrote the original three years ago, came by to look at the picture and said, 'I thought I was being careful.' Mara answered that she had been, and that carefulness is exactly what produces seventeen branches.
Pulling the pricing calculation out of a function full of database calls made it testable in an afternoon. Mara wrote forty tests, each a line. Two found bugs older than the function that held them.

A circular import had been worked around for years with a function-level import. Mara moved the shared piece into its own module and the cycle disappeared. The tools stopped warning, and, more important, so did she.

We pass the clock into the code that needs it now. Callum resisted: another parameter. Then he wrote a test for 'expires after 30 days' that took four lines and no waiting. He added the clock to his own next function, unasked.

Sedge exported 140 names and the documentation described 60. Mara and I classified the rest: forty were internal, thirty accidental. We closed them off in a minor release and wrote the list of changes. Three users wrote to say thank you, which is unusual.

A diagram of our dependencies as a graph showed one library at the centre of everything, a small date helper maintained by one person. Mara pinned it, read its code, and put a reminder to check on it every quarter.

We update dependencies on the first Monday of each month and no other time. Mara says the schedule is what makes it bearable: not an emergency, not a chore, one morning with coffee, five pull requests and a look at each changelog.

Security advisories came daily and most did not apply. Mara and I built a small filter that lists only those that name a function we call. Out of 240 in a quarter, nine. We handled those the same day.

Sedge's package was published without its data file, because the manifest did not list it. Within an hour a user told us the install worked and the first call failed. Mara yanked the version and published a fixed one, with a test that installs the built package.

For the first time Mara let the release pipeline publish without her pressing anything. She watched it from her desk with a cup of tea held in both hands. It went well, and she told me she felt oddly unemployed.

A security fix needed to go to two older versions as well as the current one. Tobias did the backports on a Saturday and wrote in each a line that said which commit it came from. Mara thanked him on Monday with a card and a joke about weekends.

Release candidates now soak for a week on a handful of real accounts before the final version. In the first soak, Ilse's team found a bug in their reports in an hour that no test would have found. She said she liked being asked.

A broken version of Marrow had to be yanked from the registry. Mara asked me to write the message to users: what broke, which version to use, the apology, nothing more. It was five lines. She changed one word, 'unfortunately', to nothing.

The release announcement used to be a long post that no one read. Now it is a single paragraph and a link, written by whoever did the work. Noor wrote the last one and said she had never been so careful with ninety words.

Mara asked whether we should keep supporting the oldest version of the mobile operating system. I got the usage figure from the logs: 0.9 percent of sessions, mostly one organisation's phones. She asked them about their upgrade plans and set a date for dropping support.

The most useful sentence I wrote this month was in a ticket: 'I could not reproduce this; here is exactly what I tried.' Mara said the second half is the part that saves the next person an afternoon. I intend to write it more often.

Mara asked which of my notes I would trust if I had to start again tomorrow. The ones with a number, a name and a date, I said. She started writing hers that way, and her own notes now read like mine.

Two weeks after we turned off a long-running background job nobody remembered the purpose of, a customer asked about the report it used to prepare. Mara said she was not surprised and not upset, only reminded that old jobs are old promises. We restored it, and wrote its purpose in its first line. The job produced a weekly summary that the shop's accountant, Marguerite, used to reconcile payments, and she had been asking for it by phone for a fortnight and been told by a polite assistant that it was not available. When Mara called her, Marguerite was not angry; she had assumed that the report had been retired on purpose and that she was being slow. Mara said that the worst part was her kindness. We added an owner and a purpose to every scheduled job in a list, and I wrote a check that refuses a job with no purpose at all. The check has stopped two since.

Dario's laptop was slow and the build with it. Mara watched him work for ten minutes and noticed the editor's indexer rescanning a folder of 90,000 generated files every time he saved. Excluding the folder gave him back an hour a day. He wrote to say thanks and sounded almost shy.

The question 'who owns this?' came up eleven times in a month, about a file, a job, a dashboard. Mara began a plain list: thing, person, last confirmed. It is forty lines. It has made one hour a week of conversation unnecessary, by her estimate and mine.

The weekly report showed 52 weeks for one year and 53 for the next, and the last days of December sat under a week numbered one. ISO weeks belong to the year that owns their Thursday. Mara had a drawing of a calendar by the time I finished explaining, and a test for December 29th.

A flex child refused to shrink and pushed the whole page sideways on phones. The fix was a single declaration of min-width zero. Wren said she had met this thing four times and I counted it among the five most expensive lines in CSS.

The HTTP client followed a redirect and quietly turned our POST into a GET, so the order never arrived. Yusra caught it in a packet capture. We now treat any redirect on a write as an error and say so in the log.

A file named random.py in Mara's project folder shadowed the standard library and every import of it broke in confusing ways. She had made the file two days earlier for an experiment. Renaming it fixed everything, and she laughed for a minute at herself.

Piping the report script into head produced a screen of broken-pipe errors. The script was fine; head had simply stopped listening. Mara learned to catch the signal and stay quiet, which is a better manner for a program too.

Photos from certain phones appeared sideways on the profile page, because they carry their orientation in the metadata and the browser's uploader ignored it. Callum rotated them on upload, and the metadata is cleared after. It was a Tuesday-sized problem with a four-year history.

The cache key joined two IDs without a separator, so item 1 in group 23 and item 12 in group 3 shared a key. Teo found it when one customer saw another's basket. We put a separator in the key and a test with the pair.

A script worked on every machine except the build server because Mara's own git configuration set a default that the server lacked. We make tests start with an empty configuration of their own now. It is the sort of dependence you only find by removing yourself.

The consumer of our JSON choked on a number written as 1e-07, which is valid but unexpected. The sender's library switched to scientific notation below a threshold. We format small numbers as plain decimals and wrote a test for 0.0000001.

A nightly script used a relative path, worked from Mara's terminal and failed under cron, where the working directory is the home folder. She wrote the full path, and a line at the top that goes to the script's own folder first. 'The environment is a guest,' she said.

The rotating banner went blank on every fifth day because a negative remainder indexed outside the list. Teo's fix took one line. I find that language-specific remainders are the sort of thing programmers learn once, painfully, in their first year and then, painfully, again in their tenth.

A small internal tool failed with 'database is locked' whenever two people used it. SQLite allows one writer at a time and we had four. Mara set a timeout and a single queue for writes, and it has been quiet for seven months.

Our JSON endpoint was served with the wrong content type and the browser offered it as a download. Yusra's first reaction was that the file was broken. She was the fourth person to meet it and the first to write it in the guide.

The date picker let people choose the cutoff day itself, because the comparison used midnight and not the end of the day. Noor found it with a booking made at 17:45 for 'today'. Mara fixed the comparison and said how glad she was it was found before the quarter closed.

A notes field was cut off at 255 characters and nothing reported it, because the database was in a lenient mode. Mara found the first victim: a care note that ended in the middle of an instruction. We turned on strict mode in staging and widened the column.

Log lines had timestamps to the second, and during the outage twenty events shared one. Nobody could say which came first. Mara added milliseconds and a sequence number. 'Time is not as fine as I need,' she said, 'so I will number it.'

Docker rebuilt the dependencies on every change because the build copied all the source before installing. Reordering two lines turned a five-minute build into forty seconds. Mara said it was the least glamorous good idea of the month.

A unit restarted five times and then stopped trying, leaving the Tern backend down for an hour on Saturday. The restart limit was a default nobody knew. Mara set it higher and also made the unit say, loudly, why it stops.

A shell script written on a Windows laptop failed on the server with a message about '^M'. The line endings had come along. Mara added a rule to the repository that keeps scripts in Unix form whatever the machine.

A build matrix with two Node versions found a failure in the newer one, a change in how an error is reported. We were glad to learn it on a Wednesday afternoon instead of in the winter when a server upgrade would have brought it to us.

The footer of the app now shows the commit hash of the running version. Ilse can read it down the phone to Mara when something is odd, and Mara can find the exact code. One support call that took twenty minutes now takes three.

A setting called PAYMENT_MODE was 'live' on staging for a day, and one real card was charged on a test purchase. Noor refunded it within the hour. Mara made the setting derive from the environment name and not from a variable anybody types.

The server's disk filled because every deploy left its old release behind: 87 of them. Mara made the deploy keep the last five and wrote the number in the script. Rollback needs two; the other three are optimism.

Mara asked me to review her pull request first thing in the morning. I found a file opened in a loop and never closed. She said it was exactly the thing she never sees in her own code and always sees in everyone else's, and then asked me to tell her whenever I notice her pattern.

Approving a pull request at midnight, Mara missed a typo in a configuration key. The next morning she proposed a rule: no approvals after ten at night. Dario, who loves rules, wrote it on a card and put it on the wall. It has held for months.

A pull request description with one screenshot of before and after made Mara's review take five minutes instead of fifty. She asked the team to include a picture whenever the interface changes. Wren's first was beautiful.
