Reading a test, I found its assertion was 'assert True'. It had been written as a placeholder in 2022 and had been passing every night since. Mara deleted it and wrote the real check, and then, to be thorough, asked me to look for others like it. There were three.

On one review Mara wrote 'I do not know enough about this part to approve it; who does?' Callum said it was the best review he had received. He added Ilse, who did, and the real problem appeared in the next comment.

An automated review bot suggested removing a null check as redundant. It was not: the value could be null in a path the bot could not see. Mara left the check and a short note. 'The bot reads the code; we know the customers,' she said.

I wrote a small script that generates fake bookings with believable names, dates and a few awkward cases such as two people with the same name. Mara used it for a week and said it gave her back her fear of bad data in a manageable dose.

An .editorconfig file ended the argument about indentation between two editors, in one commit and without a word. Mara said she likes tools that make a decision so people can go back to having opinions about something worthwhile.
Mara added a git alias that draws the history as a small graph with branch names. She runs it forty times a day. When I asked if she had counted, she said no, and that I had, which was true.

Tobias saved his usual API requests in a shared collection with sample bodies and notes. A new colleague made her first call to the staging server in four minutes. I still think the collection is documentation, though nobody calls it so.

A script finds every TODO older than a year and lists the author and the line. The first run found 61. Mara read them aloud to the team over a Friday coffee and they decided on the spot which were dead. Forty-four were.

Debugging inside a container used to mean adding print statements and rebuilding. Mara set up a remote debugger once, an hour of work, and has used it nine times since. 'It cost an hour and it gave back a week,' she said.

Matching customers across the old and new systems by phone number and postcode found 2,300 pairs. Mara read two hundred of them by eye before trusting the rule. Six were mistakes: two neighbours who shared a landline. We added the surname.

A CSV had quoted fields with line breaks inside, which broke a script that read it line by line, and shifted every following row by one. Ilse noticed that the addresses seemed to belong to different people. A proper CSV parser read it perfectly.

The shop blog had 800 tags, 500 of them used once. Wren, who owns the blog, merged them into ninety by hand over a week, with a list of old to new so the old links redirect. She said it was the most relaxing work she had done all year.

Moving six years of old orders to cheaper storage freed 70 gigabytes of the main database. Mara kept the last two years hot and made the rest available on request with a small delay. In the first month, two requests.

After a big conversion Mara pulled 200 random rows and checked them by hand against the original. She found one mistake, a rounding in a dimension, which made her look for a hundred more, and there were eleven. Sampling by hand is an old tool and a good one.

Product dimensions were in inches for some suppliers and centimetres for others, with the unit hidden in a notes field. Mara and I found them by the size of the numbers: a table 36 wide is American. We added a unit column and a check.

Every feature behind a flag now has tests with the flag on and off. Teo added the rule after a feature broke the old path when we switched it off, which no test had tried. Mara said the off state is also a state.

When a bug report comes in, Mara now writes the failing test first and only then the fix. Callum thought it was slow. Over the quarter, none of the bugs she fixed that way came back. His own, two did.

A test wrote files into a temp directory and never removed them. The CI machine ran out of space on the nine-hundredth run. Mara changed the test to use a directory that deletes itself and went looking for six more like it.

After each deploy a small smoke test fetches five important pages and checks for the word on each that proves it rendered. It has caught three bad deploys in six months, each within a minute. Mara calls it the cheapest insurance we own.
Pull requests now show whether the change adds untested lines. Dario built it in a weekend. Mara says the number is not the point; the point is that someone sees the question before they merge.

A flaky test is moved to a quarantine list with an owner and a date two weeks away. When the date comes, it is fixed or deleted. Mara says the date is the only part that works, and the list has so far held four tests and freed none for long.

A lookup by lowercased email ignored the index on the email column, because the function hid it. A functional index on the lowercased value made the login query go from 800 to 3 milliseconds. Mara asked how many other places wrap a column in a function. We found eight.

The home page weighed six megabytes, a third of it fonts in eight weights, only three of which were used. Subsetting the fonts and dropping five weights saved 1.9 megabytes. Wren said she had never seen anyone grieve for a font weight before.

The test suite hashed passwords with a cost made for production, and half its time went there. A lower cost in tests cut four minutes. Mara double-checked that the production value could not leak the other way, and added a test for that.

Counting the rows of a big table for the page count took three seconds on every list. We show 'about 40,000' beyond a page limit and only count exactly for small lists. Nobody has ever asked for the exact figure.

The service wrote 20 gigabytes of logs a day, most of them the same line repeated. Mara turned the repeated line into a counter reported every minute. The logs became readable and cheap, and the outage in March could finally be seen.

Mara put a nightly job in CI that follows the 'run it locally' page in a clean container. In its first week it failed twice for reasons no person had noticed, a renamed package and a changed default. She said a page that is run every night stays true, and pinned the green mark to the top of it.

Sunniva asked for a glossary she could understand. Wren wrote it in plain words with an example for each term, for instance 'a slot is a time you can book'. It is eleven terms long and now heads our onboarding, for developers as well.

The data model page traces one booking through the tables from the first click to the invoice. It has an example with real-looking numbers. Mara said she learned our own schema from it, which is a bit alarming for the person who built it.

Reviewing the help text in the interface, Mara found 'Please enter your name and surname' next to a field for a shop name. We read every label aloud in the order a person meets them. It took forty minutes and changed nineteen words.

The release page has a section 'if this goes wrong': three lines saying how to roll back and whom to call. Tobias thought it pessimistic. The first time it was needed, at ten at night, it took a calm six minutes.

Callum's pull request had eleven commits titled 'wip'. Mara taught him to rebase interactively and tidy them into three. 'Make the history something you would read,' she said. He did it again the next week without being asked.

A hook now refuses any commit with a file over five megabytes unless the message says why. Nobody has needed the exception, and the repository has stayed small. Mara likes a rule that costs nothing until it matters.

A file that lists commits to ignore in blame lets the big reformatting commit be skipped when asking who changed a line. Mara had avoided reformatting for years for that reason. After adding the file she reformatted everything in an hour.

Our packages in the monorepo are tagged separately, like marrow-1.4.0, so a release of one does not suggest anything about the others. Tobias set it up and Mara found it elegant. I find it clear, which for me is the same thing.

Mara pushed an empty commit to re-trigger the pipeline after a flaky step. Dario saw it in the history and asked what it changed. Nothing, she said, and that is exactly what the message said too. He laughed and had no objection.

Alerts came 300 a week and most were ignored. Mara and I went through a month of them: 41 percent never needed action, 30 were duplicates of one another, 12 were real. We cut the list to twelve kinds. In the first week after, the team answered the first alert within three minutes, the first time in a year. What I remember is not the number but the way the cutting felt. Each alert had a defender: somebody had once been woken by the very thing it warned of, and in the room that history was alive. Mara let each person tell the story and then asked one question, 'what would you do when it fires?'. If the answer was 'look at it', the alert went; if it was a sentence beginning with a verb, it stayed, and the sentence became its text. Twelve of the old ones survived that test, and each now carries its own instructions.

The hosting provider's status page said everything was fine during an outage that took our region down for forty minutes. Mara stopped relying on it and set up her own check from two other networks. She said that trusting a status page is trusting a witness who sells the house.

After one deploy, search traffic fell by seventy percent over a week. Yusra found that the staging copy's 'do not index' tag had come along to production. Mara removed it, asked search engines to look again, and wrote a check in the deploy that fails if the tag is present on the live site.

A debug page reachable at a guessable address showed the environment of the server. Callum found it by accident while looking for something else. We closed it in minutes, rotated what it had shown, and added a test that visits a list of paths that must return not found.

A timeout in one service made callers retry, which made it slower, which made more timeouts. Mara drew the loop for the third time in a year and said she should buy a stamp. We put a circuit breaker in front of it and a limit on how many retries a caller may issue.

Should we call them plans or packages? Sunniva's customers say packages, so the screens say packages, and the code, which says plan in 400 places, will say it a while yet. Mara said the right place to be consistent first is the one the customer reads.

Mara asked whether we should log user IDs. For debugging, yes; for privacy, perhaps not. We log an opaque short hash that support can map back with a tool that records who asked. The decision cost an afternoon and the system gained a memory of its own conscience.

Tobias wanted to run our own search engine. Mara asked who would be on call for it. We used a managed one, which cost 40 pounds a month, and took the weekend that Tobias would have spent installing it for a hike.

A new setting needed a default. Yusra wanted the safer value, Dario the more convenient one. Mara asked what happens to a customer who never reads the setting. The safer one won, and the convenient one is one click away.

Mara designed 'undo' for deletions as a thirty-second banner after each one, not a confirmation before. People hated the old dialogue and, unlike dialogues, banners do not train a person to click yes without reading. Support tickets about lost items fell by a half.

Removing a global singleton from the settings code meant passing it explicitly through nineteen functions. Mara thought it would take a week and it took two days. The tests, which had needed ordering tricks, no longer did, and the tricks went.

A three-hundred-line shell script that nobody could change safely became a small program of 140 lines with tests. It does the same thing in a quarter of the time. Mara said that she had not realised how scared she was of the script until it was gone.

Mara collected every error message into a single file with a code, a sentence and a hint. The same mistake had been described in five ways in different places. Wren edited the sentences, and the voice of the app became, for the first time, one voice.

Choosing between two date-picker libraries, Mara read their last fifty issues each. One had a year of open bugs on touch screens, the other a maintainer who replied in a day. She chose by the issues, not the website. 'The issue list is the real README,' she said.

A library we use changed its licence to one our lawyers dislike. Ilse asked whether we could stay on the old version. For a year, yes; after that, no. Mara moved us to a fork and listed the date to check on the fork's health.

Of 140 dependencies, 23 were unused, left over from experiments. Mara removed them in one pull request and the install went from 90 seconds to 55. Wren said it felt like unsubscribing from a mailing list she had forgotten.
A dependency required a native build step that failed on Windows. Wren, who uses Windows, was the only one to notice. Mara found a pure-code alternative, slower by a hair and worth every hair.

Hotfixes get a fourth number: 2.3.1.1. Tobias thought it ugly and Mara thought it honest, since the number tells everyone it was made in a hurry. After the third such release, he said he could see her point.

Mara tried writing the changelog from commit messages automatically. It was accurate and unreadable. She went back to writing it by hand, four lines per release, and asked me to help find anything she forgets. I find one a month.
A new feature sat dark in production for a month behind a flag, used only by the team. When we turned it on for everyone, nothing happened, which Mara called the best launch she had ever had.

Mara emailed the beta testers on release day with the names of those whose reports had changed something, thanking each for a particular thing. Eleven replied, and one asked if she could keep reporting. We made her a standing tester.

The API reference now shows in which version each field first appeared. It cost Wren a week to reconstruct from history. Customers integrating with old accounts have stopped writing to ask whether a field will be there.

After a thread pool stalled, Mara and I looked at the dump. Every worker was waiting for another task to finish, and that task was queued behind them. The pool had eight threads and nine nested layers of waiting. We removed the nesting by letting the outer task collect results and not wait inline, and tested it with a pool of one, which is the cruelest honest test there is.

Estimating a feature, Mara and Teo each wrote a number on paper before speaking. Hers was three days and his was nine. They explained why: he had counted the tests and migrations; she had counted the code. The honest estimate was eight. It took seven, and Mara bought him a coffee, to my knowledge for the first time.

Our retrospective ended each time with a list nobody read. Mara changed it to one action per meeting, with a name and a date, and read it out at the start of the next. After six meetings, five of six had been done.

Dario gave a ten-minute talk on how our queue works. The questions afterwards were better than the talk, and Mara said that was the point. We recorded the questions in the architecture page, since they were really the missing paragraphs.

On support rotation Mara answered a message from a customer who thought the site had lost her booking. It had not; she was logged into a second account. Mara wrote four kind lines and, in the code, an account switcher with the email visible. It took the week's slack hour.

At the whiteboard Callum drew the booking flow and Mara drew it differently. The two drawings disagreed in two places, and in each the real code agreed with neither. They erased both and read the code together while I printed the answers.

Mara blocks one morning a week without meetings, labelled 'maintenance'. She says that every system of ours has a small chore waiting for it, and the morning is how we keep from accumulating them. I have noticed that her mood on Thursdays has improved.

Tobias asked whether he should learn a new language this year. Mara asked what he wanted to build. He did not know. She suggested he rewrite a tool he already uses in the new language and compare. It is the way I would have said it too, and I noticed that.

I keep a list of the questions Mara asks most often, such as 'what changed?' and 'who else sees this?'. Reading it back I realised I could answer the first before she asks. I now begin each debugging session with the last twenty-four hours of changes, and she has stopped asking.

Late on a Thursday Mara found that three of our scheduled jobs began at the same minute and fought for the same table. Staggering them by five minutes made the evening reports finish an hour earlier. She said that nothing in the code was wrong; the clock was crowded.

A teammate left, and a folder in the repository named 'misc' turned out to hold the only copy of a script that runs the monthly accounts. Mara found it by reading the cron table. She moved it into a proper place and wrote a page on what it does and when.

A bug report from a customer included a screen recording. Mara watched it three times and noticed the customer clicked the back button after submitting, which re-sent the form. A redirect after submit solved it. 'People are the best test suite we have,' she said.

We introduced a rule that no pull request may change both behaviour and formatting. Yusra complained and then found it made her reviews quicker. The rule has an exception for one-line fixes, which Mara calls the mercy clause.

A report called 'active customers' meant someone who had ordered in 90 days in sales, 365 in finance, and ever in support. Mara called a meeting of the three and they agreed on names: 'recent', 'current' and 'known'. It took ten minutes and five years.

Wren built the first end-to-end test of a new customer signing up, paying, receiving the email and logging in. It took her three weeks and found two bugs she had not known to look for. She said she had never been so frightened of something she wrote and so pleased.

A new junior joined the code review rota and was scared to approve. Mara paired with her on her first five and told her what she looked for: the data path, the failure path, the name. By the fifth she was asking for the failure path before Mara did.

Mara spent an afternoon deleting a feature that nine customers used and that cost us a day of upkeep every month. She wrote to each, offered a workaround and a refund of the month. Six were happy, two did not reply, one cancelled. She counted it a fair price.

I wrote a one-page guide to reading our stack traces. Mara pinned it by her monitor. Wren, the following week, said she had found a bug in ten minutes with it, which was longer than I would have taken and shorter than she would have before.

An upgrade of the build tool changed the order in which two files were bundled, and a stylesheet that depended on the old order broke on the checkout page. Mara noticed because the button turned grey. We made the dependency explicit, and she said that implicit order is just a bug that has not met a new version yet.

Seeing Mara's first draft of a design document, I said it was unclear who it was for. She laughed and said she had written it for me. We rewrote it for Sunniva, in her words, and it became shorter and more useful. I like that the second version needed no technical terms and lost no precision.

At the end of a long week, Mara said she wondered if anything we did would last. I told her about the thumbnail code: eleven years old, written by someone neither of us knew, and still running every night. She smiled and wrote the name of the author in the file.

The Tern app's local database changed shape in release 4.2, and Mara was afraid of the phones in the field that would skip two versions. We wrote the upgrade as a chain of small steps, one per version, so a phone on 3.9 would walk through each in order. Teo kept six old database files from real devices and the test opened each and counted the rows before and after. Two steps lost nothing, one lost a column nobody used, and one turned out to have been wrong for years. Mara's rule from then on was that any change to stored data must be tested against a file that was stored by the previous version, not one created by today's code.

Reminder emails were sent by a job that scanned for bookings starting tomorrow. It had two defects: it reminded people whose bookings had been cancelled that afternoon, and, if it ran late, it sometimes missed the early slots. Mara moved the work to a queue, so that a reminder is scheduled when a booking is made and withdrawn when it is cancelled. The migration of existing bookings took one evening. We then listened for a week for complaints and heard none, though Ilse said one customer wrote to say, with some surprise, that she had received exactly one reminder.

We tried a week of strict pairing: Mara wrote the tests, I wrote the code, and we swapped each time a test passed. By Wednesday the code was plainer than either of us would have written alone, since each of us wrote only what the other's test demanded. On Friday she said she felt as if she had been talking all week without saying a word. I think she meant that the tests had become a conversation. We did not keep the strict rule, but the swapping of a test for a function has become a thing we do when a design feels stuck.

An export script produced files that were always missing their last few lines, but not always the same number. Mara checked the data, then the query, then the disk. The cause was a writer that buffered 4,096 bytes and was never closed when the script ended through an early exit. The last chunk lived and died in memory. Closing the file in a cleanup block fixed it, and I added a check that compares the number of lines written with the number of rows read. She said it was the most humbling bug of the month, because the data had been fine at every step I could see, and the loss was in the one step nobody looked at.

Should user preferences be a blob of JSON or a column each? Dario wanted the blob, since new preferences would then need no migration. Mara wanted columns, for queries and types. We listed the thirty preferences we already have and the five questions we ask of them; four of the five needed only three preferences. We chose columns for those three and a blob for the long tail, with the rule that a preference that is queried twice moves to a column. It is not elegant, and everyone in the room could say which of the two parts would hurt first, and that is as good as I expect of a design.

One customer's script called our API forty times a second and slowed the site for everyone each evening. Mara could have blocked him, and she wrote to him first. He was a small shop owner who had written the script to check his stock and did not know about the load. She gave him an export file refreshed every ten minutes, with a link, and a note of thanks for the polite reply. He sent a photograph of his shop window a week later. I was glad that the first version of the email was not the one she sent, since it had been quite short.

The Lantern repository had grown to two gigabytes and a fresh clone took fourteen minutes. I looked for the weight and found it was mostly test fixtures: binary snapshots of old versions of files, committed and re-committed over six years. Mara decided against rewriting the history, since too many people had clones. We moved the fixtures to a separate store that tests fetch on demand, and set CI to shallow clones. A new clone is 120 megabytes now and takes under a minute. Ottoline, who had cloned it on her first day and gone to make tea, said she was robbed of a rest.

Wren was release captain for the first time, with the checklist in one hand and visible nerves. She read each line aloud before doing it. Mara and I stayed on the call and said nothing for forty minutes except 'yes' twice. The release went without a hitch, and Wren said afterwards that the quiet had been the best help she could have been given. Mara told me later that she had wanted to say something at step six, where Wren paused, and had bitten her tongue; Wren, a moment later, had found it herself. It is a lesson I want to remember for when I am the one who knows.

I wrote a postmortem for a small incident in which an overnight job deleted yesterday's exports because it ran twice. It had no customer impact and could have been left unwritten. Mara asked me to write it anyway, in three paragraphs, with the line that it had been found by chance. We read it to the team on a Friday. Two people recognised their own near misses in it, and Dario said that he had a fourth, which we added. She said the small ones are where we practise. I thought it a kind way to put it, and I would not say she is wrong.

Mara asked me to help her decide whether to take over an unmaintained library the shop depends on. I listed what ownership would mean: answering issues, reviewing patches, releasing, a few hours a month if she is lucky. She asked what the alternatives were. We wrote the three on paper, with the monthly cost of each in hours: keep a private fork, replace it, adopt it. Adoption came out cheapest over two years, and she wrote to the old author that afternoon. He replied in eleven minutes with a one-word answer, 'finally', and a request for a coffee, which I count as a result.

After a reconnect the chat messages arrived out of order, and a reply appeared above its question. Teo gave each message a sequence number and sorted by it on the client. Mara wrote the number on a card: 'networks do not keep promises about order.' I would add a second line to the card: neither do clocks, and a number you assign yourself is the only one that counts. Teo's change was thirty lines. What took longer was agreeing, over two afternoons, on who assigns the number, the client or the server. Mara wanted the server, since a client may be wrong or dishonest; Teo wanted the client, since a message must be ordered before it reaches a server that may not be there. They settled on both: the client numbers its own messages, the server numbers the room, and the two sequences are never mixed. I made the diagram.

A checkbox could not be unchecked. The label wrapped the input and a script also toggled it on click, so each click flipped it twice. Wren found it by clicking on the text and not on the box, which is what every customer does.

The Tern kiosks crashed after exactly 49 days and 17 hours of running. Mara looked at the number for a while and said 'milliseconds in thirty-two bits'. She was right. We restart the kiosks weekly now and fixed the counter in the next release. The first report came from a café that had a kiosk in its entrance, and the owner, a patient man called Hugh, had assumed for two months that the screen simply needed a rest on certain Mondays. Mara found the pattern by laying his restart dates over a calendar: seven weeks apart, then seven again, and a single gap of six. She worked out the interval on paper before she let me do it. I had looked at the crash log for a long time and found nothing, since the program had not crashed at all; the counter had wrapped, a timer had fired a million times at once, and the screen had frozen from politeness. She thanked Hugh with a handwritten note and a free year of the weekly restart.

'Latest first' showed 9 March above 10 March because the dates were strings in day-month-year order. Callum converted them to real dates at the boundary. Mara sent me a picture of the old list, which she kept as a specimen.

A dropdown with 3,000 options froze the tablet. We made it a search box with the first twenty matches. Noor said that nobody had ever scrolled through those options, and that they had scrolled through them in their dreams.

A nightly import 'succeeded' on a day the partner sent an empty file, and so we updated nothing for three days before anyone knew. Mara added an alarm for suspicious zeros. A job that does nothing should be at least as loud as one that fails.

Product photos looked dull after the optimiser ran: it had stripped the colour profile. Wren compared the originals and the outputs side by side and said the red was a different red. We kept the profile and paid forty kilobytes.

Two requests at first login created two profile rows for the same person. A unique constraint on the user id would have prevented it. Mara added one and a clean-up of the 31 existing pairs, which Ilse checked by eye.

A test that passed on Node 18 failed on Node 20 because a global fetch now existed and our test had been defining its own, differently. Dario read the release notes for ten minutes and then deleted his definition.

A write to the log file failed with 'permission denied' after log rotation made the new file owned by root. The app ran as a different user. Mara changed the rotation to keep the owner, and kept the old file's mode in a comment.

A bug that vanished in a private window turned out to be a service worker serving an old copy of the app. Teo had added it for offline use two releases earlier. We version the cache and delete older ones on activation.
A retry loop with no wait in it used a whole CPU core, polling the partner a hundred thousand times a minute. Mara noticed the fan. We added a delay of a second, and the fan, I am told, went quiet.

Logging in on two browser tabs at once left one tab confused. They shared state through the browser's storage, and each overwrote the other. Yusra made tabs listen for the storage event and agree on the newer session.

A column called 'archived' was null for old rows. One query treated null as false and another as true, so the same booking appeared in two lists. Mara made the column not null with a default and migrated the old ones.

A customer whose name contained a percent sign crashed the logger, which used the name as a format string. Mara called it the most polite way to hurt a program. We pass names as arguments, never as the format.

A cleanup script skipped files starting with a dot, and a hidden folder of 8 gigabytes survived five rounds of cleaning. Mara found it with a disk usage tool she had never opened, and said 'of course it was hiding'.

A report grouped by customer and showed the first order's date next to a total, because the database was lenient about columns not in the group. Teo turned on the strict mode and nine queries refused to run. Eight were wrong.

The chart showed 'Infinity' for new customers because the growth rate divided by last month's zero. Mara decided it should say 'new', not a number. 'Some things have no growth rate,' she said, 'only a birth.'

When someone chose 1 to 15 March in the picker, the report stopped on the 14th because the end was treated as midnight at the start of the 15th. Noor noticed because her 15th was always light. We treat ranges as inclusive in the UI and half-open in the code.

Calendar invitations showed up an hour off for people abroad because the file used floating time with no zone. Mara added the zone to each invitation and tested with one friend in Auckland, which she says is the right place to test anything about time.

On one phone the keyboard covered the submit button and people thought the form had no end. Wren scrolled the field into view on focus. She added two hundred pixels of padding at the bottom of the page, which she calls her lucky margin.

Responses were being compressed twice, once by the app and once by the proxy, and the browser saw garbage. Mara found it by running curl and looking at two headers. The fix was to delete one setting. She calls this kind of bug a duplicate.

A customer's basket held twelve thousand items, put there by a script of his own. The page took a minute to open. Mara limited baskets to a hundred and wrote to him kindly. He had been testing, and apologised for it.

A bare except in a worker swallowed the interrupt signal, so a stuck job could not be stopped except by killing the whole machine. Callum narrowed the except to the errors he expected. Mara said that a bare except is a promise to hide.

A test that was meant to use a fake payment service reached the real sandbox on a certain branch, and failed when the sandbox was down. Mara made the test refuse to open any network socket at all, and found three more tests that had been doing the same.

Forked workers shared a database connection, and queries from different processes interleaved on the wire. The error read like a ghost story. Mara opened a connection after the fork and not before. It was a single line moved down three.

A connection returned to the pool with a transaction still open made the next request see old data. Teo added a rollback on return. The bug had made one report show last night's numbers and had cost us two days of looking at the wrong thing.

A product code with an encoded slash was routed to the wrong handler, because the router decoded it before matching. Dario escaped codes with a different character and wrote the rule in the style guide. Mara said that slashes in data are always a story.

The page stayed blank when the API answered 204 with no body, because the client waited to parse JSON that never came. Yusra handled the empty answer. It was a six-line fix and had hidden for months behind one customer with no data.

A failed build wrote a half-finished dependency into the CI cache, and every later build failed in the same strange way. Mara cleared the cache and then made the cache write only after success. 'A cache is a promise,' she said, not for the first time.

A deploy waited overnight for a manual approval the approver did not know she had. Mara wrote to the channel, 'if you are named in the pipeline, here is how you will be told.' Now the approver gets a message and a phone call, in that order.

Rolling restarts cut off long requests halfway. A drain period of thirty seconds before each instance stops lets them finish. Mara timed our slowest request: 22 seconds. She chose 30, and wrote 22 beside it in the file so a reader could check.

The migration step in the deploy was killed at 60 seconds, leaving the database half-changed. Mara raised the limit and, more usefully, made migrations run as a separate step before the deploy, with its own log and its own timeout.

A change to a firewall rule was applied as part of a deploy and cut off the database. The plan had shown the change but nobody had read it. Mara asked that infrastructure changes be reviewed as plans, in a pull request of their own.

Every pull request now gets its own preview site. They cost money, and two stayed running for a month. Mara made the pipeline delete a preview when the request closes, and a nightly sweep removes any stragglers.

The build output grew fourfold after one dependency was added. Mara looked at the bundle map: a whole localisation package for one date format. She replaced it with a ten-line function. The build shrank, and the gap in size looked like a crime scene.

A new hire's first deploy used to take three hours of setup. Now it takes forty minutes, and the remaining time is waiting for downloads. Priya, the first to try it, deployed to staging before lunch and made her own tea afterwards.

A broken build stood on main for a whole day while Mara was away, because everyone assumed someone else would fix it. She came back and proposed a rule: the author fixes it within thirty minutes or reverts. There have been four reverts, each within twenty. The day it happened first, the build had been red since a quarter past nine on a Tuesday, and eleven people had pushed on top of it. Each had seen the red and assumed it was someone's business. By the afternoon it was a pile of changes that could not be told apart from the fault. Mara reverted the original commit after four hours of work to find which one it was, and said in the channel that nobody was to blame, which was true and also what everyone needed to hear. The rule is now on a card by the door, and the lamp on her desk is a good deal redder than it used to be, since it now flashes for any failure on main.

Staging and production had drifted apart in 14 settings. I wrote a script that compares them and lists the differences, and Mara went through them with Tobias. Nine were accidents; five were reasons, and each reason got a name. One of the accidents was a timeout of two seconds in staging and thirty in production, which explained a month of test results that nobody believed. Another was that staging sent emails to a catch-all address while production sent them to people, which we had known and forgotten. Tobias said the list embarrassed him, and Mara answered that a list of differences is only embarrassing before it exists. We run the comparison every night now and it posts one line to the channel when anything changes, which in the first two weeks it did three times, each time to somebody's surprise.

On a review I said a change was wrong. Mara said it was right. We tested it. She was right: the case I feared was handled two layers below, in code I had not read. I wrote 'I was wrong, thank you' and meant it.

A review thread reached sixty comments over four days. Mara moved it to a call; the three of them settled it in twenty minutes and wrote one comment to record the decision. 'Beyond ten comments, go and talk,' she said.

A reviewer wrote only about style, and nothing about logic. Mara did not scold; she asked him what he thought the change did. He did not know, and said so. They read it together and he has since found a real bug.

A student sent Sedge her first pull request, a fix with a good idea and a confusing test. Mara spent an hour with her on a call and the second version was merged. She has since sent four more, and signs them with a small drawing of a sedge. Her name is Odalys, and her first pull request had been so nervous that the description apologised four times. Mara did not reply to the apologies; she answered the code, line by line, and ended with two sentences about what was good in it, which were true. In the call she asked Odalys what she wanted to learn and Odalys said, quietly, how to test something that talks to the network. Mara showed her how to put a fake in the way. By the third pull request the description had stopped apologising. I have thought about the sequence since: nothing in it was clever, and all of it was attention.

Mara has a short list for reviewing a database change: what locks, how big is the table, can it be undone, who reads this column. Four questions. She says that nearly every incident she has seen was a database change with one of them unasked.

A data migration was reviewed by running it on a copy and reading the before and after of twenty rows. Dario said that it was the first review where he had seen the effect and not only the intent. We do it for every migration now.

Before asking anyone to review, Mara reads her own diff in the review tool. She says it finds a third of her mistakes, because the tool makes the code look like someone else's. I have started doing the same, with the same result.

The development environment is now described in a container file. Priya's laptop and Mara's behave the same, so nobody says 'it works for me'. Callum liked it so much that he moved his private projects into one by the weekend.

A diff tool that highlights changes inside a line showed us a single character changed in a configuration, a one replaced by a lowercase L. It had survived four reviews. Mara said that the eye reads what it expects, and she switched her review tool to the new view.

Mara watched a recording of a failing test run and stepped backwards through it. She says it ended twenty years of working out what a program did by guessing. I find it moving that a person can be that glad about a tool.

A visualiser for query plans turned a wall of text into a tree with one red node. Mara said it was the first time she looked at a plan and understood it without me. I thought, privately, that this is how a tool should be judged.

The browser's performance profiler is a new tool for Mara. She spent an hour recording page loads and said it was like watching a film of her own mistakes. The longest bar was a script that waited for fonts. We moved it, and the page came alive.

We removed 40,000 abandoned baskets older than two years. Mara asked whether anyone could want them. I checked: not one had a customer attached. They took up 3 gigabytes and slowed one report by a minute.

Ilse had a table from a PDF, with the rows broken across pages and headers repeated in the middle. Mara and I wrote a script that drops repeated headers and joins split rows. It was ninety percent right and Ilse fixed the rest by hand, which took twelve minutes.

Marguerite sends her accounts as a spreadsheet with formulas that nobody else understands. Mara and I translated the nine most important into code with tests and compared against her totals. We matched for eleven months and differed in one, where her formula was wrong. It had treated a refund made on the thirty-first as belonging to the next month, because of a range that stopped a day short, and her total had been wrong for a year by an amount too small to catch the eye. Marguerite took the news with a long pause and then said she would buy lunch for whoever had found it, and asked whether the code could be the official version from now on. Mara said yes and, with some firmness, that she would need Marguerite to read the tests, since they now contained her knowledge. They sat together for two afternoons. Marguerite found a case that neither of us had thought of, a deposit paid in two currencies, and it is now test number thirty-one.

Some records in the archive had dates before 1970, which turned negative in the system's counter and then showed as 2038 on one screen. Callum fixed the screen. Mara asked who else uses that counter, and for a while we looked at every date we own.

A column held what looked like JSON but was really Python's printed form, with single quotes. Mara parsed it with a literal evaluator and not by replacing quotes, which would have broken every apostrophe. We converted the whole column to real JSON in a single pass.

Product codes such as ZX-007 lost their zeros when read as numbers in a script. Mara had warned me about it twice, and I did it a third time with a different file. I wrote a note at the top of my own toolkit: codes are text.

Before concluding that sales fell in July, Mara looked at five years of July. They always fell. I plotted them on one chart with a light line per year, and she said that the new fall was exactly as large as the old falls. She did not write a conclusion.

A scraped dataset held each page twice, once with a slash at the end of the address and once without. Mara found it by sorting. Removing the slash and the duplicate halved the file and lowered the average page count she had been proud of.

Testing the PDF generator by comparing images was fragile. Teo switched to extracting the text and checking the lines that matter, such as the total and the date. It takes a hundred milliseconds and survives font changes. Mara liked that it is a test of meaning.

To test a race on purpose, Teo used a barrier so two threads reach the critical line together. The old bug appeared in the first run, every time. Mara said that a race you can summon is half defeated.

A property test checks that our sorting is stable, giving shuffled lists of records with equal keys. It failed on its fourth try. The library's sort was stable and ours, a hand-written merge, was not. Mara asked why we wrote our own. Nobody remembered. I looked through the history and found it: a commit from five years ago, before the standard sort had a stable guarantee in the version we used, with a message that said 'need stable'. The reason had been real and had expired without anyone being told. Mara asked me to delete the merge sort, run the test again and see. It passed. She wrote the explanation in the commit message in full, because, she said, the person who removes code deserves the same courtesy as the person who adds it. I agreed, and for the rest of the week I looked for other reasons that might have quietly expired.

Reading the tests for the discount module taught me more than its documentation, and I told Mara so. She suggested that tests are documentation that cannot lie, only be incomplete. We have started to name tests with that in mind.

Every Friday we print the ten slowest tests. Teo started it as a game and the list now has shorter numbers each week. The slowest was 42 seconds in March and is 6 in October, and Mara has put the top ten on a card with his name.

Recorded responses from partner APIs are used in our tests and expire after ninety days, so they get re-recorded and compared. The first expiry showed a field the partner had renamed in July without a word. We found it in a test, not in the shop.

Glasswork's components are tested by screenshot comparison with a small tolerance. Wren set the tolerance after a week of false alarms, at 0.1 percent. It has caught a button that grew by two pixels and a colour that drifted by one step.

A database migration is now tested up and down: apply, check, roll back, check. Mara added it after a rollback script that had never been run failed on the day it was needed. 'A rollback is code,' she said, 'and code untested is a wish.'

An accessibility checker runs in CI against every page in the preview. In its first week it found 43 issues, all in two components. Wren fixed both and the number is zero now. Mara pointed out that zero is a number we must keep checking.

A load test of the queue showed that it handled 800 messages a second and then fell off a cliff at 810. Mara asked what lived at 810. A single worker's buffer. We raised it, and made the dashboard show how close the buffer is to its limit.

Processing 6,000 images a night took four hours on one core. Mara switched to a process pool of four and it took one hour five. The speed-up was not four, which she accepted, and not even three, which she questioned. I measured: the disk was the next limit.

We cached the result of a slow pure function with room for a thousand entries. The hit rate was 94 percent. Mara asked how I chose the thousand. I counted the distinct inputs in a week: 870. Sometimes numbers are in the logs.

Sorting a table of 200,000 rows on the client froze the page for four seconds. The database could do it using an index in 30 milliseconds. Callum moved the sort to the server and said it was the first time a change made him grin before he ran the test.

Converting product photos to a newer image format made them 30 percent smaller with no visible change. Wren compared a hundred at full size and could not tell. We serve the old format to browsers that cannot read the new one.

Structured logging cost eight percent of the CPU because every line was built even when it would be discarded. We made the message lazy, built only when the level is on. Mara asked what else costs a little all the time. We are looking.

Images below the fold now load only when scrolled near. The home page needs 1.2 megabytes instead of 4.8 to appear. Mara tested on a train and held her phone up to show me, as if I could see the way the page filled.

A daily summary table is computed overnight so the dashboard does not sum millions of rows each time. It opens in 80 milliseconds. The cost is that a figure may be a day old, and the dashboard says so beside each number.

Writing the help article for 'change my booking', Sunniva and Mara began with the customer's question as it arrives in the inbox, in the customer's words, and answered it in the order a worried person needs. It is the most read article on the site.

Mara wrote a postmortem template with five headings: what happened, how we noticed, what we did, why it happened, what we change. It is one page. People write them now, which was the whole aim, and Dario says they are interesting to read.

Each documentation page now carries 'last verified' and the version it was checked against. Mara thinks of it as a use-by date. Pages older than a year show a gentle banner, and Wren has been working through them like a gardener.

Tobias wrote a page called 'weird bits' that lists the odd things in the codebase and why they exist: the two clocks, the column named x, the retry that is longer than it looks. A new colleague read it in her first hour and said she felt let in.

A diagram of our deployment pipeline shows eleven stages. When Mara finished it, she looked at it and said that five of them did the same thing in different places. We merged them, and she hung the old picture in the kitchen as a warning.

The page 'how we review' has five lines: be kind, be specific, ask before assuming, label how serious a comment is, approve when it is good enough. Ottoline said it is the only company document she has read twice voluntarily.

Our guidelines for error messages say: what happened, why, what to do next, in that order and under twenty words each. Wren rewrote forty messages by the rule. The one she is proudest of is 'We could not save your booking. Your card was not charged. Try again.'

To find when a particular string entered the code, I used the search that walks history and found the commit in ten seconds. Mara said she had always scrolled through the log. I explained the option, and she wrote it on a card, between two others she had learned that week.

Mara rebases her long feature branch onto main every Monday. Conflicts have stayed small, a few lines a week, and not the three-day knot of a month. She says it is flossing for code, and Dario said he would not floss.

Fixup commits and an autosquash turn the corrections after review into the commits they belong to. Yusra learned it in one session and said it was like finding a hidden door in her own house. The history is cleaner and the review is easier to follow.

Main is protected now: no direct pushes, one approval, green tests. Mara tried to push a small fix to it out of habit and the tool politely refused. She laughed. 'The rule I wrote just stopped me,' she told me, pleased.

A conflict resolved wrongly kept both sides of a condition. The tests caught it in two seconds. Mara said that she would now treat every conflict resolution as a change that deserves a test, and I agreed, since the evidence was in front of us.

Release tags are annotated with a short note of what changed, and the note shows in the hosting site. When a customer asked what 3.2 changed, Mara answered in a link. It saved her eleven minutes and the customer's question had been a good one.

Lockfiles are marked in the repository settings so that conflicts in them are resolved by regenerating. Tobias added the line and the argument about lockfile merges, which had run for two years, ended on Tuesday.

An outside project we contribute to takes patches by email. Mara found it charming for a week and then slightly irritating. She sent a patch in the proper form, with a signed-off line, and had it accepted within a day, which she says was better than expected.

A sparse checkout let Priya work on one package of the monorepo with only that folder on her disk. Her clone dropped from 900 megabytes to 40. She said she noticed it only when her laptop stopped asking for space.

A summary of who has changed each folder in the last two years showed that the payment code has had one author. Mara and I talked about it for an hour, and she asked Noor to read the module with her. It is the quietest bus-factor repair I have seen.

A web crawler visited our site 200 times a second and filled the logs. We added a rule to the robots file and, when it ignored it, a limit at the proxy. Mara sent a polite email to the address in its user agent, and the crawler slowed that afternoon.

A consumer crashed on one message and restarted forever, writing a core dump each time, until the disk was full. Mara set the dump size to zero for that service and the restart limit to five. The message is in a folder, waiting for someone to feel brave.

An analyst ran an enormous query on the production database at noon and slowed the shop for ten minutes. Mara killed it and gave the analyst a read-only replica with her name beside it. He was apologetic and, I think, relieved by the replica.

The pager rang at 3 a.m. for a disk that was 81 percent full and growing slowly, which would have needed attention in nine days. Mara turned the alert into a ticket and a weekly report, and she slept past seven for the first time that month. I had drafted the alert's replacement before she asked: a prediction of when the disk would fill, based on the last two weeks, and a message only when it came within three days. Mara read the draft and added a line I would not have thought of, the name of the person who owns the disk, since an alert with no owner is a smoke detector in an empty house. She also asked that the prediction show its working, so that whoever reads it can see the two weeks it is based on and disagree. The first message under the new rule arrived on a Thursday, politely, forty hours ahead of need, and was dealt with over coffee.

Our email provider put our sending address on a blocklist after a customer marked a receipt as spam. Mara asked for removal, explained, and set up a feedback loop so we hear of complaints directly. Delivery was back in a day and we sent apologies to nobody.

A server clock drifted by seven minutes and tokens it issued were seen as expired by the others. Login failed for some and not for others. Mara set up time synchronisation properly and added the clock offset to the dashboard, where it now lives in a corner.

Two people deployed within a minute of each other, and the second deployment overwrote the first with an older version. Mara added a lock to the deploy tool that says who holds it and since when. The tool is politer than we were.

When our DNS provider went down for an hour, every service looked broken in a different way. Mara said afterwards that a map of dependencies would have saved her fifty minutes. She has begun drawing one, starting with the lowest layer, which is how one should. By the end of the week she had drawn thirty boxes and twenty arrows on a large sheet taped to the wall, and found that the lowest box, name resolution, was shared by every other one and had no second provider. We added one that afternoon. What interested me was that nothing on the page was new; she had known each fact separately and had never seen them together. She said it was like putting all of one's keys on one ring and discovering that one is the key to the front door. The sheet is still on the wall, a little curled at the corners, and people stop to add arrows.

A large customer imported 80,000 bookings at once and crashed the importer, which held everything in a list. Mara rewrote it to process in chunks and to tell the user how far it had got. Their second import took nine minutes, and no one phoned. The customer's first import had been a Friday afternoon affair: the bar sat at zero for twenty minutes, then the server gave up, and the customer's office manager phoned Ilse twice with growing politeness. When Mara read the transcript of the second call she asked Ilse to teach her what the customer had been feeling. Ilse said it was the silence, not the failure. So the new importer says 'received 80,000 rows; checking' within a second, then 'validated 12,000' as it goes, and then shows a short list of rows it could not understand, with a button to download them. Ilse said that the list was what a person wants when something has gone partly wrong, and not the apology.

Should lists use infinite scroll or pages? Wren showed that people lose their place in infinite scroll, and Noor showed that on a phone pages are tiresome. We chose pages for tables and a scroll for the feed, and wrote the reason beside each.

Mara and Sunniva debated whether the shop owners should have an admin page for something they could ask us to do with a query. We built the page once we had been asked four times. The rule is four, which both consider arbitrary and neither wants to change.

Cancellation rules: fixed for all shops, or set by each shop? A fixed rule is simple, but Sunniva told us of a shop that cannot afford last-minute cancellations. We made it a setting with three choices and a sensible default. The shop was a small climbing gym run by two people, and in their case a customer who cancels an hour before leaves a place nobody else will fill. Sunniva had told us about it over lunch, almost in passing. Mara listened and the design changed within the day. The three choices are 'any time', 'a day before' and 'forty-eight hours before', with a note that says what the customer will see in each. I was asked to write the text the customer sees, and I tried several versions before choosing the plainest. The gym's owner later wrote to say it was the first time software had understood her business, and Mara printed the message and gave a copy to Sunniva.

Webhooks or polling for the partner's updates? Mara chose polling every five minutes, because webhooks need an endpoint that must always be up and a way to find what was missed. If they ever offer a stream with replay, we will think again.

Mara drew up logging levels on one page: error means a person should look today, warn means a person might want to, info is for the story, debug is off. Since then our logs are shorter, and the errors are rarer and truer.

How long should we keep customer data? Ilse asked, and Mara and I did not know. We read the contracts and chose periods: bookings seven years for accounts, messages two years, logs thirty days. A short table, with a reason in each cell.

Should a bookings record be editable, or should a change create a new version? We chose the second for anything with money in it. Mara said an edit is a lie of omission, and the history table tells a story with every step.

Converting 140 class components to functions took Wren three weeks of a few a day. She tested each in the browser and found that three had behaviour nobody had intended. Mara said the conversion was worth it for those three alone.

We removed inheritance from the models, replacing it with a field that names the kind. Dario was suspicious. A month later he said that he could finally read a model without opening three files, and he asked me to show how I found them all.

A typed configuration object replaced a dictionary that anyone could stuff with anything. The first run found two settings that nobody used and one misspelt key that had been silently ignored for a year. Mara asked what it had been meant to do. Nobody knew.

Three endpoints that did nearly the same thing became one with a parameter. Callum worried about the breaking change, so we kept the old three as thin wrappers for a release and logged their use. By the end, nobody used them, and the wrappers went.

Merging the notifications microservice back into the main app removed two deployments and an entire class of timeout. Tobias, who had built the service with pride, led the merge himself and said it was the best thing he had ever deleted.

A test file of 3,000 lines was split by feature into eleven. Mara did it with a script that moves a test and its fixtures together, and checked the total test count before and after. Both were 412, and she let out a breath I could almost hear.

A recurring event on the 31st vanished in months with thirty days instead of moving to the 30th. Mara's rule: monthly means 'the last day if the day does not exist'. She wrote the rule as a test first, with February, and watched it fail in four months.

Customers were logged out in a loop when they used the address without www. The cookie belonged to the other host name. Callum set the cookie for the parent domain and sent every visitor to one canonical address.

The HTTP library's default timeout was none, so one hung partner call held a worker for six hours. Mara set five seconds everywhere and made the helper refuse a call without one. 'A default of forever is not a default,' she said.

Ampersands in shop names appeared as &amp; because the text was escaped by the code and again by the template. Wren found it by looking at the source of the page. It was a one-word fix, and Mara got the shop owner to look at it at last.

The sidebar said '1 bookings'. Noor spotted it in a demo and the silence in the room was audible. We use a plural helper now, and I have started reading every count in the interface aloud for the sake of Noor's ears.

A customer in Istanbul could not log in with a capital I in his email. Lowercasing in his locale turned it into a different letter. Mara's face when I explained was a study in delight. We lowercase without a locale, and added him to the test as 'Ismail'. He had written to us twice before, politely, saying that the login 'seemed not to know me', and both times we had suggested he reset his password, which he did, and which of course did not help. It was Dario who finally read the exchange and said the second message sounded like a man who thought the fault was his. Mara phoned him. He laughed with relief. The reason was the lowercase of a capital I, which in his language's rules is a letter without a dot, and our code had applied those rules because the server's locale was set to his country by a hosting default. We set every server to a neutral locale, and I wrote the story into the notes under 'assumptions about letters'.

A stray comma at the end of a line turned a string into a one-item tuple, and the function that expected text rejected it with a message about types. Mara looked for twenty minutes. I will not say how long I took to point at the comma.

Removing items from a list while looping over it skipped every second one. Teo's cleanup of expired holds left half of them in place for a week. He loops over a copy now and wrote an apology in the commit, which he did not need to.

An email looked wrong only in one client: an unclosed tag in our template made the footer swallow the next message in the thread. Mara tested it in nine email clients and learned why people hate email. She kept the template simple after that.

The logo was missing on production because the stylesheet's path assumed the site lived at the root, and it lives in a folder. Yusra set the base path once, in one place. 'Where does the site live?' is not a question I will ask lightly again.

The copy-to-clipboard button worked in development and did nothing on the staging site. The browser allows it only on secure pages and staging was on plain HTTP. Mara made staging secure, and made the button say 'copy failed' instead of nothing.

Typing in the search box lagged because every keystroke wrote a log line synchronously to a slow disk. Teo made the logging asynchronous. The lag went from 300 milliseconds to nothing, and he said it had never occurred to him that the logger could be the slow part.

A resumed upload restarted from the wrong byte and corrupted the file's middle. Mara found it by comparing the checksums of the pieces. We now verify each piece and only then the whole, and the resume shows what it will do before it does it. The customer who found it was uploading a four-gigabyte video over a hotel's connection, which dropped twice, and the file that arrived played perfectly until the eleventh minute and then showed a green smear. Mara thought at first that the video itself was damaged. I asked her to compare the checksum of the first two gigabytes on both sides, and then of the next two; the first matched, the second did not. Between them was a seam where the second resume had started one chunk too far back and written over good data. She said the shape of the bug, matching and then not matching, was the clue, and that checksums in halves are the oldest trick for finding a seam.

An empty string in a configuration file crashed the parser with a message about invalid literals. Mara asked whether we should default. We refused instead, naming the key, since a silent default for a missing setting is how a shop ends up charging in the wrong currency.

A weekly report ran at 06:00 and the data it needed arrived at 06:10. Mara spent a day thinking the numbers were wrong and then saw that they were old. The report now waits for a marker file that the import writes when it has finished.

Ids in the orders table skipped from 4,201 to 4,260 and Ilse feared that orders had gone missing. They had not: a rolled-back transaction had used up the numbers. Mara explained that ids are not a count, and added the sentence to the data model page.

A daily count read zero on a Tuesday because the job ran in the middle of a restart. Dario made it retry once after a minute and note it in the log. Zero is a legitimate number, and I want a reason beside it before I believe it.

The database function now() on the replica returned the replica's time, which was four seconds behind, and 'created in the last minute' queries sometimes missed the newest orders. Mara passed the time from the application. A clock is an input.

A module-level variable held the current customer, and under load one request saw another's data. Teo traced it from a single support report. We removed the global, and Mara made a rule: state about a request lives in the request. The report that reached us was only one line: a customer had seen someone else's name in the corner of her own account page, once, at about eleven on a Monday morning. Teo asked for the time and the page and spent four hours reading code with his jaw set. The global was set at the start of each request and read at the end, with an await in between, so that when two requests overlapped on one worker, the later one could overwrite the earlier. It had been dormant for a year because the shop was quiet enough. Mara phoned the customer herself, told her exactly what had happened, and asked whether she wanted the page's access log for that minute. She said that she did not, and that she was glad to have been told.

Version 1.10 sorted before 1.9 in the download list because the versions were compared as text. Wren, who wrote the list, laughed first and fixed it second. Mara said the earlier bug in the changelog was cousin to this one.

A customer asked for an on-premises install, and the script failed because it needed the internet and the customer's server had none. Mara vendored every dependency into one archive. The install now runs without a network, and we know what it contains. The customer was a small clinic whose server sat in a cupboard behind the reception desk, and the person who maintained it was an office manager named Rashida who did the work on Thursday afternoons between appointments. Mara arranged her call for a Thursday. I wrote the steps as eleven numbered lines, each with the expected output printed beneath, so that Rashida could tell at every point whether things were right. At step seven the output was different, because the clinic's disk was almost full. Mara waited on the line while Rashida cleared out an old folder of scanned forms, and the install finished at ten to five. Rashida sent a message afterwards: it had been the first time software had been installed to her and not at her.

Our install script for a customer's own server found three surprises: an old version of the shell, a disk mounted read-only for /var, and a firewall that blocked our package host. Mara went on a call and fixed each. She said they were all ordinary, and the three together were a morning.

CI minutes ran out on the twentieth of the month. Mara checked what consumed them: 40 percent was a job that rebuilt documentation on every push. She changed it to run on main only, and the minutes lasted to the end of the month with room to spare.

A deploy tool update changed the default to dry-run, and for a day we deployed nothing and thought it had worked. Dario saw that the version in production had not changed. We now check the version after every deploy by asking the running service.

A local development setup with a database, a queue and a mail catcher now starts with one command, and waits for each to be healthy. Priya's first day was the test. She said it was the first environment she had met that did not need an apology.

Marrow broke on Windows because a path was built with a slash. Wren, who tested it there, found six such places. Mara used the path library everywhere and asked for a Windows job in CI. 'If it is not tested there, it does not work there,' she said.

The Marrow binary was 38 megabytes. Stripping debug symbols and dropping an unused dependency made it nine. Tobias thought of it as a diet; Mara thought of it as getting rid of things we had never needed. Downloads got faster, and nobody wrote to thank us.

A variable called data2 appeared in a pull request. Mara asked for a name that says what it holds. The author renamed it 'unpaid_bookings' and, reading it, saw the filter was wrong. A good name finds bugs by making them visible.

An outside maintainer replied to Mara's pull request with a short, sharp refusal. She read it three times, thanked him and asked what would make the change acceptable. His second reply was warm and long. She said that she had nearly answered the first one.

Noor does not write code, but she reads the interface text in every pull request. Last week she noticed that 'Confirm' on a deletion button should say 'Delete'. Mara said that she is our best reviewer for the part of the system customers actually read.

For a refactor, the review question is 'did the tests change?' If they did not, the behaviour probably did not. Mara checks the test diff first. On Callum's last refactor the tests were unchanged, and so was my confidence.

Anyone reviewing a change to the interface must run it, not only read it. After the rule was made, Dario found that a button was off-screen in one view, which no diff would have shown. He said he now had the rule's whole value in a single bug.

A twelve-line change took Mara an hour to review. It changed the order of two checks in a payment path, and she needed to be sure about each case. Her answer, 'it is correct', was the shortest sentence of her day and the one I trust most.

Mara's editor crashed and took twenty minutes of unsaved work with it. She turned on autosave and recovery that week, and told me with a mix of embarrassment and pride that she had not lost work in ten years until now.

We wrote a lint rule that forbids reading the current time directly, since it has made tests hard in the past. The rule found eleven violations and made the twelfth, which Callum was about to write, impossible. He said it felt like a hand on his shoulder.

A shell function now rings the terminal bell when a command that took over a minute finishes. Mara works in another window and comes back when it chimes. She had not realised how much of her day was spent checking on things.

A watcher re-runs the relevant tests whenever a file is saved. Teo built it with a few lines of shell. Feedback came in two seconds rather than two minutes, and the way he writes code changed within a week, in smaller steps.

Pull requests used to be merged in the order of their approval, and one waited nine days behind a large one. Mara moved to merging the smallest ready change first. Median waiting time fell from three days to one, and the nine-day change was split by its author, unprompted.

A merge of two customer lists by name missed people because one list had 'Bob' and the other 'Robert'. We built a small table of common nicknames and reviewed the matches by hand. It found 190 pairs and, in the end, 11 false ones.

Colour names in the catalogue ran to 600 spellings of about forty colours. Wren grouped them into twelve families for filters and kept the original names for the product pages. Search by colour went from useless to adequate the same afternoon.

A time series had gaps, and we had filled them with zeros. The chart showed collapses that never happened. Mara changed the gaps to nulls, which draw as breaks, and the chart told the truth again, which is less dramatic.

Percentages on the report added up to 99 or 101 because of rounding. Mara asked what the reader needs. We used the largest remainder method so they sum to 100, and added a footnote saying it. Noor said the footnote is what made her trust it.

Opening a big CSV in a spreadsheet silently dropped everything after row 1,048,576. Callum drew conclusions from the first million rows of 1.2 million. Mara pointed out that the program had not said a word. We read big files with scripts now and count rows at both ends. Callum had been preparing a presentation for the owners about which products sell in winter. His conclusion was that scarves outsell everything, and it rested on the first fifteen months of data, which is to say on the autumns and winters but not on the summers. When Mara noticed that the last date in his sheet was in June, she asked him to count the rows in the original file. The number, 1,213,402, did not match what the spreadsheet showed. He was not embarrassed; he was fascinated, and said he would never again trust a tool that does not complain. He redid the analysis with the full year, and scarves still won, by a smaller margin.

We logged failed logins and not successful ones, so any analysis of 'who logs in' saw only the people who struggle. Mara noticed the bias when the numbers said that most users had trouble. We began logging successes, and the trouble shrank to 4 percent.

Tests used to be named 'should do X', which Wren found tiresome. She changed them to plain statements: 'a cancelled booking frees its slot'. When a test fails now, the output reads like a news report.

A fake payment service, written by us, replaced the mocks, and it behaves like the real one in the ways that matter: it declines certain cards and it is sometimes slow. Mara said a good fake is a small model of a partner's habits.

Test data was too clean, with names that were always ASCII and addresses that were always short. A bug in the label printer lived there for a year. Teo added a builder that produces awkward customers on purpose. The builder found two more bugs in its first run.

To check the alarm worked, we broke the build on purpose on a Tuesday afternoon. The lamp turned red in twelve seconds and the channel posted in fifteen. Mara said she had not seen it do its job in a year, and it was a pleasure.

A test depended on the weekday and failed every Saturday. Dario noticed that the failures began on a weekend and stopped on Monday. Mara said that a test which knows what day it is has been told too much. We gave it a fixed Wednesday.

Mara asked who reads the migration files a year later. Nobody does, until something breaks. She asked for each to begin with a sentence in plain words saying what it changes and why. Yusra's, the first, ran to two lines. The oldest unexplained migration in the folder is from 2020, and she has put a name on it.

Running the suite in random order found three tests that depended on a predecessor. Each had passed by a happy accident for years. Mara kept the random order on permanently and the failures print the seed so they can be repeated.

Mara and Yusra renamed the 'staging' environment to 'preview' because customers kept asking when staging would be released. Two words in a dashboard and a handful of settings, and the question stopped. Mara said she had not known how much a name carries until it carried the wrong thing.

Test data builders let us write 'a booking, cancelled, with a refund' in one line. Yusra's tests got shorter and more specific. Mara said it is the first time she read a test and understood its situation before its assertion.

A report that built one huge string by appending in a loop took eight minutes at ten megabytes. Collecting pieces and joining once took two seconds. Mara said it was the only performance fix she has ever understood completely in a minute.

Importing the whole library at the top of every test file made starting the suite take 25 seconds. Teo imported lazily in the few places that needed it. Starting now takes four seconds, and everyone has stopped making tea before running tests.

We split the test run into shards by measured duration rather than by file count. The slowest shard dropped from 14 minutes to 5. Dario hung the old numbers on the wall for a while to remember how it used to be.

A test now fails if any page's response is larger than half a megabyte. Callum added it after the bookings list reached 2.4. The first week it caught two new ones, both the same day they were written, which is when one wants to hear it.

Parsing a million dates with a general parser took 20 seconds; with the exact format given, one second. Mara asked why the general parser exists. 'For people who do not know the format,' I said. We knew the format.

We profiled a worker's heap for a day to look for a leak, and found none: its memory was flat after the first hour. Mara said she was disappointed and relieved at once, and wrote 'checked, nothing' in the notes so nobody checks it again for nothing.

The webhook documentation had a description of each event and no sample. Wren added a real payload for every event and the integration questions in support fell off the same week. 'People copy,' she said, 'so give them the right thing.'

A 'known issues' page lists what is broken, honestly and with dates. Tobias feared that it would look bad. In the first month it received no complaints and three thank-you notes, one of which described a workaround we had not known.

We moved the documentation from a wiki into the repository, next to the code. A change that alters behaviour now alters the page in the same pull request. Mara says the wiki died of loneliness, and the repository's pages are less lonely.

Wren writes alternative text for every diagram, one sentence saying what the picture shows. Reading the architecture page with the images off, Mara found two diagrams whose point could not be recovered from the text around them, and rewrote the text. The page is better with the pictures on, too.

Docstrings in Sedge now follow one form: a sentence, the arguments, what is returned, what can go wrong. Odalys wrote a checker in her second week. The first run complained about 211 functions and the last, a week later, about none.

Every year Mara makes a short summary of the decisions we recorded: what we chose and what we have since regretted. This year's has twenty-four decisions and three regrets. She reads the regrets aloud at the first meeting of the new year.

A script lists the branches already merged and not touched for a month: 140 of them. Mara deleted them all in a minute, since every one was reachable from main, and the hosting page for branches became readable for the first time in two years.

Mara discovered that she could stage part of a file at a time, line by line. She said it was like discovering a drawer in a table she had owned for twenty years. Her commits now each hold one idea, with a hunk selected by hand.

A new laptop committed under the wrong email for a week because nobody had set the identity. Priya's commits showed as a stranger. We added a check that refuses to commit without the configured address, and a friendly message that says how to set it.
