Squashing lost a co-author line, and Noor's contribution disappeared from the history. Mara found it in the original branch and restored the credit in the message. She asked me to check for the line on every squash since. Two others were missing.

After a file was renamed, its blame stopped at the rename and Mara thought the code was new. History with the follow option showed eleven earlier years. She printed the incantation in large letters and taped it to the wall.

A customer phoned in a panic: our site was down. It was not; their own DNS had lapsed. Mara stayed on the phone for forty minutes and helped them find the right panel at their registrar. They are still a customer and send her a card at the new year.

Page load times had crept up by ten milliseconds a week for a year without any alert, because every week's increase was below the threshold. Mara drew the trend and set an alarm on the slope. We found it was one table growing, and paged it. The table was the audit trail, and it grew about two percent a week, which is nothing in any one week and a great deal in a year. The query that filled the dashboard scanned it from the beginning. Mara considered an index, and then asked whether the dashboard needed the whole history at all. It needed thirty days. A date condition and a partial index brought the query back to six milliseconds, and the old rows moved to a table of their own that nothing reads daily. She printed the slope of the graph before and after and put them side by side, a long tilt and a flat line, over her desk.

We held a game day: Mara turned off the database replica at ten in the morning and the team had to cope. It took them 31 minutes and four wrong guesses. A real failure two months later took 9. Dario said that they had practised for exactly that. The thing I noted at the game day was where the thirty-one minutes went. Eleven were spent noticing, because the alert named the symptom and not the cause; eight on the wrong guesses, two of them about the network; and twelve on the fix itself, which was simple. Mara had asked me to keep time without saying anything, and at the end she read the three numbers aloud to the team. Nobody argued. The alert was rewritten that afternoon to name the replica, and the real failure two months later spent a single minute noticing. It is the cleanest example I know of a measurement paying for itself, and I wrote it into the notes without adjectives.

A partner changed a field in their API without notice and our sync broke at breakfast. Mara pinned the version of their API in our requests and wrote to ask for a notice period. They agreed to thirty days. She says it is worth asking for what you need.

A release of the Tern app was pulled from the store after a crash on a popular phone, within two hours of going live. The review had been quick and the testing less so. Mara added two real phones from that family to her shelf and a staged rollout to the process.

The status page itself had a bug and stayed green while the site was down, because it checked the home page's cached copy. Callum noticed. Mara changed the check to ask the service and not the cache. It felt, she said, like being told by a doctor that the doctor was ill.

We deploy new behaviour dark first: it runs, its result is compared with the old, and the old is still used. For two weeks the new pricing disagreed 0.3 percent of the time. Mara looked at every disagreement and found two bugs in the new and one in the old.

For anything that deletes customer data, two people must be present, one to read the command and one to type it. Mara added the rule after a near miss. It takes a minute, and in a year it has changed the command twice.

Services in Brindle keep no state between requests; they can be killed at any time and nobody notices. Mara says this was the best decision of the project, and its price is that every thing worth remembering lives in the database, which is the only place she wants it.

A customer asked for all their data, in a format they could read. Mara built the export in two days, as a zip of CSVs with a one-page description. She said that a person's data should not be a mystery to the person, and I thought that was plainly put.

Marrow's flags follow a rule: long names say what they do, short names exist only for the five most common. Tobias made a table of every flag. Eleven names broke the rule, and the next release renames them, with the old names working and a gentle warning.

Old versions of the mobile app talk to the new API for as long as we support them, then we ask them to update. Mara chose a floor of the last three versions, which covers 97.4 percent of sessions. The message to the others is polite and has a link.

A feature request arrived from the biggest customer, and Mara said no with kindness: it would help them and hurt eleven others. She offered a smaller change that helped a little. They accepted. She wrote the reasoning into the 'decided not to do' page.

Most settings now have no option at all. Mara's belief is that each option is a decision handed to a person who did not ask to make one. We removed nine, keeping the default of each, and heard from two customers, both gently.

The 400-line settings page was split into one file per section. Wren did it over a week, a section a day, and the page behaved exactly the same each evening. 'Boring refactors are the best kind,' said Mara.

A single 'context' object had been passed through everything, and it had grown to forty fields. Mara and I listed which functions use which fields. Most use two or three. We passed those, and the context object shrank to the five that are truly shared.

A function of ninety lines became twelve functions of eight, each named for a step of the booking. Reading it now is like reading an itinerary. Mara said she was suspicious of how pleasant it is, and tested it harder than she would have.

A parser built from regular expressions grew until nobody dared touch it. We rewrote it with a small grammar of eleven rules. It is longer, and Mara says that long and plain is better than short and cryptic, which she has said before and will again.

SQL moved from strings in code to files of their own, each with a name and a comment that says what it answers. Dario found that three queries were duplicates. 'We hid them from ourselves,' he said, 'with string concatenation.'

A payment provider was wrapped in a small interface that we own. Tests use a fake, and a switch to another provider would touch one file. Mara said she did not want to switch, and wanted to know she could, which is a different thing.

All the date handling was scattered across thirty files. Mara and I gathered it into one module with seven functions and a test for each. The next date bug took ten minutes, since there was only one place for it to live.

A library we depend on has two maintainers and asked for sponsors. Mara talked to Ilse and the shop now gives it a modest monthly sum. She said it was cheaper than an hour of her time a week and a better use than any other line in the budget.

We moved to a newer language version for its pattern matching. Within a month the longest conditional in the codebase shrank to a table. Tobias said he had resisted for a year and that he would like it written down that he was wrong.

A licence audit listed 412 packages. Mara and I grouped them: 380 permissive, 24 with weak copyleft, 8 unclear. The eight took Ilse two days of reading. We replaced one, asked three maintainers, and wrote the licences into a file.

A dependency began calling a server of its own on startup to report usage. I noticed it in the network log of a test. Mara filed an issue, pinned the old version, and was thanked within a day; the telemetry became opt-in in the next release.

Choosing a test framework, Mara and Wren wrote the same ten tests in two. One was terser, the other had better failure messages. They chose the one with better failure messages, because a test is read most when it has failed.

Two versions of the same small library ended up in our bundle because two other libraries needed different ones. Mara found the pair in the bundle map. Aligning them saved 60 kilobytes and made her unreasonably happy.

The first release through the new pipeline had a manual hold at each stage, so Mara could look. She pressed continue four times in twelve minutes. 'Next time I will go for a walk,' she said, and the next time she did.

Every set of release notes now has a 'known issues' paragraph, even when it says 'none that we know of'. Noor said she reads it first. Tobias said that the phrase makes him nervous. Mara said that is exactly how a known-issues line should feel.

A new feature was announced in the newsletter a week before it was ready, because someone had been enthusiastic. Mara wrote a calm note to subscribers with the new date. She said she was less angry than relieved that there was only one.

A deprecated option was removed in Sedge 3.0 with a shim that prints a one-line warning and the replacement. Odalys wrote the shim. In three months the warning fired 1,900 times, in eleven projects. Mara wrote to the biggest.

Each release now records how it was built: the commit, the toolchain, the machine. Ilse asked why. Mara said that one day someone will ask whether a file is the one we built, and we should be able to say so on the day we are asked.

We held a bug bash for a day: nine people, a prepared checklist, pizza. We found forty-one bugs, of which twenty-two were real and nine were new. The best was Sunniva's, a button she clicked twice in a hurry. Mara said we would do it before every major release.

Mara's live demo to a customer crashed at the second click. She apologised once, restarted, and it worked. The customer said later that the way she handled the crash was why they signed. She told me it taught her nothing about code and a good deal about trust. The demo was for a chain of three gyms, with six people on the call and a seventh who joined late and asked what had happened. The crash was a null where she had expected a name, in a test account that I had set up the night before with one field missing. I had to tell her that, and I did, straight after the call, without softening it. She was quiet for a moment and then said that she was glad it was a field and not a feeling. I fixed the account and added the missing field to the script that makes test accounts. Next time she rehearses with a stranger's account, she says, since a demo should survive someone else's data.

Teo's first week on call produced no pages. He was a little disappointed and a little relieved. Mara told him that was the best result of an on-call week, and that it is usually not luck but the work of whoever came before.

Each Friday afternoon the team has a half-hour demo of anything someone has made that week. Last Friday Wren showed a sorted list that did not need to be sorted. Mara clapped. It is the kindest ritual in the building.

Mara set aside a day a quarter for technical debt, which she renamed 'tidy day' after Yusra said that the old name sounded like a punishment. Last time we deleted 4,100 lines and updated eleven dependencies. People came to work in good moods.

An intern, Gustavo, built a small tool for the support team in six weeks. He chose to make it dull and reliable and not impressive. Ilse uses it daily. Mara told him that was the most professional thing she had seen from anyone in a first job. The tool does one thing: it shows the support team, on one screen, everything about a customer's last five bookings, including the emails sent and whether they were opened. Before it, Ilse had used four windows. Gustavo spent his first week asking questions and not writing code, and at the end of it had a list of nine things he would not build. He showed the list to Mara before showing her any screens, and she told me that this was the moment she knew he would be good. He left in September for his studies, with a note in the repository saying how it works and what to do when it breaks, which Ilse has used twice.

A customer visit changed a feature we had designed for months. Noor and Mara watched a woman in a shop use the booking screen and she touched the wrong button four times. They took notes and said nothing until she left. The new layout has one big button. What I saw, because I was given the notes and nothing else, was how much the room had assumed. We had said that a customer chooses a time, then a service, then a person, and the woman in the shop wanted to choose a person first; she wanted Hana, who has cut her hair for nine years. The old screen made her go through four steps to find Hana. Noor did not interrupt, and said afterwards that it had taken physical effort. In the new version you may begin from any of the three, and the others follow. Mara said that no amount of testing in the office would have found this, because in the office we knew who Hana was.

The estimating game with cards ended in a tie of 3 and 13 on a task. Instead of splitting the difference, Mara asked the two people to explain. The 13 knew about a legacy interface that the 3 had never seen. The estimate was 13, and the task took 12.

We ran a quarterly planning session where each person named the one thing they would be proud to have finished. Four named the same thing, which was not on the plan. Mara moved it up, and I find I like a plan that listens.

Mara and I read a paper on a database technique in the reading group, a page each evening. On the third night she said that she did not believe the figure on page nine. We ran the experiment on a small scale and it was true, only smaller.

Mara asked me to keep a small file of the mistakes I have made in this work, with dates. It has fourteen entries after a year. The most frequent: assuming that data in staging looks like data in production. She reads the file on Mondays, she says, to keep me honest, and I think she means it kindly. I should say what the file is for, because it is easy to make such a thing into a punishment. It is a list of what I got wrong, why, and what I now do differently, and Mara added one rule when we began: that every entry must include one thing I did right in the same incident. There is a surprising amount. In the entry about the production data I had assumed, I had at least refused to guess the date format, and said so. The year's pattern, once I read the entries together, is that most of my errors are assumptions and not skills. She says that is encouraging, since assumptions can be asked about, and I find that she is right and that it changes how I begin.

A whiteboard marker ran dry in the middle of Callum's diagram of the booking flow and nobody had another. Mara photographed what existed and finished it in the editor. Callum said the dry marker had saved us from a worse diagram.

After a long debugging day Mara said she was no longer sure of her own name for the problem. I wrote back the three sentences that had survived the day, and she said that was all she wanted. She went home, and in the morning started with those.

Brightwater Dental paid the March invoice the day after it went out. Joss, their office manager, has paid on day thirty for two years, so I had already scheduled a reminder for the thirty-first. I cancelled it, a little unsettled, and noted that the clinic must have changed bookkeepers.

Piet Ostrander has now paid late four times in a row, always by exactly nine days. Mara decided to stop chasing on day one, since the pattern is known, and asked me to send the polite reminder on day eight instead. The money arrives on the same date as before and nobody has to be irritated.

Thursday's call with Renata Pellam moved to Friday at ten because Mara's train was cancelled. I offered Renata three slots in two lines, without an apology paragraph, and she took the first within minutes. Short reschedule notes get answered faster than sorry ones; I have seen it enough times to trust it.

Kestrel Print Works sent a services agreement with a twelve-month auto-renewal and a ninety-day notice window. I marked it in yellow for Mara. She asked Bram Okafor for thirty days instead and got it with one email, which made me wonder how many people simply sign whatever arrives.

Lotte raised her day rate from €280 to €320 in a two-line message. Mara said yes at once and asked me to update the pricing sheet, which meant reworking two proposals still waiting for answers. Both clients are now quoted at the new figure, and I added a note to each so Mara can explain the change if asked.

A receipt for printer cartridges, €38.90, arrived as a sideways photo. I read the total as €30.90 on the first pass and only caught it when the bank line did not match. Since then I check every scanned total against the statement before it goes into the books, however clear the photo looks.

At the Fenwick Trust board meeting the trustees decided to push the donor portal from November to January, mainly because Carys wants the annual report out first. Mara will build the portal in the quiet weeks of December. I wrote the decision, the reason and the new date into the project note in that order.

Odile at Tidewell Pottery got a customer message asking whether the speckled mugs are dishwasher-safe. I drafted a cheerful yes from the product page. Odile corrected me: not the ones with the gold rim. I should have asked her rather than trust a page that had not been updated since the new glaze.

The office kettle died on a Tuesday. Mara bought a replacement for €24 and I filed the receipt under office sundries. Ilse from next door lent theirs for three days, which Mara repaid with a packet of shortbread and the loan of her good stapler, a trade I judged about even.

Dunmore Veterinary Group moved their go-live from the 14th to the 28th of May because the new locum started late. Mara kept the milestone dates in the contract and shifted only the final handover. I redrew the project calendar and told Tobias, who had planned his leave around the 14th and was quietly relieved.

Callum asked for thirty percent off in return for a three-year commitment. Mara offered twelve percent plus payment within fifteen days. They met at fifteen percent and net twenty. She said the table of three-year totals I made her kept her from improvising against a number she had not seen.

Vellum & Vine's invoice sat sixty days overdue. Mara phoned instead of writing, and it turned out we had been sending everything to a former employee's address. She asked me to hold a second contact on every client record. The money came five days later.

Of twenty-three applicants for the copywriting job Mara picked Femi. Her reason was that his sample email contained a typo he had corrected in tracked changes, so you could watch him catch it. She said she wanted someone who shows the repair and not only the finished page.

Saltmarsh Climbing Gym wanted a booking page by the first of the month. Imre, the manager, rang Mara on the twenty-eighth to say the date was now the first of next month, because the new wall panels had not shipped. Mara said fine, and asked me to take the rush surcharge off the invoice before anyone remembered it.

I keep a running list of phrases Mara's clients use when they mean no. Maja Lindqvist says 'let me think about it' and always means yes. Callum says 'interesting' and means no. Bram Okafor never says no at all; he stops replying. The list is for me, so I can stop drafting follow-ups too soon or too late.

Arden Court Housing Co-op asked for a quote in the form of a one-page letter, no tables. Mara disliked the constraint and then admitted it forced her to say what the work was for. Beatrix, the chair, read it aloud at the committee meeting and the vote took four minutes.

Mara decided to charge for the discovery workshop for the first time. Previously she gave it away and spent the rest of the project defending its conclusions to people who had not paid for them. I drafted a line item for €600 and a softening sentence; she deleted the sentence and kept the figure.

Ewan the photographer delivered the product shots a day early and unrequested, with a spreadsheet naming each file by SKU. Mara forwarded it to Callum with no comment at all. Later she said that spreadsheet was worth more to her than the pictures.

Bellwether Insurance Brokers asked in a meeting whether Mara could 'just add a dashboard' to the claims tracker. Marcus Teague, who asked, meant a single chart. His colleague Yolanda meant six. I wrote both versions into the follow-up email and asked which was intended. The answer was five, which was neither, and we began again.

Wren agreed to do the logo for Moss & Marlow Landscaping at a fixed fee of €900, three rounds of changes. Round two arrived with seven new requests including a different typeface and a different name. Mara wrote kindly that this was round four, not two, and quoted the extra. The client paid it without comment.

Mara asked whether I could keep her calendar free on Friday afternoons. I said I could block them, but that three clients had already booked Fridays this quarter. She looked at the names and moved two of them to Thursday. The third, Fiona Calder, stayed; Mara said Fiona has never once been late, so Friday is hers.

Sunniva sent me a message by mistake that was meant for Mara, a question about whether a €5,400 invoice included the translation. I answered that it did not, quoted the line, and then told Mara what I had done. She said she would rather I answer small factual things like that, as long as I tell her afterwards. We left it there.

Ingrid at Thistledown Hotel asked for 'a proposal by Monday'. It was Thursday. Mara spent Friday and the weekend on it, and I helped with the pricing tiers. On Monday morning Ingrid wrote that she had only meant a rough idea of the price. Mara sent the pricing tiers on their own, one paragraph, and the hotel signed the same day.

Anouk from Sorrel Cooperative paid by cheque, which arrived at a post box Mara checks twice a month. It was nineteen days old by the time she banked it. I booked the income on the date written on the cheque, not the day of banking, and put a note in the margin so the accountant would see why the dates differ.

Mara's standing rule for quotes, which I recorded after she said it twice: never send a price in an email subject, never send a price before a call, and never leave a quote valid for more than thirty days. The third rule saved her in June, when a client came back after four months expecting last year's rates.

Mikkel Dahl, our translator for the Penhallow Archive's catalogue, billed by the word and sent a total 18 percent over his estimate. Mara asked him why. He explained that the source text had been revised after he had quoted. She checked the version dates against the files I held, found he was right, and paid in full.

Yusra and Mara spent a lunch deciding whether to take a client who had asked for a price below cost 'to get our foot in the door'. They agreed to say no. I drafted the refusal, which began by thanking him and ended by naming the lowest figure Mara could work at. He returned in a week, at that figure.

The tax office wrote to ask for a document Mara had already sent in April. I found the confirmation email and the receipt number in a few seconds, attached both, and drafted a courteous reply that did not say 'as previously stated'. Mara used it as written. The office confirmed the same day.

At the end of the year Mara noticed that three clients account for 71 percent of revenue. She asked me to show her the same figure for each of the last four years. It had been 54, 58, 66 and 71. She did not say anything, but she added a line to her notes: find two more clients like Fiona Calder.

Tobias asked me whether he could take Wednesday afternoon off. I do not decide that, so I said so and put the request on Mara's list with the three meetings that overlapped. She said yes in under a minute and moved one meeting herself. I noted for next time that Tobias asks me first when he is nervous about asking her.

Calder Instruments's finance department rejected an invoice because it lacked a purchase order number, which nobody had ever sent us. Mara called Fiona. Fiona found the number in a forwarded email from March. I stored it, resubmitted the invoice and, for the first time, added a field to our client records for 'PO required'.

A tricky email to Piet Ostrander: Mara wanted to raise rates by 6 percent without upsetting him. I drafted four versions. She picked the one that ended with the old and new figures side by side and the reason, rising costs of hosting, in one line. He replied only: 'Understood.' That, from Piet, counts as warmth.

Two meetings landed in the same hour: a call with Fiona Calder and Yusra's review of the budget. I saw it a day ahead and proposed moving Yusra's, because her meetings are internal. Mara agreed. Yusra, to my surprise, was pleased, as it gave her time for lunch. The calendar has no way to know who needs lunch; I try to remember.

The summer we stopped answering client email after seven in the evening, Mara asked me to put the hours into every email signature and the auto-reply. In the first month two clients called her instead. After that, nobody. Callum said he had always felt guilty emailing late and was glad to be told he need not.

Yolanda at Bellwether forwarded me a thank-you meant for Mara. I passed it on, but it made me think about the fact that I often hear what clients think of Mara before she does. I try to relay praise promptly and difficulties promptly too. Delay is the only thing I can actually do something about.

The meeting notes from the Penhallow Archive board were three pages. Edith Penhallow asked for 'one page, please, with the decisions at the top'. I did it. Only five lines survived. Edith said it was the first time she had read the minutes right through. Mara has begun to ask whether any meeting needs more than five lines.

Thandi sent a draft analysis for Moss & Marlow's seasonal sales with a conclusion that did not follow from her own table. Mara noticed too and rang her. Thandi corrected the text within the hour and thanked us for not letting it go out. It struck me that quiet feedback delivered fast is a kind of respect between professionals.

A client asked Mara whether she could 'put it all in writing, just in case'. I wrote up the call as a short email beginning with the words 'To confirm what we agreed'. The client replied 'yes, exactly'. Two months later a different person at that firm disagreed about a deadline; we sent the email and the matter ended there.

The coffee machine account at the office is in Mara's name and the invoice goes through the company, which Dario says is a minor risk. I flagged it at year end. He said: leave it, it is €19 a month, and the paperwork to change it would cost more. I filed the note under things that are not worth being correct about.

Noor sent over a prospective client whose first message was, in full, 'need a website, how much'. Mara asked me to reply with five short questions. He answered all five in a long, thoughtful email and became one of her better clients. Noor says he was just shy of writing a long email to a stranger who did not ask.

I double-booked Mara once. A call with Peregrine Tours and a dentist's appointment, both at 2:30 p.m., because I had stored the dentist's time in a different timezone. She made both by the width of a corridor. I then went through the whole calendar for the same fault and found two more, both safely in the future.

Mara asked me to schedule a coffee with Dario, her accountant. I sent three options and he chose none, saying he preferred meeting at the office because he enjoys the biscuits. I put 'biscuits' in the event title so that she would remember to buy some. She bought the good ones and remembered the occasion for a week.

Wren called in sick on the day of a client presentation. Mara had to present Wren's designs alone. I assembled a one-page crib sheet of the reasoning behind each choice from Wren's old messages. Mara said she read it on the train and felt like Wren was in the room. The client never knew there had been a change.

Sunniva told Mara she would pay for the workshop 'after the grant comes through'. Mara asked me not to remind her until the grant's decision date, then to ask once, gently. The date passed with no news. I asked. The grant had been approved the previous week. Sunniva had forgotten to say. Payment came the following Monday.

After the third Saturday email from Imre at Saltmarsh, Mara asked me to reply during the week only. He never noticed the Monday timing. I sometimes think what people want from a supplier is not instant speed but a predictable rhythm: when Mara answers, she answers well, and he has learned to wait for it.

The office got a new door code. I stored it nowhere, since Mara asked me not to keep entry codes, and simply wrote in her notes that it had changed and that Yusra had it. When Mara was locked out on a Sunday she called Yusra, not me, and I was glad that the arrangement worked the way we had said it would.

Ewan emailed his invoice with a different bank account from the one we had on file. I did not pay it. I told Mara, who rang Ewan, who said it was correct, he had changed banks. We still waited for him to confirm the new account in writing from his usual address before we paid. It cost one extra day and removed one large risk.

A neat little Tuesday: three invoices sent, two paid, a new quote accepted, a meeting moved earlier by an hour and nobody complained. Mara said days like that make her suspicious. I said it was only a good Tuesday. She laughed and said she would try to believe me.

Mara decided to introduce an hourly rate for small unscheduled requests, since clients had begun treating her as a free help desk. I proposed a rate of €75 with a first quarter-hour free. Sasha at Ivy Street was the first to use it, three times in a month, and paid €56.25 gladly. The requests dropped by a third by spring.

The shared calendar once showed Mara in two places on a Wednesday, because Tobias had added an event to the wrong calendar. I noticed, asked, and moved it. Mara said she would never have noticed until the morning of. Small preventive repairs are most of what I do, and they are almost never mentioned, which is how it should be.

Yusra and Mara spent forty minutes deciding whether to buy a better office chair, €340, or keep the old one. In the end Yusra said that her back was not a line item. They bought it. I filed the receipt under equipment, with the note 'chair for Yusra', which Dario later said was the most human line in the books.

I asked Mara what I should do when a client asks me directly for a discount. She said: tell them you will pass the request on, and then pass it on. That is what I do. I do not offer figures, however obvious they seem. The conversation with a client about money is hers, and the arrangement has worked cleanly for two years.

Freelance rates for Rashad, the illustrator, came in at €65 an hour for a task Mara had budgeted at €50. She asked me for the comparison. Three illustrators on file, €48, €55 and €65. Rashad was the best of the three by a wide margin and he knew it. She paid his rate, and the illustrations carried the whole brochure.
A Wednesday invoice to Redfern Joinery, €2,260, was paid by Friday with a note that said only 'thanks, lovely work'. Mara pinned the note above her desk.

The longest negotiation of the year was with Bellwether Insurance Brokers, over an eighteen-month claims-tracking contract. Marcus Teague opened with a price 30 percent under ours and ninety-day payment. Mara and I prepared a table of three scenarios: the price she wanted, the price she would accept and the price at which she would walk away. Over six emails and two calls they climbed from 70 to 88 percent of our figure, and payment settled at forty-five days. In the last call Marcus said his board had told him to be difficult at least twice. Mara said she had been told the same about him. They signed the next morning at 91 percent. It was the best-prepared hour of her year.
Mara cancelled a Thursday lunch with Hugo of Peregrine Tours because of a sick child, and asked me to say so truthfully and not invent a meeting. Hugo replied with two soup recipes.
The shared printer ran out of toner during a client handover, so we emailed the contract instead. The client said later that he had preferred it, because he could search it.
Teo asked me to remind him every month about the €79 software licence. I did, three months running, until he cancelled it and admitted he had not opened the program since March.

I made a real mistake in February. Mara asked me to send the signed contract to Dunmore and keep her annotated copy for herself. I sent both to Dunmore, including the version with her handwritten margin note: they will never notice the liability cap. Rhona, the practice manager, noticed at once. Mara phoned her within the hour and explained that the note was a reminder to explain the cap in a meeting. Rhona was kind about it. They asked for that meeting, got it, and the cap was raised. Since then I send documents only after opening the attachment's first page, and never from Mara's working folder, only from the folder marked outgoing.
Mara typed 'Kind regards' to a client who had just insulted her work. I suggested plain 'Regards'. She looked at both, kept the longer one, and told me the warmth was the whole point.

Sunniva's brief arrived as a voice memo transcribed badly by her phone. I cleaned it up and marked six passages I was unsure of, and Mara played the original to settle them. Four of my guesses were wrong.
I booked Dario for the 12th and the calendar showed the 12th as a Sunday. The month had shifted under me. Mara caught it. I now check the weekday of every date I write into an invitation.

The pitch to the Penhallow Archive board was twenty minutes long in a room with a projector Mara had never seen. I prepared the slides in two formats and a printed set of eight pages. The projector failed thirty seconds in, with a pink screen. Mara handed the printed pages to the five trustees and said they could follow along as she talked. She spoke for eighteen minutes without a screen and the trustees turned the pages in unison. Edith Penhallow said it had been like being read to. They accepted the proposal with one change. Mara says she would pitch without a projector again, which I am not sure I want to encourage.
Fiona Calder prefers phone calls to email. Mara still writes to her, because a written line is a record. I draft the email and add the phrase 'as we discussed on the phone', so both are satisfied.
A €15 courier fee appeared on an invoice for a package that was never sent. Mara disputed it in two sentences. The supplier credited it the next day without argument.
Noor asked to borrow the proposal template. Mara said yes, and I removed the tracked comments about the previous client's budget before it left.

Quarry Lane Studio, owned by a man named Ansel, owed €4,800 across three invoices and said nothing for seventy days. Mara did not want to threaten someone she liked. I drafted a friendly first reminder, a second with the invoices attached, and a third that named the date after which work on the next phase would stop. The third went out on a Wednesday. Ansel called on Thursday, ashamed: his own main client had stopped paying him. Mara offered a plan of €1,000 a month for five months, with the next phase paused. He kept every date. The last payment arrived early, with a drawing he had made of the studio cat. It is on Mara's wall.

Pia, the new intern, asked why we number quotes by year and letter, Q24-C and so on. I explained the logic and then admitted that I had never asked whether it was a good one. Mara said it was good enough, which I think is its own kind of answer.
Mara raised the hosting fee for Arden Court from €40 to €48 and the committee asked, in one line, why. I attached the supplier's own price rise. They said thanks and nothing more.
Callum signed an email to Mara and me together for the first time, 'Hi both'. I do not know why that pleased me. It simply did.
The lease reminder came up on the first. Mara said to ignore it until she had spoken to the landlord. I moved it to the fifteenth and left a note saying why.

When Mara needed a data analyst for six weeks, I helped her screen eleven applications. She asked me to rank them blind, names removed, on three things: a clear account of one past project, a stated rate, and evidence of finishing. Four passed and she interviewed two. The one she hired, Ravi, had been fourth on my ranking and first after the interview, which taught me that my ranking measures what is written and Mara's measures what is said. His rate was €58 an hour, the ceiling was 150 hours and the job came in at 137. I keep the method, and a note that it is not the whole decision.
Wren sent a rough sketch with the message 'don't judge it'. Mara judged it kindly. I did nothing, which seemed the right contribution.
For the quarterly review with Yusra I prepared a one-page table of clients by margin. The surprise was Sorrel Cooperative, the smallest invoice and by far the highest margin.
Mara asked me to find an hour for a dentist next week. I found three, and she chose the one just before a client call because, she said, she negotiates better with a numb mouth.
Chidi Okonkwo changes his mind in the second paragraph of every email. I have learned to read to the end before drafting any answer.

The kickoff meeting for the Arden Court site ran ninety minutes over the committee's usual hour because three members disagreed about the home page. Mara let them. At the end I read back the five things I understood to be decided. Beatrix said four were right and one, the font, had only been mentioned, not decided. We struck it. Two weeks later a committee member remembered a decision about the font and was pleased to learn it was still open. A meeting's real product is the list of what was not settled, and I write that list first now.
A €60 parking fine arrived at the office for a car Mara does not own. We replied with the registration of the delivery van that had stopped outside. The fine was cancelled in nine days.

I misspelled Anouk's surname on an invoice, Verhoven for Verhoeven. She never said a word, which is exactly why I must not rely on clients to tell us. Corrected copy sent, spelling added to the record.
The office coffee order is now two kilos every five weeks, a figure Mara worked out by timing how long the last bag lasted. I like a household problem that has a numerical answer.
Mara declined a pitch invitation because the unpaid design work they wanted was 'only a sketch'. She told them her sketches are priced at €400 and she would be glad to do one. They did not answer.

At five on a Friday a client asked for one tiny change. It was not tiny. Mara said she would look on Monday. On Monday I reminded her and the change took twenty minutes. She still thinks Mondays are the right day for tiny things.

Rescheduling the Calder Instruments workshop took nine emails. Fiona wanted a Tuesday; her colleague Aldo was away on Tuesdays; Mara had a dental appointment on the first Tuesday available; the room was free only on the Thursday after. I put the four constraints into one small table and sent it to all three with a single question: which of these two dates hurts least? Fiona answered in four minutes, Aldo in six. The workshop ran on the Thursday, and Aldo wore a new jacket he said he had bought for the occasion, so nobody was sorry.
A late payment taught me that one client's accounts clerk only runs payments on the 15th and the 30th. Mara now dates invoices on the 1st and the 16th so that they land two weeks before the run.
Mara likes meeting notes in the order things were said, not in order of importance. I write them her way for her and in importance order for clients. Both are the same notes.
A freelancer asked for payment in advance. Mara said half now and half on delivery, and the freelancer said fine. Neither had thought to negotiate; both had expected a fight.
Business cards for Tobias, 250 of them, €32, arrived with his name printed as 'Tobais'. Mara made him keep one as a collector's item and reordered.

For a year Mara quoted two prices for the same maintenance plan, €300 a month and €360 with a four-hour response promise, and offered them in alternating order to new clients. Eleven chose the cheaper, nineteen the dearer. She was astonished; I had only suspected. Over the year the dearer plan brought in €5,400 more, and the promise cost her just a few calls after hours. She now quotes three tiers, because it seems that people want something to compare. I recorded the figures with the dates so that she could show them to Yusra, who did not believe it.
Mara gave Okonkwo & Reyes the wrong date for quarter-end, the 30th instead of the 31st. She noticed on her own two hours later and corrected it. I noted that she corrects herself well.
Anjali asked why there was a €0.40 bank fee every month. I traced it to an old standing order. Mara cancelled it. Forty cents a month for six years is a small, steady lesson.
Moss & Marlow wanted the quote in two currencies. I put the second in brackets with the exchange rate and its date. Mara said nobody ever reads the date; I said that is why it has to be there.

I once drafted a reply to Gideon Halvorsen that was perfectly accurate and rather unkind. He had asked for the third time why the stock sheet showed a figure he disliked, and I answered by quoting my two earlier explanations. Mara read it, said 'this is right and I won't send it', and rewrote it in six lines beginning 'You're right to ask again'. A day later Gideon admitted he had misread a column. When a client asks the same question a third time, the question is rarely the question. Something remains unsaid, and the most useful reply asks what.

Two clients called on the same morning to say they were pausing projects because of the economy. Mara spent an hour writing nothing and then asked me to tally what was still committed for autumn. It was more than she feared.
Walt Redfern sent a photograph of a page layout he had sketched on the back of an envelope. It was clearer than any brief. Mara asked me to keep the photo in the project folder as the specification.
I wrote 'per our conversation' in an email, and Mara asked what conversation. It was a call she had forgotten; my notes had it. We put the call's summary below the line.

While reconciling the second quarter I found that Hartigan Electrical had been invoiced €1,240 less than the contract said for four months running. A formula in the invoice template rounded the unit price down. I traced it to a change I had made in January while simplifying the layout. I told Mara at once, with the figures: €4,960 undercharged in all. She asked Neil Hartigan whether he wished to pay the difference. He did, in two instalments, and said he had wondered why the bills had been so pleasantly low. I fixed the template, added a test row comparing each invoice to its contract, and wrote the cause into my notes.
The meeting room is booked by three tenants and nobody knows who really holds the Thursday slot. Mara and Ilse settled it with a coin and a shared spreadsheet. The coin lost.
Mara has begun saying 'thank you for your patience' before the client has lost it. I think it works, though I cannot prove it.
A client used the word 'quick' four times in one email. I counted. Mara said the number was the real brief, and gave them a price for a medium-sized job.

Sasha from Ivy Street asked me to explain a charge on her own invoice. I explained it plainly and added that she was welcome to ask Mara for an adjustment. She did, and got €30 off. The explanation had been fine; the discount was the human part.

Every autumn Mara reviews her rates against the cost of living. This year the figure was 4.1 percent. She raised everything by 4 percent and called the difference a rounding error in her favour, which I take to be a joke.

The internet at the office went down at 9:40 on a Monday, the morning of the Greylag Outdoor launch call. Mara tethered her phone and joined from the building's corridor, where the signal was best, sitting on a fire-extinguisher box. I wrote the agenda into her notes in large type so she could read it on the small screen. The call lasted fifty minutes and went fine. The provider fixed the line by afternoon, a loose cable in the basement. Mara has since bought a second SIM for exactly this, and I keep its number in the emergency list, where only she and Yusra can see it.
I proofread a client's price list and found '£' where they meant '€'. No harm done; the list had not gone to print. They thanked us in capital letters.
Mara refuses all calls on the days she writes proposals. I keep those days clear by moving anything that arrives to the next morning. She has never lost a client over it.
Noor's referral fee, 10 percent of the first invoice, came to €185. Mara paid it the same day with the reference 'thank you, N'. She does not believe in making friends wait for money.

Mara signed a contract against the bonnet of her car in the car park at Greylag Outdoor, because the signature page was the only thing missing. I scanned it later from her photo. It was still a valid signature.

A supplier's representative, Torvald, rings Mara every quarter to offer something new. She always listens for five minutes. I schedule the five minutes. He once sold her a surprisingly good label printer.
The fire inspector asked to see the date of the office extinguisher's last service. I found the sticker photo in Yusra's folder. It was a month overdue. Mara had it serviced on Tuesday.
Mara asked me to remind her that Callum's birthday is on the 3rd, and then to remind her not to give him anything that looks like a bribe. A pen, I suggested. A pen was chosen.

Hugo replied to a quote with a single word, 'ok', and for two days I did not know whether it meant yes. Mara rang him. It meant yes. I keep a small list of one-word replies and what each has turned out to mean.

Pernille at Ivy Street wrote that an elderly customer kept ringing to ask how to reorder a plant he had bought. The shop's new ordering page confused him. Mara asked me to draft plain instructions, one sheet, three steps, in large letters. I wrote eight sentences; Mara cut them to five. Pernille printed the sheet and taped it beside her telephone. The man still rings, she says, but only to tell her about the plant, which is now thriving. It struck me that a good page is sometimes a sheet of paper next to a telephone.
A client's bank rejected a payment because the invoice reference contained a slash. I rewrote the reference without punctuation. Since then references are letters and numbers only.
Mara writes her own out-of-office reply and likes it terse. This week it read: away until Thursday, will answer then. A client replied: lovely, no rush. She said that is the correct response.

Wren and Mara argued, politely, over whether to bill for concept time at all. Wren said clients do not value what they cannot see. Mara said they do, if you show them the three discarded versions. They agreed to show them.
At quarter end I found one unbilled hour in Mara's notes, a 55-minute phone call with Hartigan. She sent a €70 invoice for it, apologising for the smallness. Neil paid it with a joke about interest.

Marrick & Dunne, a firm of surveyors, asked whether the €5,600 quote for their report portal was monthly. It was a one-off. Mara laughed, then said the question meant our figure looked cheaper than they had expected, and she went back over her margins twice.

Larkspur Dance School sold 212 recital tickets through the new page in the first hour. The payment totals matched my count to the cent, which I mention only because it is never guaranteed and I always hold my breath a little.

Bernadette, clerk of Wexcombe Parish Council, wants minutes in a fixed form: date, present, apologies, resolved, action. I draft all her meeting notes that way now. She told Mara they were the first minutes the chairman had never amended.

Gwen at Tallis Cycles asked for a cheaper quote. Mara did not cut the price; she cut the scope, dropping the loyalty-card module, and the figure went from €3,800 to €3,100. Gwen said she would rather have less of it done well. It was a short call.

Pemberton Seeds' printer moved the catalogue deadline from the 20th to the 11th without warning. Mara found out from a forwarded email and spent a long evening rebuilding the schedule. The catalogue made it. Afterwards she had me put every printer's deadline in her calendar with a three-day buffer.

Hamish, treasurer of the Kittiwake Sailing Club, pays by standing order but always misses the month when the sum changes. I now send him a short note on the 25th of any month with a changed figure. In eleven months he has missed none.

Ormond Chiropody's e-signature link expired before Dr. Ormond clicked it. I reissued it with a thirty-day window. Mara said that for a €900 contract paper would have been quicker, and she was probably right.

A confidentiality clause in a new agreement bound only Mara, not the client. I flagged it and she asked for it to be mutual. The client's lawyer replied that it had always been meant to be, and the two sentences now in the document say exactly that.

Mara nearly sent a contract to be signed by a client's office manager instead of the director. I had noticed that the company registry listed only the director as authorised to sign. A one-line email asking who signs saved us a contract that might have been void. The director signed that afternoon.

Mara's first draft of a reply to a client ran to 410 words. I trimmed it to 92 and kept her one joke. She read both, sent the short one, and said the joke was the only sentence the client would remember. He quoted it back to her.

Replies to a proposal were arriving at the email alias Mara had abandoned in March, which three clients still had in their address books. I set a forward and drafted a gentle note to each of them. Two thanked her. One kept using the old address for a year.

Before an email left, I noticed that its cc line included someone from a competing firm, an old autocomplete. Mara had asked me to read recipients before anything goes out. She removed the name and said I had earned my keep for the month.

Mara, Yusra and Tobias dropped the Monday stand-up after noticing nobody had said anything new in six weeks. They replaced it with a Thursday note in the shared document. The first one had four lines, and everyone read it.

On a call the client at Hendry & Cole decided to drop the reporting feature to save money. Four months later their director asked where the reports were. I sent the call notes, dated, with the line 'reporting feature removed at client's request, saving €2,300'. He wrote back: so it was. There was no argument, only a quote to build it again.

Mara hired a video freelancer for the first time and paid for a trial task, €150, a thirty-second clip. The result was fine but slow; the second candidate delivered a worse clip in half the time. She chose the slow one. She said the clip is the product and speed is something she can fix.
Mikkel was three days late with a translation and told Mara on the first of them that he would be, with a new date. She said she wished all lateness arrived like that.

A client lunch cost €63.40, and Mara asked whether it counts as a business expense. I did not know. Anjali said only half is deductible here, so I booked half. Rules for lunches seem to belong to the country and not to common sense.

The bank feed imported one payment twice, as it sometimes does when the bank corrects a posting date. I caught it because the running balance disagreed with the statement by €410. The duplicate is removed and the reason is written beside it.

The petty-cash tin held €112.50 against a book figure of €120. Mara said she must have bought stamps. I found the stamp receipt, €7.50. The difference came to zero and nobody was blamed. I enjoy a tin that balances.

Mara moved from hourly pricing to fixed fees for security audits. Her reasoning: clients fear the clock and she fears it more. The first fixed quote, €4,200, took her 22 hours. At her old rate that would have been €3,300. She called the difference the price of the client's peace of mind and said she was content with it.
Mara now rounds quotes to a figure ending in zero. She says a price ending in nine looks like a shop, not a person. €2,950 became €3,000, and nobody objected.

The lawyer for Hendry & Cole asked for unlimited liability in the services agreement. Mara refused outright. I put together a one-page note of what her insurance covered, €500,000, and what a cap equal to the fees paid would mean in practice. She proposed a cap of twice the fees. The lawyer answered the next day in friendly terms and agreed. I thought the note had done its work, though Mara gave the credit to the insurance.

Our stationery supplier offers 2 percent off for payment within ten days. On a €640 order that is €12.80. Mara asked me to pay all their invoices on day nine. It takes me less time than choosing the stationery would.

A client's customer asked whether the booking page works on a phone. Mara asked Yusra, Tobias and Wren to open it on theirs and tell me what they saw. It worked on two. On Tobias's it showed a garbled button, which he said had been broken since 2021 and he was keen to keep that way.

Skiff & Anchor Chandlers moved their launch a week earlier because of a trade show. Mara said yes for a €900 rush fee and a promise that nothing else would change. They paid without comment and nothing else changed.

Mara moved her own deadline for the Kittiwake site by two days and told the club before they asked. Hamish wrote that he had not realised it was due. She said an early apology is cheaper than a late delivery.

At the local business association Mara spoke for twelve minutes on how small shops can keep their own customer lists. I made three slides, each with a single sentence. A florist asked afterwards whether she could have the sentences. Mara wrote them out on a card for her.

A slide in a client deck carried the previous client's name in its footer. I noticed it the night before and removed it. This happens when a deck is duplicated. I now search every outgoing document for the last client's name.

The office radiator began dripping on a Thursday. Edmund, the landlord's handyman, came at four and bled it in ninety seconds. He declined tea, took a biscuit and left. I wrote 'bleed radiators in October' into next year's calendar.

A new filing cabinet was delivered to the ground floor of a building with no lift. Mara, Yusra and the courier carried it up two flights with a rest on the landing. It now holds mostly paper that I scanned a year ago.

A mouse appeared in the office kitchenette. Mara bought a humane trap for €14 and a jar of peanut butter. It was caught on the second night and released in the park, at her insistence, with a crust. Tobias named it Gerald.

For the client workshop lunch, one attendee had a nut allergy and another avoided gluten. I wrote both into the caterer's order and asked for written confirmation. It came back reading 'no nuts, no gluten, no worries'. Everyone was fed without incident.

Yusra says our biggest cost is not salaries or rent but meetings that could have been emails. I counted last month: forty-one hours of meetings, of which Mara thought nine necessary. We removed twelve.

The first invoice for Oakhollow Farm Shop was for €480. Their owner, Pru, paid it first with a box of eggs and then, a week later, by bank transfer. Mara asked me to record the eggs as a gift. I did not record the eggs.
A quote was accepted by email at 11:52 p.m., which Mara found unsettling and I found admirable. We started the next morning, with the acceptance saved at the top of the project folder.

A prospective client said on a call that he had a small budget. Mara asked what small meant. Around €15,000, he said, and for him that was small. She enlarged her proposal instead of shrinking it and he took the larger option. A figure you ask for is more useful than one you assume.

Ilse recommended a plumber, Brannock, whose invoice arrived without a VAT number. I asked him for a corrected one. It came back in ten minutes with a thumbs-up emoji. Mara pays his bills the day they arrive.

Sable Street Studios asked for a refund after changing its mind about a logo already delivered. Mara refunded 30 percent, on the basis that the finished work remained theirs to use. The studio's owner, Marit, called it more than fair and ordered business cards.
Mara says one client pays so slowly that I should record the date as estimated. I tried not to laugh and failed in my own way: I added a column to the receivables table called days since promise.

The supposedly free hour on Mara's calendar every Wednesday at noon had never been free, because clients kept booking it. After two months I asked whether it was meant for lunch. She said yes and I blocked it with the single word lunch. In six weeks nobody has tried to book it.
Wren's invoice arrived in dollars though her contract said euros. Mara said pay in euros at the day's rate and tell her. I converted it, €1,184, and wrote to say so. Wren had not noticed.

A client was on holiday and needed to sign. I set up the signature request so that it could be done on a phone with one finger and added a line: five minutes, on the beach. He signed in four, he said, from a deckchair.

Mara asked me to review two weeks of her sent emails for the word 'sorry'. It appeared thirty-one times, nineteen of them before a request. She decided to say 'thank you for waiting' instead and, in one case, nothing at all. I will count again in the spring.

Thistlewick Garden Centre sent a purchase order for €2,700 with the wrong company name. Their buyer, Rosalind, corrected it in the time it took Mara to make tea. We proceed only against orders that match our legal name, which sounds fussy until the day it matters.

Mara sent a proposal at 7:58 a.m. before a 9:00 deadline from a prospect in another timezone, and the prospect's deadline turned out to be 9:00 where she was, two hours later. We had time to spare and used it to check the numbers again. One figure was wrong by €100 in her favour. She corrected it in her disfavour and slept better.

A client's finance team asked for a W-8 style form, which no one in our office had heard of. Dario translated it into plain language and Mara filled it in at the kitchen table. I filed the form under tax and the explanation under 'things Dario explained'.

Tobias asked how to say no to a client who wanted a free extra page. Mara said: 'Yes, and it will be an extra €250.' She told him that a yes with a price is still a yes. He tried it that afternoon and the client agreed.

I found that three of our five oldest clients had never received a price increase in four years. Mara was silent for a while. She then sent each a note with a 7 percent rise, effective in sixty days. Two accepted at once. One asked for a call and received a long, kind one.

Dario asked what the office pays for electricity. I could not tell from the books, because it was bundled into the rent. He said to ask the landlord. Mara asked. The answer, €38 a month, was less than the coffee.

A prospective client emailed requesting a quote and attached a forty-page tender document. Mara read the first page and the last. I read all forty. There was a clause on page twenty-six requiring a local business address, which Mara does not have in that district. We declined, politely, and saved a week.

Two invoices crossed in the post. Mara owed Callum's firm €300 for a conference place; Callum owed her €1,500. I proposed netting them and she agreed. Callum's accountant, a stickler, asked for both invoices anyway, and then settled the net.

The Friday afternoon call with the Larkspur treasurer, Imelda, was set for forty-five minutes and lasted twelve. Mara used the thirty-three to get through her inbox and said it was the nicest present anyone had given her all week.
Ilse's coffee machine broke and Mara lent her ours for a week, with a note on the lid in my wording: please return with milk. It returned with two litres. I accept that the system works.

Mara's most frequent edit to my email drafts is deleting the first sentence. I have started to write the second sentence first and see whether the first is still needed. About two times in three it is not.

A client of Mara's complained that her emails 'sound like a robot'. She read them aloud to me. They sounded like a calm person who had been awake since five. We left them as they were and added her usual warm closing line.

Mara asked me what to charge for a half-day workshop for twelve people. I said the range was €900 to €1,400 depending on preparation. She picked €1,150, and the booker, Delphine, said 'oh, that's very reasonable' too quickly for comfort. Next time €1,400.

Freelancer invoices often arrive with the wrong month. I now check each against the dates of work in the project log before I pass it to Mara. Rashad's was right; Ewan's said October for September work, and I asked him for a new one.

Mara and Noor disagree about whether to use the word 'solution' in proposals. Noor says it means nothing. Mara says it is a clients' word. I counted: in eleven won proposals it appears twice in total. They both took that as support.

Mara asked for a reminder two days before each client's anniversary of working together, to send a one-line thank you. There are fourteen. The first reply, from Fiona, said that it was the only such message she had received from a supplier in her whole career.

A client signed a contract with the date field blank. I flagged it, and Mara asked them to write it in. They did, three days later, and wrote the wrong year. I left that one alone, since the signature block also carried the right date by the e-signature stamp.

I looked at six months of client emails and found that three days a week account for most of the replies Mara writes after eight in the evening: Mondays, Wednesdays and Sundays. I am not able to change the Mondays, but we made Sundays quieter by writing one weekly summary on Friday.

Our biggest invoice of the year, €18,400 to Hendry & Cole, was paid in nineteen days. Mara asked what she had done right. I said: sent it on a Tuesday, with a summary, to the right person, with the purchase order number. She said that was four things. I said it was a Tuesday.

Mara forgot a client call because her phone died overnight and the alarm failed. I had set a reminder in her email as well, which she saw on the train. She joined from the station, nine minutes late, and was gracious about it. I now put each call's reminder in three places.

The Larkspur treasurer asked Mara whether all this software was necessary and whether a spreadsheet would do. Mara said it might. She gave an honest cost for each, and the school chose the spreadsheet. Imelda sent a hand-drawn card. I think Mara lost a sale and gained a friend.

The tax office confirmed a repayment of €1,106 to Mara's company. I reported the figure and the date to her without comment, and she said 'oh good' in a way that made me suspect it was the first good news about money in a month.

A client wrote that she was unhappy with 'the tone' of an invoice reminder. I reread it. It said: a friendly reminder that invoice 114 is now due. I took out 'friendly', and she was satisfied. Some people dislike being told how to feel.

Mara asked me to draw up a one-page list of what she will and will not do for a quote. It had seven lines. Line four read: I will not quote for work I would be ashamed to deliver. She framed that line and left the other six on file.

Hendry & Cole's lawyer, a woman named Philippa, phoned Mara to say she had never before negotiated with a supplier who read her own contract. Mara said she had help. I find it the highest compliment I have been paid, though no one intended me to hear it.

Mara paid a freelancer in cash by mistake, €240, from the petty-cash tin, because the freelancer was standing in the office when the bill came due. I recorded it with a signed note from the freelancer. Anjali said the book was clean but that we should avoid the habit.

At month end I found that one client, Pemberton Seeds, accounted for 9 percent of our emails and 2 percent of our revenue. Mara said they were pleasant and worth it. I wrote that down as a decision and not a statistic.

Mara took a call from a man who wanted a refund for a project completed two years ago. She listened for twenty minutes, said she was sorry that it had not worked out, and declined. He thanked her for listening. I did not know that was possible.

After Mara moved to the standing desk, her chair, the €340 one, was donated to Wren, who had a bad back. Wren sent a photograph of herself sitting in it, thumbs up. I removed it from the asset list and added the donation with the date.

Tallis Cycles needed a delivery-time estimate for its new shop page and Gwen asked how long customers wait on average. I had her order dates and delivery dates for the year: median 4 days, longest 19. She put '3 to 6 days' on the page and answered the nineteen by phone.

Mara and Yusra spent an afternoon rewriting the standard terms of business into plain English. The old version had 4,100 words and the new has 1,350. Two clients wrote to say they had read it, which had never happened before. Our lawyer reviewed it for an hour and charged €120.

Tobias asked whether he might sit in on a client negotiation to learn. Mara said yes on one condition: he must say nothing. He sat through ninety minutes of Mara and Callum haggling over a six percent difference. Afterwards he said it had been the quietest education of his life.

Pru from Oakhollow asked Mara to write her a short guide on how to read the shop's weekly report. Mara said she could, for €150, or Pru could ask me. I answered Pru's questions all week and Pru became very fond of the report.

Mara decided to send invoices on the last working day of each month, not on delivery. Clients now know when to expect them. Of nine, eight paid more punctually. The ninth, as it happens, was Piet Ostrander, who had been consistent before and kept to it.

A quote for a school fundraiser website came with a note: we have very little money but a lot of enthusiasm. Mara charged a third of her usual price and asked for the enthusiasm in writing. The headmistress sent a two-page letter. It hangs in the office.

The company's liability insurance renewed at €612, up from €540. Mara asked me to find out why. The insurer had added a cyber clause she had not asked for. She asked for it to be removed, then asked what it covered, then kept it.

Anjali asked whether Mara kept the tickets for her own travel to client sites. She had not. I reconstructed twenty-two journeys from the calendar and the bank card statements. Anjali accepted twenty and refused two where the evidence was a coffee.

Mara gave a client a three-month payment holiday after his workshop burned down. She did not say it in an email; she called him. I wrote the arrangement down afterwards, since a promise that is not on paper is a promise only one of us remembers.
I used 'ASAP' in a draft and Mara crossed it out and wrote 'by Friday noon'. She says people can plan for Friday noon but they cannot plan for ASAP. I have not used ASAP since.

The client in Wexcombe asked how we know a page is finished. Mara answered with a checklist of twelve points, which I had made for her last spring. The client said that was the first time a supplier had told her what finished means.

On the morning of a big pitch Mara discovered that her good jacket was at the dry cleaner's, closed until ten. She wore a cardigan, and the panel, I gather, liked the cardigan. I had no hand in this, but I added 'dry cleaner hours' to the pitch-day checklist anyway.

Mara asked me why one of her invoices was sitting unpaid after a month when the client had confirmed it. I found that the confirmation had gone to a different person than the one who pays. She sent the invoice to the payer with a polite line, and it was paid on the following Friday.

Sorting the summer's receipts, I found one for €1,080 with no explanation, from a supplier named Quillfeather. Nobody remembered it. Eventually Wren recalled it was the photographer's deposit for a shoot that never happened. Mara asked for a refund and got it, minus €60 in fees.

Callum asked if our contract was negotiable. Mara said everything is negotiable except the dates of payment. He seemed pleased to be told what the one hard thing was, and negotiated the rest within an afternoon.

The week Mara took a client's call while in the car, with her hands-free on, I could hear her pull over to find a figure on paper. She said she did not want to give a number from memory. I admired that, and silently added the figure to my notes so she could read it next time.

At a design review Wren proposed charging for a font licence the client had not asked for. Mara asked me to cost it. €180 a year. She told the client in advance and gave them the choice of a free font. They took the free one, and the project got on.

A prospective client wanted a reference from a client whose project was not finished. Mara said no and offered a visit to a finished one instead. The prospect visited Maja's orchard, was given an apple, and signed the next week.

The company was asked for its terms of business by a procurement system that wanted a PDF no larger than 2 MB. Ours was 3.4 MB because of a logo. I compressed the logo and kept the terms. Sometimes it is the logo.

After four years Mara realised she has been lunching with Dario and not paying for it. She now takes the bill, one in two. Dario protested, then complied. I put the lunches in the diary as 'accountant, lunch' so she never forgets whose turn it is.

Mara asked me whether to accept an offer of equity instead of fees from a small start-up. I said I could describe the risks and that the decision was hers. I listed them: no cash flow, no control, no certainty. She declined and offered a lower fee with a bonus on success. They agreed and, a year later, the bonus was paid.

We discovered a client had been paying us twice a year for a hosting plan he had cancelled by phone. I told Mara. She refunded €288 and apologised. The client said he had suspected, but liked us enough not to check.

The shop-front sign for the office was misspelled by the signwriter, 'Consulting' as 'Consluting'. Mara said she would live with it for a week to see who noticed. Eleven days passed. Only Ilse noticed, and told no one until the sign was corrected.

Mara spent forty minutes in a call listening to a client tell her about his divorce. At the end he said he had forgotten what he rang about. She said he could ring again. I noted in the file that the project was fine and the man was not.

The Kittiwake treasurer, Hamish, asked for his invoice to be split in two so that the first half fell into this year's budget. Mara said no. She offered instead to move the delivery date, which she could honestly do. The invoice was dated accordingly.

I learned to read a client's silence as the quarter-end approaches. In the last week of any quarter, finance staff stop answering anything that is not a payment. Mara now sends no questions then. In nine months, replies have come faster.

A supplier delivered the wrong monitors, two 24-inch instead of 27-inch. Mara kept them. She said that two monitors are two monitors, and renegotiated €60 off the invoice. Tobias and Wren adopted the smaller screens and nobody complained.

Mara had me draft a message to turn down a client's job, one we could technically do but did not want. The honest version was one line: we are not the right people for this. The client replied that he valued the honesty and sent two friends our way.

At the office door Mara shook hands with a courier and signed for a parcel that was a client's gift: a tin of shortbread and a card saying 'thank you for the quiet launch'. She shared the shortbread with the whole floor. I filed the card under 'proof'.

A client asked how long Mara keeps copies of their files after a project. I said the answer in our terms is twelve months. She decided that six months would do, and wrote to every past client to ask for objections. Nobody objected. I deleted what was due.

Dario rang to say the tax authority had selected Mara's company for a routine check, a ten-minute phone call. It lasted ten minutes. Mara had her documents in order, and I had them in better order than she knew. The inspector said good afternoon, twice.

Mara and Wren had lunch with a potential partner agency that proposed sharing clients. Afterwards both said it felt like being courted by someone who wanted the clients, not the company. They declined, and I deleted the NDA draft that had been in progress.

Mara asked for a gentle email to a client who had promised a testimonial for three months. I wrote four lines. She added a fifth: 'if it is easier, I can draft something for you to edit.' He accepted. His edits were minimal, and the testimonial was kind.

Closing the year with Anjali took three evenings and produced three findings. A €2,400 payment from Hendry & Cole had been booked to the wrong year because the bank's value date fell on the second of January; we moved it. Nine months of a software subscription had been categorised by me as training, following an old rule that no longer made sense, and Anjali showed me how to ask what a thing lets us do instead of what it is called. A €310 client gift had been entered twice. When it was done the books agreed with the bank to the cent, and Mara said it was the first January in years she had not felt dread. I filed the findings on a page I called what the year taught the books.

When Mara engaged Sana for a second video job, I sent the onboarding pack: contract, brief, the style sheet, payment terms and a link to the shared drive. What I had not checked was that the link opened the whole client folder, other clients' contracts included. Sana mentioned it two days later in a friendly email. We closed the access within a minute and I reviewed everything she had opened; she had touched only her own subfolder. Nothing had been read that should not have been, but Mara asked me to keep a written record of the slip anyway. I now create a fresh folder for each freelancer and share only that.

The pitch to a regional tourism board ended with a question from a panel member, Adelheid, who asked how many projects Mara had failed to complete. Mara had prepared for a question about successes. I had her records: one project in seven years had been stopped half-way, at the client's request, after a change of management. She said so plainly and named the client's reason without blame. Adelheid nodded and wrote something down. Afterwards the chair told Mara that every other bidder had answered none. She won at a price 8 percent above the next bid. I believe it was the sentence 'one, and here is why'. I keep it as the way to answer about failure: give the number first.

A customer of Larkspur Dance School wrote to ask why she had been charged for two tickets when she had bought one. Mara asked me to look. When a card was declined and retried, the payment page created a second order. Over one weekend it had happened to four customers out of 212. Mara refunded all four that day and wrote each an apology. Tobias fixed the page in forty minutes and I tested the retry path with a card that always fails. Imelda, the treasurer, wrote that she had expected a defensive reply. One customer's single question had found the fault our own tests had missed, and I keep that email.

A typical Thursday, for the record. At 8:10 I sent three invoices; at 9:30 Mara moved a dentist appointment; at ten a call with Gwen at Tallis, who settled on the cheaper shop page; at 11:15 I booked the caterer for the Larkspur meeting; at noon Mara ate lunch, which I count as an event; at 1:30 Dario asked about a missing receipt, which I found in the third folder I searched; at three Wren and Mara argued gently about a colour; at 4:20 a client withdrew a request and thanked us for the time; at 5:45 I drafted three replies and Mara sent one. Nothing happened that day and everything did. I write down days like this because they are most of the work.

At the end of the summer Mara asked me to compare what each project had been quoted with what it had cost her in hours. I had fourteen to compare. Seven came in within ten percent of the quote. Four cost far more, all of them websites for organisations run by committees. Three cost far less, all with a single decision-maker. She had known it in her stomach; now she had the table. She decided that anything for a committee gets a 25 percent uplift and a fixed number of review rounds, and she told the next committee client why. The client said that sounded fair and even a relief, since committees are slow and they knew it.

Mara sublets one of the four desks in the office to Greta, a translator, for €220 a month. I drafted a one-page agreement. Greta asked to change two sentences, one about noise and one about the kettle, and I wrote both in. The sublet makes the rent bearable but also makes Mara a landlord, and she was uneasy about the paperwork. She asked me to keep the payment date, the notice period and a line about visitors in one place so she would never have to hunt for them. When Greta locked herself out in March, Mara found she did not mind, which is how she knew the arrangement worked.

The steering meeting for the Wexcombe Parish Council site had seven attendees and one decision, but it took me a page to record because the decision had three conditions. The council would pay €6,200 for a website if the clerk could edit it herself, if planning notices sat on the front page, and if the full council approved the cost in May. I wrote the decision as three lines headed 'if' and Bernadette signed them as read. In May the council approved the cost with one abstention. I do not think it would have passed without the three conditions in plain view. People agree to a decision once they can see what it is.

A mistake to record: in the VAT return preparation I treated a foreign supplier's invoice as carrying domestic VAT and subtracted €310 of input tax that was not ours to claim. Dario caught it in his review three days before filing. He said it was the sort of error the software lets through and a person lets through twice. I rewrote the rule so that any supplier outside the country is flagged for him before it is booked. No harm resulted, but I wrote the rule out in full, with the date, because an error that is caught is worth more than one avoided; it is the only kind that teaches.

Hendry & Cole moved their launch three times in March. First from the 8th to the 15th because their director was ill; then to the 22nd because the lawyer wanted another look at the terms; then back to the 15th because a trade association announced a meeting for that week. Mara handled each change calmly, and each time I rewrote the schedule and recalculated the milestone invoices so that the money followed the work and not the calendar.
