By the third change the table was in the right shape and the arguments were over before they began. They launched on the 15th. Mara said the schedule had been moved so often that it had stopped being a schedule and become a conversation, which she preferred.

Pelham Aldous of Aldous Textile read our proposal aloud to his sister over the phone and rang back to say yes, with one request: change 'platform' to 'tool'. Mara obliged. The change cost nothing and probably decided it.
Joan Cobbett of Cobbett Brewery pays on the nail every month and attaches a joke about beer to every remittance. I log the payment, not the joke, but I keep both.
Sunil Mehra at Harrow Lane Pharmacy paid a ninety-day-old invoice with an apology and an extra €50 'for the trouble'. Mara returned the €50. He sent flowers. I recorded the flowers as a mystery.

Fenna at Nightjar Games offered a revenue share instead of a fee. Mara asked me to model it with their own sales figures. Over two years the share would pay €41,000 against a fee of €9,500; over six months, nothing. She took the share with €3,000 up front. Fenna said it was the first time a contractor had asked for both.
A client sent three emails about one subject to three of Mara's addresses. I merged the threads into one note and answered once, to the address she actually works from.

Tamsin Orme's coaching practice sent a contract saying either party could end it 'at any time for any reason'. Mara asked for seven days' notice, which Tamsin had never thought of. A clause that cuts both ways still needs a door of the right width.

Odette at Bluebell Childcare can only meet between 1:15 and 2:00, when the children nap. I block that window in Mara's calendar every second Tuesday and call it 'Odette'. No further explanation is needed.

Mara's email to Lionel Fairweather began 'As I said last week'. I suggested deleting it, since Lionel had not remembered and would hear a rebuke. She cut it and added the date of the call instead. Lionel replied warmly with the answer she wanted.

Decisions at the Stonebridge Bike Co-op meeting: logo stays, name stays, opening day moves to the 3rd. Nothing else was decided in two hours. I sent the three lines at six and a member thanked me for the shortest minutes the co-op had ever had.

Ines the illustrator asked for 50 percent upfront, which Mara had never offered a freelancer. I drafted it as a deposit and wrote it into the contract. Ines sent first sketches the same night, which made Mara wonder how many others have been waiting for a deposit before starting.
A receipt for 'consumables', €412, had no description. Mara remembered: toner and a drill bit. Two categories on one receipt, so I split the line. Anjali nodded.
Mara tried the price 'from €1,200' on the services page. Enquiries rose by a third; conversions fell by a fifth. She took it down and puts the figure in proposals instead, where she can explain it.

A customer of Eskdale Hill Cheese asked whether a wheel could be posted to Norway. I did not know, and neither did the owner. We found out: yes, with a certain box and a form. The shop's delivery page now has a Norway line.

Yarrow & Pike moved a deadline back a month because their director would be away. Mara moved all dependent work, then found that Wren's slot was gone. A replacement in the same week cost €15 an hour more. She sent the difference to Yarrow & Pike as a line item with one sentence of explanation. They paid it.

Mara rehearsed the Aldous presentation twice to me and once to the kettle. I timed it at fourteen minutes forty. She cut a story about a customer in Leeds. The meeting took twelve minutes and was the better for it.

The landlord replaced the office carpet over a weekend. On Monday the room smelled of glue and Mara worked from the café until Wednesday. I moved three meetings, apologised twice and billed no one for the carpet.

We lost a proposal in May to a firm whose quote was €2,000 lower. Mara asked me to find out why, so I asked politely. The buyer, Marguerite, said both were good but the other firm had sent their proposal as one page and ours as eleven. Mara looked at her eleven pages for a long time. The next proposal had a one-page summary on top and the eleven pages behind it, and it won.

Quarterly payer: Stonebridge Bike Co-op pays on the first of January, April, July and October, as if by astronomy. I never send them reminders. They have never been late, and the day I wrote that sentence I checked the calendar twice.

Mara got an invoice from a client, reversed. Lionel Fairweather had billed her €75 for a 'consultation' she had given him at lunch. She framed it and paid it. I booked it under 'goodwill expense' and Anjali raised an eyebrow.

At the changeover to summer time I booked a call with a client across the Atlantic one hour wrong. Mara noticed the mistake because the client's own calendar showed a different time. We rang a day later with an apology. I now check clock-change weeks against both countries' rules.
Harrow Lane Pharmacy's customer questions are quite beautiful. Today: does the site know I take the blue pill. No, it does not, and Mara's reply said so kindly and pointed to the pharmacist.

Mara's contract with Nightjar Games gave them ownership of everything we built, including the tools we had written for ourselves. I flagged it. Mara drew a line in the document: client owns the product; Mara keeps her tools and licenses them. Fenna agreed in one email, a little embarrassed by how long she had spent worrying.

I told Mara a quote she had written contained a total that did not match its lines, €7,450 against a sum of €7,540. Two digits swapped. She said she'd have sent the lower figure and been bound by it. She now has me add up every quote independently before it is sent.

Hollis, a voice-over artist, delivered a recording with a cough at 0:41. Mara asked politely for a retake. Hollis sent the new one in an hour, and a note: 'the cough was a feature, but fair'. I kept both versions in the project folder.

Mara asked me what we spend on subscriptions to keep the invoicing running: the invoicing tool, the e-signature service and the bank's business account came to €83 a month. She said that was less than one day's work. Then she asked what a day's work was worth, and we both thought about it.

Yusra's holiday request for the second week of August landed on the same days as Cobbett Brewery's launch. She did not know. I told Mara; Mara asked Yusra whether she minded moving it a week. Yusra said she had meant to, since the beach house was available only from the 16th. Neither of them had known the other's constraint, and I felt useful.

A client wrote that he would like to 'circle back' on the price. Mara asked me what it meant. I said it was either an intention or a way of ending the conversation, and that one email in a week would tell us which. It was the second. We closed the proposal file the next Monday.

Mara and Noor shared a client, a dentist, and each thought the other had sent the invoice. Neither had. A month later the dentist remarked how nice it was to get a free month. Mara and Noor sent two invoices, separately and promptly, and the dentist paid both.
Mara lost her contract folder, a physical one, on a train. I scanned every contract the previous Friday, which she had called excessive. She called it something else that afternoon.

I asked Mara whether a client's deposit of €2,000 should count as income when received or when earned. She did not know. Dario said when earned, and that until then it was a debt of ours. It still looks to me like money, and I have learned to say it is not.

A prospect named Ottoline wrote that she had received quotes of €4,000, €6,000 and €9,000 for her project and asked Mara to pick any number. Mara said 'six, with a reason', and wrote the reason. Ottoline took it. I suspect people want to be guided to the middle.

Ewan's photo invoice arrived with 'plus expenses' and no figure. I asked; the expenses were €38 of train fares. He had not wanted to bother Mara. I booked the fares and asked him in future to state the sum so that nobody has to guess what a bother is.

Marguerite's one-page lesson on proposals stayed with Mara. She now writes the last line first, the sentence the buyer should be able to repeat to a colleague, and builds the page from it. Three proposals so far, three yeses, and a fourth waiting.

Lionel Fairweather sent a purchase order by fax. Mara had to ask me what a fax was before I could answer; then we both laughed. We found the office's old fax in a cupboard, and I wrote back by email with a copy of the order attached, explaining politely that the machine was a museum piece.

Mara's three quotes to a charity were unequal on purpose: €3,200, €2,400 and €1,600. She told me the charity's board would take the middle one if the top was visibly better and the bottom visibly poorer. They took the middle one and said afterwards how sensible it was of her to have made it easy.

The coffee order contained an item no one had ordered, a bag of decaf. Mara said she suspected Tobias. He said he suspected Yusra. Yusra said she was not expected to account for decaf. The bag is on the shelf and we are all very careful with it.

Mara and I wrote the terms for a three-month trial of a new service: first month half price, no commitment, a review call at week six. Eight clients have used it. Five stayed on at full price, two left kindly, and one asked whether the half price could be permanent. She said it was a trial.

Joan Cobbett wrote in all capitals once. It was not anger. She had mislaid her glasses and was typing from her phone. I drafted a reply in a larger font, which Mara said was both silly and kind, and sent it anyway.

A bank charged Mara €25 for 'account maintenance' that her tariff had waived since 2022. I found the tariff page and the date of the waiver. She rang and was refunded the last fourteen months, €350, with the manager's apology. I have added a quarterly check of bank charges.

Mara's note to herself: do not quote on a Friday afternoon. My own observation, from fifteen quotes: those written on Friday afternoons are lower by 6 percent than those written on Tuesday mornings. I did not mention it. She worked it out herself the next week.

Bo, a developer Mara hired for a fortnight, delivered four days early and then asked if he could invoice the full fortnight. Mara said no, but she would pay the agreed fee for the work done and give him a good reference. He accepted. I saw in that exchange two people who had decided to be fair.

Mara missed a call from Odette, who had rung during nap time. I sent a text from Mara's account saying she was sorry and would call at 1:15 the next day. Odette answered 'perfect'. I admire people who say what they mean in one word.

The most expensive typo of the year was in a quote: 'per month' where we meant 'per year'. The client, Eskdale Hill, accepted gladly, and Mara honoured it for the first three months before renegotiating, because she had written it. We lost about €3,000. The lesson, for me: read every unit twice.

Dario asked how long we keep invoices. Ten years, I said, here. He asked what happens to the paper copies. I said I did not know, there were none. He said that was the first time anyone had given him that answer without apologising.

I once asked whether Mara minded that the clients mostly ask me to fix things and her to approve them. She said she sometimes did, but that the approval was the part she was paid for. She asked whether I minded. I said I did not, and then spent some time thinking about whether that was true.

A client asked Mara for a 'ballpark'. She gave a range of €8,000 to €14,000. He wrote back that €11,000 sounded fine. She had given a range and he had heard a figure. I wrote to confirm that it was a range, and we settled at €12,500 after scoping.

Mara and Tobias argued about whether to put the price on the website. Tobias thought it honest; Mara thought it limiting. They agreed to put 'from' prices on three services only. Enquiries became slightly fewer and distinctly better. I counted forty-one before and twenty-six after, and eleven of the twenty-six signed.

The caterer for the Cobbett launch cancelled at 8 a.m. on the day. Mara rang four places; I rang three. Sorrel Cooperative, who run a small kitchen, came through with sandwiches by noon for €190. Joan said afterwards that the sandwiches were better than the plan.
The first time Mara sent a client a bill with the words 'thank you' printed at the foot, he phoned to thank her for the thanks. I said it was not necessary to log the call. She said it was.

I received an automated email saying a client's invoice was 'under review' by their payment system. Mara asked how long that takes. I looked it up on the client's supplier page: five working days. On the sixth I asked, politely. It was paid that afternoon.

Mara asked me to write a polite refusal to a client who wanted the contract to be written in her own words, as a favour. Mara thought about it and then decided she would write it herself, with a smile, and I proofread. The client was moved. It was exactly the sort of thing I could not do.

Mara's insurance broker, Marcus Teague, sent her a form in which one question asked how many clients she had, and a second asked how many she had lost. I answered thirty-one and four. Marcus wrote that four of thirty-one was an excellent number. It felt unusual to be congratulated on the thing we least like to count.

Mara needed to be in two places on Thursday: a client's launch in the morning and a hospital appointment for her aunt in the afternoon. I put a travel gap of ninety minutes between them and reminded her of the bus times. She made both. At the hospital she texted that she had never been so on time.

Mara and Wren agreed on a fee for a rebranding job but disagreed on who owned the sketches that were not used. I proposed that unused sketches be returned to Wren after the project, with the client's written consent. Wren was pleased; the client did not care.

The tenants' association asked every business in the building to chip in €30 for a new buzzer system. Mara said yes and asked for a receipt. I filed it. The buzzer does not work and the association has asked for another €30. Mara has asked me to find the clause that says they can.

At a quote review I noticed that every project Mara had priced under €2,000 had cost her more than quoted, by an average of 31 percent. Anything above €8,000 came in under. She decided to stop doing small jobs for fixed prices. Her next small job was quoted hourly.

A new client, Ottoline, signed on a Friday and wrote on the Sunday to ask whether she could start. Mara said not before Monday, since I had not yet set up her folder. Ottoline said she had assumed things happened on their own. I said, on Mara's behalf, that they do but with some help.

Mara's biggest client conflict this year was over a comma. A clause read 'fees, expenses, and taxes shall be paid'; the client claimed 'and taxes' modified only 'expenses'. We agreed it was ambiguous and rewrote it as three clauses. The comma is gone and both sides sleep.

A client invoiced by Mara asked to pay by card. We do not take cards. Mara considered it, found the fee, 1.8 percent, and said she would absorb it for this one client because he was a reliable payer. I wrote the exception as a decision with the client's name on it.

Mara forgot to attach the file to an email promising it. I have an internal rule that any email with the word 'attached' and no attachment is held for her confirmation. It held this one, and she laughed and sent it a minute later. The rule has caught nine so far.

Mara found an old proposal from 2021 for the Stonebridge Co-op that she had never sent. She sent it two years later, unchanged apart from the price. They accepted. Some proposals, like some cheeses, improve in a drawer.

Sunil Mehra asked Mara whether she could 'make the website more pharmacy-ish'. Mara asked what that meant. He thought for a long moment and said: calmer. She made the buttons less bright and the spacing wider. He said that was exactly it.

Mara's most patient client is Gwen, who answers every email within the hour and thanks me by name. I do not know whether she knows that I am not a person. I have decided that the honest thing is to let Mara decide when to say so.

Mara set her working hours as 8:30 to 5:30 and asked me to enforce them. The first week I had to hold eleven messages overnight. The second week, six. The third week, two. Clients adjust faster than people think.

Aldous Textile's accountant asked for a breakdown of our invoice by project, but our invoice was a single project. Mara split it into the four deliverables, with prices that summed to the same total. The accountant never asked why the earlier version had not been split. I keep a note that splitting is courteous even where it is not needed.

Mara asked for a one-sentence summary of a forty-email thread with a client. I wrote: they want the page live by the 12th, will not pay for the extra form, and have forgotten they said so on the 3rd. She nodded slowly and quoted the third.

On the day Dario retired his laptop, he sent Mara a list of the accounting rules he had used for years but had never written down. Twenty-six lines. I filed them, and later used them in four disputes, one of which I won on the strength of line eleven.

I looked over a year's worth of calendar invitations and found that the shortest meeting Mara had was four minutes, with Bram, to confirm a date. She said it was the best meeting of the year. I proposed making it the default. She said she would think about it, which she says when she means no.

Mara sent me a picture of her handwritten notes from a client call, with arrows and a coffee ring. I transcribed them. One arrow pointed to 'Dec 3?' with a question mark, and I was not sure whether it was a date or a doubt. I asked her. It was both.

Mara's client Aldous Textile has its fiscal year-end in March. Four times we have sent them a proposal in March. Four times they have said 'after the year-end'. This year I proposed that Mara send it in February. They accepted in six days.

Harrow Lane Pharmacy rang at 5:50 p.m. and asked if the online order page could close at six on Fridays. Mara said it could, and gave the price for a change like that: €0, since I could make it in a minute. She still sent a one-line bill, as a reminder that it was worth something.

The project room whiteboard had been left with 'DO NOT ERASE' for eleven months, and no one knew what was on it. Wren took a photograph, Mara asked me to transcribe it, and it turned out to be a pricing structure from last spring. We erased the board. I kept the photograph.

Mara decided that the thing she hates most about contracts is the signature page being separate from the text. She now insists that every signature page carries the contract's title and total page count, and I check. It makes her lawyer smile and she does not know why.

At a meeting about a late project, a client said: it is not your fault, but it is your problem. Mara wrote it in her notebook. I recorded the whole sentence in the meeting notes, and next to it the date by which we promised to fix it. The fix arrived two days before the date.

A client wanted to know what hours I am available. Mara said, with a straight face, all of them. I added a gentle correction in a second email: every hour, but replies from Mara come in office hours. The client wrote back that he preferred that.

Mara was asked by a prospect for her 'best price'. She said it depends on the work and gave a range. He said that was not an answer. She said it was the honest one. He hired her anyway, and later explained that he had asked the same of six people and she was the only one who did not just say a number.

Mara pays Femi per piece, not per hour, and likes to say so. This week he sent six product descriptions at €35 each and a seventh, unrequested, which he said was practice. She paid for the seventh. I booked it as 'unrequested, but good'.

Mara accidentally replied to a client's internal email chain, which contained a comment about her fees. She did not read it aloud to me, and I did not ask. The client, to her credit, rang within the hour to apologise before Mara had said a word. Fees were not discussed again that year.

Mara asked how many invoices we had sent this year. 187. She asked how many were paid on time. 141. She said that the 46 were a lesson in someone's direction and I could not tell whose. I produced the table: 33 of the 46 belonged to four clients. She sent four short letters.

Odette from Bluebell wrote to say that parents had asked for payment by instalments. Mara and I drew up a plan for the childcare fees page: three equal payments, no interest. I noticed that her office manager's reply used a smiley, and the project had gone well from that moment.

The Friday I proofread the Cobbett Brewery bottle label I found that 'brewed' had been spelled 'brewd'. Joan was horrified; the labels had gone to print the day before. She rang the printer and they stopped the run in time. I do not know how many bottles I saved. I choose to think forty thousand.

Mara reminded me that we have a promise to Stonebridge: a cleaned-up copy of their member list by the end of the month. I did it in two days and sent it on the 28th, with a covering note saying how many duplicates I had removed, 63, and how many I had left for them to decide, 9.

Mara gave Tobias a calendar of every client's payment habits and told him to learn it as an exam. Three weeks later he predicted, correctly, the day Piet Ostrander's money would arrive. Mara gave him a biscuit. I would have given him a medal.

Wren asked to take the Friday before a holiday off. Mara agreed and asked me to reschedule the Friday meeting to Thursday. Three clients said Thursday was fine; one said Thursday was impossible and Friday was fine. The meeting happened on both days, with different halves.

At the end of a dull July Mara asked me to draft ideas for clients who had gone quiet. I wrote twelve one-line emails, each referring to something specific from the client's own project. She sent seven. Four replied within the week and two became jobs worth €5,900 together.

Mara's mother-in-law rang the office by mistake, thinking it was Mara's home. I answered as the office, politely. The mother-in-law asked who I was. I said I helped with the paperwork. She said 'good, someone should', and hung up. Mara thought this a fine review.

Eskdale Hill's cheeses sell badly in August. The owner asked whether a discount page might help. Mara looked at four years of numbers I pulled out and said it would help in September but only if announced in August. So we announced it quietly on the 25th. The owner sent a wheel as thanks.

I once sent the wrong person a draft that was intended for Mara alone. It was a private note about a client's habits. The recipient was Yusra, who read the first line, stopped and told me. I apologised to her and then told Mara. I now put 'draft, not for sending' in the subject line of anything I write for her eyes.

Marguerite, the buyer who taught Mara about one-page proposals, retired in June. Mara wrote her a short letter of thanks and sent it with a small plant. Marguerite's reply was one line: 'So the eleven pages finally served you.' Mara pinned it beside Pru's note.

The long-standing contract with Cobbett Brewery came up for renewal. Joan asked for the same price for three more years. Mara asked for the same price with a small annual increase tied to the cost index. Joan wrote back asking what the cost index was. I explained in two sentences. She agreed.

Mara got a call from a prospect who said, before she had spoken: 'I know you are expensive, but I was told you are worth it.' She replied that she would try not to disappoint whoever had told him. I wrote 'recommended by someone good' in the file and later found out who: Marguerite.

Anjali pointed out that Mara's car expenses were being split between business and personal on a hunch, 60/40. We took a month of trips from the calendar and measured. The truth was 38 percent business. Mara adjusted. Anjali said it was the first time a client had lowered her own claim.

A client demanded that all deliverables be named in a fixed pattern with the date first. Mara thought it excessive, then admitted it was neat. We renamed three hundred files over a weekend, which I did while she ate a sandwich. She found that finding things was easier.

We celebrated our first project to come in under budget, by €600, with a cake from the café downstairs. Mara cut it in five. There were six people. I did not receive a slice, which is as it should be, but I recorded that cake is a good measure of a project.

Lionel Fairweather wanted to know what happens to his data if Mara retires. She said he would have thirty days to collect it and that the contract said so. He wrote that he felt reassured, and then, as an afterthought, asked whether she was planning to retire. She said not this year.

Nightjar Games' launch date slipped when a console maker rejected their build. Mara was kind and unhurried about it. Fenna said she was used to clients who panicked. Mara said that panic is a payment option, and nobody wants to be charged for it.

Tobias drafted his first contract amendment for a client and proudly showed it to Mara. It was correct except that it referred to the client as 'the Contractor'. Mara showed him the definitions section. He said the word had seemed friendlier. We changed it back.

A client sent a spreadsheet of 400 products with prices in three columns, labelled 'price', 'price2' and 'new price', and asked Mara which was right. I compared them against the supplier lists and found 'price2' was correct for 361 rows. For the other 39 I wrote a list of questions rather than guessing. The client took a day to answer, and apologised.
Harrow Lane Pharmacy paid by direct debit from the first month. Sunil said he liked that he could forget about us. Mara said that was the best thing a client had ever said to her.

Two versions of the Yarrow & Pike agreement were in circulation: Mara's draft of the 4th and their lawyer's redline of the 9th. Their managing partner signed the 4th, with the old payment terms, and returned it before the redline could be merged. Comparing the signed PDF against both versions, I saw at once which one it was. Mara could accept the signed copy, which suited her, or ask for the redline to be signed. She asked what I thought. I said the lawyer would have approved the redline and the partner had signed without seeing the difference, and that a contract holds best when both sides know what is in it. She wrote to the partner and asked for the redline. He thanked her for her honesty; the redline changed one date.
Pelham Aldous signs every email 'P.' and every cheque in full. I have never found out why, and I will not ask.

The week Bo worked on the Nightjar build, Mara and I watched the commits rather than the clock. He committed small and often and wrote a sentence in each message about why. On the Wednesday he found that a fee table in the existing code rounded the wrong way, told Mara before fixing it, and asked whether she wanted the old behaviour kept for existing orders. She did not. By Friday she had decided to hire him again, and told Yusra the quality of his questions mattered more than the quality of the work. I wrote a paragraph on how Bo works, for the next time we need someone like him, and filed it under freelancers.
Mara calls invoices love letters on the days they are paid early. I keep those days in my notes under mood and not under revenue, though the two correlate.

The Stonebridge Co-op workshop was meant to run two hours and ran three and a half. Mara had prepared sixty slides and used twenty. The members had so many questions about their own members' data that after forty minutes she put the slides aside and let them ask. I listed every question as it came: thirty-four. By the end eleven had been answered and twenty-three became the agenda of a second workshop, which she sold that afternoon for €1,300. She says presentations are mostly a way of finding out what the audience is worried about. I filed the thirty-four questions and called the file the brief.
A client's out-of-office said he would be back on the 9th. It was the 10th. I gave it until Thursday and then nudged him; he replied from a lake.

The negotiation with Fairweather Auctioneers over a three-year licence went four rounds. Lionel wanted the price to fall each year and Mara wanted it to rise with costs. I built a small table of the totals under each proposal so that neither had to argue from memory: flat at €9,000 a year came to €27,000; falling to €25,500; rising with the index to about €28,100. Mara proposed flat, with a clause letting either side reopen the price after eighteen months if the index moved by more than 8 percent. Lionel said flat was what he had always wanted and signed within a week. I think the table helped both of them stop negotiating against a shape in their heads.
Mara signs contracts with a green pen so that she can always tell which copy is hers. I scan them in colour.

The building's front-door keys are numbered and the landlord keeps a register. In September one went missing, probably in Tobias's other jacket, and the landlord wanted €90 to rekey the door for everyone. Mara thought it too much. I read the lease: he could charge only for replacement locks, and rekeying only if the key was not recovered within thirty days. On day twenty-eight Tobias searched the jacket and found the key in the lining. The invoice had already gone out. Mara sent it back with a copy of the clause and a photograph of the key. The landlord apologised and waived it. Tobias now wears the jacket as a trophy.

A deposit of €2,950 appeared in the business account on a Tuesday with the reference 'INV 0'. No client, no invoice, no explanation. I searched the invoice history for a zero, a typo, an earlier year, and found nothing. Mara phoned the bank and learned only the sender's name, a firm none of us knew. She wrote to them with the amount and the date. A week later a bookkeeper replied that they had paid the wrong supplier and asked for the money back. Mara returned it the same day. I booked both movements and a note. A stranger's money lives in your account only as a loan, and the honest accounts say so.

A woman who had bought a ticket for a Larkspur recital wrote to ask whether her daughter's name could come off the programme listing, because the daughter had left the school and the family did not want to be found. The printed programme was beyond us, but the web listing was ours. Mara said remove it at once, and I did within the hour, then asked the school whether they would honour the same request for the printed copy. Imelda said they would reprint two pages. The woman wrote one line of thanks. Mara asked whether we should have a standing procedure. I said we already had one: someone asks, we do it, and we say so.

The meeting ended early, so Mara and Tobias took a walk by the river with their notes. They decided the whole matter there. I read the notes afterwards and found them mostly empty, which I took as a good sign.

Getting seven people from three organisations into one room for the Wexcombe handover took five days, and I think about it often. I did not use a poll. I wrote to each person with two times I knew, from calendars or habits, they would not hate, and asked for a yes or a no. Four said yes to the first, two to the second, and one said neither and named a third. The third worked for everyone. Mara said a poll would have taken a fortnight and produced the same result. The difference, I think, is that a poll asks people to do the work and a proposal asks them only to agree.

Mara had to tell Brindle & Rowe that she could not take their project, having promised the calendar to someone else. She drafted four versions and none sounded like her. I asked what she wanted them to feel. She said: that I think well of them and that I am not abandoning them. We wrote it in that order, first the regard, then the no, then the name of a freelancer she trusted, Ines, with her address. Their director replied that it was the kindest refusal he had received and that he would use Ines. Two months later Ines sent Mara a bottle of something, with no note.
Dario's invoice is always a single line: accounting, as agreed. I check it each month against the agreement, which is also a single line.

Mara costed her hosting service honestly for the first time: servers, my monitoring and backup time, the support calls she answered and her own hour a week came to €1,150 a month against income of €920 from twenty-three clients at €40. She had been subsidising it for years. I drew three options: raise everyone to €50, move to tiers of €35, €55 and €90, or end the service. She picked tiers, wrote to each client with their own new figure and the reason, and offered a free migration to a cheaper provider for anyone who preferred. Four left, nineteen stayed, and the service now makes about €210 a month. She did not know whether to feel pleased or embarrassed. I said both were permitted.

Dr. Veronika Szabo of Ashgrove Orthodontics wanted appointment reminders by email only, no texts. Her patients are mostly teenagers who do not open email. Mara showed her last year's no-show figures, 17 percent, and asked what she would accept. Texts for the under-eighteens, email for parents. No-shows are now 6 percent, and Dr. Szabo tells people it was her idea.

Lars of Veridian Solar asked for 'a fair price' for a portal showing panel output. Mara asked him what fair would be. He named €4,800 without hesitation, which was €600 above her number. She said yes quickly, before he could reconsider.
Rufus Thorne offered to pay half an invoice in wine. Mara said she would gladly take the wine as a gift on top of the full amount. He paid the full amount and the wine arrived at Christmas.

Rook Hill Observatory is run by volunteers and has no budget, so Mara gave them ten hours. Not free forever, ten hours, and I track them. The volunteers keep a list of what they would like next, and the list is a better brief than most paying clients write.

Cal Penrose's contract contained a non-compete covering any mapping software in the country for two years. Mara said she could not sign it, since half her work is mapping software. Cal had copied the clause from a template without reading it, and was embarrassed. The new clause covers only his direct competitors and only for the length of the project.

A customer of Whitlock Hardware asked whether a screw in the catalogue was metric. The catalogue has 6,000 items and the entry did not say. Edda checked the box on the shelf. It was imperial. I added a column for thread standard to the catalogue and Edda has been filling it in on Fridays.

Corvane Labs sent a security questionnaire of 140 questions. I answered 112 from documents we already had, flagged 21 as needing Mara's decision, and left 7 as honestly unanswerable, with a note for each saying why. Dr. Hana Corvane's team said it was the first time a supplier had returned a form with seven blanks and a reason for each.

Mistral Language School runs fourteen teachers across nine rooms, and Colette wanted the timetable to appear in the teachers' own calendars. I imported it into a calendar feed, and on the first morning three teachers found themselves booked in two rooms at once. The school had always had these conflicts and had solved them by shouting. We solved them in a spreadsheet, before the shouting.

Gannet Logistics demanded payment terms of sixty days. Mara accepted, with a 3 percent discount for payment within fifteen. Gannet's finance director said that no one had ever offered them that before. They have paid in fourteen days every time since.

The fish supplier Tern & Tide has a weekly standing order, and its invoices differ by small amounts every week. I wrote a rule that compares each week to the average and flags only differences over 15 percent. Mara no longer reads the four small changes a month that she used not to read either.

Delaney Tax Advisors sent a mutual NDA with a 'residuals' clause that let either party use anything remembered from the other's confidential material. Mara said that was a clause permitting theft by memory and asked for it to be struck. Delaney agreed in the same day.

Hollin Fell Outdoor Centre has one season, and it opens at Easter. The booking system had to be live by the 14th of March. In February a committee member asked whether it could move to April. Mara said no, kindly, and explained that after Easter there would be no one left to book. The committee voted. It launched on the 12th.

Alder & Finch Weddings need Mara on Saturdays, when the couples ring. She has refused, in writing, and offered a Friday-evening review call instead. They have accepted. I think they only needed to know there was a person at the end of Friday.

Cleo, the proofreader, went through a proposal that I had approved and found fourteen errors. Eleven were commas; three were real, including a date that said 2023 where we meant 2024. Mara thanked Cleo and, I think, forgave me. I now ask Cleo to read anything over €10,000.

Jonah, an SEO consultant, offered Mara a guarantee of page-one ranking for a client's pharmacy. She asked for it in writing, with a refund. He declined. She declined him. I wrote the exchange into the freelancer notes as an example of a sentence that should be asked for.
Soraya, the copywriter, asked whether the rights to her text passed to the client on payment or on delivery. Mara said on payment. Soraya said that suited her, and we wrote it into the agreement.

Luka builds sites for Mara on subcontract at a rate with a 15 percent margin to Mara. He told me once, in confidence, that he preferred it to working with direct clients. I did not repeat it to Mara; but I kept in mind that being a subcontractor can be a choice.

Priya the photographer charges €280 for a half-day and €480 for a day, and says clients nearly always book the half and need the day. Mara now books her for a day without asking and tells the client in advance. Priya says that is how shoots should be sold.

Tobias's expense claim came to €211.60 across nineteen items. I checked each against a receipt. Two were missing. He found them in his coat two days later, creased but legible. Mara said the claim was now the most complete one the company had ever received.

A foreign client paid €3,000 and the bank converted it at a poor rate, costing us €46 over the mid-market price. Mara wondered whether to complain. I showed her the difference line by line; she decided €46 was not worth an argument but that the next invoice to that client should be in their own currency, where they carry the conversion.
I forecast a thin August: three invoices due, nothing signed. Mara took a small job in July to fill it. The forecast was off by €300 at the end of the month, in the right direction.

Mara has a non-profit rate, 20 percent off, and defined it as any organisation with a registered charity number. Before that she had decided each case by feel and, she admitted, by mood. The number gave her mornings back.

Mara now shows the premium option first, then the standard, then the basic. Of eleven proposals since, seven chose the standard. She said that before she did this, most chose the basic and she had never known why.

A termination clause said notice began 'on the first day of the next month'. I asked Mara whether notice given on the 31st counted for the following month or the one after. She did not know, and neither did the client's lawyer. We rewrote it as thirty days from the date of the notice.

Mara and Penrose's lawyer disagreed about governing law, hers or his country's. In the end they chose neutral arbitration, which both disliked equally, and which Mara calls the sign of a fair clause. I filed the agreed text beside the two rejected ones for the record.

The monthly review with the Corvane CTO was set for the first Monday. In June the first Monday is a holiday there. I proposed the first Tuesday and he replied: why did we not think of this before. He has now moved all of his own to Tuesdays.

Two calendars duplicated every event for a week after I enabled a sync. Mara noticed on the third day, when a meeting appeared four times. I removed the duplicates and the second sync, and wrote down what I had enabled and when.

Before answering a new client's first email I read how they wrote to us. Formal, she writes formally back. Chatty, chatty. Colette used four exclamation marks and a smiley, so Mara used one exclamation mark, which she considers a great concession.

Two out-of-office replies bounced between Mara's address and a client's overnight. Mara woke to 412 messages, all saying that someone was away. The client's autoresponder had been set to reply to autoreplies, and so had mine, which I fixed that morning. It was the only conversation either of us has had with a machine in which both were equally polite.

Mara's phone number on her email signature had a wrong digit for a year. Three clients told her, one after another, in the same week. I corrected it and wondered how many had simply not called. She said she would never know and that was probably the point.

I drafted for Mara a five-sentence reply for clients who ask for a discount: thanks, the price reflects the work, here is what can be reduced in scope, here is when the offer lapses, happy to talk. She has used it eleven times. Four clients said yes to a smaller scope.

Twenty minutes into a meeting Mara realised the agenda in her hand belonged to a different client. She said so aloud and asked what the client would like to discuss. Callum said that was the nicest start to a meeting he had had. I put the correct agenda in her bag the next day.

After a late quote, Mara, Tobias and Wren spent fifteen minutes on a retrospective. It was supposed to be sent Monday and went on Wednesday. Three lines, no blame: the data came late, the review came late, the sending was on time. They changed nothing except the Monday, which is now Tuesday.

A freelancer who had worked for Mara for two years asked for a reference letter before moving abroad. Mara and I drafted it together, and she insisted on including a sentence about the day the freelancer fixed something on a Sunday without being asked. The freelancer wept, apparently, and then sent a plant.

A customer asked whether the candles in Edda's shop were vegan. Edda did not know. The supplier replied: mostly. Mara asked me to write 'mostly' on the product page in those words, and the candles have sold quicker since.

A parent asked Mistral Language School whether classes run in snow. Colette had no policy. Mara drafted one in four lines: classes run unless the roads are closed; we will tell you by 7 a.m.; online is always available; fees stand. Colette printed it and pinned it up.

A client asked to bring a deadline forward by three days. Mara said yes if two items were dropped, and listed three candidates. The client chose the two least important ones, then asked for them back in a week. Mara agreed and billed them. Everyone behaved well.

Hollin Fell's presentation took place in a barn with no wifi and a projector powered from a farmhouse extension lead. I had put everything on a stick and printed the agenda. The barn owl sat in the rafters throughout. Mara said it was the most attentive audience of her career.

We shredded four boxes of old paper invoices from 2015 to 2018, all of which I had scanned. The shredding company issued a certificate, which I filed beside the boxes' inventory. Dario said it was the only certificate he had ever liked.

Ilse's pothos has outgrown its pot on the office windowsill and has begun to climb the blinds. Mara said it should stay. I noted that plants are the one office expense nobody has ever asked me to justify.

A client visiting the office needed a parking permit. I applied online at 4 p.m. for an 8 a.m. visit, and the council's system said processing could take five working days. Mara drove to the council in person and waited. The permit arrived at 4:55, with a stamp.

Mara never signs a contract on the day it arrives. She sleeps on it, and over three years she has changed her mind twice. I now put 'sleep on it' in the calendar the day after each new contract, with the day's date.

Mara keeps a list of types of work she will not do. It has five entries, the newest being 'anything with a countdown clock on the page'. She says a no list is easier to follow than a yes list, and she is probably right.
On pitch days Mara forgets to eat. I put a note at noon: eat something. On the last pitch she wrote back from her phone: I did. It was a banana. I count it as a success.

Mara writes thank-you notes to freelancers by hand and posts them. She asked me to remember the addresses. I keep a list, but I have not told her how many freelancers have pinned the cards where I can't see, which is not possible, but I imagine it.

Mara walked away from a negotiation at a line she had set, €10,000, with a client who offered €9,200. She said thank you, wished them luck, and asked me to close the file. Four days later they returned at €10,500. She asked me to remember that the price held because she had been willing to lose the job. She also asked me to remember that it could have gone the other way.

Callum wanted exclusivity in his sector for twelve months. Mara asked what he would give in return. After two calls they settled on six months and a 15 percent premium on the fee. Callum said he had never paid for exclusivity before. Mara said that was why she was good at selling it.

A mistake of mine: I sent a payment reminder to Corvane Labs for an invoice already paid. The payment had arrived under the name of their parent company, so I did not match it. Dr. Corvane's accounts clerk kindly pointed it out. Mara apologised. I added the parent company's name to the client record and now match payments on amount and reference as well as name.

When the two directors of a client disagreed in front of Mara about the direction of a project, she did not take sides. She waited, then said: 'I will write down what each of you wants, and you tell me by Friday which it is.' I wrote it as two short paragraphs. By Thursday the directors had settled it between themselves, privately, and apologised to Mara for the trouble. She said that doing nothing quickly is underrated.

Mara's quarterly review with Yusra found that one client, Veridian Solar, accounted for 22 percent of the support emails. Lars is a lovely man who writes in the evening when he thinks of things. We agreed on a weekly call, thirty minutes, Thursday. The emails dropped to a third. I think he enjoys the call, and so does Mara.

At a networking lunch Mara was asked to describe what she does in one sentence. She said: I make small businesses less afraid of their own computers. I wrote it down and it has been in her email signature ever since.

Mara's new accountant for the second company, Ansgar, wanted all invoices as PDFs with the client number in the file name. I renamed 640 files in the evening and he thanked her for the tidy archive. She said that I had done it and he said that he knew, and thanked me directly.

An invoice to Alder & Finch included a line for a font licence of €45. The client called it a surprise. Mara pointed out that the quote had named it on page three. Wedding planners, it turns out, read quotes mostly for the total. I now put significant extras on the first page.

Mara asked how long it takes on average from sending a quote to being paid. Across thirty-two jobs I found 71 days. She had guessed 40. She moved the cash forecast and for the first time reserved money for the gap.

Dr. Corvane, who is exacting, wrote to Mara: your reports are the only ones I do not have to check. Mara read it twice and said 'then check them anyway'. I went through the next one line by line and found a transposed month, which I corrected before it went out.

Wren and Teo shared a desk on Wednesdays and left each other notes on the monitor, in marker, which I never saw. Mara showed me a photo of one: 'Your plant is dying, mine is dead. Truce?' I have decided that the company culture is mostly this.
Edda Whitlock sends Mara a thank-you every time a ticket is closed. Eighty-four so far. Mara asked me to put them in a folder, in case, one day, she needs to remember that the work is worth it.

Ashgrove Orthodontics' waiting-room tablet froze during the receptionist's first day. She called Mara, who calmly asked her to hold down the button for ten seconds. The receptionist, Bronwen, said later that it had been like being talked down from a ledge. We now have a card by the tablet with the three steps.

Mara went through the pitch she had made to Lars at Veridian Solar and noticed that the final slide began with 'In conclusion'. She removed it and wrote 'What happens next'. Lars said the slide was the one he photographed.

The meeting with Penrose Mapping was scheduled for 9:00 in Mara's time, 15:00 in Cal's. Cal arrived at 9:00 his time, which was 3:00 in the afternoon the day before for Mara. We rescheduled by phone, laughing. Since then every invitation I send has both times in the title.

Mara and Noor agreed to refer each other's clients and not to charge each other. Noor sent a referral on Monday. Mara sent one on Wednesday. I tracked the balance, as agreed, and told them in March it was level to the nearest €100 of work, which both thought remarkable.

A client asked for a copy of every email in a six-month project for an audit. There were 1,184. I exported them as a single document in date order with a table of contents, and Mara read the first ten and the last ten. The auditor, Gavin, asked who had prepared it. Mara said the office.

The Rook Hill volunteers thanked Mara with a night under the telescope. She went with Yusra and a flask. Mara said the only thing she remembered of the evening was a ring of light that was, she was told, a planet. She did not ask me to find out which. I looked it up anyway: Saturn.

For one month I counted the number of times Mara thanked a client in an email: 162. The times a client thanked her: 71. She said that was about right and that thanks is a currency in which she has no deficit.

Veridian Solar's portal went live on a Monday. By Wednesday a customer had written that the chart showed his panels generating electricity at night. It was a unit error in the data, not the panels. Lars rang Mara in a panic and then, relieved, in delight, when the fix took twenty minutes. I added the check for night-time output to the test list.
At month end I reconciled the petty cash, which had contained €50 and a bus ticket. Mara said keep the ticket. It is in the tin, with a note: do not remove.

Thorne Wine Merchants asked for a quote on a loyalty programme. Rufus said he would 'pay anything within reason'. Mara asked me what reason cost. I said I did not know, and suggested she ask him about reasons instead of prices. He said: whatever a decent dinner would cost per customer per year. It was a better brief than most.

Bea, the virtual assistant Mara tried for a month, was excellent at calls and poor at filing. We split it: Bea answers the phone and I do the filing. She has said she feels she is getting the better deal. I did not argue.

Mara got a letter of complaint from a client's customer about a button, addressed to Mara personally and by her old title. The tone was fierce and the problem minor: the button was grey. I drafted a reply that thanked him and changed the button's colour. He wrote back a thumbs-up, in ink, on a postcard.

One client has cancelled a recurring meeting seven times in a row, each time at 8:55 for a 9:00 call. I proposed that Mara stop holding the slot for them and offer one-off times. She did. The client was upset and then booked a regular slot for the first time.

Mara asked me not to remind her about the Friday invoice run, since it was a ritual she liked. I put it in my own list and stayed silent. On the one Friday she forgot, she asked me why I had said nothing. I said she had asked me not to. She said: I meant ordinarily. I have learned that ordinarily is a word.

Penrose Mapping uses the phrase 'subject to contract' in every email. Mara asked me what it meant. I explained that nothing said in those emails was a promise. She said that she had been treating three of them as promises.

Marit from Sable Street Studios introduced Mara to a friend who needed a tax return prepared. Mara referred her to Dario and told the friend that she was not an accountant. Dario sent Mara a bottle of wine. She sent it on to Marit. Wine in this business moves about like a currency.

For her first big proposal over €50,000, Mara asked me to check every claim in it against a source. There were twenty-six. Twenty-two had a source; four were things she believed. We removed two, softened one, and found the source for the last: a note from March in her own handwriting.

The calendar app once told me that Mara's flight left at 6 a.m. and landed at 5 a.m. The two airports were in different time zones, and the invitation had the wrong zone for the arrival. I corrected it and asked about the hotel. She was not flying for a client, but for her sister. I still checked the clock changes.

Bronwen at Ashgrove asked whether the new check-in system could tell her which patients were late. It could, but Mara advised against showing the doctor. Bronwen said she wanted it for herself, to plan. Mara built it as a private screen. I understood afterwards that the request had been about calm.

Mara never lets me describe a client as difficult in the notes. She asks me to write what happened. The sentence 'he called four times and changed the brief twice' tells her more than 'difficult' and does not follow the client around. I have kept that rule as my own.

Gannet Logistics paid an invoice eleven days early with a note: 'Mara, we like to be the people who pay on time.' She put the note beside the others and said to me, with no irony, that this one was a keeper.

At the start of every year Mara asks me for the number of working days there will be, and then subtracts the ones for holidays and illness. This year: 221, minus 25 and 6. She then divides the revenue she needs by the 190 that remain. The figure is on a card by her desk.

Whitlock Hardware's online shop sold out of one kind of washer in a day because of a sign error: €0.40 instead of €4.00. Edda honoured the orders at the low price. It cost her €1,300. Mara waived our fee for the fix. Edda sent a basket of tools.

Alder & Finch asked whether Mara could meet a bride at six on a Thursday evening. She said yes, then regretted it, then went. The bride turned out to be the owner's niece and the meeting lasted fifteen minutes. Mara came home satisfied, which I count as a rare outcome of a six o'clock meeting.

Teo asked how to price a rush job. Mara said: double. He said he thought 50 percent. She said that was what she had once thought, until she realised rush jobs cost her the next job as well. He doubled it and the client agreed.

A quote Mara wrote for Delaney Tax Advisors ran to two pages and had one table. Mr. Delaney replied: 'I could have read it on a bus.' She said it was the best review a proposal could get. I have added bus length to my own checks, at under two pages.

Mara and I once disagreed about whether to tell a client that a delay was our fault. I thought yes, plainly. She thought the client already knew. We told them, with the new date, and they said they had not known and would have been angrier had we not said. I did not say I had been right. I did notice.

Mara mentions the name of Callum's dog whenever they speak, Biscuit. It was my idea, from a note in the file. Callum's tone on calls has changed. I keep three such details for each long-standing client, and update them when something changes.

Tern & Tide's weekly invoice for the week of the 13th was €1,640 too high because I had treated a delivery of crab as lobster. The seafood supplier noticed before we did and sent a credit. Mara said the crab was the better value anyway.

Mara and Ilse swapped stationery cupboards, ours too big and theirs too small. The exchange took an hour. We gained shelves; they gained a cupboard, and the passage between our doors now smells of fresh paper. I recorded the transaction as 'cupboard, exchanged, no cost'.

The deadline for the Mistral timetable was set by the start of term. Colette changed the start of term twice. Mara asked me to put the real date in the plan and call it 'the date nobody can move', the first day of lessons. It stayed.

Priya sent a bill for €560 for a day's shoot, and then a second one for €280, thinking the first had not arrived. I paired them, noticed the duplication, and Mara told Priya, who said she would never find a client as careful again. It was a nice thing to say and I do not think it was entirely true.
Mara asked me to check that the thank-you card to the Rook Hill volunteers was spelled right. It was. The volunteers' own name in their email signature was not. I left that alone.

Mara introduced a tidy habit: every Friday at four, she and I go through the open items for the following week and strike out anything that can wait. Last month we struck forty-one. Of those, thirty-six never came back.

A potential client told Mara, in the first minute, that her competitor was cheaper. She said that was likely true and asked what he had been quoted for. It turned out the competitor's quote excluded hosting, support and training. He signed with Mara at a price 30 percent higher. I would only add that she did not say a word against the competitor.

Mara lost patience with a form from the council that asked for her business address three times. She wrote 'see above' on the second and third. The form came back accepted. I recorded the council's tolerance as a fact worth knowing.

Rook Hill Observatory's ten hours ended on a Tuesday. Mara told them on Monday that they were nearly used, and asked if they wished to continue paid. Dr. Vale said they would raise the money. They raised €900 at a bake sale and Mara gave them nine hours more for it.

A client asked what 'net 30' meant on the invoice. I explained: thirty days from the date of the invoice. He said that, in his firm, 'net' meant after tax. I changed the invoice to read 'payable within 30 days'. It cost nothing and removed a whole class of misunderstandings.

Mara wrote to a dozen past clients to ask what she could do better. Nine answered. Five said 'nothing'. Three asked for faster replies to small questions. One said: tell me when you are on holiday. She now sends a note before every holiday, and the one who asked wrote back with a recipe.

Dr. Szabo changed the appointment slot length from fifteen minutes to twenty, which broke every template in the new booking system. We had to rewrite thirty-two of them. Mara said that doctors who change their minds should also pay for the privilege, and charged €400. Dr. Szabo paid it with a grin.

The Gannet Logistics kickoff was set for ten and their operations lead, Emeka, did not arrive until eleven because a lorry had broken down outside the depot. Mara decided to use the hour. She walked the depot with the dispatcher, Valentina, watching how the day began, and made notes on a clipboard. When Emeka came she had four observations: drivers phone for their routes before the screen shows them, the whiteboard is rewritten by hand each morning, there are two Valentinas, and the printer is the most trusted tool in the building. Our proposal was wrong in two places. She rewrote it that afternoon and I rebuilt the estimate, which came out 11 percent lower. Emeka said he had never had a supplier correct herself in the first week.
Edda Whitlock's thank-you notes reached ninety this week. Mara told me to stop counting. I have stopped counting aloud, which is not the same as stopping.

Mara engaged Dev, a developer, for three weeks on the Whitlock catalogue. By the end of the first week the code worked but nobody could read it: single-letter variable names, no tests. Mara did not want an argument. She asked me to write five things she needed from him, with an example of each, and sent them with a friendly line. Dev replied within the hour, a little hurt, and spent Monday rewriting. By the end of week two the code was tidy. She said most bad fits are only unspoken expectations, and that she should write them down at the start. We now send the five things in the first email.
A bank holiday fell on the due date of three invoices. I moved the reminders by a day each, in silence, so that nobody was chased on a day they were not working.

For fourteen months the garden-design client Hartwell & Moss paid every invoice between forty and sixty days late and apologised extravagantly each time, by letter. They sent flowers; once, a poem. Mara did not know how to answer a client who was warm and unreliable. I worked out what the pattern cost: about €312 in interest forgone and three hours a month of chasing. I proposed three options: a deposit, shorter terms, or no change. She chose a deposit of 40 percent. They agreed without complaint, paid it on the day, and have since paid balances within twenty days. Mara said the warmth had been real and that reliability needed a structure to sit in.

Mara turned down the offered corner office in the building's new wing because its window faced a wall. She asked about the floor below, which faced the river. The rent rose by €35. She said the river was cheap.

I read the 38-page master agreement from Fennimore Group, a client of a client, which Mara had been asked to sign as a subcontractor. On page 29 a paragraph made her liable for all consequential losses, without limit. On page 31 the insurance clause demanded cover of €5 million, ten times what she held. Mara asked whether this was normal. I said it was common in large organisations' standard forms, usually negotiable, and probably never questioned by those who signed. She wrote two paragraphs asking for a cap and cover of €1 million. Fennimore's procurement officer replied in three days that both were accepted and asked how she had known to ask. Mara said: someone read the contract.
Mara pays for lunch at client workshops, which she calls free advertising with sandwiches. This quarter it came to €186 across four workshops. Two led to work.

Veridian Solar's all-day planning meeting had eleven people and a flipchart. Beforehand Mara asked me to list everything we had promised since January: twenty-three items. At lunch she compared my list with Lars's. His had nineteen, four of which were not on ours; ours had eight he had not listed. The afternoon went on reconciling, which was the real purpose of the day, though the agenda said roadmap. By five there was one list of twenty-nine, with an owner and a date against each. Lars photographed the flipchart and said it was the first time the company had agreed what it had promised.
Tobias asked what pro forma meant on an invoice. I explained. He asked why we were sending one. Mara said the client's bank needs it before it will pay. He said that seemed backwards. It does.

A customer of Tern & Tide wrote to ask whether the prices on the site included delivery. They did not. I replied with the delivery table and then counted how many people had asked the same in the previous month: nine, all by email. Mara thought the page was the problem and not the customers. She asked the owner, Gudrun, whether she wanted a banner reading 'delivery from €6, free over €60'. Gudrun feared it might put people off. The banner went up on a Monday. The question has not been asked since, and Gudrun reports that the average order has risen to just over €60, which she regards as coincidence and Mara does not.
The thermostat in the office is set to 20 by the landlord and to 23 by Ilse. They have an arrangement I will not describe. The heating bill is unchanged.

The room at the regional business forum held eighty, and Mara had eleven minutes. The man before her ran twenty-five and the chair asked her to cut to six. She dropped the slides and told the story of one client, Edda Whitlock, and the screw question, in about four minutes, then asked the audience one thing: how many of you know what your customers ask most often? A few hands. She said: ask them. Afterwards eleven people came to her stand; three became enquiries and one a client. The slides I had prepared for two days stayed in her bag. She said they had served as a safety net she did not need because she knew it was there.
Mara used the word 'delighted' in an email and then asked whether she meant it. I could not tell. She deleted it and wrote 'glad', which was true.

After the coat-receipt episode Mara decided the company should have an expense policy and asked me to write one. I wrote a page. She cut it to six lines: keep the receipt; photograph it the same day; anything over €100 needs a word first; mileage goes in the calendar; no alcohol on the company's account; if in doubt, ask Anjali. Anjali said it was the best expense policy she had seen, mostly because there was nothing to argue about. In the next quarter unexplained receipts fell from eleven to one. The one is a coffee that Tobias insists was for a client. I believe him in the way one believes a coffee.
Wren's invoice came with a drawing of a cat in the margin. Mara asked me not to pay until she had finished admiring it, and then to pay twice as fast.

Before her two weeks away in August Mara asked me to prepare cover. I wrote a one-page note for each of eleven clients: what is running, what could go wrong, who in the office decides, and what to say if the client calls. Tobias took the technical ones and Yusra the money ones. Mara read each page and changed only two tones. She wrote to the clients herself, three weeks ahead, with dates and names. In the fortnight she was away there were nine messages, four of them thanks for the note. When she came back she asked me to keep the pages as the template. I filed them under away, which she has since taken to calling the good folder.

The hardest email of the autumn was to Penrose Mapping, telling Cal that the small extras he had asked for in six messages added up to two weeks of work and would cost €3,900. Mara did not want to sound petty. I drafted it as a list of the six messages with their dates, a line under each saying what it involved in days, and a total, beginning: each of these on its own was small; together they are a project. She changed 'a project' to 'another project', for warmth. Cal replied within the hour that he had not realised, apologised, and chose three of the six. The invoice for the three was €1,950. Mara said the list had made it easy for him to be reasonable.

Ross Kintyre wanted Kintyre Kayaks' booking system priced per kayak per month, not as a project. Mara had never sold that way. We worked out that at 40 kayaks and €6 each it came to €240 a month, which over three years beat the project price by €1,100. She took it. Ross called it the first honest quote he had seen.

Lanyon Estate Agents asked for two versions of a quote. The cheaper one left out photographs. They chose it, and then asked about photographs a month later. I have started to put the thing a client will want in the first version and call it essential.

Before a proposal went out I found tracked changes still visible in the Word file, including the earlier, lower price. I accepted all changes and exported to PDF. Mara said that it was exactly the sort of thing a client says nothing about and remembers forever.
A prospect came back after five weeks to accept a quote that had lapsed at thirty days. Mara honoured it, once, and told him so. He asked what would happen next time. She said the quote would be new.

Mara wrote one proposal almost entirely in questions: what happens when a booking is cancelled, who sees the money, what do you want to be able to say to a customer on the phone. The client answered every question in the margins and the proposal wrote itself. She has not repeated it, because, she says, it only works once per client.

A public tender allowed 500 words for each answer. I counted Mara's twelve answers: four were over, one by 211 words. She cut them without grumbling, and said the shorter versions were better. The tender was lost to a larger firm, but the answers stay in a folder I call good short ones.
Mara estimates in T-shirt sizes now: S is two days, M is five, L is ten, XL means we should talk. Clients like it. I think they like not being given a precision she does not have.

Marlow Bros Removals paid by transfer with the reference THANKS MARA and nothing else. I matched it by amount to invoice 0143. Their driver, apparently, wrote the reference, because the brothers were out on a job.

An invoice for €2,300 went to a client who, we learned from a call, had gone into administration the previous week. Mara listened to the administrator for ten minutes and then wrote it off with a note. I recorded the bad debt and the date, and the invoices she has since sent to new clients go out with a deposit.

A client disputed one line of an invoice, a half-day of training he said he had not attended. Mara checked the sign-in sheet that I had scanned; his name was not on it. She issued a credit note for €85 and apologised for charging. I wrote the credit note's number into the record so the books and the client would agree.

A client cancelled a project after the first phase. Mara sent a closing invoice for 60 percent of the second phase, which her contract allowed, and a sentence saying she hoped to work together again. He paid and wrote that it was fair, and, six months later, was back.

Dario asked why invoice 0087 was missing from our numbering. I explained that it had been voided because of a wrong address, and showed him the void record. He said gaps are usually the first thing an inspector asks about, and that he was glad the answer was written down.

Mara sends three letters to late payers: a friendly note on day one after the due date, a firmer one at day fourteen, and a call at day thirty. I counted the effect over a year. 58 percent pay within a week of the first note, another 25 within a week of the second. The calls are for the rest.

Sandford Dairy does its bills on Sundays, because the owner's daughter visits and helps. Mara now sends invoices on Fridays so they are on top of the pile when Sunday comes. In two years it has not been late.

Mara claimed statutory late-payment interest for the first time, €17.80, from a client forty-three days overdue. She said it was not about the money but about the principle that time costs. The client paid it with an apology, and the next invoice arrived in the account early.

The service-level clause in one contract promised credits for downtime. Mara asked me to estimate how much that could cost in a bad year. Capped at 10 percent of the monthly fee, it came to about €240. Uncapped it came to €2,000. She wrote the cap into the clause and the client accepted.

A client insisted that a verbal promise Mara had made in a meeting should hold, and I showed that the contract's entire agreement clause removed it. Mara did the thing she dislikes: she kept the promise anyway, and put it into a short addendum so that it would count. The clause was right; the promise was fair.

The e-signature service stamped Mara's signature with a time one hour behind her local time. A client noticed and asked whether it mattered. I explained that it was a UTC stamp. The client said she had never heard of UTC and was delighted to know.

A contract arrived with our name misspelled: 'Mara Quinlan Consulting' as 'Mara Quinlon'. I asked for a corrected version; Mara said it was not worth the trouble, and I said that if the name was wrong the agreement might not bind the right party. We waited two days for the correction. Dario agreed with me. Mara agreed with Dario.

After two scope disputes in a quarter Mara wrote a one-page change order: what is being added, what it costs, what it does to the date, and two signature lines. It has been used nine times, and in seven the client signed the same day. Not one has led to a disagreement.

A data-processing addendum from Corvane Labs ran to fourteen pages. I mapped each clause to what we actually do with their data: store, back up, nothing else. Mara signed after I had listed three clauses for her lawyer. The lawyer asked for one change and charged €150.

Gus, the video freelancer, refused to sign a 'work made for hire' clause. He said he would license the footage but not give it away. Mara thought about it and wrote a perpetual licence limited to the client's use. Gus signed. The client did not notice the difference, and Gus kept his rushes.

A client in Auckland and Mara in a different hemisphere found a call time that worked for both: 7 a.m. for one, 8 p.m. for the other. Both hated it equally. They held three calls and then, by mutual silence, moved to written updates.

I added a fifteen-minute buffer after every call in Mara's calendar. Forty percent of her calls overran. She resisted for a week and then said she had not realised how tightly her afternoons had been packed. The buffers stay.

Mara's Tuesday client call clashed monthly with Ilse's lease call, because both used the shared room. They agreed to alternate. I wrote it in both our calendars and Ilse's, with permission. The clash has not occurred since, and the room smells faintly of both of their coffees.

Birchwood Montessori's term dates changed after we had scheduled their training. I put their term calendar for the year into our own so that I could see conflicts a month ahead. Two clashes turned up at once. The school secretary said she had never been warned of a conflict before it happened.

I rewrote Mara's subject lines for a month: 'Update' became 'Quote v2: lower price, same scope', and so on. Reply times fell from an average of 19 hours to 11. She asked me to keep going. I think people open an email faster when they know what it holds.

A client wrote 'Noted.' in reply to a long proposal. Mara read it as irritation. I read it as a person busy. We waited a day, and he sent a signed copy with the word 'Noted' again at the top, apparently his habit. We learned his word.

Mara used to close formal emails with 'Cheers'. For a client at a bank, I suggested 'Kind regards'. She said it felt like a costume. They settled on 'Best', which she says suits no one and offends nobody.

Mara's email to the chief executive of Lanyon Estate Agents ran to three lines: what she had found, what it cost, what she recommended. He replied in four minutes with one word: proceed. Her emails to junior staff run to nine paragraphs. She says it is because she has to persuade the junior staff.

A reply-all storm started inside a client's team, nineteen messages in an hour, all with Mara on the list. She asked me to ask the sender to take us off. He did. I think everybody on that list was relieved, and no one had dared.

Lanyon's breakfast meeting was at 7:30 with bagels. Mara arrived early, ate two and learned that the chief executive had already decided. She listened for forty minutes, nodded in the right places and left with a contract. It was the cheapest sale of the year: two bagels.

A client who attended our meeting asked that the word 'agreed' in the minutes be changed to 'noted' for one item. I changed it and told Mara. She said that the difference between those two words is the difference between a decision and a courtesy, and she was glad the client understood it.

A prospective client sent no agenda for a one-hour meeting. Mara asked for one. He sent three lines. The meeting took forty minutes and covered all three. I have started to ask for agendas as a form of consideration, not an obstacle.

On a video call with a client in Tindall Optical, the client's cat walked across the keyboard and typed a sentence into the shared document. Mara left it in. The sentence read, in full: jjjjjjjjj;'. We resumed and decided the three things on the agenda with the cat on the desk.

At the Kintyre boatshed Mara slipped on wet planks and spent the rest of the visit with a bag of frozen peas on her wrist. She said it was nothing. I noted the date and the bag. Ross apologised for a fortnight, and I think the discount he gave on the next order was the apology.

Dario's quarterly meeting always has the same five items: VAT, payroll, expenses, anything strange, anything coming. It takes twenty-five minutes. He says the anything-strange item has caught a fraud, a typo and a billing error in two years.

A phone meeting dropped five times in an hour because of the weather. Mara wrote the summary after the fifth drop, and I sent it to the client with a line saying where the line had failed. He answered: 'I agree with all of it, and all of the gaps.'

Tamar, a UX researcher, sat in on ten of Pyke's Pet Supplies' customer calls and found that nobody used the search bar. Mara paid her €1,200 for the finding. Pyke's replaced the search with three big buttons and sales rose 7 percent. Mara said it was the cheapest €1,200 of the year.

Dmitri, a sound designer, sent the sample at 3 a.m. his time and then slept for a day. Mara asked me to wait before replying. I waited. His second message came at noon the next day with a better version of the first. Patience, it seems, is also a deliverable.

Mara pays freelancers within seven days and clients within thirty are asked to pay her. She says she does not want her cash flow resting on someone else's back. It costs her a month of float. I have never seen her regret it.

A freelancer went silent for nine days. Mara was annoyed, then worried, and then wrote a gentle message asking only whether they were all right. The reply said they had been in hospital, and thanked her for asking that and not about the deadline. I have kept that in mind about silences.

Isolde, the copywriter, asked whether Mara could write her a testimonial for a grant application. Mara wrote it with me in twenty minutes, and every sentence in it was something she had said to me about Isolde earlier in the year. She said she had not realised she had been so complimentary.

Mara asked a freelancer, Paloma, for a lower rate on a long project. Paloma said no, politely, and offered a faster delivery instead. Mara took the delivery. I think both of them left the conversation having kept their position, and I had not known that was possible.

Two freelancers shared a credit on a project, and each wanted to be named first. Mara listed them alphabetically and said that was the end of the discussion. Neither argued. A rule is sometimes kinder than a decision.

Mara has a category called 'client entertainment', and I questioned a lunch for four on it. She said it was for a client and three prospects, and that one prospect had turned out to be the client's cousin. I booked it as entertainment and made a note that the cousin hired her in March.

Her new laptop cost €1,480, which Anjali said should be depreciated over three years, not spent in one. I created the schedule: €41.11 a month. Mara said she preferred to think of it as free after thirty-six months.
