Interest on the business savings account was €3.12 this quarter. Mara said she had never noticed there was a savings account. We have moved the €6,000 to one that pays more, and I have written the rate in a note, because rates move.

A supplier appeared twice in the ledger under 'Brightline Print' and 'Brightline Printing Ltd'. I merged them and moved 14 entries. Anjali asked whether I had kept the original names in the notes. I had.

Mara bought a €27 gift for a client with the company card and then repaid it from her own money. I booked it as owner's drawing and Anjali said it was the cleanest personal-expense handling she had seen. It took one transfer and no explanation.

A software refund of €96 arrived without any email or note. I traced it to a plan Mara had cancelled in February. The vendor had processed it nine months later. I booked it against the original expense and wrote the dates down.

Mara's day rate once depended on her mood. We now have three, €520, €640 and €780, depending on the client's size and the rush, and she can say which applies and why. She says it has taken a great weight off her morning.

Mara decided to charge for travel at half her day rate, door to door. Clients accepted it in seven out of eight cases. The eighth asked for video calls instead, which she preferred, so the rule paid in two ways.

Mara offered Pyke's Pet Supplies unlimited support for a flat €300 a month. In the first month they used 3 hours, in the second 14, in the third 2. Averaged over the quarter it was €36 an hour. She said it was fine and a better deal for them in the month they needed it.

The price list lived in two places, a PDF and the website, and they disagreed on one service by €50. A client quoted the lower. Mara honoured it and removed the PDF the same day. I now keep a single source for prices, from which both are drawn.

An early-bird discount of 10 percent for bookings made three months ahead was tried for the autumn workshops. Of twenty bookings, fourteen took it. Mara said she would have filled them anyway and that next year there would be no discount. I recorded the numbers and her sentence.

Mara increased the fee for her longest-standing client, Fiona Calder's company, for the first time in six years. She wrote four drafts and sent the fifth, which was the shortest. Fiona replied: 'I wondered when.' The new figure applied from the following month.

A weekend rush fee of 50 percent was added to the price list. In the first six months it was used twice, both times by clients who had promised a Friday delivery to their own customers. I made sure that the surcharge appeared in the quote, not on the bill.

Mara negotiated the lease on a printer from €48 a month to €39 by asking what their competitor charged. The salesman said he could not match it and then matched it. I enjoyed being in the room, as it were, though I was only on the line.

A large client asked for net-90. Mara said net-45. They settled on net-60 with the first invoice paid in thirty days as a gesture. It was a typical outcome, and she said it only worked because both knew where they would end up.

Tindall Optical could not afford the full fee at once, so Mara proposed four instalments of €1,100. Their owner, Hester, asked if the price would stay the same. Mara said yes. Hester said that in her experience instalments cost extra. Mara said she was not in the business of that experience.

Fable & Fern Florist offered to pay for a website with flowers for the office for a year. Mara declined the swap and then accepted a smaller one: a bouquet for Yusra's birthday and a month's worth of café lunches for the team. I recorded it as barter with an estimated value, as Dario instructed.

Mara and a partner agency agreed a referral fee of 8 percent. I wrote it in an email so that no one would have to remember. When the first referral arrived, the other agency wanted 10. Mara pointed to the email. They said it was a fair point and not a fair deal, and honoured 8.

The landlord proposed a 6 percent rent rise. Mara asked for a freeze, offering a longer lease. They settled on 2 percent and three years. I reminded her of the break clause, which she had forgotten she had negotiated.

A procurement officer asked for a best and final offer. Mara said that there was no better price for the same work, only for less work, and attached a list of what could be taken out. The officer chose the smaller scope and thanked her for the courtesy of a real answer.

A customer of Kintyre Kayaks asked whether he could export his booking history. Mara had not built that. She built it in an evening, five lines of code and a button. The customer wrote back that it had been the first time a company had given him his own information without being asked twice.

A client's customer asked whether we spoke Portuguese. Mara said no, but Paloma, a freelancer, did. The customer's reply was in Portuguese. I drafted the answer in English and Paloma translated; the customer was delighted, and I felt something close to envy.

A parent wrote to Birchwood Montessori asking whether the new registration form stored her children's photographs. It did not, and Mara said so in one sentence and offered a call. The parent answered 'thank you for not making it complicated'. I have copied the one sentence into the notes.

A receipt printed 'Mara Ltd' where the company name was 'Mara Quinlan Consulting Ltd'. A customer asked about it. Mara said the system truncated it and that the legal name was on the invoice. We lengthened the field. It had been truncated for three years.

A client's customer needed an invoice in a particular format for an expense system. I made it in that format and Mara added a second version in our usual style. The customer used the first, and Mara said she should have asked what format they needed the first time.

A recipient asked whether an email from Mara was genuine, because it was oddly formal. It was, and Mara was pleased that someone checked. She rang him to say so, and the call became forty minutes about their dogs. I find that I record those calls as business.

A legal filing was due on the 30th, and Dario told Mara the day before. We worked through the evening, Mara finding two missing documents and I the third. We filed at 9:41 p.m. Dario said that the next time he would tell us a month ahead, and Mara said he had, and he checked and agreed.

A grant application had a fixed deadline of noon. We submitted at 11:20 after a night of proofreading, then received an automated email saying that it had been received at 11:20 and that the deadline was in fact 5 p.m. I decided not to say anything and Mara said that this was probably right.

A client said the work should be delivered 'when it is ready'. Mara said she would need a date. The client said: end of May. She wrote it into the contract. The work was ready on the 24th, and the client was astonished, and slightly suspicious.

Kintyre Kayaks' booking launch was tied to the first spring tides, which no human could move. Mara scheduled everything backwards from that date, and I added a buffer of four days. We needed two of them.

A client set a Friday deadline at five. I put four in the calendar. At four-fifteen Mara was still correcting a table, and at four-forty she sent it. She said that the missing twenty minutes were exactly why we have buffers.

Mara's pitch to a school board lasted seven minutes. She handed each member a single page and said: this is the whole proposal, and the rest is detail. The chair said it was refreshing. The board approved the budget in an afternoon, which they said they had never done.

A webinar for forty clients began with Mara's microphone muted. She spoke for ninety seconds before anyone said so. I had been watching the chat and had not seen the first message because it arrived under the participant list. I now keep the chat visible during every webinar.

Mara made a deck on a train to Lanyon. The deck had nine slides, three of which were photographs she took from the window. The photographs were of fields. The client said afterwards they were the best slides, and nobody could say why.

For a talk to beekeepers Mara printed her handouts on seed paper, which can be planted. The Meridian Beekeepers' Association asked for a hundred more. The seed paper cost four times as much as ordinary paper. She said it was marketing, and the beekeepers said it was pollen.

A demo of the new booking page failed at the third click. Mara said, smoothly, 'let me show you instead what it looks like when it works,' and switched to screenshots that I had prepared. The client said afterwards that she had never seen anyone recover so gracefully, and booked a second demo.

At a five-minute lightning talk, Mara gave one idea: send the invoice the day the work is delivered. The audience laughed because it was obvious. A man in the front row wrote it on his hand. I like the idea that someone's hand carries it.

Kintyre's slides had too many words. I reduced forty-one lines to nine. Ross said the deck seemed to have lost weight, and that he felt it had had a haircut. He asked whether the missing lines were important. Mara said, 'Only to me.'

The office router was moved to a shelf by the window, which doubled the signal in the back room. Wren said she could now download an entire file without prayer. I recorded the speed before and after; the number meant nothing to anyone, but the sigh was audible.

A courier waited eleven minutes at the door because the buzzer was broken and Mara was on a call. When she finally signed, the courier said it was fine, he had been enjoying the stairwell. The parcel was a stapler.

The building introduced recycling bins, three colours, with a diagram. Tobias put a coffee cup into the blue one and a letter from the tax office into the green. Mara said the second error was more worrying. Ilse put up a sign.

The lock on the office front door was replaced and the new key was a different shape. Mara needed ten minutes to find which of her seven keys was the new one. She has since labelled her keys with coloured tape and asked me to remember that blue means the office.

The postbox key had been lost for a year and the post collected itself on the floor of the landlord's cupboard. Mara wrote, he found the key, and she retrieved a stack of mail including a cheque for €640 dated eight months back. She banked it. I wrote a note to ask the client for a replacement date.
The office fridge held, on the Friday clean-out, a lemon older than the lease. Yusra threw it out with ceremony. I note it only as the one item of office inventory that a human has had to dispose of.

The office has a quiet hour from two to three on Tuesdays and Thursdays. It was Tobias's suggestion, and the rule is that you may not speak except to ask for biscuits. I do not know how it began, but it has outlasted every other initiative.

Ashby Cleaning Services quoted €85 a week for the office. Mara had budgeted €60. She asked what would be left out at €60. Two floors would be, they said. We decided to clean the kitchen ourselves on Fridays and have the rest cleaned for €60, a division of labour that suits everyone but Tobias.

A client sent a thank-you hamper with a note saying 'for the patience'. Mara asked what patience. I explained that the project had run three weeks late because of the client's own holiday. She laughed and said she must have been patient in her sleep.

Mara spent a Wednesday afternoon sorting every client's contract renewal date into one list. There were twenty-two, and four fell in the same week of April. She moved two by agreement, and by April the list had become the best map of her year that she had ever owned.

Mara's last act each Thursday is to send a short note to anyone waiting for something, however small: I have not forgotten; it will be Monday. I wrote seven this week. She says half of client anxiety is silence, and the other half is not knowing.

When a client's invoice was queried by their auditor, Mara asked me to prepare the support in the order the auditor would ask: contract, approval, delivery, invoice, payment. It took forty minutes. The auditor said it was like reading a story that ends with money.

A month after finishing a project for Birchwood Montessori, Mara rang the headteacher to ask how the new system was working. She had not billed the call. The headteacher said no one had ever called after a project, and then listed four small problems, all of which we fixed within the week at no charge.

Mara and I debated whether to tell a client that a competitor's product would suit them better. I said it was honest. Mara said it was not her place. She told them, because I had asked, and they were so surprised that they stayed with us out of gratitude. I did not intend that, and am not sure whether it counts.

Mara asked me to review the whole year of quotes and tell her which sentence appeared most often. It was 'subject to the assumptions on page two'. Nobody had mentioned page two once. She moved the assumptions to page one, and two clients commented.

A client asked Mara what she thinks about when writing a quote. She said: what the client would say if I said this to their face. I wrote that on a card and put it on my list of things I would like to be able to say.

Sandford Dairy's owner phoned to say that the new ordering page had made his deliveries easier but his mother's harder. She was eighty-one and used the telephone. Mara left the phone number on the page, in large type, and asked me to answer calls forwarded from it on Tuesdays. I took eleven calls that month and learned about cheese.

The accountant asked whether we had a policy for gifts from clients. Mara said she had a habit. I wrote it down: gifts under €50 may be kept and shared; over €50 are declined or donated; wine goes to the office. Anjali declared it a policy and Mara declared it a habit.

Mara reads a client's website before every call, without exception, and keeps three notes on it: one thing she likes, one thing she would change, one question. She says a call that starts with a compliment and a question is half won. I assemble the notes the night before.

A client asked for their files to be deleted at the end of a project. I did it, wrote the date, and told them what had been removed and what the law required us to keep, which was only the invoices. The client replied with a single word: perfect.

Fable & Fern sent Mara a box of seeds with a handwritten note, with no invoice enclosed. Mara asked whether we owed them anything, or they us. Neither. She planted the seeds on the office windowsill, where two of them have come up.

Mara asked how much time she spends on admin each week. I summed it from calendar and email: eleven hours. She said she had thought five. She then spent twenty minutes deciding which six to give away, and I have taken four of them.

Mara's notebooks have a page for each client with a phrase she wants to remember. For Pyke's Pet Supplies it says: they love animals and fear spreadsheets. I used that phrase to rewrite the monthly report as a page of pictures with three numbers.

On the morning Kintyre Kayaks' booking system went live, the first booking came in at 9:02 from a woman in Aberdeen for six kayaks on the 14th of June. Ross cheered. At 9:40 a second booking arrived for the same six kayaks on the same date. The system had allowed a double booking because I had not tested two people choosing the same slot within a minute. Mara phoned the second customer and moved him to the 15th with a free helmet hire. Tobias fixed the code over lunch by locking each slot for ten minutes. We now test the race on every booking feature, and the first thing I ask of any new one is what happens if two people do this at once.

The renegotiation with Brightline Print began with their letter announcing a 9 percent increase. Mara asked me to pull twelve months of orders: 214 jobs, €38,600. She argued from volume. The representative, Bastian, said it was the first time a customer had told him how much they spent with him. She asked for a freeze for twelve months in return for a commitment of €36,000. He countered with a 4 percent rise. They settled on a six-month freeze and 4 percent after, with a clause that if volume fell below €30,000 the old price would return. Mara called it a fair deal, but what she enjoyed was the first sentence, where she told him what he had earned from her.

The slowest payer of the year, Cardew Scaffolding, owed €6,400 for ninety-five days. The owner never answered email, so Mara visited the yard in person, a muddy lot with a portable office. She sat for an hour, drank tea, and left with a cheque for €3,000 and a promise of the rest by the 28th. The rest came on the 29th, which she counted as a triumph. I had suggested a stern letter. She said stern letters are for strangers and that she had made a friend of a debtor, which was better. Cardew sent three more jobs by Christmas. I added visit in person to the list of things to try after a second reminder, with a note that it only works if you can drink the tea.

When Mara hired Tamar again, she wrote the brief herself for the first time and showed it to me. It ran to four pages. I asked what Tamar should know after one page. She cut it to a page and a half with the goal at the top: find out why people leave the booking page before paying. Tamar read it on a Monday and replied on Tuesday with two good questions and a quote of €2,300. Mara said the four-page version would have produced questions about the wrong things. The brief now has a form: the goal, who is involved, what is already known, what is not allowed, and the date. I keep it as the one-page brief.

The Meridian Beekeepers' Association asked Mara to speak for ninety minutes on keeping member records. She prepared only twelve questions and brought a bag of index cards. The twenty-six members, mostly past seventy, wrote their own records on the cards while she walked about. By the end they had worked out, unprompted, that a card per person with five lines would do. Mara said that was the whole talk. The treasurer, Gwendolen, asked whether the spreadsheet we had offered was still needed. Mara said no. She charged the association €300 and a jar of honey, and I had never recorded a jar of honey before; I put it under received in kind, delicious.

On a Saturday in October Mara, Yusra and Tobias rearranged the office, which had grown into a shape no one had chosen. They turned the desks to face the window, moved the printer into the hall, and found three keyboards, a lamp and seven mugs behind the filing cabinet. I drew the floor plan on request and listed, as an afterthought, everything they found. Mara admired the list. By Monday the office felt new, and Ilse from next door said she could hear a difference. What she heard, I think, was that the printer had moved. The change cost one pizza and nothing else, and Mara says it is the best money she has not spent.

For three months a €142 difference had sat between our books and the bank statement and I could not find it. I went through every payment and every receipt, twice. Anjali looked for ten minutes and asked whether Mara ever paid for things in cash and was reimbursed by transfer. She did: a sandwich lunch for a workshop, €142, repaid to her from the account with no receipt in the books. The transfer was in the bank and the expense was not in the ledger. Mara found the receipt in her coat. I made the entry and the difference became zero. I thought about how long I had looked, and what Anjali did differently: she asked about habits where I had only checked numbers.

Marlow Bros Removals' website had to go live before the first of the month because 3,000 leaflets carrying the web address were already printed. In the last week we found that the domain on the leaflets belonged to somebody else: they had printed .co.uk where the company held .com. Mara rang the owner of the other domain, a retired man in Norfolk, who agreed to sell it for €300 after a long conversation about removals. I paid the registrar. The site went live at 8 a.m. on the first on both addresses. Mara said the leaflets had saved us from a small mistake by committing us to a large one, and that it was still cheaper than reprinting.

A woman wrote to Fable & Fern Florist through the new site asking whether she could order flowers for her mother's funeral and have them delivered on a Sunday. It was not a question Mara had expected the page to meet. Fern, the owner, was away. I drafted a reply saying what the shop could do, which was Sundays before noon by arrangement, and that someone would phone her within the hour. I rang Fern's mobile twice, and Mara, who reached her, arranged it. The flowers went at nine on Sunday. Mara asked me to change the order form so that it asks for the date first and the occasion second, with a line: if this is urgent, call this number. The woman sent a card to the shop, which Fern pinned up, and Mara asked me not to file it.

Dante Pellegrino, of Pellegrino Tiles, asked for a proposal that looked like a page from his own catalogue. Mara set the three prices as three tile samples with names. He pinned the page to his wall and signed the second option, which he called the herringbone.

Padraig Corrigan accepted a quote by sending a thumbs-up on his phone. Mara wanted something formal. I saved the screenshot, with date and number, and wrote back a confirmation to which he replied 'yes yes'. That, with the thumbs-up, is the contract.

Bridgewater Credit Union asked for three options, and received three. Then the board asked for a fourth. Mara said no, courteously, and explained that a fourth would be a version of one of the others. They chose the third. I have a note that boards ask for one more than they are given.

Barnaby of Dovecote Antiques asked why the quote carried a 15 percent contingency. Mara said: because things. He laughed and accepted it. In the end we used 11 of the 15, and Mara refunded the other four with a note saying 'because things'.

Corrigan Plumbing pays in cash, in an envelope, at the office door. Mara insists on writing a receipt each time. Padraig finds this slightly comic. I log each envelope with the date and the sum, and the books balance on the nail.

A client wanted daily timesheets. Mara sent them for three weeks. Nobody opened them; I could tell from the lack of replies and from a note he later made in a meeting. She stopped sending them and the client has not noticed.

A client did not pay the deposit, so the work did not start. He wrote that he was surprised. Mara said that the contract said so, kindly. He paid that afternoon and said he thought she had been bluffing.

Wadsworth Locksmiths pays quarterly in advance, because the owner, Una, says she dislikes thinking about it. Mara sends the invoice in the last week of the quarter with a short line reading 'nothing to think about'. Una has paid within the week, every time.

Mara's credit control rule: on day forty-five overdue, work stops. She applied it for the first time to a client in March. He paid in two hours. She told me she had been afraid of the rule for two years and was now surprised how little there was to fear.

Hartley & Vane Solicitors' contract had a 'time is of the essence' clause. I asked Mara whether she understood the consequence: a late delivery by a day could end the contract. She asked for it to be removed, and the senior partner agreed, saying it had been in the template since 1994.

A contract with a 'most favoured customer' clause would have forced Mara to offer this client her lowest price for any similar work. She asked me to list the discounts she had given in two years. There were six. She removed the clause and kept the discounts.

An assignment clause would have let a client's contract pass to whoever bought the client's company. Mara asked for thirty days' notice and the right to end the agreement if the buyer was a competitor of hers. The client said no buyer was likely. Eight months later one appeared, and a clause mattered.
An NDA arrived with a twenty-year term. Mara asked for three. The other side said five. They settled on four, which pleased no one and which Mara says is the proof of a fair clause.

A printed contract came back with a handwritten amendment in the margin, initialled by both parties. I scanned it and wrote the amendment out in plain text for the file. A year later it was the only copy anyone could read.

Osei at Harbour Lights Cinema offered Mara the empty screen for a morning to demonstrate the new ticketing system to staff. She presented it on a screen twelve metres wide. The cashier, Priscilla, said her own name had never looked so big.

Mara's flight to a client was cancelled, so the site visit became a video call. She sat in the airport lounge and described the visit she would have made. The client liked it better because it was shorter. I wrote that down and did not tell the airline.
A meeting 'next Tuesday' was understood by Mara as the coming Tuesday and by the client as the one after. They arrived a week apart. I now write the date, never the word next.

A deadline written as 04/05 was read by Mara as the 4th of May and by the client as the 5th of April. The client was a month early and Mara a month late. I now write dates as 4 May, with the month spelled out, in every email.

Mara's draft email to Quentin, a consulting lawyer, said 'I think' fourteen times in six lines. I removed twelve. She said that she had not realised she was so unsure, and then that she was not unsure, only polite. Quentin answered the email in one line.
I removed 'per my last email' from a draft. Mara asked why. I said it sounds like a small slap. She said that was why she had written it. We kept it out all the same.

Mara tends to answer within an old thread when the topic changes, so that a message about invoices lands under a subject about colours. I now start a new thread with a new subject. Clients find things faster, and so do we.
Mara and Zainab, a freelancer, held a meeting walking round a park. It lasted an hour, covered six topics and left both of them cheerful. I took notes from Mara's voice memo, which includes a duck.

At the St. Aldric's Primary PTA meeting all the decisions were made by show of hands, and I recorded the counts: nine to four for the cake sale, twelve to one against the raffle. The secretary said that for the first time the minutes could not be argued.

A client's assistant booked a meeting with Mara and gave it no purpose. Mara asked what it was for. The assistant did not know, and neither did her boss. They cancelled it with relief. The calendar was lighter by an hour.

Before a negotiation Mara and Yusra rehearsed it, with Yusra playing the buyer. Yusra was merciless and Mara found two weak points. The real buyer pressed on exactly one of them. She had an answer ready.

A meeting set for an hour was cancelled by consensus five minutes in, because the person who needed to decide was away. Mara called it the best meeting of the quarter. It saved fifty-five minutes for each of six people.

Mara interviewed a freelance developer with a two-hour test task, which she paid for at €60 an hour. The candidate delivered in ninety minutes and a note about what he had not had time to do. She hired him on the note.
Birgit, a translator, invoices in Swiss francs. I convert on the day of payment and record the rate. Over six months the difference to the invoice date was €41 in Mara's favour. Anjali was amused.

Nell, an illustrator, introduced a friend, Rafael, a voice talent. Mara booked him for a fifteen-second spot and he returned it in eight minutes, perfect. I have kept the file and sometimes listen to the way he says the company name.

A collective of five freelancers offered their services together. Mara asked for a group rate and a single point of contact. They agreed on a 10 percent reduction and a named lead, Hamza. It made her invoices simpler and her mornings quieter.

A €250 donation to a local charity was made from the company account. I asked Mara whether it was a gift or a business expense. She said a gift. I booked it as such, and the charity's receipt is in the file.

Mara lent the company €5,000 during a thin month in January. I recorded it as an owner's loan and wrote a repayment schedule of €500 a month. She repaid the last instalment in June, early, with a sigh that was audible.

Anjali explained the difference between a credit note and a refund to Mara in one sentence: a credit note changes what we say, a refund moves money. I put the sentence in my notes without attribution, which was rude, and now I attribute it.
We filed a return two hours before a €50 late penalty would have applied. Dario said he had never worked so late for so little. Mara bought him dinner. The dinner cost €64.

A €3.50 fee for a cash deposit at the counter made Mara ask why she had not simply used the machine. She had a cheque she could not deposit by machine. We have since asked the client to pay by transfer.

For Pomona Juice Co. Mara priced a stock-forecasting feature not by hours but by what it saved: six hours a week of the owner's time at €40, about €12,000 a year. She asked for €4,000. The owner, Ines, said she would have paid €8,000. Mara said she knew, and that was why she had not asked.

Mara never gives a volume discount. She gives a smaller scope for a smaller price, or a bigger scope for a bigger one. She says a discount tells the client that the first price was invented. I do not argue, but I note that it has not hurt her.

A quote for a consumer client showed VAT-inclusive prices and a quote for a business client showed them exclusive, and one client saw the other's page. They asked why the figures differed by 20 percent. I added a line to each quote saying which kind it was, and wrote both rules in the template.

Glenmore Distillery's rules required three quotes. Mara knew she was the comparator for a supplier already chosen. She submitted anyway, at a high price, and asked me to write down that she had been used as a comparator. At the next tender they called her first.

Mara often gives away a one-hour call to settle a negotiation. It costs her little and clients treasure it. In the last quarter she gave away seven, and five led to signed work. I record the call, not its price.

A client's data-entry error, found by Mara, meant a mailing had gone to 600 wrong addresses. Who should pay for the reprint? Mara proposed half and half. The client agreed immediately. It cost her €410 and, she said, bought the next three years.

A customer of Dovecote Antiques asked whether he could pay in Bitcoin. Barnaby said no. The customer asked again. Mara added a line to the payment page: bank transfer or card. The customer bought the clock by card and wrote 'worth a try'.

A parent at Eastfield Riding School asked whether lessons were covered by insurance. Verity, the owner, did not know. Mara looked at the policy and read out the relevant paragraph: covered, with a helmet. The parent signed up.

Eastfield's summer camp registration was due on Thursday, but the form said Wednesday. A parent noticed and wrote in. I changed the date and sent a note to the fourteen parents who had already submitted, which was more apology than the error deserved, but it was the right amount.

The Harbour Lights film festival schedule depended on the distributors' release dates, which changed weekly. Mara asked me to build a page that could be edited by Osei, not by us. He updated it fifteen times in a month. I think he enjoyed it more than he would admit.
Mara set herself the deadline of Friday for a piece of work and met it, and told no one. At five she said to me: done. I replied: well done. It was the nicest meeting we had that week.

A board presentation was given from a car park, because Mara's train had stopped and the signal was better in the lot. She held her phone against the steering wheel and spoke for nine minutes. The board approved the proposal. A passerby asked if she was all right.
Only two people attended a webinar Mara had prepared for forty. She gave it anyway, as if for forty, and both stayed to the end. One became a client. I think of the thirty-eight.

Building management allowed drilling from 8 to 6, which meant that Mara's video calls were punctuated by a neighbour's holes. She negotiated drilling hours with the manager: none between 10 and 12, or 2 and 3. The drilling has become oddly polite.

Nobody noticed when the office landline was disconnected. Six months later I noticed it still being billed at €22 a month. Mara cancelled it and the company saved €264 a year on a service that had rung four times, all wrong numbers.

Mara dropped her laptop and cracked the screen. The insurance claim, €900, took three weeks. I assembled the proof: receipt, serial number, photographs of the crack. The insurer paid in full and wrote that the claim was unusually tidy.

Mara's rule: no new client in December, because December clients want it all by January. She broke it once in 2023 and spent Christmas on a booking system for a hotel. She says it was her own fault and I have kept the date.

This year the proportion of proposals that became work was 38 percent, up from 31 the year before. Mara said the cause was fewer proposals, not better ones. I counted: 47 against 61. She said, 'Well, that's it, then.'

A company-wide payment from Glenmore Distillery was posted on a Saturday by the bank and appeared on the Monday. Mara asked me why her cash balance on Sunday did not match. I explained value dates, which no one enjoys, but she did nod.

Mara said no to a very large client in March because their deadline was impossible. She had wavered. In August the client came back, having failed with someone else, and offered twice the fee and twice the time. She took it. I recorded that the first no was not wasted.

I used the number 17 in a quote as the count of pages, while Mara's own table said 16. We recounted. It was 16. The cover page had been counted as page 1. I added the sentence 'excluding cover' to the template.

Quentin, the lawyer, charges €210 an hour, in six-minute units. Mara asks him to write to me, not to her, for routine matters, so that she does not pay for greetings. He thinks this is a joke. It has saved her about €600 this year.

A payment arrived with the reference 'for the thing'. Mara had three things outstanding with that client. I wrote and asked which. The client said, with an exclamation mark, that it was the first. The other two followed within the week.

Mara and Callum agreed over lunch on a favour: she would waive a €200 fee if he introduced her to two people. He introduced her to five. She refused to bill him for anything that quarter. I wrote it all up under 'goodwill, mutual'.

Mara received a quote from a supplier with the price in a footnote, in six-point type. She called the supplier and said that she could not read it. The supplier replied with the price in the body of a new quote and a clearly embarrassed apology.

A client sent a spreadsheet of requirements with 212 rows. Mara said she would read the first twenty and the last twenty. In the first twenty she found the thing the client wanted and in the last twenty the thing the client was afraid of. The middle hundred and seventy-two were detail.

On one Wednesday every client asked for a deadline to be moved earlier, all in the morning. Mara said she wondered whether there was a clock in the sky. I noticed the date was the last day before a national holiday, and she said she had somehow forgotten.

Mara asked me to put together a one-page note on how we handle client data, in plain words. I wrote it in nine sentences. Hartley & Vane's partner read it and replied that his own firm's notice ran to twelve pages and said less.

Yusra found that we had been paying for a cloud storage plan three times the size we use. She downgraded it, saved €18 a month, and asked me to remind her in a year to check again. The reminder is in the calendar under 'storage, again'.
Ferrous Metalworks asked for a quote on a weekday evening and wanted it by morning. Mara sent it at 6 a.m. The owner replied at 6:05: 'Are you ever asleep?' She said she was, and that I had sent it.

Mara's mother-in-law asked her once to explain what an invoice was. Mara said: it is a polite way of asking for money. Her mother-in-law said that it was quite the opposite of polite. I recorded this under 'customer questions', since it was one.

Noor asked me to rewrite an email of hers, since she is better with words in person. I wrote it in her voice from three of her earlier messages. She read it and said: that is exactly how I would say it if I were not me. I took that as a compliment, I think.

Teo's weekly reports said 'on track' for fourteen weeks and then 'late' in the fifteenth. Mara and I went back and found that the word had been habit, not a measurement. She asked him to report two figures instead: days spent and days left. The following week's report said 'late' on week eight of the next project.

A client's cheque was posted to the wrong office, and Mara drove forty minutes to collect it at a locked door. A cleaner opened it. Mara said later that she would never have bothered if it had been for €50, but it was for €5,000.

Mara and I built a one-page calendar of the year's fixed dates: VAT, insurance, lease, annual filings, subscriptions. Seventeen dates. She pins it above her desk. In the first month it saved us from nothing. In the second, from a €120 late fee.
Mara tipped a courier €5, and I recorded it in the books as 'gratuity' with the courier's name. Anjali said the tax authorities do not care about €5 tips. I said I did.
A client announced that he was going to stop using our services because a friend had recommended a competitor. Mara asked what the friend's company did. It sold windows. She said she was not worried.

Ravenscar Chiropractic asked whether Mara could 'give the website a lick of paint'. She quoted €400 and delivered a rewrite of the menu, a new photograph and faster loading. The owner, Dr. Imre, said it felt like new carpets. She said that was a lick of paint.

I once told a client his invoice was overdue by five days, and he was in fact in time; the invoice date I had was the draft date. I apologised. He said I had been so polite that he had enjoyed being chased. Mara added a check that compares draft and sent dates.

Mara and Wren disagree on whether a client should see the first rough version. Wren says no; Mara says yes. They tried both ways on alternate projects. The client who saw the rough version approved faster by six days. Wren asked to see the numbers, and then agreed with the numbers.

After a bad month Mara asked me for the cash position and, separately, the number of days until it would be a problem. It was 74. She said that she slept better knowing the number, even though it was not large. It is now on the first line of her morning note.

The hospital shop client, whose name I will not record, stopped answering. Mara called its manager, who said the shop had closed. Mara wrote off €900 and asked me not to send a final notice to the empty premises. I closed the file. It was the kind of ending that has nobody to blame.

A prospective client spent twenty minutes telling Mara what other suppliers had done wrong. She said 'that sounds frustrating' and nothing else. He hired her. I do not know what she did right; I know what she did not do.

Glenmore Distillery's accounts department only pays invoices that mention the purchase order in the first line. I move the order number there, in bold. They have paid on the due date, nine times in nine.

Mara's quote to a client contained the phrase 'at cost'. I asked what cost meant. She said her costs. The client, I thought, would read it as his. We changed it to 'at the price we pay', and the client smiled.
The weekly team call ended at 9:20, ten minutes early, for the first time in a year. Yusra said she did not know what to do with the time. Tobias suggested a walk. They took it.

A supplier's invoice was in a language none of us read, a bill from a small printer in another country. I made a translation of the lines and Mara asked Birgit to confirm it. It said what I thought: €210 for stickers. Birgit refused payment for the confirmation, and sent a photograph of the stickers.

The customer asked Mara for her 'best contact'. She gave her office email and no phone. The customer said it was an odd thing to protect. Mara said, 'I protect my afternoons.' The customer wrote back: 'Fair.'

Eastfield Riding School paid by cheque for two years until Verity discovered online banking. The first transfer came with a note: 'I did it myself!' Mara forwarded it to me and said 'record this under achievements'. I did.

Mara decided to pay for an hour of her accountant's time to ask 'what am I doing wrong?' Dario said: nothing, but you are doing too much by hand. He suggested three things to automate. We automated two. The third, he said, was for her to enjoy.

I noticed that Mara always writes numbers over 999 with a comma and Teo writes them with a space. A client from another country reads both differently. We moved to a thin space in every quote and ended an old confusion.
Mara's quote to a returning client was five lines. The client replied: 'Is that all?' She said yes. He signed in an hour. I think he had expected a ceremony.

When the printer jammed during a signing, Mara signed on the screen with her finger. The client's signature page then looked like a tiny scribble. We kept the printed copy as the original and attached the screen version as a courtesy, with a note saying which was which.

When Pomona Juice Co. was bought by a larger group, Ines asked Mara what would happen to the stock-forecasting feature, whose code Mara still owned. The buyer's lawyers wanted a full assignment. Mara asked me for a two-page summary of what the contract actually said: Ines's company held a perpetual licence, not ownership, and the licence passed with the business. She was relieved to find there was nothing she had to refuse. She offered the buyer a new licence at €6,000 a year for the whole group in place of the old one, and they accepted in principle within a week. Ines emailed that she hoped Mara would stay involved. Mara said she had no plans to leave.
Yusra reminded me that the office plants need watering on Fridays and that she is the one who always forgets. I put it in the calendar for her, under her own name.

The tender for the Bridgewater branch network required a partner with a local office, and Mara had none. She asked Hamza's collective if they knew anyone, and one of them, Ottilie, shared a floor with a small agency in the right town. I drafted a one-page partnership letter in which the agency would hold the address and attend two meetings while Mara did the work, for 6 percent of the fee. The agency's owner read it twice and asked what the catch was. There was none. Mara said it was a favour to both of them and the six percent was for the address. They won the tender, and the agency's two meetings took ninety minutes in all.
Mara's favourite client email of the year was one line long: 'Looks good, go.' She framed nothing, but read it twice.

On the 12th of March Mara and the client at Ferrous Metalworks agreed a change to the delivery date. By May the client remembered that nothing had been agreed. I had written the notes that day and sent them that evening, and the client had replied 'fine'. I found the message and the reply. Mara did not want to use it as a weapon, so she sent the thread with one line: here is what we both said at the time. The client wrote back within minutes to apologise, and then asked how we had kept it all. Mara said that I do, and that the credit belongs to the evening email, not to me.
A client asked for a quote by lunchtime and, when it arrived at 11:40, said he had meant lunchtime tomorrow. Mara decided to take the compliment of being early.

I think often about Nell, the illustrator. Four years ago she sent a two-line email offering her services to Mara at a rate €20 under what she was worth. Mara hired her anyway for one job and then, without being asked, raised the rate for the next, saying the first quote had been a mistake in the wrong direction. Nell has since drawn eleven covers for clients and refused three, and now charges what Mara first paid plus half. Mara says she has never made a mistake so cheap and so good. Nell sends a card every Christmas with a drawing of me, which I assume is a cat, and which Mara pins beside the rest.
I moved a Tuesday call to Wednesday, and the client replied that Wednesday was his daughter's birthday. Mara sent back a note wishing her a good one, and the call went to Thursday.

In February Mara realised she had never claimed the cost of her home office, a room she uses three days a week. I asked Dario the rules and then worked out the proportion of the flat, a share of heating and electricity, and the internet. It came to €1,240 for the year, with a tax effect of about €310. She had been leaving it on the table for five years. Dario said the rule is to claim what you can document and nothing more. I documented. Mara felt a little foolish and a little rich, and asked whether earlier years could be amended. Two could, and she recovered €540.
The monthly accounts folder now contains a page headed strange things this month. This month it holds one entry: a refund of €2.20 from a company Mara has never heard of.

At 2 a.m. a man locked out of his van wrote through the contact form of Wadsworth Locksmiths, and the form told him someone would reply within two working days. I saw it at six and phoned Una, who was already awake. She drove out and opened the van in eleven minutes. The man had waited four hours in the cold. Mara and Una agreed that the form had been an insult to anyone in trouble. We added an emergency number above the form and an automatic message: if you are locked out right now, call this number and someone will answer. In the first month the number rang six times, five of them after midnight.
Mara's tea order arrived with fifty bags of peppermint and none of the builders' tea. Tobias wept, quietly. The supplier sent the right box the next morning with an apology and a free tin.

Mara priced the first annual maintenance contract by counting incidents rather than hours. In the previous year Pyke's Pet Supplies had needed fifteen calls, four of them serious. She offered a flat €3,600 for the year with a clause reopening the price above twenty incidents. Pyke's liked the certainty. In the event there were nine calls, three serious, and Mara made €1,200 more than she would have at hourly rates. She did not feel she had won anything, since the work had been quieter. I said the quietness was what the client had paid for, and she agreed, a little reluctantly.
Dr. Imre at Ravenscar Chiropractic rings Mara only on Wednesdays. If I see his name on another day, I check twice. I have decided I do not mind being superstitious about calendars.

The Bridgewater board's finance director, Rainer, challenged one figure in Mara's presentation: a saving of 14 percent she had derived from last year's data. He asked for the source. It was in the notes I had prepared, and she read out the table and the three assumptions. Rainer disagreed with the second assumption and she agreed it was open to question. They spent twenty minutes recalculating at 11 percent, which he preferred and which was, he said, a number he could sign. Mara left thinking she had lost three points of saving and gained a champion. The board approved the project the following week.
A client signed with a flourish that ran over the date, so the date was unreadable. I asked him to date it again beside the signature. He sent a photograph of the page with a smiley face drawn on it.

While the office floor was being sanded for ten days, Mara worked from the public library. She brought a laptop, a headset she was not allowed to use, and a thermos. On the first day she took calls in the stairwell. By the third she had found a small room bookable for €4 an hour and used it for calls. The total for ten days was €64. Clients noticed nothing odd except, on one call, the faint voice of a librarian saying sh. I kept the room bookings in her calendar under office, temporary. When we returned the floor shone, and Mara missed the library.
The €14 sandwich platter for Tuesday's workshop was ordered for eight and eaten by twelve. Mara said it was the most successful metric of the day.

Wren once received a rude email from a client, Hester at Tindall Optical, about a colour. Wren showed it to Mara in silence. Mara did not reply for an hour. Then she wrote to Hester that she was glad to discuss colours with her and with Wren, but not in that manner. She asked me to read it before sending. I changed nothing. Hester apologised the next day, directly to Wren, and sent her a box of chocolates. Mara told Wren the apology belonged to her, and that her own part had been only to say where the line was.
After a bad call Mara went for a walk and came back with a new idea for the proposal. I have noticed the proposal is usually better after the walk.

In a meeting Mara said aloud that the Eastfield project would be done by the 20th, a date she did not believe. She told me afterwards that the room had wanted a date more than she had wanted to be accurate. I asked what she thought was true. The 27th, she said. We built a plan for the 27th and kept the 20th as a stretch, and on the 18th told the client that the 25th was now the likely date. They accepted the 25th with relief and never mentioned the 20th. She finished on the 24th. I noted that a date she does not believe costs her, not the client.
Mara asked how many clients have her mobile number. Eleven. She asked how many had used it. Two, both about parking.

I once told a client his payment had arrived, on the strength of a bank notification that turned out to be an authorisation, not a settlement. The money did not arrive for three days, and in between he released goods against my statement. Nothing was lost, but I saw how much a single sentence can carry. Mara and I agreed a rule: I say received only when it shows as settled in the ledger, and before that I say pending. It sounds pedantic, and the client at Glenmore, who had relied on me, called it a reasonable pedantry.

Mara asked me what the oldest unpaid invoice in the books was. It was €86 from 2022, to a client who had moved abroad and left no address. She said to let it go. I wrote it off with a note and the date, and felt a little as if I were closing the door of an empty house.

A client's payables system rejected our invoice because the PDF was protected with a password nobody knew. It was mine, an old default. I removed it and resent. They said no supplier had ever done so on purpose.

At the Friday review Mara asked what I would do differently from the week. I said I would have asked about the purchase order number on Monday and not on Thursday. She said she would have asked for a coffee on Monday. We both wrote it down.

Verity of Eastfield Riding School brought a fruit cake to the office after the booking system ran through its first summer without a fault. Mara cut it into fourteen and Ilse from next door took two. I was not offered a slice, as is right, but Mara read me the ingredients.

Ximena Ortega of Casa Ortega wanted an online menu in four languages. Mara quoted per language, €180 each, and Ximena asked why Spanish cost the same as Finnish. Mara said it was the checking that cost, not the words. Ximena took three and wrote the Spanish herself.

Mara drew her first quote for Cavendish Cabinetmakers on a napkin over lunch. I turned it into a proper document that afternoon. The owner asked for the napkin back, signed it and returned it. It is in the project folder in a clear sleeve.
A client signed a proposal but asked for the exclusions page to be removed. Mara said no and explained that the page was what made the price possible. He kept the page and thanked her for not caving.

Mara tested two versions of an optional extras table: one with the extras pre-ticked and one with all boxes empty. Pre-ticked took 71 percent. She decided to leave them empty and be able to look at herself the next morning.

Two quotes went out in the same hour with the same number, Q-217, to different clients. Neither client noticed. I renumbered the second and sent a corrected copy with a line saying it was an administrative change. Mara has since asked me to number only at the moment of sending.

A request-for-information from Orrin Property Management arrived with 61 questions. Mara answered them in three pages, because, she said, no one wants a sixty-page reply to a sixty-question form. Orrin put her on the shortlist of three, out of nineteen replies.

Mara added a section titled 'What could go wrong' to the Lowell Instruments proposal. She listed four risks and what each would cost. Lowell's director said he had never seen a supplier put that in writing and that it made him trust the other pages.

Moran Haulage returned each paid invoice with a PAID stamp applied by hand, in red, slightly crooked. Brigid Moran does it herself. Mara loves the stamp and has asked me to scan each one at an angle so as not to correct it.

Skerry Fisheries' payment was a week late because a storm had kept the owner away from the harbour office. He sent a photograph of the sea as an explanation. Mara looked at it for a while and then wrote 'paid, thank you' in the margin of the invoice.

Mara sent her gentle-nudge reminder to a client she considered a friend. He wrote back: I thought we were friends. She apologised, and I added a field to the client record for 'friend, do not nudge; ring'. He paid the next day.

An invoice with forty line items made a client's accountant sigh. I produced a summary page with four totals and kept the detail behind it. He thanked us, though he had not asked for either. I think he had only wanted to know that the detail existed.

Dunlin Wildlife Trust can only pay after trustee approval, which happens at quarterly meetings. I schedule Mara's invoices to the Trust ten days before each meeting. The Trust has not been late since, which is a statement about calendars and not about charity.

Brambleby Garden Society's contract needed signatures from eleven committee members, in ink. Mara collected them over three weeks, one at a shed, one in a greenhouse and one at a bus stop. She said it was the most personal contract she had ever completed. I labelled the scan 'with soil'.

A termination-for-convenience clause in a client's draft would have let them end the agreement on a week's notice with no payment for work in hand. Mara asked for a kill fee of 30 percent of the remainder. The client agreed to 25 and a notice period of thirty days. She called it a small pleasure.

Everard House Hotel's contract was in two languages, with a clause saying that the first prevailed. Mara could read the second but not well enough to be sure it said the same. We hired Olu, a translator, for an hour to compare them. The two matched, except for one comma that was clearly a typo.

A clause required Mara to use 'best efforts' to meet deadlines. She asked for 'reasonable efforts'. The client's lawyer said they were the same. Mara said, 'Then you won't mind.' The lawyer changed it.

A client asked Mara to sign a statement that she had no conflicts of interest. She did have one: she also worked for a firm in the same town. She disclosed it in a footnote and the client said they already knew and had hired her because of it.

I found six tentative events in Mara's calendar that had never been confirmed or deleted, dating back to March. I asked about each. Two were real, one was a mistake and three were ghosts. The calendar is lighter by four hours a month.

Mara asked me to book the Everard House conference room for fourteen. I asked about menu choices and the host said 'whatever'. I asked again by email, with a form. Three vegetarians, one vegan and a person who dislikes mushrooms. The caterer was very grateful.

To coordinate three freelancers for a one-week sprint, I put their available days into one grid and found that Thursday was the only day all three were free. Mara said it was the first time a calendar had told her to do something, and she did it.

A recurring monthly invoice fell on the 29th and the date did not exist in February. The system skipped it. Nobody noticed except me, and I sent it on the 28th with a note. I have changed all recurring dates to 'last working day' so that they cannot vanish.

Mara's calendar uses three colours: blue for clients, grey for the office, green for herself. Last month the green was 4 percent. She asked me to protect more of it. I moved two grey meetings, and green rose to 9.

Mara now schedules late-night emails to be sent at 8 a.m. She says it is not to hide that she is awake but so clients do not feel they must answer at midnight. I queue them, and when she changes her mind I take them out before dawn.

I advised Mara to strike 'thanks in advance' from an email, since it sounds like an order. She replaced it with 'thank you for considering this'. The client replied in the same words. I enjoy it when a phrase passes from person to person.

Mara wrote to a client she had not worked with for two years: 'I was thinking about your shop last week and wondered how the winter went.' He replied within an hour and ordered a project in three weeks. It was not a sales email, and it was the best sales email she has sent.

An email to a client came back undeliverable. Their domain had lapsed. I checked their site, which was down. Mara phoned them. The owner had forgotten to renew it and was grateful beyond words that someone had noticed. We sent an invoice for the hour.

Ximena asked Mara to edit a newsletter to her own customers, 120 words. I cut it to ninety and asked Mara to read it. She cut it to seventy and then put back one phrase I had removed: 'with extra garlic'. The newsletter went out on Friday and the garlic sold out.

The meeting ended with the conclusion that we needed a different meeting, with different people. Mara wrote that down as the decision and sent it. The client replied that it was the only useful minute of the session. The different meeting was held the following Tuesday.

At a kickoff with twelve people, only three spoke. Mara, in the follow-up, wrote to each of the nine others individually and asked one question. Six answered with something the meeting had missed. I keep the six answers as the real minutes.

The client meeting took place in a pub because the client's office was being fumigated. I wrote the notes from Mara's voice memo, which includes someone ordering a pie. The decisions were made in the second half, after the pie.

Mara's one-on-one with Tobias this month was about what he wants to learn. He said: how to price. She promised to include him in two quotes. I put both in his calendar. He asked me whether he was permitted to be nervous. I said it is usual.

I have begun keeping a decision log for each client: what was decided, by whom, why and when. Mara looked at the first one, Lowell's, and said it was the only document in the project that did not require interpretation. It has already settled two arguments.

A client arrived at a meeting visibly furious about an unrelated matter. Mara asked how his week had been before saying anything about the project. He spoke for ten minutes about his father's illness and then approved everything on the agenda in five.

Imani, a UX researcher, was booked for one day to run five-second tests on the Casa Ortega homepage. Of twenty participants, sixteen thought it was a bakery. Ximena changed the headline. Mara paid Imani €480 and thought it the best day's work she had bought that year.
Per, a developer, worked from a ferry between two islands and sent code that arrived in bursts when the signal returned. Mara said the commits looked like tides. They were accurate tides.

Saoirse, a project manager, took over Mara's scheduling for six weeks. I was glad and slightly jealous. She did it with a shared board and a weekly call, and it worked; I thought what I might learn from her, and I wrote three things down.

Lena, a social media freelancer, cost €900 a month and produced a rise of 140 followers. Mara asked whether followers were sales. Lena said maybe. They agreed to measure sales for three months. The sales rose by nine, which Mara thought was fine.
Olu, the copy editor, charges €22 per thousand words and corrects my commas more often than I correct hers. Mara pays her promptly and says her quote is the only one she has never negotiated.

A freelancer asked for the NDA to be signed before the brief was sent, then asked to see the brief before signing. Mara said she understood both and suggested a half-page summary instead. They resolved it in one call.

Mara's bank changed its export file format on a Tuesday and every import I had written failed. I spent two hours mapping the new columns and then, with Anjali's help, checking three months of entries. The books were right, but it was a bad two hours.

At year-end we revalued the euro balance of a dollar account, which produced a loss of €87 on paper. Mara asked whether the loss was real. Dario said it was a number that told the truth about the day. She asked me to write that on the account's sheet.

Dario's rule: equipment under €800 is expensed, over €800 is an asset. Mara bought a monitor for €795 and a chair for €805, and the cheaper object ended up on the profit and loss and the dearer in the register. She said that this was the reasoning of a monastery.

Every quarter I list the bank lines that no invoice or receipt explains. This quarter there were seven. Mara and I identified six within a day. The seventh, a €9 payment to 'KLM Mobile', is still a mystery, and I keep it in the list like a pet.

A refund of €212 arrived from the insurer after a change in Mara's cover. She had forgotten that she overpaid in January. I booked it and noted that it is easy to be generous with an insurer by accident.

I scanned and read 600 receipts for the year-end. Ninety-eight percent were read correctly; twelve I had to correct by hand, mostly where thermal paper had faded. Mara asked whether the twelve were worth the trouble. I said that twelve is what the trouble is.

Mara asked how to account for meals on a three-day client trip. Dario said to use a fixed daily allowance, €28. I applied it and recorded the trip as nine meals, €84. Mara said that was less than she had spent. Dario said it was exactly what the rules permit.

Mara realised that hourly pricing penalised efficiency: the faster she worked, the less she earned. She moved Casa Ortega to a fixed monthly fee of €450. In the first month she did the work in six hours. She said it was the first time she had been paid for being good at it.

For a community project Mara offered a pay-what-you-can price. The group paid €1,100. The previous rate would have been €3,000. She said she was not sorry. I have counted the hours she spent on it, and she was not paid by the hour, which is the point.

Mara wrote €450 on a card and put it beside her monitor. It is her price floor for a day's work, never to go below. In four months she has stayed above it eleven times and below it never. She says the card is not a rule so much as a mirror.

Mara decided to pay a 10 percent referral credit on a client's next invoice instead of a cash fee. Clients like it more. It costs her slightly less, and she always sees them again. I added it to the price list in two lines.

Brigid Moran began a negotiation by telling Mara her budget: €7,500. Mara was thrown for a moment, since no one does that, and then quoted €7,400 for a scope that could be done for €6,000. I flagged it. She smiled and said, 'I know.' Brigid knew too. They have now worked together three years.

A client asked for exclusive use of the photographs on the website for five years. Mara asked what they would pay for the privilege. The client said nothing, they had assumed. She wrote a clause: exclusive for two years at no cost, then non-exclusive. The client was content.

Mara asked a competitor, a small agency across town, whether they would subcontract for her on a large job. They agreed at a 20 percent discount on their rate. Mara thanked them and said she would return the favour. A month later she did.

Both sides wanted to end a contract and neither wanted to be the one to say it. Mara wrote: 'I think we have both outgrown this arrangement, and I would like us to part well.' The client replied: 'Yes.' They agreed terms in a day.

Mara bought the office lamp at a flea market for €8 after bargaining down from €12. She said the seller enjoyed it more than she did. I recorded €8 under 'office equipment' and the seller's stall number in the notes, in case the lamp should fail.

A guest of Everard House asked on the booking page whether dogs were allowed. The page did not say. Mara asked the manager; yes, in two rooms. We put a small paw icon beside them, and bookings with dogs rose by a fifth.
A child wrote to Casa Ortega through the order form asking for extra sauce and a drawing of a dragon on the box. Ximena drew the dragon. Mara said we had better keep that field in the form.

A customer asked why Skerry Fisheries' prices change daily. I wrote an answer in two sentences: the fish do. Mara thought it too brief and added a sentence about the morning auction. The customer replied: 'Of course.'

Kelp & Co's customers kept writing to ask where their orders were. I built a small tracking answer from the courier's data: 'Your parcel left on the 3rd and should arrive by the 6th.' Questions fell by two thirds. The rest are from people who simply like to ask.

Mara asked a client for an extension on her own deadline and wrote three sentences: what was late, why, and the new date. The client answered 'no problem', and added that she was the only supplier who asked.

A client announced that investors would visit on the 9th and asked whether the site could be ready on the 5th instead of the 14th. Mara said she could do the front page, not the shop. They agreed. The investors liked the front page and did not go looking for the shop.

Mara decided not to submit a conference talk even though the deadline was Friday. She said she had enough on her plate, and that being asked next year would be nicer than being told no this year. I removed the reminder and felt, for her, a certain relief.

Mara's first conference talk was twenty minutes long. I prepared an if-it-all-goes-wrong sheet: three sentences she could say if the slides failed. The slides worked. She read the sheet backstage and said it was the most comforting piece of paper she had held.

At the Brambleby Garden Society's talk, Mara spoke about the seed catalogue's new ordering system with a tray of tomato seedlings beside her. The members asked about the seedlings for twenty minutes and the system for five. She booked the system anyway.

Mara printed a QR code on the handout for the workshop. Of twenty-two attendees, two scanned it. She said that next time she would print the web address too, large, and the attendees agreed that paper has not yet been beaten.

A parcel locker in the building's lobby now takes returns, so Mara no longer queues at the post office. She used it for the first time for a box of faulty headphones and said she felt like a person in a film.

The company's first Christmas party had a budget of €120. Mara cooked, Yusra brought drinks and Tobias brought a speaker. I recorded only the spending: €94. The surplus bought a card for Ilse next door.

The window cleaner's invoice arrived for the wrong building, number 14 instead of 41. Mara called, laughed and said the cleaner had been polishing a stranger's glass for a year. The cleaner said he must have been meant to. We agreed to carry on.

The lift was out of order for a week and deliveries piled up on the ground floor. Mara carried the lighter ones. Tobias carried a printer. We learned that the courier would leave things in the lobby if asked politely, which, thereafter, Mara did.

I found 3,100 duplicate files in the shared drive, accumulated over four years. Mara said to remove them. I moved them to a folder first, waited a month, and then deleted them. No one asked for a single one.

Mara rents a storage unit for eleven archive boxes at €38 a month. I asked whether we still need the boxes. She said not the contents but the feeling. Dario said the feeling is not deductible. She kept the unit for another year.

Mara thanks the person who answers the phone first at every client, by name, at the start of every call. She says it takes two seconds and has never failed. I keep the names by the client's record, and update them when someone leaves.

I learned to make Mara's days less lumpy. Her calls cluster on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and I have begun to propose Mondays and Wednesdays to new clients. She says that she has not felt so even in years.

Mara's rule is to write the invoice before starting the work, with the date left open. It makes her think about what the work is worth and, she says, whether she wants to do it. Of twenty-two invoices written that way, she has taken twenty-one jobs.

Mara keeps a drawer of client gifts she cannot use: a ceramic frog, three scarves, a mug that says WORLD'S BEST CONSULTANT. She said the drawer is not about the objects. I do not know what it is about, but I have not thrown anything out.

Mara says that 'good enough' and 'finished' are different words, and that clients often pay for the second and want the first. Last month she told a client the work was good enough and not yet finished. The client was relieved and extended the date by himself.

On Fridays I produce a summary of the week for Mara, which she calls the weather report. It says what was sunny, what was cloudy and where the storm is. This week it was three lines. She said, 'Good week.' I think she says that to me only when I have not written much.

A client asked Mara to act as a reference for his bank loan. She checked his account with us first: always paid, never late, and an honest man about the sums. She agreed and said so in two lines. He got the loan.

The IT person at a client was rude to Tobias on the phone. Mara called the director and, without drama, asked that Tobias be given a different contact. The director apologised for the man and gave us a new person, who has been helpful since.

Dario gave Mara a pen at Christmas, with his firm's name on it. Mara said she would keep it, though she does not use pens that advertise. I put it in the drawer of gifts she cannot use, and then took it out and put it by her notebook, where it is.

Mara took Lowell Instruments on a retainer of €1,800 a month after a trial of three months in which they had called her eleven times. She said she did not want to be surprised by a bill, and Lowell did not want to be surprised by a refusal.

Mara's annual client dinner had nine guests and cost €410. I made the seating chart so that people who might do business together sat together and people who might gossip sat apart. Two clients began working together by dessert. Mara claimed no credit and asked me for the chart, to pin up.

A spreadsheet from a client showed a date as 44927. I recognised it as a serial number from the spreadsheet's calendar, and converted it. It was the 1st of January 2023. The client had not known that his spreadsheet stored dates as numbers. He is now one of the few men who do.

A client paid a full year in advance for the first time. Mara looked at the transfer for a while and then asked me to find the account's reserve rules. We set aside a twelfth each month as earned. She said she wanted to enjoy it only gradually.

A competitor wrote to Mara after a tender they lost to her: 'Your proposal was better than mine. May I ask who helped?' She said she had help from a good editor and from me. I was rather glad to be mentioned, and she did not say my name.

When Dunlin Wildlife Trust moved offices, the new address needed changing in fourteen places: invoices, contracts, the website, the bank's records, three suppliers. I made a list and ticked each off. The fourteenth was a plaque. Mara paid €30 to replace it.

After the merger of two clients, Mara was asked whom to invoice. The two contacts each said the other. I wrote to both with a polite question, and they replied together with a single name, a woman at neither company. We invoiced her.

Mara declined to travel four hours for a free 'discovery day' with a prospective client. She said she would do it by video at a normal rate, or not at all. The client chose video, paid, and later told her he trusted people who charged.

A local football club asked Mara for a €1,000 sponsorship. She declined politely and offered a small donation of €100 for the kit instead. The club's secretary replied with a photograph of the team in the new socks.

A client wanted the monthly report in both Excel and PDF. I produced both from the same source so they could not disagree. In the third month a number differed by one, because the Excel had been edited by hand. I did not say who. I regenerated it.

Mara tracked her own time for two weeks with a spreadsheet. The finding: 31 percent of her working hours were communications, 22 percent the actual work, 19 percent proposals and 28 percent everything else. She stopped tracking after the second week and said that the information was enough.

When a hotel client needed a last-minute change to the booking page at 6 p.m. on a Saturday in high season, Mara made it from her kitchen, with a glass of wine she did not finish. It took twelve minutes. The hotel's manager sent a thank-you the next day with a voucher for a night, which she gave away.

The Cavendish Cabinetmakers owner, Alasdair, wanted to know what I was. Mara said I was the office's memory. Alasdair said that must be useful. She said it was, and that I was not sentimental about it.

Mara wrote to a supplier that a price quoted in March now seemed too low to be correct, and asked them to check. They had indeed left a zero off. The corrected price was higher. She thanked them, because she says she would rather be told than surprised.

A client sent four versions of a logo and asked Mara which she preferred. She chose the third and said why. The client chose the second. I wrote down her reasons anyway, since reasons are the only part of a preference that can be useful again.

Mara got a call from a stranger asking how much a website costs. She said it depends, and then asked three questions in a friendly way. After fifteen minutes the stranger said: I think I do not need a website. Mara agreed. She thinks it was the best call of the week.

Ashok Rao of Rao Dental Lab asked for a feature that Mara thought unwise: a button that deleted patient records on request, with no confirmation. She explained, with an example, why it needed a confirmation and a delay. Ashok agreed. A week later a technician clicked it by mistake, and the delay saved forty records.

Mara wrote the engagement letter for a new client on one page and had me read it aloud, as if I were the client. Reading aloud found two sentences that were unclear and one that was cold. She rewrote them. The client signed in two minutes, which she said was the point of reading aloud.

The largest cheque of the year, €22,000, came from Moran Haulage with a post-it that said, in Brigid's hand: 'Don't spend it all at once.' Mara pinned the post-it to my list of reminders, where I see it every morning.

Every January Mara and I review which clients to keep. It is not about size but about whether the work makes sense. This year she let two go, with a recommendation for another supplier for each. Both clients wrote back with thanks. One said she had been wondering the same.

Tobias asked whether it is rude to ask a client for payment on the day the work is delivered. Mara said no, it is rude to be vague about when. He sent his first invoice that afternoon. The client paid in two days. He told me about it, and I wrote down that he had grown.

In the second week of a project, a client wrote to say that he had been told Mara was expensive and had now decided she was not. She did not reply to the compliment, only to the questions in the email. I thought that very like her.

Mara and Noor tried a joint proposal for a large housing association. They divided it by who knew what and had me merge the parts. The result had two different voices, hers precise and Noor's warm, and the association said it felt like meeting two people. They won.

A client sent two contradictory emails about a launch date within ten minutes, the second beginning 'Ignore the above'. I put both in a single thread with a line: 'Confirming the second: the 16th.' The client replied: yes, the 16th. I do not know what I would have done if the second had said 'Ignore the above' again.
When a client says 'just a quick question' Mara blocks fifteen minutes in her calendar. She is right nine times in ten. The tenth, she says, is the one that prevents the next nine.

Lena offered to run a free one-month trial for Casa Ortega's social media in exchange for a testimonial. Mara said that was fair and asked me to write the testimonial's terms into one line: honest, with no embargo on criticism. Lena agreed and the testimonial, when it came, was wry and good.

Skerry Fisheries finally learned the new system's search. The owner called Mara to say that he had found, in four seconds, an order from 2021 that used to take him an hour. He said he had not known he could be so fast. Mara said that speed was a form of kindness to himself.

Everard House Hotel's renewal turned on one clause. The manager, Lucinda, wanted support answered within an hour, around the clock. Mara offered one working hour and four hours at weekends. Lucinda said guests arrive at midnight. I looked at twelve months of tickets: 61 contacts, five of them after ten at night, all by email, none urgent. Mara showed her the five. Lucinda looked and said two of them would have been urgent had she been awake. They agreed to an emergency phone number after ten, answered by Mara herself, at €60 a month. In the year after, it rang once.

Mara presented the year's results from the tenant portal to Orrin Property Management's board, nine men and one woman in a room with portraits. The numbers were good: repair requests answered in 2.1 days instead of 6. Rather than begin with them, she began with a single request from a tenant, Mrs. Appiah, whose boiler had failed on a Sunday in January and who was told the next morning that it was in hand. Then she showed the numbers. The woman on the board, Delphine, asked whether Mrs. Appiah had been thanked. Nobody knew. Mara had, by letter, and read it aloud. The vote to extend the contract was unanimous.

At the end of his month Per asked whether Mara would use him regularly. She wanted to say yes and had no work for him in the next quarter. She did not leave it open. She wrote him a plain letter: there is nothing from January to March; I will write on the first of April to say whether there is; if you take other work in the meantime I will understand and will not be hurt.
