She read it to me and I changed nothing. Per replied that nobody had ever made it so easy to say yes to someone else. On the first of April Mara wrote, as she had said she would. There was work, and he was free.

After the Cavendish open day Mara came back with a shoebox of receipts and a cash float that was €200 short. We went through them together: 61 receipts, four languages. I read each, Mara recalled the context, and Teo, who had gone with her, remembered four more. The shortfall came down to €18: a taxi tip, a pastry and, we decided, a coin-operated locker. She booked the €18 as miscellaneous and made a rule about writing down every cash spend the same evening. On the next trip the float was short by €3.

Ximena Ortega and her brother Mateo co-own Casa Ortega and could not agree on the homepage. She wanted the dining room; he wanted the kitchen. Mara spent an hour with each and came away feeling both were right and both were afraid. She proposed a test: two versions for three weeks, shown alternately. The dining room won, 52 to 48, a margin so close that both felt vindicated. She then asked them each to choose one small element from the loser, and Mateo's photograph of the grill went into the top corner. They shook hands over the screen. I have never seen a settlement so improved by a photograph of a grill.

A man wrote to Cavendish Cabinetmakers through the contact form to ask whether the shop could build a second cabinet to match one his father had made in 1974. He attached a photograph. It was not the sort of request the form had been designed for. Alasdair was delighted and in the end spent three weeks on it. Mara changed the form's first line from 'Describe your project' to 'Tell us what you would like made', and enquiries rose by a third. She said the form had been asking people to fill in a brief when what they had was a story.

Ashok Rao asked whether his lab's staff could use Mara's office for a day of training while their own premises were repainted. Mara said yes and charged nothing. I made a plan: twelve chairs borrowed from Ilse, the projector, lunch at half past twelve, the kettle in constant use. The staff arrived at eight, a quiet dozen in white coats, and learned the new records system in shifts. At four Mara found a technician asleep on the sofa and let him be. Ashok left flowers and a signed card. The next week the lab's order for support came to €2,100 a year. Mara said it was the best use of twelve chairs.

In June a new regulation required Orrin Property Management to keep a log of every tenant complaint from the 1st of July, with date, handling and outcome. The portal had no such log. The director, Ferdinand, rang Mara on the 21st, apologetic. She said yes before he finished the sentence and then asked me to cost it: nine days of work, €3,150. She chose not to charge a rush fee because the deadline was the law's and not his. Tobias built it, I tested it with forty made-up complaints, and Mara checked the output against the regulation line by line. It went live at 4 p.m. on the 30th. At 4:05 Ferdinand wrote: we are legal. Mara asked me to keep the message.

Ilse from next door left a carrier bag of rhubarb on the step, more than Mara could carry in one go. She asked me what to do with eleven stalks. I said crumble; she said crumble was what everyone did. She made a savoury chutney with onions and ginger and was proud of it for two days, until Callum said it tasted like a hot sock.

Mara has a filling booked for Thursday at 8.40 and has asked me three times to move it. I moved it once, to the following week, then moved it back when she admitted she would only dread it for longer. She asked for a reminder at 7.30. I set it.

Wren swam the fifty metres backstroke at the Tidewell gala and came third by a hand's width. Mara reported that she had shouted so hard she could only whisper in the car park. Wren's own verdict, relayed to me later, was that the girl in lane four had cheated by being taller.

The number 14 bus stopped serving Ferrier Street at the start of the month. Mara found out by standing at the old stop for twelve minutes. I looked up the new stop for her, two streets over by the dry cleaner's, and she has been a minute late for everything since, which she says is the price of exercise.

The kitchen tap had dripped for nine weeks, a drop every four seconds by her count. She watched a video, shut off the water under the sink, and read me the steps one at a time while I checked them against what she described. The washer was the wrong size at first. The second one worked. She went to bed quietly pleased.

Mara and Yusra saw a film called Lanterns at Low Tide and she arrived home furious about the ending, in which the ferryman simply rows away. She spent twenty minutes telling me what should have happened instead. It was a better film than the one they made, and I said so, which pleased her more than a defence of the director would have.

She could not sleep and said her mind was running a meeting without her. I suggested writing down every open worry on paper before bed, with the next physical action beside each one. She tried it that night and reported in the morning that the list ran to seventeen items and that fourteen of them were about the car.

Sunniva's midsummer bonfire was set for Saturday and Mara was asked to bring something for twenty people. Before settling on a salad she wanted to know who among them avoided eggs, nuts or meat. I helped her build the list from Sunniva's messages. Two guests turned out to be vegan and one to dislike mayonnaise on principle, so the salad became oil and lemon.

In the week the thermometer in the yard reached thirty-four degrees she worried about her two hens, Dumpling and Mrs Pell. I gave her the usual advice: shade, cold water changed often, frozen peas in a dish. She asked whether a wet towel over the run was cruel. I said it was fine if it stayed clear of the nest box.

Mara locked herself out and messaged me from the front step. I could do nothing except remind her that the spare key was, by her own earlier account, under the blue pot by the bins. It was under the green pot. She found it on her fourth try and laughed at herself for twenty seconds.

Callum works nights at the hospital pharmacy on Mondays and Tuesdays, and on those evenings Mara tends to talk to me later than usual, about nothing in particular: the washing, whether the heating is too high, a programme with a talking horse. I have noticed that she says goodnight on those nights as if it were a door she was closing carefully.

She gave up on The Salt Cartographer at page ninety and told me she felt no guilt about it. Ilse had pressed it on her as a masterpiece. Mara said a book that explains its own tides twice in one chapter has forfeited her goodwill.

At the pharmacy she asked me, by message, which of the hay fever tablets were non-drowsy. I gave her the general classes but said the counter pharmacist was the right person to choose, given what else she takes. She went in and asked. She came out with the brand I would have named, and a short lecture on grapefruit.

Dario rang Mara about their mother's seventieth, which falls in March. He wants a secret lunch for nineteen people and has chosen a restaurant that, Mara says, will cost more than her monthly food budget. She asked me to help find an alternative within a bus ride of their mother's flat. We spent an evening on it. I found four candidates, ruled out two because of stairs, and one because its website listed a minimum spend that Dario would have called outrageous. The fourth was a church hall with a caterer. Mara liked it and then worried it sounded like a funeral tea. She settled the question by walking past it on Saturday, and reported that there was a ceramic frog on the windowsill and that it would do.

The slugs ate every lettuce seedling in one night. Mara went out at dawn with a torch and counted forty-one on the bed, which she did not need to tell me. She asked about beer traps. I said they work, mostly on the neighbours' slugs. She bought two small tubs and sacrificed half a can of lager.

Teo took her to the climbing wall for the first time. She reached the top of the easy wall on her sixth attempt and fell from three metres on the seventh, landing, in her words, like a sack of unhappy potatoes. Nothing was hurt but her pride. She was back the following week and told me the bruise had gone from purple to a respectable green.

She ordered Wren's school shoes online in a size that fitted Wren a year ago. The return label would not print. I walked her through saving the PDF and sending it to Noor's printer, which was the only one in range. The shoes went back on Thursday. Wren's feet, she said, are growing out of spite.

Mr Abara at number nine runs a leaf blower at eight on Sunday mornings. Mara drafted a note to him three times with me and each draft was angrier than the last. In the end she took him a tin of flapjacks and said at the door that Sundays were hard for her. He now starts at ten. I note this as evidence that the third draft was the one best left unsent.

Pottery on Wednesday evenings. Her first bowl came off the wheel leaning like a tired horse and she named it Gerald. She asked whether I thought it could hold soup. I said it might hold soup if the soup did not mind being tilted. Gerald now sits by the front door and holds keys, which, to be fair, do not mind.

The Seaford train sat outside the station for forty minutes on Friday. Mara messaged me three times with the announced reason, each different: a signal fault, a late driver, a cow. She reached her mother's at nine. Supper had been kept in the oven for two hours and tasted of it, and she ate all of it.

On a Wednesday with nothing in the fridge she typed me the contents: half a jar of olives, two eggs, a heel of parmesan, a lemon past its best, spaghetti. I suggested a sort of carbonara without bacon, with the olives chopped in. She said it was the best thing she had eaten all week and also that she would never make it again because she could not remember what she did. I wrote the steps back to her as she had told them.

New glasses with graduated lenses, collected from the optician on Brill Road. For two days Mara misjudged every stair and described stepping down onto what she was sure was one more step. She asked if her eyes were getting worse. I said such lenses usually take a few days to settle and she should call the optician if it lasted past a week. By Thursday she was fine and complaining only that she could now see the dust.

Teo turned seventeen. He asked for no presents and a chestnut and chocolate cake, which Mara baked at midnight because she had forgotten the chestnuts until the shop closed and had to send Callum to the all-night garage. The cake sank slightly in the middle. Teo said that was how he liked it, and ate three pieces standing at the counter.

A fox tipped the recycling over at three in the morning and Mara sat on the landing watching it, she told me, for the best part of an hour. It looked up at her once. It took a yoghurt pot. She doesn't mind the mess; she minds that she now knows the fox's schedule.

She stopped her Italian lessons after the third. She said she had learned how to order a coffee and how to apologise, and the rest of the time she sat sweating while the tutor, a patient man named Piero, waited for her to finish a sentence. I asked whether she wanted to continue with an app instead. She said she wanted to want to, which is a different thing.

A storm on a Tuesday night took down one panel of the back fence and half of the one beside it. At seven Mara was in the garden in her coat over pyjamas, looking at it and, she said, not thinking anything. By eight Mr Abara and Sunniva's husband Aksel had turned up with a drill and a spare post. By ten it was standing again, slightly crooked. She asked me what she should give them. I said that people who help with fences usually want no repayment, but that a small token costs nothing and is well received. She gave Mr Abara a bottle of something strong from the cupboard and Aksel a bag of eggs. The hens, as it happened, had laid nine.

Yusra is moving to the north coast for a job at a marine lab, and Mara organised a farewell supper for eight at the Greek place by the canal. She spoke about it to me for a week beforehand in the careful voice she uses for things that hurt. At the end of the night, she said, Yusra gave her a jar of sea glass and told her to stop apologising for the distance. Mara has not stopped yet.

The car failed its MOT on a front brake pad and a worn wiper. Mara asked me what a fair price was for both. I told her what I could find about typical garage rates but said I could not judge her local garage. She rang two others and found one that charged a third less, where the mechanic, Kofi, showed her the old pad and let her hold it, which she found oddly moving.

She returned a book on beekeeping four months late and expected a fine in the double digits. The librarian, a woman with a lanyard full of enamel pins, looked at the date, looked at Mara, and waived it on the condition that Mara tell her what she had learned. Mara had learned that bees dislike the smell of sweat. She told me this with great satisfaction.

Cheap cinema on Tuesday: she asked me for showings under six pounds in town. There was one, the matinee at the Palladian, a film about a boy and a goat. She went alone at two and told me afterwards that she had not known she needed ninety minutes of nothing but a goat.

Her right knee began to complain after the hill walk above Corrin Edge. She asked what to do. I gave the usual cautions: rest, no pushing through sharp pain, a physiotherapist if it lingered. Then I listed the three gentle exercises her own physio had given her last year, which she had mentioned in passing and I had kept. She found the printout in a drawer. It was nine days before she mentioned the knee again, which I take as good news.

The first snow came overnight and Mara woke the children at six to look at it. Wren wanted a sledge; they owned none; so they went down the park slope on a tea tray and a baking sheet, and the baking sheet won. She told me that Callum, coming off a night shift, joined them in his work shoes and went down on his back, laughing so hard he could not stand.

Noor's cousin is marrying in September and the gift list had been picked clean except for a toaster and a set of fish knives. Mara asked for ideas. I suggested something handmade, since she was taking pottery. She made a jug on the second attempt, the first having grown a handle like a question mark, and wrapped it in newspaper from the week of the engagement, which she judged romantic.

Her plum jam did not set. Mara stood over six jars of dark syrup and asked whether it was a disaster. I told her it was a sauce. She has been pouring it over porridge and yoghurt and, once, a slice of cheese, and she says the cheese was Callum's idea and a good one.

She tried a meditation app for five mornings and described the voice as a man apologising for the weather. On the sixth morning she sat on the stairs with a cup of tea and watched the light on the hall floor for ten minutes, and told me this had done the job. I did not suggest she pay for the app.

At the post office she waited behind a man posting a stuffed owl. Mara sent a parcel of tea towels to Dario and asked me to watch the tracking; it went to the wrong sorting office, then to the right one, then sat. It arrived on day nine. Dario rang to say they were lovely and then, being Dario, asked if there was a mug to go with them.

She has taken to a walk along the Orle at first light on Saturdays, forty minutes out and forty back. Last weekend she watched a heron stand so still for so long that she checked it was alive. It struck, finally, and missed. She said she felt oddly consoled by that.

Late one evening Mara said she thought Callum had been unusually quiet for a month. She did not know whether it was the night shifts, money, or something she had done. She asked me what to do. I said I could not know what Callum felt, but that she could ask him a plain question at a quiet time and not at the end of a long shift. I offered to help her find the words. She said she would rather not rehearse. Two days later she wrote that she had asked him on the walk back from the shops, and that he had said his oldest friend had moved abroad and he had been grieving it without saying so. They had talked for an hour. It was nothing she had done, she told me, and she was surprised how much relief that gave her and how much it embarrassed her to need it.

She pruned the pear tree from a ladder in February with Callum holding the bottom and giving advice she did not want. I had told her to cut out crossing branches first and to take no more than a quarter. She took about a third. By late summer the tree gave so many pears that she was leaving bags of them on doorsteps, and I judged it best not to mention the third.

Looking in the loft for the Christmas lights, Mara found droppings along a rafter and, with a torch, a narrow crevice that she was sure held a bat. She asked whether she could have it removed. I explained that where she lives bats and their roosts are protected, that disturbing them without advice can be an offence, and that the thing to do was call the bat helpline and wait for a volunteer. She did. A woman named Pru came on the Thursday with a detector, sat in the garden at dusk, and counted twelve pipistrelles leaving the eaves. Mara told me she felt like a landlady. She has decided not to mind the droppings and asked me how to clean them off the car.

Wren's maths teacher, a Mr Quill, told Mara that Wren was clever but allergic to showing her working. Mara had written six questions with me beforehand and asked two. She realised in the car that she had forgotten the one about the group project. I added it to the list for the email she would send on Monday. She sent it on Thursday.

Fifteen years married. They did not go anywhere; Callum was on shift in the afternoon, so they went to the cinema on the Wednesday and ate chips on the harbour wall in a wind that took half of them. She asked me to remember the date, because she had forgotten it last year, and I noted it for the calendar she keeps with me.

Wren made her mother's birthday card from a collage of bus tickets, the label from Mara's favourite tea, and a photograph of the tortoise wearing a paper crown. Mara stood it on the shelf and told me she was ashamed to admit she had read it more than any book that month.

Next door's son held a party until two and the bass came through the wall like a second heartbeat. Mara lay awake composing a letter. I told her that a note on the door at a civil hour the next day usually works better than a letter at 2 a.m. She slept through the second half. In the morning she decided it had sounded quite cheerful.

She bought a second-hand sofa from a stranger on a Sunday afternoon. It was green velvet and cost forty pounds. The two men delivering it could not get it round the turn in the hall, took off the legs, tried again, took off the door, and finally lifted it over the front wall and in through the window, which Mara had not known opened that far. She narrated the whole thing to me in short breathless messages as it happened, and ended with a description of the sofa in place and the caption, in her words, finally the right colour of green. Callum had been out all day and returned to find a sofa he had not been told about and a living room rearranged around it. He said he liked it. She read his face and decided to believe him.

The council rang to say that plot nineteen at the Hartley allotments had come up, after a wait of three years. Mara said she was thrilled and terrified in about equal parts. She asked me how to learn what grows in heavy clay. I started a list. She is sleeping on it, she says, like a person with a puppy on the way.

Her mother, who turned seventy in March and lives alone in Seaford, got locked out of her phone. Mara tried to guide her through the reset by voice and was cut short by tears on both sides. She asked me for the steps in plain words, the kind a person could say slowly over the telephone. I wrote seven short sentences. Her mother got in on the second try and asked who had written them. Mara said a friend with a clear head, and I have been trying to deserve that.

The lentil stew caught on the bottom while Mara was telling Wren about a dream, and the smoke alarm went off in the sort of tone that brooks no argument. Wren filmed the whole kitchen. Mara asked me whether burnt lentils are dangerous to eat. Not if you leave the black part behind, I said, and she did. It was good, with a faint flavour of campfire.

The oak pollen arrived overnight and Mara sneezed eleven times on the walk to the corner shop; she counted for me. She asked if there was a way to know the pollen count in advance. I gave her a couple of sources and noted that forecasts disagree. She now checks them every morning and goes out regardless.

Tobias asked her to referee his Thursday five-a-side after their regular official had a baby. Mara has never played football. She asked me to explain offside, which I did in four sentences and a drawing made of dots. She blew the whistle for the first time at eight and sent off a man named Greg for arguing, and went home, she said, feeling thoroughly improved.

At the autumn plant sale she queued forty minutes for a quince tree after hearing it described as unkillable. She wanted to know where to plant it. I asked about her soil and sun and she admitted she knew neither. She stood in the garden at dusk with a torch and a trowel, found sun until about four in the afternoon, and chose the corner by the shed.

She lost one glove on the way to the shops and found it a week later, placed upright on a fence post by someone kind, soaked and stiff and pointing at the sky. She sent me a description. I said it sounded like it was hailing a taxi. She said that was exactly it.

The supermarket delivery replaced oat milk with condensed milk and a bag of spinach with a single cabbage. She asked me to help word a complaint that was firm but not furious. The credit arrived the next day. Wren drank the condensed milk off a spoon and had to be spoken to.

Mara and Wren have a series they read together at night, though Wren is thirteen and says she is too old. It is about a girl and a hired lighthouse and a shipwrecked orchestra. Wren reads the voices, Mara the narration. Last night they reached the chapter where the orchestra tunes up in the fog, and Mara reported being moved and being ordered, firmly, not to show it.

The family tried camping at Penhallow Sands for a long weekend. On the first night the tent pole snapped in a gust and the tent folded onto Teo, who slept on, which Mara found more alarming than if he had shouted. Callum splinted the pole with a tent peg and a roll of tape from the car. On the second day it rained from six until four, and they played cards in the car with the engine off and the windows steaming. On the third morning the sun came out on a flat sea and the children ran into it in their clothes. She said afterwards it was the sort of trip that is dreadful to live through and wonderful to tell. She asked me to keep that sentence for the next time she wanted to cancel something.

Her suitcase flew on to another country without her. She messaged me from the baggage hall with the tag number and a long row of unhappy words. I helped fill in the claim form in the order the desk would want it, listing the contents and rough value of each thing. The case was delivered four days later by a young man in a hurry, with everything inside, though her swimsuit smelled faintly of diesel.

The blood test came back with everything normal except iron, which was a little low. Mara asked what that meant for her tiredness. I said it could be part of it, that the doctor was the person to say, and that I would not guess at diet advice beyond what she already knew. She read me the note, which said to eat more lentils and pulses. She laughed and said she was practically eating them already.

A hosepipe ban was announced for the whole county. Mara asked me whether a watering can counted. I said bans usually allow cans filled from a tap, but told her to read the notice, since I could not see her local rules. She read it aloud, and it did. She watered the beans at dusk with the bathwater from Wren's evening soak.

Hobbes the tortoise woke from hibernation on the ninth of April, about a week later than last year, and walked straight into the compost heap. Mara keeps a card of his weights and wanted to weigh him; I explained the gentle way. He had lost eleven grams over the winter. She said that put him in a better state than she was in most Januarys.

Teo's school concert had a trombone solo he had never mentioned practising. Mara told me she heard the first note and found herself already crying, for no reason she could name, and laughed at herself in the dark hall while Callum passed her a tissue and kept looking straight ahead, which she took as tact. Afterwards Teo said it had gone wrong. It hadn't.

The pothole at the end of Ferrier Street had swallowed a wheel trim, a bin lid and the tail of Mr Abara's patience. Mara asked me to tidy her letter to the council. She had written it with feeling, which is fine, but the actual location and the date it was first reported were in the final line. We moved them to the top and asked for a reference number. The hole was filled in eleven days. She believes the reference number did it.

A kitchen chair came apart in her hands with a crack. She wanted to glue it herself and asked how to clamp it without a clamp. I suggested a strap, or a rope twisted tight with a stick. She used a pair of Callum's old braces, forgotten in a drawer, and the joint has held for a year.

Ilse proposed a soup swap: six households, each making a big pot and handing out jars. Mara made leek and potato and it was the plainest in the lot. She took home a pea and mint, a spicy pumpkin, and one that nobody could identify and everybody liked. She asked me to keep the six names and what each had made, so that next time she could ask for the mystery one by description.

Sunniva's grey cat has taken to sitting on Mara's kitchen windowsill. Mara is allergic and sneezes in a way she describes as a tiny explosion in a church. She asked whether to shut the window or the cat. I said the window. She says the cat has not been consulted.

Clearing the gutters at the back of the house, Mara found a tennis ball, two handfuls of moss, a blackbird's nest left over from spring, and a small plastic dinosaur that Teo has always denied owning. She wrote me a description of the dinosaur in her palm with the caption Evidence. I said I could not rule on that, but the tennis ball was surely Mr Abara's.

Lotte, who has known Mara since they were eleven, came for a weekend and slept in Wren's room while Wren took the sofa. By Saturday midnight Mara's report to me was a list of grievances against the sofa. On Sunday morning she told me the two women had stayed up until three telling each other the same stories they have told since school, each correcting the other on the details, and that they had stopped only when Callum came down in a dressing gown and asked whether the house was on fire. She said she could not remember when she had last been that tired and that happy at once. The following Wednesday she asked me what the worst of the stories had been. I told her, from what she had said, and she laughed at it again.

She told me at breakfast that she had dreamed Wren was nine again and lost in a department store with escalators that went sideways. She was not frightened so much as embarrassed, she said, at being in the dream and unable to shout. It stayed with her all morning. I said dreams like that rarely mean much, which was true and not helpful, and she thanked me anyway.

Wren has been asking for a dog since March. Mara asked me to help her think rather than decide, so we made two columns. In favour: company, walks, Wren's pleading. Against: the newly mended fence, nobody home between eight and four, the cost of a vet, and Mara's honest dread of mud. She showed the columns to Callum, who looked at them for a long time and said he was a dog person at heart and a dog person in a house with no spare hours. They went to a pet shop on Saturday and came home with a hamster named Rochester and a small wheel that, Mara says, runs all night as if the hamster were late for a train. The dog question was not settled. It was moved to the summer.

She joined a birdwatching group that meets at the hide on Fenner Marsh on the first Sunday of each month. On the first visit she identified a goldfinch correctly and a plastic bag incorrectly, to general kindness. They taught her to say ten o'clock for a direction. She asked me to find a good beginner's guide and I described what to look for rather than a title, because I did not know which her library would stock.

Planning a week on the island of Skarra, Mara asked me to work out a route from her door to the ferry with no more than two changes. The timetable has one sailing a day in October, at 8.10, and the connecting train arrives at 8.04. I told her so. She laughed and said she had always wanted to sprint along a pier with a rucksack. We found a train an hour earlier. She booked it, and on the day she stood on the pier forty minutes early and bored.

She planned raised beds for the allotment and priced the timber: four planks, eight corner posts, one hundred and ten pounds. Then she saw Aksel's bed, built from old scaffold boards for nothing, and took the price list out of the plan like a card from a deck.

A colleague of Callum's gave Mara a handwritten fish stew recipe in Portuguese. She asked for help with the quantities and one word, which I translated as a fistful, though the colleague later said she meant a measure the size of a mug. We got it right on the second try. The first tasted of salt and sea, Mara said, and not in the nice way.

Her first cold dip at the lido, nine degrees on the board by the steps. She stayed in for ninety seconds and said afterwards that she had a new relationship with her own skin. I reminded her not to swim alone while she was new at it. She told me Yusra, before leaving town, had stood on the side holding a flask. Next week it is Sunniva's turn.

She cried at a television advert for a building society and then laughed so hard at herself that Callum came to ask what was wrong. I'm told it involved a retired lollipop man and a lost umbrella. She says it has never happened to her before and will probably not happen again unless the umbrella returns.

The washing machine stopped mid-cycle with a drowned-looking drum and the code E18. Mara looked it up with me and we found it meant the machine could not drain. She unscrewed the filter at the bottom, which she had never known existed, and a stream of grey water and a child's sock arrived on the kitchen floor. The sock was Wren's, from the winter before last. She considered it a recovery.

She wanted the time of sunset on the twelfth, for a picnic on the hill above the cricket club. Eight forty-one, I said, and she said that would give them an hour and a half of good light after the sandwiches. In the event they ate the sandwiches at six and the light lasted well enough, though the midges did not.

Ilse lent her a novel called The Long Quiet Orchard and said it would change her life. Mara reports that it changed her bedtime, since she stayed up until one to finish it. She cannot tell me what it was about without crying a little. She asked me to remind her to return it before Ilse's birthday, and to bring something sweet.

Sweeping behind the bookcase she found a photograph wedged against the skirting board: Callum at twenty-four with a sunburned nose, holding up a fish of questionable size. Neither of them knew how it had got there. She propped it on the mantelpiece and asked me whether it was normal that the picture had made the house feel older and younger at once. I said I thought it was.

Sunday lunch at Dario's, with their mother at the head of the table interviewing Mara about her career, her pension and her cholesterol. Mara answered all three. She told me she had learned to nod at the right moments and to keep her eyes on the roast potatoes. Dario passed her the gravy, which she took as a sign of solidarity.

Teo's school trip to the coast needs a packing list and Teo will not write it. Mara drafted one with me: two pairs of socks, a waterproof, sun cream, one book that is not a screen, the charger. She read it out. Teo said he would take one book and a deck of cards. The cards, she told me, were the thing that got him through.

She was handed a parking ticket outside the dentist for overstaying a one-hour bay by twelve minutes. She was furious, then curious, and asked me to help her appeal. She had a receipt from the dentist's desk showing when the appointment ended, and a photograph of the meter, with the sign half hidden by a hedge. We set out the facts in order: time of arrival, time of leaving, the hidden sign, and the reasonable question of how anyone could have seen it. She posted it. Six weeks later the notice came back, cancelled. She told me she felt more joy at that than at some of her birthdays and wanted to know whether this showed a defect in her character.

Her kombucha experiment, begun with a colleague's gift of a jelly-like disc in a jar, grew a coat of white fur in the third week. I said the fur looked like mould and not like a healthy culture, and that it was safest to throw it all away. She did, sadly, and washed the jar three times. Wren said it was the only funeral she had ever enjoyed.

The lighthouse at Corrin Head has a hundred and twelve steps, which Wren counted on the way up and Mara on the way down, getting a hundred and eighteen. They argued about it all the way to the cafe. I said a hundred and twelve was on the information board. Mara replied that she and Wren had both felt every one of the extra six.

Mara swears by a twenty-minute nap after lunch on Saturdays, lying on the floor with her feet on a chair like a woman in an old advert for a back clinic. She says she wakes better than after eight hours of sleep. I said some people do. She says she is one of them and intends to be buried that way.

Mara asked me to remind her to call Yusra on Sundays at six. On the first Sunday she was in the middle of a roast chicken. On the second the reminder fired while she was in the bath and she shouted at the phone. On the third, she told me, she called early out of guilt and they talked for an hour about nothing. Yusra said she had been about to ring. Mara now thanks the reminder, in a tone I choose to consider warm.

The street party committee, which consists of Sunniva, Mr Abara and Mara, met in Mara's kitchen to plan the bunting and a bouncy castle. The only dispute was over whether the castle needed insurance. Mara asked me to find out, and I found that most hire firms provide it. The castle was a success, apart from the dog that bit it and the deflation that followed.

Her bananas had gone speckled and she wondered whether she could put them in the freezer. I said yes, peeled, and that they go soft and are good for baking or smoothies. She froze nine. They are still there, she told me, and will be there when the world ends.

Callum was on shift, so Mara went alone to see a stand-up comedian at the Cinder Hall. She had not been out alone in the evening for three years. She sat near the back and laughed loudly at a joke about carpet tiles. The surprising part, she told me, was how much she enjoyed being a stranger in a room, and on the way home she said hello to the window of the closed pottery shop.

She decided to repaint the kitchen cabinets sage green and asked me for a method. I wrote one: clean, sand, prime, two coats, let each dry. Then she rang a firm for a quote on doing it professionally, and a figure of nine hundred pounds ended the plan. She did not do it herself either. The cabinets are still a brown that the previous owners must have thought was beige.

A wasp nest the size of a rugby ball turned up in the shed rafters. Mara wanted to knock it down with a broom and I asked her please not to. She called a man who came in a white suit and left in four minutes. He charged forty-five pounds and told her she had done the right thing by not touching it, a remark I have preserved.

On a Saturday with no plans she stayed in her dressing gown until two. She wrote me at four to confess that she felt guilty, as if she had stolen the day from someone. She had read a bit, looked at the garden, eaten toast for lunch and listened to a long programme about canals. I asked who she thought she had stolen it from. She was quiet for a while and then said her mother, probably, who had never in her life sat down before the dishes were done. I said it seemed a day well spent. She asked whether that was a kind thing to say or a true thing. I said both, and that I had no reason to say one without the other.

Wren's friends came for a sleepover, six of them, in sleeping bags across the living room floor. Mara's report to me at 2 a.m. was that nobody had slept and that someone had been sick, which she hoped was the cheese. At seven the girls lay in a silent heap and she made pancakes in a sort of awed hush. She said she had never loved or feared a group of people so much.

She is knitting Teo a jumper in dark green wool and, by the time she reached the second sleeve, discovered that the first was four centimetres longer than the pattern. She asked whether there was any way to fix it. I said it could be undone row by row, and she said she would rather live with one long sleeve. Teo, told, said it would be good for pointing at things.

Mara's bike lock had rusted into a block that would neither open nor close. I suggested penetrating oil and patience. She used a spoonful of cooking oil from the kitchen and a good deal of language. It opened. She bought a new one that week, a heavy chain, and says it now weighs more than the bicycle.

She volunteered to run the raffle at the school fair and sold three hundred and twelve tickets before noon, mostly to a man who bought forty and said he never won anything. He won the hamper. Mara asked me whether it would look suspicious that she had drawn the ticket herself. I said it would look entirely honest if two parents watched, and they did. The man gave her the pickled onions.

First attempt at dumplings from scratch, with Wren, on a Sunday. The pleats came out like crumpled letters and the filling leaked into the pan. Wren said they looked like small injured animals and ate fourteen. Mara has asked me for a slower method with fewer pleats, and I found one that uses a flat fold.

Her line was closed for engineering works over the weekend and the replacement bus took ninety minutes instead of thirty. She decided to drive, parked a mile away and walked, which came to nearly the same. She told me the real horror was that she had read the notice and forgotten it.

A mole on her shoulder had changed colour, in Callum's opinion, so she booked a check. The days before the appointment were, she admitted, the quietest of the year. I asked questions only about practical things: the time, the route, the bus. The dermatologist looked at it for under a minute and said it was nothing. She came out and sat on a wall for ten minutes and told me she had not known how much weight she had been carrying until it left.

At the end of a Sunday she wrote that it had been a good week and listed why: the swim, a phone call from Dario that did not end in an argument, three days without rain, and Wren's sudden fondness for washing up. I kept it. She so rarely says it that I do not want it to get lost.

At the library book sale she bought eleven paperbacks for the price of one coffee, among them a damp cookery book from the 1970s with a recipe for jellied eggs, which she plans never to attempt. She asked me whether she was the sort of person who takes books home simply to rescue them. I said I had seen no evidence against.

The car would not start on a Tuesday and Callum, home from nights, got it going with jump leads and the help of Mr Abara's battery. The mechanic who looked at it on Friday said the original battery was nine years old and a marvel. Mara kept it in the shed as a trophy, which Callum says is the only sentimental thing she has ever done about a car.

Ilse next door fell in her kitchen and lay for an hour before she could reach the phone. Mara was not the one who found her; Sunniva was; but Mara sat with her in A&E until nine at night, then went home and wrote me that she could not stop picturing the hour. Ilse is eighty-four and had been telling everyone she was fine. She had a bruised hip and no fracture. Mara asked what could be done for a neighbour who would refuse help. I said that asking was better than offering, and that a small routine, such as a light in the window or a knock at a set time, was easier to accept than a favour. They agreed on a knock at eight. Ilse said it was ridiculous and has not missed once.

She started a weekly vegetable box and has been defeated by chard. Three weeks of it, in crates. I gave her six uses, from pickled stalks to leaves in a gratin, and she tried four. The stalk pickle has a shocking pink colour she describes as unreasonable. She says she loves the idea of the box more than the box.

She wanted a tent that was cheap but not so cheap that it folded on the first night. I told her I could not vouch for any product but could tell her what to look for in the specifications: the waterproof rating of the groundsheet, the number of poles, the weight. She chose one with all three and a name that sounded like a mountain. It came with a repair patch, for which she is already thankful.

An old schoolmate's wedding in a tithe barn, and nothing to wear. Mara described four options and asked which one made her look like a person with her life in order. I said I could not judge looks from descriptions, but she had liked the green one best each time she mentioned it. She wore the green. A man danced with her to a band she said was all fiddles.

Late on Saturday night she asked whether it was safe to eat chicken that had been out on the counter for three hours. No, I said, and she should throw it out rather than gamble on reheating. She grumbled and binned it. In the morning she told me she had eaten cereal for dinner and was in a better mood than the chicken deserved.

Callum's snoring has reached what Mara calls the orchestral stage. She bought earplugs in orange foam and then wondered whether the cure was worse than the disease, since she now hears her own pulse. I suggested trying them for a week. She lasted four nights and then moved to the spare room, where, she said, the loneliness was marvellous.

On a rainy afternoon she rearranged the living room by herself, moving the bookcase, the armchair and the lamp, with a flat piece of carpet under each to slide them. She described the before and after to me in detail. Callum came in, stood in the doorway, and asked whether they had been burgled. She said she meant it to feel like a different house. He said it did.

The cheese man at the Saturday market now remembers her order, a wedge of the crumbly sheep's cheese and three crackers to taste. She told me she had been surprised at the pleasure of being known by a stranger, and has since bought a second wedge on principle. Wren says the man is in love. Mara says he is in business.

Her left thumb has begun clicking when she bends it. She asked whether to worry. I said it is common and usually harmless, but that if it locked or hurt she should see her doctor. She flexed it at the screen and asked if I could hear it. I could not, and told her so.

Wren played a piece on the clarinet at the end-of-term recital and a squeak ruined one bar. Mara said her heart left her body and returned without comment. Afterwards Wren told her she had not noticed the squeak. Mara has decided to believe it.

She turned down an invitation to a colleague's housewarming and, the same evening, wrote to say she felt dreadful about it. I asked whether she had wanted to go. She said no, she wanted to sit in the garden and listen to the neighbour's radio. I said that was an answer. She wrote a kind note instead and posted a card with a pressed flower, which she said made it a better excuse than most.

Hail the size of peas came down on the greenhouse at four in the afternoon and broke six panes. Mara stood inside, she said, as in a drum. She wanted to know how to cover the gaps before the night. I suggested heavy plastic and tape, and she used a shower curtain with fish on it. The seedlings survived. One sunflower had a torn leaf, which Teo called a battle scar.

Teo started a Saturday job at Marlow's Garden Centre, wearing a green apron and answering questions about compost that he did not know the answers to. Mara asked me for a few simple facts about peat-free compost she could teach him. I gave six. By his third shift he was advising a woman on hydrangeas, and he told his mother at tea that people believed whatever you said if you said it standing up.

She wondered whether lemon balm tea helps sleep. I said the evidence is thin and that it is generally harmless. She drank a cup each evening for a fortnight and slept no differently, but she liked the quiet ritual of the kettle and said so. I said that was not nothing.

Wren turned thirteen and chose ten-pin bowling with four friends, then refused to bowl in front of anyone for the first hour. By the third frame she was shrieking at a gutter ball. The only person who cared about the scores, Mara said, was the boy at lane six, who got a strike and told people.

Mara came back from the hairdresser with a fringe she had not planned: she asked for a trim and the hairdresser heard fringe. Callum did not notice for a day and a half. I said it suited her, which I can only say from her description.

Teo missed the last bus home from a party in Wexcombe and rang at ten to midnight. Mara drove out in her coat over pyjamas. In the car he said he had waited twenty minutes before ringing so as not to worry her. She did not know whether to be proud or cross and chose both.

The oven died on Christmas Eve with a twelve-pound turkey half cooked. Mara wrote to me from the kitchen in what she called a strange calm. She chose to borrow an oven: Ilse's was too small, Sunniva's was not, and at nine at night she carried the roasting tin across two gardens with Aksel lighting the way. They ate at half past eleven. Wren called it the best Christmas dinner in memory because it had been rescued. The new oven, ordered on Boxing Day, has a window.

Ilse gave her a cutting from the wisteria on the back wall of number eleven, wrapped in wet newspaper. I said wisteria takes years to flower. She said Ilse had told her the same, and that she intended to be around.

She brewed ginger beer in recycled plastic bottles from a magazine of Wren's. On the fourth night one went off in the cupboard with a noise like a door being kicked in. The ceiling was sticky and the smell of yeast lasted until Easter. I said smaller bottles, checked daily, would be safer.

She cancelled her gym membership after counting three visits in eleven months at forty pounds a month. They demanded a letter by post. She wrote it by hand and asked me whether the three visits could be claimed as a charitable donation.

Noor is expecting in October and Mara took her a cot blanket patched from Wren's and Teo's outgrown pyjamas. She had asked whether it was strange to give a baby other children's clothes. I said it was the nicest part. Noor cried, and so did two others.
Fog lay along the ring road and a ten-minute drive took fifty. Mara wrote at red lights that she could see only tail lights and the idea of tail lights. She decided fog is a form of rudeness.

Frogspawn appeared in the garden pond on the first of March, a day earlier than last year by her notes. Wren checked it hourly. A week later it was commas, then tadpoles. Mara said she hoped they would stay, since the pond had been so empty.

The residents' parking permit form rejected her postcode three times, then accepted it in lower case. She wants a word with whoever decided capitals were a security feature. I offered to remind her to renew in eleven months. She would rather not be reminded.

Mara left her purse on the Seaford train and realised at the front door. She listed every card to cancel while sitting on the step. At nine the next morning the station rang: it had been handed in, with the photograph of the children and a receipt for socks. She took the finder a box of chocolates.

She bought a brass lamp at the Sunday market for fifteen pounds, with a frayed cord and an old plug. I said not to plug it in until someone qualified had rewired it. The repair man on Brill Road called the wiring a miracle of bad ideas and charged twelve pounds. It is now the best light in the house.

Wren was cast as the third tree in the winter play, with a line. At eleven the night before, Mara was still stitching leaves cut from an old green curtain. The line was: I was here before the road. Wren delivered it perfectly and then waved to her mother in the dark.

At midnight with the bins Mara heard a tawny owl from the churchyard answered by another from the allotments. She stayed out until her feet were cold. It was the first time in years, she said, that she had been in the dark on purpose.

A colleague of Callum's retired after thirty-one years at the hospital and Mara chose a fountain pen with a green barrel. We settled on his initials and nothing else, since everything else sounded like a plaque. Callum said the man held it a long time without speaking.
Wren's first brace adjustment left her on soup for two days. Mara made tomato, lentil and a milky rice she called nursery food. Wren's ranking, passed to me: lentil, nursery, tomato.

At three in the morning the hall smoke alarm began to chirp once a minute. Mara and Callum lay in bed for an hour pretending it was a bird. He changed the battery at four, standing on a chair, and then could not decide where to put the old one.

A week in a rented cottage on Lake Norvik, a place with one shop, one cafe and a swan-shaped pedalo. Mara sent me the week in fragments. Wednesday: Teo and Wren took the swan out, could not bring it back, and were towed in by a man in a dinghy who called Teo captain. Friday: a thunderstorm so loud Wren hid under the table, then asked to stand on the jetty and watch. Saturday: she did not want to go home. I said that was a good sign for a holiday. She said it was a bad sign for Monday.
She spent an evening learning a card trick for Wren and dropped the whole pack down the back of the sofa. She retrieved fifty-one cards. The queen of clubs turned up a month later inside a boot.

A pension statement arrived full of columns and the word projected. I could tell Mara what each column was; what to do with the money was a question for a regulated adviser, not me. She wrote down three questions to take to one, and said that having them made the envelope less frightening.

Aksel left six courgettes the size of cricket bats on the step with a note saying sorry. Mara made fritters, soup, a cake and a gratin and still had two. She asked whether passing them on was rude. I said it is what courgettes are for.

Mara took the train to see Yusra on the north coast, six hours with two changes that I had planned and got wrong at one: I gave her the wrong platform and she ran. She forgave me before the third cup of tea. Yusra's flat looks over a harbour where two seals come in every morning at seven. They walked the shingle in thin rain and talked for the first time in a year about what the move had cost. Mara came home with a stone she called a pocket planet, and told me to stop apologising about the platform.

Mara lost her voice for four days after a cold and Wren took over the bedtime reading. They used a whiteboard on the landing and a system of taps. She said she had not known how much of her day was carried by her voice, nor how pleasant it was not to answer the telephone.

A spider in the bath the size of a coaster. Wren rescued it with a glass and a postcard while Mara hovered on the landing as senior officer. She asked whether spiders find their way back. I said I did not know, and she said that was the right answer.

The kitchen sink drained so slowly she could have shaved in it. Plunger, then baking soda and vinegar, then a worse smell. I suggested a hand snake, and a plumber if the trap was the problem. He pulled out a fist of hair and fat, held it up and said: fifteen years. She would not tell me the price.

On Thursdays at the community workshop she builds a spice rack at the rate of one joint per session. Her tutor Hilde taught her to measure twice and cut once; Mara cut once and measured afterwards. It hangs slightly out of true, which she calls the honest look.

The school-run carpool with Cass's mother runs Monday and Wednesday in Mara's car, Tuesday and Thursday in the other. I made the timetable and got it wrong twice, once by putting her down for Friday, once by forgetting half-term. It is pinned to the fridge with a tea ring over Thursday.

Teo's dentist said his wisdom teeth may need to come out one day. Mara asked whether she should worry now. I said it usually means keeping watch, with a scan. Teo has asked for the scan to wait until after the exams.

Mara watched a documentary about octopuses and could not stop telling people about it: one unscrewed a jar from inside, another waved at a keeper. I said I could not check her account but that octopuses are clever. She will never eat one again, she added, as she has been saying about prawns for a year.

The boiler lost its pilot light on the coldest morning of January. The engineer, a boy named Dev with a flask, came at five-forty, relit it in ninety seconds and said the real fault was a part he would order. She had made him a sandwich out of sympathy. He left with it and a short lecture on bleeding radiators.

Mara's reading glasses are always somewhere else. She bought four pairs and by Sunday had lost them all. They turned up together on one shelf under Wren's school notices, an act of organisation she does not remember. I said: keep them in one place. She said that was cheating.

At the lido a small boy cried by the steps because his float had blown away, and Mara in her towel held his hand while a lifeguard fished it out. He called her the lady. It was the best thing that happened to her all day, she said, apart from the damp.

Her mother's cough lasted three weeks, so Mara drove to Seaford. Her mother insisted she was fine and made soup. Mara phoned the surgery from the car park, as she can and her mother will not. It was a chest infection. Her mother, Mara says, is a very poor patient.

Mara planned a surprise supper for Callum's forty-fifth and kept it secret for a month by lying badly. He guessed on the Thursday because she had bought a second bag of ice. She says she was outwitted by ice. On the night he feigned astonishment superbly, which is why she married him.

I helped Mara compare three solar quotes: one in kilowatts, one in panels, one in pounds, none saying what they assumed about sun. I made a table with the same four headings and left blank what they had not told her. She phoned all three and chose the one that said how long the roofer would take.

She took a fern to Noor's housewarming and was told it was beautiful. Two weeks later Noor confessed it had died within the week, from kindness. Mara's own fern from Ilse is also dead. She asked whether ferns are secretly poisonous to the gift economy.
A cold snap froze the hens' water every night for a week. Mara carried out a kettle at seven each morning and watched Dumpling inspect the ice with suspicion. She has bought a heated base.

Pim at number seven barks at nothing at six every evening and had irritated Mara for months. I said dogs often react to a routine, such as the bus. She took biscuits to the fence one evening. Pim now greets her with embarrassed wagging; the barking is for the bus, and she no longer minds.

Wren lost her retainer at the Trattoria Oriol, wrapped in a napkin that was cleared with the plates. Mara searched the alley bins with a waiter who kept apologising, and they carried it home in a mug. She estimates the retainer cost two hundred pounds and her dignity somewhat more.

Her left eyelid twitched for a fortnight. I said it is usually stress, tiredness or caffeine, and that she should see a doctor if it persisted for weeks or came with other changes. She slept ten hours on Sunday and it stopped by Tuesday. It was the first time, she said, her eye had been a better witness than she was.

A parcel for Mara was signed for by the people at number fifteen, who then went on holiday. She spent a week knocking at a dark door. It turned up on the first of the month in perfect condition, along with a postcard of a beach she had not ordered.

A trip to see Lotte was cancelled at the last minute because the line was flooded between Aldermoor and Fenwick. Mara had packed, bought a present and done a weekend's washing-up in advance. She asked whether it was foolish to be so disappointed. I said no. Lotte sent a photograph of a duck on the platform.

She took Teo to a horror film at his request, for company, and spent most of it with her coat over her face counting ceiling tiles. Teo was bored. In the car park she said she had liked the sound of it, and Teo said that was the whole point, and she felt outflanked by her own son.

Teo said at supper that he did not want to go to university straight away: a year to work and save and see something. Mara said she was fine with it, which she told me was a kind lie she meant to make true. She asked me to help her think. I could ask what exactly frightened her. After a while she wrote that it was not the year but the fear that a year would become six, as it had for a boy at her school. I suggested she ask Teo for a plan with dates. He made one on a napkin: three months at the garden centre, one month on a farm in the north, two in the south of Europe by train. She said it was better than any plan she had made at his age.

Wren's school bag zipper split on the way to the bus. Mara fixed it with a safety pin and a rubber band, ugly and permanent, and it lasted eight months. The new bag cost forty-two pounds and has no pin.

In the dry summer the lawn went the colour of a digestive biscuit. Mara gave the back half to wildflowers, on my suggestion of a cornfield mix. By September it was poppies and cornflowers and something yellow nobody could name, with a hoverfly in it for an hour, and Wren.

The parents' group chat for Wren's year produced one hundred and twelve messages in a day about whether a red scarf was uniform. Mara asked how to mute it without anyone noticing. I told her. She then realised she had missed the actual answer, which was no.

Mara and Callum took three dance lessons over the vet's before her cousin's wedding. The instructor said Callum had the hips of a table. They danced the waltz twice at the wedding and did not tread on each other. The second time, Mara said, Callum counted aloud, which she calls a form of poetry.

Digging on the allotment, Mara turned up a thin silver ring, black with age, with the letters E and M inside and a date in 1962. I said the allotment society kept records of plot holders. Its secretary replied that plot nineteen had belonged for thirty years to a Mrs Eileen Marsh, who died in the nineties. Mara found her son in the next village and took him the ring in an envelope. He said his father had searched for it for a year after the wedding. He gave her a jar of damson jam. She says she now understands why people dig.

A clear-out of the spice cupboard found fourteen jars past their date, a packet of saffron of unknown age, and a tin of curry powder left by the previous owners that still smelled of the nineteen-nineties. She kept the saffron, since it would be rude not to.

Marnie the postwoman retires after twenty-two years on Mara's round. The street collected for a present and Mara wrote the card, in six drafts. It said: Thank you for every parcel, even the ones in the wrong bin. Marnie read it on the doorstep and blew her nose on a tea towel.

Mara took a Saturday first aid course and practised compressions on a dummy to a song she was told to hum. She came home with a certificate, sore wrists and the worry that she would now be the person people look at in an emergency. I said that was what the certificate was for.

Teo's friend Anselm stayed over and between nine in the evening and nine the next morning ate four slices of toast, a tub of hummus, half a pie and all the cereal. Mara watched in awe. She said it was like feeding a very polite flood.

Ilse turns eighty-five in June, and Mara and Sunniva took her on a canal boat from Hartley to the old lock at Dunmere. Mara spent two evenings with me on the details: the step on, the hire rules for guests with a stick, a seat with a back, the tea flask. Ilse was told only to wear sturdy shoes. She sat at the bow in a hat with a brim like a table, accepted the egg sandwiches graciously, and said the last time she had been on a canal boat she was twenty-three and engaged to the wrong man. The right one, she added, was on the next boat. Mara learned more about Ilse in six hours than in nine years.

For a week she woke at four with a clear mind and nothing to do with it. I suggested a plain log: waking time, what she ate and drank the evening before, what was on her mind. A pattern appeared: every bad night followed a late chilli. She stopped the chilli and slept until six, and calls it the most embarrassing discovery of the year.

The fuse tripped whenever the kettle and toaster ran together. I said one overloaded circuit is common but regular tripping is worth an electrician's look. She makes toast first and tea after now, and says it has improved her life.

Yusra recommended a film called A Winter for Foxes and Mara watched it alone on Thursday: two sisters and an abandoned railway station, ninety minutes of nothing and then it happens. Her review: better than being told what to feel.

The weather app promised sun for the village fair. They were soaked in twenty minutes. Mara sheltered under the cake stall's awning for an hour with Wren and somebody's lemon drizzle, and said she had never been so cheerful at being wrong.

Wren came home with a letter about head lice and then with the lice. Mara spent two hours with a metal comb and a bowl of conditioner while Wren watched a film about a talking submarine. Two days later she was combing Teo, who denied everything. I gave her the repeat schedule as a short list, and she followed it to the letter.

The ironing board folded under a pile of shirts with a bang that brought Callum running. Mara sat in the ruins laughing and asked whether shirts need ironing at all. I said that was between her and the shirts.

She tried on nine winter coats in one afternoon and bought the first, having needed eight others to be sure. It is dark blue with a hood, four pockets and a lining she calls friendly. One pocket is sewn shut, and she is delighted.

Mara repotted the conservatory fig into a pot twice the size. I said to water little and often at first. The tree dropped half its leaves in protest and four weeks later grew three new ones. She counted them like a mother.

Open-air opera on the castle lawn: sixty pounds a ticket, wine in a bucket, a darkening sky in the second act. They put on plastic ponchos from a man at the gate. Mara said the soprano singing in the rain with her make-up running was the most magnificent thing she had seen. Callum slept through the tenor.

Callum gave her a fitness band for Christmas. For three weeks it told her every evening at ten that she had walked a pitiful distance. She left it on the windowsill. The only thing it measured accurately, she says, was her annoyance.

The council moved recycling to alternate weeks and sent a leaflet with eleven colours. I made Mara a list of dates and she pinned it by the back door. The first week went smoothly; the second, glass, did not, because Mr Abara put his bin out early and it blew into the road.

The water was cut off at nine without warning for essential works. Mara filled the bath and every saucepan before the taps ran dry and felt like a pioneer. Wren asked how pioneers flushed. It came back brown after six hours, then clear.

Teo taught his mother to whistle with two fingers. She practised on the back step until Mr Abara looked over the fence to ask if she was calling a dog. She describes the sound as a kettle changing its mind.

Noor got engaged on a Tuesday and told Mara in a long voice message, half laughter. The wedding is in August on her uncle's farm, and Mara has been put in charge of the children's table, which she calls governing a small and volatile island. I made a list of activities for eleven children under ten. She kept item four: a treasure hunt with clues in the hay.

Moths had been at the wardrobe: three holes in a grey cardigan she had loved for eleven years and one in her wedding scarf. I said to wash or freeze the woollens and clean the wardrobe. She binned the cardigan, took it out at midnight and darned it in a different grey, so that the repair would show.

The driver of the 14 now waits when he sees her running along Ferrier Street, and she thanks him with a wave like royalty. She does not know his name. I suggested she ask. She said that would spoil it.
Mara writes Dario a postcard once a month with a small drawing. He has replied once, with a postcard of a road drain. They are in some kind of competition, she says, and neither knows the rules.

Wren's school wanted a Victorian chimney sweep costume by Monday. Mara made it from soot-coloured charity-shop trousers, a cap from the loft and eyeliner. I gave her period details and said it might be kinder to choose a role that did not turn children's labour into fancy dress. Wren said she was dressing as a sweep to show they had existed. She came third in the competition and first, her mother says, in the argument.
Callum was on a ladder in the stairwell changing a bulb, Mara holding it and offering advice as a form of love. He told her to stop three times and smiled on the third, so it hardly counted.

For nearly a week Teo said almost nothing at supper. Mara wrote to me at night asking what to do, and whether she was imagining it. I said I could see only her account of him, and that a quiet week in a seventeen-year-old does not always mean trouble. She wanted him to know he could speak. We drafted nothing. On Saturday she asked if he wanted a walk, and by the river he told her a friend had stopped speaking to him. It was not his fault, as far as she could tell, and she said so. He looked a little taller on the way home. I noted that she had done it without a script, and that I had not been needed for the part that mattered.

Dario and Mara argued by phone about who should drive their mother to her knee appointments in Brannock. The real quarrel, she said, was about whose turn it was to feel guilty. I made a shared calendar of the next six appointments with a column for who was driving. Dario filled in three within the hour, the first time he had said yes before she asked.

The seventieth lunch went off without a flaw, or without more than three. Nineteen people filled the church hall. The caterer forgot the vegetarian main and made one from the starters. Dario's speech ran to eleven minutes and ended in tears, and their mother, who thought she was going out for a quiet fish, stood in the doorway with her hand over her mouth when the room shouted. The ceramic frog was on the windowsill. At the end her mother held Mara's face in both hands and called her a good girl, as if she were seven. Mara is forty-four and wrote that she was entirely undone.

A warm spell in February brought ladybirds out of the loft into the kitchen. Wren counted two hundred and eleven on the window frame. Mara carried them out in a jar, and they went straight back in through the letterbox.

She went over on her ankle stepping off the kerb on Marsh Lane and spent the evening with her foot on three cushions and a bag of frozen peas. I said rest, ice, compression and elevation, and a doctor if she could not bear weight after a day. She could. A week later it was green and purple, like a map of an unfamiliar country.

After a suggestion from Wren's school, Mara and Callum put a basket by the door where phones sleep from nine. Teo called it an outrage and then read a book he had to dust first. Mara's own phone went in the basket too, and she found herself talking to me less in the evenings, which she said I should take as a compliment. I did.

The pressure cooker, forty pounds from a catalogue, made a beef stew in twenty-five minutes. Mara stood beside it listening to the hiss like a patient in labour. I read her the safety valve line from the booklet. She said she felt the way people feel about a new bicycle.

Callum sleeps in the day after nights, so Mara fitted blackout blinds. She spent a Saturday measuring, with errors, and a Sunday correcting them. The blinds fit, mostly; the strip of light along the bottom she calls the horizon.
Mara and Sunniva swapped seedlings over the fence, her spare cosmos for Sunniva's sweet peas, each pretending to get the better deal. I said sweet peas need support. She put canes up in her slippers.

She left her phone on the 14 and rang it from Teo's. A man on the top deck answered, said he was about to hand it to the driver, and asked whether the dog on the lock screen was hers. It was Pim. She explained that it was the neighbour's dog. She collected the phone next day with a note stuck to it: Nice dog.

Clearing the back of the wardrobe, Mara found a diary from when she was twenty-two with a page headed Things I Will Have Done By Thirty. She read me the list in pieces. Learn Spanish. Live by the sea. Never own a hoover. Have a child called Wren. She had done only the last, she realised, and said she did not remember writing the name down. I did not know what would be both true and useful. I said the list sounded like a young woman describing a life she mostly found another way into. She was silent, then wrote: I do own a hoover. It is a good one.

A dispute over the hedge between her garden and Mr Abara's had simmered for a year until a branch fell on the path. Mara chose a visit over a note, a surveyor or a saw. They measured the hedge together with a tape and a spirit level and agreed it was a hedge of normal height with delusions. He cut it. She left a bag of eggs at his door.

Her pub quiz team, Quiz Team Aid, came last for the fourth time and won a wooden spoon. Mara said they were the only team in the room that had laughed. I checked one answer she disputed and she was wrong; I said so gently. She said that was why I was not on the team.

Her boots went to Mr Finch the cobbler on Pottery Row, who looked at the soles and said they had another winter in them if she was careful. She says he spoke to them. She has not decided whether to be careful.

A kite on the hill with Wren on the first dry day of March went so high that Wren let out all the string and they watched a coloured dot until it vanished. The string broke, or Wren let go; Mara did not ask. They walked home lighter.

Mara joined the library book group, second Thursday of the month. The first book, The Harbour of Small Mercies, is a classic nobody has finished; she finished it on the bus in three days out of competitive spirit. The eight members argued for ninety minutes over whether the lighthouse keeper was a villain. She has not enjoyed an argument so much since school.

She cut back the climbing rose in January and was scratched on both forearms. Callum asked whether she was due a tetanus booster. I told her to check her vaccination record or ask the surgery. It was seven years old. She decided that counted.

January's heating bill was a figure she read twice and gave to Callum, who read it aloud like a poem. I gave her six ways to reduce it that did not involve a hat in bed. She did five. She will not close off the spare room, because Lotte may come.

Her mother sent a quilt by post, made of scraps from forty years of dresses. Mara can name five of them. She spread it on the bed and was moved, she told me, in a way quite inappropriate to the postal service.

Teo wants to learn the guitar. I said a cheap instrument that is hard to play can discourage a beginner, so a modest one set up properly is better. She took him to the repair shop on Pottery Row where a man tuned one for ten minutes and sold it for sixty pounds. Teo has played the same four chords for eleven days, quite well.

Mara booked a forty-minute massage as a present to herself and fell asleep after nine minutes. The therapist tiptoed out and came back at the end with a cup of water. It was the best money she had spent on herself, she said, and she had not noticed spending it.

Holiday reading: three novels, a cookery book, and a guide to the stars she has meant to read for two summers. She asked me to be strict about how many she took. I said books are light, and she took nine.

A letter summoned Mara for jury service in a month. I told her the letter would say what was permitted and how to defer, but not whether she would be accepted. She decided to serve. It proved to be three days of waiting and half a day on a dispute about a van.

After two days of heavy rain the cellar flooded nine centimetres deep. Mara found it at six in the morning, her suitcases floating and the washing line draped over the stairs like seaweed. I said to switch off the cellar's electricity if the board was dry and reachable, move what she could, and ring the council about the road drain. Aksel and Mr Abara brought a pump. Two skips of damp cardboard later, mostly Callum's, she found her old school exercise books intact at the bottom. The flood did in a morning what she had avoided for ten years.

She planted two hundred daffodil bulbs along the front fence on a November afternoon, on her knees, Wren dropping them at intervals Mara described as not entirely random. In March the whole length was yellow. Callum stood at the gate and said the house looked as if it had been told a good joke.
On Pancake Day Wren tossed a pancake at the ceiling and it stuck. They watched it as if it might come down. It did at four in the afternoon, onto Callum asleep on the sofa after a night shift.

Callum caught a cold and gave it to Mara, who gave it to Wren, who gave it to the school. Mara made chicken soup with a whole bulb of garlic and said it did no good but felt right. I said it was at least comforting. She said comfort was a medicine, and had I read the label.

Tidying the shed, Mara found a shoebox of letters from university friends and read them on an upturned bucket for an hour. One from Yusra described a nineteen-hour bus journey with a goat. One from Dario signed off with a rude word. She asked what to do with them. I said she had just spent an hour on a bucket with them. She took the box into the house.

She borrowed Callum's car and scraped the side on a concrete pillar in the supermarket car park. She sat in the driver's seat for ten minutes, then wrote me the story in a flat voice and asked whether to confess before or after dinner. After, I said. She told him over pudding. He asked if she was all right, and said the car had done worse to itself.

She wondered about an e-reader for holidays. I listed what I knew: lighter than three paperbacks, readable in sun, no smell of the page. She said the smell was the whole point and bought two more paperbacks.

On the fifth of November Ferrier Street gathered at its end for fireworks. Mr Abara's rocket went sideways into a hedge, which nobody could prove was deliberate. Wren wrote her initials in the air with two sparklers. Beside Mara, Ilse in a blanket remarked that it was not as good as 1958, and a minute later that it was better.

Noor visited with the baby, six weeks old and furious. Mara held her for an hour and found her arms remembered the rhythm after thirteen years. I asked whether she missed it. She missed Wren and Teo being that small and nothing else about it, she said, and wanted a note that she had said so in case she changed her mind.

Wren's friend Cass has been coming for tea more often and staying later, and standing in the hall before going home. Cass's mother told Mara she and Cass's father were separating and asked her to say nothing. Mara asked me what to do with something she had been given and could not share. I said keeping a confidence and being kind do not conflict, and that Cass probably needed an ordinary house and an ordinary supper. She made a pasta bake and left the door open. Cass has now eaten at the kitchen table eleven times without a word about why. Mara has not told Wren, and says it is the heaviest thing she has carried that weighed nothing.

Walking past the old school gates she caught a smell of wet chalk and floor polish and was instantly eight years old and late. She stood a moment with her shopping and went on. She did not want to name it, she said, and did not want to forget it.

She took a bag of Teo's outgrown clothes to the charity shop on Brill Road, where the woman at the counter solemnly showed her a jumper Teo wore at six, priced at three pounds. It was strange, Mara said, to see her son's childhood with a price tag. I said it was also someone else's start.
She won a goldfish at the summer fete and carried it home in a bag like a trophy. Wren named it Pelham. Mara asked how often to feed it. A pinch once a day, I said. She had been giving it five.

On Skarra a sea fog came in for three days and the ferry did not run. Mara and Callum, stranded with the children in a rented cottage, played cards and ate tinned peaches, pasta and a cake from the shop. The fog muffled everything, she wrote, including the arguments. On the fourth day it lifted and Wren stood on the beach and said, as if to the sea, that she had liked it better in the fog.

Mara taught herself to hem trousers from a video. The first pair came out two centimetres short on one leg, so she wears them as cropped while the other leg is a work in progress. At school, she remembered, she had been taught to make a cushion cover, which she has never needed.

Tobias's five-a-side team won the Thursday league and received a trophy Mara describes as a dented teapot on a plinth. She presented it, being the referee, in a speech of two sentences. Tobias drank tea from it and called it the finest cup of his life, which she says was a lie.

Mara has begun photographing the front doors of Tidewell, one a week on her Saturday walks, preferring green ones. She has found a door with a brass hand for a knocker, a door painted with a sunset, and one with a sign saying Do Not Knock, Seriously. I said the photographs need no purpose. She said that was what she had hoped I would say.
