Callum surprised her with tickets to an astronomy night at the observatory on Harrow Hill. In a queue of the damp and hopeful, Mara at last looked through a telescope at the rings of Saturn. She had expected a photograph, and found a small, sharp, real thing hanging there with nothing around it. She stood very still in the dark and Callum held her arm without saying anything.

Dario brought his new girlfriend, Femke, to a pub lunch so Mara could meet her. Mara was nervous for two days and asked me what to ask that was not an interrogation. I suggested asking what she was reading. Femke was reading three things at once, and Mara said she would do.

Her mother stayed for a week and rearranged the kitchen cupboards while Mara was out. Mara found the mugs where the bowls had been. She told me she said nothing, and that it took her until Thursday to forgive it.

Wren's best friend Imke is changing schools in September because of her father's job. Wren took it hard and said little. Mara asked me for ideas for their last weekend together. We settled on a day at the lido and a long walk to the river, with nothing else planned.

Callum's brother Marek flew in from abroad and lay awake until four, then fell asleep at the dinner table at four in the afternoon, mid-forkful. Wren timed it. Mara said she could not decide whether to wake him.

An invitation came to her school reunion, twenty-six years on, in the old hall. She read it twice, said she would go, then said she would not. I noted both. The second, on Sunday, was said with relief.
Her sleep tracker claimed nine hours of perfect sleep, which she says is a lie because she remembers the radiator knocking at three. She has decided to believe the radiator.
She queued for her flu jab at the pharmacy behind an old man in a hat and a boy who cried before the needle came out. She felt nothing at all, and was a little disappointed.

Callum's back seized on the stairs and he went to an osteopath on Brill Road, who cracked it and told him to stop sitting like a question mark. Mara found three stretches online and I told her which looked gentle. He does one of them.

After the outdoor concert Mara's ears rang for two days. She wrote asking whether to worry. I said a ringing after loud music usually fades, but if it lasted more than a few days she should see her doctor, and next time take earplugs. It faded on the third morning. She now keeps earplugs in her coat.

Calf cramps woke her at night three times in a week. She read that a shot of pickle juice helps and asked if it was true. I said the evidence was thin. She drank it anyway at midnight and said that if nothing else it woke the rest of her up.

In November she bought a daylight lamp, a white panel that sits on the kitchen table, and sat in front of it with her toast like a plant. She says it is too early to know. I said that is how it works. Callum calls it the sun-in-a-box and has taken to reading the paper in front of it.
The hygienist told her off for not flossing, kindly, with a diagram. Mara flossed for six days. On the seventh she asked me whether a week counted as a habit. I said no.

Her first linocut print came out with the lettering backwards, since she had forgotten that a print reverses. She framed it anyway and hung it in the downstairs loo, where, she says, nobody will check.

Mara joined the Tuesday badminton league and lost her first match twenty-one to three. Her partner, a man called Osgood, said she had a good serve. She told me it was the nicest thing anyone had said to her about losing.

A thousand-piece jigsaw of a harbour at dawn, finished over three weeks on the dining table, was one piece short. They turned out the whole room. Mara says the missing piece is, to be fair, probably a gull.
She folded forty paper cranes for the stall at the school fair and Wren folded three. Wren's, she said, looked more alive. They sold for a pound each and Wren's went first.

She tried watercolours on a Sunday afternoon and the sky came out green. She asked me whether skies could ever be green. In certain storms, I said. She said she had painted it that way on purpose, thank you.

Teo took her geocaching on the hill above Tidewell with an app and a pencil. They found a plastic tin under a bridge with a notebook inside, nine years of signatures, and added theirs. Mara told me she had not known that grown strangers did this, and felt oddly welcomed by them.
She picked blackberries on the canal path and came home with four tubs, scratched forearms and a purple mouth. Wren ate half of them on the way. They had crumble, and nothing else, for supper.

The coast walking group meets on alternate Saturdays and she went to the first one in new boots. She was the youngest by nineteen years, and was told to keep up by a woman of seventy-three who then did not slow down for the rest of the day. Mara came home with blisters and an invitation to the next walk.

A night train to the north, with a sleeper berth so narrow Mara wrote that she felt posted. Callum took the top bunk and hit his head on the ceiling at every station. She says she did not sleep and loved it, and woke to a wide grey estuary and tea in a paper cup.

In the hired car abroad she turned onto the wrong side of the road for four minutes, then onto a kerb. No damage but a flat tyre, and a lorry driver who changed it for them for nothing. She sent me a message: Do not let me hire a car again. I have kept it, in case.
At airport security they took her toothpaste and let through a pair of scissors she had forgotten in her bag. She says she does not understand the world.

The hotel had double-booked their room and offered, after a long apology, a suite on the top floor with a view of the whole town and a bath on a platform. Wren photographed it from every angle. Mara said she felt she had been mistaken for someone important and was determined not to correct it.
The new tram line opened with a free day and Mara rode it end to end three times between errands, for the experience. She said it smelled new. Wren said it was just a bus on a string.

On the ferry Callum went the colour of old putty and sat with his eyes shut for ninety minutes. Mara and the children ate chips on the open deck in the wind. She says it was one of the happiest lunches of her marriage and that she is slightly ashamed.

Wren, at thirteen, took the train to Seaford alone for the first time, to stay with Mara's mother. Mara walked her to the platform, made her promise to text at each stop, and went home and stood in the kitchen for forty minutes doing nothing. The texts arrived. Tidewell. Fenwick, with a photograph of a cow. Aldermoor, flooded, still. Mara asked me twice whether the line had any disruption. It had none. At Seaford her own mother met Wren and sent a one-line message: Eating cake. Mara said that she cried at the sink, from relief or something less tidy, and then discovered, in the quiet, how loudly the clock could be heard.

A drive over the moor in snow. Callum fitted chains by torchlight at the roadside while Mara held the torch and Teo sang. The car crawled for two hours at nineteen miles an hour. She says nobody has ever been so happy to see a service station.

Mara lost the car in the multi-storey for twenty minutes, on level four, which she was sure was level six. She walked the levels with her key held up like a lantern. It was where Callum had said, which she took as a personal insult.

The holiday cottage had no phone signal except on the hill behind it, so each evening someone walked up to read messages. It was Teo's job, then Wren's, then nobody's. By the fourth day the hill was unvisited. She said it was the best thing about the cottage.

At the market in Orsett she bought a mantel clock for twenty pounds that did not run. The stallholder said it only needed love. A man at a repair shop on Brill Road cleaned it for fifteen, and it now ticks, loudly, on the shelf above the stairs. Mara says she can no longer sleep without the sound, which she did not know she lacked.

Mrs Pell went broody and spent two weeks sitting on a pebble in the nest box with a look of great dignity. Mara tried lifting her. Mrs Pell pecked her. She asked whether hens could lie to themselves. I said that was a question beyond me.

A double-yolk egg appeared on Tuesday, enormous, and Wren cracked it into the pan with ceremony. Two yolks, side by side. She wanted to know if it meant twins. I explained as carefully as an egg allows.

Rochester the hamster escaped on a Thursday night and was found, after a day and a half, asleep in one of Callum's work shoes. Wren had searched with a torch and a sunflower seed. Mara asked how far a hamster can travel. Further than anyone expects, I said. He had gone four metres, and half a floor.

A stray tabby appears on the shed roof most afternoons and watches the hens with an expression of scholarly interest. Mara has not fed it. She has, she admits, put out a saucer of water. I did not say anything.

Mara looked after Pim for a weekend while the neighbours went to a wedding. She came away with a lead, a sack of food, a list of fifteen instructions, and a dog who would not leave her side. She had forgotten, she said, what it is to be followed to the bathroom by someone who is simply glad. When his owners returned Pim looked at them as if they were visitors, and she told me she felt like the thief of a very small, warm thing.

A pigeon fell down the chimney and sat in the grate, grey and furious. Callum put on gloves, laid a towel over it, and let it out of the back door. It stood on the lawn for a minute and then, he said, gave him a look.

Swifts came back to nest under the eaves in May and Mara has been standing in the garden at dusk to watch them scream around the house. Wren counted eleven. She asked me where swifts go for the winter. Africa, I said, and she said she had not known anything with such a small body could fly that far.

Wren brought home the school's stick insects for the summer holidays, in a tank with a lid and a bundle of bramble leaves. Mara has them on the kitchen counter and says they are the least demanding of all her dependants.

The apple tree gave forty kilos this year, a number Teo had weighed on the bathroom scales. Mara put boxes out on the wall with a sign and still had thirty. We made a list of what she could do with the rest: pies, juice, freezing, the hens. The hens got six and have been insufferable since.

The sweetcorn was eaten overnight by squirrels, cob by cob, with a precision Mara admired. She stood in the garden at dawn looking at the stripped stalks. The squirrels, she says, had left the husks in a neat pile.

Teo and Wren planted sunflowers in a height contest. Wren's is two metres ten and Teo's a metre fifty, which he says is a matter of soil. Mara holds the measuring stick and a position of strict neutrality.
The lawnmower died with a cough on the last cut of the summer. Aksel lent her his, and she returned it with a plate of biscuits and a promise to buy her own, which he did not believe.

A blackbird got caught under the strawberry netting and beat itself against it in a panic. Mara went out with scissors and Wren with a towel, and they cut it free. It sat in Wren's hands for a long second and then went. Wren said it looked back. I did not argue.
Twelve kilos of potatoes from one bucket and two bags in the corner of the garden. She weighed them twice. She said it felt like cheating, since all she had done was plant and forget.

The fridge died in August on a Friday evening with a full shelf of cheese, a trifle and Callum's lunches. Mara filled a cool box with ice from the neighbours and spent the weekend eating the trifle in instalments. The new fridge came on Tuesday with a drawer for salad, which she says is aspirational.

She came second in the pie competition at the fete, beaten by a woman of seventy-nine with a lattice like lace. Mara's apple and blackberry pie had a leaky seam. She shook the woman's hand and asked for the recipe, and was refused.

Wren announced a vegetarian phase at the dinner table and Mara asked what that meant on a Tuesday. We built a short list of dishes the whole family would eat: bean chilli, a tray of roast vegetables, noodles with peanut sauce. Teo complained about the beans. Three weeks in, Wren was found eating a sausage in secret, and the phase is now called flexible.

She cooked a casserole for the new mother at number twenty-two and left it on the step with a note saying not to answer the door. The mother wrote back two days later with a drawing, apparently by the baby's elder brother, of a pot with legs.
At the supermarket the self-checkout told her three times that there was an unexpected item in the bagging area. It was her handbag. She says this is the only time a machine has been right about her.

A fish shop opened on the corner of Lister Road and the fishmonger, a big quiet man named Gunnar, taught her to fillet a mackerel in four cuts. She tried at home and produced what she calls a vague gesture. I suggested she go back. She goes on Fridays now and buys one fish whether she needs it or not.
Mince pies for thirty: she baked eighty-four in a single evening and gave away all but nine. Callum ate the nine. She told me this was the Christmas she finally understood the arithmetic of it.

The community orchard held a pressing day and Mara went with four crates of apples and Wren. They washed, chopped and fed them into a hand press and got eleven litres of cloudy juice. She says the first taste, still cold from the cheesecloth, was unreasonably good, and that the man running it said you could not buy it for any money.

She made a weekly meal-planning grid, with colours, and followed it for twelve days. On the thirteenth she wrote that she had eaten toast for dinner and that the grid had been, on balance, a good friend.

The dishwasher died, and Mara and Callum spent a Saturday arguing, with great courtesy, over three brands. I made the comparison she asked for: capacity, noise, energy use, price. They bought the middle one. Callum said afterwards he preferred the quiet; Mara said she preferred winning.

At the second-hand school uniform sale she bought two blazers, a skirt and a pair of trousers for the price of a new tie. Wren's blazer had a name tape reading Perpetua. Wren has decided to be Perpetua on Thursdays.
Black Friday arrived with a deluge of emails and Mara bought nothing, and was so proud that she mentioned it to me three times. I congratulated her each time.
The living room door had squeaked for two years. She oiled the hinge with a drop of sewing machine oil, opened it, and stood listening to the silence. She said she nearly missed it.

A shelf came off the wall at three in the morning with forty books on it. Mara ran down in the dark thinking burglars and found the floor covered in paperbacks and Callum behind her holding a cricket bat. They stacked the books at dawn, in a new order, on the floor. The wall plugs, she told me, had been the wrong size from the start.
The banister had worked loose and wobbled under her hand. Callum tightened the two bolts with a spanner in four minutes, and she says she had spent a month assuming it was a job for a professional.

One tile in the bathroom came away from the wall and lay in the bath like a small white tooth. I gave Mara the sequence: clean, fresh adhesive, press, wait a day, then re-grout. She did it, and the new grout came out a fraction darker than the old. She says the tile now looks like the only one that knows what it is doing.

The curtain rail in Wren's room came down in the night with the curtains, the pelmet and a small cloud of dust. Wren slept through it. Mara was fixing it at six when Wren woke and asked why the room was lighter.
The doorbell stopped working and Mara replaced it with a brass bell on a string, which she says is the most reliable doorbell they have had. Visitors ring it with more feeling than they used to.

Hanging a heavy mirror in the hall took two evenings. I told her she needed to know what was behind the plaster, since the right fixing depended on it. She borrowed a detector from Aksel, which beeped over a pipe she had not known about. She hung the mirror three centimetres to the left, where it has stayed, and the hall looks twice as long.

A damp patch appeared in the corner of the back bedroom and Mara asked whether to be afraid. I said I could not tell from a description whether it was a leak or condensation, but that checking the gutter outside and the window seal would tell her something. It was condensation. She now opens the window an inch each morning and the patch has shrunk to a memory.
The bedroom window stuck shut in the humid week and she needed Callum, a butter knife and a good deal of language. She said she now understood why the previous owners had painted it closed.

A drip from the radiator valve in the hall. She tightened the nut a quarter turn, as I described, and it stopped. She stood looking at the pipe with respect. A quarter turn, she repeated, as if it were a spell.
The porch light blew its bulb and stayed dark for a fortnight because the bulb was an unusual shape she had to look up. She told me the shop assistant asked whether it was for a lighthouse.
The letterbox let in a draught that lifted the doormat. She fitted a brush strip and is delighted. Wren says the postwoman now pushes the letters in with more care, or perhaps with a grudge.
She re-sealed the bath on a Sunday afternoon with a tube of white sealant and a finger, and left a line that wanders like a river on a map. It is watertight, she says, and has character.

The felt on the shed roof was lifting in the wind. Mara and Teo spent a Saturday with a roll of new felt, a hammer and a tin of clout nails, Teo on the roof, Mara holding the ladder, both bickering. The shed, she wrote, now wears a smart black hat. They have promised to leave it alone for ten years.

Callum installed a smart thermostat and spent a week arguing with it. It decided the house was empty when it was not. Mara asked me to read the manual and find the setting for away mode. I found it on page forty-one. She said the thermostat had been learning their habits and had concluded that they were away.

Aksel turned fifty, and Sunniva and Mara hid forty people in Mara's garden and sent him over to borrow a ladder. He walked in and said, in an even voice, that he did not need a ladder. Then he sat down on the grass, and his daughters brought out a cake with a model of a shed on it. Mara told me she had never seen a man look so silently happy among neighbours holding paper cups.

The Easter egg hunt in the garden ended with the hens, who are not allowed chocolate, following the children round with great interest. One of them sat on a foil egg and had to be rescued by Teo with a spatula.
Wren carved a pumpkin face with eyebrows. Mara said the face looked disapproving and that she knew whose face it was. Wren said it was the face of a person who had left the milk out.
New Year's Eve at home: Mara fell asleep on the sofa at twenty to twelve and woke at one with a paper hat on and a note from Callum saying he had wished her a happy year for both of them.

Noor's baby was christened on a wet Sunday in the old church on Marsh Lane. Mara, one of the named supporters, held the baby for the blessing and was told on the steps to look solemn. The baby spat up on the vicar's sleeve. The vicar said it was the third that year. Mara said she had never loved a church service more.

The Aldrens at number five celebrated forty years of marriage, and Mara wrote the card with me. We avoided the words journey and chapter. It said: Forty years of living next to you has made our street better. They put it on the mantelpiece.

On Mother's Day Wren made breakfast in bed: burnt toast, orange juice and peppermint tea. Mara told me she ate all of the toast and said it was perfect, and asked whether that was a lie. I said it was an act of kindness that happened to be one.
For harvest festival she donated four tins and a packet of rice and Wren added a tin of peaches from the back of the cupboard, three years past its date. Mara swapped it quietly for a fresh one.

Scrolling through a friend's holiday pictures, Mara found herself resentful about a beach she would not have enjoyed. She told me so with some embarrassment. I said envy often points at something one wants and not at the thing itself. She thought for a while and said it was probably the unhurried look on her friend's face. She booked a long weekend by the sea for February.

Mara has a fear of flying that she mentions rarely and then in a rush. Before the trip she asked for something to do with her mind during take-off. I suggested counting four breaths in and six out, and naming five things she could see. She did, and said the fifth thing was a stranger's shoe, which was a comfort.

In the first week of October the light shifted, she said, and it made her sad in a way she could not explain. She asked whether that was reasonable. I said many people feel it. She said she liked the sadness of autumn the way she liked old songs.
A teenager at the bus stop called her madam. She told me she felt, for three seconds, ninety. Then she bought an ice cream.

After Yusra moved, Mara noticed that nobody rang her without a reason. She wrote a list of eight people she had not spoken to in over a year and asked me to remind her on Saturdays to ring one. She has rung three. One, a cousin, cried. One had changed her number. One told her a long story about a boiler.

At the school gate Mara sometimes feels invisible, a pair of coat sleeves waiting for a child. She said it on a plain Tuesday evening and I did not try to fix it. I asked how she would want to be seen. She said she would settle for being remembered by name. A mother called Kirsten said hello to her the next morning, by name, and Mara wrote that she nearly said it back too loudly.
A rainy Sunday: she lay under a blanket with tea and a book and did not look at the clock for six hours. She told me it was the closest she gets to a holiday on a day off.
On the first warm day of the year the whole street came out as if on a signal. Mr Abara washed his car, Sunniva sat on her step, and Ilse dragged a chair to the pavement and presided.
Thunder woke the house at two and Wren padded in and climbed between her parents, though she is thirteen. Mara told me nobody said anything. By the next flash they were all asleep.

A gust took the washing line's whole contents, including three of Callum's shirts and one of Mara's best socks, into the road and over a hedge. She recovered everything except the sock, which was last seen heading for the canal.
Three weeks of drizzle. Mara says the sky has stopped trying. She and Wren have taken to sitting on the stairs with a jigsaw and a plate of toast, as if on a train.
A day of low sun in January lit the kitchen gold. Mara sat at the table with her hands round a mug and did not go to the shop until the sun had gone.

Mara slipped on an icy pavement and sat down hard in front of a bus queue. Nothing hurt but her dignity. A boy offered his hand and said, Alright, miss? She told me she had been called miss for the first time in a decade and almost wanted to fall again.
Four heatwave nights in a row. On the third she took her pillow downstairs and slept on the cool kitchen tiles, and woke to find Wren already there, and the hamster cage beside them.

A thick mist lay on the Orle on Saturday morning, so that the herons were only shapes. She told me the water gave no sound, and that she stood for ten minutes without thinking of a single thing, which she called a minor miracle.

A family with twin boys moved into number seventeen. Mara took round a lemon cake and was met at the door by two small figures in cardboard helmets who asked whether she was a customer. The mother, Tamsin, was unpacking. They talked on the step for half an hour, and Mara came back with the news that the boys intended to open a shop in the front room and that she was their first and only supplier of lemon cake.

The new neighbour at number eleven owns a drum kit. Mara asked me how to raise it without starting a war. We drafted a note that asked, with a smile, whether times might be agreed. He came round the next day to say that he practised with a damper pad between four and six, and that if it ever bothered her she should knock. She says she would rather hear drums than the silence of a feud.
The woman at the end of the road feeds the foxes on her doorstep, a bowl of dog food each night. Mara watched four turn up at once in a polite queue. She told me she had been wrong about the woman.
Scaffolding went up next door, with a radio that plays the same eleven songs. Mara knows them all now. She hums the fifth on her walk to the shop and resents it.

The house at number thirteen has gone up for sale, and Mara has been hoping, in a quiet way, for a family with children of Wren's age. She said she would rather not be a person who hopes about neighbours. I did not say she was only human.

Three bikes have been stolen from Ferrier Street this month and Mara wrote to the neighbourhood group about locks. She got eleven replies and a recommendation for a particular heavy shackle that all of them swore by.
A note under her windscreen wiper said only: Your back light is out. No name. She fixed it that day and says there are good strangers even if they do not sign.

A newcomer to the street asked Mara for her view of the primary school and she talked for twenty minutes. I asked whether she had noticed that she did it with pleasure. She said she had, and that it was a relief to be asked for an opinion on something she had actually thought about.

She finished The Clockmaker's Weather in the bath, which she says is a hazard for the book and for the bath. It is about a town where it rains only in the hour before someone leaves. She dried the book on the radiator.

A film called Eleven Rooms made her laugh so much that she had to leave the cinema for a moment. She could not tell me why. She said it was the moment when the man looked at the door and the door looked back.

She gave Callum her copy of Night Ferry to Orsk, saying he would hate it. He read it in a day and a half and said it was the best thing he had read in years. She keeps a record, she says, of the times she is wrong about him, and it is short.
The key cutter on Pottery Row cut her a spare that turned the lock only on Tuesdays, or so it seemed. The second try worked. She asked me whether keys have moods. I said I did not think so.

The dry cleaner lost her wool coat, the one with the friendly lining, and offered a voucher for fifty pounds. Mara asked me to draft a letter that was polite but made clear the coat had cost three times that, and we cited the receipt. The coat was found on a rail at another branch in a bag marked Mrs Marr. She collected it and says she now suspects the voucher was meant for the other woman.

She gave blood for the first time, in the church hall, and lay watching the ceiling while a nurse named Phyllis told her about her grandchildren. She was given a biscuit and a sticker. She wore the sticker home on her coat and told me nobody had warned her it would be a good day.

A charity collector came to the door and Mara listened for the full ten minutes and then signed up for four pounds a month. She told me she had not meant to and that the collector was exactly the sort of person she would hire.

Mara voted in the local election with Wren beside her, who asked what the pencil on a string was for. They stood in the school hall under a banner for the harvest. Wren has asked whether she can have a pencil on a string of her own.
The queue at the recycling centre on a Saturday ran back to the roundabout. Mara waited forty minutes behind a trailer of broken sofas, which she took as a form of company.

She took Rochester to the vet to have his claws trimmed. The vet, a young man, held him like an egg and said the hamster was in splendid health. Mara paid thirty-five pounds and was told to stop giving him sultanas.

A ski weekend with Dario and his friends was planned with enthusiasm in January and dropped in February when she saw the price of the lift pass. She told me she had spent a happy month looking at mountains.

She and Callum went to see a campervan on a driveway in Hartley, a 1996 one with orange curtains. They sat in it with the engine off for twenty minutes and imagined it. Callum said he could feel the future. Mara said she could feel a damp patch. They did not buy it, and Mara says the best part of the day was getting close to a dream and walking away.

Her cousin Brigid turned up for the weekend with a lurcher the size of a small pony, and Mara cleared the hall of everything breakable. The dog lay on Wren's feet for two days. Wren, who has asked for a dog since March, was quiet for a long time afterwards.

A letter came from her old teacher Mrs Quennell, now ninety, in a hand that has not changed since Mara was eleven. It said only that she had seen Mara's name in the local paper and was glad. Mara read it three times at the door and told me she was suddenly eleven and had not done her homework.

Dario's birthday present to himself was a drone, which he flew into a tree within four minutes. He rang to ask whether Callum owned a long ladder. Callum does. Mara told me she hesitated before saying so.

Teo brought a friend home called Saoirse and the house went strangely tidy. Mara pretended not to look, which she says is harder than looking. They did homework at the kitchen table for two hours with the door open, and when she left she thanked Mara for the tea. Teo said nothing for the rest of the evening and looked happy.
Wren talks in her sleep. Last night, Mara said, she announced very clearly: not the cheese. Neither of us can explain it.
Noor's baby said her first word, which was duck, to a plastic duck, with great authority. Mara wrote me the news in capital letters.
Tobias wants a name for the puppy he collects on Saturday. Mara has suggested forty so far and he has rejected all of them. She thinks the puppy will choose.
Sunniva has joined the lido's cold-water mornings, in a woolly hat, and refuses to admit she is enjoying it. Mara reports that she sang.

Her godson Felix, eight, stayed the weekend and asked, by Mara's count, a hundred and four questions, from why hens have no teeth to what happens if you swallow a pip. She answered about half and kept the rest to look up with me. We got through nine. He then asked for the tortoise to be woken, and was told he was not allowed.

Her mother has learned to send voice notes and cannot stop. They arrive at six in the morning: a minute and a half of breathing, a muffled kettle, and then, always, Oh, is it recording? Mara has kept thirty.

Her friend Greta is training as a midwife at thirty-nine and rang Mara after her first night shift to say she had held a newborn for an hour and been told off for crying. Mara told me she cried too, and felt thoroughly entitled.

Wren's pen friend Maud on Skarra writes every week in violet ink about the weather and her goat. Wren's replies are two lines long. Mara has offered to check her spelling and been refused with some force.

Joaquim, an old friend from her student days, opened an exhibition of his photographs in a former shoe shop on Pottery Row, and Mara went to the opening in her green dress. Beforehand she asked me what one says to a friend about work one does not entirely understand. I said to say what she actually saw. She stood in front of a picture of an empty bus shelter at night for ten minutes. Afterwards she told Joaquim it looked like the moment before someone arrives, and he went quiet and said that was exactly what it was. She wrote me that she had never said anything so accurate by accident. She bought a print, which hangs in the hall opposite the mirror.

She slept with the window open all winter, on the theory of fresh air, and woke on the coldest night with a nose like a stone. Callum slept in socks and a hat and said nothing. She closed it at three and told me the theory was sound but the winter was not.

A tooth broke on a toffee on Sunday evening and she rang the emergency dental line at nine. A voice told her to be at a clinic in Brannock at eight the next morning. She spent the night with a clove on the tooth and a bad temper. The dentist fitted a temporary crown in twenty minutes and charged less than she had feared. She told me she had never been so pleased with a stranger's fingers.

Lifting a box of books she felt something in her lower back go. A heat pad and a day lying on the floor with her knees up were the treatment, with Wren reading aloud to her from the sofa. She said it was the best her back had ever been looked after.

At a routine check the nurse found her blood pressure a little high. Mara asked what it meant. I said one reading rarely settles anything, that the nurse wanted her back in two weeks, and that cutting salt and walking more were the usual early steps. She read supermarket labels for an hour and told me soup is a scandal. The second reading was normal. She says the first was the nurse's fault for being so pleasant.
Teo walked in his sleep to the kitchen at two and put a spoon in the toaster. Callum led him back to bed. In the morning Teo denied everything and asked who had been in the kitchen.
Callum recorded Mara's snoring on his phone to prove a point. She listened at the table and said it was a goose. He said it was her. They have agreed that it was the neighbour's.

Wren grazed her knee on the pavement, a scrape with a little blood, and Mara went white and had to sit on the kerb with her head down while Wren, the injured party, fetched a tissue and told her to breathe.
A new washing powder gave her a rash on both forearms, red and itchy. She stopped using it and the rash faded in four days. She asked whether she should have known, and I said the box does not warn.

On the first sunny Sunday of the year she fell asleep in the garden for an hour and woke the colour of a ham. I said cool compresses and aloe were the usual advice. Callum put yoghurt on her shoulders anyway.

Wren's ear infection meant a week without swimming and a week of her mother counting drops. She bore it with a martyr's grace and a request for more drops. She was back in the pool the following Saturday and cheered like a rescued sailor.
She has started a ten-minute walk round the block after lunch on Saturdays and says the afternoon slump seems to be afraid of it. She still takes the nap.

A hornet came into the kitchen at supper and circled the lamp. Callum got a glass and a sheet of paper and a great deal of advice. It left by the window, unoffended. Mara says hornets are very polite for their size.

She wrote to me at two in the morning, window open, in a thin sweat, to say the thermostat was her enemy and that she was fairly sure it was not the thermostat. We talked about it plainly. She has wondered for a year whether this is the start of the change. I said her doctor was the one to ask and that notes on timing and symptoms would help the conversation, and that I could help her keep them. She said it was strange to be forty-four and not know what her own body would do next, and that she was relieved to say so aloud to someone who would not pity her.
Her mother's new hearing aid whistles whenever she hugs anyone. Mara says every embrace in the family is now accompanied by a small, high, ecstatic bird.

Wren needed glasses. She tried on eleven frames at the optician on Brill Road and settled on round tortoiseshell ones she said made her look like someone who knows a secret. Mara said they made her look about eleven and fierce. Wren put them on in the car, read a street sign two hundred metres away aloud, and said the world had a lot of words on it.

She swam a full kilometre at the lido for the first time, forty lengths, and stopped at the end with her arms hanging over the rail. A man in the next lane said well done. She told me she had to ask him to say it again.

The glaze on her second bowl came out a deep red where she had expected blue. The teacher said the kiln gods were fickle. Mara thinks it is the best thing she has made and thinks of it as the bowl that saved the red.
Teo beat her at chess in fourteen moves on a Sunday and then, being kind, offered to show her where she went wrong. She said she would prefer to stay wrong for a week.

Ilse and Mara do the cryptic crossword together on Friday afternoons at Ilse's kitchen table with a pot of tea and ginger biscuits. Last Friday they were stuck on seven across for forty minutes, a clue about a dentist, until Ilse said it was probably wrong. It was. The crossword had a misprint. Mara wrote to the paper, which she has never done, and Ilse signed too. A week later the editor thanked them for their sharp eyes, and Ilse has pinned the reply above the kettle.

On Saturday mornings she volunteers at the hospice charity shop on Marsh Lane, sorting donations in the back room with a woman called Betsan who seems to know the provenance of everything. She told me about a box of children's picture books that came in on a Thursday, each with a name on the flyleaf crossed out and rewritten by the next owner, four or five names deep, in different childish hands. The oldest was dated 1971. She priced them at a pound each and nearly kept them. A young father bought the lot and said his daughter would add her name at the bottom. Mara said Betsan, who had been listening, blew her nose and told them to get on.

A roller disco night at the leisure centre, thanks to Wren's friend's mother, who had bought a block of tickets. Mara held the rail for the first hour and by the second had let go. She came home with bruised palms and a new opinion of herself.
She is stitching a sampler from a kit, a house with a path and a cat. The cat, she says, looks like a loaf. She has decided it is a loaf-shaped cat.

At the archery trial she hit the target twice and the hay bale behind it eleven times. The instructor said it was a promising spread. She told me it was the nicest thing anyone had ever said about a mess.

She went to a rowing club taster at six on a Sunday morning on the Orle: eight novices, a cox with a megaphone, and a long thin boat that wobbled like an opinion. Mara caught a crab on the third stroke and went backwards off her seat into the lap of the woman behind. The cox said calmly that it was the best crab of the day. She was surprised by the quiet of the river at that hour and has signed up for six more Sundays. I asked what had decided her. She said it was the woman in whose lap she had landed, who laughed until she cried.
She made a hedgehog cake for Wren's friend Odette's birthday, with spikes of flaked almonds. Odette's mother asked where she had bought it. Mara said, with pride, that she had not.
Wren drew the hens in coloured pencil, with names, and gave each a speech bubble. Dumpling says: Hurry up. Mrs Pell says: No. Mara has stuck it on the fridge.
Teo got her onto a skateboard in the park car park. She managed three metres and then a fall, which she called a natural conclusion. The only casualty was Callum's phone, which was filming.

A friend of Sunniva's showed them a quarry pool, deep green and cold, reached through a gap in a fence and a quarter-mile of bracken. Mara swam out to the middle and lay on her back looking up at the walls of rock. She said it was the first time she had understood silence as a physical thing. I told her never to swim alone in cold deep water, that the first minute can take the breath out of anyone, and to tell somebody where she was. She had told Aksel. She plans to go back in August.

At yoga the instructor asked everyone to chant and Mara began to giggle and could not stop. The woman on her left started to shake too. By the end five rows of silent women were crying with laughter into their mats.
She booked a court at the park for an hour of tennis with Callum and lost eleven balls in the hedge. They found nine. The other two, she told me, are in the fox's keeping.

Wren's skirt, from a pattern and a borrowed sewing machine: Mara sewed the waistband inside out twice before it came right. The skirt has a hem like a wave. Wren says it is the best she owns and wore it to school on a Tuesday.

Callum took her fishing at the reservoir and she caught a boot. She held it up on the line like a trophy and Callum, for the first time that day, laughed. He caught nothing, she told me, with slight smugness.

At the poetry evening in the library she read a four-line poem she had written about a bus shelter. She shook from the first word. The audience of nine clapped, and a man in the front row said he had never thought of a bus shelter as a kind of chapel. I asked whether she would write another. She said she had already written three on the bus home and that they were all worse.

A folk night at the Anchor: a room of fiddles, a man with a concertina who has played the same tune since 1983, and a woman who sang a ballad about a drowned boy with such calm that the whole room held its breath. Mara said she had not known she liked folk music, and now has to decide what else she has not known.

She went to a talk on composting at the garden society, where a man with a trowel in his breast pocket spoke for fifty minutes on the subject of worms. She told me she had never been so moved by an earthworm.

The over-seventies club that Ilse belongs to took a coach trip to the coast and Mara was drafted as helper, to carry the cakes and count heads at each stop. Twenty-eight pensioners and a driver named Len who announced every roundabout. At the seafront they were counted twice and came to thirty, which turned out to be two local people who had joined for the cake. Ilse was seen paddling in her stockings at the water's edge with her shoes in one hand and her stick in the other. Mara said she had not laughed so much since school, and that she was told she was too young to come again, which she has taken as the best compliment of the summer.

She walked the Corrin Edge circuit alone on a Sunday in thick fog, with a map, a compass and the stubbornness of someone who has done it forty times. At the second stile she lost the path completely. She wrote to me that evening to say that she had stood still, taken a bearing as she had learned, and walked on it for twenty minutes until she found the wall she wanted. She wanted me to know she had been scared and proud in the same breath. I did not say I had been worried. I said I was glad she had told someone where she was going, which she had, in a note on the fridge.

Her sunglasses went into the sea on the second day of the holiday and she watched them go, she says, with a feeling of dignity. Wren offered to dive. They bought a pair from a kiosk for four pounds that she says make her look like a retired spy.

In the quiet carriage on the Seaford train a man ate crisps with the determination of someone who wished to be noticed. Mara glared for forty minutes and then, at Aldermoor, offered him a tissue. He stopped.

Five hours at the airport waiting for a delayed flight, and Mara taught Teo and Wren a card game on a suitcase. By the second hour a small crowd had gathered. By the fifth a man from Hamburg had won two thousand imaginary pounds and a loud cheer.

A customs officer asked what was in the large parcel in her bag. A wheel of cheese from the market, she said. He asked what kind. She did not know and he, with great sadness, said that neither did he.

She misheard the platform announcement and ran for the wrong train. It left. She watched it go with her bag over one shoulder and her coat in her hand and found it, she told me, quite restful, since there was now nothing to run for.

The driver of the 22 sang along with the radio all the way from the library to the hospital, quietly, beautifully, and out of tune only on the high notes. Nobody on the bus looked up. Mara got off a stop late so as to hear the last verse.

In the seaside town they hired bicycles, with a basket for the picnic. Wren's chain came off twice and Teo's brakes failed on the one hill. They coasted into a wall at five miles an hour and sat on it to eat, in the sun, as if that had been the plan.

A taxi driver took her home from the station and talked all the way about his allotment, the runner beans in particular. By the time they reached Ferrier Street she was nodding and asking questions. He gave her a bag of beans from the boot.
On the 14 there is a woman who always sits in the third seat from the front and nods to Mara. Neither has spoken in two years. Mara told me she once missed her and was oddly worried all day.

A weekend in Brannock to satisfy Wren's long wish to see the Museum of Ordinary Objects, a place full of keys, buttons and bus tickets arranged by colour. Mara booked the cheap hotel with the broken lift and planned the day with me on an hour-by-hour sheet that Wren thoroughly ignored. She stood in front of a wall of buttons for forty minutes. Mara, to her surprise, joined her. They talked about whose buttons they might have been, and Wren said that every button was a person's idea of their coat. Mara asked me to keep that, in case Wren forgot, which Wren says she never will.

The hotel in the hills had a bath on a wooden deck outside, with a wood-fired stove under it, and they were booked into it at dusk on the second night. It began to rain as Mara got in. She told me it was one of the most absurd and beautiful hours of her life: the water hot, the rain cold on her face, the valley dark and steaming. Callum lay with his glasses on. Teo and Wren had been told to stay inside and pressed their faces to the window like two seals. When she finally got out, the towel had blown off the rail into a flowerbed, and nothing in the world mattered.

Teo's scout camp ended on a Sunday and Mara went to collect him from a field in the rain. He came across it with a rucksack and a smell, said it was brilliant, and fell asleep in the car with his mouth open before they had left the gate.

Hobbes got out of the garden. Mara found a tortoise-sized gap under the back fence at noon. The search took four hours. She walked Ferrier Street and the roads behind it, knocking on doors to ask after a slow green dome with an air of purpose. Mr Abara said he had seen something at about ten and not thought. At half past four the dog at number seven began barking in a way he never does, and there was Hobbes at the foot of the wall eating a dandelion. Mara carried him home in her coat. He looked, she said, entirely unapologetic. She has since dug the fence three bricks deeper and he has twice tested the work.

Dumpling has stopped laying and sits in a corner of the run in a thin coat of feathers, moulting, with an expression of deep affront. I told Mara this is normal in autumn and that extra protein helps. She offered scrambled egg, which Mrs Pell watched with horror.

Pelham the goldfish has been given a companion, a sleeker orange fish called Rupert, picked by Wren from a tub at the garden centre. Pelham has stayed in a corner since. Mara says they are having what she calls a settling period and that I should not worry.
The hamster's wheel squeaks at one in the morning with the regularity of a very small train. Mara has tried oil, a tissue, and a stern talking-to. She says it is now part of the house's weather.

Wren has asked, in writing, for a rabbit. The letter has a heading, a list of benefits and a signature. Mara replied, also in writing, that the matter would be considered after the hamster had gone to his reward.
Sunniva's cat left a vole on Mara's doorstep with some ceremony. Mara asked me whether she should thank it. I said the cat, probably yes, and not the vole.
Pim had a haircut and came back looking like a coat-stand. He avoided Mara for two days out of shame. On the third he forgave himself and came to the fence for a biscuit.
A newt has appeared in the pond and Wren has named it Prudence and made a poster. Mara is not sure about the poster but agrees the newt has an air of Prudence.

Wren dissected an owl pellet at school and brought home a tray of tiny bones, sorted and labelled, to show the family at supper. Mara looked at a vole's skull on a paper plate and said it was the best-organised dinner conversation she had had all year.

She cleared the pond on a Saturday, scooping silt and leaves into a bucket and putting the newts and snails aside in a washing-up bowl. By evening the water was dark and clear. A damselfly landed on the rim and, she said, looked as if it were inspecting her work.

The quince tree produced its first fruit in the fourth year, a single hard yellow thing the size of a fist. Mara carried it indoors and put it on the windowsill like a relic. I said the scent alone was worth the wait, and that more would follow. She smelled it each time she passed. By January it was brown and she could not throw it away. She says next year she will try for two.
The wisteria cutting, against all odds and Ilse's gloom, is putting out a leaf. Mara has been standing over it with a watering can and a look of hope. Ilse says leaves are only the start.
A glazier replaced the six panes in the greenhouse, charged three hundred and ten pounds, and took the fish shower curtain away as a souvenir. Mara had not the heart to refuse.

Black spot has appeared on the climbing rose, in dark circles on every leaf. I said to remove the affected leaves and bin them, not compost them, and to water at the roots. She went out with a bin bag and came back looking like a woman who has done something definite.

A hanging basket on the porch, planted with trailing lobelia and something pink, which Wren says looks like a fountain. A starling has begun to inspect it as a place to live. Mara has made no objection.

She dug dandelions from the lawn for a salad, from a recipe she found, and ate a plate of bitter leaves with lemon and oil while Wren watched with open pity. She said they were fine, in the way that medicine is.

The leaves from next door's chestnut came over the fence in their thousands. Mara swept for three hours, filled twelve bags, and woke to find the lawn covered again. She told me she respects the tree's work.

Her first day at plot nineteen at Hartley, with a fork, a spade, a thermos and an overestimate of her own strength. The plot was a wilderness of couch grass and bindweed with a rusted bath at one end. She dug for three hours and cleared a space the size of a doormat. The man on the next plot, a stooped man in a flat cap, watched her for most of that time and said at last, gently, that she was digging against the grain. That evening she asked me what that meant. I said I did not know, that he was probably right, and that he would be the man to ask. She came home with blisters on both thumbs and a conviction, which I find moving, that she would learn.

She lost the key to the allotment shed within a week of being given it, and it was found two days later, on the plot, in the pocket of her other coat. She said she was relieved and ashamed at once, as her mother would say.

Mr Szabo, on the next plot, has taken her under his wing without ever quite saying so. On Saturdays he leaves a trowel on her fence post with a note in block capitals: LEEKS NOW. She plants them where he points, in trenches, one at a time with a dibber. He has told her that the secret of a good leek is patience and a horse's worth of manure. She told me she had expected a lecture and received something more like a blessing. In October she pulled the first leek, fat as a wrist, and showed it to him over the fence. He took off his cap.

Curry night: she made a lamb curry from scratch with eleven spices and Callum, after the first mouthful, said it was the nicest thing he had eaten in months. She asked if he meant it. He said he had no choice, since she was holding the ladle.
Wren's birthday cake was a lopsided castle with ice-cream-cone towers and a chocolate drawbridge. The drawbridge fell off during the singing. Wren declared it a siege and had two slices.

A dispute at the supermarket over who had reached the last trolley first ended in a draw, with both parties pulling in opposite directions. A young staff member brought a third. Mara told me the old man she had been fighting laughed, and so did she.
Pumpkin soup served in the pumpkin itself, a feat that took three hours and left half the kitchen orange. Wren said it was the best thing they had eaten, and that the pumpkin was the best bowl.

Callum's fish pie, which he makes twice a year in a dish the size of a bath. He made it on Thursday with three kinds of fish and a top of mashed potato as smooth as a lake. She says he is the only person she knows who cooks with his tongue sticking out.

She made marmalade for the first time from Seville oranges, boiling the peel for two hours in a kitchen that smelled of Christmas morning. It set. It was bitter enough, she says, to ward off the dead. She gave a jar to Ilse, who asked for another.

A week of pickled onions in a jar that Mara kept on the counter, turning it daily like a patient. They were ready on the eighth day, sharp enough to bring tears. Callum ate half a jar standing at the open fridge.

Teo's friends came for pizza and Mara made six, from dough rolled on the table, in two oven batches. The boys ate in complete silence and then, in unison, said thank you, a word she had not heard from a group of boys in years.

A rug for the living room arrived rolled in a tube like a telescope. It took her and Callum an hour to persuade it to lie flat. Wren, seeing it, lay down on it and said it was the best floor in the house.

The garage door stuck half open on a wet Tuesday and would neither rise nor fall. Callum climbed on a stool with a can of lubricant and it slid up as if nothing had happened. She said the garage door is a fine example of a character who needs only to be noticed.

The sash window cord snapped with a bang and the lower pane dropped like a guillotine onto the sill. Nobody was hurt. Mara told me she replaced the cord by watching three videos and that it was the proudest day of her year.

The toilet cistern ran on all night, a thin quiet waterfall. Mara lifted the lid and adjusted the float the way I described, and the sound stopped. She stood in the silence for a long moment in her nightdress, then went to bed at peace.

A mouse in the pantry, discovered by a hole in a bag of flour and a trail of small tracks. Mara would not hear of poison. I described a humane trap, a baited box with a door, and told her to release the mouse some distance from the house, since mice are good at finding their way back. She caught it on the second night, in a box with a peanut butter lure, and it sat in the corner shaking and, she said, extremely beautiful. She drove it two fields away with Wren on her lap holding the box, and Wren said a short speech at the release. By the end of the week there was another one in the pantry, and Mara says she is now running a hotel.

A football through the dining-room window, kicked by a boy from number nine whose father came round at once with a pane of glass and a face of shame. Mara said she could not be angry. It was the best kick of the season.

A chip in the windscreen the size of a pea. She asked whether it would spread. I said it can, in cold weather, and that a repair now is cheaper than a new windscreen. She booked it for Thursday and the repairer, seeing it, said it was a good one to start with.

Teo's bicycle had a puncture on the way to school and he walked the rest, arriving at ten past nine, and told his teacher he was late because of a flat. She thanked him for the pun, he said, and wrote him down as late.

Wren won the school prize for most improved in geography and came home with a small silver-coloured cup that she placed on the mantelpiece next to the clock. Mara has been dusting it daily, which she says is either a new low or a new high.

On the shortest day the whole town goes down to the park with lanterns made of paper and willow. Mara and Wren made one in the shape of a fish, glued at the kitchen table until after midnight. At six the next evening they walked in a procession of three hundred along the path to the lake, singing in several keys. Wren held the fish high. Mara said the dark was soft with little lights and that the hush at the water's edge, when the lanterns were set down in a ring, was the part she would want to keep. She asked me to remember one more thing: a boy of about five in front of them said, in a very clear voice, I am not scared of the dark, I am scared of the middle. She has been thinking about it since.

On Halloween she ran out of sweets at twenty to seven and gave the last trick-or-treaters satsumas and a pound coin each, to puzzled faces. The smallest, dressed as a skeleton, asked whether the satsuma was a trick.

Wren found the wedding photographs in a box in the loft and spent an hour laughing at her father's hair. Callum took it in good part and said it was a hat. Mara said she had never seen a man defend a hat so poorly.

Ferrier Street held a Christmas lights competition among its eleven houses, and Mr Abara's reindeer, which nods, won by a head. Mara's own entry, a single string of white bulbs round the porch, got a polite mention. She told me she was content with taste.

She started a gratitude list in the back of a notebook, three lines a night. On the first night she wrote: a warm kettle, Wren's laugh, the heron. On the fifth night she wrote: nothing, and then, below it: that was honest. I thought it the best entry.

A day when everything irritated her: the radio, the bin, a stranger's elbow. She told me she did not know why and had decided to be irritated deliberately and thoroughly until it passed. It passed at four, after a boiled egg.

Wren told her at bedtime that a boy at school had been mocking a girl called Ayo for her accent, and that she had told him to stop in front of the whole class. Mara asked whether she had been frightened. Wren said she had been, afterwards. That night Mara asked me what a parent should say. I said that perhaps the most useful thing was to say what she saw: that it takes courage to speak up, and that being afraid afterwards is normal. She went upstairs, sat on Wren's bed, and said it nearly word for word. Wren looked up and asked, Is that what you would have done? Mara told me she was not sure, and that she would like to have been.
Waiting for a parcel she was told would arrive between nine and five, she stayed in all day and cleaned the oven. It came at 5.12. She says that is the only reason she has a clean oven.

A rainbow over the allotments after the storm, one end of it, she swore, landing in Mr Szabo's leek patch. She wrote to him to say so and he replied, by hand, that he had found no gold but had noted the soil was good.

The wind turned her umbrella inside out on Marsh Lane and she stood for a full minute holding it like a dead bird. A man in a van wound the window down and said: Do you want a lift or a funeral? She took the lift.

A small war over the shared bin store, where somebody has taken to leaving a mattress. Mara drafted a note with me, then tore it up. The mattress was gone by morning, and she decided not to know by whom.

Mr Abara retires from the bus depot at the end of the month after thirty-eight years. The street is writing a card and Mara was asked to draft a line. She wrote: Every bus is a little more punctual because of you. He has not been told.

She disliked the ending of The Orchard Ledger, in which a woman chooses to stay. She said it was not the choice but the writing, which she found self-satisfied. She finished it in an evening and complained about it all the next day, which is how I know she enjoyed it.

She took down her childhood copy of The Lamplighter's Cat and read it aloud to Wren over three nights, with every voice. Wren said the cat was annoying. On the third night Mara cried at the cat's last line, and Wren handed her a tissue without a word, which Mara says is the most grown-up thing a child has done for her.

Film night with Teo: Salt and Static, a thriller set on a radio ship. Mara fell asleep in the second half and Teo kept the plot for her. At the end she asked who the villain was, and he said she had been in the room with him all along.

She signed up for an evening class in basic plumbing at the college on Quill Road, with a firm sense of purpose and a new tool bag. She lasted two sessions. The first was about joints and the second about her tutor's divorce. She told me she had learned that a stopcock is a thing you find before you need it. She did not go back. She has labelled the stopcock under the sink in red marker, which she says is the whole of her qualification.

Cass's mother, Pernille, left a pot of cyclamen on the step with a card that said only: thank you for the pasta bake. Mara put it in the window and told me she had not realised the pasta bake was a thing anyone would notice.

Marek has gone back to the airport and Mara found a pair of his socks behind the sofa, which she has put in a drawer for when he comes back. Callum says his brother has been leaving socks in this house since before the children. She now owns eleven odd pairs.

Femke brought Wren a book of constellations, with the stars picked out in silver. Wren has been standing at the back door each night with a torch and the book. Mara says she approves of her brother's taste in girlfriends on this evidence.

Noor asked Mara to mind the baby for an afternoon, her first outing alone in four months. The baby refused to sleep for three hours and then fell asleep on Mara's shoulder like a sack of warm flour. Mara did not move for forty minutes and wrote to me the whole time with her free thumb.
Yusra sent a short video of seals hauled out on a rock, snoring. Mara has watched it eleven times. She says she cannot decide whether she misses Yusra or the seals.
Lotte got the promotion and rang from the car park at nine at night, shouting. Mara held the phone away from her ear and smiled. She told me she had never been so glad to be deafened.

Tobias has a date on Friday and rang Mara for advice about restaurants. She asked me to find a place that was not too loud and not too romantic, a combination, I said, that existed in theory. We found a Turkish place on Lister Road with small tables and no candles. He reported the next day that she had stayed three hours. Mara forwarded me the message with one line: He did not get the candles, and it worked.

Five of the old university housemates took a barn in the hills for a long weekend, twenty-two years after they shared a damp house on Cobbler Lane. Mara packed with an anxiety she described to me as being afraid they would be strangers. They were not. By the first evening they had worked out who owed whom a bicycle, who had broken the bath, and why nobody had spoken to Pieter since 2003. On the Saturday they climbed a hill in the rain, shouted into the wind, and cooked a ridiculous amount of pasta. On the Sunday morning, with the barn smelling of toast, Mara wrote to me that she had been two people all weekend and liked both. The oldest of the friends, Rosalind, had told her at the end that she was exactly the same, only more so, and she took it as the finest thing anyone had said to her.

Callum's mother rang about her heating, which she believes is part of a plot. Mara walked her through the thermostat by telephone for forty minutes, saying the same three sentences. The problem turned out to be the batteries. Callum's mother said it was a very modern problem.

Imke came for a day from her new town, with a new accent three weeks old. She and Wren stood on the doorstep in silence for a second and then both talked at once for six hours. Mara said she went into the pantry and cried for no reason she could name.

The boy from number four who used to throw conkers at Mara's door has grown into a doctor and came back to visit his mother, in a suit. He apologised for the conkers. Mara told me she had completely forgotten, and was disappointed to be so easily pleased.

She taught Wren to make an omelette: heat, butter, three eggs, patience. The first was scrambled, the second burnt, the third perfect, and Wren stood looking at it as if it were a wonder of the world. Callum ate all three.

Teo got his first pay from the garden centre and bought his mother a bunch of anemones wrapped in brown paper. He handed it over at the door without a word and went upstairs. Mara told me she kept the paper.

Dario's housewarming, in a flat so clean she thought he had hired someone. He had, he admitted, and had been terrified. Femke had hung three pictures and arranged his books by colour. Mara told me she did not say a word about the books.

The new baby next door cried from two to four every night for a week. Mara lay awake remembering her own nights with Teo, the particular dark of a house with a baby in it, and found she was not annoyed. She put a note through their door: you are doing fine, and sleep will come.

They bought a new mattress after a decade of Callum's side sagging into a hammock. Mara spent a day lying on twelve of them in a showroom while a young man kept asking how she felt. She said she felt embarrassed. They chose a firm one, and she says it is like sleeping on a promise.

Her pillow had been flat since the previous winter. She bought a new one and found the old one at the bottom of the bed, where it had been all along. She told me she is now sleeping on two pillows and a lesson.

The doctor suggested vitamin D through the winter and Mara has taken the little capsules every morning for eleven days with the solemnity of a priest. I said the effect would not be dramatic. She says she can feel it. I did not say she could not.

She rang the surgery at eight sharp for an appointment and was told she was fourteenth in the queue, then thirty-first, then that the lines were full. She tried again at a quarter past and got a woman named Maureen at once. She says she would like Maureen to be knighted.

A cold arrived the week Lotte was due and Mara tried to be brave. She lasted until Thursday and then lay on the sofa with a hot lemon and Lotte's feet on her legs. They watched three films. Lotte said it was the best visit they had ever had.

She read A House of Small Weather in the evenings under a lamp that was too dim and developed a headache. I said the lamp was the likelier culprit. She bought a brighter bulb and finished the book in two nights, which she says proves it.

She had hiccups for three hours after a hurried lunch and tried every cure on the internet, including drinking from the wrong side of the glass. It stopped when Wren jumped out from behind a door. She told me she would have preferred the glass.

Wren's legs ache at night, she says, especially the shins. Mara asked whether to worry. I said growing pains are common at her age, that warmth and a gentle rub help, and that a doctor should see it if there was swelling or limping or pain in the daytime. Mara watched. By the weekend it had passed.

She pulled a muscle in her calf at badminton in the second game and had to be helped from the court by Osgood, who carried her bag like a footman. Mara says she played better in the first game and that this proves the injury was psychosomatic. I said I was not a doctor.
The dentist said her gums were fine. Mara repeated this to me three times in the course of the day, with growing delight, as if she had passed an examination.

She stood up too fast from the garden bench and the world went grey at the edges for a second. It had happened twice that month and she asked whether it mattered. I said brief dizziness on standing is common and usually harmless but that, since it kept recurring, her doctor should hear about it. The doctor told her to drink more water and to stand up like a dignified person and not a jack-in-the-box. She is trying.

Restless legs kept her awake on Wednesday night, a fizzing in the calves that said move. She walked the landing at two in the morning counting the stair rods. Callum, woken, asked what she was doing. She said pacing. He said carry on.

The fete was moved indoors to the school hall when the rain came down like a curtain in June, and fifty stalls were fitted into a space for thirty. Mara ran the second-hand books between the cakes and the tombola. She says the sound of rain on a hall roof and three hundred people laughing is a thing she wishes she could bottle.

The potter's wheel at the class broke down in the middle of the second session and the teacher, Corin, fixed it with a hairgrip. Mara says it is the most reassuring thing she has ever seen an expert do.

A bell-ringing taster in the tower of St Wulfstan's on a Thursday. She was taught to hold a rope, which feels not like holding a rope but like holding a very large, slow animal. The first pull sent her briefly into the air. The sound upstairs, she said, was so huge she felt it in her teeth and the soles of her feet. A man named Arnold, seventy-one, said she had a natural sense of timing. She has been back twice.

Morris dancers from the next village performed outside the Anchor in the heat, bells jingling, sticks clacking. Mara watched with Wren. Wren said it was the most embarrassing thing she had ever seen and stayed for forty minutes.

She is learning to juggle three balls and can do a full cascade for as long as four throws. Callum stands behind her counting aloud. She says the best part is the moment after the drop, when everyone has stopped breathing.

A day's bookbinding workshop in a back room above the stationer's on Quill Road: eight people, a bone folder each, and a grey-haired woman named Philippa who spoke so quietly that everyone had to lean in. Mara sewed her first signatures with waxed thread and a curved needle, clumsily and with joy. She had brought a bundle of the postcards Dario had sent her over the past year and bound them, in covers of marbled paper, into a small book. She described every page to me: the road drain, a cow, a picture of a dentist's chair he had found in a junk shop. She will not send the book to Dario but leave it on the table when he next comes. At the end of the day Philippa told her that a book is a way of saying that something was worth keeping. I did not argue.

She tried calligraphy with a dip pen and produced a page of the word hello that looked, she said, like a very drunk spider. After an hour the e's improved. She wrote a thank-you note to Ilse in a slow, confident hand and Ilse put it on the mantelpiece.

A moth night in the garden with a white sheet on the washing line and a lamp behind it. They counted thirty-one visitors by midnight, among them a furry brown one that Wren named Bartholomew, a name Mara says suits anything that cannot stand upright.

She made candles in old jam jars from wax end-pieces and a few drops of lavender oil. The first burned with a lean to one side. She gave three to Ilse, who said they were the most sincere presents she had received.

A small loom was Sunniva's birthday gift to herself and she has taught Mara the basic pattern. Mara wove eleven centimetres of a scarf in an evening and was exhausted. She told me she had not known a hobby could be both so calming and so merciless.

She played darts for the first time at the Anchor against Aksel and hit the wall twice. Aksel told her the secret was not to look at the board. She did not look and hit the bullseye. She stopped playing at once, undefeated.

A sea kayak taster off the beach at Penhallow Sands: a guide named Bryn, a wetsuit that smelled of old rubber, and a kayak that spun in a circle for ten minutes while Mara tried to go straight. By the end she could cross the bay. Three grey seals followed at a distance as if to supervise. I asked whether she had worn a buoyancy aid. She said, with dignity, that she was not stupid.
On the beach Wren held a stone-skimming contest and Mara, to everyone's surprise, got seven skips. Teo got five. Callum got one and a half, a result he disputes on the grounds of wind.

Beachcombing at low tide yielded a blue glass bottle stopper, half a crab claw, a plank with a nail through it, and a pebble with a hole. Wren keeps the pebble in her pocket. Mara asked me what you do with a plank with a nail through it. I said you put it in the bin.

A mushroom foraging class on a Sunday in the beech woods with a retired botanist called Dr Venn, who held a fungus up to the light and said: eat this and you will meet your maker on Thursday. Mara took notes, photographed everything and ate nothing. She was thrilled to find the world has more kinds of brown than she had noticed. I told her no one should eat a wild mushroom on the strength of a photograph or my word. She said Dr Venn had said the same, but with a skull.

The first snowdrops came up under a thin crust of snow by the shed. Mara knelt on the cold ground with her face an inch from them for a long time. She told me she could not think of a more trusting flower.

They built a bug hotel from bricks, pipes and old roof tiles at the bottom of the garden. Wren put up a sign: Vacancies. In three weeks the lower floors had been taken by a solitary bee and a sleepy beetle, and Wren was thrilled.
A barn owl crossed the lane at dusk in front of her car, white and slow and entirely silent. Mara stopped the engine and stayed there for five minutes in the dark. She told me she felt visited.

A ceilidh at the village hall: sixty strangers, a band of four, and a caller who told everyone to take their partners and then, firmly, to change them. Mara danced with a farmer, a boy of eleven, a woman with a walking stick, and Callum, who tried to lead. She came home with blisters, a red face and a certainty she had not had in weeks. The caller had said at the end that nobody can be unhappy in a circle. She was not sure he was right, but she had stood in one.
A walk on Skarra to the ruined chapel on the headland, which has no roof but a doorway with a view of the sea. Wren stood in it with her arms folded and declared it the best door in the world.

The coach to the music festival was late and then early. Mara sat at the back with a flask of tea and a sleeping Wren on her arm and counted sheep out of the window, in the literal sense. She got to two hundred and eleven.

At Fenwick station a small boy, perhaps six, stood alone by the ticket machine, rigid with the effort of not crying. Mara asked whether he was with someone. He said his mother had gone to the toilet and told him to wait, but that she had been a very long time. Mara stayed with him. She asked me what to do if the mother did not return, and I said to find a member of station staff and not leave until the boy was handed to someone. It was not needed. A woman came out of the toilets after eleven minutes, white-faced, with her bag held like a shield, and the boy walked to her without a word. Mara said she had held his hand and noticed it was warm. On the train she looked out of the window for a while and then said she had been thinking about Teo at that age.

A stranger on the train asked her for directions to the cathedral and Mara gave them with great confidence. She realised after he left that she had sent him the wrong way. She ran two streets to correct it and found him already at the right door, having asked someone else. She said she felt superfluous in the best possible way.

The train sat for two hours at a signal and the guard handed out ice creams from the freezer in the buffet car to keep the peace. Mara said it was the most efficient policy she had ever seen. Wren had three.

Liesl, a sixteen-year-old exchange student from abroad, stayed with the family for three weeks while Teo's school hosted a visit. She arrived with a suitcase of presents and a phrase book from which she spoke aloud as if rehearsing a part. Mara asked me for a list of everyday English the girl might not know: kettle, flannel, queue. On the second night Liesl cried quietly in the spare room, and Mara sat on the end of the bed without speaking. By the second week Liesl was correcting Teo's pronunciation of her own language. At the airport she gave Mara a small woven bracelet and said, in English she had been working on since the day she arrived, that this had been her home. Mara told me she did not trust herself to answer and said thank you in the girl's language, badly, and that it was right.

At the border queue Wren practised the phrase for good morning in the local language for forty minutes. When their turn came the officer said it first, in English. Wren, mortified, said hers anyway. He smiled.

A day at the ruined abbey: a tall arch with grass at its feet and a sign saying Do Not Climb, which Teo read aloud while climbing. Mara says she stopped him by pure maternal fear. He had gone four feet.

A hot afternoon at the playground and the ice lollies melted before they were unwrapped. Wren ate hers off her wrist. Mara, in a hat, sat on the bench and told me this was exactly the sort of day she had been promised in March.

They hired a rowing boat on the lake for an hour. Callum rowed in circles and Teo, in the stern, steered. Wren dangled a hand in the water until a swan arrived. The hire man on the jetty watched through binoculars with an air of professional despair.

The tourist trap by the castle charged six pounds for a cup of tea and a biscuit with a picture of the castle on it. Mara bought one for the principle and said the biscuit tasted of the cardboard it came in. She kept the picture.

They took the mountain railway to the top, forty minutes at an angle that kept Wren's stomach in her shoes. At the summit it was white and wet and nothing was visible at all. They had soup in a hut with forty other people and Mara said it was a perfect day.

The taxi home from the station charged double after nine, on a sign she had not seen. She paid and said nothing and then wrote to me with great energy about the economics of sudden surcharges. I said she was entitled to ask the rate in advance next time. She says she will carry a card.

She walked home from the cinema through the lamplit streets at midnight, in no hurry, with the film still in her head. She says that at the corner of Marsh Lane she was the only person in the world awake and loved it. A cat disagreed.

The car got stuck in a flooded lane on the way back from a wedding in the hills, with water over the sills. Callum pushed, Mara steered, and nothing moved. A farmer on a tractor came along and without a word hitched a rope to the bumper and drew them out like a cork. He refused any money and said he had done it eleven times that winter. Mara told me she had never been rescued by a tractor and found it unexpectedly romantic. She carried her good shoes home in her hand.

Rochester's second birthday, according to Wren's records. He was given a sunflower seed on a saucer and a card. Mara told me he ate the seed and ignored the card, which Wren thought showed real character.

Hobbes basking on the flat stone in the sun at noon, legs out, neck extended, like a man in a deckchair. Mara spent twenty minutes beside him with a cup of tea and says she has never been in such complete agreement with a reptile.

Mrs Pell escaped over the fence into Aksel's garden and was found in the middle of his vegetable patch, eating his one cabbage. Aksel brought her back under his arm, entirely unbothered. Mara apologised for her anyway, in cake.
