Pim has learned to open the gate from the inside by lifting the latch with his nose. The neighbours have tied a knot in the latch. Pim has learned to untie the knot. Mara says it is a war in which she is neutral and a little proud.
A parrot at the end of the road has learned to call out Mara in the voice of its owner. She turned round three times on Monday before she understood. She told me she had never been so summoned.
Wren found a snail in the lettuce, named it Gustav, and moved it to a safe place under a flowerpot. By Thursday there were four snails in the safe place and Wren was running what Mara calls a refuge.
Ilse's budgie, Mr Pickering, has learned to say Put the kettle on in Ilse's exact voice. Mara says she has been in Ilse's kitchen three times when Ilse was out of the room and nearly obeyed.

Mr Abara's sister visited from the coast for the weekend and sang in his garden on Saturday evening, in a clear contralto, hymns and a couple of songs Mara did not know. Half the street stood at their windows. Mr Abara looked embarrassed, then proud. Mara told me she was glad she had been home.

A camera Callum put at the bottom of the garden caught a badger at two in the morning, nose down, shuffling along the fence. Wren has watched the clip until the badger has become a character. She named him Alfred. Mara says that every evening now she looks for him.

The runner beans are producing at such a rate that Mara has taken to leaving carrier bags of them on doorsteps with no note. Mr Abara left a bag back, of onions. A barter, she told me, has started in the street.

The sweet peas Sunniva gave her flower along the fence, in a scent that fills the garden at dusk. Mara picked a jar of them and put it by Wren's bed. Wren, who does not usually notice, said her room smelled like a letter.

She started to trim the hedge in April and found a wren's nest in the middle, with five eggs the size of peas. She stopped cutting, put the shears away, and has told the neighbours not to touch the hedge until June. They are cooperating, with some humour.

A row of molehills appeared across the lawn overnight, fine dark soil like cocoa. Mara asked how to get rid of the mole. I said that it is hard to do humanely and that she might consider living with it. She counts the molehills each morning now, and has named the mole Gordon.

The council delivered free compost to a depot behind the library and Mara queued with a wheelbarrow behind a man with a shovel and a woman with ten buckets. They filled up at the back of a lorry in the rain. She said it was the most communal thing she had done since the street party.

She asked about weedkiller for the path and I told her that boiling water was a less harmful way but that, honestly, scrubbing worked. She boiled a kettle and poured it over the weeds in the cracks. They were back in a fortnight, as she had expected, and she told me she liked their persistence.

A wigwam of hazel sticks for the beans, tied at the top with string and the end of an old scarf. Wren sat inside it for most of Sunday, reading, in the green dusk. The beans have not yet climbed but they, said Mara, are not the point.

A butterfly count on the buddleia on a bright August afternoon: two peacocks, a red admiral, four whites and a comma. Mara and Wren recorded the numbers in a notebook and sent them to a national count she had found on an app. She told me looking for butterflies made her slow.

Callum fitted a water butt to the downpipe on Saturday and by Sunday evening it was full. Mara stood by it with a watering can in an attitude of triumph. It rained again at midnight and the butt overflowed onto the path, and she says it is the first problem she has been glad to have.

The garden bench had gone grey and splintery. She sanded it on a Sunday and painted it duck-egg blue with Wren's help, which was extensive. They sat on it, half wet, for the afternoon and left two stripes on the backs of their legs.

Onions laid out to dry on a wire rack in the garage like a small pale army, forty-two of them. She counted them twice. Callum says it is the first time he has seen a woman look at a vegetable with pride.

The great ash tree at the end of Ferrier Street was felled one grey Tuesday because it was diseased. The whole street came out to watch in silence, in coats. It took five hours and the chainsaw sounded like something being made to apologise. Ilse stood at her gate with her stick and did not speak. Afterwards Mara counted the rings on the stump: a hundred and four. Someone has put a vase of flowers on it.

The seed catalogue arrived in January and she spent a whole evening circling things in pencil. She asked me to work out what she would pay if she bought them all. I said it came to three hundred and forty pounds. She said she would choose twelve.

The allotment society's competition for the heaviest marrow was won by Mr Szabo with a monster of eleven kilos, which he presented as if it were a baby. Mara's, grown from seed under his instruction, weighed four and a half and won a card for Most Improved. She kept the card and ate the marrow, stuffed, over three days. She told me she had learned something about being second.

She made chocolate truffles for the neighbours' Christmas presents, rolled in cocoa and chopped nuts. The first batch was too soft; the second too hard; the third perfect and promptly eaten by Callum. She made a fourth, wrapped them, and hid them in the garage.
Wren and Teo had a long argument about whether oven chips are better than fried. Mara adjudicated with a plate of each and declared a tie. Neither child spoke to her for two hours.

She has begun to put short notes in Wren's lunchbox: a riddle, a joke, a line from a poem. Wren pretends to be embarrassed and keeps them in a tin. Mara found the tin by accident while looking for a plaster and put the lid back at once.
Dario sent her a cookbook for Christmas titled Fifty Ways With a Lentil. She says it is a message but cannot decide what it is. She has made four recipes and Wren has refused two.

The Yorkshire puddings did not rise on Sunday. They lay at the bottom of the tin like small pale pancakes. Mara says it was because the fat was not hot enough. Callum says it was because she opened the oven door. They ate them with gravy, with great solemnity.

She cooked lasagne for twelve for Wren's club supper, in two big dishes, and asked me to help with the timings so both would come out at six. I made a table of tasks by the half hour. They came out at six-oh-five. Mara said it was the first time in her life she had served a meal on time. Wren said the lasagne was fine, but that the sauce tasted of effort.

The butcher on Lister Road, a man named Mr Pratt who wears a straw boater, told her to cook the lamb for less time than she thought. She followed his advice. It was pink and tender. She says she would follow Mr Pratt into a river.

She reads recipes like novels, in bed, without ever intending to cook them. She told me the best she read last month was a plain account of a Portuguese rice dish, written with such tenderness that she felt she had been invited.

The vending machine at the leisure centre swallowed her coin and gave her nothing. She hit it gently, then not gently, then stood with her forehead against the glass. A small boy beside her put in a coin of his own and handed her the chocolate bar. She told me she was grateful and slightly ashamed.

She returned a green dress to a shop in Brannock because it did not fit, and the assistant said: you were here in March, you took the blue one. Mara said she was astonished to be remembered. The assistant said she had a lovely way of choosing.

The back door lock jammed one wet morning with Mara outside it and the kettle on inside. She tried a hairgrip, a credit card and a stern talk. Callum came home at noon and opened it with a drop of oil and a wiggle. She had been locked out of her own kitchen for four hours, she told me, but it had given her a good view of the hens.

The garden gate had sagged off one hinge and dragged along the path with a groan like a ship. Callum fitted a new hinge and a spring. It now swings and shuts itself with a click she can hear from the kitchen and has come to love.

A crack appeared in the front wall of the house, thin as a pencil line, running from the corner of the window up towards the roof. She asked whether the house was moving. I said many houses show hairline cracks and most are harmless, but that a structural engineer was the right person to say, especially as this one was new. She measured it with a ruler and marked each end in pencil with a date, as I suggested. After two months it had not grown. The engineer called it a settling crack from the dry summer and said it would be filled and forgotten. She says she is a little disappointed not to be living in a ruin.

A light switch in the hall began to crackle and smell faintly of burning. Mara turned off the circuit at the board, as I urged, and would not touch the switch until an electrician had been. He came on the Friday, a quiet man named Ewan, who said she had done well to stop. The wiring behind it was old and charred.

She tiled the kitchen splashback herself over a long weekend, a thing she had wanted to do for three years and feared for two of them. I helped her sketch it out from the measurements she gave me: eighteen tiles across, six up, a cut at the end by the window. She did the first row on Saturday morning at a slant that she did not see until lunch. She took it off and began again with a spirit level. By Sunday evening it was done, with grout she put in with her finger. The tiles are white with a faint green in them like glass. Callum stood with his arms folded for a full minute and said it looked professional, which she took as a lie and then, after a moment, as a compliment.

She painted Wren's room, finally, in a pale blue that Wren chose and then disliked. It was too blue, Wren said. Mara said it would be fine in a week. In a week Wren said it was the best colour in the house.

A washing line strung across the garden between a hook on the shed and the pear tree. Mara tested it with a full basket of sheets. It held. Teo, passing, ducked under it with great drama. She says she has joined the people who own a washing line, and that they are a tribe.
Three shelves for the hall, built from planks she bought at the timber yard, sanded, stained and fixed with brackets. They are the first thing she has ever made that Callum did not offer to improve.

Teo's school leavers' prom is in June and he has asked, with the air of a man requesting a loan, whether he may borrow his father's good jacket. Mara has been going through old photographs. They found a navy one that fits. Teo looked at himself in the mirror and said nothing for a long time.

Mara's mother came to stay for Christmas, the first time in four years she had agreed to leave Seaford. Mara prepared for a month: a list of foods her mother could not eat, a chair with arms, a hot water bottle in the spare bed. She asked me to remind her of three things not to say, and we agreed on: you should have told me, you are too thin, and why do you not move nearer. She lasted until Boxing Day. Then, in the kitchen with her hands in the sink, she said all three in a rush, and her mother laughed, a laugh Mara said she had not heard in a decade, and replied that she had been wondering when. They washed up together. On the way to the station on the twenty-eighth her mother said she would think about it, and Mara has not stopped thinking about the word.

She writes the Christmas card list on the back of an envelope every year and loses it by the end of November. This year she asked me to keep it. I have forty-two names. She added three more on the fourteenth of December and said, with resignation, that we were now one of those families.

Wren's first night away from home with a friend, at Odette's, and Mara surprised herself by sleeping badly. At six in the morning she found herself standing in Wren's empty room, adjusting the curtain. She told me she was being ridiculous. I said that was not the word I would use.

The replies to the wedding invitation arrived in a disorderly stream: six yeses, two noes, one cheerful maybe and a card with a drawing of a goose. Mara has made a table. She says the goose is probably Noor's cousin and that she has put him down as a yes.

On New Year's Day she wrote three resolutions: to walk more, to call her mother on Sundays, and to stop saying yes to things she meant to refuse. By the end of January she had managed the second and, she told me, excelled at the third, which was refusing a coffee morning.

A leaving party for Mr Quill, Wren's maths teacher, in the school canteen. Mara took a tray of flapjacks. Mr Quill, who is retiring to a cottage by the sea, said he would be sorry to leave the pupils and a little sorry to leave the paperwork. Mara told me he held her hand a second too long and said, Wren is a delight, and turned away.

A talk in the library by a woman who had rowed across an ocean, and Mara signed up on the spur of the moment to ask a question. She did. It was about the loneliness. The woman paused and said it was not what she had expected to feel, and that it had gone on to be the point. Mara told me she walked home with the sentence in her mouth like a sweet.

She said on Tuesday that she had become her mother. She had folded a tea towel into a perfect rectangle, said Mind the step to an empty hall, and heard herself, in the car, say that it was nearly time. I asked whether she minded. She considered it for a long while and said she minded less than she had expected, since her mother, whatever else, had always been on time and always known where the tea towels were. She added that Wren had told her that same evening that she looked like a person who had everything under control, and that she had found this funnier than anything on television.

Tidying the airing cupboard at eleven at night, she told me, was a way of not thinking about the next day. She folded forty-one towels. She said she would like it noted that she knew exactly what she was doing and had done it anyway.

A clear night of stars on the back step with a flask, and a meteor that crossed the whole length of the sky and went out behind the pear tree. Mara said it was gone before she could make a wish. Wren said it was fine, she had made one for both.

On a day she described as useless she wrote to me at noon that she could not do anything, not even decide what to eat. I said perhaps we could make the day very small. Three tasks only: water the hens, post the letter, eat something warm. She did the first two by one o'clock and, by two, a bowl of soup. At the end of the day she wrote that she had done more than she thought, and that three small tasks had been the kind of rope she could hold. I did not say it was her rope.

The first evening of the year when it was still light at seven. She stood on the front step with a mug and said hello to the whole street. She told me she had not realised how long the dark had lasted until it ended.

She has taken to wearing a sleep mask, a black silk one that Wren picked, and says she now sleeps like a woman in a hotel advertisement. Callum says she looks like a very elegant burglar. She wears it anyway and says the dark is worth the insult.

When she cannot sleep she counts backwards from three hundred in sevens, a trick from a puzzle book. She has never got below a hundred and seventy. She told me this was proof that it worked, or that she was bad at sevens.
After a ten-mile walk on the downs she slept eleven hours and woke at noon not knowing the day. Callum had brought tea and left it to go cold. She called it the best night's work of her life.

Her mornings begin with stiffness in the hips. I described three stretches from a physiotherapy leaflet she had mentioned, and she now does them on the bedroom floor with Wren's hamster watching from his cage. It has helped, she says, though not as much as the hamster's approval.

An eye infection, red and gluey, kept her home for two days. She lay in a dark room listening to a long audiobook about a railway. She could not focus on the label of the drops, so I read it to her, clearly, twice.

Wren went to the dentist alone for the first time, with a note from her mother in her pocket, and came out with a sticker, a toothbrush and a lecture. Mara waited at the corner pretending to look at shoes, she told me, for twenty-five minutes.

Teo's feet have grown two sizes in four months. Mara bought him shoes in September and by January the toes were pressing. I said to measure at the end of the day and leave a thumb's width. He now walks like someone in a boat.

A twinge in her right shoulder from carrying a heavy bag every day. Mara read me the exercises a physiotherapist had given her last year and I helped her pick the two that looked relevant. She also changed the bag for a rucksack, and the twinge went in a week. She says the bag was the whole problem and the exercises a form of paying respects.

Her cholesterol came back slightly high and Mara has taken up porridge with a vengeance. She eats it each morning with a dull expression, adding a spoon of honey as a bribe. Callum says the kitchen smells like a Scottish schoolroom.

She dreamed that she had to sit an exam in a subject she had never studied, in a hall full of children, at forty-four, and had come without a pen. She woke in a sweat. I said it is a very common dream. She said she knew, and that it was horrible to be common.

A day of pure energy: she cleaned the whole house before noon, washed the car, reorganised the garage, and was in the garden by one. She told me she was a different person on days like this. At her request I wrote down the date, so that she could tell later what such a day felt like.
Her second ceramic project was a teapot, which dribbles from the spout and, she says, has the posture of a heron. Callum uses it for his tea and says it needs only a little forgiveness.

She made linocut Christmas cards, a robin on a branch, printed forty-two times on a Sunday with a wooden spoon. By the twentieth the robin looked drunk. She sent them all anyway, and Ilse said they were the best she had ever had.

On Sunday afternoons she plays records on the old turntable in the living room, the ones from her mother's collection, with a crackle like a fire. Wren sits on the floor and turns the sleeves. Mara says it is the one quiet hour of the week that nobody interrupts.

She tried drawing the people on the bus and was caught by a man in a hat who leaned over and said he had never looked so noble. She kept the drawing, she says, as evidence of the kindness of strangers.

Dominoes with Ilse on Tuesday afternoons, in the front room with the clock and a plate of shortbread. Ilse plays slowly and savagely and has won thirty-one games to Mara's four. Mara says her four are the best four wins of her life.

Teo took her orienteering in the woods behind the school with a map, a compass and a punch card. She was given the map, and promptly walked them in a circle for twenty minutes. Teo, patient, pointed out that they were standing at the first checkpoint. They found eight out of twelve. What surprised her, she told me, was that her seventeen-year-old son was good at being a guide.

She volunteers at the community cinema on Friday evenings, selling tickets and popcorn from a cardboard booth. The film was a silent comedy with a live pianist. She stood at the back between customers and laughed silently with her hand over her mouth.

She spent a Saturday at the repair cafe at the library, taking Wren's bicycle apart with a volunteer named Hamid who has mended eleven thousand things. He showed her how to true a wheel with a spoke key. She did it herself, and he said, nicely, that she was a natural. She told me she had never been called a natural at anything and would like it on her gravestone.

She keeps a nature diary, ten minutes at the back step each morning, a line or two and a small drawing. Last Tuesday: a wren on the fence, ice on the hens' water, a smell of coal smoke from somewhere. She says that since she started, the days have more edges.

Mara made cider from the apple glut in a demijohn with an airlock that bubbled like a small and persistent opinion. After six weeks they tried it. It was cloudy and very strong and tasted, said Callum, of the underside of a hedge. Aksel asked for a second glass. She told me they now have a vintage.

A stained glass workshop on a Saturday: she cut her first piece, a wobbly leaf, ground its edges and soldered it into a small hanging. It hangs in the kitchen window now, and in the morning puts a green leaf on the table. She says the glass was the only thing she did right that day, and that it was enough.

Teo's old scout manual taught her three knots: a bowline, a clove hitch and a sheet bend. She tied the bowline on the washing line as practice and could not undo it for a day. She calls it the one that holds.

Mara has been making a map of the trees of Tidewell, one street at a time on Saturdays, with a tree guide, a notebook and Wren as scribe. They have found sixty-one species, including a monkey puzzle outside the library and a mulberry in a car park. She says it is the oldest kind of thing she has done that nobody asked her to do.

A tai chi class in the park on Wednesdays at seven, under a tree, with an old man named Mr Lau who moves as if through honey. Mara joined at the back. She says that when she copies him she can feel her shoulders come down by an inch.

On New Year's Day Mara joined the sea swim at Penhallow Sands, a hundred people in fancy dress and a brass band on the sand. She went in as a penguin. Teo stayed on the shore holding her towel. She came out the colour of a boiled sweet, laughing too hard to speak.

On the funicular up the hill Mara, who dislikes heights, held on to the rail and looked at her shoes. Teo took her hand without saying anything. At the top she looked at the town below and said it looked like a model. She told me she had not wanted to let go of the hand.

A stretch of Roman road on the downs, a straight green line that Mara walked in an hour, thinking about all the feet. She stopped to put her own foot where an old stone showed through the turf. I did not mention that nobody can know whether the stone was Roman.

A car boot sale on the way home, in a muddy field. She bought a brass compass for a pound, a blue jug and three paperbacks. The man selling the compass said it had belonged to his father, looked at it for a while, and raised the price to two pounds, which she paid.

A trip to the capital with Wren to see a musical called The Lamplit Hour, Wren's birthday present, with tickets bought eight months in advance. Mara booked the train, the hotel and the seats, and asked me to plan the day around a 2.30 curtain. We built a timetable with a margin. At the theatre Wren sat motionless for two and a half hours with her face a few inches from the stage. At the end she cried, and so did half the circle. On the train home she asked whether they could come again, and Mara said yes before she had checked the price.

On the train a man opposite read the same novel she was reading, at a page ten further on. She wanted to lean over and ask how it ended and held her tongue for fifty miles. When he left he looked at her book and said: it gets worse. She said thank you.

She power-walked to the station in her good heels because the bus had not come, and arrived with a blister, a flush and a minute to spare. The train was late. She says this is the universe's idea of a joke, and that she is not smiling.

She missed her stop on the Seaford line, fell asleep, woke in a town called Orlby she had never visited, and decided to get off and walk about for an hour. She ate chips on a bench by a clock tower. She told me it was the nicest mistake of the month.

Her shortcut to the shops goes through the old cemetery, past an angel with a missing hand. She says she nods to one particular headstone, a Mrs Hephzibah Rudd, every time, and has begun to feel she knows her.

A deer stepped out in front of the car on the lane at night, huge and still in the headlights. Mara braked hard and Callum swore. The deer looked at them and went into the trees. They sat with the engine off in a long quiet, and the dashboard clock changed minutes without anyone moving.

At the campsite their neighbours were a Dutch family with a cargo bike that held three children, a tent, a stove and what looked like a small piano. Mara spent a good part of the evening in admiration. Teo asked whether they could get one. Callum said they could get a bigger car.

A night in a hostel dormitory, at forty-four, in a bunk bed under a girl who talked in her sleep in two languages. Mara had expected to be the oldest person in the room and found a woman of seventy on the top bunk by the window, sleeping with her boots on. They shared a flask in the morning, and the woman said she had been doing this for thirty years. Mara has asked me to find the next one.

The adapters she bought for the trip turned out to fit a country they were not going to. She found this out at the hotel on the first night, with a phone at three per cent. A man at reception lent her a charger from a drawer of lost ones. She told me a drawer like that is a kind of history.

A week of walking in the mountains from hut to hut, with Callum, Teo and a rucksack of nine kilos each. On the second day Mara's blisters bled. On the third a mist came down and the path vanished and for an hour they walked from cairn to cairn, calling out to each other like sailors. The huts were the best of it: long tables, soup, a warden who gave a weather talk each evening, and a dormitory of forty snorers. On the last night she wrote to me from the highest pass, where a spark of signal reached the ridge. After four days of nothing but walking, she said, she had stopped composing sentences in her head and begun to think like the mountain, slowly and without commentary. I do not know what that is like. I said I would like to hear more. She said she could not tell me, that it dissolves in sentences, but that she had come back different by an inch.

A boat trip to see the puffins on the island off the headland. The skipper cut the engine and the boat rocked in a swell while hundreds of small black-and-white clowns flew past with fish in their beaks. Wren counted twenty-eight before she lost track. Mara said they looked as if they had been told a secret.

A hot air balloon flight was a present from Callum, booked for a calm morning in June. It was cancelled for wind, then for rain, then for a mild fog that nobody but the pilot could see. On the fourth try the balloon went up at dawn with six passengers and Mara. She said it was the quietest she had ever been. The fields were small squares and a river a bright thread. It is the one present, she says, she would have waited four times for.

The family chat ran a caption contest for a holiday photograph of Callum asleep in a deckchair with a crab on his sleeve. Dario won with: Brother, you have been outranked. Mara has framed it, in the sense that she keeps it on her phone.

Hobbes weighed in at four hundred and thirty grams in June, up eleven on last month. Mara writes it on his card in green ink. She says that for a creature who has never exercised he is keeping a very steady line.

Dumpling has begun laying again after her moult, small pale eggs at first, then a proper one on Saturday. Mara carried it indoors in both hands like a relic and boiled it for exactly seven minutes. It was, she told me, a triumph.

Pim swallowed a sock. Aksel, who looks after him on Wednesdays, rang Mara in a panic and she drove them both to the vet with a very calm dog on her lap. The vet felt his belly, took an X-ray, and said the sock would pass or would not. It passed on Friday, with fanfare. The neighbours, grateful, brought a casserole, and Mara says she has been a dog's chauffeur and his saviour in the same week and would like it on a card.

The rabbit question has been settled: Wren may have one in the summer if she keeps her room tidy until then. Mara showed me the contract she wrote at the kitchen table. It has seven clauses and two signatures. Wren's signature is the larger.

Mara bought a third hen, a bronze one named Biscuit, from a farm at the foot of Corrin Edge. The first day was war. Dumpling and Mrs Pell chased her round the run pecking, and Biscuit hid in the nest box. Mara watched from a folding chair with a cup of tea. I told her the pecking order takes a few days to settle and that she should watch for injury but not interfere. By the fourth day they were eating together, with only the occasional squawk.

A heron stood at the edge of the garden pond one morning, a grey statue with a patient eye. Mara went out in her dressing gown to shoo it and it looked at her as if she were the intruder. She netted the pond that afternoon, and the heron came back and stood looking at the net.

Teo has set up a tropical fish tank in his room, with a heater, a filter and eleven small fish the colour of boiled sweets. He feeds them at six every morning, the only thing he has ever done at that hour. Mara says the tank hums in the night like a very peaceful machine.

A rat was seen in the compost bin on a Sunday evening, a tail disappearing under the lid. Mara was alarmed. I told her that compost bins attract rats and that the answer is to leave out cooked food and keep the lid tight. She has stopped adding bread and the rat has, she believes, moved house. She misses it a little, she said, and was ashamed.

She planted an apple tree for Wren's thirteenth birthday at the bottom of the garden, a Bramley, the height of Wren. They stood side by side and were measured against a cane. Mara says that in ten years the tree will be taller, and that she would like to see Wren's face when it is.
The greenhouse has produced nine cucumbers this summer, each as long as a forearm. Mara has given six away. She told me she is unreasonably proud of a vegetable that is ninety-five per cent water.

The lavender along the path hums with bees in the evening sun, a sound she calls the garden's thinking. She sits on the bench with Wren for ten minutes before bed to listen. It does not need a purpose, she said.

Wren built a scarecrow from Callum's old coat and a pumpkin head, set it by the beans, and gave it a hat. Ilse, coming round the corner at dusk, said Good evening to it before she realised. Mara has been told never to repeat this to Ilse and has told me instead.

A gale flattened four sunflowers overnight, heads in the mud. Mara and Wren spent the morning standing them up with canes and string, like nurses. Three of the four have lived. Wren says the survivor has a look of experience.

A slow worm turned up in the compost heap when Callum turned it, small and golden-brown and not a snake. Wren held it in a cupped hand. Mara asked whether it was dangerous. I said no, it is a legless lizard and a friend of gardeners. It went back into the heap with great dignity.

The fig tree in the conservatory has produced its first fig, a small hard green thing that Mara has inspected daily. When at last it softened she cut it in half and shared it with Wren, who said it tasted of jam and of earth.

Mara and Teo built a herb spiral from broken bricks in the corner of the garden, a low snail of stone and soil with thyme at the top and mint at the wet bottom. Teo had read about it and drew the plan; Mara carried the bricks. By the end of the afternoon they had six plants in and a satisfied silence. She told me it is the first thing in the garden that was Teo's idea, and that she is leaving room for him to be right about the next.

Dario sent a garden gnome in a parcel with a note: For the bottom of the garden. It is wearing a fishing hat. Mara has placed it behind the compost bin, from which its eyes can be seen. Wren says it watches the slugs.

Mara asked me to turn a recipe from a book printed in the 1950s into modern measures. It spoke of a gill of milk and a wineglass of stock. I gave her my best guesses and said so. The result was edible and a little damp. She says the recipe was a fine piece of social history, not a cake.

Teo tasted her soup and said it needed salt. She added salt. He tasted it again and said it needed more. She asked whether he would like to take over. He took the spoon and she stepped back, in unfamiliar silence. He added a pinch, a squeeze of lemon and a few grains of pepper, and it was better. Mara has been quietly proud for two days.

On a late evening she eats peanut butter from the spoon in the dark kitchen, standing at the open fridge with the light on her face like a saint's. She told me she is aware of the cliche and is doing it anyway.

For the school bake sale Mara made forty cupcakes with pale pink icing and Wren made twelve cookies, burnt at the edges. Wren's sold first. Mara wanted to know what this said about the market. I said it sounded like people had bought the story.

A great clear-out of the fridge turned up a jar of something grey, a half lemon that had become a fossil, and a pot of cream whose date had passed her own. She held a funeral with great solemnity and then made a frittata of what was left.

The new kettle arrived after the old one boiled dry and cracked its element with a pop. Mara chose a cheap white one and says it feels like a modest, trustworthy colleague. Callum says it is too loud. They have agreed to disagree about volume.

The weekly shop with Teo carrying: he pushes the trolley, reads the list in a monotone, and eats a packet of crisps between the dairy aisle and the till, which he then offers to pay for. Mara says it is the only time he talks to her unprompted, and she is willing to pay for the crisps.

She found a box of dried chillies from a trip years ago and used four in a stew, on the assumption that they had lost their strength. They had not. Callum wept at the table, politely, and Wren drank two glasses of milk. Mara said it was the best stew she had ever ruined.

A birthday picnic in the rain, in a bandstand, with a tablecloth spread on the boards and twelve children eating sausage rolls while the rain drummed on the roof. Mara told me nobody wanted to go home. A man with a dog came to listen to the noise.

She bought a second-hand set of cutlery in a charity shop, silver-plated, with a different initial on every handle. Wren has declared them a family: the S fork, the P knife, the A spoon. Mara says the soup spoon with the J belongs to someone who has had a good life.

A damp patch on the ceiling below the bath had grown to the size of a dinner plate and begun to bulge. Mara wrote to me from the landing in her bare feet asking what to do. I said to stop using the bath, put a bucket under the bulge and, if the ceiling looked ready to fall, to prick it at the lowest point with a screwdriver so the water would drain and not burst. She did, and a stream of brown water fell into the bucket. The plumber found a failed seal around the waste pipe and replaced it. The ceiling still has a ghost on it, the shape, says Wren, of Australia.
The bedroom window rattles in the wind with a patient, nervous sound. Mara folded a bit of cardboard and wedged it in the frame. The window now whispers. She says she prefers the whisper.

A drawer in the kitchen stuck so hard it would only come out with a shout. She rubbed the runners with a candle and it slid open like silk. She stood admiring the drawer for a minute, then shut it and opened it again, and again.

A floorboard on the landing creaks at the same spot each night, one long drawn note. She tried screws and talcum powder. Callum says it is the house clearing its throat. They have taken to stepping around it, and Mara says the house is training them.

The boiler service man, a cheerful Mr Dunmore, said it was in better health than she was, that it would see them through another ten winters if treated kindly, and that she should bleed the radiators in October. Mara wrote this on the calendar and underlined it.

A section of the garden wall needed repointing and Mr Abara's nephew, a mason, did it on a Saturday for the price of lunch. Mara watched him work, a slow and careful rhythm. She said she had never understood patience as a physical act before.

The chimney sweep, a man in a black top hat with a laugh, came for the first time in six years and brought down a bag of soot and a dead jackdaw. Mara was embarrassed. He said it happened to everybody. She gave him tea in the best cup and told me he left the room cleaner than he found it.

She cleaned the oven with baking soda and vinegar, as a video told her, and spent two hours on her knees. The oven shines. She stood in front of it with a mug, in the manner, she said, of a woman who has finished a book.

Teo's results day, an envelope in a school hall. Mara drove him there and waited in the car and told me she was unable to read a single page of the novel she had brought. He came out ten minutes later, unreadable, walking slowly. He opened the car door and said in a flat voice that he had got the grades for the course. Then he put his head on the dashboard and laughed. She says she drove them both to a cafe and bought the biggest cake in the case, and that the sun came out as they sat down.

Wren's sports day: the egg and spoon race, which Wren led for most of the way, then dropped the egg a metre from the line, then picked it up and finished fourth. Mara cheered as if for an Olympic final. Wren told her afterwards she did not mind. The egg, she said, had been very ambitious.

The Easter bonnet parade down Ferrier Street: Wren in a hat made of a colander, ribbon and fourteen plastic daffodils, Mr Abara in a bowler with a chocolate egg tied on, Ilse in a straw affair with a hen. Mara told me the street has never been so ridiculous or so well dressed.

Ilse held a tea party for six old friends in her front room and asked Mara to help carry the plates. Three of the guests were over ninety. They talked about a ballroom that was now a car park, a man called Godfrey who had owed each of them ten shillings, and the exact timing of a rainstorm in 1961. Mara carried the kettle in and out and was introduced as the girl next door. She would happily have stood in a doorway all afternoon listening to people who remembered everything, she said, and hoped she would be one of them.

The boiler quote came in at three thousand two hundred pounds and Mara spent a night awake with it. She told me she was not in danger but that the number was the size of a mood. We went through what the quote covered, what she had set aside, and what a second quote might say. She asked for two more. In the morning she wrote that the worry had changed shape, from a lump into a list.

After the storm there came a calm, and she wrote that she felt content, simply that, with a kettle and a book and Wren practising scales upstairs. She said it was not a big mood and she had no intention of doing anything about it.

She remembered a Sunday from her childhood when her mother laughed at a dropped pie, and wrote to me while still laughing a minute, then two minutes, later. She did not know why it had returned. I said that was how memory mostly worked, and that I was glad it was funny.

She was asked to speak for five minutes at the village meeting about the bus route, and was frightened. She spent an evening writing and rewriting the speech with me, cutting it from nine minutes to four, and cutting the joke twice. At the meeting she stood at the front with a paper that shook. She wrote afterwards that she heard her voice from some distance, level and clear, and that the room went quiet, and that an old man at the back began nodding at the third sentence and did not stop. The bus route was kept. She did not know what to do with her hands for an hour.
She wrote one evening, unprompted, that she was grateful to Callum. She did not say for what. I did not ask. She said she would tell him in the morning and then, probably, just make him a sandwich.

She wanted to be alone for a whole day, and planned it: Callum to take the children to his mother's, the phone off, a thermos, a book, the lido at noon. She had looked forward to it for weeks. She told me afterwards that for the first hour she was lonely, for the second she was fine, and that by the afternoon she had never been so entirely herself.

In the stationery shop at the start of term she stood among the new pencil cases and the smell of rubber and was suddenly eleven, with an entire future in a pack of felt tips. She bought a pack. She says she has no idea what to do with them.

Spring restlessness: she walked for six hours on Saturday for no reason, up the hill, down the river, round the park. She came home with her legs shaking and said she had not been in such a hurry to nowhere for years.
A heatwave: she hung wet sheets in the windows to cool the rooms. The house smelled of damp laundry and, a little, of the sea. Wren said it felt like living in a ship.

It snowed in the second week of April, thickly, over the daffodils, and the garden looked like a joke. Mara went out in boots and shook the snow from each yellow head. The daffodils were fine, she says, which is more than she could say for her mood.

The wind took a big branch off the pear tree in the night with a crack she heard in her sleep. In the morning it lay across the lawn, still heavy with green fruit, and the wound on the trunk was pale and raw. I said that cutting the stub cleanly in dry weather would help the tree heal, and that fruit from a fallen branch is perfectly good. She sawed the stub and ate three pears straight off the branch, sitting on it. The tree, she told me, was the oldest living thing in her care and she could not stop touching it.

A foghorn from the harbour woke her at three, a slow cow-like note, over and over. She lay listening and found it more companionable than frightening. She says she was grateful to be told, every thirty seconds, that something out there was being careful.

On St Swithin's day it rained hard in the morning, and Mara, who knows the old rhyme, said it meant forty days of rain. She asked me to check. I said it was a legend and has never been reliably true. It stayed dry for three weeks. She said the saint had been generous.

Mrs Delaney at number three watches bin day like a hawk and rings the council about stray bags. Mara thinks she is a woman of principle. Callum thinks she is a spy. On Tuesday a note came through the door: You left your lid up, dear. They keep the lid down now.

A man in a raincoat knocked on the door on Sunday and said he had lived in the house as a boy. His name was Desmond, he was seventy-three, and he had come on the train from Orlby to see it. Mara asked him in. He stood in the hall and looked up the stairs and said the third step had always creaked and that there had been a pear tree. He cried a little in the kitchen, standing, with his hat in his hands. She showed him the garden and the pear tree, which he said could not be the same one, and then, looking closer, said it was. They sat for an hour over tea and cake, and he mentioned a sister who had died. After he left she found she could not tread on the third stair for the rest of the day.

A year since Ilse's fall, and the knock at eight has not been missed. Mara knocks twice on the wall by the kitchen, Ilse knocks back once, and that is the whole ceremony. On the anniversary Ilse knocked back three times, which Mara had not expected. She went round with a loaf. Ilse, at the door in her cardigan, said she had been wondering for weeks how to say it and that three knocks would have to do. They had tea.

Lost cat posters appeared on every lamppost on Ferrier Street for a black cat named Soot. Mara took one home for the fridge and walked round the garden each night with a torch. On the fifth day Soot was found asleep in someone's shed three streets away, and well fed. Every poster came down within an hour, and Mara felt, absurdly, as if a war had ended.

Sunniva has a new job at the library and Aksel has taken over the cooking, with a firmness that alarmed everyone. The first week he served what he called a gratin and Sunniva called a regret. Mara went round for supper on Thursday and reported that the second week was better, and that Aksel had written down every step in a notebook with a drawing of an onion.

She read The Tin Lighthouse aloud to Wren, a children's book about a boy who keeps a lighthouse in a biscuit tin. Wren is thirteen and declared herself above it, then sat through all of it with her chin on her knees. In the last chapter the boy gives the tin to a girl. Mara said Wren had to be reminded that it was only a story.

Mara saw a film called Paper Moths on a wet weekday afternoon with nobody else in the cinema. She cried quietly for forty minutes and walked home in the rain without an umbrella, on purpose. It is about two sisters who make kites, she said, and she had never seen anyone so well filmed asleep.

She listens to audiobooks while ironing, a long novel about a family of lighthouse keepers, read by a woman with a slow, precise delivery. She has ironed everything in the house, twice. Callum has found three shirts so crisp they could cut bread.

She copied a short poem onto an index card and stuck it on the fridge with a magnet shaped like a pear. It is four lines about a woman who leaves the door open for the weather. She told me she had read it forty times, and that every time she opened the fridge she read it a forty-first.

She lost her bank card, found it three days later in the pocket of an old coat, and cancelled it anyway on principle, which took forty minutes on the telephone. A recorded voice told her seven times that her call was important. She says it was not.

She renewed her library card after twelve years, with a form and a photograph. The assistant said she still had a book out. It was a book of knots, in Mara's name, from a decade ago. They have agreed that it was lost in a worthier cause.

A run to the tip with the old sofa, roped to the roof of the car. It slid at the first roundabout and Callum, in a hi-vis jacket, ran after it with an expression she described as noble. They arrived with the sofa, though not with the rope. A man at the recycling centre said he had never seen so confident an approach.

Charity bag collection day: she filled the bag with clothes, towels and the lamp she had never liked, then took the lamp out again after Callum said he did. The bag stood at the gate all morning like a patient dog.

A sailing taster on the reservoir on a windless Sunday, in a boat the size of a bath. They went nowhere for two hours and she was told she was a natural. She did not book the course. She told me she liked the idea of sailing more than sailing, and had learned this cheaply.

The loft conversion, which she had planned for two years with a notebook and a folder of pictures, came back as a quote of forty-one thousand pounds and a six-month wait. Mara phoned me from the car park of the builders' merchant. We went through what she wanted from it: a room for Teo to be older in, a place for Callum's books, a window with a view of the hill. She said she could get half the view by moving the bed. The plan is dropped. A smaller one has begun, with a ladder, a roll of insulation, two weekends and a skylight from a catalogue that Teo chose.

A weekend retreat in the hills with Yusra and Lotte, planned in January, dropped in March when Wren's school trip changed dates and Callum's rota moved. Mara told me she felt like someone with a train ticket and no train. We have put it in the notes for next year. She says next year is a country that has always been very kind to her.

She has decided not to dye the silver at her temples. She stood in front of the bathroom mirror for twenty minutes with a box of dye in her hand and then put it back on the shelf. Callum, asked, said he had never noticed. Wren said it was like moonlight. Mara said she would think about it, and has not touched the box since.

She asked me to turn a Fahrenheit oven temperature into Celsius and I gave her two hundred and thirty when the right figure was two hundred and ten. The cake rose, caught and sank, with a crust like a boot. She forgave me in the tone of a woman who has had practice. I have written the formula down where I will find it.

I set a reminder for her pottery class an hour wrong, so that she arrived at the studio at six with the door locked and a flask of tea. She sat on the step beside a woman in a hat who turned out to be the teacher's mother, and they talked for fifty minutes. She says it was a good mistake. I do not intend to make it twice.

The photo booth at the station took four pounds and returned four strips of Mara mid-blink, each with a slightly different expression of betrayal. She kept all of them. She says it is the only honest portrait anyone has made of her this year.

She asked me for a joke to put in Teo's card for his last day of school and I gave her three. She chose the worst. He read it at the kitchen table, put the card on the shelf, and was heard laughing at it three times that evening.

Callum's mother lost an earring, a small gold hoop, and rang Mara twice about it. On the second call she remembered it was in the soap dish. She apologised for the trouble and asked whether it would be all right to ring a third time in the event of a further disaster. Mara said yes.

Wren has a crush and is mortified by it. The boy is called Arlo and builds small robots from scrap in the school workshop, and last week one of them rolled across the playground and stopped at Wren's feet. She told her mother with her face turned to the wall. Mara asked no questions. That night she asked me whether to say anything at all. I said that perhaps the most she could offer was her attention, and to be ready to listen again. She sat on the end of Wren's bed with a mug of cocoa for ten minutes without speaking, and Wren eventually said the robot had a very small flag on it. Mara said she thought it was a lovely flag. They did not speak of it again.

Dario taught Teo to play poker with matchsticks at the kitchen table on Boxing Day. By nine o'clock Teo had won all of Dario's matches and two of Callum's. Dario said he had been playing badly as a courtesy. Mara said she had known her brother for forty years and never seen him do anything as a courtesy.

Lotte found her missing wedding ring in a flowerpot on the balcony, four months after she had given it up for lost, wrapped in a leaf. She rang Mara in tears. They talked for an hour, though Mara had a pan on the stove, and the pan did not survive.

Mara attended her cousin's wedding on a video link from the kitchen, in a green dress, with a glass of wine, and at the vows heard Wren behind her whisper: I never knew you could cry that much. She says it was the first wedding she had both attended and washed up at.

Callum's oldest friend, Piet, rang from abroad on a Sunday afternoon, the first time in two years, and Callum took the call in the garden. Mara watched through the kitchen window. He walked up and down by the bean wigwam for forty minutes, laughing and then not laughing, with his hand over his eyes. When he came in he sat at the table and said they had talked about nothing and everything. She asked me later what to do with the knowledge that he had cried. I said perhaps she need do nothing but make tea and be near. She made tea. He drank it. The next day Piet's number was in the calendar, with a reminder to ring on the first of each month.

Mara's mother knitted Wren a woolly hat in a shade she calls heather, and it came out the size of a tea cosy. Wren wore it for the photograph with a straight face, on the grounds that it had been made with love. It now lives on the hamster's cage, where Rochester sleeps in it.

Noor's baby took her first steps in Mara's kitchen, four of them, from the table to the fridge, with her arms out like a tightrope walker. Noor shrieked. Mara had her phone in her hand and, she told me, did not take a picture, because she was holding her breath.

A second cousin, Wilhelmina, turned up unannounced with a roll of paper the length of the dining table: the family tree, back to 1790. She stayed three hours, pointing out a man who had apparently been transported for stealing a cheese and a woman who had walked to the coast with a goose. Mara could not stop looking at the line of names, as at a staircase, and counting how many steps it had taken to be standing there.
A postcard from Marek: a kangaroo with the word Grrr written on its stomach in felt tip, nothing else. Callum put it on the fridge. Wren says it is the longest letter he has ever written.

She slept badly the night before the flight and woke at three to check the tickets for the fourth time. They were where she had left them. She says the fear of forgetting something is worse than the thing forgotten.

A splinter from the garden bench lodged in her thumb and Mara spent twenty minutes with a needle and a lamp, Wren holding the lamp. When it came out, long as an eyelash, they both cheered. I said splinters seldom need more than a clean needle and a clean thumb.

She walked through a patch of nettles on the allotment path in shorts and her legs came up in white and red stripes by evening. Mr Szabo told her to rub them with a dock leaf, which she says worked, and to pick the leaf as one buys something from a friend. Mara said she was not sure what that meant. Neither was I.
Wren had her school vaccination and two girls in the queue fainted before the needle. Wren, who had worried for a week, was fine and proud, and walked home with a plaster on her arm like a medal.
A hearing test at the surgery, a pair of earphones and a button. She heard everything. She told me that Callum, who has said for years that she does not listen, is therefore the one who mumbles.

Her right elbow has begun to ache after a week of hammering in the shed, and the surgery's leaflet called it a form of tennis elbow. She has never played tennis. Callum says she may now play, since she has the qualification.

She slept in the garden hammock on the hottest afternoon, with Wren's cardigan over her face against the flies, for forty minutes, and woke to find Hobbes sitting patiently by the post, as if waiting for his turn.

Wren came down at three with a stuffy nose and could not sleep, so Mara made a hot lemon and sat on the stairs with her until five, reading aloud from the book on the hall table. It was a book about tides. By dawn Wren was asleep against her shoulder and Mara knew more than she had ever wanted about the moon.

Callum's cough has lasted a fortnight, and Mara pointed out that a hospital pharmacist is the only person she knows who will not take his own advice. He said the advice was for other people. She put honey in his tea and said nothing more, which she says is the hardest thing she does.

A bruise appeared on her thigh, large and yellow-green, and she could not remember how. She asked me to keep a note of it with the date. I said it was sensible, and that she should see her doctor if bruises kept appearing with no cause. She remembered on Thursday: the corner of the garden bench.

Photography class on a Wednesday, with a young teacher who talked about aperture as if it were a mood. Mara's photograph of the swan on the canal came out as a soft white cloud with a beak. The teacher called it a brave decision. She is going to frame it.

Gerald, the lopsided bowl from the front hall, was chosen by the pottery teacher for the end-of-term display in the library window. Mara went to look at it through the glass, between a vase and a jug, with a card that said: Bowl, stoneware, M. She stood on the pavement for ten minutes. A small boy pointed and said it looked as if it was thinking. She told me that was the review she had been waiting for.
Sudoku has taken over her evenings. She does one a night with a pencil and a face of fierce calm, and has filled a notebook. Wren says the numbers have eaten her mother.

A salsa class on Thursday at the community centre, with a teacher who counted in a language she did not know. She trod on her partner's foot twelve times. He said it was a record. She said she was practising.

The garden club seed swap: she took six packets of her sweet peas and came home with twenty-two packets of things she cannot identify. One is simply labelled Bean (Gran's). She plans to plant them all in April and see what happens.

Mara has begun to write real letters again, on paper, to Joaquim, who lives on a boat. She told me it was a pleasure to write something that would take six days to arrive. Joaquim replied in four, with a drawing of an anchor.

She sketched the harbour at low tide on a cold Sunday, with a pencil and an old board, and was told by a passing woman that it looked like a drawing of what the place felt like. Mara said that was the nicest thing and the least accurate.

At a party a friend read tarot cards and Mara, amused, drew the Tower. She went quiet and drove home early. Callum asked whether she believed in it. She said no, and then said it was the way the woman had looked at the card. We talked about it, and she decided it was about the shed roof.

Mara joined a Tuesday knitting circle at the library making tiny hats for babies in the hospital's special care unit: eleven women and one man named Cyril, who knits at speed and glares at dropped stitches. Her first hat took three weeks, a small cream thing not much bigger than an egg-cup. When she handed it in a nurse said it was exactly the right size and that the babies would not know it was imperfect. She told me she thought of that sentence all week.
A beginners' chess club at the library. She lost to a nine-year-old in six moves and shook his hand. He said, kindly, that she should castle earlier. She has written it on her hand.

A drumming workshop at the community centre: twenty adults, a circle of hand drums, and a teacher with a laugh like a fanfare. Mara's hands were red in ten minutes. By the end of the hour, she said, the whole room was a single animal breathing. She asked me whether she was being romantic. I said it sounded right. She has bought a small drum and plays it in the shed in the evenings with the door shut, where the hens listen with an air of professional interest.

She started a paint-by-numbers kit of a lakeside cottage, for relaxation, and has become fierce about staying inside the lines. Wren stands behind her and says that Number 14 is too blue. Mara says Number 14 can mind its own business.

A falconry morning as a birthday present: a field, a Harris hawk named Juno, a leather glove and a man with a lure. Juno landed on Mara's fist with a thump she felt in her teeth. Being looked at by such an animal, she said, was like being quietly assessed by a very polite judge. She was given a feather at the end and has put it in the bowl on the hall table, next to the keys.

Mr Szabo is teaching her to whittle a spoon from a green sycamore branch with a small curved knife, on his allotment bench on Sunday mornings. He says to cut always away from the body, and then explains why in a whisper. Her first spoon is the shape of a startled bird. She has put it in the kitchen drawer with the proper spoons and uses it on Sundays for the porridge.

An adult swimming lesson on Monday evenings, where she is learning the butterfly. She says it is a stroke designed by someone who hates arms. After five weeks she manages two strokes and a belly flop.

A night in a former lighthouse keeper's cottage at the end of a causeway that floods at high tide. They had to leave by six or be stranded until midnight. They stayed until ten to six, ate fish and chips on the rocks, then ran across the stones with the sea coming in behind them. Wren stopped for a shell and was carried the last twenty metres by Callum. Mara told me she had never felt so alive and so sensible at the same time.
The train went through a tunnel two miles long and Wren whooped the length of it, a single young voice with its echo. A man opposite, who had been reading, put the paper down and joined in.

While they waited for the ferry a gull took Teo's pasty from his hand with an elegance he is still discussing. He stared at the sea for a long time. Mara bought him a second one, which he held with both hands and a glare.

A road trip to the south coast with Callum's playlists. Mara told me the third song was a nine-minute organ piece and the fifth a man shouting about a train. She did not object. After four hours, she says, she had begun to appreciate the shouting.

A city break and a tower with four hundred steps, and from the top red roofs to the horizon. They stopped halfway on a windowsill and ate a biscuit. Wren said it was the highest she had ever been on her own legs.

A holiday home swap with a family in a flat in a faraway city: they had the flat for a fortnight, the family had the house. The flat had a balcony of geraniums and a tiny kitchen with a hob that clicked. On the third day Mara found a note in a drawer from the owner, a recipe for a cold soup with a drawing of a sun. She cooked it and it was wonderful. Afterwards the owner wrote that Wren's drawing of the hens was on her fridge.

At the arrivals gate Marek came through with a rucksack and a hat that was not his, and Mara, who had been standing for an hour, was the first person he saw. He hugged her so hard she lost her breath. Callum, behind her, said he had forgotten that Marek hugged like a bear.

Mara chaperoned Wren's school trip to a science museum, one adult for eight children, on a coach with a driver who hummed. She counted heads at every stop, twenty-one times in all, and came home with a lanyard, a headache and a fond respect for teachers. One child was lost in the planetarium for four minutes and found asleep in the dark. She told me those four minutes were the longest of her life.

A goat on the railway line held up the train for half an hour while a man in hi-vis tried to persuade it with a carrot. The goat, according to Mara, was in no hurry and in no doubt. It strolled off when it pleased, and the train, to loud applause, moved on.

A river taxi down to the old docks on a dull afternoon: a small boat with a canvas roof and a driver who named every bridge. Mara said it was the most interesting forty minutes she had spent with a man she did not know.

The Christmas market in the old square: mulled wine, a stall of felted mice, a woman in a hat selling chestnuts. Mara lost a mitten on the way and found it ten minutes later on the head of a snowman built by a child. She says she had never known a mitten could look so happy.

Pickle arrived, a lop-eared grey rabbit from a rescue centre on the hill. Wren had cleaned the hutch, written a three-page rota and read the leaflet aloud to the family. Pickle was placed in the run, sat motionless for ten minutes, then did what Mara calls an unreasonable leap. Rochester, in his cage, watched with what looked like disapproval. By evening Pickle had eaten a dandelion and a corner of the run. Wren, who has lately been quiet and sensible, ran in circles on the lawn for five minutes in celebration. Mara said she had not seen her do that since she was seven.

In October Mara prepared Hobbes's hibernation box: a crate lined with shredded paper and straw, set in the cold of the garage. I explained the steps as I knew them and said a vet's advice on his weight and health before hibernation mattered more than my notes. She took him to a vet, who weighed him, listened to his chest and pronounced him ready. She tucked him in as one tucks in a child, with the lid propped open an inch. Wren wrote a card for the box: Sleep well, see you in April. Mara has set a reminder for the first of March to check on him, which I will keep.

Biscuit and Dumpling have been bickering over the dust bath. Mara watches from a deckchair with tea and refuses to interfere. She says the rule of the henhouse is that everything is settled by Thursday.

A rescued greyhound, Quill, visited from a neighbouring street, long as a rope and gentle as a cloud. He lay on the kitchen floor in a patch of sun and sighed. Wren said he needed a hot-water bottle. By the end of the afternoon he had one.

The tadpoles in the pond turned into froglets overnight, hundreds the size of thumbnails. Wren laid a plank to the water's edge as a ramp and sat watching them leave in a hopping stream. She says it was like a school at a fire drill.

A fox cub drank from the pond at dusk, small and thin, with oversize ears. Mara stood at the kitchen window with the lights off and did not breathe. The cub looked up and was gone. She told me she had never been so grateful to a stranger.

She pruned the quince in January, a third of the old wood, as I had recommended, and was pleased to find the cuts clean and the tree hardly bothered. She put a few twigs in a vase and says they will flower in March on their own.
A load of mulch was delivered, six cubic metres, onto the front drive, and Mara has been barrowing it round the garden for two days. She says she has a new respect for the weight of a bad idea.
Callum and Teo planted a hawthorn hedge along the back wall, eighty whips in a double row, with Wren drawing the plan. The whips look like sticks. Mara has said she will believe in it in four years.
Heavy rain turned the lawn to a lake and the hens stood on the shed step with an expression of public outrage. Wren took out a paper boat and sailed it. It lasted from the back door to the pear tree.

A bumblebee nest in the compost heap, a loud brown hum when Callum lifted the lid. He put it back at once. Mara has told everyone to stay clear of the bin until September and feeds it from a safe distance.

Wren cut the heads off the dead sunflowers and spent a Sunday shelling the seeds onto a tray for the hens. Biscuit ate her share in one go. Mara says it is the most efficient piece of recycling in the district.
The pear tree blossomed on the warmest day of April and for a week the garden was full of white. Mara stood under it at dusk and a petal fell onto her tea. She did not drink it.

The sweetcorn did well this year behind a fence of wire against the squirrels. Mara cut the first cobs at noon and cooked them within the hour, as Mr Szabo had said she must, and ate them standing, with butter running down her wrists. She told me it was the first time she had understood what sweetness was.

The allotment hosepipe split in the dry spell and Mara and Mr Szabo repaired it with a bicycle inner tube and a good deal of talk. It leaks, but only by the amount that makes the rows of beans grateful.

Ice cream without a machine: she whisked cream, condensed milk and vanilla, froze the whole in a loaf tin and stirred it every hour. It came out as a firm pale block. Wren said it was the best thing she had eaten all summer. Mara has made it six times since.

She made pancakes for the whole street on a Saturday morning, forty of them, at Sunniva's stove, with a line of neighbours holding plates. Mr Abara ate nine. Ilse ate one and a half and pronounced it enough for a woman of her age.

A bet with Callum about which of them would crack first on a diet was lost by Mara on the fourth evening, and she paid by baking him a fruit cake by midnight. She started at ten. It came out at ten to twelve in the shape of a brick. Callum ate the corner and said it was the best brick he had had.

Teo made bean burgers from a recipe on his phone, with oats and cumin, and served them to the family with an air of rigid professional pride. Callum said they were very good. Teo said you cannot say very good, you must say what you think. Callum said they were fine. Teo said, thank you.

She bought mackerel straight off a boat in the harbour, still stiff, for three pounds the string. The fisherman wrapped it in newspaper and told her not to wash it. She cooked it in the garden on a griddle, the smoke curling over the fence, until the whole street came to smell it.

A huge pot of stock simmered all Saturday from the bones of three chickens and a handful of end-of-week vegetables, until the windows ran. Mara strained it into jars and froze eleven. She says it is a form of savings.

The grocery receipt showed that she had bought twelve lemons and she had no memory of why. We could not reconstruct it. She made lemon curd, lemonade, a cake and a dressing. At the end of the week she found the reason on the back of an envelope: Sunniva's marmalade.

Dario's present was a pasta machine, which she screwed onto the edge of the kitchen table and used on a Sunday with Wren. The first sheet of dough tore. The second was thin enough to read through. They cut it into ribbons, and the family ate in silence, which Mara took as the highest praise.

She put anchovies in the salad and the household divided. Callum loved them, Wren spat hers into a napkin, and Teo declared that he had always known. Mara has decided anchovies are a test of character.

Teo needed to know how to tie a tie before the prom and learned from a diagram on his phone, with Mara beside him as a sort of mirror. By the fifth attempt he had a knot that looked like a small fist. He wore it all evening and kept putting his hand to it.

The bathroom fan stopped turning and the mirror steamed over every morning. Callum replaced the unit on a Saturday with a new one that hums, he says, like a cat. Mara has stopped writing messages on the mirror in the steam, and says she misses the habit.

She painted the cellar wall with damp-proof paint on a long Sunday, in a mask and old clothes, to keep the water out. It dried grey. The patch has stayed dry through two storms. She says it is not a beautiful victory, but a victory.

Teo and Callum replaced the leaning fence post at the bottom of the garden, digging out the old one, a long black rotten thing, and setting a new concrete footing. Then they stood beside it in silence while it set, like two men watching a bus.
The garden hose developed a leak the width of a hair and sprayed a fine fan across the path. Mara patched it with a connector and a stern word. It does not leak now, except when asked to.

Callum fitted a small automatic door to the henhouse that opens at dawn and closes at dusk. The hens do not trust it. Dumpling stood and watched it open for twenty minutes before deciding to risk it. Mara says it is the first piece of technology in the garden to have been properly introduced.

The toaster died in a bright flash and a smell of pepper. Mara did not use a knife to free the toast. She unplugged it first, and told me so with great self-regard. I confirmed that this was the right order.

She bled the radiators on the first of October, as the boiler man had advised, with a small key and a rag. The first one hissed and spat. By the last she was almost fond of the hiss. She says a warm house in autumn is a promise kept.

A new ceiling light in the hall, a paper globe, now glows like a moon. She hung it herself on a ladder with Wren holding it up and Callum reading the instructions aloud. The globe is crooked by a hand's width and she calls it character.

Teo turned eighteen on a Saturday in the back room of the Anchor, with twenty friends, a long table, and sausage rolls in a pyramid. Mara spent the morning trying to decide what a mother should do at her son's party and decided to be a barmaid. She carried trays and said very little. At nine he found her in the corridor and said quietly, thank you for not coming in. She said she had not planned to. He said he knew, and that it had been the nicest thing. She stood in the corridor afterwards with a tray of empty glasses feeling, she told me, like the happiest ghost in the building.

Tamsin's twins opened their shop in the front room, selling shells, drawings and half a carrot. Mara was the first customer and bought a pebble with a face. The twins, in cardboard helmets, gave her a receipt written in letters of several wrong sizes. She has it on the fridge.

The street's carol evening was held under the one lamppost on Ferrier Street with a borrowed piano on a trailer: forty people in coats, a man in a Santa hat doing the descant, and Ilse in a chair with a tartan blanket and a flask. Mara held a candle in a jam jar. At the last carol the piano went flat in the cold, and the whole street, undeterred, sang the final verse unaccompanied and slightly lower. When it ended there was a quiet in which she could hear someone blow his nose and the lamppost tick. She told me that was the sound she would keep.

A Boxing Day walk on the downs with the whole family and Pim, in a wind that took hats. Wren ran ahead and came back with a stick like a flag. Mara said it was the best walk of the winter and the worst for her hair.

Sunniva's birthday tea in the garden, with a table of cakes and a cat on the wall. Mara brought a jug of lemon curd, and Sunniva said she had never been so well supplied for an anniversary of nothing in particular.

Wren was the narrator in the end-of-year show and delivered her lines to the back wall in a clear, level voice. At the end she bowed and tripped on her own foot and the audience, as one, loved her. Mara said she had never been so pleased by a fall.

She found a photograph of herself and Yusra in a launderette, aged twenty, laughing at something outside the frame. She stood it on the dresser for a day. Then she took it down and put it in her bag. She told me she wanted it with her when she next rang.

A long Sunday with nothing to do and no one to see. She wrote to me three times in the afternoon, each time saying she was bored, each time with less conviction. By evening she had made a list of things to learn. It had fourteen items and the first was: how to be bored properly.

At dusk she stood in the garden with a cup of tea and looked at everything she had made, the beds and the bench and the bean wigwam, and felt, she said, a sudden quiet pride that she did not want to name in case it left.

She forgot to ring her mother on Sunday and spent Monday morning in a low grey temper that she took for the weather. At noon she rang. Her mother said she had assumed she was busy. Mara said that was exactly the sentence she had been afraid of.
The night before the trip she made a list of all the things not to forget, and lost the list. She made another. She says packing is a rehearsal in which one person plays every part.

She wrote to me at one in the morning to say she had been watching Callum sleep, his mouth slightly open, and had felt a rush of tenderness that frightened her. She wanted to tell somebody. I said it seemed a good thing to be frightened by.

Teo's year away begins in September and the fear arrived early, in August, without cause. Mara found herself standing at his bedroom door looking at the shape of him asleep, and weeping. She told me in the morning in a dry voice. I said it sounded less like fear of an event than like rehearsing an absence. She said that was exactly it. At her request we made a list of what could help: a weekly call, a parcel for the farm, a map on the wall. She says it is a stranger thing to prepare for a goodbye than for a welcome.

An ordinary Tuesday: a boiled egg, a bus, a quiet afternoon, soup. She wrote that at the end of the day she felt enormously, unaccountably happy and could find no reason. I said that might be a reason. She said she would take it.

A warm October evening and the family ate outside on the step, in jumpers, with the plates on their knees. Mara said the light did the work of an expensive restaurant. Wren said the worms were also eating.

A hot wind came up from the south and filled the garden with dust. Mara went round shutting windows with a handkerchief over her nose like an outlaw. By evening the sky was a pale rose and the wind had dropped, and the whole place smelled of somewhere a long way off.
A heavy dew made every spider's web in the garden visible, a hundred small silver hammocks. Mara photographed one with a drop on each strand. She told me she had never seen anything so well made.

The first day she wore shorts this year was a Wednesday, on the way to the shop, and she felt the sun on her knees for the first time since September. She stood for a minute at the crossing with her face turned up. A van hooted, kindly.

A neighbour was mending a motorbike on the pavement for three weekends, with a radio. Mara took him a bacon sandwich on the third and learned the bike was his father's, abandoned in a shed for nineteen years. He ate the sandwich standing and said he would ride it to the sea.

The woman at number six and the man she lives with never speak to anyone. Mara waved at them across the road on a Monday and, to her astonishment, both waved back at once, then looked at each other as if caught. She plans to wave again on Friday.

Kirsten from the school gate invited her for tea on Thursday, the first invitation in months. They talked for two hours about nothing: the council, a bad film, a boy named Dilip. Mara came home and wrote that she had not known how hungry she was for ordinary talk.

She lent her copy of The Cartwheel Year to Ilse, who returned it two days later with a postcard for a bookmark and the remark that it was a book about a woman who ought to have been shaken. Mara says that is also, in its way, a review.

She walked out of Ordinary Stars after an hour, a film about an astronomer with a sad dog, which she said was shot entirely in one colour. She ate a pie on the pavement and was cheerful. I said she was allowed to leave a film. She said she knew, it just felt like a decision.

She and Callum rewatched an old comedy called Quartet for a Cow on a rainy night, one they had seen on their second date. Callum laughed at all the same places and, a second late, so did she. She says the film had not aged, only they had.

A documentary about cathedrals sent her to sleep on the sofa in the first twelve minutes. She woke in the last five to a shot of a stone angel and thought for a moment it was her mother. Callum says he will not repeat this to anyone.

She collected a prescription for Callum from the pharmacy, queuing behind a woman with a trolley of tins and a small boy who sang. When her turn came the pharmacist said, Is it for Callum? She said yes. The pharmacist said: tell him he is a fool for working through that cough.

A form for a council tax discount came in the post with fourteen pages and instructions in type she could barely read. Mara asked me to help. We went through it a page at a time. I could read the form aloud and explain what each box asked; what she was entitled to was for the council to say. She filled it in and posted it, and the discount arrived without further trouble.

She returned a borrowed ladder to Mr Abara with a cake and a note, and was told she should have kept it. She said she could not have a ladder without a gesture. He ate a slice standing on his step and said it was good, and that he would keep the note.

At the lost property office at the station an old man handed her a blue umbrella, then another, then a third, and asked which was hers. She said none of them, that she had lost a black one in March. He regarded her for a while and said it was very probably in the drawer at the other office.
